description:
Eighteen months ago, Shi Feng had two hundred and thirty-seven open meridians and the brightest future in Qingshi Town. Then his meridians went silent. Now the clan is cutting his rice, his cousins line up to gloat, and his fiancée’s sect has come to break off the engagement in front of everyone.

None of them know that his meridians never died. They went somewhere no physician can follow: past the limit every cultivator believes in.

Alchemy, a marriage made for the price of a seal that slowly becomes real, and a regional tournament of one hundred and eight young geniuses. A sharp, quiet cultivation story about a fallen genius who doesn’t need anyone’s permission to rise again.

chapters.title: The World
chapters.html:
A short guide for readers. No spoilers.

The Path of Cultivation

Cultivators take in the qi of heaven and earth to strengthen their bodies and lengthen their lives. The path is divided into realms, and most people spend their whole lives stuck in front of one.

1. Meridian Opening. The cultivator opens the channels that carry qi through the body. One hundred and twenty is completion, and most people break through there. Geniuses pass one hundred and eighty. Once a generation, someone passes two hundred. Three hundred and sixty is the absolute limit, and no one in living memory has touched it. Old legends speak of meridians beyond it, called Epoch Meridians, but most people think they're a children's story. The more meridians a cultivator opens, the faster they cultivate for the rest of their life, which is why one test can make a family proud or ruin it.

2. Qi Condensation. The cultivator gathers qi and stores it in the body until it stays. Qi spells become possible. This realm has no stages, only long, patient refinement.

3. Bone Refinement. The body is tempered one bone at a time, all two hundred and six of them. Cultivators boast by count ("eighteen bones refined," "half refined"), and every refined bone makes the body harder and its strikes heavier. Progress slows sharply near the end, and many cultivators grow old before they finish.

4. Foundation Establishment. The cultivator lays the base for everything that follows. Foundations are graded Mortal, Earth, Sky, Heaven, Immortal and Divine. A Mortal foundation is common. A Heaven foundation makes a clan celebrate for a month. Anything higher is spoken of in whispers. Leaving this realm requires surviving a lightning tribulation, and not everyone does.

5. Golden Core. A core of condensed qi forms in the dantian. Cores are graded False, Flawed, Flawless and Supreme. A higher grade fills more slowly but reaches much further. The realm ends in a tribulation of the will rather than of lightning.

6. Nascent Soul. A spiritual infant forms within the core and slowly solidifies. Few in this region ever reach it, and those who do are the pillars of the Great Sects.

From Foundation Establishment upward, each realm has early, mid, late and peak stages. Golden Core sometimes has a rare "half-step" beyond its peak.

Alchemy and Marks

Alchemists refine spirit herbs into medicine, and a good alchemist is worth more to a clan than a dozen guards. Even so, most alchemists are mediocre. They burn through herbs, fail more often than they succeed and sell what they can.

The Sky Pavilion certifies alchemists, and Refiners (the craftsmen who forge cultivators' weapons and tools), with Marks. A Mark tells the world which realm of cultivator a maker can serve:

  • 1 Mark for Golden Core cultivators
  • 2 Mark for Nascent Soul cultivators
  • 3 Mark for late and peak Nascent Soul cultivators

Higher Marks exist, but in this region they are only names on the Pavilion's walls.

A cultivator must be at least Foundation Establishment to sit the exam for a Mark, and almost no one earns one before reaching Golden Core. Most alchemists never earn one at all. Those without a Mark sell to ordinary cultivators at ordinary prices. A marked alchemist names their own price, and sects and royal houses compete to feed and shelter them.

The Kingdom of Great Liang

Great Liang is a modest kingdom ruled by the Sima royal clan. Like most kingdoms, its strongest experts stand at early Golden Core, but the royal clan holds more of them than any other house. Generations ago, a Sima ancestor was taken away by a great power from far beyond this region and never returned. No one knows what he became, and no one wants to find out.

The proud Ling clan is among the kingdom's great houses, an old family with a sword tradition and a voice at court. The Thousand Blossom Register ranks Great Liang's young beauties. Families celebrate a place on it, and its first name is spoken almost with reverence.

Places you'll hear of: Qingshi Town, a small western town and home of the Shi clan; Yunze Town, a rough hunters' town by Heilu Marsh; and the capital, with its markets, its courts and a tower of the Sky Pavilion.

The Surrounding Kingdoms

Great Liang is one of about thirty kingdoms in the shadow of three Great Sects. Its neighbours include Great Yan, Great Zhao, Great Wu, Great Qin, Great Song, Great Han and Great Chu. Each has its own royal house and its own geniuses who believe they are the best under heaven. Among them lie small sects, some weak and a few far stronger than they look. One of these is White Crane Pavilion, which sends recruiters across Great Liang's border.

The Great Sects

  • Martial Palace is the strongest and proudest of the three. It prizes force above all.
  • Hundred Flower Valley is elegant and selective, and famous for its women cultivators.
  • Artificer Hall is a sect of Refiners, widely called the weakest of the three.

Their elders are Golden Core experts, and their highest powers are at Nascent Soul. Every few years the kingdoms hold the Great Kingdom Tournament. Each kingdom sends three representatives, and a few strong small sects send their own. The top ten are taken by the Great Sects, and the champion may enter any of them as an inner disciple. A Great Sect disciple stands beyond the reach of kingdom politics.

The Sky Pavilion

The Sky Pavilion is the oldest and most trusted trading power on the continent, with towers in every capital and sect city. It runs auctions, appraises treasures and certifies alchemists and Refiners. No one is sure where it began, only that it is older than the kingdoms it trades with.

The Legendary Empire

Far to the north lies what people call the Legendary Empire. Stories say that cultivators beyond Nascent Soul walk its streets like ordinary men, and that a sect master from here would be a country bumpkin there. No one from these kingdoms has gone there and come back to tell of it.

People You Will Meet

Shi Feng, eighteen, was once the genius of Qingshi Town. For a year and a half, everyone has called him a cripple.

Ling Qingzhu is the first fairy of Great Liang and first on the Register, a daughter of the Ling clan. She is proud and composed in public and quite different behind closed doors. Half the capital wants to marry her, and the other half wants to arrange it.

Lu Qingxue is tenth on the Register and a White Crane Pavilion disciple. She is Shi Feng's fiancée, for now.

Shi Yulan, Shi Feng's aunt, runs his household with a sharp tongue and an even sharper ledger.

Shi Zhen is the Second Elder of the Shi clan and Shi Feng's uncle. He is at Qi Condensation and very fond of lecturing about clan honour.

Shi Hong, Shi Zhen's son, has one hundred and seventy-six meridians and a temper to match. He is the clan's new pride.

Han Zheng, a Foundation Establishment steward of White Crane Pavilion, does not like to be kept waiting.

Sima Yu is the Crown Prince of Great Liang, at late Foundation Establishment and first among the kingdom's young talents. He is courteous and soft-spoken, and he never raises his voice.

The Princess of Great Liang, Sima Yu's younger sister, is second on the Register, and the capital rarely mentions her.

Beyond Great Liang, the names every gambler knows are Yuan Kuang, Crown Prince of Great Qin, said to be the strongest of his generation; Xiahou Lie of Iron Bone Temple, whom no one has ever knocked down; Bai Chenxi of Frost Lotus Sect, whose sword leaves frost on the platform; and Gongsun Ce, Third Prince of Great Song, who fights with a dozen puppets at once.

chapters.title: The Fallen Genius of Qingshi Town
chapters.html:
The ladle passed over the third bowl and went back into the pot. Shi Feng stood at the kitchen counter with his tray and watched it go.

Zhao Fu, the old clan cook, kept his eyes on the pot. He put a cracked bowl behind him before Shi Feng could take it. The allowance was cut; the chipped dishes were his own decision.

“The allowance has changed,” Zhao Fu muttered.

“For both households, or only ours?” Shi Feng asked.

“Yours,” Zhao Fu said. Then he added, “The Second Elder gave the order this morning.”

Behind the steaming pots, the kitchen servants stopped chopping and began to whisper.

“Two bowls! Last month it was four.”

“Eighteen months ago this kitchen sent ginseng soup to the eastern courtyard every day.”

“Eighteen months ago he had two hundred and thirty-seven meridians.”

“…”

Shi Feng glanced at the slate on the wall. Yesterday’s allocation was still written there in chalk. He lifted the tray.

“Two bowls are enough,” Shi Feng said calmly. “Thank you, Uncle Zhao.”

Zhao Fu’s ears reddened. He scraped the bottom of the pot and knocked the stuck rice into Shi Feng’s bowl. Behind him, the servants stopped whispering. None wanted to be the next person Shi Feng thanked.

Eating less at noon would leave Shi Feng hungry during his evening exercises.

He didn’t want to fight an old cook over rice. The cook wasn’t the one who cut it anyway.

Shi Hong was waiting in the passage with four cousins behind him.

He wore a blue training robe with silver cuffs. The spotless cuffs showed how rarely he trained.

“One hundred and seventy-six!” Shi Hong announced. “Meridians, cousin. I opened the last one last night.”

The cousins took up the cue at once.

“The most in our generation!”

“Second Elder laughed out loud at the testing stone!”

“They say the White Crane Pavilion is already asking about him!”

One hundred and twenty meridians counted as the completion of Meridian Opening. Most cultivators stopped there and broke through to Qi Condensation. One hundred and seventy-six was far beyond that. In Qingshi Town, it was already the number of a genius.

“Congratulations,” Shi Feng said.

He meant it. He still remembered teaching this cousin to keep his shoulders loose during his very first breathing exercise.

Shi Hong’s face darkened. “That’s all?” Shi Hong shouted.

“What else would you like me to say?” Shi Feng asked.

One of the cousins lowered his head and studied the floor.

“You still think you’re better than us!” Shi Hong yelled. “A cripple living on two bowls of charity, and you still look at me like I’m nine years old!”

Shi Feng didn’t want to argue while holding hot food. He walked toward the courtyard. A hand seized the edge of his tray.

Rice slid. Shi Feng steadied the bowls, and even that small movement stabbed a cold ache beneath his breastbone. He waited for the pain to pass before he spoke.

“Please let go,” Shi Feng said.

“Or what?” Shi Hong said, grinning now.

The passage fell silent.

Shi Feng looked at his cousin’s wrist. The grip was loose. The elbow was raised. The weight sat too far forward. Three ways to break the hold appeared in his mind at once.

His body couldn’t do any of them.

Shi Feng sighed in his heart. Eighteen months ago, Shi Hong couldn’t have touched his sleeve. Today Shi Feng couldn’t even take back his own breakfast.

“Your elbow is still too high,” Shi Feng said calmly. “I told you that when you were nine.”

Someone behind Shi Hong snorted and swallowed the laugh. Shi Hong’s face turned red to the ears. His fingers tightened until the bowls rattled against each other.

“Brat! That breakfast is charged to my household!” Shi Yulan snapped from the end of the passage. “If you spill it, the cost goes on yours!”

Shi Yulan stood there with a medicine basket over one arm. She was Shi Feng’s aunt, his late father’s younger sister, and she managed what remained of their household’s property. The elders of the Shi Clan forgot many things. But Shi Yulan never forgot a debt!

Shi Hong’s expression changed at once.

“Aunt, we were only talking,” Shi Hong said, letting go of the tray.

“Then go and talk somewhere else.” Shi Yulan said. She did not move until the cousins were gone.

In the eastern courtyard, Shi Yulan took a bowl from the tray before Shi Feng could set it down.

“The physician’s letter came from the capital,” Shi Yulan said.

“And?” Shi Feng asked.

“I didn’t open it.” Shi Yulan said, picking up her chopsticks. “I’m not your servant, brat. Read your own letters.”

Shi Feng dried his hands and slit the envelope.

No rupture. No poison. No trace of demonic interference. No detectable meridian network under repeated examination. Recommend long-term restorative treatment. Avoid strenuous exertion.

He read it twice. The second reading changed nothing.

No detectable meridian network. Shi Feng knew exactly what that meant. To the best physicians in the capital, he was a cripple. A man without meridians couldn’t draw in qi. He couldn’t condense it. He would never take another step on the path of cultivation.

“They found the same thing,” Shi Feng said, folding the letter.

“What did you expect?” Shi Yulan asked.

“I didn’t know,” Shi Feng said.

Shi Feng was eighteen now. Eighteen months ago, Qingshi Town’s testing stone showed that he’d opened two hundred and thirty-seven meridians. The whole town was stunned. A genius might reach one hundred and eighty. Only once in a generation did someone pass two hundred. The county governor sent him a jade cup, and three sects sent invitations.

Nobody knew about the stone chamber beneath this courtyard. Nobody knew about the old meridian diagram his father brought home from the border.

The diagram showed three hundred and sixty paths. Every manual in the kingdom called three hundred and sixty the absolute limit. In secret, within that stone chamber, Shi Feng had reached all three hundred and sixty. Only beyond that private count did the diagram draw five more curves.

Shi Feng tried to open them.

The first wave of pain nearly tore him apart. The second was worse. After the fifth, there was nothing.

He woke three days later with dried blood in his hair. When he reached for his meridians, his body answered with emptiness. Since that day, no physician could find a single meridian in him.

Still, every morning, Shi Feng performed the breathing exercise. In his heart, he didn’t believe those five curves were a lie.

“The bracelet covered the physician’s deposit,” Shi Yulan said, scraping the bottom of her bowl. “I’ve added it to your debt.”

Shi Feng looked at her bare wrist. His father gave her that bracelet long ago. It was green stone. The merchant sold it as jade, and his father never admitted the mistake.

“At the pawn value,” Shi Feng said.

“At the replacement value!” Shi Yulan said.

“The stone is still in the pawnshop,” Shi Feng pointed out. “Nothing has been replaced.”

“You brat, you always notice the wrong things!” Shi Yulan snapped, and she turned her face away.

Shi Feng understood her perfectly. She pawned her dead brother’s last gift for him. She called it a debt so that he would not feel he owed her anything. Aunt, he thought, you’re terrible at keeping accounts. You can’t hide that you care.

Outside, the guest bell rang three times.

Servants rushed past the gate. One of them grabbed a flowerpot that had stood crooked for six months and set it straight.

Through the gate, Shi Feng saw a carriage with white cranes stitched on its silver curtains. The gossip arrived before the dust settled.

“White cranes! That’s the White Crane Pavilion’s crest!”

“The Lu family carriage is right behind it!”

“Today? The same morning his rice was cut?”

“You think the kitchen decides these things by chance?”

A young woman stepped down in pale blue robes. A white-jade pin shone in her hair. Shi Feng glanced at the visitor, then put down his chopsticks.

He recognised that pin. He bought it back when the two families still enjoyed mentioning their engagement. Now the carriage brought a steward instead of gifts. The purpose of this visit wasn’t hard to guess.

Lu Qingxue looked toward the eastern courtyard. An older man in a grey steward’s robe murmured something at her shoulder. She turned away.

Shi Yulan’s complexion went pale. “That’s not a social call,” Shi Yulan said quietly. “Nobody brings a Pavilion steward to drink tea.”

So that is why the rice was cut this morning, Shi Feng thought. The Second Elder wanted the guests to see how low the eastern courtyard has fallen.

He finished his rice before standing.

“Aunt, I’ll go hear their conditions,” Shi Feng said.

“Don’t let that old steward bully you,” Shi Yulan replied.

Shi Feng wiped his hands and walked towards the hall.

chapters.title: Tenth Under Heaven
chapters.html:
Shi Feng stopped outside the reception hall. A servant reached to shut the side door and pointed him toward the main entrance. The guests wanted everyone to see him come in. Very well. He pulled his cuff straight and entered by the middle.

Shi Zhen waited in his ceremonial belt, dressed well for a nephew’s disgrace.

“Late! The clan’s guests are waiting, and the boy dawdles outside!” Shi Zhen muttered to the elder beside him. “Where are his manners?”

Clan Head Shi Rong sat at the head of the hall with the elders below him in order of seniority. The Lu family sat on the left and the White Crane Pavilion’s visitors on the right. At every window, junior disciples and maids had suddenly found a reason to dust the lattice.

No chair had been set out for Shi Feng.

He bowed to the clan head and to the guests. He stood at the table’s end. The Second Elder wanted him to look like a criminal.

“Shi Feng…” Lu Qingxue said softly, rising.

“Lu Qingxue,” Shi Feng replied.

She held a sealed scroll. Good, Shi Feng thought. They could finish without wasting the morning.

That spring, the Thousand Blossom Register ranked her tenth among Great Liang’s young beauties. Merchants raised prices, claiming a fairy’s hometown shouldn’t sell cheap cloth. Shi Feng didn’t understand how her face improved their cloth.

Han Zheng, the Pavilion’s steward, lifted two fingers. A sealed wooden case rose from a servant’s arms, floated across the hall and landed on the table without a sound.

The elders gasped. Controlling objects without touching them marked Foundation Establishment. In Qingshi Town, people bowed to that realm from across the street.

“The old agreement between your families is no longer suitable,” Han Zheng said impatiently, in the tone of a clerk reading a grain tally. “Disciple Lu has been chosen for our Cloud Ascension instruction. Her future needs freedom from promises that can’t be kept anymore.”

Shi Feng ignored the case and looked at Lu Qingxue.

“Is this your decision?” Shi Feng asked.

“Yes… I,” Lu Qingxue said. Her eyes went to the steward first, and then came back.

Shi Feng noticed that first glance and nodded.

“Let’s get this over with,” Han Zheng continued, with a sneer. “The Pavilion offers three hundred spirit stones, a Meridian-Mending Pill, and a full year of treatment from our outer physicians.”

At the windows, the maids were so shocked they forgot to dust.

“Three hundred!”

“And a pill from the Pavilion itself!”

“The Second Elder’s eyes are shining!”

Shi Zhen leaned forward in his seat. Greed was written all over his face.

“May I hear her answer in full?” Shi Feng asked the steward.

Han Zheng’s fingers stopped on the arm of his chair. After a moment he nodded, and Lu Qingxue stepped away from the guests.

“My master has offered me a path I couldn’t have imagined eighteen months ago,” Lu Qingxue said quietly. “If I take it, I’ll be gone for years. I… I don’t want to promise you a life I’m not even sure I want. I’m sorry.”

At least she gave a clear answer.

“You want the engagement ended,” Shi Feng said.

“Yes,” Lu Qingxue said.

One person no longer wanted the engagement. There was nothing more to discuss.

“Then it should end,” Shi Feng said.

Shi Zhen let out a long breath of relief. Lu Qingxue didn’t.

“I asked to speak with you privately,” Lu Qingxue said, lowering her voice. “I wanted to…” She stopped.

“But you agreed to speak here, didn’t you?” Shi Feng said.

“…Yes,” Lu Qingxue said, and looked down at the scroll.

He held out his hand. Han Zheng passed him the scroll and a brush already dipped in ink, like he was a child being given medicine.

Shi Feng read. The scroll returned the ancestral pledges, released both families, and declared the decision mutual. The last line made him say, in front of everyone, that the settlement was fair.

They wanted him to sign away the insult with the engagement.

“Isn’t the sum enough?” Han Zheng asked, sneering.

“The money is generous,” Shi Feng said. “The sentence next to it costs too much.”

“The pill alone is a great treasure! Do you know how many people would beg for it?” Han Zheng said.

“Can it restore my meridians?” Shi Feng asked.

“It’s a treasure of our Pavilion,” Han Zheng said.

Shi Feng waited. The silence stretched, and the steward said nothing.

“Their own physicians don’t think it can,” Lu Qingxue said in a small voice.

Han Zheng’s expression changed. “Disciple Lu!” Han Zheng said sharply.

“He asked,” Lu Qingxue said, not lowering her eyes.

“Thanks,” Shi Feng said, inclining his head toward her.

Then he took the brush, crossed out the word mutual, and wrote beneath it in small, neat characters: Requested by Lu Qingxue. Accepted by Shi Feng.

Han Zheng’s smile vanished.

“That’s unnecessary,” Han Zheng said, his voice sharp.

“It’s what happened,” Shi Feng said.

“Both wordings mean the same thing. Stop wasting my time,” Han Zheng said.

“Then the true one shouldn’t be a problem,” Shi Feng said.

He turned the scroll and drew one clean line through the compensation line.

“How dare you!” Shi Zhen barked, half rising from his chair. “The clan’s already approved this!”

“I haven’t agreed to that part,” Shi Feng said.

“Do you think turning down money will fix your status?” Shi Zhen shouted. “Do you think three hundred spirit stones grow on the plum tree in your yard?”

“No,” Shi Feng said.

Shi Zhen waited furiously for an explanation that never came.

The windows filled with whispers.

“He crossed out three hundred spirit stones!”

“Is he crazy?”

“He’s lost his mind along with his meridians!”

“…”

Shi Feng needed those stones.

He thought of the leaking roof and wanted to sign. But he wouldn’t take money to call this fair. He still owned his name.

His fingers trembled as he signed. He laid the brush on its rest, not across the wet page.

“We can each keep a copy,” Shi Feng said.

“Hmph. Young people love their dignity,” Han Zheng said. “Let’s hope you can afford it.”

A heavy pressure fell on his shoulders, and his knees weakened. He set one hand on the table and felt the pale mark under his fingertips. Teacups rattled on their saucers. At the windows the maids shrank back from the lattice without knowing why.

The steward was crushing a cripple before the whole clan!

Shi Feng gritted his teeth. I won’t kneel!

The wooden table groaned under his palm. Han Zheng narrowed his eyes and pressed harder, releasing a second wave of Foundation Establishment pressure that made the nearest elders duck their heads and clutch their chairs.

Shi Feng’s knees trembled once, locked, and held. Slowly, inch by inch, he lifted his chin until he was looking straight into the steward’s eyes.

He didn’t kneel.

At the windows and along the hall, the whispers broke out in a rush of shock.

“He’s still standing!”

“That’s Foundation Establishment pressure—even the Third Elder had to bow his shoulders!”

“He doesn’t have a single working meridian, and Steward Han can’t force his knees down!”

“Look at the steward’s face—if he presses any harder, everyone will know White Crane Pavilion had to murder a cripple just to make him bow!”

Han Zheng’s jaw tightened. Clan Head Shi Rong sat straight up, staring at Shi Feng’s back. The watching disciples stepped back from the sill. Nobody laughed.

Only when Han Zheng’s aura faltered against that stubborn spine did Lu Qingxue step forward beside the table.

“He’s signed, Steward Han,” Lu Qingxue said, her voice tight. “The Pavilion has its copy.”

Han Zheng withdrew his pressure and rose, glancing coldly at Shi Feng’s unbent knees. As the guests left, Lu Qingxue paused beside Shi Feng with an envelope hidden inside her cuff.

“The Pavilion physicians’ first report,” Lu Qingxue whispered hurriedly. “Steward Han ordered it buried in the outer archive. I… I copied it before we left.”

Shi Feng glanced at the crane-marked seal without reaching for it in front of the hall.

“Would their report say anything different from the one I already have?” Shi Feng asked.

“I haven’t read the whole thing,” Lu Qingxue admitted in a low voice. “Only that they questioned the diagnosis.”

“Not in front of your steward,” Shi Feng said calmly. “Keep it until you’re not being watched.”

She slipped it back into her sleeve and left. He didn’t ask her to look back.

When the carriage bell sounded, Shi Feng pulled out an empty chair and sat. Two elders moved their teacups without meeting his eyes.

Shi Zhen stood with his ledger, trying to recover his authority.

“Since you want to be so independent,” Shi Zhen said, forcing his voice loud into the quiet room, “let’s talk about the eastern courtyard.”

Shi Feng lifted his head.

This time, his hand was steady.

chapters.title: The Red Cord
chapters.html:
“Please explain,” Shi Feng said.

Shi Zhen had planned to scold a rude junior. But a polite request gave him nothing to scold! After a pause he opened his ledger instead. A written account still carried an elder’s authority.

“The eastern courtyard belongs to the clan,” Shi Zhen said, tapping the page. “It was assigned to your father for his service. It costs far too much to keep up, and your household gives almost nothing back.”

“My father’s settlement covers two generations,” Shi Feng said.

“That agreement is under the clan’s control,” Shi Zhen said.

“Does control include cancelling it?” Shi Feng asked.

Several elders who had risen to leave suddenly decided to stay beside their chairs. Nobody wanted to miss this.

“For seven years this clan has fed and sheltered you!” Shi Zhen thundered, so loudly that the maids at the windows ducked. “A junior should remember the kindness of his elders, not count their furniture!”

Shi Feng folded his hands so the elders wouldn’t see the left one close into a fist. His father died on a clan border contract, and this house was part of the price of that death. The Second Elder was selling it back to him as charity. What a shameless old man, Shi Feng thought coldly.

“Clan Head,” Shi Feng said, turning to Shi Rong, “please have the settlement brought out. My father’s seal is on it. We can read his terms together.”

“Do you know where it is?” Shi Rong asked.

“The western strongbox. Third bundle of border records. Red cord,” Shi Feng said.

“The cord?” Shi Rong asked.

“My father asked me to tie it,” Shi Feng said.

Years ago, he sat at this very table with the loose ends between his fingers, and his father made him retie the knot twice. A document that mattered, his father said, should not be held carelessly.

The clan head sent a servant. The bundle came back with its red cord intact, and Shi Rong read the settlement in silence while Shi Zhen turned pages that did not need turning.

“Two generations,” Shi Rong said at last. “The courtyard stays with the eastern household.”

A murmur ran down the table.

“The Second Elder lost.”

“The settlement is real.”

“Quiet, quiet…”

Shi Zhen’s face turned red, and his expression twisted. Losing the courtyard was bad enough, and losing it in front of his own sons was worse. He coughed and tried another road.

“Then there’s still the matter of treatment costs.” Shi Zhen said, louder than before. “The jade-needle specialist. The winter restoratives. Several furnace fees!”

“Please read them one by one,” Shi Feng said.

Shi Zhen looked toward the clan head. Shi Rong said nothing. With no help coming, Shi Zhen read the first sum, his face growing redder.

“Paid from our household’s savings,” Shi Feng said. “Treasurer Du Cheng holds the receipt. The physician also refunded four stones for two needles he broke in my arm.”

Shi Zhen read the second.

“Forty-eight bottles of restorative arrived this winter,” Shi Feng said. “Our courtyard received twelve.”

“The shares were changed,” Shi Zhen said stiffly. “The clan’s honour comes before one household’s bottles!”

“Then our account should say twelve,” Shi Feng said.

“The rest went to the clan’s cultivators!” Shi Zhen snapped.

“For whom?” Shi Feng asked.

“Mine!” Shi Hong shouted from the doorway. “I opened one hundred and seventy-six meridians! You couldn’t use them anyway. Why waste them on a cripple?”

“Then you should pay for them,” Shi Feng said, turning toward him.

Shi Yulan appeared behind Shi Hong and elbowed him out of the doorway without a glance. A servant followed her carrying a cracked blue jar.

“Brat, I figured you’d need these.” Shi Yulan snapped.

She set the jar beside Shi Feng. Inside were folded receipts, wrapped in old prescription sheets against the damp, and every one was dated.

“Twelve stones,” Shi Yulan said as she straightened. “My share, brat. Don’t forget.”

Shi Feng nodded once. She kept the papers because a household with proof was worth more than one without it. He could trust her interests without mistaking them for affection. She probably liked it that way, he thought.

Treasurer Du Cheng was sent for, and while they waited, Shi Zhen lectured the hall about clan honour and how hard it was to manage so many households. Shi Feng listened without interrupting. When the speech ended, he turned the ledger back to the disputed page.

Du Cheng arrived carrying his abacus upside down. He turned it over, read three receipts, and stopped moving the beads.

“Who wrote forty-eight under this household?” Du Cheng asked.

Shi Zhen stared at him.

Du Cheng looked down at the brush tucked in his own belt. His face turned pale.

“I’ll correct it,” Du Cheng said quickly.

“Thirty-six spirit stones,” Shi Rong said.

“A mistake in the accounts,” Shi Zhen said, red to the ears. “A small matter. No need to bother the whole household.”

Shi Feng stayed seated. The Second Elder closed the ledger, and still Shi Feng did not rise.

“What more do you want?” Shi Zhen shouted.

“The corrected payment,” Shi Feng said.

“It’ll go into the accounts!” Shi Zhen said.

“Please write it down after it’s paid,” Shi Feng said.

There was no accusation in his voice. It needed none.

The clan head nodded to Du Cheng, who counted out the stones. Shi Feng took each one and turned it over before setting it down. Shi Hong watched with open disgust.

“Look at him!” Shi Hong sneered. “Cripple! He’s dragging this out for the pleasure of it.”

In truth, Shi Feng was checking for cracks. Once, Shi Yulan took three cracked stones as rent, and the loss landed on his account. He said nothing and put the purse away.

Shi Rong set his cup down. The elders were stunned that Shi Feng knew the exact price of every bottle.

Shi Feng stood.

“The year-end clan test is in nine months,” Shi Zhen said before his nephew reached the door. “The eastern household will lose its allowance unless its heir demonstrates Qi Condensation. Your precious settlement doesn’t change that rule.”

Shi Feng stopped. The Second Elder was making a new condition for an allowance already owed. Whether he returned for that test would be his own decision.

“Will this be written down?” Shi Feng asked.

“It will,” Shi Zhen said.

“Then I want a copy,” Shi Feng said.

“You think paper can protect you from everything?” Shi Zhen barked.

“No,” Shi Feng said. “Only from the people who sign it.”

He bowed to the clan head and left. Behind him nobody spoke until the door closed, and then everybody did.

Outside, Shi Yulan took her twelve stones before she’d let him put the purse inside his robe.

“For a few receipts,” Shi Feng said calmly.

“For keeping them when everyone else wanted to forget, brat!” Shi Yulan said, and tucked the stones into her sleeve.

He didn’t argue.

At the eastern courtyard she went in to put the money away, and Shi Feng sat under the plum tree. He thought about his next trip to the physician. The engagement was finished. He didn’t intend to waste another afternoon thinking about it.

He sat until the shadow of the wall reached his boots. When his aunt came back out, she asked if he’d finished his breakfast.

“No,” Shi Feng said.

“The kitchen won’t give you another, you know,” Shi Yulan said gruffly.

“I know,” Shi Feng said.

He went in and ate the cold rice, then washed the bowl himself. He was still hungry. Refusing three hundred spirit stones didn’t fill his stomach.

That afternoon he went down into the chamber beneath the house. Scratches marked the stone around the meditation platform, where his own nails had dug in eighteen months ago. He knelt beside them and unrolled his father’s diagram on a dry cloth.

Three hundred and sixty paths. Five curves joining places that should never touch.

I was sure I understood these, he thought. I was wrong, but I wasn’t stupid. He compared the faded lines with the pattern in his memory until the lamp guttered, then rolled the sheet into its tube and climbed back up.

He packed one spare robe, a knife, and the twenty-four stones that remained, with the diagram wrapped against rain between them. At dusk a boy from the clinic in town brought a note. Physician Meng Shou has found one more possibility.

Below that, in smaller writing, Meng Shou had added: Come alone. Don’t bring your aunt, she’s too loud. Shi Feng folded the message and laid it beside the bundle.

Shi Feng read the note again.

“A possibility?” Shi Feng murmured. “Then I’ll hear it.”

He set his pack beside the door. If the physician gave him a road, he was ready to take it.

chapters.title: One Last Prescription
chapters.html:
The copper needle turned under Shi Feng’s skin for half an incense stick. He watched the ash grow longer. He didn’t dare look at the old man’s face.

“Did it find anything?” Shi Feng asked.

“Nothing!” Meng Shou growled, flinging the needle into the stove.

For eighteen months Shi Feng had sat under the same painting of a mountain crane while the old man told him to drink more soup. Today Meng Shou took the painting down. Behind it was a hidden cupboard.

“The capital’s letter says what I found,” Meng Shou grunted. “No channels at all. Hmph. An empty room.”

“So nothing is blocking them?” Shi Feng asked.

“Nothing,” Meng Shou grunted.

He brought out a pressed plant between sheets of waxed cloth. Its narrow roots were black on one side and silver on the other.

“Yin Jade Root,” Meng Shou said. “Dead one. Picked near Hanyin Well in Heilu Marsh, eleven years ago.”

“What does it treat?” Shi Feng asked.

“In beasts, a fever that stops their inner flow. It can wake dormant channels for a short time,” Meng Shou said gruffly.

Dormant, Shi Feng thought. His heart began to pound, and he was stunned. Every other physician said dead, and this one said dormant.

“And in people?” Shi Feng asked.

“A charcoal burner took a sliver. Feeling came back to his leg,” Meng Shou said.

“Then?” Shi Feng asked, leaning forward.

“Then he took a second dose by himself. His kidneys failed,” Meng Shou said.

“I see,” Shi Feng said.

“You don’t, so listen!” Meng Shou snapped. “A piece the size of your smallest fingernail. Never more. I’m not promising a cure, boy. I’m just sick of selling you soup.”

“Can it be bought?” Shi Feng asked.

“Living roots rot once they’re pulled from the mineral bed. One lasts a day, sealed well,” Meng Shou said. “No merchant will risk the western flats for you.”

“Then why tell me at all?” Shi Feng asked.

“Your credit here runs out in seven days. A merchant offered me fifty stones for a living root,” Meng Shou said bluntly. “You need a cure. I need someone fool enough to fetch it.”

Meng Shou pressed a folded survey into his hand. Hanyin Well sat beyond the maintained roads in a blank space ringed by warnings in four different inks.

“An old patient gave me that map,” Meng Shou said. “The square marks are abandoned kilns. That black circle is the well. Follow the raised stone path from the hunting hut.”

“What’s the red line?” Shi Feng asked.

“Where he got lost,” Meng Shou replied. “Don’t follow that.”

Shi Feng turned the map the right way up. The physician immediately turned it back.

“North is down on this one,” Meng Shou said.

“Did your patient survive?” Shi Feng asked.

“Long enough to complain about the map,” Meng Shou replied.

He also sold Shi Feng wound powder, fever pellets and instructions for the root.

“What will you pay for a living sample?” Shi Feng asked, his hand on the door frame.

“Twenty stones,” Meng Shou said. “And any more roots come to me.”

“That wasn’t in the price you named,” Shi Feng said.

Meng Shou grunted.

Shi Feng waited with the stones in his palm, and after a while the physician grumbled, dipped his brush and crossed out the line about exclusive supply.

Qingshi Town was getting ready for the spring market. At the corner by the well, the storyteller He Yan had gathered a ring of listeners around a new tale.

“...and the fallen genius fell to his knees before the kingdom’s tenth fairy!” He Yan cried, slapping his fan against his palm. “‘Don’t abandon me!’ he wept, and then he fainted dead away on the Lu family’s carpet!”

The listeners groaned with pleasure.

“Pitiful!”

“What a waste of a face like that.”

“I heard he fainted twice.”

Shi Feng stood at the edge of the ring until the storyteller noticed him. The fan stopped in mid-air, and He Yan’s expression changed.

“I didn’t faint,” Shi Feng said.

“It’s only a story, young master!” He Yan said.

“Then please use a different name,” Shi Feng said.

He walked on before the man could decide whether that was a threat. It was a polite request. If it was ignored, Shi Feng would come back.

Behind him the ring buzzed.

“Was that him?”

“He doesn’t look like he fainted.”

“Then why’s He Yan so scared?”

“…”

Gao Sheng’s pawnshop smelled of camphor and other people’s misfortune. His father’s brass compass, pawned by Shi Yulan for his treatment, lay in the case between a chipped thumb ring and a hair clasp set with glass.

“Twenty stones,” Gao Sheng said.

“You lent my aunt eight,” Shi Feng said.

“Twenty,” Gao Sheng said.

“Treasurer Du Cheng is checking our household’s receipts this month,” Shi Feng said, glancing at the account books on the man’s desk. “I’ll need a receipt for this.”

Gao Sheng’s expression changed. “Ten,” Gao Sheng said. Shi Feng counted ten stones onto the counter and waited until the owner wrote ten on the ticket.

By the time he reached home, most of the rest of his money had become travel rations, a bow with an uneven pull, a short spear, and a compass that still pointed south as faithfully as it had for his father.

Shi Yulan listened to the whole route. Then she asked what it had cost, and then she picked up the map.

“Three men from the northern branch died in Heilu Marsh last autumn.” Shi Yulan said.

“They went to hunt,” Shi Feng said.

“Do you think the beasts will care that you only came to pick a plant, brat?” Shi Yulan shouted.

“I can’t stay here,” Shi Feng said.

“Is it because a girl left?” Shi Yulan asked.

“Because I still have to rest halfway up the eastern stairs,” Shi Feng said. “Waiting another year won’t make them shorter.”

“You could be killed, you idiot!” Shi Yulan said.

“Yes,” Shi Feng said.

The answer made her look up. He was afraid, and his decision was the same. She turned the map around, studied it, and set it down with a sniff.

“You’ve packed two fever pellets. Take two more!” Shi Yulan said gruffly. “Red for sweating fever, grey for chills. Don’t mix them up. And take your father’s boots. Yours will fall apart in seven days.”

“Aunt,” Shi Feng said.

“You owe me money, brat,” Shi Yulan said, not looking at him. “Don’t you dare die on me!”

She found the compass under his spare robe and went quiet. She rubbed her thumb over the dent in its lid, from his father’s fall off a border horse. Then she put it back in his hand and folded his fingers around it.

“He never got lost with this,” Shi Yulan said. “Don’t be the first.”

Before dawn she pushed a belt with a hidden pocket into his hands. The seam was split, so she mended it herself, with very small, very angry stitches. Aunt, he thought, you’re the worst liar in the Shi Clan.

“Come back with enough stones to settle your account, brat,” Shi Yulan said at the door.

“I’ll pay back what I owe,” Shi Feng said.

“A living debtor is better than a dead one!” Shi Yulan shouted, and shut the door before he could answer.

At the clan gate, a servant waited beside a wooden notice board. By order of the Second Elder, the eastern courtyard’s quarterly allowance was suspended until the year-end clan test. Under the seal someone had chalked: A cripple has no road.

Shi Feng looked at the chalk and smiled faintly. So the Second Elder still needed a wall to insult him. He didn’t bother answering it.

He would find his own road.

The servant waited for him to notice the chalk. Shi Feng already had, and the servant’s face fell. He adjusted the strap on his shoulder and stepped onto the road west.

The pack was heavy, and his legs were weak. Shi Feng knew the marsh would be dangerous. He kept walking anyway.

Behind him, the servant waited for a curse or a threat.

Shi Feng didn’t give him either. He had medicine to find.

chapters.title: Three Spirit Stones
chapters.html:
“Three spirit stones, and I guarantee you'll reach Yunze Town alive,” Tang Jiu said, holding up three fingers.

Shi Feng looked at the cart behind him. One wheel leaned outwards. The mule was chewing a strip of its own harness.

“Does the mule know?” Shi Feng asked.

Tang Jiu turned, slapped the mule's mouth, and quickly hid the broken strap.

“That's why it's so cheap!” Tang Jiu replied.

The western road ran between green hills. Qingshi Town was already out of sight, and the morning mist still hung over the fields. Shi Feng's shoulder ached beneath his pack. Eighteen months ago, he could've run this road without sweating.

Now a mule was deciding whether he deserved to sit down.

“Can you guarantee the cart will reach Yunze Town?” Shi Feng asked.

“Young Master Shi, you're asking for too much,” Tang Jiu said seriously.

So this fellow knew his name.

Shi Feng wasn't surprised. News of a fallen genius spread faster than news of a new one. People enjoyed hearing that someone above them had fallen into the mud.

Tang Jiu's narrow eyes dropped to the short spear tied beside the pack.

“I heard your meridians are ruined,” Tang Jiu said. “A lonely road isn't kind to a man in your condition.”

“Then lower the price,” Shi Feng replied.

“The price is already pitiful!” Tang Jiu protested.

“So is the cart,” Shi Feng said.

Tang Jiu's mouth twitched. He was about to speak when hoofbeats came from behind.

Four freight wagons rolled around the bend. A woman in a dark green robe walked beside the leading horse. Her saber hung at her hip, and a black scar crossed her left eyebrow.

The wagon drivers straightened when she looked their way.

“Lin Shuang! Sister Lin!” Tang Jiu called eagerly. “There's a customer here!”

“I'm not your sister,” Lin Shuang replied without slowing.

Tang Jiu immediately lowered his voice.

“Bone Refinement,” Tang Jiu whispered to Shi Feng. “She's refined more than a third of her bones. She can break your spear with two fingers.”

Shi Feng watched Lin Shuang's footsteps. Her boots barely sank into the soft roadside mud despite the heavy saber.

Bone Refinement strengthened the body itself. A cultivator at that realm didn't need to show qi to frighten ordinary men.

“Two spirit stones to walk behind the wagons,” Lin Shuang said to Shi Feng. “Three if you want to sit.”

“Three,” Tang Jiu repeated at once. “Give them to me. I'll arrange everything.”

Lin Shuang held out her hand.

Tang Jiu's expression fell.

Shi Feng paid Lin Shuang directly and climbed onto the last wagon. Tang Jiu climbed up beside him without paying anything.

“You're not charging him?” Shi Feng asked.

“He owes me twelve,” Lin Shuang said.

“I'll pay you after the autumn market!” Tang Jiu shouted.

“You said that last autumn,” Lin Shuang replied.

Tang Jiu raised his voice toward the driver instead.

“Brother Hu De! Tell Sister Lin how I fought bandits on this very road!” Tang Jiu called.

“You told them where I hid the fare box,” Hu De replied.

“They had knives!” Tang Jiu protested.

“So did she,” Hu De said, pointing at Lin Shuang.

Tang Jiu sat down. Lin Shuang tapped her saber against his boot once. He tucked both feet beneath him.

By noon, the road narrowed beside a bamboo grove. Shi Feng ate half a dry cake while Tang Jiu spread a collection of coloured papers across his knees.

“Heilu Marsh entry permits,” Tang Jiu said. “Without one, the guards won't let you hunt. White costs five spirit stones. Blue costs eight. Red costs twelve.”

“What's different?” Shi Feng asked.

“Red looks more impressive,” Tang Jiu said.

Shi Feng picked up a red paper. Two names were written under a large seal, followed by a promise about sharing a marriage bed.

“This is a marriage certificate,” Shi Feng said.

Tang Jiu snatched it back.

“Wrong bundle,” Tang Jiu muttered.

“Whose wife were you going to sell me?” Shi Feng asked.

“For twelve stones, don't be so picky!” Tang Jiu replied.

The driver, Hu De, burst out laughing. Even Lin Shuang glanced back.

Shi Feng put away his cake. These people were greedy, but at least their greed was easy to understand.

An instant later, the lead horse screamed.

Something black burst from the bamboo. Two curved tusks struck the wagon's front board, and the driver flew backwards into the grain sacks.

“Black-Tusk Boar!” Lin Shuang shouted. “Get behind the carts!”

The beast was as large as an ox. Its thick hide carried a faint brown glow. A spirit beast with that much qi could tear apart an ordinary hunter before he lifted his bow.

Tang Jiu jumped off the wagon and disappeared underneath it.

Shi Feng reached for his spear.

“Put it down!” Lin Shuang snapped. “Do you want to be skewered along with it?”

Her saber flashed. The boar twisted, and the blade cut a long wound across its shoulder instead of its throat.

Blood splashed against the bamboo.

The beast roared and charged the smaller gap beside the last wagon.

Straight towards Shi Feng.

He jumped down, but his right leg gave way when he landed. A sharp pain shot from his knee to his waist. His meridians remained silent.

Damn it! Shi Feng thought. His old instincts were faster than this useless body.

The tusks lowered.

There wasn't time to climb back onto the cart. Shi Feng caught the corner of a sack and dragged it down between himself and the beast.

White powder burst into the air.

The boar's charge didn't stop. It smashed through the sack, but its eyes closed against the lime. Shi Feng threw himself sideways into the ditch.

A tusk tore his sleeve.

The wagon shook above him. Wood cracked, and the mule shrieked. Lin Shuang landed on the wagon roof and drove her saber down with both hands.

Bang!

The blade split the boar's skull.

Its legs thrashed twice before going still.

For a while, nobody moved.

“It's dead?” Hu De asked from the grain sacks.

“Do you want to check with your head?” Lin Shuang replied.

Shi Feng climbed out of the ditch. His hands were muddy, and his torn sleeve hung from his elbow. Lin Shuang looked from him to the burst sack.

“You knew it was lime?” Lin Shuang asked.

“The driver complained about the price when we stopped,” Shi Feng replied.

“You listened to that?” Lin Shuang asked.

“He complained for half an hour,” Shi Feng said.

The driver shut his mouth.

Lin Shuang wiped her saber clean. Shi Feng understood what saved him. The lime blinded the beast for a breath, and a Bone Refinement cultivator used that breath to kill it. He couldn't have done it himself.

He didn't enjoy admitting that.

Tang Jiu crawled out from beneath the cart, brushed his robe, and pointed proudly at the corpse.

“Good thing I guarded the wheels!” Tang Jiu declared.

“You were holding my ankle,” Hu De said.

“Then I guarded you too,” Tang Jiu replied.

The broken wagon couldn't continue. The merchants argued over the lost lime while Lin Shuang cut the beast's valuable tusks free.

“You can walk from here,” Lin Shuang told Shi Feng. “Yunze Town is six li ahead.”

Shi Feng held out his hand.

“What?” Lin Shuang asked.

“I paid to sit,” Shi Feng said.

“You sat,” Lin Shuang replied.

“To Yunze Town,” Shi Feng added.

Lin Shuang stared at him, then tossed him one spirit stone.

“You're troublesome for a cripple,” Lin Shuang said.

“Being crippled is expensive,” Shi Feng replied.

Tang Jiu hurried after him with the coloured papers tucked away.

“I also sell maps!” Tang Jiu called.

Ahead, Yunze Town's dark walls rose beyond the trees. Above the gate hung six enormous beast skulls, their jaws open over the road. Under them, a painted board promised rich rewards for anyone who entered Heilu Marsh.

Someone scratched another sentence beneath the promise.

Dead men didn't need collecting fees.

Tang Jiu followed his gaze and smiled.

“Don't believe everything written on a wall,” Tang Jiu advised.

Shi Feng looked at the coloured papers under his arm.

“Only things written on your papers?” Shi Feng asked.

“Those cost money,” Tang Jiu replied. “Naturally, they're more trustworthy.”

chapters.title: The Young Master Wanted a Seat
chapters.html:
“Move your leg. Young Master Wei wants this seat,” Luo San said.

Shi Feng looked up from his bowl.

The noodle stall stood just inside Yunze Town's western gate. Smoke drifted beneath a patched awning, and hunters filled every bench. Three men in fine robes waited beside his table.

The one in front wore a jade thumb ring large enough to knock against his sword hilt.

“There are seats beside the wall,” Shi Feng said.

“Did I ask where the wall was?” Wei Kuo replied.

Luo San laughed. His qi pressed against the nearby diners, and two men hurriedly carried their bowls away.

Both master and servant were at Qi Condensation. In this part of town, that was enough to make people swallow their anger.

Shi Feng lowered his gaze to the noodles. He hadn't eaten a hot meal since leaving home.

“I'm almost done,” Shi Feng said.

The stallkeeper rushed over, wiping his hands on his apron.

“Young Master Wei, this table hasn't been cleaned!” Shen Gui said. “I'll arrange a better one!”

Wei Kuo glanced at the next stall. Two girls buying hair ribbons were watching him. He pulled his jade ring higher on his thumb before answering.

“I want this one,” Wei Kuo said.

Shen Gui looked from the girls to the empty seats. Ah. The young master wanted an audience with his noodles.

Then his eyes returned to Shi Feng's face.

“Wait. Aren't you the Shi family's fallen genius?” Wei Kuo asked.

The chatter around the stall grew quieter.

“You recognise me?” Shi Feng asked.

“Two hundred and thirty-seven meridians!” Wei Kuo said loudly. “People in Qingshi Town used to say you'd become a Great Sect disciple. Now you can't even find a clean table?”

Luo San's laughter grew louder.

“I found a clean one,” Shi Feng replied. “You weren't here yet.”

Shen Gui nearly dropped the kettle.

Wei Kuo's smile vanished.

“Do you still think you're a genius?” Wei Kuo asked coldly.

“Do you need the seat or a compliment?” Shi Feng asked.

Someone at the next table choked on his soup. Wei Kuo slapped his palm onto the table. The bowls jumped, and Shi Feng's broth spilled over the rim.

“You're a cripple!” Wei Kuo shouted. “Even Lu Qingxue doesn't want you!”

“Then go ask her for the seat,” Shi Feng said.

Luo San reached for Shi Feng's collar.

“Break that table and pay twenty spirit stones,” Shao Cheng said from the street.

A thickset man in a brown robe stood beside the stall. A heavy iron ruler hung at his waist. The noisy street became quiet around him.

Wei Kuo's hand stopped.

“Senior Zhao, it's just a little joke,” Wei Kuo said.

Shao Cheng was at Bone Refinement. More importantly, he collected the western market's rent for the town lord. Wei Renshan, Wei Kuo's father, was at Foundation Establishment, but he was away on business.

“Then laugh outside,” Shao Cheng replied. “Shen Gui owes me rent. If you wreck his stall, I'll collect it from you.”

Wei Kuo's expression changed. After a moment, he pulled his sleeve straight.

“Enjoy your noodles, Young Master Shi,” Wei Kuo said with a sneer.

Shi Feng lifted his bowl.

“I was trying to,” Shi Feng replied.

Wei Kuo left with Luo San close behind. Shen Gui waited until they disappeared, then hurriedly picked up the bowls from the abandoned table.

“You shouldn't have answered him,” Shen Gui whispered.

“You shouldn't sell soup in such shallow bowls,” Shi Feng replied.

Shen Gui stared at the spilled broth.

“I'll add some more,” Shen Gui muttered.

Shao Cheng glanced at Shi Feng's thin wrists and went on collecting rent. He didn't ask his name or offer advice.

Shi Feng drank the fresh broth. Shao Cheng had protected his rent, Shen Gui had protected his stall, and Wei Kuo had protected nothing except his own bad mood. There was no need to follow any of them.

“Five spirit stones a night,” Bian Cui said. “Clean bedding, hot water, and nobody asks questions.”

Shi Feng stood in the doorway of a narrow lodging house. Hunters' boots crowded the steps, and a row of wet hides dripped over the yard.

“Show me the bedding,” Shi Feng said.

Bian Cui opened a room behind the kitchen. A straw mattress lay beneath the window. Something small jumped from it onto the wall.

“Those are only field fleas,” Bian Cui said quickly.

“Do town fleas cost more?” Shi Feng asked.

“Young man, don't joke about business,” Bian Cui replied.

“Two spirit stones,” Shi Feng said.

“Four,” Bian Cui said.

“Two. I'll sleep on the floor,” Shi Feng replied.

Bian Cui agreed so quickly that Shi Feng knew he was still paying too much.

He put his pack down and checked the window. It opened over the back alley, and the latch worked. That was enough for one night.

Outside, Bian Cui was already telling another guest that her last room cost six spirit stones. Shi Feng ignored her and laid Meng Shou's map across the floor.

Hanyin Well sat beyond the black marsh reeds. The road marked beside it ended at an abandoned hunting hut.

One living Yin Jade Root might wake his meridians. Or it might ruin his kidneys and leave him dead beside a well. Neither possibility would improve by staring at the paper.

The next morning, Shi Feng walked through the herb market. Fresh roots lay beside beast bones, dried mushrooms and bottles of cloudy medicine.

Qian Rui, a white-robed physician at Qi Condensation, stood on a platform beside a painted list of rare herbs. A rabbit nibbled his sleeve while he announced the strength of his medicine.

Yin Jade Root was written near the bottom. Under it was a price of three hundred spirit stones.

“Physician Qian,” Shi Feng called, “do you really have that root?”

Qian Rui followed his pointing finger. His eyes brightened when he saw Shi Feng's pale face.

“Young man,” Qian Rui said warmly, “I knew you were sick the moment you arrived.”

“Did the root tell you?” Shi Feng asked.

“Your face told me,” Qian Rui replied. “Look at those cheeks. You haven't eaten properly in months!”

Shen Gui's stall was still visible across the street. Its owner lifted an empty noodle bowl and waved it furiously.

Qian Rui turned his back on him.

“There are illnesses food can't cure,” Qian Rui added.

Shi Feng looked at the rabbit. It was now nibbling the corner of the physician's sleeve.

“Does the rabbit agree?” Shi Feng asked.

Qian Rui pulled the sleeve away and pushed the wooden medicine box across his counter.

“You'll understand after looking at my medicine,” Qian Rui said.

“Your breathing is weak, your blood is thin, and your meridians are dead,” Qian Rui said gravely.

“You heard that from Tang Jiu,” Shi Feng replied.

Qian Rui's hand paused above the medicine bottle. Behind the platform, Tang Jiu quietly stepped behind a hanging hide.

“A good physician doesn't refuse useful information,” Qian Rui said.

Shi Feng pointed at the painted board.

“The Yin Jade Root,” Shi Feng said. “Let me see it.”

Qian Rui took a long wooden box from beneath the counter. Inside lay a pale root with a thin black line painted along one side.

It smelled faintly of vinegar.

“Three hundred spirit stones,” Qian Rui said. “For you, two hundred and eighty.”

“How long ago was it picked?” Shi Feng asked.

“This morning,” Qian Rui replied at once.

“From Hanyin Well?” Shi Feng asked.

“Naturally,” Qian Rui answered.

“Then your feet are fast,” Shi Feng said. “It's a day's walk from here.”

Qian Rui shut the box.

“The delivery boy's feet are fast,” Qian Rui corrected.

Shi Feng ran a wet fingertip over the root's black line. Colour stained his skin.

Qian Rui's expression stiffened.

“Its medicinal nature leaks,” Qian Rui said.

“So does your ink,” Shi Feng replied.

Two hunters behind him burst out laughing.

“I told you the old fox painted it!”

“Last month his thousand-year ginseng still had a cabbage leaf attached!”

“Don't touch the other side. That costs another hundred!”

Qian Rui glared at them and snatched the box away.

“If you're not buying, stop blocking real patients!” Qian Rui snapped.

“Do you know anyone who goes to Hanyin Well?” Shi Feng asked.

The physician's anger faded slightly. There was still business to be done.

“Ma Liang leaves today,” Qian Rui said. “He gathers Black Needle Grass near the old hunting grounds. Two spirit stones, and I'll introduce you.”

“One,” Shi Feng replied.

“You bargain over a life-saving chance?” Qian Rui asked.

“You painted a radish,” Shi Feng said.

Qian Rui took the spirit stone.

Shi Feng put Meng Shou's map away. An introduction was useful, but he would watch the route himself. He hadn't come this far to buy another painted root.

chapters.title: A Cripple Was Cheaper
chapters.html:
“No qi?” Ma Liang asked.

“None,” Shi Feng replied.

Ma Liang pressed two fingers against Shi Feng's wrist. He wore a wolf-tooth necklace, and old claw marks covered his hands. A faint strand of qi passed into Shi Feng's arm and found nothing it could follow.

Ma Liang let go.

“You carry the baskets,” Ma Liang said. “You pick what I point at. Don't wander.”

“I want to reach Hanyin Well,” Shi Feng replied.

“We pass it,” Ma Liang said. “If you find your medicine, that's your luck.”

The other two hunters looked him over. Zhou Ping carried a crossbow. Chai Jin held a hooked spear and wore a fresh blue headband.

All three were at Qi Condensation.

“A cripple?” Chai Jin said with a laugh. “Brother Ma, you're getting cheap.”

“Can you carry three baskets?” Ma Liang asked Chai Jin.

“Of course!” Chai Jin replied.

“Then carry them,” Ma Liang said.

Chai Jin immediately stopped laughing.

Shi Feng paid three spirit stones for the route and took the lightest basket. Ma Liang didn't complain. His gaze rested on Shi Feng's bow, then moved away.

These men weren't escorting him out of kindness, Shi Feng thought. That was fine. He didn't come looking for kindness.

Beyond Yunze Town, the fields gave way to black reeds. Frogs called from shallow pools, and white flowers covered the banks of the narrow path.

Chai Jin reached for a flower.

Ma Liang struck his wrist with the end of a stick.

“Do you want to lose that hand?” Ma Liang asked.

The white petals snapped shut around the stick. Thin teeth scraped the wood.

Chai Jin's face turned pale.

“I was checking it,” Chai Jin muttered.

“With your fingers?” Zhou Ping asked.

Chai Jin hid the bitten stick behind him. Zhou Ping took it, shaved the tooth marks away with his knife, and handed it back.

“Now you can tell the wine house you killed it,” Zhou Ping said.

“Mind your own business!” Chai Jin snapped.

Ma Liang didn’t laugh. He counted the baskets again and made them move. He cared more about what they brought back than what Chai Jin boasted about over wine.

Shi Feng stepped over the flower bed. Here, even the flowers wanted meat. Meng Shou's warning suddenly seemed too short.

By afternoon, they reached a broken stone arch beside a sunken channel. Black Needle Grass grew in the cracks below it. Ma Liang crouched, touched a broad footprint, and looked into the dark channel.

His face changed for a moment.

“Old tracks,” Ma Liang said, standing up. “Shi Feng, go down and fill your basket.”

Shi Feng didn't move.

“What left them?” Shi Feng asked.

“A marsh lizard,” Ma Liang replied.

The footprint had four deep claws. The old beast boards at the town gate showed the same shape beneath a much larger skull.

Split-Maw Beast.

Shi Feng gripped his spear.

“You said we'd pass the well first,” Shi Feng said.

“The grass comes first,” Ma Liang replied. “Climb down.”

Zhou Ping lifted his crossbow. The bolt didn't point into the channel.

It pointed at Shi Feng's chest.

“You don't need to stare,” Zhou Ping said. “Do what Brother Ma says.”

Shi Feng understood. A young Split-Maw Beast hid below. They wanted someone to draw it out, and a cripple was cheaper than a bait beast.

“You won't get much grass if it eats me,” Shi Feng said.

“Then run faster,” Chai Jin replied.

Ma Liang sighed impatiently.

“Don't blame me,” Ma Liang said. “Blame yourself for coming here without strength.”

Shi Feng looked from the crossbow to the channel. Three Qi Condensation cultivators above. One hidden beast below.

There was no good choice.

“Give me the rope,” Shi Feng said.

“That's more sensible,” Ma Liang replied.

Chai Jin reached for Shi Feng's pack. Shi Feng pulled it behind his shoulder before the hunter could take it.

“I'll need the wound powder,” Shi Feng said.

“You won't have time to use it,” Chai Jin muttered.

Ma Liang gave his companion an angry look. Chai Jin laughed and stepped away.

Shi Feng tied the pack tightly against his chest. They wanted the beast distracted, not an obedient herb picker. Keeping his medicine was the only thing he could still choose.

He wasn't going to beg them.

“If I climb back up, you won't get a second payment,” Shi Feng said.

Ma Liang's smile grew wider.

“Of course,” Ma Liang replied. “We're honest men.”

Ma Liang threw down the rope. Shi Feng passed it around his waist and tested the knot before putting his weight on it.

The stone wall was wet beneath his boots. Shi Feng lowered himself slowly, his spear tied across his back. Ten feet below, a narrow shelf ran along the channel.

Something moved in the deeper darkness.

“Further!” Ma Liang called.

“There's no grass further down,” Shi Feng replied.

“Then look harder!” Ma Liang shouted.

Shi Feng took out his knife and scraped a mark beside his hand. The stone was soft under a crust of dark moss. Above him, Chai Jin leaned out and snorted.

“What's he doing?” Chai Jin asked.

“Trying not to fall,” Zhou Ping replied.

Shi Feng shifted his weight onto the shelf. His legs trembled with the strain.

“I can see your beast,” Shi Feng called.

For a breath, the hunters were silent.

Then Ma Liang laughed.

“Good eyes, Young Master Shi,” Ma Liang said. “Now make it angry.”

Shi Feng swung the knife twice. The first cut sliced the rope above his head. The second drove the blade into the soft crack beside the shelf. He hung from its handle for a breath, then let go.

His body dropped out of sight.

Zhou Ping's crossbow snapped.

The bolt struck the stone where Shi Feng's head was a moment earlier.

“He cut it!” Chai Jin shouted.

Shi Feng landed hard in a shallow pool. Pain tore through his ankle. His knife stayed wedged in the wall above him, along with the last piece of rope.

There was no way back up.

But there was a narrow drain behind the shelf, and a faint silver root grew at its entrance.

Yin Jade Root.

Shi Feng took one step towards it.

The darkness beside the root opened its mouth.

Two rows of yellow teeth spread apart. The beast crouched under the low stone ceiling, and its heavy tail blocked the passage behind it.

Shi Feng drew the short spear from his back.

chapters.title: The Mouth in the Dark
chapters.html:
“Come out, you little bastard!” Ma Liang shouted from above.

The beast didn't look at him.

It looked at Shi Feng.

The drain was barely wide enough for two men. Black water covered the floor, and thin roots hung from the broken ceiling. Behind Shi Feng, daylight shone through the channel opening.

It was ten steps away.

The young Split-Maw Beast was only six steps away.

Its head spread sideways when it opened its jaws. A grown one could swallow a man's shoulders. This one would have to bite twice.

Shi Feng lowered the spear point towards its eyes.

“I'm not good meat,” Shi Feng said quietly. “Try the three upstairs.”

The beast sprang.

He thrust without thinking. His old clan training chose the angle, but his arms couldn't give the spear its old speed.

The point scraped across the beast's cheek.

Claws struck the shaft.

Crack!

The spear broke in the middle. Shi Feng slammed into the wall, and the air left his lungs.

He rolled before the jaws closed. Teeth struck the stone beside his ear. A chunk of rock fell into the water.

His chest hurt. His ankle couldn't hold him properly. The beast turned its head, dragging the spearhead stuck beneath its cheek.

Shi Feng was afraid. There was no shame in admitting that. Fear wasn't going to open his meridians, though.

He caught the broken half of the shaft and pushed himself upright.

“Is he dead?” Chai Jin called.

“Not yet,” Zhou Ping answered. “I heard him hit the wall.”

They sounded annoyed.

Shi Feng's anger turned cold. If he got out of this drain, those three would be next.

The beast lunged again. This time he slipped sideways before it moved, pressing himself into the shallow gap beside the root bed.

Its shoulder struck the narrow stone lip.

The jaws stopped an inch from his robe. Shi Feng jammed the broken shaft into its open mouth. The beast bit down, and wood splintered between its teeth.

Its claws scraped the floor as it tried to force its body further into the gap. He couldn't overpower it. Even a young spirit beast was far stronger than his present body.

But the stone wasn't going to move for it either. Shi Feng reached past its cheek and caught the exposed spearhead.

The edge sliced his fingers.

He pulled hard.

The blade came free, bringing a strip of flesh with it. The Split-Maw Beast shrieked, and its jaw opened wider around the wood. Shi Feng drove the blade upwards beneath its chin.

It struck bone and stopped.

The beast's claws caught his side.

Hot pain tore across his ribs. His robe split, and blood ran into his belt.

“Die!” Shi Feng shouted.

He pressed both hands against the broken metal and pushed with his entire body. The trapped beast jerked forward. Its own weight drove the point through the soft gap behind its jaw.

Blood poured over Shi Feng's wrists.

The claws stopped moving.

Shi Feng kept hold of the blade. A twitch ran down the beast's tail and struck the drain wall hard enough to shake loose dust.

He waited through it.

He didn't know whether Split-Maw Beasts could play dead. He only knew that taking his hand away too soon would be stupid.

“Brother Ma, it cried out!” Chai Jin shouted.

“I have ears!” Ma Liang answered.

“Should we go down?” Zhou Ping asked.

“You first,” Ma Liang replied.

Nobody climbed down.

For three breaths, he stayed pressed against the wall. He didn't trust the silence. Then the beast's head sagged, and its jaw closed loosely around the shattered shaft.

Shi Feng slid down into the water.

He was alive.

For now.

“It's quiet,” Chai Jin called.

“Wait,” Ma Liang answered. “A wounded beast may pretend to be dead.”

Shi Feng looked at the corpse blocking the drain.

“So can people,” Shi Feng whispered.

He dragged his pack free and pressed wound powder against his side. The powder stung so badly that his vision blurred.

The claws missed his belly by less than an inch. If they went deeper, no powder would help him. He tore a strip from his spare robe and bound the wound as tightly as he could.

Above, the hunters began arguing about who should climb down.

Shi Feng took out one of his aunt's fever pellets, looked at its red shell, and put it back. She specifically said it was for fever. It wouldn't restore the blood running into the water.

He was glad he listened to her complaints while she packed. The wound powder stopped the worst of the bleeding. He pushed the pack beneath his arm and tested the strip around his ribs.

It held.

The cloth slowed the bleeding. He could stand if he kept his back against the wall, but his right ankle wouldn't carry him up the shelf. He needed the root, then a way past the hunters. Standing here waiting would solve neither.

Shi Feng ignored them. He reached towards the silver root growing beside his knee.

One side was black. The other carried a clear, cold sheen. No ink came away beneath his wet fingers.

“Meng Shou, you'd better not be another liar,” Shi Feng muttered.

He scraped a piece no larger than his smallest fingernail from the living root. Then he put it on his tongue and swallowed.

Cold spread through his throat.

His trembling hands suddenly stopped.

Shi Feng shut his eyes and tried the breathing exercise he performed every morning. Air entered his chest. His thoughts followed the old route through his body.

For eighteen months, that route led nowhere.

This time, something answered.

Not qi.

A faint ache appeared beneath his sternum. It spread outwards through places he no longer expected to feel.

His heart pounded.

“There!” Shi Feng whispered.

The sensation vanished.

He opened his eyes sharply.

No! He didn't imagine it. Something inside him moved.

His bloody hand lay against the Split-Maw Beast's neck. Beneath his palm, the beast's flesh began to sink.

Shi Feng froze.

Warmth poured into his hand, then rushed up his arm. It wasn't the cold strength of Yin Jade Root. It carried the fierce vitality of the dead beast.

He pulled away.

The flow stopped.

His chest rose and fell rapidly. He stared at the pale patch beneath the beast's jaw.

“What is this?” Shi Feng said.

The hunters heard his voice.

“He's alive!” Chai Jin shouted.

Shi Feng didn't answer. He pressed his hand against the corpse again.

Warmth returned at once.

The hunger beneath his sternum grew stronger. His body wanted the beast's blood, flesh and remaining qi. It wanted all of them.

Shi Feng was stunned, but he didn't let panic take over. He tried to stop without removing his hand.

The warmth stopped.

He willed it to return.

It returned.

He could control it!

Shi Feng checked his injured fingers. The cuts were still there, but his hands weren't as cold. A little feeling returned to his numb arm.

The change was small and clear. This wasn't a dream, and it wasn't the root making him imagine things. Whatever woke inside him could take strength from the corpse.

And right now, he needed strength more than he needed an answer.

He pressed harder. The pale patch spread from the beast’s jaw to its shoulder, and his numb fingers began to warm. The change followed his touch. He could test it again after he escaped.

A crossbow bolt splashed into the pool nearby.

“Young Master Shi!” Ma Liang called. “Come out! We were only testing your courage!”

Shi Feng looked towards the daylight.

His wound still hurt. He still couldn't fight three Qi Condensation cultivators. But the vitality entering his body was real, and two silent channels inside him were beginning to respond.

He pressed his other hand against the beast's belly.

“Then wait,” Shi Feng replied quietly.

Ma Liang couldn't hear him from the channel above.

That suited Shi Feng perfectly well.

He only cared about the strength filling his empty channels.

chapters.title: The Second Kind of Bait
chapters.html:
“I'll count to ten!” Ma Liang shouted. “If you don't come out, we'll smoke you out!”

Shi Feng tightened the strip around his ribs. Four meridians answered his breath. Only four, yet the difference was enough to make his eyes sting with relief.

He didn't have qi. His body was still injured. But his legs no longer trembled when he stood.

At his feet, the Split-Maw Beast was a dry hide stretched over pale bones.

Its vitality didn't restore him all at once. Most of it gathered beneath his sternum, waiting for his body to take it in. Shi Feng could feel the warmth slowly reaching his limbs.

He wanted time to understand it.

The three outside wanted him dead.

He untied the spear's remaining cord and wound it around his torn palm. The makeshift blade had no handle. One careless thrust could slice his own fingers open again.

Then he checked the shallow water beside his boots. There were two loose stones, a patch of mud, and nothing else worth using.

It would have to be enough.

“Brother Ma, are you really counting?” Chai Jin asked.

“Seven!” Ma Liang shouted.

“You missed four,” Zhou Ping said.

“Then go down and count it for him!” Ma Liang snapped.

Shi Feng stopped listening to the numbers. Chai Jin was pulling reeds with both hands, and Zhou Ping kept the crossbow aimed at the opening. The threat was real even if Ma Liang couldn’t count while angry.

“Shut up and gather reeds!” Ma Liang snapped.

Shi Feng crouched beside the entrance. The drain opened beneath a low stone shelf. White flowers grew along its outer edge, close enough to brush his shoulder.

He remembered their teeth.

“My leg's broken,” Shi Feng called. “I can't climb.”

“Then throw your pack out!” Ma Liang replied.

“Why?” Shi Feng asked.

“So we can pull you up!” Ma Liang shouted.

Shi Feng smiled coldly. That lie didn't even deserve another answer.

He tipped loose stones into his pack and pushed it halfway into the daylight. The strap caught on a low root. Then he crawled back into the shadow with the broken spearhead.

“There's blood on it,” Zhou Ping said above.

“He's dying anyway,” Chai Jin replied. “I'll get it.”

A rope dropped past the shelf. Boots followed it.

Chai Jin landed in the shallow water, hooked spear held in one hand. He glanced into the drain and saw the beast's pale skull.

His face changed.

“Brother Ma! The beast—” Chai Jin shouted.

Shi Feng struck the back of Chai Jin's knee with a loose stone. It wasn't enough to break the leg. A Qi Condensation cultivator's body was tougher than an ordinary man's.

But Chai Jin wasn't ready, and the slick floor gave him no footing.

He fell sideways into the white flowers.

The petals closed on his wrist and throat.

“Help!” Chai Jin screamed.

Shi Feng stepped forward and drove the spearhead through his open mouth.

The scream stopped.

It happened in less than two breaths.

Shi Feng pulled the blade free. The flowers moved beneath Chai Jin's body, drawing fresh blood into their pale roots. He pressed his bare palm against Chai Jin's arm and willed the same flow he'd drawn from the beast.

Nothing happened.

The difference was immediate. His chest answered the dead beast without hesitation. Against Chai Jin's body, it stayed quiet.

Shi Feng wasn't disappointed. He wanted to recover his cultivation, not become a man who looked at every passerby as food.

Good, Shi Feng thought. This hunger wasn't asking him to eat people.

He didn't stop to examine the difference. A crossbow creaked above. Shi Feng seized Chai Jin's spear and rolled back into the drain.

The bolt struck the hunter's corpse.

“You bastard!” Zhou Ping shouted.

“You were aiming at me earlier,” Shi Feng replied. “Don't sound so surprised.”

Ma Liang cursed and grabbed the rope.

“Stay up here!” Zhou Ping said. “We can wait!”

“And let him find another way out?” Ma Liang snapped.

Shi Feng heard the rope scrape against stone. He moved to the rear of the drain, where the ceiling sank even lower.

Ma Liang dropped onto the shelf. Qi shone faintly along his knife.

That knife could cut through Shi Feng's thin spear shaft. If they met on open ground, Ma Liang could kill him with one clean strike. Shi Feng wasn't planning to meet him there.

“Young Master Shi,” Ma Liang said, crouching at the entrance, “give me the medicine. I'll let you leave.”

“Come and take it,” Shi Feng replied.

“You think that narrow hole will save you?” Ma Liang asked.

He crawled forward with the knife held beside his face. Shi Feng thrust the hooked spear along the ground.

Ma Liang blocked it easily. The knife cut the shaft, and the spearhead dropped between them.

“Useless!” Ma Liang shouted.

Shi Feng threw the rest of his wound powder into Ma Liang's eyes. The hunter recoiled with a curse. His head struck the low ceiling.

Shi Feng seized the broken hook and pulled it towards him. The curved tip caught Ma Liang's ankle.

He pulled with both hands.

Ma Liang's chin struck the stone floor. His knife clattered into the water. Shi Feng stamped on the wrist reaching for it, then drove his own blade into the back of Ma Liang's neck.

The hunter's qi scattered.

Shi Feng stayed there until the body stopped moving. He couldn't win a fair fight against Ma Liang yet. He won because the drain forced Ma Liang to crawl, and the powder blinded him before he could use his knife.

It was simple enough.

Dead men didn't get to complain about fairness.

“Brother Ma?” Zhou Ping called.

Shi Feng picked up the fallen crossbow bolt.

“He's busy,” Shi Feng replied.

The rope suddenly shook. Zhou Ping was pulling it back up.

Shi Feng pushed Ma Liang's corpse aside and stepped onto the shelf. The remaining hunter stood above with a fresh bolt laid in his crossbow.

Fear showed clearly on Zhou Ping's face.

“Don't move!” Zhou Ping shouted.

Shi Feng threw the bolt at his eyes.

Zhou Ping flinched and fired.

The shot passed above Shi Feng's shoulder. He caught the hanging rope and pulled with all his strength. Zhou Ping was standing on its loose end.

His foot slipped, and he pitched over the broken edge.

Shi Feng stepped aside.

Zhou Ping hit the shelf shoulder-first. Before he could rise, Shi Feng drove the knife Ma Liang dropped into his throat.

Silence returned to the channel.

An hour later, Shi Feng climbed out with two purses, a crossbow and a coil of rope. He took only things he could carry. The hunters' baskets stayed beside the path.

His side throbbed, and his fingers shook from the effort. Winning didn't make the injuries disappear. He sat beneath a willow and breathed slowly until the stored warmth spread through him again.

Four meridians.

Alive.

Shi Feng looked at his bloodstained hands. He didn't regret killing them. They sent him into a beast's mouth and shot at him when he survived.

They made their choice.

He opened the purses. Most of the stones came from Ma Liang. Chai Jin carried only two, along with a small wooden comb and a scrap of dried meat.

Zhou Ping carried spare bolts wrapped in oiled cloth.

Shi Feng checked the crossbow carefully. It could be drawn by hand, so it wasn't a refined artifact. He could use it even without qi.

He took the bolts and left the comb.

“You three didn't even leave a decent spear,” Shi Feng muttered.
