His old clan instructors would certainly scold his performance. Bad footing, exposed ribs, and too much force wasted on every movement. Fortunately, none of the instructors were here to charge him for the lesson.

He got to his feet and tested his injured ankle. It hurt, but it held his weight. The hunting hut on Meng Shou's map was less than two li away.

That became his next goal.

Now he needed to find out exactly what his body could do. From the nearby reeds came a sharp squeak. A marsh rat dragged a strip of meat out of Chai Jin's abandoned basket.

Shi Feng picked up the crossbow.

“You came at the right time,” Shi Feng said.

chapters.title: An Honest Kind of Hunger
chapters.html:
“If you eat that, you'll die before sunset,” Deng Hu said.

Shi Feng lowered the roasted meat from his mouth. A bent man stood outside the abandoned hut, carrying two fish and a split bamboo basket. Three narrow scars ran down his nose.

“It's a marsh rat,” Shi Feng said.

“I can see that,” Deng Hu replied. “Those things eat poison roots.”

Shi Feng threw the meat into the cold ashes.

Deng Hu nodded approvingly, then held up the fish.

“Two spirit stones,” Deng Hu said.

“You waited until I threw it away,” Shi Feng replied.

“You're a sharp young man,” Deng Hu said.

Meng Shou’s map had led him to this hut. Its roof leaked, but the stone cellar stayed dry.

He paid for one fish and cooked it over the fire.

Deng Hu sat opposite without being invited. His qi was thin and uneven. He was still in Meridian Opening, with a hundred and twenty-six opened meridians. That put him above ordinary hunters, but he hadn't entered Qi Condensation.

Deng Hu glanced at Shi Feng’s bandaged side.

“Boar?” Deng Hu asked.

“Men,” Shi Feng replied.

“Worse,” Deng Hu said, turning his fish.

Shi Feng appreciated the lack of further questions.

Under his robe, twelve meridians now answered his breathing. A marsh rat and the snake coiled around it had been his first small tests that afternoon, and the warmth settling through his chest told him the cavern hadn't been a dream.

“I need beasts I can kill with this,” Shi Feng said, showing his knife.

Deng Hu examined the chipped edge and the bandage before pointing north.

“Grey-Shell Crocodiles in the shallow pool,” Deng Hu said. “If you insist on being stupid, choose one with a white belly. The darker ones are older.”

“Did a dark one give you those scars?” Shi Feng asked.

“My first wife threw a basket hook,” Deng Hu replied. “Watch the crocodile’s tail.”

The next morning, Shi Feng stood beside a shallow pool and waited.

Seven Grey-Shell Crocodiles slept opposite him. Even the smallest could take off his foot.

Deng Hu crouched behind a willow.

Shi Feng ignored him and set a fish on the muddy bank. The fish was tied to Ma Liang's rope. Its scent drifted across the water.

One crocodile opened its eyes.

Shi Feng pulled the fish a little closer.

The crocodile slid into the pool.

He retreated slowly, drawing it towards a narrow gap between two fallen trees. The creature followed the fish, its jaws snapping impatiently. When its head passed the first trunk, Shi Feng pulled the rope sharply.

The fish flew into the air.

The crocodile lifted its head after it.

Shi Feng thrust Ma Liang's knife into the soft flesh beneath its jaw. The beast thrashed. He let go of the knife and jumped onto the fallen tree before its tail swept the bank.

It took half an incense stick for the crocodile to die.

“Your knife's good,” Deng Hu called.

“So are your eyes,” Shi Feng replied.

Deng Hu went to fetch his skinning basket. Behind the fallen trees, Shi Feng pressed his bare palm against the corpse's belly. Vitality rushed into him, moving along his waking channels and easing the ache around his ribs until twenty-four meridians answered.

When Deng Hu came around the trunk with his skinning knife, he stopped short. The crocodile’s belly had sunken in, the flesh beneath the scales dry and brittle as salted leather.

Deng Hu crouched, poked the withered ribcage with his sheath, and let out a low whistle.

“Don’t bother hiding your hand, boy,” Deng Hu said. “I saw an old border sergeant use a blood-drinking body medicine like that thirty years ago. Eats the beast’s marrow right after the kill, doesn’t it?”

Shi Feng wiped his palm on the grass without correcting him. “You know the rules for that medicine?”

“Anyone who carried hides for the border camps heard enough,” Deng Hu said, tapping the crocodile’s jaw. “Has to be your own kill while the life’s still leaving the flesh. Touch a carcass somebody else dropped—or a rat a snake already choked—and you’ll draw nothing at all.”

“And through a glove or a sleeve?” Shi Feng asked, testing the old man against what he had noticed with the snake.

“Through cloth?” Deng Hu snorted. “Medicine sits in the skin of the palm. Wrap your robe around your hand and you might as well stroke a rock. Direct contact, flesh to flesh—that’s why those border fellows always had raw palms.”

“What happens if a man takes in too much at once?” Shi Feng asked.

Deng Hu pointed his skinning knife at him. “That’s the catch! Once that medicine bites into a beast, you can’t stop the draw until the carcass is dry or your own channels burst! Half the men who used it died from greed when they killed something too big.”

Shi Feng looked down at his hand. A moment ago, when his old wounds had twitched, he had halted the flow mid-breath and restarted it only after the heat settled.

Deng Hu had the rest right, and that last part wrong. This wasn’t a border salve dragging its user along. The power belonged to him, and it stopped the instant he willed it to.

“I’ll stick to smaller ones, then,” Shi Feng said.

“See that you do,” Deng Hu grumbled, setting to work on the hide. “Your medicine’s working, though. Yesterday you climbed the ridge like an old man. Today your feet didn’t even sink.”

Over the next four days, Shi Feng hunted the remaining six crocodiles, letting each gain settle before taking another until seventy-three meridians woke.

Before leaving, Shi Feng returned to the mineral bed beside Hanyin Well. He cut out a small block with one living shoot still rooted in it. Pulled roots spoiled within a day. This one remained in its own wet bed.

“Can you get this to Physician Meng Shou in Qingshi Town?” Shi Feng asked.

Deng Hu examined the wrapped block.

“My nephew's fish cart leaves tomorrow. Two stones, and the onward driver takes it straight to the clinic,” Deng Hu said.

Shi Feng paid and wrote the address. Meng Shou deserved a living sample. Deng Hu packed it under wet reeds and promised a receipt when the cart returned.

“You're alive!” Tang Jiu shouted.

Outside Yunze’s herb market, Tang Jiu grabbed Shi Feng’s sleeve and looked behind him with obvious disappointment.

“Did you bet on it?” Shi Feng asked.

“No!” Tang Jiu answered too quickly.

“How much?” Shi Feng asked.

“Two spirit stones,” Tang Jiu muttered. “But that isn't important. Where are Ma Liang and his friends?”

“Still in the marsh,” Shi Feng replied.

Tang Jiu released his sleeve. His eyes dropped to the familiar skinning knife hanging at Shi Feng's belt—Ma Liang's knife—and his expression shifted as he tucked that detail away for future profit.

“All three stayed behind?” Tang Jiu asked softly.

“The marsh was busy,” Shi Feng replied.

Shi Feng bought clean bandages, then found Lin Shuang beside the hide stalls. Tang Jiu immediately tried to leave.

“Twelve spirit stones,” Lin Shuang said, blocking his way.

“Sister Lin, I only have eight!” Tang Jiu protested.

“Then give me eight,” Lin Shuang replied.

He counted them out with a miserable face. Tang Jiu’s debts were stronger than his legs.

“You found your medicine?” Lin Shuang asked Shi Feng.

“Enough to stop falling into ditches,” Shi Feng said.

Lin Shuang glanced at the bandage beneath his sleeve.

“That ditch had teeth?” Lin Shuang asked.

“A few,” Shi Feng said.

“There's a Blood-Crowned Spirit Deer north of the old hunting hut,” Lin Shuang said. “It's wounded. Six hunters went after it last week. Three came back.”

Shi Feng's expression became serious.

“What realm?” Shi Feng asked.

“Strong enough to gore a Qi Condensation cultivator,” Lin Shuang replied. “I'm telling you so you avoid it.”

“Where's the wound?” Shi Feng asked.

Tang Jiu began smiling.

“I know a man who saw it!” Tang Jiu said eagerly. “His directions are very cheap!”

“Your directions,” Lin Shuang said, “led a hunter into a latrine last month.”

“The latrine wasn't on the map!” Tang Jiu protested.

Tang Jiu hurried after him, lowering his voice.

“Three stones,” Tang Jiu said. “The deer has a broken back leg. It drinks at the abandoned stone watercourse before sunset.”

“Who told you?” Shi Feng asked.

“The hunter who broke its leg,” Tang Jiu replied.

“Why isn't he hunting it?” Shi Feng asked.

Tang Jiu hesitated.

“It broke both of his,” Tang Jiu admitted.

Shi Feng looked towards the north road. Fish wouldn’t reopen three hundred meridians. He paid for the directions.

“Young Master Shi,” Tang Jiu called, “if you don't return, where should I collect the rest of your money?”

“Ask the deer,” Shi Feng said.

Across the street, Lin Shuang held up four fingers. Tang Jiu's smile vanished. He still owed her four spirit stones.

chapters.title: One Hundred and Twenty Wasn't Enough
chapters.html:
“Don't touch the water,” Deng Hu said.

Shi Feng stopped with his waterskin open.

The old hunter sat on the ruined watercourse wall, holding a fishing line. Below him, green water ran slowly between stone channels.

“Poison?” Shi Feng asked.

“Bitter,” Deng Hu replied. “You'll curse for half a day.”

“You're fishing in it,” Shi Feng said.

“I don't drink fish,” Deng Hu replied.

Shi Feng put away the waterskin.

Two days of hunting restored one hundred and twenty-one meridians. That was already enough for an ordinary cultivator to attempt Qi Condensation.

He could stop here.

Leave the marsh, find a quiet room, and gather qi with a body stronger than most youths in Qingshi Town. Shi Feng looked at his hand and closed it slowly.

No.

He once opened three hundred and sixty-five. He wasn't going to spend the rest of his life pretending one hundred and twenty was good enough.

“You're waiting for the deer?” Deng Hu asked.

“Yes,” Shi Feng replied.

The old hunter began winding in his line.

“You're leaving?” Shi Feng asked.

“My eyes aren't that good,” Deng Hu said.

He went away without looking back.

Shi Feng climbed onto the narrow ridge beside the watercourse. Broken stone channels ran down the slope, crossing above a shallow pit. The whole place was once part of an irrigation works.

Now weeds grew between the stones, and a long red smear marked one wall.

The deer used this path.

He checked the spear assembled from Chai Jin's shaft and his own old head. The binding held. Beside the pit, he laid the crossbow behind a stone block.

Then he waited.

Two herb pickers passed below the ridge. One carried a broken bucket. The other was complaining about losing his shoes in the mud.

“Are you hunting?” Tu An asked, stopping with his bare feet in the mud.

“Yes,” Shi Feng replied.

“Alone?” Tu An asked.

“Do you want to join me?” Shi Feng asked.

“What beast?” Tu An asked.

“Blood-Crowned Spirit Deer,” Shi Feng replied.

Tu An seized his companion’s sleeve.

“We’re picking mushrooms!” Tu An said. “Very small mushrooms!”

The second man tried to recover his bucket. Tu An dragged him away without it. The two men looked at his bandaged ribs and hurried away.

Shi Feng didn't blame them. He wouldn't join a stranger's hunt without knowing what they were hunting either.

He settled behind the broken wall and checked the wind. It blew towards him from the drinking pool. Good. The deer wouldn't smell him before arriving.

The Blood-Crowned Spirit Deer came at sunset.

Its antlers were red from base to tip. Pale markings glowed along its chest, and one rear leg dragged slightly behind it.

Shi Feng stopped breathing for a moment.

Even wounded, it carried more qi than any beast he killed before. If it struck him once, the hunt would end there.

The deer lowered its head to drink.

Shi Feng lifted the crossbow.

The bolt struck beneath its broken leg.

The deer screamed and turned. Its red antlers shone, and a stone beside the water exploded beneath one hoof.

Shi Feng dropped the crossbow and ran.

Behind him came a heavy crash.

The deer leapt onto the ridge instead of taking the narrow path.

Too fast!

Shi Feng threw himself behind a thick stone pillar. Antlers struck the other side, breaking off a chunk larger than his head.

Dust covered his robe.

His plan was simple. The broken rear leg would limit the beast's turn. He wanted it charging along the narrow ridge, where his spear waited below.

Unfortunately, nobody explained the plan to the deer. It tore the pillar free from the soil. Shi Feng rolled beneath its rising neck and slashed at the wounded leg with Ma Liang's knife.

The blade cut deep.

A hoof struck his shoulder.

He flew into a shallow channel and slammed against the stone edge. Pain burst through his arm. He almost dropped the knife.

The deer limped after him, snorting blood and foam.

“Come on, then,” Shi Feng said through clenched teeth.

He scrambled backwards along the channel. Its walls forced the beast to lower its antlers before it could enter.

The sharp points scraped towards his chest.

Shi Feng caught a low stone bar and hauled himself over the side.

The deer thrust its head forward.

Its antlers wedged beneath the bar.

Shi Feng landed on the ridge, seized the waiting spear, and drove the point down towards its neck. The first thrust pierced the hide but slipped against a glowing marking.

Qi protected the beast's body!

He pulled the spear free before its struggles snapped the shaft.

The stone bar cracked.

Shi Feng changed his grip and thrust again, this time behind the ear where no pale marking covered the skin.

The point sank half its length.

The deer screamed and twisted.

The bar broke apart.

Shi Feng couldn't pull the spear free. He let go and jumped back as the antlers swept over the ridge. One point caught his belt and ripped it open.

His father's compass fell into the mud.

The deer stumbled into the pit, dragging the spear behind it. Blood spread beneath its head.

It was wounded badly.

It wasn't dead.

Shi Feng stood above it, breathing hard. His right shoulder throbbed. His fingers barely held the knife.

He could leave now and let the wound finish it. But another beast might find it first, and then his strange physique might give him nothing.

He waited until the deer's next charge failed. Its broken leg folded beneath it. Shi Feng jumped into the pit behind its shoulder.

The beast tried to turn.

He caught the spear shaft, pushed with his uninjured arm, and drove the point deeper behind its ear.

The red light faded from its antlers.

Its body struck the ground.

This time, it didn't rise.

Shi Feng backed away until he reached the wall. His knees bent, and he sat down hard. His hands shook now that the fight was over.

The first plan failed when the deer jumped. The second worked because the narrow channel trapped its antlers for two breaths. Without that stone bar, he'd be the body lying in the pit.

“Next time, I'll choose somewhere with a lower wall,” Shi Feng muttered.

He laughed at himself, then stopped when his ribs hurt.

“You really did it?” Deng Hu called from the hill.

Shi Feng looked up sharply.

The old hunter kept a respectable distance from the pit. His empty basket hung from one hand.

“You came back for the antlers,” Shi Feng said.

“I came back to see if you needed help,” Deng Hu replied.

Shi Feng looked at the basket.

“Burying a man takes a shovel,” Shi Feng said.

Deng Hu coughed.

Shi Feng named a price for the antlers. Deng Hu complained once, then hurried down the hill when Shi Feng started cutting them himself.

The deal was settled in six sentences.

Deng Hu took out a knife and started cutting. Before leaving, he tossed down a small waterskin.

“Don't drink from the channel,” Deng Hu said.

“How much?” Shi Feng asked.

“It's included,” Deng Hu replied. “Don't say I cheated you when I sell the antlers for more.”

“I won't ask,” Shi Feng said.

After the old hunter left, Shi Feng touched the deer's flank.

Fierce vitality surged through his palm.

One hundred and twenty-one meridians trembled. More silent routes stirred beyond them, answering a pressure far stronger than the crocodiles could give him.

Shi Feng's heart pounded with joy.

He stopped the flow before it overwhelmed him and sat down to steady his breathing. His wound needed binding. The corpse needed moving into cover.

Most of all, he needed somewhere nobody would disturb him. In the mud beside the broken bar, his father's compass lay open. Shi Feng picked it up and wiped it clean.

The needle still pointed south.

“Good,” Shi Feng said quietly. “We haven't finished yet.”

He closed the lid and tucked it safely beneath his robe. Then he reached for the rope.

chapters.title: Five Meridians Beyond the Limit
chapters.html:
“Young man, your deer is getting thin,” Deng Hu said.

Shi Feng stood in the hut doorway and blocked his view of the cellar.

“So is your fish,” Shi Feng replied.

Deng Hu glanced down at the two small fish hanging from his string.

“The big ones aren't biting,” Deng Hu said.

“Then eat these yourself,” Shi Feng replied.

The old hunter sighed and looked past him again. Shi Feng didn't move.

“Are you tanning the hide?” Deng Hu asked.

“Yes,” Shi Feng said.

“I can help,” Deng Hu offered.

“For free?” Shi Feng asked.

Deng Hu clicked his tongue and walked away. Shi Feng closed the door and dropped the wooden bar into place. He liked questions much less when they approached the truth.

Two hundred and thirty-seven meridians were awake.

His old public count.

In Qingshi Town, that number once made the clan elders fight over who would teach him. It made merchants smile, servants bow, and marriage proposals arrive before he turned eighteen.

Then his meridians fell silent.

The smiles vanished much faster than they arrived. Shi Feng walked down into the cellar. The deer's pale hide covered most of the floor, and the remaining vitality gathered beneath his sternum.

He sat beside it and shut his eyes.

The old breathing exercise began again.

This time he didn't try to stop at the familiar routes.

Two hundred and thirty-eight.

Two hundred and thirty-nine.

Warmth moved through his body, waking channels that no physician could find. Shi Feng guided it slowly. There was no reason to rush and injure himself after coming this far.

By dawn, three hundred answered.

By the next evening, three hundred and sixty.

He opened his eyes.

Every ordinary meridian was awake.

The hut's cold air no longer troubled him. His shoulder moved freely, and the cuts along his ribs were closing beneath fresh skin. He was stronger than before he appeared crippled.

Yet five routes remained silent.

Shi Feng pressed two fingers against his chest. Eighteen months ago, he found those five routes beyond the old clan diagram. Opening the last one made the whole network disappear from his senses.

He didn't collapse because someone shattered his meridians.

He opened something he didn't understand.

He wanted to draw in the qi around him. It touched his skin more clearly than ever, gathering whenever he breathed.

But he stopped himself.

First finish waking the whole network, Shi Feng thought. Qi Condensation could wait until he knew every route was open.

He tested the old breathing rhythm once more. Warmth reached the five hidden curves, then returned along the ordinary meridians.

They weren't blocked by poison or a wound. They were simply quiet. That was better than every diagnosis he paid for.

“Then let me understand it now,” Shi Feng said.

“Open the door!” Deng Hu shouted upstairs.

Shi Feng's eyes snapped open.

The cellar was dark. Someone struck the hut's door twice, then cursed.

“The rain's coming through my roof!” Deng Hu called. “Yours is better!”

Shi Feng climbed the steps and opened the door. Rain fell hard across the marsh. Deng Hu stood beneath a basket held over his head, looking thoroughly offended by the weather.

“The roof isn't mine,” Shi Feng said.

“Then you can't refuse me,” Deng Hu replied.

He hurried inside before Shi Feng answered.

Shi Feng shut the door and moved the small stool away from the cellar entrance. Deng Hu stretched his wet boots towards the hearth.

“You look different,” Deng Hu said.

Shi Feng picked up the kettle.

“Less hungry,” Shi Feng replied.

“You're still pale,” Deng Hu said. “That cheap medicine didn't fix everything.”

“No,” Shi Feng agreed.

The old hunter heard what he expected and stopped looking. Shi Feng poured two cups of hot water and sat beside the hearth.

He could wait one night.

Deng Hu warmed his hands and pointed at a broken slab supporting the stove.

“Don't lean on that,” Deng Hu said. “The letters underneath make it crumble.”

Shi Feng glanced down.

“Letters?” Shi Feng asked.

“Some old cultivator carved them,” Deng Hu replied. “People say there's treasure under the marsh. They say that whenever a stone has writing.”

“Did you look?” Shi Feng asked.

“Naturally,” Deng Hu said. “There were centipedes.”

Shi Feng waited until the old hunter fell asleep. Then he carefully shifted the broken slab and looked at its underside.

Only half a sentence remained.

Beyond three hundred and sixty, an epoch begins. The rest broke off with the missing corner.

Shi Feng's expression changed.

Epoch Meridians.

His father once mentioned the term while explaining why the clan's diagram ended at three hundred and sixty. Even one meridian beyond that limit could make a genius remembered for an entire age. Most people thought such stories were made up.

Shi Feng looked towards his chest.

He opened five.

What happened after the fifth? The broken stone gave no answer.

For once, he didn't mind.

He turned the slab over and returned it beneath the stove. Deng Hu opened one eye.

“Treasure?” Deng Hu asked.

“Half a sentence,” Shi Feng replied.

“Keep the half that doesn’t hold my fish pot up,” Deng Hu muttered.

He went back to sleep. Shi Feng looked at the ancient writing, then at the pot. An epoch’s genius had left a message here, and the only witness wanted his breakfast level.

Shi Feng considered taking the slab with him. It was broad, heavy, and missing most of its writing. He copied the surviving words onto the back of Meng Shou's map instead.

One day he'd find someone who knew more. He wouldn't ask Qian Rui. That old fox would probably claim to have sold the original stone.

An ancient cultivator's writing was holding up a fish pot.

At least it was useful.

The rain stopped before sunrise. Deng Hu left to check his traps, taking the remaining firewood without asking.

Shi Feng let him go.

He returned to the cellar and pressed his palm against the last part of the deer's body.

The stored vitality answered.

He followed the first silent curve slowly, refusing to stop when the familiar network ended.

A sharp pulse struck beneath his ribs.

The three hundred and sixty-first meridian woke.

Shi Feng's breath stopped.

Every opened meridian suddenly moved faster. Warmth crossed his body in a single breath, reaching places it took dozens of breaths to reach before.

The difference wasn't a small improvement.

It was another level entirely!

He steadied his mind and continued.

The second Epoch Meridian woke.

Then the third.

Each one widened the routes inside his body and strengthened the flow passing through them. By the fourth, the cellar's loose dust stirred around his knees.

The fifth remained quiet.

Shi Feng didn't force it. He guided the remaining vitality through all the waking channels, returning to the last curve again and again.

At noon, it answered.

Three hundred and sixty-five meridians joined into a complete network.

Now he understood what the root had done. It stirred his dormant network and woke the hunger born when his three hundred and sixty-fifth meridian opened before the collapse. The root hadn't given him a new physique. It had awakened what was already his.

For a breath, everything went silent.

Shi Feng's heart tightened.

Not again!

Then the entire network woke together.

Strength flooded his limbs. The faint hunger beneath his sternum settled into his body, and every route became clear.

This time, nothing disappeared.

Shi Feng opened his eyes and laughed.

“So you weren't broken,” Shi Feng said. “You were sleeping.”

He gripped the heavy stone beside the cellar steps and lifted it clear of the floor. Before leaving Qingshi Town, he struggled to carry his own pack. Now he held a stone twice his weight without shaking.

Shi Feng set it down carefully.

Perfect Meridian Opening.

Not one hundred and twenty. Not his old public count.

All three hundred and sixty-five.

He packed the little that remained of his equipment. The crossbow still worked. His makeshift spear needed replacing, and his knife was already nicked.

There were better weapons in Yunze Town. Better manuals too. This time, he could buy them without wondering whether he'd live long enough to use them.

He looked up at the thin strip of daylight beneath the cellar door.

The world outside still thought he was a cripple.

Let it.

chapters.title: The Qi That Stayed
chapters.html:
Shi Feng drew the next breath slowly and pulled the surrounding qi into his body.

This time, he wasn't trying to wake another meridian. All three hundred and sixty-five already answered him. He needed to gather qi, refine it, and keep it instead of letting it scatter after each breath.

The old stone cellar was quiet. Above the ceiling, wind shook the abandoned hunting hut. He sat with his back straight and followed the breathing exercise taught to every Shi clan junior.

At first, the qi passed through him too quickly.

His meridians could take far more than his body could yet refine. Drawing harder only filled him with loose, restless strength. Shi Feng slowed down and compressed a small current instead.

The current narrowed.

A little of it stayed.

He checked again, afraid he'd mistaken the feeling.

It was still there.

“Qi Condensation,” Shi Feng said softly. “I've finally reached it.”

He was delighted. After eighteen months of being called a cripple, the first lasting strand of refined qi mattered more than the clan's old praise ever did.

The sleeping meridians were awake, but that alone hadn't completed his breakthrough. Meridian Opening built the paths. Qi Condensation began filling his body with strength he could actually use.

Shi Feng continued until the pale light beneath the cellar door brightened. When he stood, the qi remained inside him. He raised one hand, guided a little toward his fingertips, and pressed against a loose brick.

Crack!

The brick split beneath his fingers.

Shi Feng looked at the pieces and smiled. That wasn't the strength of a starving young man dragging a spear through mud. His old martial training finally had something to work with again.

He tried a second movement. Too much qi rushed into his arm and broke another corner from the brick.

“Enough,” Shi Feng muttered. “The hut hasn't offended me.”

Power wasn't control. He repeated the exercise with less force until he could make a shallow mark without breaking the whole brick.

The difference became clear when he tried to keep the current in one finger. It spread into his palm instead. Shi Feng stopped, gathered it again, and used a thinner stream.

After a dozen attempts, the warmth remained where he directed it.

That would matter in a fight. Pouring everything into one wild blow would waste his strength and make the next movement slow. A short, controlled burst would support the strike without dragging his balance out of place.

He practiced a plain forward punch, then withdrew it along the same line. The first attempt shook his sleeve. The next stopped cleanly.

Shi Feng thought: I don't need a grand technique yet. I need to use what I already know. He packed only after the new current obeyed him.

Then he drew his qi inward. The faint pressure around his body disappeared as he settled his breathing. He didn't need a special secret art to stop showing off every current he possessed.

The town could keep its cripple.

He knew what was inside him.

By noon, Shi Feng reached Yunze Town along the dry northern track. His pack held the same few tools, a damaged short spear, and money that wouldn't last if he spent every day resting.

Deng Hu's nephew met him at the fish carts with a folded receipt. Meng Shou's name and the clinic seal stood beside a note: living sample received, still rooted. Shi Feng put it away. The physician had what he needed; the paid delivery had reached its end.

The first thing Shi Feng wanted now was a sword.

A boar-hunting spear was useful, but the Shi clan's common sword forms were the movements he knew best. He couldn't afford a fine weapon. He could afford plain steel that wouldn't fold after striking bone.

Tan Tie's smithy stood beside a row of charcoal baskets. The smith was broad through the shoulders, with one burned eyebrow. He didn't stop hammering until Shi Feng picked up a straight sword from the cheaper rack.

“Twelve spirit stones,” Tan Tie said. “Scabbard included.”

“Ordinary steel?” Shi Feng asked.

“Ordinary steel,” Tan Tie replied. “Try the grip. No, not that way. Thumb lower.”

Shi Feng adjusted his hand and tested a short thrust.

Tan Tie grunted approval. The smith watched the blade rather than the faded clan mark on his customer’s collar. A straight thrust interested him more than a ruined genius.

“The edge will chip if you strike rock,” Tan Tie said. “Come complain before you do it, not after.”

Shi Feng drew it halfway. The edge was even. The grip fit his palm. He checked the blade's line against the doorway and laid down the price.

Tan Tie took the stones and returned to his work.

A few hammer marks remained near the hilt. The scabbard was plain wood wrapped in dark cloth. Shi Feng was satisfied with a weapon that cut.

Outside, two boys argued over a roasted sweet potato. One claimed the larger half because he was older. The other took the smaller half, then demanded the whole skin. Their mother slapped both hands away and divided it herself.

Shi Feng bought a rice cake from the next stall and ate while walking toward the medicine street. Qian Rui spotted him before he reached the purple awning.

“Young Master Shi! Your complexion has improved!” Qian Rui cried. “This Qian Rui's advice is clearly helping!”

“I didn't take your medicine,” Shi Feng said.

“Advice doesn't have to be swallowed,” Qian Rui replied immediately.

Shi Feng looked at the piles of books beneath the counter. Several hunters were buying cheap manuals beside bottles of wound wash.

“Do you have a book on Bone Refinement?” Shi Feng asked.

Qian Rui's little eyes brightened.

“Three spirit stones. Common printing, complete pages,” Qian Rui said, pulling out a thin blue booklet.

Shi Feng checked the title and the chapter on the order of the bones, then paid. A common method was enough to begin. He didn't need a shopkeeper's promise of an ancient immortal.

Qian Rui leaned across the counter before he could leave.

“Why study that? Your meridians are still ruined, aren't they?” Qian Rui asked.

“I can read,” Shi Feng said.

Qian Rui paused, then nodded with great seriousness.

“A good attitude!” Qian Rui said. “Even a man who can't cultivate should cultivate his mind!”

Shi Feng left before the quack could sell him something for his mind too. The booklet fitted inside his robe. He returned to the lodging house before the afternoon crowd filled the street.

Back at the lodging house, Shi Feng closed his door and laid the booklet beside his new sword.

He practiced the clan's basic cuts first. Straight thrust. Downward cut. Step back and guard. His cuts were plain and quick. Every stroke went straight where he'd aimed.

His body remembered the movements better than his hands expected. The sword stopped where he wanted instead of dragging his shoulder forward. When he turned, the qi inside him followed.

Shi Feng felt confident, but he didn't rush the next realm.

The booklet was blunt about that. Qi Condensation wasn't finished just because a cultivator could break a brick or frighten a neighbor. The qi had to be refined until it could steadily strengthen the body and enter the bones.

He still had work to do.

For now, his strength would let him hunt better prey and earn better money. The All-Devouring Physique supplied resources. It didn't swing a sword for him or complete his training while he slept.

A shout rose from the market square outside.

“Ten spirit stones for anyone who lifts it! Come test the strength Heaven gave you!” Ding Hai shouted.

Shi Feng glanced toward the shutter.

The voice shouted again. Somebody cheered. Somebody else groaned that the stone was too heavy.

He put the manual away and fastened his sword at his waist.

Heaven wasn't paying his room bill. Perhaps the shouting man would.

chapters.title: The Wei Family’s Stone
chapters.html:
“Ten spirit stones! Lift the Wei family's stone and take them home!” Ding Hai shouted.

The crowd closed around a low platform in the market square. A round black stone stood upon it, with an iron ring set deeply into the top. Beside the stone, a board listed its weight and the rules. Two thousand jin. Lift it clear for three breaths. Two spirit stones to try.

Shi Feng stopped near the basket stall. The stone rested on three short feet, leaving daylight beneath it. It wasn't fastened down. A porter even crawled halfway under the platform to check, earning a kick from the man waiting behind him.

“You can inspect it after I win!” Ke Kang said.

The porter climbed out, wiping dust from his beard. Ke Kang had opened one hundred and eighty meridians. He rolled up his sleeves and seized the ring. He hauled until his face turned purple. The stone tilted, then dropped with a thump.

“Two breaths!” Ke Kang protested.

“Half a breath, and half the stone,” Ding Hai said. “Who taught you to count?”

The crowd laughed. Ke Kang stepped down, rubbing his palms. Shi Feng looked at the banner behind the prize box. The Wei household sponsored the stall. Its young master sat in a chair beneath it, enjoying a plate of grapes while other people sweated.

Wei Kuo hadn't noticed him yet.

He had reached Qi Condensation. That was good enough to impress the Meridian Opening hunters crowding around the platform. It wasn't good enough to impress Shi Feng, whose restored network had already carried him into Qi Condensation.

A woman asked whether lifting the stone would win her son a household job. Ding Hai explained that the prize was only ten stones. She dragged her son away. Ten stones were good, but a lifetime meal ticket was better.

Wei Kuo finished his grapes and stood.

“Let me show you,” Wei Kuo said.

Ding Hai immediately cleared the platform. Luo San, the Qi Condensation servant beside the chair, took the empty plate with both hands. His young master caught the ring, took a deep breath, and lifted.

The stone rose to his knees.

Wei Kuo held it there, trembling slightly while Ding Hai counted very slowly. He lowered it on the third count and spread his hands toward the crowd.

“Talent can't be replaced by a strong back,” Wei Kuo said.

The porters looked at each other. That speech seemed aimed at them. Ding Hai clapped first, and the household servants followed until several townspeople joined in.

Wei Kuo smiled. Then he saw Shi Feng near the baskets.

His smile grew wider.

“Brother Shi Feng! Come try!” Wei Kuo called. “You were a genius once. Surely Heaven left you two useful arms?”

Several heads turned. The old story passed through the crowd faster than the prize rules had. Two hundred and thirty-seven meridians, ruined overnight. The former fiancé of Lu Qingxue. Qingshi Town's cripple.

Shi Feng looked at the prize box.

“Does the sponsor compete for his own money?” Shi Feng asked.

“I'm demonstrating for the people!” Wei Kuo said. “Naturally I won't take the prize.”

“That leaves ten for me,” Shi Feng said.

He stepped onto the platform and paid the entry fee. Ding Hai hesitated over taking it. Then Wei Kuo laughed and nodded, making the choice easy.

“Don't force yourself,” Wei Kuo said. “If you faint, people will say my household bullied an invalid.”

Luo San chuckled beside the chair. He didn't bother stepping closer. A cripple trying to lift a stone wasn't a threat to anybody except his own waist.

Shi Feng set his feet and caught the ring with one hand.

“Use both!” Ding Hai warned. “The weight is written plainly. Nobody forced you!”

Shi Feng lifted.

The stone left the platform, passed his knees, and rose to his waist. He held it there without bending his back. Refined qi stayed within his body, supporting the muscles instead of spreading into an aura.

The square became quiet.

Ding Hai forgot to count.

“Are the three breaths mine or yours?” Shi Feng asked.

“One! Two! Three!” Ding Hai said hurriedly.

Shi Feng lowered the stone gently. It didn't even strike the boards hard enough to shake the prize box.

The porter stepped forward, staring.

“With one hand?”

“Didn't Young Master Wei use two?”

“He didn't grunt either!”

“Was the weight changed?”

Ke Kang pushed through and seized the ring. He couldn't lift it any farther than before. His face reddened as the crowd watched. Finally he let go and pointed at Shi Feng with open admiration.

“His arms are better than mine,” Ke Kang said.

That simple admission made Wei Kuo's expression worse. He had been preparing to blame a loose footing or a weakened stone. Now his own challenger had confirmed the weight for him.

“It's medicine,” Wei Kuo said sharply. “Anybody can strengthen flesh with enough medicine.”

“Then the stone measures strength correctly,” Shi Feng said.

He held out his hand toward Ding Hai.

The stall keeper counted the prize at once. He ran a fair challenge, and he wasn't about to lose a day's customers because the sponsor disliked a winner. His bow toward Shi Feng was much deeper than it had been before.

Wei Kuo stepped down from his chair.

“Another lift,” Wei Kuo said. “Raise it over your head. I'll give you twenty.”

“No,” Shi Feng said.

“What? Afraid?” Wei Kuo asked.

“The board pays ten. I took ten,” Shi Feng said. “If you want dancing too, hire a performer.”

A laugh escaped from somewhere near the vegetable stalls. Wei Kuo turned, but the whole row suddenly studied its cabbages.

Shi Feng put the prize away and walked down the steps. He didn't need to prove his body to a young master with grapes stuck between his teeth.

Luo San moved as if to block him. Shi Feng looked at his hand, then into his eyes. For some reason the servant stopped. He told himself there were too many people watching.

Wei Kuo seized the ring again. He wanted to lift the stone above his own head and recover the square's attention. It reached his waist, trembled, then dropped so hard that his shoes jumped.

The laughter became harder to hide.

Shi Feng bought noodles at the far side of the square. The seller added a little broth and asked whether the stone really weighed two thousand jin. He said yes. She shook her head and went back to serving.

A fair challenge had paid for his meal. That pleased him more than Wei Kuo's miserable face.

Beneath the banner, Wei Kuo ordered Ding Hai to close the stall. He waited until Shi Feng had gone before speaking to Luo San.

“Find which road he hunts on,” Wei Kuo said.

Luo San looked toward the noodle stall and nodded. The young master no longer wanted an audience.

chapters.title: Forty Stones and a Boar
chapters.html:
“Forty spirit stones, both tusks, and I keep the meat,” Shi Feng said.

Liao Yong looked from the hunting notice to the young man standing in his grain yard. The merchant wore a fine brown robe with straw stuck to one sleeve. Something had clearly chased him through his own fields that morning.

“You're the Shi clan's cripple,” Liao Yong said.

“I'm the man who read your notice,” Shi Feng replied.

“Can you kill a spirit boar?” Liao Yong asked.

“If I can't, don't pay me,” Shi Feng said.

That answer pleased the merchant. He pointed toward the far grain field and called for a worker.

Qiu Sheng arrived carrying a rake. He was an ordinary laborer, and his face went pale when Liao Yong told him to lead the hunter out.

“It's still there!” Qiu Sheng protested.

“That's why I hired him!” Liao Yong snapped.

Shi Feng lifted his damaged spear from his shoulder. He wasn't planning to rely on it today, but a long shaft was useful for checking deep mud.

“Show me the last fence,” Shi Feng told Qiu Sheng. “You don't have to enter the field.”

The worker immediately became more willing.

They left the grain yard by a narrow path between irrigation ditches. Two carts waited beside a storehouse. One wheel was broken, and the scattered sacks showed where the boar had struck.

Qiu Sheng pointed to a dark patch beneath the trees beyond the field.

“Big as an ox,” Qiu Sheng said. “It ate the millet, then chased the men who came to drive it off.”

“How long has it stayed?” Shi Feng asked.

“Since yesterday,” Qiu Sheng replied. “You really don't need me?”

“Go back,” Shi Feng said.

Qiu Sheng ran back to the fence, then stopped beside a broken millet stalk.

“Don’t chase it into the beans!” Qiu Sheng shouted. “Those are mine!”

Shi Feng looked at the hollow where the boar slept.

“Tell it,” Shi Feng replied.

Qiu Sheng considered the boar, clutched his rake, and hurried away. He wanted the beans saved by somebody else. Shi Feng waited until the footsteps faded, then crossed the damaged fence.

The Ironhide Spirit Boar lay in a hollow beside the trees. Its black bristles stood thick along its neck. One tusk had torn through a grain sack still caught around its mouth.

A broken tree branch lay across the edge of the hollow. Shi Feng moved it aside with his spear. The ground behind it was soft with spilled irrigation water.

He didn't want his foot sinking there when the charge came. He chose the dry strip between the trees and placed his pack against a trunk.

The damaged spear went beside it. Carrying two weapons wouldn't help if one got tangled around his legs. Then he walked forward with only the sword.

The boar grunted before lifting its head. Its ears twitched toward the sound of his boots. The grain sack tore free when it opened its jaws, leaving wet cloth upon one tusk.

Shi Feng watched the forelegs bunch beneath its chest. He'd spent years practicing against clan juniors. A beast gave fewer warnings, but this warning was clear enough.

Shi Feng struck his scabbard against the tree. The boar lifted its head and spat the torn sack onto the grass.

He could feel the strength in its body. An ordinary Qi Condensation hunter would need to be careful with that thick skull and plated hide.

Shi Feng drew his sword.

He thought: let's see whether plain steel is enough when I supply the strength.

The boar scrambled upright and charged.

It crossed the clearing with surprising speed, tearing soil behind its hooves. Shi Feng stepped right at the last moment. The tusks passed his hip. He cut downward across the exposed side of its neck.

The edge broke through bristles and hide, but struck the hard plate beneath.

A shallow wound opened.

The boar squealed and swung around.

Shi Feng didn't retreat to find a trap. He'd seen where the plate ended.

The second charge came lower. He caught the broken fence rail with one foot and kicked it into the beast's snout. The boar tossed its head, opening the softer fold beneath the jaw.

Shi Feng guided refined qi into his sword and thrust. The blade entered the fold and sank to half its length.

He stepped with the boar instead of letting its weight wrench the weapon from his hand. Then he turned the edge and pulled it free.

Blood struck the grass.

The beast stumbled past him, hit a tree, and tried to rise. Shi Feng reached its side and cut once more into the same wound.

The legs folded.

A moment later, it stopped breathing.

Shi Feng examined his sword. A little blood stained the fuller, but the blade was straight. Tan Tie hadn't cheated him.

He felt pleased with himself. That was a clean fight, won by timing and strength instead of barely escaping with his life. The Qi Condensation realm had changed what he could do.

He could still waste it by getting careless, but he no longer had to treat every angry animal as an unbeatable elder. After cutting out the tusks, Shi Feng removed a good piece of meat for supper. He dragged the rest of the body farther beneath the trees, where nobody in the yard could see him.

His palm touched the open wound.

The All-Devouring Physique began taking the beast's vitality. Heat entered his arm and spread through his body. He slowed the flow when the first rush grew strong, then let the strength settle before drawing again.

By midafternoon, a brittle shell of hide and bone lay beneath the trees. Shi Feng broke it apart, covered it with loose earth, and rested beside the ditch until his breathing was even. More refined qi remained inside him than before the hunt.

Not another realm. Not a new grade. Qi Condensation was a long process of refining and gathering strength, and he'd moved farther along it.

He wrapped the tusks and carried them back to the grain yard.

Liao Yong met him beside the storehouse.

“Already?” Liao Yong asked.

Shi Feng unwrapped the tusks.

The merchant's expression changed. He inspected the fresh roots and ran a finger along the curve of one tusk.

“Where's the body?” Liao Yong asked.

“Mine,” Shi Feng said.

“It ruined six sacks of grain,” Liao Yong said.

“Then collect the debt from it,” Shi Feng replied. “Our price was forty spirit stones.”

Liao Yong grumbled, but the boar was dead and the tusks were in front of him. He counted out the agreed payment.

Qiu Sheng leaned around the storehouse door. When he saw the tusks, he gasped.

“You killed it!” Qiu Sheng cried.

Shi Feng looked at the money in his hand.

“That was the job,” Shi Feng said.

The worker stared until Liao Yong ordered him to repair the fence.

Shi Feng returned to town before sunset and bought ginger, salt, and fresh greens. He could afford finished meat at an inn, but he wanted to try cooking the portion he'd kept. Bian Cui allowed him to use the little yard stove after he paid for fuel.

“Don't burn my pot,” Bian Cui warned.

“I won't,” Shi Feng said.

He cut the boar meat into small pieces and browned them before adding water and ginger. His first taste was too salty. He added more water and let it simmer while washing the greens.

The smell reached the doorway.

Bian Cui stopped there with a bowl already in her hand.

“The stove rent doesn't include feeding the owner,” Shi Feng said.

“I was checking the pot!” Bian Cui said.

He served himself, left the lid off, and watched her find another reason to stand nearby.

Eventually she bought a bowl.

Shi Feng sat upon the step with his supper and the forty stones safely inside his robe. He wasn't rich, but he'd earned money without selling his future or asking his aunt for another loan. From the main street came the beat of a gong.

A sect caravan was entering Yunze Town, its white crane banners rising above the west gate while Wei Kuo’s riders cleared the street ahead of it.

Bian Cui paused by the doorway and glanced back at Shi Feng. “Young Master Wei’s men were asking the gate clerks this afternoon which inn you stayed at. And that white carriage behind him has Qingshi Town’s tenth fairy inside.”

Shi Feng set down his empty bowl and picked up his sword.

chapters.title: A Sect’s Good Manners
chapters.html:
“Make way for White Crane Pavilion!” Fang Ze shouted from the front of the caravan.

People hurried toward the sides of the street. Three wagons rolled beneath the gate, followed by six young disciples in white robes. A gray-haired elder rode upon a narrow flying sword above the mud.

Shi Feng stopped beside the food stalls and watched the sword pass.

A refined artifact.

The elder was in Foundation Establishment. A cultivator below that realm couldn't properly activate such a weapon, no matter how expensive the metal was. Shi Feng wanted one.

Tang Jiu appeared beside him carrying a bundle of maps.

“Recruitment stop,” Tang Jiu said. “Good business for tailors. Every fool will want a robe that looks like theirs by tomorrow.”

“Are they recruiting townspeople?” Shi Feng asked.

“Anyone with working meridians and the talent they want,” Tang Jiu replied. “The rest can buy my maps and try the next town.”

Shi Feng looked at the elder's sword again.

“Are the Great Sects recruiting here as well?” Shi Feng asked.

Tang Jiu nearly dropped the maps.

“Here? Martial Palace and Hundred Flower Valley don't stop in little gathering towns!” Tang Jiu said. “Only lesser sects want our hunters. Don't call White Crane Pavilion a Great Sect. Its disciples will be so pleased they won't leave!”

“And Artificer Hall?” Shi Feng asked.

“Not them either,” Tang Jiu said. “Their elders don't bother with a little gathering town. White Crane Pavilion recruits across our border. It's enough to make our hunters bow.”

Shi Feng nodded. The sects beyond the kingdom were another world.

Lu Qingxue stepped down from the second wagon beside Mu Yong. Shi Feng recognized her, then returned to reading the banner. Her presence didn't change his plans.

The caravan halted beside the square. Servants unfolded a table beneath a white banner. People began lining up before the chairs were down.

Gu Fan, eighteen, pushed ahead, then hurried back when the elder looked at him. His mother, Wu Chun, argued for a place near the front.

Shi Feng joined the people reading the notice beside the table. Gu Fan reached the testing stone first. Mu Yong placed a hand on his back, and pale lines appeared across the stone.

“One hundred and thirty-nine,” Mu Yong announced. “Your age?”

“Eighteen, Elder!” Gu Fan replied eagerly.

“Eighteen by counting from his birth year!” Wu Chun shouted.

Gu Fan reddened.

“My birthday’s passed,” Gu Fan said. “Mother, I told you!”

Mu Yong held out his hand for the household record.

“Your bones won’t grow faster because your mother shouts,” Mu Yong said. “Let me read it.”

The elder’s pressure quieted even Tang Jiu.

“You can take the outer disciple examination,” Mu Yong said. “That doesn't mean you've passed. Stand beside the second wagon.”

The youth bowed three times before hurrying away. His father immediately began asking a disciple about travel expenses. His mother started crying, then shouted at him to straighten his robe.

Shi Feng watched without envy. For ordinary families, an examination was worth celebrating.

His own road would be different. He wasn't going to reveal his restored meridians just to wear a white robe and carry somebody else's basin.

Joining meant leaving home and obeying the pavilion’s rules. There were no promised treasures, but people crowded around as though the notice offered them.

Fang Ze came down the steps with a copper basin. His spotless sleeves dragged across its rim. He was in Qi Condensation, and his expression said carrying water was beneath him.

Then he saw Shi Feng's collar.

“Shi clan?” Fang Ze asked.

“Yes,” Shi Feng replied.

“Shi Feng?” Fang Ze asked, smiling now.

Shi Feng didn't answer twice.

Fang Ze turned toward the table.

“Elder Mu Yong, the fallen genius has come to apply!” Fang Ze called.

Beside the registration table, Lu Qingxue looked up sharply from a stack of wooden candidate slips. The crowd stirred. Mu Yong glanced up from the register, then ran one finger down a page.

“Shi Feng. Qingshi Town. Meridians ruined,” Mu Yong said. “You can't enter with that condition. Go home.”

“I came to read the notice,” Shi Feng said.

Mu Yong was already looking at the next name. Beside him, Lu Qingxue parted her lips as if to speak, her fingers tightening around the slips, before remembering the banner over her head. Shi Feng didn't look toward her. The registry was old, and he intended to keep his actual cultivation private.

He stepped away from the notice.

Fang Ze glanced toward Lu Qingxue as if expecting her to appreciate the display, then held out the copper basin to block Shi Feng’s path.

“Carry this to the horses,” Fang Ze said. “You can't become a disciple, but you can still learn useful work.”

A few people laughed nervously. At the table, Lu Qingxue took half a step forward, her brows drawing together. “Senior Brother Fang—” Lu Qingxue said.

Fang Ze ignored her.

“Your horses don’t belong to me,” Shi Feng said.

“Neither does this street!” Fang Ze snapped. “Move when a sect disciple speaks!”

He shoved the basin hard against Shi Feng's chest.

Shi Feng caught its rim. Water sloshed to the lip without spilling a single drop onto his boots. He looked calmly at the disciple's hands.

“You're still holding it,” Shi Feng said.

“Then take it!” Fang Ze barked, driving his Qi Condensation weight into the push.

Shi Feng yielded half an inch, angled the copper rim with two fingers, and stepped cleanly off the line. Fang Ze's own force carried him into empty air. His robe caught beneath the tilting basin, and the heavy rim struck both his knees.

Splash!

Fang Ze pitched headfirst into the muddy horse water with the copper basin overturned upon his head.

For a breath, the entire square froze. Beside the banner, Lu Qingxue stared at Shi Feng’s boots—not a fleck of mud had touched his hem, and his shoulders hadn’t even shifted when a Qi Condensation disciple drove into him.

Then a roar of laughter burst from the back of the crowd.

“He washed himself!”

“That basin was for the horses!”

“Look at the Shi boy’s feet—he didn’t even move and the sect disciple went swimming!”

“Who called him a cripple? A cripple doesn’t turn a cultivator’s shove with two fingers!”

Fang Ze hurled the dented basin aside. Mud plastered one cheek, and his white Pavilion sleeves were brown to the elbow.

“You!” Fang Ze shouted, snatching at his sword hilt.

“Fang Ze!” Mu Yong’s voice cracked across the square.

The disciple froze with his thumb on the guard. Mu Yong wasn’t looking at Fang Ze alone; his narrowed eyes lingered on Shi Feng’s calm stance and dry boots before turning coldly back to his disgraced junior.

“Stand up,” Mu Yong ordered. “You shove an uninvolved passerby, miss your own footing, and reach for a blade in front of the whole town?”

“Elder, he tripped me!” Fang Ze protested, his face burning as the candidates in line backed away from his dripping hem.

“Then stop presenting your knees to a man who didn’t even lift his hand,” Mu Yong said icily. “Go wash yourself by the wagons and stay out of the square until the bell rings.”

Fang Ze had to pick up the muddy copper basin himself and walk the length of the candidate line while townspeople openly pointed at his dripping hair. When Shi Feng turned to leave, the hunters and shopkeepers who had snickered a moment ago parted at once to give him the dry middle of the street. Behind the table, Lu Qingxue was still watching his back with the registration slips forgotten in her hand.

Fang Ze had tried to make him a servant and fallen in horse water. That was enough.

At the next stall, Shi Feng bought a sheet showing the hills west of Yunze Town. The seller rolled it up and tied it with string.

Tang Jiu found him before he left the square.

“Did you push Fang Ze?” Tang Jiu asked eagerly.

“Did you see me?” Shi Feng replied.

“I heard three versions already,” Tang Jiu said. “One says you threw him over a wagon.”

“Sell that one,” Shi Feng said. “It sounds more expensive.”

Tang Jiu grinned, then held out a map with red circles around several hills.

“Special hunting locations,” Tang Jiu said. “Cheap, since we're old acquaintances.”

Shi Feng unrolled the sheet he'd just bought. The same circles appeared in the same places.

Tang Jiu slowly lowered his copy.

“Good judgment,” Tang Jiu said. “You chose the right seller.”

Shi Feng left him to find somebody with worse judgment.

Beyond the square, the road rose toward the western hills. A hunter passing through town had mentioned a Green-Eyed Rock Fox den there. Its hide would sell well, and he needed more resources for Qi Condensation.

He'd had enough of sect good manners for the day.

A beast would at least show its teeth before attacking.

chapters.title: The Report
chapters.html:
Lu Qingxue waited beside the well when Shi Feng returned from the western track.

She wore White Crane Pavilion's white robe, with a plain traveling cloak over it. Her cultivation was at Qi Condensation. In Qingshi Town, people would have gathered just to watch her draw water. Here the washerwomen wanted her to move away from the good side of the well.

Shi Feng stepped around a bucket.

“You're blocking the rope,” Shi Feng said.

Lu Qingxue looked down and moved at once. A woman hauled up the next pail, splashed both their boots, and continued with her work.

“Can we speak somewhere else?” Lu Qingxue asked.

“Here is fine,” Shi Feng said.

He wasn't angry. He simply had bread in his pack and wanted to eat it while it was warm. Their engagement was over. He didn't see why that required another private meeting.

Lu Qingxue held a narrow sealed envelope inside her sleeve. She had practiced several ways of beginning this conversation. None included a washerwoman arguing that the water tasted of clay.

“I saw what happened with Fang Ze,” Lu Qingxue said.

“Then you saw him wash his face,” Shi Feng said.

“He shouldn't have treated you that way,” Lu Qingxue said.

“Tell him,” Shi Feng said. “I wasn't the one holding his basin.”

Lu Qingxue lowered her eyes. He spoke as though the incident were finished, because to him it was. Fang Ze's opinion hadn't become important merely because she witnessed it.

She glanced once toward the square to make sure none of Mu Yong’s disciples had followed her, then took out the narrow envelope from her sleeve.

“This is the Pavilion physicians’ examination from eighteen months ago,” Lu Qingxue said quietly. “I copied it from the sealed outer-hall archive before we left the mountain.”

Shi Feng put his bread down on a clean corner of the well wall.

That did interest him.

The outer paper bore the silver-crane watermark of White Crane Pavilion’s medicine hall, and across the corner sat a red archival restriction mark. Taking a sealed record out of the sect registry was no small offense for a newly elevated disciple.

Lu Qingxue handed the envelope over.

“I tried to give it to you in Qingshi Town,” Lu Qingxue said, her voice dropping. “Steward Han was watching every word in that hall.”

“Why was it sealed?” Shi Feng asked.

“Because when our Pavilion’s two physicians examined you after your collapse, they didn’t write what Steward Han announced to the two families,” Lu Qingxue said. “Steward Han ordered the original buried in the restricted ledger so my master would accept the annulment without waiting another year.”

Shi Feng broke the wax and read beside the well. The Pavilion physicians had measured against the standard diagram of three hundred and sixty channels—the private count he had reached in the stone chamber remained hidden, along with the five Epoch Meridians beyond it.

A sentence halfway down made his fingers tighten.

The principal network shows extreme dormancy. Total destruction cannot be confirmed. Repeat examination is advised after eighteen months once the acute shock settles.

Below the physicians’ signatures sat a terse docket line in Han Zheng’s sharp clerical hand: Record publicly as meridian destruction. Seal original; clear Disciple Lu’s betrothal before the Cloud Ascension intake.

Dormant and destroyed weren’t the same thing.

Shi Feng read the docket line twice. White Crane Pavilion’s own physicians had written dormant, and White Crane Pavilion had buried the truth to tidy up a promising disciple’s marriage contract.

Eighteen months of Qingshi Town calling him ruined beyond repair because a Pavilion steward wanted a cleaner ledger.

He felt a brief, cold anger. Then he folded the page. The living root had already stirred the sleeping network. Knowing this earlier might have changed where he searched, but it wouldn't make the lost months come back.

“Did you know what it said before the meeting?” Shi Feng asked.

“I knew it questioned the diagnosis,” Lu Qingxue said. “I hadn't read the whole thing.”

“Yet you came with the annulment paper,” Shi Feng said.

Lu Qingxue's face paled.

“Yes,” Lu Qingxue said.

She didn't offer another excuse. For that much, Shi Feng gave her a second look. He still felt no wish to reopen the engagement.

“I didn't bring it to ask you to change anything,” Lu Qingxue said. “You should have the report. It concerns your body.”

“Then I'll keep it,” Shi Feng said.

He slipped it inside the manual in his pack. His expression returned to its ordinary calm, and he picked up the bread. Lu Qingxue seemed to be waiting for something else.

“Have you found a physician here?” Lu Qingxue asked.

“I've found what I need for now,” Shi Feng said.

“Mu Yong knows people across the border,” Lu Qingxue said. “I can ask—”

“No need,” Shi Feng said.

He didn't tell her he had restored all three hundred and sixty-five meridians. He didn't need her help carrying a secret back to the sect. Her guilt belonged to her, and his recovery belonged to him.

A recruitment gong sounded from the square. Lu Qingxue turned toward it.

“The caravan leaves tomorrow,” Lu Qingxue said.

“Then don't miss it,” Shi Feng said.

For a moment she looked as though she wanted to ask whether he hated her. She swallowed the question. His bread mattered more to him than this conversation now, and that answered something she hadn't wanted to know.

“Take care,” Lu Qingxue said.

Shi Feng nodded. He left by the side lane, walking toward his lodging instead of looking back at the square.

The washerwoman reached for the bucket again.

Lu Qingxue moved without being asked this time.

Near the wine shop, Wei Kuo watched the white-robed figure return toward the sect wagons.

He knew who she was. Everyone from Qingshi Town knew. Lu Qingxue had broken her engagement to a cripple, yet she still sought him out alone beside a well.

Wei Kuo's fingers tightened around his fan.

After the stone challenge, he'd spent the afternoon listening to servants insist that nobody was laughing at him. Now he could see Lu Qingxue watching the lane Shi Feng had taken. The sight made those assurances useless.

“What did she give him?” Wei Kuo asked.

“A letter, young master,” Luo San said.

Wei Kuo snapped the fan shut. A letter could mean anything. That was precisely why it annoyed him.

“Follow him tomorrow,” Wei Kuo said. “When the sect caravan goes, nobody will have reason to keep staring at that cripple.”

Luo San bowed. His Qi Condensation cultivation put him above most Yunze hunters. Dealing with one medicine-fed youth would be easy, especially on an empty track.

At his lodging, Shi Feng read the report once more and put it away. He didn't spend the night imagining what Lu Qingxue might regret.

He practiced his sword cuts until the courtyard shadows lengthened, ate the rest of his bread, and prepared for another hunt. His strength had returned. He intended to use it.

chapters.title: The Young Master Didn't Return
chapters.html:
The Green-Eyed Rock Fox shot from its den with a chicken feather stuck between its teeth. Shi Feng stepped across the narrow path and cut before it could turn back.

The fox twisted in midair. His first stroke missed its neck and opened the shoulder instead. It landed upon a rock, hissed, and sprang toward his face.

He raised the scabbard with his left hand. The fox's claws struck wood. His sword entered beneath its ribs.

He turned the blade and lowered the body before it could tear its own valuable hide.

A quick hunt. The beast wasn't large, but its green eyes and pale fur made it worth finding. Buyers paid far more for something pretty than for something that bit them.

Shi Feng checked the slope behind him. The den stood beneath a low cliff, well away from the cart road. Nobody was watching.

He removed the hide, wrapped it, and touched the remaining body. Warmth passed through his palm. He drew it slowly, then sat upon a stone while the new strength settled into his own refined qi.

The fox's resources didn't amount to another spirit boar. They still helped. He packed the hide only after his breathing was calm.

A voice called from the path below.

“That's the one!” Wei Kuo said. “Bring it here.”

Shi Feng looked down.

The young master stood between two boulders, wearing yellow silk far too clean for the hills. Luo San waited beside him with a hand upon his sword. Both men were in Qi Condensation.

Nobody else followed them.

Shi Feng walked to the edge of the clearing and stopped several steps above their heads.

“What do you want?” Shi Feng asked.

Wei Kuo pointed at the wrapped hide.

“That,” Wei Kuo said, pointing at the fox. “A girl at the wine house wants a scarf.”

Luo San leaned closer to his master.

“She asked for white fur, Young Master,” Luo San whispered.

Wei Kuo glared at the green-grey hide.

“Then she can change her mind!” Wei Kuo snapped. “Two spirit stones, Shi Feng. Bring it here.”

“It's not for sale to you,” Shi Feng replied.

Wei Kuo stared, surprised that a cripple had refused him so quickly.

“Did you hear me?” Wei Kuo asked.

“I heard the price,” Shi Feng said.

The young master's face darkened.

At the gate, somebody had interrupted him. Out here there was no clerk, no crowd, and no reason to pretend that two stones were a fair offer.

“Luo San, take his pack,” Wei Kuo said. “If he complains, break his legs.”

Luo San drew his sword and climbed toward Shi Feng.

The servant looked older than his master, with gray beginning near his temples. He had no interest in the fox. He wanted to finish the errand and return to town before the cooking fires went cold.

“Put it down, brat,” Luo San said.

Shi Feng didn't move.

“Don't make me repeat myself,” Luo San warned.

“Then stop talking,” Shi Feng replied.

Wei Kuo's expression twisted with anger.

“Kill him!” Wei Kuo shouted. “Who'll ask about a cripple lost in the hills?”

Luo San thrust at Shi Feng's throat.

At the same moment, Wei Kuo pulled a dagger from his sleeve and threw it toward the clearing. He aimed at Shi Feng's chest. There was nothing uncertain about either man's intent.

Shi Feng drew his sword.

The dagger struck his edge and flew into the dirt. He stepped inside Luo San's thrust, caught the servant's sword arm, and cut across his throat.

Luo San's eyes bulged. The movement was so fast that his feet kept climbing after his blade had already missed.

Shi Feng pushed him aside.

Wei Kuo stood frozen below.

His servant fell beside the boulder and didn't get up.

“You're not—” Wei Kuo began.

Shi Feng reached him before he finished.

The young master raised his empty hand as if rank could block steel. Shi Feng knocked it aside and drove the sword into his chest.

Wei Kuo's mouth opened.

No order came out.

Shi Feng withdrew the blade. The yellow robe slid down the rock, and the body settled beside Luo San's fallen sword. The whole fight lasted only a few breaths.

Two ordinary Qi Condensation cultivators had attacked a man with perfect meridians and vastly greater strength. They hadn't understood the difference until it was too late. Shi Feng looked down at them without pleasure.

They wanted his hide, then his life. He'd given neither. There was no reason to leave an attempted murderer alive just because the man discovered fear at the last moment.

He wiped his blade upon a clean patch of grass and listened.

Wind moved through the bushes. Far below, somebody called to a mule upon the road. The boulders and cliff hid the clearing from passing travelers.

Nobody had seen his qi or the fight.

Shi Feng searched both bodies. The two purses held seventy-six spirit stones between them. A little wound medicine was still sealed. The weapons were ordinary forged steel, not refined artifacts.

He kept the money and medicine, then picked Wei Kuo's thrown dagger from the dirt. It was a sound knife, better than the chipped blade he'd taken from Ma Liang. He replaced the old blade at his belt and left the swords behind.

His own sword was enough. He didn't want to carry every weapon a dead fool dropped.

He rolled the bodies away from the narrow footpath and left them beneath the cliff. Whether beasts or searching retainers found them first wasn't his concern. He wasn't going to spend the afternoon building graves for men who'd come to murder him.

The wrapped fox hide went back into his pack. He took a different path down the hill.

The furrier Zou An inspected the hide beneath an awning near the east market.

Zou An turned the pelt over, checked the clean seam at the shoulder, and paid twenty spirit stones without argument before the waiting customers could put their greasy hands on it.

He accepted, bought a meal, and returned to the lodging house before sunset. Bian Cui looked at the blood dried upon his cuff.

“Don't wash that in my drinking basin!” Bian Cui said.

“I wasn't planning to,” Shi Feng replied.

She pointed toward the yard tub and went back to arguing with a tenant over a missing quilt. Shi Feng washed there without explaining what had happened in the hills. As far as Yunze Town knew, he'd hunted a fox.

That was true.

In his room, he counted the useful gains once and put them away. Money would buy food and medicine, but ordinary purchases wouldn't fill the enormous capacity inside his body for long. He needed stronger beast resources and something to prepare for Bone Refinement.

The blue manual described that next step clearly. Refined qi had to enter a bone and remain steady while strengthening it. His control was improving, but he wanted it steadier before attempting the change.

Shi Feng opened his hill map.

One place bore a small mark beside an old spring. The hunter who'd mentioned the fox also spoke of mineral deposits there. Jade Marrow Dew sometimes gathered around the rocks, but a Blackback Stone Ape had claimed the hollow.

Other hunters avoided it for good reason. Its strength matched Bone Refinement. Shi Feng studied the approach and folded the map.

A young master thought he was easy prey.

Tomorrow, he would see what the ape thought.

chapters.title: The Spring Belonged to an Ape
chapters.html:
“Take the small medicine bottles,” Sun Mao said. “You'll run faster when the ape comes.”

Shi Feng looked at the stoneware bottles on the roadside stall. Two of the small narrow-necked bottles would fit easily inside his pack. The largest would need both arms to carry.

He took two of the small bottles.

“Two spirit stones,” Sun Mao said. “No refund if you drop them.”

“I won't bring the pieces back,” Shi Feng replied.

The peddler accepted the payment and pointed toward Yunlu Hill. A narrow path climbed between low pines. Farther up, pale rock showed where water had cut through the slope.

“The spring's around that rock,” Sun Mao said. “If you hear stones breaking, you're close enough.”

“Does anyone else gather there?” Shi Feng asked.

“A few tried,” Sun Mao replied. “They came back with broken bottles.”

“What does the dew look like?” Shi Feng asked.

“Pale where it's thin. Darker where it gathers under the rock,” Sun Mao said. “Don't fill a bottle with spring water and call it medicine. Qian Rui already does that.”

Shi Feng glanced at the vessels on the stall.

“Did you sell him those too?” Shi Feng asked.

Sun Mao looked offended.

“He bought the big ones,” Sun Mao replied. “And I told him not to call them ancient jade vessels!”

Sun Mao scraped his thumbnail over a bottle’s base. His own potter’s mark showed beneath a smear of green paint. He scrubbed harder, offended by the bad disguise rather than the dishonest medicine.

“Carry it by the neck,” Sun Mao said. “If you carry it by the lip, it’ll break before the ape gets a chance.”

Shi Feng thanked him and started climbing. The two small bottles would be enough. He wanted genuine medicine, not a heavy load of water.

He'd left Yunze Town at dawn. The path from the north road took him past vegetable plots and an abandoned charcoal stack. Now the trees hid the town, and the spring lay less than half an hour ahead.

He wanted Jade Marrow Dew, not another argument with a shopkeeper.

Buying enough cultivation medicine to fill his body's enormous capacity would eat through money faster than he could earn it. Hunting gave him strength directly. A useful spring could supply something different: medicine for the bones he would soon refine.

He wouldn't rush that change before his qi was ready. The first sign of the ape was a broken tree.

Its trunk lay across the path with tooth marks in the bark. Beyond it, stones had been thrown down the slope. One was larger than the roadside peddler's whole stall.

Shi Feng set his spear against a tree and tightened his sword belt. He didn't need the damaged shaft in this fight.

A Blackback Stone Ape stood beside the spring with both hands in the water. Gray hide covered its arms. The fur along its back was black, and its shoulders rose higher than Shi Feng's head.

It lifted a flat stone, sniffed beneath it, and smashed it against the bank.

Sun Mao's directions were accurate.

A mature beast of this kind had strength comparable to a Bone Refinement cultivator. Its hard limbs and thick skull were what kept ordinary hunters away.

Shi Feng stepped into the clearing.

The ape turned at once.

He drew his sword.

“I'm taking some dew,” Shi Feng said. “You won't agree, so let's save the discussion.”

The ape roared and threw the broken stone.

Shi Feng moved left. The stone struck a pine behind him and snapped two branches. Before the fragments fell, the ape charged across the clearing with both fists raised.

He met the first swinging arm with his palm.

Bang!

His boots cut two grooves in the soil. The ape's arm jerked sideways.

Shi Feng felt the force, but his elbow held. Refined qi supported his body instead of scattering at the impact.

He'd fought weaker beasts since his breakthrough. This was the first time he'd properly tested the strength of perfect meridians against an opponent above his realm.

It was enough.

The ape swung its other fist.

Shi Feng stepped inside the blow and drove his shoulder into its chest. The beast stumbled backward. He followed, cutting across the soft place beneath its jaw.

Blood darkened the gray hide.

The ape roared louder and grabbed his sword arm. Shi Feng turned his wrist before the fingers closed. He struck the inside of its elbow with his free hand, then kicked the knee as its weight shifted.

The huge body fell to one side.

He didn't give it room to stand.

His sword went beneath the collarbone and deep into the chest. The ape seized the blade with one hand. Shi Feng planted his foot against its shoulder and pulled the edge free before the grip tightened.

A second thrust entered the throat.

The fingers opened.

Shi Feng stepped back and waited until the body stopped moving. His left palm stung. Otherwise, he was unhurt.

He was happy with the result. Stronger cultivation made a difference, but so did knowing where to stand and putting force into a clean movement. He didn't have to survive every fight by falling through a hole.

A shout came from the trees.

“Is it dead?” Sun Mao called.

Shi Feng turned. The peddler stood well below the clearing, peering around a trunk.

“Come look,” Shi Feng said.

“No need!” Sun Mao replied quickly. “I believe you!”

“Then why are you here?” Shi Feng asked.

“My stall's still down the road,” Sun Mao said. “I wanted to know whether I should move it!”

Shi Feng pointed downhill. Sun Mao took the advice and hurried back.

He hadn't seen the fight. He'd arrived after the final roar and still wouldn't come close enough to inspect the corpse. Shi Feng waited until the peddler was gone, then knelt beside the ape.

The All-Devouring Physique answered his palm.

A thick rush of vitality entered his body. He stopped drawing after a few breaths and sat beside the spring while it settled. The beast was stronger than the fox, and there was no reason to let greed make the process harder.

He repeated it slowly through the afternoon.

When the body finally collapsed into brittle scraps, more qi remained within him. The currents were denser and easier to hold together. He guided one through his arm without feeling it spread where he didn't want it.

Qi Condensation was reaching the point described in the manual. He still hadn't entered Bone Refinement. That would require a deliberate change, with refined qi entering and strengthening an actual bone.

First, the dew.

Shi Feng washed his hands upstream of the blood and examined the spring hollow. Water ran clear over the upper stones. Beneath a low shelf, thick amber drops clung to a mineral crust.

He touched one with the clean tip of a wooden spoon.

Jade Marrow Dew.

There wasn't a whole pool of it. The good substance gathered slowly, one drop at a time. The ape had claimed the spring, but it hadn't known how much a pair of small bottles could sell for.

Shi Feng scraped carefully. He left mud and loose grit behind, collecting only the thick drops. By the time he finished, he had filled two small bottles with the thick amber dew.

That was enough for a start.

He stoppered both bottles, wrapped them in cloth, and recovered his spear from the tree. At the roadside stall, Sun Mao stared when Shi Feng tucked the two filled bottles into his pack.

“You came back,” Sun Mao said.

“You sound disappointed,” Shi Feng replied.

“I was worried!” Sun Mao protested. “About my stall too, but I was worried!”

Shi Feng bought a cup of water and sat upon a stone. The peddler kept looking toward the hill.

“The ape won't come down?” Sun Mao asked.

“Not unless somebody carries it,” Shi Feng said.

Sun Mao stared for a moment, then moved his stall a little farther from the path anyway. Shi Feng returned to Yunze Town before the evening lamps were lit.

Inside his room, he placed the two small bottles beside the blue manual and spread his right hand upon the table.

The forefinger bone would be first.

chapters.title: The First Bone
chapters.html:
“Don't break the bed!” Bian Cui shouted through the door.

Shi Feng looked at the stool he'd just moved away from the wall.

“It was the stool,” Shi Feng replied.

“Then thank Heaven it wasn’t the bed!” Bian Cui shouted. “The carpenter’s already sick of this house!”

Shi Feng checked the stool. One leg had cracked when he gripped it to steady his first circulation. He put it aside and sat on the floor. The floor, at least, belonged to the ground.

“Don't break that either!” Bian Cui said.

Her slippers slapped down the stairs. He waited until the sound faded, then closed the window and set the first of the two small bottles upon the table.

The Jade Marrow Dew was amber and thick. He didn't pour a mouthful just because he had two bottles of it now. The common manual advised a small amount during the first attempt.

Shi Feng touched one drop with a clean spoon and swallowed it.

Warmth spread through his chest.

He sat cross-legged upon folded bedding and placed the blue booklet where he could see the open page. The first step was clear. Gather refined qi, direct it around a small bone, and let it enter slowly.
