He chose the first bone of his right forefinger. A tiny place to begin after opening three hundred and sixty-five meridians.

It was still a beginning.

Shi Feng guided his qi down the arm. The current passed through the hand without difficulty, but it spread through the surrounding flesh when he pressed toward the bone. He stopped and tried again with less force.

The manual didn't say to smash the qi inward. Refinement meant strengthening the bone, not injuring it and hoping the medicine would clean up afterward. His next attempt held around the chosen point.

He felt the hard surface resisting the current. A little strength entered, then slipped away when his attention wandered toward the rest of the hand.

Shi Feng frowned.

He thought: one point first. Don't become greedy just because the road is open.

The All-Devouring Physique had given him plenty of resources. His perfect meridians carried the qi easily. Neither could choose where he focused.

He settled his breathing and began again.

This time he kept the current thin and steady. The warmth from the dew supported his body while refined qi pressed slowly into the bone.

Something changed beneath the surface.

A tiny hard point began holding the qi instead of letting it slide away.

Shi Feng didn't celebrate yet.

He fed it another careful current, then another. The new strength stayed through each breath. It wasn't the loose warmth he'd felt while restoring dormant meridians.

The bone itself was changing.

Outside, somebody dropped a bucket in the yard. A man cursed. Bian Cui shouted that the bucket still had to be paid for even if it was old.

Shi Feng kept his attention on his finger.

The noise faded.

Then the tiny point became stable.

His whole skeleton gave a clear response.

The force passed from the forefinger into the hand, through the arm, and down the spine. His body straightened without him intending it. Refined qi settled deeper, supporting his flesh with a firmness he'd never felt before.

Bone Refinement.

Shi Feng opened his eyes.

For a moment, he just looked at his hand.

“I've reached it,” Shi Feng said quietly. “Bone Refinement.”

He was excited. He hadn't crawled out of Hanyin Well merely to return to the life he lost. He'd gone beyond it.

Before his meridians went dormant, the clan praised his channel count. He still hadn't reached this realm. Now there was no testing stone and no elder deciding how much applause he deserved.

There was only his own hand and the little point of new strength within it.

That was enough.

He examined the change carefully.

The refined portion was tiny, little more than a grain along the forefinger bone. He hadn't completed that bone, much less the whole skeleton.

Yet every bone was already connected to the strength flowing through his perfect meridian network. The first successful refinement let that strength support his entire body more directly. It didn't mean all two hundred and six bones were refined.

It meant he'd finally begun the work.

Shi Feng glanced at the two small bottles.

The dew would help, but this wouldn't be cheap. If every small section needed steady resources, completing the whole body would require far more than one lucky spring.

He wasn't discouraged.

He could hunt, and he could earn money. The important thing was that his road hadn't ended where the physicians said it had.

Near noon, Shi Feng stood and tested a few plain clan movements.

His first forward step stopped exactly where he wanted. The next turn was faster. When he closed his fist, his forearm no longer shook against the full force gathering within it.

He picked up an iron nail left beside the shutter.

The nail bent between his fingers.

Shi Feng looked at it, straightened it as well as he could, and set it back. Bian Cui would probably recognize her nail from across the yard.

The sword was next. He drew it, made a short thrust, and stopped before the point reached the wall. Qi supported the movement without spilling from him in a visible glow.

His strength had risen sharply.

An ordinary opponent in Bone Refinement wasn't going to be dangerous just because they shared a realm. His foundation before this point was far beyond theirs, and his body could finally carry more of that advantage. He wouldn't need a clever escape every time somebody swung a blade.

Shi Feng sheathed the sword and washed before opening the door. A sleepy cloth merchant stood upon the landing with an empty water bowl. His robe hung open at the collar, and he looked annoyed at everything.

“Were you the one knocking?” Qiu Sheng, a sleepy merchant, asked.

“No,” Shi Feng said.

“Good. I was trying to sleep,” Qiu Sheng grumbled.

He shuffled downstairs and began arguing with Bian Cui about whether cold tea counted as yesterday's tea or today's.

Shi Feng followed more slowly.

The lodging house was exactly as noisy as before. Nobody bowed because he'd entered Bone Refinement. Nobody even knew.

That suited him.

In the yard, Bian Cui looked him over.

“You look healthier,” Bian Cui said. “Have you finally stopped wasting money on Qian Rui?”

“Not soon enough,” Shi Feng replied.

“He still owes me for two meals,” Bian Cui muttered.

Shi Feng sat with a bowl of rice. He ate it, ordered another, then added eggs and vegetables. The new strength had left him hungry enough to think poorly of small bowls.

Bian Cui watched the dishes accumulate.

“Do you want the pot brought over?” Bian Cui asked.

“How much rice is left?” Shi Feng replied.

She stopped joking and fetched the pot.

“If you're hungry, say so before I put the fire out,” Bian Cui said.

“I'm hungry,” Shi Feng replied.

“I can see that now!” Bian Cui snapped.

She brought another plate of eggs. They weren't free, but they were hot, and the shells weren't mixed into the food.

Shi Feng ate them with satisfaction. A breakthrough deserved a decent meal. He didn't need elders beating drums outside his door to enjoy it.

Across the yard, the sleepy merchant watched the empty plates accumulate and quietly moved his breakfast farther away.

After eating, he bought food for two days and checked his pack. The damaged spear would serve as a walking staff. The plain sword was sound. Wei Kuo's better knife sat at his belt, replacing the old chipped blade.

He kept the two bottles of dew wrapped at the center of the pack. More hunting would bring more resources. He could practice along the way instead of sitting in town while every merchant tried to sell him another cure for being crippled.

Bian Cui saw him preparing to leave the following morning.

“Where now?” Bian Cui asked.

“The outer hills,” Shi Feng said.

“Don't bring anything alive into my kitchen,” Bian Cui warned.

“I'll eat it first,” Shi Feng replied.

Before she could answer, heavy boots stopped outside the courtyard gate. Gao An, the Wei household’s steward, stepped over the threshold with two armed retainers and an unrolled watch notice in his hand.

“The Wei household has reported Young Master Wei Kuo and his attendant Luo San missing to the town watch,” Gao An announced, his sharp gaze sweeping the yard before settling on Bian Cui. “They went toward the western hills yesterday afternoon and haven’t returned. Which of your lodgers took the western track before dusk?”

Bian Cui stiffened with the empty dish still in her hand. Two steps from the gate, Shi Feng adjusted the strap of his pack, met Gao An’s eyes calmly as he stepped past the retainers, and walked out into the street.

chapters.title: An Elder in the Wrong Town
chapters.html:
“Shi Feng! Stop right there!” Shi Hong shouted.

Shi Feng had just bought a whetstone when the voice came from the inn steps. He turned and saw his cousin standing beside a loaded trade carriage.

Shi Hong wore a blue robe with silver cuffs. A new sword hung at his waist. He looked delighted, which immediately made the meeting less promising.

Behind him stood Second Elder Shi Zhen, holding a teacup.

The clan's mark was painted on the carriage. They'd come to Yunze Town on trade business, not to find him. Shi Feng could see bolts of cloth beneath the driver's seat and two servants carrying sample boxes into the inn.

He put the whetstone in his pack.

“Second Elder,” Shi Feng said. “Cousin.”

Shi Zhen looked him over. The last time they met, the youth's robe hung loosely from his shoulders. Now he stood straight, his hands looked steady, and his ordinary sword showed fresh use.

“You've been eating well,” Shi Zhen said.

“Yes,” Shi Feng said.

Shi Hong's smile stiffened. He'd expected embarrassment, not agreement.

“People say you're gathering medicine,” Shi Hong said. “Show us what you've found.”

“Why?” Shi Feng asked.

Shi Zhen set down his cup.

“Don't speak to your cousin that way,” Shi Zhen said. “You've been away long enough. Load your things onto the carriage. We're returning after the market closes.”

Shi Feng didn't move.

“I didn't say I was going back,” Shi Feng said.

Several people slowed near the inn. A family elder claiming a wandering junior was familiar enough. A junior refusing in the middle of the street was worth watching.

Shi Zhen frowned.

“The clan raised you,” Shi Zhen said. “Don't forget your roots just because you've earned a few spirit stones.”

“The clan sent me away,” Shi Feng said. “I've found my own food since then.”

“Watch your mouth!” Shi Hong snapped.

Shi Feng looked at him. He felt no fear and very little anger. His cousin was still the same boy who mistook a louder voice for a better argument.

Shi Zhen was different. The elder looked at the bottles tied inside the open pack and recognized the pale liquid.

“Jade Marrow Dew?” Shi Zhen said.

Shi Hong's head turned at once.

Even in the clan, he couldn't drink that medicine whenever he wanted. Now the cripple carried two bottles through the street as though they were ordinary water!

Shi Hong drew himself taller and looked around for witnesses. Several merchants knew the clan's name. If his useless cousin obeyed in front of them, the story would return to Qingshi Town well before the carriage did.

“I've opened one hundred and eighty-two meridians,” Shi Hong announced. “Do you know what that means?”

“You opened six more,” Shi Feng said.

Shi Hong tugged his sleeve up to show the bead bracelet marking his count. One bead had a fresh scratch where the number was changed.

“I haven’t had the new ones carved yet!” Shi Hong snapped.

“Nobody asked,” Shi Feng replied.

The sleeve came down again. His cousin wanted the street to admire six new meridians, but now everyone was looking at an old bracelet.

Shi Hong froze. He wanted awe, not subtraction.

“It means my future matters to the clan!” Shi Hong snapped. “That medicine should go to somebody who can use it!”

“Then gather some,” Shi Feng said.

The merchant beside the carriage covered his smile with a sample cloth. Shi Zhen saw it and became impatient. The boy was refusing to play his part, and the onlookers were enjoying it too much.

“That belongs in the clan store,” Shi Hong said. “You can't even cultivate. Give it here!”

He reached for the pack.

Shi Feng caught his wrist.

Shi Hong tried to pull away. His arm stayed where it was.

“Let go!” Shi Hong shouted.

“Then keep your hands to yourself,” Shi Feng said.

Shi Hong kicked at his knee.

The kick landed. Shi Feng didn't shift. Pain shot through Shi Hong's ankle, and his expression changed.

He was still in Meridian Opening. He couldn't meaningfully hurt a Bone Refinement body, much less Shi Feng's. No qi showed on the street, so the onlookers saw only a failed kick and a wrist caught in a firm grip.

Shi Hong's face reddened.

“Father!” Shi Hong cried.

Shi Zhen stepped down from the inn.

“Release him,” Shi Zhen said coldly.

Shi Feng let go and moved his pack to the other shoulder. Shi Hong backed away, rubbing his wrist. Then he saw the crowd and became even angrier.

“He attacked me!” Shi Hong shouted.

“You kicked him first!” someone called.

“And grabbed his medicine.”

“Didn't the Shi clan say he was useless?”

“Then why do they want him back?”

Shi Zhen's expression darkened. He didn't care what these townspeople thought, but he cared that they were laughing at his family.

The elder had reached Qi Condensation. He gathered a little qi beneath his sleeve, intending to seize Shi Feng's arm and drag him into the inn before the spectacle grew worse. His hand closed around Shi Feng's upper arm.

It might as well have closed around a stone pillar. Shi Feng turned and pulled the elder's hand free.

Shi Zhen stared at him.

“Second Elder, we're not in your courtyard,” Shi Feng said. “Keep your hands to yourself too.”

He gave the older man one short push.

Shi Zhen stumbled backward onto the inn steps. His heel caught the edge. He sat down hard beside the teacup he'd abandoned.

The driver hurried away from the carriage and helped him stand.

Shi Hong was stunned. His father was an elder! How could a cripple shove him around in public?

“It's medicine!” Shi Hong blurted. “He found something that strengthens the body!”

Shi Zhen seized the explanation at once.

“You waste clan resources on this nonsense?” Shi Zhen demanded.

“My resources,” Shi Feng said.

He hadn't shown a thread of qi. Let them call it medicine. That explanation cost him nothing.

The elder stood, furious but unwilling to risk another public fall. He pointed toward the carriage.

“If you refuse today, don't expect me to speak for you later!” Shi Zhen said.

“You didn't speak for me before,” Shi Feng said.

Then he walked away.

Behind him, two Qingshi Town cloth dealers standing by the inn rail didn’t even wait for the dust to settle before leaning together.

“Did you see that? The Second Elder grabbed him with Qi Condensation force and ended up sitting on the steps!”

“Wait until the east-road carters bring this back to Qingshi Town—the whole market will hear how Second Elder Shi went sprawling before his own carriage gets home!”

Shi Zhen’s face turned the color of iron. Beneath his cuff, his wrist still throbbed where Shi Feng’s arm had felt like tempered stone. “At the year-end test,” Shi Zhen muttered through his teeth as his servants pretended to find their boxes very heavy, “we’ll see what his aunt has left when the elders call his name.”

Shi Feng bought a clean robe at the next street.

The shopkeeper measured his shoulders, named the price, and waited while he paid. There was no need to bargain over a fair charge. He changed behind a hanging cloth and put the old robe in his pack.

Outside, two boys were arguing over which carriage horse was faster. One insisted the white one would win because white horses belonged to heroes. The other pointed out that this one was chewing its tether.

Shi Feng stopped only long enough to move past the loose end of the rope. His relatives hadn't spoiled the day. That surprised him less than it once would have.

He thought: they still believe they can order me around. Let them keep believing it from Qingshi Town.

At the noodle stall, the cook placed a full bowl before him and asked whether he wanted more meat. Shi Feng said yes.

He ate slowly, sharpened his sword afterward, and spent the afternoon refining the medicine from the spring. The changes inside his first few bones remained small, but each day added something useful.

Later, the innkeeper asked whether the elder would pay for his room. Shi Feng said no and paid for it himself. The man took the stones, put down a clean towel, and asked no further questions.

From the open window, Shi Feng could hear Shi Hong shouting at a servant over a missing pair of gloves. The gloves turned up in the carriage a moment later. The servant was scolded for finding them too slowly.

Shi Feng shut the window and returned to his breathing exercise. By dusk, the clan carriage rolled toward the eastern road.

Shi Hong sat inside rather than riding where townspeople could see him. Shi Zhen kept the curtain closed. Shi Feng watched them pass from the noodle stall and returned to his bowl.

He wasn't going after them.

His road lay west.

chapters.title: The Missing Son
chapters.html:
The Wei household's gates stayed open until midnight.

Gao An stood beside a table covered in travel slips. Wei Kuo hadn't returned. Neither had Luo San, the Qi Condensation servant who followed him out of town.

“The young master often stays out,” Wen Ruxiu said.

She worked at the customs shed and knew which gates had counted which carts. She had come because Gao An sent five spirit stones with the message. Sympathy alone wouldn't have brought her through the rain.

“He took no spare clothes,” Gao An said. “Search the northern permits.”

“Permits tell me who passed a gate. They don't tell me who stabbed whom in the hills,” Wen Ruxiu said.

Gao An flinched. She hadn't meant a prophecy; she was warning him what he was buying. He paid for another day's watch. Shi Feng's name went onto her list beside seven hunters and two missing traders. Nobody could confirm his cultivation. The old record still called him a cripple.

“Then Heaven struck his meridians dead!” He Yan declared, slapping his wooden clapper onto the table.

Several drinkers gasped. A man near the door dropped a peanut into his wine. Shi Feng paused with a noodle halfway to his mouth.

That sounded familiar.

The dining room of the Changfu Inn was crowded and warm. Travelers occupied the benches nearest the windows. Townspeople stood by the storyteller's little platform, listening for free until the owner chased them toward empty tables.

He Yan wore a robe with a patched elbow and spoke with the confidence of a man who'd never met Heaven but quoted it every evening.

“One hundred and thirty-seven meridians!” He Yan cried. “An extraordinary genius, destroyed in a single night!”

“Two hundred and thirty-seven,” Shi Feng said.

He Yan looked toward him.

“What?” He Yan asked.

“The story starts with two hundred and thirty-seven,” Shi Feng said. “You forgot a hundred.”

The drinkers turned. Someone recognized his face, leaned toward a neighbor, and whispered much too loudly.

“That's him!”

“The Shi clan's cripple?”

“He doesn't look half dead.”

“My cousin says he eats spirit beast meat every day.”

“Can that repair meridians?”

“No, but I'd like to try!”

He Yan's smile froze. Then he recovered and lifted the clapper again.

“Exactly! Two hundred and thirty-seven!” He Yan said. “I was testing whether this audience knows its heroes!”

“Then return half our money!” somebody shouted.

The dining room burst into laughter.

Shi Feng went back to his noodles. He felt amused rather than humiliated. He Yan could tell the old story however he liked. It couldn't change the qi moving quietly through Shi Feng's body or the little bones he'd already begun refining.

He thought: if I correct every rumor, I won't have time for supper.

He Yan snapped his clapper down.

“Fortunately, Heaven left the youth one last treasure!” He Yan declared.

Shi Feng looked up.

“A very good appetite!” He Yan finished, pointing at the noodles.

The room burst out laughing. Shi Feng raised his bowl in acknowledgement. He Yan bowed from his platform, delighted to have survived his own story. He moved straight into a tale about a sect elder pursuing a stolen chicken.

The audience liked that one much better.

A serving boy brought another bowl of broth. Shi Feng thanked him and moved his pack out of the aisle. Two men beside the window argued about whether a swordsman could cut a shadow. Neither had drawn a sword all evening.

By the time He Yan finished, the lamps were burning low. He collected the offered stones and came to Shi Feng's table with a broad smile.

“You've become a famous young man,” He Yan said.

“Your famous young man lost a hundred meridians,” Shi Feng said.

“A slip of the tongue,” He Yan said. “Don't mention it again. Some listeners take numbers too seriously.”

“You announced the number three times,” Shi Feng said.

He Yan put his clapper away.

“I came here for a quiet bowl,” He Yan muttered.

“So did I,” Shi Feng said.

The storyteller looked at the empty seat. Shi Feng didn't invite him, but the dining room was full, and He Yan sat anyway after buying his own wine.

He was from Qingshi Town. Carrying familiar gossip from one town to another paid better than staying where everybody already knew the ending. That was his entire reason for coming west.

No secret sect, no mysterious employer. Just listeners and money.

“Are you going home?” He Yan asked.

“No,” Shi Feng said.

“Your elder was furious this morning,” He Yan said. “I heard half the street laughing.”

“Then you have tomorrow's story,” Shi Feng said.

He Yan's expression brightened. He reached for the clapper, thought about it, and left it in his sleeve.

“Some stories aren't worth making an elder angry,” He Yan said.

Shi Feng didn't argue. The man knew where his courage ended.

At the next table, a merchant complained about the price of medicine in the capital. His companion said the selection was better there, so naturally people paid more.

He Yan pointed his cup toward them.

“That's where money goes to disappear,” He Yan said. “I've been twice. A decent room can cost more than my whole week's earnings here.”

“Do they have better bone medicine?” Shi Feng asked.

“Shops, markets, auctions,” He Yan said. “Even a Sky Pavilion tower. If you've got the stones, somebody will sell you what you want.”

Shi Feng listened more closely.

Yunze Town had hunters and ordinary medicine shops. Its good resources came in small amounts, and the same few people fought over them. The capital drew traders from across Great Liang. That mattered more than its fine buildings.

“Which road?” Shi Feng asked.

He Yan waved west.

“Shuanghe Ferry first,” He Yan said. “After that, join a merchant convoy. Don't ask me the fare. The last merchant I rode with charged me for telling stories that kept his drivers awake!”

“What did you charge him?” Shi Feng asked.

He Yan coughed into his cup.

He Guang, the hide merchant at the next table, leaned over.

“Don't frighten him over the rooms,” He Guang said. “You can sleep cheaply near the warehouses. It's the medicine that empties your purse.”

“You bought the wrong medicine,” He Yan said.

“You drank it!” He Guang snapped. “That was my sleeping draught, not wine!”

He Yan stared at him, then pushed his own cup farther away.

Shi Feng laughed. The capital wasn't some distant sacred land. Ordinary people went there, earned money, made mistakes, and came back to complain. That made the journey feel straightforward.

“How long did you stay?” Shi Feng asked.

“A month,” He Guang said. “Sold hides, bought cloth, lost a tooth arguing with a Bone Refinement guard. Don't do the last part.”

“I'll try not to,” Shi Feng said.

He Guang returned to his own table. He Yan waited until the merchant wasn't looking and smelled his wine. Shi Feng smiled and called for the meal to be cleared.

Morning found him at the west end of town, looking at a road sign.

One arrow pointed toward Shuanghe Ferry. Another led to the nearby hunting hills. A third board warned travelers that part of the southern path had washed out.

He wouldn't leave immediately. His supplies needed replacing, and there was still medicine here he could use. But he no longer needed to wonder where he'd go after that.

He counted the food in his pack and looked at his boots. One lace needed replacing. The leather itself was sound. With a little preparation, he could begin walking as soon as he finished his next few hunts.

The capital.

He wasn't going there to prove anything to his family. He wanted more resources, better markets, and enough room to choose his own opportunities. Fan Mu, the old shrine sweeper, looked at his pack.

“Going far, young man?” Fan Mu asked.

“West,” Shi Feng said.

“Then don't sleep under the ferry sign,” Fan Mu said. “They move it when the river rises. I woke up in the mud once!”

Shi Feng looked at him and laughed.

“I'll remember that,” Shi Feng said.

The old man returned to sweeping. A gust blew half the leaves back across the steps. He cursed the wind and chased them with his broom.

When Shi Feng walked back through the west gate, a fresh wooden placard had been nailed beside the customs board. A crowd of hunters stood reading the black characters: the Wei household offered fifty spirit stones for word of Wei Kuo, and twenty more for the name of anyone who had met him on the western hill path.

At the edge of the crowd, Tang Jiu looked from the placard down to the knife hanging at Shi Feng’s belt—and slipped quietly down the side lane before Shi Feng reached the board.

chapters.title: The Basket
chapters.html:
The tray tipped, and three black pellets rolled into the street. Qian Rui grabbed the apprentice by the collar before the rest followed. A puff of smoke rose between their faces.

“Look what you've done!” Qian Rui shouted.

“I told you the tray was hot!” Yu An shouted back.

The apprentice dropped it onto the doorstep. Dark lumps bounced across the stones. One came to rest beside Shi Feng's boot.

He stepped around it.

A young hunter reached for one of the scorched pellets until Qian Rui slapped his broom handle down in front of the man’s fingers, barking that a failed batch would have him coughing blood before sunset. While Yu An swept the black lumps into a waste jar, Shi Feng stepped to the front shelf, bought a twelve-stone bone-strengthening tonic after Yu An confirmed it was three days fresh, and left master and apprentice arguing over the broom.

Near the east gate, Deng Hu’s nephew was unloading fish baskets from Qingshi Town. He handed Shi Feng a tied pouch containing twenty spirit stones and a gruff four-word slip from Physician Meng Shou: Root lived. Don’t die.

Shi Feng pocketed the twenty stones with a faint smile. That closed his last small account with Qingshi Town.

He unfolded the slip once more before putting it away. Meng Shou's impatient handwriting crowded the narrow paper. The old physician had taken the living shoot seriously enough to pay for it, instead of dismissing the strange marsh root because his books had no certain answer.

Shi Feng hoped the sample would prove useful. He could picture Meng Shou bending over the mineral block, scolding an assistant for letting the reeds dry.

At the medicine shop, Qian Rui had promised that the tonic would help strengthen his bones. Shi Feng hadn't bought the promise. He had bought one measured bottle to test. If it worked poorly, he would know before wasting stones on a whole course.

An hour up a rocky gully in the western hills, Shi Feng found a Stoneback Spirit Crab in the upper pool. Its shell looked like a broad slab of wet rock. Two claws rose from beneath it when his shadow crossed the water.

He put his pack on the bank, out of reach of the pool, and drew his sword.

The crab lunged sideways. Shi Feng stepped outside its larger claw and struck the smaller one's joint. The blade caught between the hard plates, cutting deeply enough to stop the limb closing.

The larger claw snapped at his knee.

He moved onto the flat stone behind it. The crab turned after him, exposing the pale underside where its legs joined the shell. Shi Feng thrust into that gap and released a short burst of qi.

The creature's legs folded. He waited until the last claw stopped twitching before pulling the sword free.

Qian Rui's tonic tasted bitter enough to deserve its reputation. Shi Feng swallowed it and sat beside his pack, guiding its warmth into the bones he was currently refining. The gain was real, but small. Even after the bottle's force settled, the work had moved forward only a little.

Then he laid his palm against his kill.

The crab's vitality did more in ten breaths than the tonic had managed through the whole cultivation session. He stopped the flow once to let the denser warmth settle, then continued. Deng Hu's supposed border medicine would have dragged him along; his own power still answered his choice.

Shi Feng looked at the empty bottle. A town tonic could help an ordinary cultivator patiently strengthen a few bones. It wasn't enough for the resources his complete refinement would demand.

He would still check better medicines when he found them. One poor result didn't make every shop useless.

After cultivation, Shi Feng washed at the stream and ate the bread he'd brought. A faded trail marker stood on the opposite bank. Somebody had added a warning beneath the town's painted directions: don't wash wounds downstream of the tanners.

He checked the clear water, then returned to his pack strap. The thread held after a little repair. He tested it, packed the empty shell for sale, and headed toward town before dark.

On the road, a group of hunters passed carrying a covered basket between two poles. They were laughing too loudly for men carrying anything light.

“Careful with it!” Ge Lu called from the front. “Drop one and I'll break your legs!”

A younger hunter slipped. The basket lurched. Something heavy and oval knocked against the wicker from within, followed by a faint, sharp clicking.

Shi Feng stopped at the roadside. A sour, mineral stench escaped beneath the oiled cloth—the exact nest-scent of the Split-Maw Beast from Heilu Marsh. His gaze narrowed.

“You took Split-Maw eggs from a live nest?” Shi Feng asked.

“Shut your mouth, cripple!” Ge Lu sneered, though he glanced nervously back toward the marsh road. “Master Wei Renshan posted a hundred-stone bounty for a live clutch to send to the capital. By the time the mother notices the mud’s cold, these will be locked in the Wei storehouse!”

The others laughed. One shoved the cover into place where it had slipped.

The cloth was wet around its lower edge. A hunter wrinkled his nose and wiped his hand against his trousers. Whatever they had used to wash the basket hadn't removed the nest-scent. The sour smell clung to the carrying poles as well.

“Cover it properly,” Ge Lu snapped. “The storekeeper won't take cracked eggs.”

The younger hunter tightened the rope without laughing this time. Beyond the bend, the marsh road lay empty. Ge Lu looked back at it again before ordering the group onward.

Shi Feng watched them choose the town track. They were counting the reward before delivering the clutch. He couldn't tell how far away the mother was, or whether it had already found the raided nest. He knew the covering hadn't made the cargo scentless.

Shi Feng kept walking.

He didn't care what strangers were taking to market. They hadn't attacked him, and he wasn't about to follow a basket because its owner had poor manners. By the time he reached his inn, the hunters were drinking in the courtyard behind a locked shed.

Their basket sat inside.

Shi Feng ordered supper, carried it upstairs, and shut his door against the noise.

chapters.title: The Beasts Didn't Buy Tickets
chapters.html:
“Out of the road! Move!” Ge Lu shouted.

His cart hurtled past the inn steps. The basket from yesterday bounced beneath a torn covering, and Deng Chao clung to its rim.

Shi Feng stepped back with his breakfast bowl. The cart hit a rut. An egg rolled beneath its covering, cracked against the rim, and gave off a sharp, foul smell.

The hunter holding the basket went pale. He was at Qi Condensation, but he looked ready to abandon the whole cart.

“Did it break?” Ge Lu shouted.

“No!” Deng Chao shouted back.

A red limb pushed through the covering.

The hunter jumped off the moving cart. Ge Lu finally looked behind him, screamed, and whipped the mule toward the gate.

Something crashed beyond the southern gate.

The road shook. A horse screamed. Then the gate's wooden bar flew across the street and smashed through a noodle stall.

The Split-Maw mother came into Yunze Town.

Its back rose above the roofs. Gray plates covered its body, and the hooked legs tore through walls as it forced its way along the road. Behind it rushed a pack of smaller beasts with pale armor and jaws that split wide.

Shi Feng's expression became serious.

This wasn't an opponent he could casually kill. The mother was far beyond the town's ordinary hunters, and more powerful than the beasts he'd fed on so far.

“Eggs!” somebody screamed. “Those fools stole its eggs!”

Ge Lu lashed the mule harder.

An egg rolled from the basket and broke beneath a wheel. The mother's cry shook the inn's windows.

The smell he'd noticed yesterday came from a nest. Now Shi Feng saw what Ge Lu had taken for the Wei household: a clutch raided from the marsh nest to fill Wei Renshan’s bounty before the mother noticed.

They hadn't thought very far ahead.

The mother struck the cart with a foreleg.

Wood burst apart. The mule bolted with a broken harness dragging behind it. Ge Lu disappeared under the wreckage, and two hunters were caught before they could reach the far side of the street.

The rest ran in different directions.

The smaller beasts followed them into the lanes. Shi Feng put down his bowl and picked up his pack. His sword was already at his waist, with Wei Kuo's knife tucked on the other side.

He wasn't joining a defense of the town. He needed to leave the mother's path and find a way toward the northern road.

“Upstairs guests, pay before you run!” Xu Geng shouted from the inn counter.

The innkeeper held both arms over the coins spilled in front of him. A drinker shoved past and knocked over his stool.

“My room's paid,” Shi Feng said, passing the counter.

“Breakfast isn't!” Xu Geng cried.

Shi Feng put the agreed stones beside his hand and walked out through the kitchen. He kept his word. That didn't mean waiting while Xu Geng tried to charge the fleeing guests twice.

The rear lane led toward the potters' quarter. He took it, keeping the mother's enormous body behind the inn and out of his direct path. A young Split-Maw Spirit Beast dropped from a low wall.

Shi Feng caught its lower jaw before it could close around his face. His fingers tightened. He struck its head against the wall and broke the neck with a short turn.

The beast fell at his feet.

He stepped over it. There were people in both doorways, and no quiet place to devour a carcass. He didn't need the resource badly enough to stop in the middle of the tide.

At the next corner, a fat landlord was trying to force a crying tenant out of a stone storehouse.

“Only paying guests!” Liu De shouted. “Twenty spirit stones per person!”

“You raised it from ten!” Chen Wan cried.

“Then you should've gone in sooner!” Liu De shouted.

Shi Feng moved past them. The storehouse was already packed, and arguing wouldn't make its walls stronger. A crash sounded from the street behind him.

The mother pushed through the inn's roof. People scattered from the front entrance. Xu Geng ran with the cashbox beneath one arm and left the building without looking back.

The eggs were still somewhere ahead of the beast. A surviving hunter had carried the smaller basket off the broken cart and was running east. Shi Feng saw him cross the far end of the lane.

He turned north instead.

At the next crossing, two armed men were trying to lift a fallen beam from a cart. One wore a town watch sash. The other kept shouting that his cargo was valuable, as though the timber might rise faster if it knew the price.

“Leave it!” Meng Tao shouted.

“It's imported cloth!” Pei Jin cried.

A young beast skittered around the corner. Both men abandoned the cart and ran.

Shi Feng cut the creature across the neck as it passed him. It fell beneath the abandoned wheel. He didn't stop to touch it. The narrow lane ahead remained clear, and that was where he needed to go.

Behind him, a door slammed. Someone started hammering on it from outside and begging a relative to open up.

He felt anger at the hunters who'd brought this disaster, but anger wouldn't make him the town's guardian. He couldn't protect every household while a mother beast taller than the roofs tore through the streets.

The potters' square was crowded with people trying to reach the same narrow road. Tang Jiu stood on an empty cart and waved both arms.

“Safe passage! Ten spirit stones for a place!” Tang Jiu shouted.

“Where are the horses?” a man in the crowd demanded.

“On their way!” Tang Jiu shouted back.

The cart didn't move. Paying passengers pushed to board first. Shi Feng glanced at the empty shafts and kept going.

Above the potters’ awning, Lin Shuang braced one boot against the parapet and hauled a child and an old woman up a knotted rope onto the tiles. As a red-plated brood beast scrambled onto the opposite gable, she spotted Shi Feng moving below.

“Shi Feng! Don’t take the east street!” Lin Shuang called down, catching her spear up from the tiles. “That idiot Ge Lu ran the egg basket toward the Wei storehouse, and the mother’s tearing down every wall between here and the market!”

“Which gate is still clear?” Shi Feng called back.

“None of them until the brood passes! Get behind stone—I’m guiding these people over the ridge tiles to the north granary, and once the road opens I’m taking a cloth convoy west toward Shuanghe Ferry!” Lin Shuang struck the climbing beast’s claws from the eaves with her spear butt. “Don’t get eaten before the ferry road!”

“Keep your rope dry,” Shi Feng replied, and turned into the side lane.

He passed a public well where three women were filling every jar they could carry. A frightened boy tried to drag his grandfather toward the northern road. The old man kept insisting that he needed his shoes first.

He entered a side lane behind the northern pottery works. The street beyond it should have led to the road out of town. Instead, a fallen wall blocked the far end.

He could climb it. He took two steps toward the rubble. A brood guardian rose from the other side.

Its red head cleared the bricks, followed by a pair of bladed forelegs. The creature was larger than an ox, and its plates were much thicker than those of the young beasts.

Shi Feng drew his sword.

The guardian struck down. He stepped aside and cut at its leg, leaving a deep mark where the plates joined. The beast shrieked and pulled back.

He could kill this one.

Then a second guardian climbed onto the roof behind him.

The tiles cracked beneath its weight. It was larger, with dark red armor and a body that gave off far more pressure. This creature's strength was at the Foundation Establishment level.

The lane was too narrow to avoid both beasts while climbing the wall.

Shi Feng backed toward the open kiln yard beside him. A rounded firing chamber stood at its center. Its stone walls offered a place to keep the guardians from attacking him from opposite sides.

He entered the yard, then stepped through the kiln doorway. The first guardian followed along the lane. The second crawled over the outer wall and dropped into the yard with a heavy crash.

Inside, Shi Feng put his pack behind the furnace and drew Wei Kuo's knife with his free hand. A human voice squealed from somewhere behind the kiln.

“Don't bring them here!” Zheng Bao cried. “I just repaired that roof!”

Shi Feng looked at the approaching guardians and raised his sword.

“Then stay out of the way,” Shi Feng said.

chapters.title: The First Guardian
chapters.html:
The guardian shoved its head through the kiln doorway. Shi Feng thrust his sword toward its open mouth. The beast twisted, and the point scraped along a red plate before cutting into the softer joint beneath it.

Dark blood spilled across the threshold.

The guardian shrieked and struck down with a bladed foreleg.

Shi Feng stepped left. The limb hit the stone floor and threw broken chips against his boots. He cut across the joint before the creature could lift it again.

The foreleg folded.

Outside, Zheng Bao screamed louder than the beast.

“My doorway! Watch the doorway!” Zheng Bao cried.

Shi Feng didn't answer. The potter was somewhere behind the kiln, safely out of reach. He could complain to the bricks if he wanted.

The firing chamber was round, with a furnace recess at the back. Shi Feng's pack lay beside it. There was room to move inside, but only one proper entrance.

The larger guardian had climbed onto the roof. Its legs scratched across the curved bricks while the wounded one pushed farther through the doorway. He needed to kill the first beast before the second came down.

Shi Feng put his sword in his left hand and caught the advancing head with his right. The guardian's jaws snapped beside his wrist. He gripped the edge of its upper plate, pulled it downward, and drove a knee beneath its mouth.

Crack!

The lower plate split.

The creature jerked back, but Shi Feng followed. He planted one foot on the threshold and punched directly through the damaged plate.

The head slammed against the doorpost.

A second blow crushed the hard ridge behind its eye. The guardian collapsed halfway inside the kiln. Its bladed legs scraped the floor twice, then went still.

Shi Feng stood over it, breathing evenly.

Its strength was close to that of a Bone Refinement cultivator. Once, a beast like this could have chased him through half the town. Now it couldn't withstand his fist.

This was what all those hunts were for. He hadn't eaten beast meat and endured cultivation just to keep running from things he could crush.

A crash shook the roof above him.

The larger guardian drove one leg through the bricks. Shi Feng stepped away as it swept across the chamber and cut a shelf in half.

The potter howled again.

“That shelf was new!” Zheng Bao shouted. “The wedding bowls are on it!”

“Whose wedding?” Shi Feng asked, keeping his eyes on the beast.

“Mine! If she sees that kiln, there won’t be one!” Zheng Bao cried.

Shi Feng pulled the guardian’s head toward the empty side of the yard. He needed room to strike anyway. The potter’s marriage could survive if it stayed out of his way.

“Stay behind the wall,” Shi Feng said.

“I'm already behind two!” Zheng Bao shouted back.

Shi Feng dragged the first corpse away from the doorway. He wanted space to leave if the roof fell, not to crouch beneath it while waiting for another strike. The carcass was heavy, but he pulled it clear with one hand.

Outside, a group of people ran past the yard gate. One saw the red plates blocking the kiln entrance and screamed. Nobody came closer.

That suited him.

“Have they gone?” Zheng Bao called.

“One's dead,” Shi Feng said.

“Then why's my roof still shaking?” Zheng Bao demanded.

“The other one's on it,” Shi Feng said.

Something scraped above them. A loose brick fell into the doorway and broke beside the dead guardian.

Zheng Bao cursed from behind his wall.

“There's a ladder in the yard!” Zheng Bao shouted. “Can't you make it use the ladder?”

“Come and ask it,” Shi Feng said.

The potter didn't answer that.

Shi Feng wiped blood from his sword against the corpse. The edge had two fresh chips. He tested the grip and found it sound, then shifted the pack away from the falling dust.

A small cupboard stood beside the furnace. He pushed it over the pack, leaving space beneath so the bottles wouldn't be crushed if more bricks fell. His hand still felt steady. Killing the smaller guardian hadn't tired him.

He could finish the larger one too. It was coming down to him anyway. Shi Feng set the sword within reach and placed his palm beneath the first guardian's broken head.

The All-Devouring Physique responded.

Vitality entered through the contact, hot and rich. The dead beast's flesh tightened beneath his hand as part of its strength passed into him. He drew only a little before removing his palm.

There was no time to settle a whole guardian's vitality. Taking too much while fighting would burden his body instead of helping it. The resource wouldn't run away just because he left it for later.

He circulated what he'd taken through his meridians and stood.

The larger guardian struck the roof again.

A section caved inward. Shi Feng caught his pack by its strap and moved behind the furnace as bricks hit the floor.

The beast dropped through the hole.

Its front claws struck first. Its red head followed, forcing the opening wider until the chamber filled with dust. Shi Feng set the pack into the furnace recess and drew the sword again.

The guardian was larger than the first by half. Dark red armor covered its shoulders, and a thick ridge protected the head. The pressure from its body matched a Foundation Establishment cultivator's.

One major realm above him.

He could fight it. That didn't mean his ordinary sword would cut every plate cleanly.

The guardian lunged before the dust settled.

Shi Feng stepped toward its left side, caught a descending leg with his free hand, and cut at the joint with his sword. The edge opened the flesh but didn't sever it.

The beast slammed its body sideways.

Shi Feng braced his feet and held. The force drove him across the chamber, scraping two lines through the ash. He struck the nearer shoulder plate with his fist.

A crack spread across it.

The guardian shrieked and swung another foreleg around its body. Shi Feng turned his head away from the edge, but the hook caught his left shoulder.

Cloth tore. Blood ran down his arm.

He felt anger at once. Not fear. This thing had just damaged his new robe and opened a deep cut beneath it.

Shi Feng caught the hooked limb before it could pull free and used both hands to wrench it outward.

The joint cracked.

The guardian struck him with its head. He took the blow on his forearm, stepped back once, and drove the sword into the exposed flesh beside the broken plate.

The blade sank halfway.

Its steel bent when the beast twisted.

Shi Feng pulled it out before it snapped entirely. He didn't need to keep trading blows against the heaviest armor. The beast's joints and damaged shoulder were already within reach.

“Come on, then,” Shi Feng said.

The guardian came.

He met it with a short clan sword thrust, turned the blade outward as its head moved, and cut through the flesh beneath the jaw. It was the same simple turn he'd practiced beside the drying shed. The movement kept the edge against the wound instead of wasting the stroke in the air.

Blood splashed over his sleeve.

The guardian reeled, then struck the furnace wall with its good foreleg. A long crack opened in the bricks behind Shi Feng's pack.

He grabbed the strap and moved it toward the first corpse. His left shoulder throbbed. Warm blood dripped from his fingertips, but his grip remained strong.

A normal Bone Refinement cultivator would've been badly outmatched. Shi Feng wasn't normal. He could still overpower this beast, provided he stopped letting it swing freely at his wounded side.

He backed into the center of the chamber and raised the bent sword. The guardian lowered its head. Its broken leg dragged, and blood bubbled beneath the jaw.

Neither of them was finished.

Behind the yard wall, Zheng Bao began praying so loudly that the words carried through the dust.

Shi Feng glanced at the cracked roof, then back at the beast.

“Pray for your kiln,” Shi Feng said. “I'm busy.”

chapters.title: A Fist Through Red Armor
chapters.html:
The guardian charged across the kiln.

Shi Feng stepped left of the doorway. The guardian’s head came straight at his chest, but its right side scraped the kiln wall. The wall blocked its turn.

He stepped inside the jaws’ reach before the beast could pull back. He drove the bent sword beneath its jaw and shoved with his whole body. The blade entered the wound he'd already opened, then struck hard bone and snapped.

Half the steel stayed inside the beast.

Shi Feng threw the broken hilt aside and caught the edge of its upper plate. The guardian pushed him backward. His boots struck the fallen bricks near the furnace, but he kept his feet and pulled the head downward.

Its good foreleg swept toward his wounded shoulder. He punched the joint with his right fist.

The leg bent sideways. A sharp pain shot through his wrist.

Shi Feng's expression tightened. The force had cracked the thick joint and damaged his own wrist at the same time. His first forefinger bone was stronger than before, but most of the hand and arm still needed refinement.

He couldn't keep putting every heavy clash through that little section.

The beast tried to lift its head.

Shi Feng caught the lower jaw with his left hand, ignored the pain in his shoulder, and drove his knee upward.

The damaged armor shattered.

Dark blood ran over his boot.

The guardian staggered. Shi Feng moved with it, planted his foot against a fallen block, and forced its head toward the floor.

It was strong enough to fight a Foundation Establishment cultivator. So was he.

The difference was that it only knew how to bite, slash, and use its weight. Shi Feng could choose where his strength went.

He drew Wei Kuo's knife.

A red plate covered most of the back of the creature's skull. Below it, the neck bent where the head joined the body. The wound beneath the jaw gave him room to turn that joint.

Shi Feng pulled once more and drove the knife into the soft gap.

The beast thrashed.

Its body struck his left shoulder and slammed him against the furnace wall. Pain ran through the torn flesh, but he didn't lose his grip.

He pushed the knife deeper.

The guardian struck the wall again. Bricks broke around his back.

Shi Feng planted both feet and wrenched the hilt sideways. The blade tore through the flesh beneath the skull.

The creature's legs folded.

He held it down until the last spasm stopped, then pulled the knife free and stepped away. For a few breaths, only his breathing disturbed the chamber.

The first guardian had been an easy kill. The larger one had cost him a shoulder wound and a damaged wrist. He'd killed it with his own body and ordinary steel.

Next time, he'd buy better steel.

A shaky voice came from outside.

“Is it dead?” Zheng Bao called.

“Yes,” Shi Feng said.

“Both of them?” Zheng Bao asked.

“Do you want one left alive?” Shi Feng asked.

“No! Absolutely not!” Zheng Bao cried.

Shi Feng put away the knife and sat beside his pack.

His right wrist was swelling. He could move the fingers, but turning the hand hurt. The left shoulder had a deep cut and heavy bruising from the wall. Blood had soaked the sleeve.

He cut the cloth away, folded a clean strip over the wound, and pressed it firmly until the bleeding slowed.

Then he used two flat pieces of kiln wood to splint his wrist. Tying the final knot with one injured hand was troublesome. He caught the cloth between his teeth and pulled it tight.

Outside, something much larger moved along the road.

The mother.

Its cry rolled through the broken buildings. Gray legs passed above the yard wall, followed by a body higher than the surviving roof.

Shi Feng stayed seated.

He didn't live here. Nobody in Yunze Town was depending on him. After fighting two guardians, he had no interest in rushing outside to challenge the mother over somebody else's stolen eggs.

“Don't make a sound,” Shi Feng told Zheng Bao.

The potter obeyed so quickly that even his prayers stopped.

The mother lowered its head beside the kiln mouth. Its nostrils widened. A low sound came from its throat, and its eyes fixed on Shi Feng. The smell of the young beast he'd killed still clung to him. Washing his robe hadn't removed it all.

Shi Feng tightened his good hand around the knife. Standing now would pull the shoulder open, but staying seated wouldn't stop a charge.

Then an egg cried from the eastern lane.

A hunter ran past with a smaller basket. One pale egg fell, struck the road, and split. The mother's head snapped toward it. More cries answered from the Wei storehouse farther east.

Its foreleg smashed through a corner house. It followed the eggs, tearing down anything that blocked the lane. Shi Feng stayed still until its body passed the kiln mouth. It hadn't forgiven him. The stronger scent had simply drawn it elsewhere first.

Shi Feng waited until its footsteps grew farther away. Then he took a water flask from the pack and drank.

A section of roof fell somewhere down the road. Shi Feng listened until the mother's cry moved beyond it.

“Is it coming back?” Zheng Bao whispered.

“How would I know?” Shi Feng said.

“Can you go and look?” Zheng Bao asked.

Shi Feng looked at his bloody sleeve.

“Can you?” Shi Feng asked.

Zheng Bao fell silent.

The potter's courage apparently ended at his own wall. Shi Feng didn't blame him for staying there, but he wasn't going outside on the man's behalf.

He moved his pack to a dry spot beneath the remaining roof and leaned his back against the furnace. The bricks were warm from an earlier firing. At least the potter's broken kiln had something useful left.

His jaw ached from clenching it through the fight. He loosened it, spat dust from his mouth, and checked the knife. A short blade, a plain handle, and no damage.

Wei Kuo had owned a better knife than Shi Feng's sword. That was almost annoying.

He cleaned it with a strip from the torn sleeve and laid it across his knee. Nobody was getting it while he slept.

As the yard grew quiet, Shi Feng placed his left palm against the second guardian's exposed neck.

Its vitality entered him slowly. He controlled the flow instead of taking everything in a rush. Warmth spread through his chest and helped him steady his breathing.

The shoulder still hurt. The wrist remained damaged. Devouring a beast gave him resources his body could use; it didn't turn a serious wound into something that never happened.

He removed his hand and circulated qi until the first gain settled.

Only then did he draw again.

Two guardians held far more strength than the beasts he'd hunted around the spring. He intended to use it carefully over the next few days. Wasting a resource through impatience would be stupid, and he wasn't in a hurry to prove otherwise.

The first little bones took part of the gain. The rest nourished his flesh and supported recovery. He examined the result after the heat eased.

Only a few bones refined. Most of the two hundred and six bones still needed work.

He'd barely begun work across the full skeleton. The warmth reached the larger bones, but they needed more than a few breaths of cultivation. He let the gain settle and stopped before his wounded shoulder began to ache again.

His combat strength was another matter. The dead Foundation Establishment-grade beast at his feet made that clear enough. Shi Feng rested his head against the wall and closed his eyes for a while.

Somewhere outside, a baby was crying. A man shouted for water. Another insisted his storehouse key was still inside the house that had just fallen.

Yunze Town was beginning to sound human again. When Shi Feng opened his eyes, light came through the broken roof at a different angle. He ate a piece of bread, drank more water, and checked the shoulder binding.

The bleeding had slowed to a stain.

He touched the remaining Jade Marrow Dew bottle inside his pack. It was unbroken. So was the ordinary Bone Refinement manual, though dust filled the folded pages.

His sword was gone. The knife would have to serve until he bought another. Shi Feng pulled the pack closer, placed the knife beside his good knee, and looked toward the doorway.

A mirror on the end of a pole crept around the doorpost.

Behind it, Zheng Bao whispered fiercely to himself.

“Dead means dead,” Zheng Bao muttered. “It can't bite the mirror.”

chapters.title: Twelve Stones for a Broken Kiln
chapters.html:
The mirror shook when it found the guardian's open mouth. Zheng Bao pulled the pole back so quickly that it struck the doorpost. A sharp crack came from the glass.

“My mirror!” Zheng Bao cried.

“The beast didn't touch it,” Shi Feng said.

The potter peered around the doorway. He was a round man with dust in his eyebrows and a yellow talisman tied around his neck. It hung upside down.

His eyes moved from the two corpses to the bloody cloth at Shi Feng's shoulder.

“You're still alive?” Zheng Bao blurted.

Shi Feng looked at him.

Zheng Bao hurriedly waved one hand.

“I meant it’s good that you’re alive!” Zheng Bao said.

He crept past the dead jaw and picked up a small blue bowl. One side was crushed. His excitement faded.

“My best glaze,” Zheng Bao muttered.

Shi Feng waited while the potter rubbed the unbroken edge with his thumb. For three breaths, Zheng Bao forgot even the spirit stones. Then he looked at the cracked roof and remembered them all at once.

“Who’s paying for my kiln?” Zheng Bao demanded.

There was no room left in him for terror when money needed discussing. Shi Feng lifted his water flask. It was almost empty.

“Is the well still clear?” Shi Feng asked.

“You brought monsters into my yard!” Zheng Bao said.

“They climbed over your wall,” Shi Feng said.

“Because you came inside!” Zheng Bao said.

“So bill them,” Shi Feng said.

Zheng Bao looked at the corpses. He could imagine charging a person. He couldn't quite imagine where a spirit beast kept its stones.

The potter wasn't a cultivator. All his life, he'd relied on thick walls and louder complaints than his neighbors. Today the first had failed him, and the second hadn't improved matters.

He poked the nearer guardian with his pole.

Nothing moved.

He poked harder, found a patch of shell weakened by Shi Feng's devouring, and broke a piece free. Pale dust spilled onto the floor.

Zheng Bao's face fell.

“It's ruined!” Zheng Bao said. “I thought the plates would pay for the roof!”

“Some of them might,” Shi Feng said.

He didn't offer to explain which parts he'd drained. The physique was his own secret, and the potter's disappointment didn't require an answer.

Zheng Bao looked at Shi Feng again. The familiar face finally gave him something easier to understand.

“You're the Shi clan's cripple,” Zheng Bao said.

“That's what people call me,” Shi Feng said.

“Then how did you survive?” Zheng Bao asked.

“I didn't wait for them to chew me,” Shi Feng said.

The potter stared. He glanced at the broken sword on the floor, then at the knife beside Shi Feng's knee.

There was clearly a story here. He wanted to hear it, but he wanted compensation more.

“Fine,” Zheng Bao said. “If you're staying, twelve spirit stones.”

“For what?” Shi Feng asked.

“Hiding in my kiln,” Zheng Bao said. “And sleeping here. And the mess.”

Shi Feng looked through the missing roof.

“Three days,” Shi Feng said. “Water included.”

Zheng Bao opened his mouth to object, then saw the knife and closed it. The youth was injured, but both beasts were dead. Trying to drag him outside would be foolish.

“Three days,” Zheng Bao agreed.

Shi Feng paid twelve stones.

That settled the matter. He'd buy a little shelter and let the potter tell himself it counted as compensation.

Zheng Bao fetched clean water from a covered well in the rear yard. He also brought a stool without being asked, then demanded to know whether it counted as another day's rent.

“No,” Shi Feng said.

The stool remained anyway.

“Eight spirit stones,” Sun Cheng said, setting his medicine box beside the bed. “I clean the shoulder, change the dressing, and fix that splint. You keep both arms.”

Shi Feng pushed eight stones across the plank.

“Go ahead,” Shi Feng said.

Zheng Bao looked disappointed. He'd brought a surgeon and expected a lively argument about the price. Instead, Sun Cheng already had the cloth unfolded and a basin between his feet.

Zheng Bao put the bed in a covered corner of the damaged kiln. Dust covered the high shelf, and a reed screen kept the morning glare out. Outside, someone kept shouting for workers to move broken tiles.

Sun Cheng cut away the dirty dressing. His expression changed when he saw the shoulder.

“A beast did this?” Sun Cheng asked.

He set a carved wooden fish beside the medicine box. Its tail opened to reveal his needles.

“My granddaughter made it,” Sun Cheng said before Shi Feng asked. “Don’t put your bloody sleeve on it.”

Shi Feng moved his arm. Sun Cheng grunted approval and went back to prodding the wound. He treated the wooden fish more gently than the patient.

“It hit harder than the wall,” Shi Feng said.

“You hit a wall too?” Sun Cheng asked.

“It was behind me,” Shi Feng replied.

Sun Cheng grunted and began cleaning the wound. He was an ordinary surgeon, not a cultivator. His hands were steady, and he didn't waste time asking how a cripple survived something that could break a kiln.

Shi Feng bit a folded cloth when the medicine entered the torn flesh. He could bear pain. That didn't mean pain felt pleasant.

The surgeon loosened the right wrist splint, checked the swelling, and bound it again with straighter supports. This time the wood didn't press against the most tender part.

“Better?” Sun Cheng asked.

“Much better,” Shi Feng said.

“Then don't ruin my work before tomorrow,” Sun Cheng said.

Zheng Bao leaned over his shoulder. The potter's face turned pale at the bloody water.

“Is he going to need another room?” Zheng Bao asked.

“He needs this one,” Sun Cheng said.

“But what if there's fever?” Zheng Bao asked.

“Then he still needs this one,” Sun Cheng replied.

Shi Feng looked at the potter.

“You aren't charging by the illness, are you?” Shi Feng asked.

“No! Of course not!” Zheng Bao said, taking a step back.

Sun Cheng left two packets of swelling powder and a small pot of salve. He explained when to change the dressing, collected his empty cloth, and stood.

“Can I walk tomorrow?” Shi Feng asked.

“If you walk instead of wrestling beasts,” Sun Cheng said. “I won't promise anything if you choose the second.”

“Walking will do,” Shi Feng said.

The surgeon nodded and went out. A woman in the yard immediately caught his sleeve and dragged him toward another patient. Sun Cheng didn't look surprised.

Shi Feng slept after the treatment. When he woke, the shoulder no longer burned, and the wrist could rest without a sharp ache. He circulated the guardian's stored vitality until the pressure inside his chest eased, then ate the bread in his pack.

Outside, Zheng Bao was charging neighbours two coppers apiece to peer at the dead guardians through the broken doorway and trading gossip about the eastern street: the Split-Maw mother had followed the stolen eggs straight into the Wei family’s eastern storehouse and smashed all three buildings flat before returning to the marsh.

Shi Feng listened from behind the reed screen until a more familiar voice joined the gawkers.

“Did that Shi boy come through the tide with his pack?” Tang Jiu asked near the gate. “Still carrying that short hill-knife at his belt?”

“What’s it worth to you?” Zheng Bao asked cautiously.

“Two stones if you tell me when he goes to the customs shed for his travel seal,” Tang Jiu muttered. “The Wei stewards lost their storehouse and their young master in the same week, and Wen Ruxiu at the customs desk is paying for word of anyone who took the western hill road.”

Footsteps hurried back toward the street. A moment later, Zheng Bao edged around the screen with a bowl of porridge and an uneasy expression.

“You heard him?” Zheng Bao asked in a small voice.

“Every word,” Shi Feng said, taking the bowl. “Come with me to the customs shed when I fetch my seal. You can carry the water jar back.”

Zheng Bao looked at the knife beside the bowl and nodded very quickly.

chapters.title: The Broker’s Last Offer
chapters.html:
“Don't put your hand there. The seal's wet,” Wen Ruxiu said.

Shi Feng moved his fingers and laid thirty-five spirit stones beside the paper.

The customs shed still had a roof. That made it busier than most buildings in Yunze Town. People crowded beneath the eaves with bundles, children, and whatever they could pull from their ruined homes.

Wen Ruxiu blew on the red mark and passed the departure paper across her desk.

“Show that at the road posts,” Wen Ruxiu said. “And don’t fold it until the seal dries!”

A man behind Shi Feng blew on his own paper.

“Not with your mouth full!” Wen Ruxiu snapped.

The man stopped chewing. Wen Ruxiu wiped a grain of rice from the desk and stamped the next permit with unnecessary force. She had survived the beast tide. She wasn’t going to lose the rest of her morning to filthy documents.

“I can walk,” Shi Feng replied.

“The road's long,” Wen Ruxiu said.

“I've noticed,” Shi Feng said.

When Wen Ruxiu wrote his name into the ledger, the tip of her brush paused for half a beat. She glanced up at his face, then down at the private watch list pinned beneath her inkstone—the one Gao An had paid five spirit stones to keep updated.

“Wait while I enter the counter-slip,” Wen Ruxiu said smoothly. Turning toward the rear lattice, she lifted a wooden tally peg from the sill—the prearranged signal for the runner waiting in the alley behind the customs shed.

Shi Feng caught the reflection of the runner’s dark blue lapel moving past the oiled paper window. He folded his stamped permit into his coat without comment.

Outside, the customs-shed lane was jammed with handcarts, stacked baggage crates, and townspeople arguing over mule hire. Zheng Bao stood near the water trough holding two salvaged bowls, his eyes darting nervously toward the narrow baggage passage beside the shed wall.

Tang Jiu stepped out from between the stacked crates, flanked by two Wei household men. Wei Song carried a heavy iron-shod staff, and Du Heng kept a hand on his short sword. Both were in Qi Condensation.

“That’s him!” Tang Jiu said quickly, pointing at Shi Feng’s waist before the crowd by the trough could drift closer. “He walked out of Heilu Marsh wearing Ma Liang’s skinning knife after all three hunters vanished, and he came down the western hill path wearing Young Master Wei Kuo’s dagger!”

Zheng Bao nearly dropped his bowls behind the water trough. Two carters tying a load at the mouth of the passage froze, staring at the Wei household badges.

“Step into the baggage lane, cripple,” Wei Song ordered, swinging his staff across the exit. “Our eastern storehouse is rubble and Young Master Wei Kuo is dead. Master Wei Renshan is returning today—you can either walk to the Wei courtyard with your hands tied or be carried there in a sack!”

“And my ten stones?” Tang Jiu demanded, edging behind Du Heng. “Clerk Wen’s runner said you’d pay as soon as he stepped out with the west-road permit!”

“Take it off his corpse once we’re behind the crates,” Du Heng snapped, drawing his short sword as he lunged to herd Shi Feng into the narrow passage between the customs wall and the timber stacks.

At the mouth of the lane, Zheng Bao ducked behind the trough while the two carters scrambled back against their mule cart.

Wei Song brought the iron-shod staff whistling down at Shi Feng’s collarbone to drop him out of sight of the main street.

Shi Feng stepped inside the arc and caught the oak shaft in his left hand.

The blow stopped dead. Wei Song’s eyes bulged as he poured Qi Condensation force into both arms, but the wood didn’t budge a finger’s breadth. Before Wei Song could draw breath to shout, Shi Feng yanked him forward by the staff and drove the heel of his palm into the man’s breastbone.

With a sharp crack, Wei Song slammed backward into the stacked crates, bringing a pile of timber down over his chest.

Du Heng cursed and thrust his short sword at Shi Feng’s ribs. Shi Feng pivoted off his rear heel—using the shortened turn he had practiced—caught Du Heng’s sword wrist against the brick wall, and drove Wei Kuo’s dagger beneath his chin. Du Heng slid down the customs-shed wall without a second cry.

Tang Jiu bolted for the street corner. Shi Feng caught the back of his collar in one stride. In panic, the broker slashed backward with a sleeve knife; Shi Feng angled his splinted right forearm so the blade bit into the hardwood splint strips instead of his flesh, twisted Tang Jiu’s wrist until the fingers opened, and caught the falling knife in his left hand.

“Young Master Shi! It’s a misunderstanding!” Tang Jiu choked out.

“You already spent the ten stones in your head,” Shi Feng said.

Tang Jiu’s other hand darted for a lime packet at his belt. Shi Feng drove the blade through his throat and let him drop beside the timber stack.

At the mouth of the passage, Zheng Bao was pale as kiln clay, and a carter peering over the mule’s rump clapped a hand over his own mouth. Through the side lattice of the customs shed, Wen Ruxiu stared down at the three bodies in the baggage lane, her fingers trembling on the window bar as she realized what her five-stone tip had just cost the Wei household.

Shi Feng wiped the knife, took the two retainers’ purses from their belts, and walked out past the water trough.

“Your bowls are going to fall,” Shi Feng told Zheng Bao in passing.

Zheng Bao clutched them to his chest and couldn’t even nod. Within the quarter hour, half the customs queue was whispering that two Wei retainers and Tang Jiu had tried to jump the Shi boy behind the permit shed and hadn’t stood up again. By then, Shi Feng had already collected his bedding from the kiln yard.

chapters.title: His Son Died Standing
chapters.html:
“Master Wei Renshan is here!” Zheng Bao shouted.

Shi Feng looked up from his pack. The potter ran through the yard, nearly knocked over a rack of bowls, and caught it with both hands before remembering why he was running.

“He's flying!” Zheng Bao said. “On a sword! A real sword!”

“You’ve seen flying swords before,” Shi Feng said.

“Not stopping above my roof!” Zheng Bao replied.

His voice cracked. He caught a bowl sliding from the rack, set it safely down, and knocked over the one beside it with his elbow. Shi Feng took his pack before the man could blame him for that too.

“Where?” Shi Feng asked.

“Above the main road,” Zheng Bao replied. “He's going to his house.”

Shi Feng tied the pack shut.

So the father was back. The two retainers in the customs lane wouldn't be delivering their news, but someone else would. Yunze Town had enough loose tongues to fill the empty shops.

He rolled his bedding and tucked it beneath the strap. His shoulder pulled painfully when he lifted the bundle, so he shifted the weight to the other side.

Zheng Bao watched with a pale face.

“You're leaving now?” Zheng Bao asked.

“That's what a departure seal is for,” Shi Feng said.

“But you paid for three days!” Zheng Bao said.

“You can keep the rest,” Shi Feng replied.

For a moment, Zheng Bao looked pleased. Then he remembered who was flying above the road, and the pleasure disappeared.

“Don't tell him I hid you,” Zheng Bao said.

“You rented me a corner of a broken kiln,” Shi Feng replied. “You didn't hide anything.”

The potter looked miserable. Shi Feng left him holding the bowl rack.

Outside, people crowded at the lane's mouth. A broad sword floated above the main street, carrying a man in dark blue. His face was narrow, and two long gray strands fell from his temples. Every shopkeeper below him bowed or found a reason to look at the ground.

Early Foundation Establishment.

In Yunze Town, that was enough to make a noisy street fall silent.

Wei Renshan didn't look at the broken houses. He swept past them toward his family's courtyard. His sword left a pale line above the roofs.

“That's real cultivation!” someone whispered.

“If he came yesterday, the market wouldn't look like this.”

“Keep your voice down! Do you want him to hear?”

“…”

Shi Feng stepped away from the crowd and took the western lane. There was no need to announce his departure beneath the man's flying sword.

At the next corner, a medicine seller was pulling a broken cabinet upright. Two helpers kept pushing from opposite sides. The cabinet swayed, and the seller shouted until both stepped away. He stared at it for a moment, then sat on the ground and rubbed his head.

The beast tide wasn't going to be repaired by a man flying above it.

Shi Feng stopped at the public well and filled his flask. The woman ahead of him needed help lifting her bucket over the stone rim. He lifted it with his good hand and set it beside her feet. She thanked him, then hurried back toward the damaged houses. He corked the flask and continued west.

He wasn't afraid of Wei Renshan's realm. A Foundation Establishment cultivator stood one major realm above him, but Shi Feng knew how much force his body could carry now. The problem was the street full of people.

A public fight would reveal more than he wanted to show. He'd rather leave quietly. If Wei Renshan insisted on following, they could speak where no one needed to bow.

The Wei courtyard held two covered bodies.

Wei Renshan landed beside them and stepped off his sword. A household servant fell to his knees before he reached the first cloth.

“Master, we searched for you!” Gao An cried. “The roads were cut off. We couldn't send anyone through!”

Wei Renshan pulled the cloth aside.

Wei Kuo lay beneath it. The young master's face was gray, and the cleaned robe couldn't hide the wound that killed him. The second body belonged to Luo San, his Qi Condensation servant.

Wei Renshan's expression darkened.

“Where?” Wei Renshan asked.

“Outside town,” Gao An said. “Hunters brought them back before the beast tide.”

“Who was with them?” Wei Renshan asked.

“Only Luo San went out with the young master,” Gao An said, his voice shaking as smoke still drifted from the ruined eastern storehouse where the Split-Maw mother had torn down three walls to get her eggs back. “And half an hour ago, Clerk Wen at the customs shed sent word that the suspect took a west-road permit—Wei Song and Du Heng tried to take him in the baggage lane beside the shed.”

“Where are they?” Wei Renshan asked coldly.

Gao An swallowed hard. “Both dead in the lane, Master. Along with the broker Tang Jiu. The carters say the boy broke Wei Song’s chest with one hand and walked out the west gate.”

Wei Renshan’s eyes turned colder than the steel at his side. His eastern storehouse was rubble, his son lay under a white cloth with his purse and knife missing, and now two more retainers were laid out in front of the town’s carters.

“Which road did he take?” Wei Renshan asked.

“The western quarry road toward Shuanghe Ferry, Master!” a breathless runner called from the gate.

Wei Renshan didn’t wait another breath. He stepped back onto his flying sword and shot into the western sky.

Shi Feng walked past the last houses and climbed the low road beside the old quarry.

A cart passed in the other direction with a woman sitting on rolled bedding. She slept with her mouth open while the driver kept talking to her. He didn't seem to notice she wasn't answering.

Beyond them, the road was empty.

Shi Feng stopped near a dry cutting in the hillside. Workers used to take clay and stone from it. Now thorn bushes filled the narrow tracks, and rain left shallow pools at the bottom.

He loosened his pack strap.

A shadow crossed the road.

Wei Renshan landed twenty paces ahead, the broad sword floating at his shoulder. The old man's eyes went first to the knife at Shi Feng's belt. Shi Feng set his pack on a flat stone.

“That's my son's,” Wei Renshan said.

“It was,” Shi Feng replied.

Wei Renshan's expression changed. He expected excuses, a denial, perhaps a youth begging for the chance to explain. Shi Feng gave him none of those.

“You killed him,” Wei Renshan said.

“He tried to kill me,” Shi Feng replied.

“And Luo San?” Wei Renshan asked.

“The same,” Shi Feng said.

The flying sword turned. Its point aimed at Shi Feng's throat.

Pressure spread across the road. Loose dust stirred around Wei Renshan's shoes, and the nearest thorn branches bent away from him.

Shi Feng kept his qi within his body. He stood with his feet apart, not kneeling and not drawing a weapon.

Wei Renshan was furious.

“Do you know who you're speaking to?” Wei Renshan demanded.

“A father who taught his son badly,” Shi Feng said.

The sword gave a sharp cry.

Wei Renshan raised a hand, then stopped. His gaze passed over the shoulder binding and the splinted wrist. The youth looked wounded, but his breathing hadn't changed under the pressure.

Rare medicine. Some body-strengthening treasure. There had to be a reason.

Wei Renshan wanted that reason before he broke the boy's neck.

“Kneel,” Wei Renshan said coldly. “Tell me where you found the medicine. Then you can explain why my son shouldn't have taken it.”

Shi Feng thought: the son wanted my prize, and the father wants everything left. They really are family.

He pointed toward the dry quarry cutting.

“If you want to fight, come down there,” Shi Feng said. “The road's narrow.”

“You think you can choose where you die?” Wei Renshan asked.

“I'd rather not block the carts,” Shi Feng replied.

He picked up his pack and walked down the short slope. The old man followed above the ground, his flying sword moving beside him.

At the bottom, Shi Feng laid the pack beyond the pools and turned. Rock walls enclosed three sides. No houses overlooked them, and no traveler could see below the road's edge.

Wei Renshan landed opposite him.

“One last chance,” Wei Renshan said. “Kneel! My son isn't someone a cripple can touch!”

Shi Feng loosened his good hand.

“Your son died standing,” Shi Feng said. “You can do the same.”

Far above the cutting, Gao An crawled behind a thorn bush. He had followed his master's sword on foot and arrived breathless. He could see Wei Renshan facing Shi Feng below. He dared not call out or move closer. If the master wanted a witness, he would ask for one.

chapters.title: One Realm Wasn’t Enough
chapters.html:
The flying sword crossed the quarry before Wei Renshan finished lowering his hand.

Shi Feng turned his shoulder. The point passed beside his neck and cut through the binding over his left arm. Blood warmed the cloth, but the blade didn't touch the bone.

He stepped forward.

Wei Renshan pulled two fingers back. The sword turned behind Shi Feng and came for his spine.

Shi Feng heard its sharp whistle and dropped his right heel. He turned his body without straightening his shoulders, shortening the old clan movement. The sword passed above his bent arm.

His teachers liked a broad, upright turn. A blade aimed at his back didn't care how good his stance looked.

Wei Renshan frowned.

“Quick feet won’t save you!” Wei Renshan shouted.

He kept his left hand behind his back, still trying to look like an elder disciplining a child. Shi Feng closed the distance between them. The old man’s hidden hand came forward in a hurry.

The sword rose and struck downward.

Shi Feng caught the flat behind its point with his left hand.

The blade stopped inches from his chest.

Wei Renshan's face changed.

Qi blazed along the metal. Shi Feng felt the sharp force scrape his palm, but it couldn't cut through his grip. He twisted the sword sideways and forced its point into the ground beneath his foot.

The old man pulled with all his strength.

The sword shuddered.

It didn't come free.

“Impossible!” Wei Renshan cried.

Shi Feng's shoulder throbbed. Holding the weapon pulled at the torn flesh, so he changed his grip and put more of his weight through the foot pinning it down.

His strength was greater than the force controlling the sword. That was all that mattered.

“It's a decent weapon,” Shi Feng said. “You rely on it too much.”

Wei Renshan struck with his palm.

A wave of qi swept across the shallow pool between them. Water burst upward. The blow hit Shi Feng's chest and tore a strip from his robe.

He didn't step back.

The old man's eyes widened.

“Bone Refinement?” Wei Renshan said. “You're only in Bone Refinement!”

Shi Feng thought: and you're only in Foundation Establishment. You should've asked before you started. He released the sword, crossed the distance in two steps, and drove his left fist into Wei Renshan's raised guard.

Bang!
