The protective qi broke. Wei Renshan's forearm folded against his chest, and the old man flew backward into the quarry wall. Cracked stone fell over his shoulders.

Shi Feng stopped in front of him.

His left dressing was wet. His right wrist ached beneath the splint. Neither injury prevented him from standing where Wei Renshan couldn't escape.

The old man raised his other hand.

Shi Feng caught that wrist too.

This time, Wei Renshan's face went pale before the bones broke.

“Wait!” Wei Renshan gasped. “We can discuss this!”

“You wanted me to kneel,” Shi Feng said.

“I was angry!” Wei Renshan cried. “A father loses his son. Wouldn't you be angry?”

Shi Feng increased the pressure.

“I'd be angry with the fool who taught him to rob people,” Shi Feng replied.

Wei Renshan screamed as his wrist broke. His knees gave way, but Shi Feng held him against the wall.

The flying sword trembled behind them. The old man still tried to call it back.

Shi Feng drew his ordinary knife.

“I have spirit stones!” Wei Renshan shouted. “Take them! I'll forget everything!”

“You won't,” Shi Feng said.

He drove the knife through the old man's throat and held him until the gathering qi scattered.

The flying sword dropped into the mud.

Shi Feng stepped away. Wei Renshan slid down the stone and lay still.

A Foundation Establishment cultivator died in a quarry outside Yunze Town. The fight took less than ten breaths.

Shi Feng wasn't pleased about the fresh blood on his sleeve. Otherwise, he didn't feel much about it.

Wei Kuo tried to rob and kill him. Wei Renshan came to finish the same job. Both failed. He wasn't going to leave the father alive so someone could repeat it tomorrow.

He wiped the knife and put it away.

“Still eight stones,” Shi Feng muttered.

He sat on a flat rock and peeled the loose edge of his dressing away. Sun Cheng's work wasn't entirely ruined, but the shoulder needed another clean binding. He took water and salve from his pack and dealt with it before searching the corpse.

The right wrist was worse. When he caught Wei Renshan's second hand, he used it without thinking. Now the swelling pressed against the wood again.

Shi Feng loosened the splint and tied it carefully. There was no need to admire his own strength while doing something stupid with an injury. After a short rest, he returned to the body.

Wei Renshan carried a cheap storage bag inside his robe. Shi Feng could open that. It wasn't a sealed storage ring or some high-level refined artifact needing Foundation Establishment qi.

He tipped its contents onto clean cloth.

Eight hundred and fifty-six spirit stones. Two spare robes. A packet of dried meat. A few bottles with labels he didn't trust enough to swallow. Several household papers and a narrow jade token completed the pile.

Shi Feng put the papers and jade back beside the corpse. He didn't need proof of who owned the quarry's dead man.

The spirit stones went into his own bag. He kept the dry meat and the useful spare cloth. The uncertain medicines stayed closed until someone qualified could tell him what they were.

There was no reason to guess with strange bottles when he could afford ordinary treatment now.

He picked up the flying sword.

Even cold, it looked much better than a town stall's ordinary steel. Pale lines ran near the guard, and the edge showed no damage from being forced into the ground. Shi Feng sent a thin thread of qi into the handle.

Nothing moved.

He tried once more, then stopped. Bone Refinement couldn't activate a refined artifact. Beating its owner didn't change that rule.

“Fine,” Shi Feng said. “You'll buy me something I can use.”

He cleaned the blade, wrapped it in spare cloth, and secured it along his pack. He could sell it at a proper trading house. Sky Pavilion's appraisal would settle any argument about its quality if a buyer wanted to try something.

The old man's body stayed against the quarry wall. Shi Feng didn't burn it or try to arrange a beast attack. His meridians remained his own business.

He lifted his pack with the good arm and climbed the slope. At the top, a crow landed near the abandoned road marker. It looked at him, looked toward the quarry, and gave a harsh cry.

Before putting the knife away, Shi Feng repeated the shortened turn once. The footwork kept his wounded shoulder away from the next stroke. He made the movement slowly, checked his balance, and decided to practice it each morning. Common clan basics were useful, but he didn't need to follow every old correction when a fight showed him something better.

“Don't look at me,” Shi Feng said. “I didn't invite him.”

The crow flew away.

Shi Feng turned toward the road out of Yunze Town. His shoulder and wrist would need days, but he had money, supplies, and no reason to return to the Wei household. There was a roadside shed beyond the western ridge where he could change the bandage in peace.

Then he'd leave.

Behind the thorn bush, Gao An waited until Shi Feng's footsteps disappeared. His master's attack had been first. That much he had seen clearly. The rest happened too quickly for a household servant to understand.

He hadn't seen a meridian examination or any device measuring cultivation. He knew only that Wei Renshan died and the supposed cripple walked away. Gao An pressed both hands over his mouth until he stopped shaking, then crawled back toward town.

The Wei household would hear his account. He had no wish to shout it across the market and invite Shi Feng to come looking for him.

Shi Feng continued west. The little storage bag rode beneath his robe, heavier with spirit stones than any purse he'd carried before. His shoulder needed rest. His next meal no longer needed to be cheap.

chapters.title: The Ferry Owner's Scale
chapters.html:
“Eighteen spirit stones! Baggage costs extra!” Song Deyuan shouted.

Shi Feng stopped at the edge of Shuanghe Ferry's landing. On the third morning after leaving Yunze Town, he finally reached a river too wide to cross on foot.

Two ferries were tied below the stone steps. One carried fishing baskets. The other had a flat deck large enough for loaded carts, and every traveler on the bank was waiting for it.

Song Deyuan stood beside a scale with one hand out.

“Don't block the steps!” Song Deyuan said. “Are you crossing or admiring the water?”

“I'm looking for the Jade Scale convoy,” Shi Feng replied.

“Then admire their water!” Song Deyuan said, pointing toward the warehouses.

A duck climbed onto the bottom step behind him. Song Deyuan kicked at it without looking. The duck bit his trouser hem and refused to let go.

“Whose miserable bird is this?” Song Deyuan shouted.

“Mine,” Yu Sanniang called from the queue. “It’s already paid for the crossing!”

Shi Feng went toward the warehouses while Song Deyuan tried to argue with the duck’s owner and escape its beak at the same time.

Shi Feng walked past him.

Behind the first warehouse, three carts stood beneath blue canvas covers. A pointed-bearded merchant watched two porters struggle with a wheel pin. He wore a plum robe and turned a jade ring whenever the hammer missed.

“Pei Rong?” Shi Feng asked.

The merchant immediately smiled.

“Ah, the right man at the right hour! Going west, young friend?” Pei Rong asked.

“To the capital,” Shi Feng said.

“Eighty stones. Crossing included. Meals aren't,” Pei Rong said.

“How long?” Shi Feng asked.

“A few days. We stop for business,” Pei Rong replied. “You can sit on the third cart if there's room.”

Shi Feng looked at that cart. The wheel leaned, and the porter underneath it was arguing with the man holding the hammer.

“Will it leave today?” Shi Feng asked.

“As soon as that pin goes in,” Pei Rong said.

“Then you might be here a while,” Shi Feng replied.

The merchant's smile stiffened.

A porter pulled the iron bar again. The corner of the cart rose a finger's width, slipped, and dropped. The man with the hammer shouted at him. They blamed each other while the pin stayed on the ground.

Shi Feng set down his pack.

“I'll lift it,” Shi Feng said. “Fresh shoulder dressing and a little swelling salve are included in my fare.”

Pei Rong's eyes flicked toward the bandage.

“You're injured,” Pei Rong said.

“It's still cheaper than another wheelwright,” Shi Feng replied.

Pei Rong looked at the two sweating porters.

“Done!” Pei Rong said.

Shi Feng handed over the eighty stones, then crouched beside the frame. He braced the cart on his left forearm, kept the right wrist straight, and rose. Six heavy cases of blades lifted with the cart.

The porters froze.

“Put the pin in,” Shi Feng said.

The hammering porter dropped his tool. He snatched it up and drove the pin home in three quick strikes. Shi Feng lowered the cart and stepped away.

“He lifted all of it!”

“Those are blade cases!”

“Did you see the bandage?”

“…”

Pei Rong stopped turning his ring.

“Your travel paper, young friend,” Pei Rong said. “I need the name for the passenger list.”

Shi Feng handed it over. The merchant glanced at the departure date and Yunze Town's red seal, then paused at the description beneath the name.

“You're Shi Feng,” Pei Rong said slowly. “From the Shi clan.”

“The fare's paid,” Shi Feng replied. “Remember the medicine.”

“The ruined meridians…” Pei Rong began.

“Don't prevent me from carrying things,” Shi Feng said.

Pei Rong looked at the cart again. He was surprised, but surprise didn't tell him a cultivation realm. He couldn't sense qi from the youth, and good body medicines could produce strange results.

“Of course, of course,” Pei Rong said. “Strong tonics! I'll get the salve.”

Shi Feng thought: let him think that. I didn't come here to explain my bones to a merchant.

He picked up his pack. Before he reached the steps, Song Deyuan blocked the porters rolling the first cart downhill.

“Overweight!” Song Deyuan shouted. “Twenty stones more!”

Pei Rong's smile vanished.

“The weight hasn't changed since you agreed to carry it,” Pei Rong said.

“My scale says it has,” Song Deyuan replied.

A woman carrying egg baskets started shouting at him too.

“You weighed my baskets twice!” Yu Sanniang cried. “They got heavier when I complained!”

“Then your hens lay heavy eggs!” Song Deyuan snapped.

He slapped the scale beam. One pan sat higher than the other, even with nothing in it. A cloth hung beneath the counter, hiding most of the support.

Shi Feng looked at the beam, then at the wooden peg jammed behind it.

That wasn't even a good hiding place.

He reached beneath the cloth and pulled the peg free. The pan dropped with a clang. Song Deyuan jumped back, and the waiting travelers fell silent.

Pei Rong took the peg from Shi Feng's hand.

“Does the river's current push this in too?” Pei Rong asked.

Song Deyuan's face turned red.

“It keeps the beam steady!” Song Deyuan said.

“It keeps your purse steady!” Yu Sanniang shouted. “Give me back my stones!”

Three more people pushed toward the counter. Song Deyuan hurried around it, waving both hands. His greedy trick might have worked on one traveler, but now the whole landing could see it.

Shi Feng went to the ferry while they argued. He didn't need to spend the morning punishing a fool who couldn't hide a peg.

The porters followed. Song Deyuan finally opened the chain and stopped demanding more money.

By the time the carts reached the deck, Yu Sanniang was counting a refund into her sleeve. She looked fierce enough to demand payment for the counting too.

The ferry pushed away from the steps. Water slapped its blunt side, and ferryman Yu Jiang poled until the current caught the hull.

Shi Feng sat beneath the stern awning. The wrapped sword lay between his feet, and the shoulder felt better after the fresh dressing Pei Rong provided.

The merchant sat beside him.

Two stone pillars stood farther upstream, with no bridge between them. Shi Feng pointed them out to the ferryman.

“What happened there?” Shi Feng asked.

“The Immortal Crossing Bridge!” Yu Jiang replied proudly. “They started it thirty years ago. Two Foundation Establishment cultivators came to lay the first stones.”

“Then why isn't it finished?” Shi Feng asked.

“The money was gone before the third pillar,” Yu Jiang said.

Yu Sanniang snorted from her seat by the rail.

“The bridge hasn't crossed the river, but its taxes crossed thirty years ago!” Yu Sanniang said.

The passengers laughed. Yu Jiang grinned and leaned against his pole.

“Don't say it so loudly,” Yu Jiang said. “They'll collect another tax to bring the first one back!”

Pei Rong rubbed his rings and looked toward the pillars.

“A finished bridge would be bad for Song Deyuan,” Pei Rong said.

“He wasn't born when they stopped building,” Yu Jiang replied. “Don't give him credit for everything!”

Shi Feng looked at the broad river between the two useless pillars. Even two Foundation Establishment cultivators couldn't make an official finish spending the money in the right place.

“Good eyes,” Pei Rong said. “You saved me twenty stones.”

“You agreed to the medicine before that,” Shi Feng replied.

“Fair is fair! I wasn't going to take it back,” Pei Rong said.

He rubbed his ring and looked toward the long bundle.

Shi Feng waited.

“I buy weapons,” Pei Rong said.

“I noticed the six cases,” Shi Feng replied.

“Ordinary ones. Better ones too,” Pei Rong said. “If a young friend has something he doesn't need…”

“Say a price after you've seen it,” Shi Feng said.

Pei Rong's smile widened. He didn't reach for the wrapping on the open deck. Whatever else he was, the merchant knew when a valuable object deserved a private room.

The ferry turned toward the far landing. Yu Jiang called to the men at the ropes, and the passengers stood to collect their baskets.

The road ahead climbed between green hills. Beyond them lay larger towns and, at last, the capital. He'd spent two mornings practicing the altered sword turn with his knife. Soon he'd have a proper blade again.

Pei Rong leaned closer.

“Our warehouse has a quiet room,” Pei Rong said. “We can talk there.”

Shi Feng rested a hand on the bundle.

“Bring your stones,” Shi Feng said.

chapters.title: Eight Hundred for Expensive Metal
chapters.html:
“Close the door,” Pei Rong said. “And don't let Bu Tie lean against it!”

A porter grumbled outside. The door shut, and Shi Feng put the long bundle on the warehouse table.

The room stood at the back of Jade Scale Trading House's western-bank store. Afternoon light entered through a high window. A chest of ordinary blades occupied one wall, and someone left a half-eaten pear beside the inkstone.

Pei Rong pushed the pear away and untied the wrapping.

His smile grew.

“Now this is better than farm tools,” Pei Rong said.

He lifted Wei Renshan's flying sword and turned it beneath the window. A little crystal lens appeared from his sleeve. He examined the edge, the pale lines near the guard, and the maker's stamp.

Pei Rong’s smile disappeared for a moment. He brought the blade close to the light and carefully wiped a smear from the maker’s stamp.

“See how the line joins beneath the guard?” Pei Rong asked. “No wasted stroke. Good work.”

“You can admire it after buying it,” Shi Feng said.

“Naturally, naturally,” Pei Rong replied, still looking through the lens.

This time he wasn’t fishing for a lower price. He liked the sword.

Shi Feng leaned against the table.

He knew how to handle an ordinary sword. He didn't know how to refine one, and he wasn't going to pretend that beating the owner made him an expert in its value.

Watching Pei Rong was easier. The merchant looked much too pleased for this to be worthless metal.

“Where'd you find it?” Pei Rong asked.

“Yunze Town,” Shi Feng said.

“After the beast tide?” Pei Rong asked.

“I'm selling a sword,” Shi Feng replied. “Are you buying a story?”

Pei Rong laughed and lowered the lens.

“Naturally, naturally. A merchant asks questions,” Pei Rong said.

“So does everyone who wants a lower price,” Shi Feng replied.

The merchant's fingers paused against the hilt.

“Four hundred,” Pei Rong said. “Cash. No delay.”

Shi Feng took the wrapping from the table.

Pei Rong watched him cover the blade.

“You haven't named your price!” Pei Rong protested.

“I can wait until the capital,” Shi Feng said.

“The capital has plenty of swords,” Pei Rong said.

“And a Sky Pavilion tower,” Shi Feng replied.

Pei Rong stopped smiling for a moment.

Everyone with valuable goods knew what that meant. Sky Pavilion appraised refined artifacts and traded them through its towers. Its reputation was older than most of Great Liang's merchant houses. Shi Feng didn't need to accept Pei Rong's estimate if he could afford to wait for a trusted one.

“The appraisal won't be free,” Pei Rong said.

“Neither is losing half the value,” Shi Feng replied.

The merchant rubbed both jade rings. He liked buying from people in a hurry. This wounded youth clearly wasn't in enough of one.

“Six hundred,” Pei Rong said.

Shi Feng tied the first cord.

Pei Rong looked at the knot, then at the chest of blades. The third cart would carry this sword all the way to the capital whether he bought it or not. If another merchant bought it there, he'd spend the trip watching his own lost profit.

He couldn't bear that.

“Eight hundred!” Pei Rong said. “I can't give you more!”

Shi Feng stopped tying.

“That's acceptable,” Shi Feng said. “Show me the stones.”

Pei Rong looked as if he wanted to take the offer back. Instead, he opened a cash box.

Eight hundred spirit stones changed hands. Shi Feng checked the amount, and the merchant wrote a short sale note. No long list of promises followed. Jade Scale Trading House owned the used refined artifact, and Shi Feng owned the payment.

He put his copy away.

The flying sword was valuable, but Bone Refinement couldn't activate it. Letting it sit in his pack wouldn't help his wrist or give him a longer reach in a fight.

Shi Feng thought: eight hundred stones can buy something useful. An expensive sword I can't command just makes the pack longer. Pei Rong locked the refined artifact in a narrow wooden case.

Then he turned toward the larger chest.

“A young man still needs a blade,” Pei Rong said. “Naturally, I've got a good one.”

“You just bought my sword. Now you want the money back?” Shi Feng asked.

“Only a little of it!” Pei Rong replied.

He took out a plain steel sword with a leather grip. No fine lines, no glowing edge. It was an ordinary forged weapon.

“Thirty-eight stones,” Pei Rong said.

“From an ancient sword mountain!” Pei Rong added.

“Which mountain?” Shi Feng asked.

“A very old one. Far away,” Pei Rong said.

Shi Feng ignored that part and looked at the steel.

Shi Feng drew it and checked the join beneath the guard. The grip didn't shift when he turned the hilt. He pressed the point against the floor and let the blade bend a little, then released it.

The steel returned straight.

“Thirty,” Shi Feng said.

Pei Rong sighed loudly.

“Young friend, you're cutting into my rice money,” Pei Rong said.

“You bought a sword for eight hundred,” Shi Feng replied. “You aren't eating rice.”

Pei Rong took the thirty stones.

Shi Feng buckled the ordinary sword at his waist. Wei Kuo's knife remained on the other side. This new blade couldn't fly, but it could cut without making him look like a man carrying a valuable refined artifact he couldn't use.

He liked it already.

Shi Feng tested a short thrust toward an empty corner. The point stayed steady when he stopped. He tried again with the grip shifted a little lower, then lifted the blade for a shallow cut.

His right wrist pulled against the splint. He lowered the sword at once. There was no need to prove a new weapon was sound by damaging the arm carrying it.

Pei Rong watched from the cash box.

“You still remember your lessons,” Pei Rong said.

“I didn't forget how to hold a sword,” Shi Feng replied.

“Naturally, naturally!” Pei Rong said quickly. “I meant it's a fine match.”

Shi Feng sheathed it. He wasn't going to argue over whether a cripple was allowed to remember swordsmanship. The sword was paid for, the sale money was in his bag, and the merchant no longer owned either. That was enough for one afternoon.

“Don't strike rocks with it,” Pei Rong said.

“Then don't sell me something that needs that warning,” Shi Feng replied.

Pei Rong suddenly found his lens worth cleaning.

Outside, Bu Tie was trying to lift a barrel onto the second cart. The porter pushed while another man pulled from above. The barrel reached the edge, rolled sideways, and trapped Bu Tie's sleeve beneath it.

“Stop pulling!” Bu Tie shouted. “That's my arm!”

Shi Feng set a shoulder against the barrel and shifted it just enough to free the cloth. Bu Tie pulled his arm back and sat down, breathing hard.

“Thank you, young master,” Bu Tie said.

“Move your sleeve first next time,” Shi Feng replied.

Bu Tie nodded. He was an ordinary porter, and he'd been lifting things since dawn. He didn't need a lesson about effort.

Shi Feng filled his flask at the pump and found a place beside the third cart. The convoy would leave in the morning. Until then, he could rest, change the shoulder dressing, and use the new sword somewhere clear of the workers.

He practiced in an empty corner behind the stable.

Three cuts. A shorter turn. A thrust without lifting the wounded shoulder too high.

The blade stopped where he wanted it to. He repeated the turn and changed the position of his rear foot. Better. The shortened movement left less time for another weapon to catch him.

It was still common clan swordsmanship. He just wasn't going to keep the mistakes because an old teacher liked how they looked.

When he returned, a broad man stood beside Bu Tie. A saber hung at his waist, and he kept one hand on its hilt while the porter talked.

Bone Refinement.

The man's gaze went to Shi Feng's new sword, then to the little bag at his belt.

“How much?” Xue Kun asked Bu Tie.

The porter pointed toward the warehouse.

Shi Feng walked past them and sat by his pack. He didn't care whether a guard counted his money in his head. Hands and blades were another matter.

Across the yard, Xue Kun smiled and stroked his saber's guard.

He clearly thought the money would be easier to handle than the sword.

chapters.title: Food Costs Extra
chapters.html:
Shi Feng stirred the porridge and counted three grains of rice. He waited for the rest to rise. None did.

Across the convoy's first roadside camp, Pei Rong held out his bowl with a pleased smile. The carts left Shuanghe's western warehouse that morning, and their afternoon stop was apparently an excuse to sell hot water.

“Food costs extra,” Pei Rong said.

“So does the rice?” Shi Feng asked.

The nearest porters laughed. Tian Laowu turned from the cooking pot with his ladle raised.

“There's rice in it!” Tian Laowu snapped.

“I found three grains,” Shi Feng replied.

“It settles at the bottom!” Tian Laowu said.

“Then give me the bottom,” Shi Feng said.

Tian Laowu looked into the pot. His face reddened.

Pei Rong suddenly became busy with a cart rope. Shi Feng drank the hot water, ate a cake from his own supplies, and decided he'd cook tomorrow.

When the carts started again, he sat beside a grain bale on the third cart. The road wound between fields of young green shoots. At one bend, four children threw dirt clods at a painted wooden target. They shouted every time someone missed, which was often.

The slow pace suited his shoulder. It also gave him time to read the ordinary Bone Refinement manual without a beast trying to eat the page.

Xue Kun rode beside the second cart. The Bone Refinement guard kept his saber where everyone could see it and shouted whenever a porter took too long at a stop. His gaze often returned to Shi Feng's belt.

Shi Feng ignored it. Looking wasn't an attack. If the guard wanted more than that, he could say so.

At the next village, Shi Feng bought rice, bean paste, spring onions, and a little salt. That evening, he set his own pot over a small fire beyond the cart wheels. He rinsed the rice, cut the onions, and let the bean paste dissolve in hot water before bringing it together.

The pot needed proper ingredients and someone to watch the heat.

Pei Rong wandered over with a bowl.

“Smells good!” Pei Rong said.

“It isn't finished,” Shi Feng replied.

“I can wait,” Pei Rong said, sitting down.

Shi Feng looked at the empty bowl.

“One spirit stone,” Shi Feng said.

Pei Rong's smile paused.

“We're traveling together,” Pei Rong said.

“Food costs extra,” Shi Feng replied.

The porters nearby laughed again. Pei Rong glared at them, then paid and held out his bowl.

Shi Feng filled his own first.

The merchant took a cautious mouthful, then another. Soon he was scraping the bottom with enough effort to make the spoon squeak.

Tian Laowu watched from the convoy pot.

“It's just bean paste,” Tian Laowu muttered.

“Then put some in yours,” Pei Rong said.

The cook's expression changed. The porters looked away before he could blame them for smiling.

Three men bought bowls. Another asked for credit until the capital. Shi Feng shook his head and ate the remaining portion himself.

Bu Tie squatted nearby and looked into his empty bowl.

“How long did you learn cooking?” Bu Tie asked.

“Long enough to stop burning it,” Shi Feng said.

“I cook every day,” Bu Tie said. “Mine still tastes bad.”

“Do you leave it on the fire while you load the carts?” Shi Feng asked.

Bu Tie looked embarrassed.

“Only when someone's shouting for me,” Bu Tie said.

“Someone's always shouting for you,” Shi Feng replied. “Move it off the fire first.”

The porter nodded and stood. He didn't suddenly become a better cook, but he took the empty bowl to the pump instead of leaving it for Shi Feng to wash. Across the camp, Tian Laowu tasted his own porridge and quietly added salt.

A few paid bowls covered his ingredients. Feeding thirty men would leave no time for cultivation.

After the fires settled, he took the sword and walked beyond the lanterns. He practiced each day since the quarry fight. Tonight he could repeat the same movements without stopping halfway to rest the shoulder.

A clear patch stood beside a shallow stream. Shi Feng practiced there with no bright edge along the blade and no qi spilling from his body.

Three cuts, a turn, a shortened thrust.

The shoulder no longer pulled sharply during the turn. His wrist still ached if he changed direction too fast. He slowed the movement, kept the point steady, and repeated it until his feet found the right places without thought.

Then he sat beneath a tree and cultivated. The strength from his earlier hunts was settling properly now. He guided it through the small bones in his hands and feet, refining one section before beginning another.

About five percent of the ordinary Bone Refinement work was done. That meant roughly ten small bones out of two hundred and six. The larger bones still needed far more resources.

It wasn't a high percentage. It was already enough to make a Foundation Establishment cultivator regret coming alone.

Shi Feng thought: I'll finish every bone. There's no point rushing into the next realm with half the work left. He returned before the watch changed and slept beside his pack.

On the sixth evening after the quarry fight, the convoy stopped at a roadside warehouse. The capital was still beyond the next two days of walking, but Pei Rong wanted to unload part of his goods here. Shi Feng washed his pot at the yard pump and started supper beneath an open shed.

Xue Kun sat down beside the fire.

“Kid,” Xue Kun said. “You forgot someone yesterday.”

Shi Feng put the lid down.

“Who?” Shi Feng asked.

“The man protecting this convoy,” Xue Kun said, tapping his saber.

“Pei Rong's over there,” Shi Feng replied. “Ask him for your pay.”

Xue Kun's ears reddened.

“Travelers show respect,” Xue Kun said. “A fellow carrying a fat purse should be grateful someone stands watch.”

“A bowl costs one stone,” Shi Feng said.

The guard leaned closer. He smelled of cheap wine and Tian Laowu's onions.

“What if a beast comes for the third cart?” Xue Kun asked. “I've only got two hands. Maybe I'll be busy elsewhere.”

“Then stay elsewhere,” Shi Feng said.

Xue Kun stared at him.

The nearest porter stopped splitting wood. Another lowered the bucket he was carrying.

“He said that to Xue Kun?”

“He didn't even move the pot.”

“The cripple really has a temper!”

“…”

Xue Kun had expected a frightened apology.

His hand closed on the saber's hilt.

Shi Feng looked at it.

The guard hesitated. Nothing in the youth's face suggested he cared whether that blade came out. Xue Kun didn't know why that made him uneasy, but it did.

“Hmph! I'm giving advice,” Xue Kun said.

“I didn't order any,” Shi Feng replied.

Xue Kun stood abruptly and strode toward the convoy kitchen. He shouted for a bowl loud enough to make Tian Laowu drop the ladle. Shi Feng took the lid off his own pot.

He filled a bowl for himself, then accepted the stones from two waiting porters. Neither mentioned Xue Kun.

Across the yard, Pei Rong checked his stacked crates while pretending he saw nothing. Tian Laowu finally put a proper scoop of rice into the convoy pot.

Before the cookfire died, a single covered silk-cart rolled into the warehouse yard and a familiar figure swung down with a spear in hand. Lin Shuang spotted Shi Feng beside the pot and walked over, dusting road grit from her cuffs.

“You didn’t get eaten in the kiln,” Lin Shuang said, looking from his healed shoulder to the pot. “Got a bowl left?”

“One stone for the carter, free for the warning on the roof,” Shi Feng said, filling a bowl for her and another for her grey-bearded carter, Zou Sheng.

“Fair trade,” Lin Shuang said, sitting on an upturned bucket. She jerked her chin toward the sealed brocade chests on her cart. “We’re hauling rejected tribute cloth back from the southern dye-works to the capital. Last month Crown Prince Sima Yu sent forty bolts of cloud brocade to the Ling household for Fairy Ling Qingzhu. My carter here drove the wagon—she didn’t even untie the ribbons before sending all forty bolts back out the gate.”

“Forty bolts of royal cloud brocade!” Zou Sheng grumbled over his bowl. “Worth enough to buy a street, and the First Fairy treated it like wet straw!”

Shi Feng listened with mild interest as he cleaned his blade. While the carter went back to check the mules, Lin Shuang lowered her voice and glanced toward the dark well near the side gate, where Xue Kun had just finished a quiet exchange with two men in short drivers’ coats who didn’t belong to Pei Rong’s crew.

“Your convoy guard has restless eyes,” Lin Shuang murmured, setting her empty bowl down. “Someone greased the iron bolt on that side gate an hour ago. Keep your sword near your hand tonight, Shi Feng.”

chapters.title: The Third Cart
chapters.html:
The third cart moved after the warehouse lamps went out.

Shi Feng had been sitting beneath the shed, settling the day's cultivation. He opened his eyes at the creak of a wheel. Pei Rong's drivers had finished unloading before supper. Nobody should have been moving cargo now.

Two men pushed the rear cart toward the side gate. Its mule was already harnessed. Near the well, Xue Kun inspected the roof as if a guard's work had suddenly moved into the sky.

Shi Feng stood. His bedding lay beside that cart, and he wasn't going to walk two days to the capital because someone fancied the wheels.

“Where are you taking it?” Shi Feng asked.

The nearer man stopped pushing. The scar-faced man wore a driver's short coat, but Shi Feng had eaten with the drivers. This one hadn't been among them.

“Night delivery,” Han Qiu said.

“Then wake the owner,” Shi Feng said.

His partner moved away from the mule. Both were in Qi Condensation. They looked past Shi Feng toward Xue Kun, who continued studying the roof.

Han Qiu's patience disappeared.

“Go back to sleep, cripple,” Han Qiu said. “You saw nothing.”

Shi Feng reached for the cart's side rail. Meng Da drew a narrow knife and rushed him. There was no warning cut. The blade went straight for Shi Feng's throat.

He caught the knife hand and pressed downward.

Meng Da's wrist cracked. Before the man could shout, Shi Feng struck him beneath the jaw. The blow lifted his feet off the ground. He landed behind the cart and lay still.

Han Qiu pulled a short crossbow from beneath his coat.

The bolt struck Shi Feng's chest.

It tore the outer cloth, bent against his body, and fell. Han Qiu stared as though his own weapon had betrayed him. Shi Feng crossed the gap, seized the bow, and drove its wooden stock into the thief's throat.

Han Qiu dropped against the wheel.

The whole exchange lasted only a few breaths. No qi flared across the yard. To someone looking from the gate, two thieves had rushed a young man and fallen behind the cart.

Xue Kun turned at the second impact. His expression changed completely.

“Thieves!” Xue Kun shouted. “Wake up! Thieves in the yard!”

He drew his saber and charged toward the cart. Shi Feng put one hand on the side rail and stopped the heavy wheel before it struck the fallen thief's leg.

“You noticed quickly,” Shi Feng said.

Xue Kun swallowed.

The warehouse door opened. Pei Rong emerged in a loose robe, one sleeve twisted inside out. Bu Tie followed carrying a lamp, then the other porters crowded behind him with poles and a frying pan.

“Where?” Pei Rong demanded.

Xue Kun pointed at the bodies.

“I caught them stealing the third cart,” Xue Kun said. “They resisted. Young Master Shi helped.”

Shi Feng looked at him. It was a fine speech for a man who hadn't reached the cart before both thieves died.

Bu Tie held the lamp closer. The bolt lay beside Shi Feng's shoe. Pei Rong bent to inspect the traces of the opened side gate, then turned toward his guard.

“Who unlocked that?” Pei Rong asked.

Xue Kun's grip tightened on the saber.

“Perhaps the watch forgot,” Xue Kun said.

“You were the watch,” Pei Rong said.

From the hayloft ladder above the shed, Lin Shuang stepped down with her spear resting on her shoulder. “He was watching the roof tiles very carefully, Master Pei,” Lin Shuang said dryly. “So carefully he missed the two men he let through the side gate before moonrise. Look under his saddle blanket.”

Bu Tie hurried into the stable and came back holding a tied purse from beneath Xue Kun’s saddle blanket, with a cargo tally tucked under the cord listing everything loaded on the third cart.

Pei Rong took it. His face no longer carried any smile.

“How much were they giving you?” Pei Rong asked.

Xue Kun took a step back.

“Only a share of the goods!” Xue Kun said. “I didn't tell them to hurt anybody! They said they'd roll it away while everyone slept!”

The porters stared. Bu Tie looked at the frying pan in his companion's hand, then back at the man hired to protect them.

“You sold our cart?” Bu Tie asked.

“It wasn't your cart!” Xue Kun snapped.

“It wasn't yours either,” Pei Rong said.

Xue Kun's anger collapsed. He looked toward Shi Feng again, this time with real fear. He'd thought a medicine-fed cripple could be frightened away from a purse. Now the boy stood beside two dead Qi Condensation thieves without even breathing hard.

Bone Refinement should have given Xue Kun confidence. Instead, he became painfully aware that his saber was still outside its scabbard.

He put it away.

“Master Pei, I've served your trading house for years,” Xue Kun said. “I was drunk. I made a foolish bargain.”

Pei Rong opened the purse and counted enough stones to confirm the amount. He wasn't interested in hearing the whole history of the guard's foolishness.

“Your wages settle the missing watch and the trouble,” Pei Rong said. “Leave the badge.”

Xue Kun touched the Jade Scale token at his belt.

“Where am I supposed to go tonight?” Xue Kun asked.

“Try looking at roofs elsewhere,” Shi Feng said.

Bu Tie burst out laughing. Two porters joined him before remembering the bodies. Xue Kun's face turned from pale to red. He unfastened the badge and dropped it into Pei Rong's hand.

Pei Rong had the warehouse watch take his account of the theft. Xue Kun admitted arranging stolen cargo. Nobody claimed he'd ordered the knives or knowingly arranged a killing. By dawn he was walking out with his own bedding and no position in the convoy.

Shi Feng didn't follow him. The men who tried to kill him were already dead.

Pei Rong stopped beside the repaired side gate while the workers prepared breakfast.

“Naturally, your fare is returned,” Pei Rong said, giving Shi Feng a small purse. “A passenger shouldn't have to guard his own cart.”

“Apparently he should,” Shi Feng said.

Pei Rong rubbed his jade ring, glancing from the dented scabbard throat to the deep finger marks Shi Feng had left in the hardwood cart rail when stopping the wheel.

“You'll sit beside the driver today,” Pei Rong said.

“I'll sit where the cooking pot is,” Shi Feng said.

Bu Tie lifted the pot at once and carried it to the driver's bench. As the carts rolled onto the capital highway at sunrise alongside Lin Shuang’s brocade wagon, hoofbeats thundered past them from the east—a relay rider in the dark blue vest of the Wei household, spurring a lathered horse straight toward the capital’s southern gate with a sealed dispatch tube strapped to his back.

Lin Shuang reined her mount beside the third cart and looked after the dust cloud. “The Wei family of Yunze has a cousin sitting as a clerk in the Southern Gate office,” she told Shi Feng quietly. “If that rider’s carrying your name, the gate table will have it before noon.”

chapters.title: The Wei Inquiry
chapters.html:
The capital walls rose above the river plain before noon.

At the outer fork where the cloth road branched toward the northern looms, Lin Shuang tapped her spear haft against the third cart’s rail in farewell. “If the southern gate looks crowded, try the water-gate,” she told Shi Feng. “And if you’re still in the city next month, the brocade yard is behind West Market.”

“Travel safe,” Shi Feng said.

Pei Rong’s three carts rolled on into the southern gate queue. Great Liang’s capital spread along the water with high watchtowers and enough wagons outside the arch to swallow Yunze Town’s whole market. Shi Feng stepped down to walk beside the third cart with his sheathed sword at his waist and his departure permit in hand.

At the entry table under the stone arch, a Bone Refinement gate officer named Cheng Mao was checking permits while two spear guards stood beside a freshly pasted wooden board. Waiting right behind the officer’s shoulder stood a rider in a dust-streaked Wei household robe—Wei Min—his lathered horse tied to the guard rail.

When Shi Feng placed his Yunze permit on the table, Cheng Mao’s ink-stained finger stopped on the name.

“Shi Feng. Qingshi Town. Came through Yunze,” Cheng Mao read aloud. He glanced sideways at the stamped inquiry slip pinned to the board, then signaled the two spear guards to step across the archway.

Their iron spear butts came down on the flagstones, blocking the path into the city.

“Hold your pack right there,” Cheng Mao said, resting a hand over the permit. “A provisional inquiry notice was entered at this gate an hour ago by the Wei household of Yunze, endorsed by Clerk Wei in the Southern Ward office.”

Wei Min stepped forward at once, his Qi Condensation aura flaring thinly as he fixed his eyes on Shi Feng. “Master Wei Renshan and Young Master Wei Kuo died outside Yunze Town,” Wei Min said sharply. “A household witness saw what happened by the western quarry. Officer Cheng, hold him in the gatehouse until our capital elders arrive to take him back!”

The travelers in line behind them backed away hastily, and Bu Tie froze beside the lead mule’s bridle.

Shi Feng didn’t reach for his hilt, and his breathing didn’t change. “Is that a royal arrest warrant, Officer, or a private household complaint?” Shi Feng asked calmly.

Cheng Mao frowned at the paper in his hand. “It’s a provisional gate summons for questioning. Without a magistrate’s arrest seal I don’t put chains on you for a border-town feud—but nobody under an active gate inquiry enters the capital unless a registered capital house signs surety for his residence and appearance.”

Wei Min sneered. “Who in the capital is going to sign surety for a crippled country wanderer? Lock him in the watch room!”

Behind the third cart, Pei Rong stood with both hands in his plum sleeves. At the words Master Wei Renshan died outside Yunze Town, the merchant’s fingers went completely still around his jade rings.

Locked inside the narrow wooden case under the third cart’s canvas sat a Foundation Establishment flying sword with the Wei family’s private workshop stamp beneath its guard—a sword this bandaged youth had sold him at Shuanghe Ferry for eight hundred stones.

Pei Rong looked at the calm back of the young man standing before two crossed spears. He didn’t say a single word about the sword, and he didn’t let his face show what he had just pieced together. Turning a customer over to the Wei family would mean surrendering an eight-hundred-stone artifact as stolen evidence—whereas keeping the secret gave Jade Scale Trading House a very tight hold on a remarkably dangerous young man.

“Officer Cheng!” Pei Rong stepped smoothly to the table, his pointed beard lifting in an amiable smile. “Naturally, naturally, we must respect the gate office’s procedures! This young man traveled in my Jade Scale convoy from Shuanghe Ferry. Our trading house has been registered in the Southern Ward for twenty years.”

Wei Min’s face darkened. “Pei Rong! This is a blood matter of the Wei clan—do you know what you’re stepping into?”

“I’m stepping into my afternoon unloading schedule,” Pei Rong replied mildly, sliding Jade Scale Trading House’s brass bond tally across the desk so Cheng Mao could press it against the register. “If the Wei family obtains a magistrate’s trial warrant, your clerks know where my counting house sits. Until then, my passenger enters on my bond.”

Cheng Mao checked the brass tally, ignored Wei Min’s glare, and stamped Shi Feng’s permit with a heavy thud. “Report any change of lodging within ten days. Next!”

The two guards lifted their spears. Wei Min’s hand trembled on his reins. “The witness saw your face at the quarry, Shi Feng,” Wei Min hissed as Shi Feng walked past him through the arch. “A merchant’s bond won’t cover you once our elder petitions the ward court!”

Shi Feng didn’t bother answering a messenger.

Inside the inner arch, where the carts pulled aside to clear the thoroughfare, Pei Rong handed Shi Feng back his stamped permit and kept two fingers resting lightly on the corner of the paper.

“A messy business at the gate, young friend,” Pei Rong said softly, his eyes warm and calculating. “Standing bond on a capital inquiry costs my house a forty-stone surety deposit with the ward office—and, naturally, a little risk to my peaceful reputation.”

Neither of them mentioned the flying sword locked in the third cart, and Shi Feng said nothing about the maker’s mark beneath its guard. What wasn’t spoken aloud couldn’t be overheard by the porters.

Shi Feng counted forty spirit stones from his pouch and placed them into Pei Rong’s palm. “For the deposit.”

“Naturally, naturally!” Pei Rong’s fingers closed around the stones, his smile deepening as he tucked the bond receipt into his own sleeve rather than handing it over. “And when a capable young friend has more rare business in the capital—or needs a quiet buyer who knows how to keep his ledger shut—you’ll come to Jade Scale Trading House first, won’t you?”

“You’ll know where I’m staying,” Shi Feng said evenly.

“Send the street name to our Southern Ward store before sunset so my clerk can log the bond,” Pei Rong said pleasantly. “Enjoy the capital, Young Master Shi.”

Shi Feng shouldered his pack and turned down the side avenue toward the workshop lanes. The gate hadn’t stopped him, but his name was now sitting on the Southern Ward’s inquiry board, and Pei Rong held both his residence bond and the dead elder’s sword.

Before the Wei family’s capital elders turned that household notice into a magistrate’s warrant, he needed a roof with a strong lock—and a much faster road to strength.

chapters.title: A Courtyard with Two Owners
chapters.html:
Past the southern gate, workshops lined the lane behind the main avenue. Shi Feng followed the sound of hammers until the lodging signs became smaller and the prices became sensible. He wanted a stove and a lock, not a painted ceiling.

An inn on the first avenue offered quiet rooms, fine furniture and a physician by appointment. Shi Feng asked the rate and decided he’d never be able to enjoy that much quiet. At the third street, a housing broker found him.

“Young master, new to the capital? Of course you are, you’re still staring at the roofs.” The man had a narrow face, a bright sash and a ring of keys as big as a melon. “This Bao Shun is at your service. A courtyard with a private well, a good room, a kitchen and a cheap price, all for you, young master!”

“Show me the courtyard first. Brag about it later,” Shi Feng said.

Bao Shun led him into Qingliu Lane, far from the main avenue, behind a row of workshops and a small market where people bought food instead of admiring it. The courtyard had a crooked pear tree, a kitchen with a freshly repaired stove, and one big room with a wide bed against the back wall and a clear patch of floor beside it.

Shi Feng checked the roof, then the door. Both held up fine. His opinion of the place went up a little.

“One hundred and twenty spirit stones a month, young master.” Bao Shun declared, spreading his arms. “And no troublesome neighbours.”

Beyond the wall, a hammer rang against an anvil for the fortieth time since they’d walked in.

“The man next door has been hitting metal this whole time,” Shi Feng said.

“A hard-working neighbour, young master,” Bao Shun said quickly. “That’s a good thing. Totally different from noisy.”

Shi Feng tested the well bucket, looked under the bed boards and checked the rear wall. The chimney drew well. The market was close enough to carry groceries by hand. He could cultivate here and sleep without wondering which wall would fall on him. In his heart, Shi Feng was already satisfied.

“Who’s the owner?” Shi Feng asked.

“Away,” Bao Shun said.

“And the deed?” Shi Feng asked.

“You can see it after you pay, young master,” Bao Shun said, jingling his keys. A folded lease protruded from his sleeve. Shi Feng read the owner's name before the broker pushed it away.

Shi Feng thought: I won’t pay a fee for a lock I can buy myself. He turned toward the gate without another word.

“It’s a custom, young master, only a standard agency custom!” Bao Shun said, scrambling after him.

“Then try it on someone else,” Shi Feng said. “The name on that paper isn’t yours. Charging a signing fee for an owner who isn’t even here? That’s ridiculous.”

Bao Shun’s expression changed, and his face turned pale. The broker was stunned that a country boy had read the paper so closely. Within the hour, he went and fetched the owner.

Jiang Meilan arrived with a basket of greens on her hip, and her expression soured the moment she saw the broker.

“One hundred and twenty?” Jiang Meilan shouted down the lane. “Bao Shun, you shameless weasel, you told me eighty!”

Bao Shun coughed into his sleeve. “Auntie Jiang, Auntie Jiang, don’t shout! The tenant wanted extra guarantees!”

“I wanted to see the roof,” Shi Feng said from beside the pear tree.

Jiang Meilan put down her basket. A woman haggling over cabbages at the mouth of the lane stopped to listen. The smith next door stopped hammering for the first time all morning.

“Forty stones!” Jiang Meilan shouted, jabbing a finger into the broker’s chest. “Forty stones you planned to swallow between my house and this boy’s purse, and you call it guarantees? Does your mother know what you do for a living?”

“Auntie, it’s a misunderstanding.” Bao Shun protested.

“Misunderstanding, my foot! Shameless!” Jiang Meilan snapped.

The whole lane came out to watch.

“Bao the Weasel again!”

“Last spring he rented one room to two widows at once,” Jiang Meilan said.

“…”

After an argument the cabbage seller would retell for half a month, the rent was settled at eighty stones a month, with a refundable deposit of twenty. Bao Shun took a ten-stone fee, with the hurt look of a man who’d hoped for four times that. Shi Feng paid only after all three amounts were written on one sheet of paper.

Jiang Meilan handed him a key. He tried it, then held out his other hand to Bao Shun, who pulled out a second key that opened the same lock.

“The spare belongs to the property office,” Bao Shun explained.

Jiang Meilan held out her palm without a word.

“…” Bao Shun gave up the key.

“Young master,” Bao Shun said at the gate, bravely trying again, “if you ever need anything in the capital, a cook, a sword polisher, a matchmaker—”

“I’ll check the roof first,” Shi Feng said, and shut the gate.

He walked to the little market, bought a new lock and fitted it himself.

Jiang Meilan watched from the lane and nodded. “Smart boy,” Jiang Meilan told the cabbage woman, her face finally softening. “Bao Shun will have another key made by tomorrow.”

After sunset the courtyard grew quiet, except for the smith and the cabbage woman, who’d found a new customer to argue with.

Shi Feng swept the dust from under the bed and opened the shutters to air the room. The pear tree cast a swaying shadow across the floor. He lit a small fire to test the stove, and the smoke went up the chimney instead of into his eyes. That alone made it better than several places he’d slept.

The hammering started again. Over the wall, a deep voice shouted about a bent hinge, then louder still.

“New neighbour! The hammer starts at dawn,” Dou Shan the smith bellowed. “Don’t complain!”

“I won’t,” Shi Feng called back.

The hammer started again. Shi Feng closed the shutter on the workshop side. That cut the noise enough for him.

He put his papers on a shelf away from the stove, with the damaged bone manual beside them. The sword hung within reach of the bed. Wei Kuo’s knife went into the fold of his spare robe.

Then he sat at the little table and counted his money. Enough for rent. Enough for food. Enough for some useful medicine, if he chose carefully.

Not enough to feed two hundred and six hungry bones. Shi Feng frowned. Being clever and being fed were two different things, he told himself, and the bones didn’t care how smart their owner was.

Outside, the capital went on through the night with cart wheels, faraway music and a hawker clearing his throat for one last sale. Past the rooftops, a great tower stood lit from its lowest floor to its highest balcony.

Sky Pavilion.

He’d seen its sign from the main avenue. Tomorrow he’d find out what the capital charged for cultivation. Tonight, he heated water and cooked rice.

As he set his empty rice bowl down, three sharp raps sounded on the outer courtyard shutter. Jiang Meilan’s voice came low through the wooden slats.

“New boy—keep your latch down tonight. A runner wearing a dark blue Wei badge just paid Bao Shun two stones at the corner tavern to ask which courtyard the traveler from Yunze Town rented.”

Shi Feng glanced from the locked gate toward the lit tiers of Sky Pavilion rising above the rooftops. Tomorrow morning couldn’t wait.

chapters.title: No Rank Above First
chapters.html:
“Three hundred and sixty stones? For a bottle I could hide in my fist?” Wang Peng demanded.

The angry customer at the next display case said exactly what Shi Feng was thinking.

Sky Pavilion's tower rose in pale tiers above a square big enough to swallow Yunze Town's old market. Inside, the floor shone, the counters were clean, and nobody shouted prices. The numbers written beside the bottles did enough damage without help.

“Every seal on this shelf was checked by the tower,” Qu Ming said. “Cheaper preparations are available on the floor below.”

The customer looked toward the stairs. Pride kept his feet still for another moment. Then he went down without buying anything.

Shi Feng copied the price onto a scrap of paper.

“Does the tower buy resources too?” Shi Feng asked.

“We buy what we can examine and certify,” Qu Ming said. “Beast materials go to the eastern counter.”

The clerk's Qi Condensation cultivation was plain. It hadn't made him too grand to explain where the stairs went. Shi Feng appreciated that almost as much as a lower price, although he would have preferred both.

He had money from Wei Renshan's sword. That didn't mean he could feed two hundred and six bones on bottles chosen because they looked impressive. He asked about the ordinary strengthening tonic and wrote its price beneath the first.

Qu Ming showed him three sizes, explained the difference, and left him to decide. No wounded pride. No story about an immortal finding the herbs. The most expensive bottle was still more than Shi Feng wanted to spend today.

He bought the smallest ordinary tonic.

At the payment desk, a gray-robed customer named Zeng Fu was arguing about a certificate. The man carried a furnace-shaped pendant and had the slightly scorched sleeves of somebody who worked close to fire.

“I sold three batches to hunters,” Zeng Fu said. “All three worked. Why isn't that enough?”

“Because you asked for an alchemist's Mark,” Qu Ming said. “That requires the tower's examination.”

The man slapped his own packet of medicine onto the desk. Qu Ming didn't touch it.

“Ordinary medicine can be useful without earning a Mark,” Qu Ming said. “A first Mark concerns medicine serving Golden Core cultivators. Selling a tonic doesn't complete that test.”

Shi Feng glanced at the wall behind the desk. Different certificates hung in separate frames. Alchemy occupied one side, artifact refining the other. A pair of large doors led to rooms closed to ordinary shoppers.

A passing worker carried two empty pill trays through those doors. One smelled pleasantly of herbs. The other smelled as if somebody had burned breakfast and tried to hide it with incense.

Even the tower had failures behind its polished counters.

Shi Feng took his tonic and receipt. He knew almost nothing about refining medicine. For now, a clear label mattered more than the man's wounded ambition.

Outside, the square had become louder.

A bookseller stood beside a folding screen painted with flowering branches. Half a dozen young men waited while he untied a fresh bundle of thin books. Two pretended to be studying a map on the neighboring stall.

“New edition of the Thousand Blossom Register!” Liang Wen called. “Names, households, portraits, verses! Proper binding this time!”

“What happened to the last binding?” Fan Jun asked from the front.

“You opened it too often,” Liang Wen said.

Fan Jun shut his mouth. His friends laughed until Liang Wen held up the first portrait. Then everyone leaned closer.

Shi Feng paused at the edge. He had heard the register mentioned on the road. The capital apparently ranked beautiful women with the same enthusiasm hunters brought to arguing over beast teeth.

A young scholar objected to the order on the open page. He wore a carefully brushed robe and held his fan as though he might be examined on it.

“Princess Sima Lan should be first,” Fan Jun said. “Royal bearing is also beauty.”

“Then write to the compiler,” Liang Wen said. “I'm selling the books, not marrying the rankings.”

The crowd laughed again. Fan Jun looked toward the map stall, hoping his friends would rescue his dignity. They were suddenly occupied with a distant mountain on the paper.

Shi Feng looked at the two names at the top. Ling Qingzhu. Sima Lan. He remembered Lin Shuang and her carter at the roadside warehouse describing the forty rejected bolts of royal cloud brocade. The first fairy apparently had enough admirers to keep both tailors and booksellers comfortable.

“Have you seen the portraits?” Liang Wen asked Shi Feng.

“I'm looking now,” Shi Feng said.

“Then you have good fortune. Those two argue every edition,” Liang Wen said, nodding toward Fan Jun and his companion. “Neither has spoken to either lady.”

Fan Jun went red.

“The judgment of beauty doesn't require an introduction,” Fan Jun said.

“Certainly. Payment does require spirit stones,” Liang Wen said.

Fan Jun bought a copy so quickly that his fan fell from his sleeve. His friend picked it up, handed it back, and bought one too. Shi Feng understood the bookseller's confidence now. Men would spend money just to avoid admitting why they were standing there.

He didn't buy a copy. Portraits couldn't refine bones, and the woman in the first picture had so little detail she could have been any noble daughter with a good hairpin.

Across the square, two boys had rented wooden swords and were performing a duel for younger children. The taller boy called his attack Heaven-Splitting Dragon Judgment. His opponent stepped back, tripped over the coin bowl, and demanded a second judgment.

Shi Feng watched them start over. Their grand sword art had less footwork than his common clan forms, but the children cheered loudly. A fight didn't need blood to entertain an audience.

He ate a sesame cake beside the fountain, then examined the street leading toward the beast market. That would be tomorrow's errand. Today he'd learned enough about the capital's medicine prices to know the sword money wouldn't last forever.

The tower bell rang once overhead.

The bookseller began putting his finest copies on the front edge of the table. Several men stopped talking and looked toward the carriage road. Fan Jun straightened his collar so sharply that one friend nearly laughed aloud.

Shi Feng followed their gazes. Something important was coming, or something expensive. In this square, those seemed to draw much the same crowd.

chapters.title: The First Fairy
chapters.html:
At the far side of the square, the crowd changed.

Men stepped out of a carriage’s path and forgot to step back. A fan stopped halfway open. A seller kept calling out his price after his customer turned away, then forgot the end of it himself.

“It’s the Ling household carriage!”

“Don’t push. I was here first.”

“Fairy Ling comes on the tenth day of every month, I told you.”

“…”

A young woman stepped down from the carriage. Her long black hair fell over robes of pale violet and white. A white silk veil covered her face below her clear eyes.

The cloth hid her nose and lips completely. It did nothing to hide her graceful figure, full curves and slender waist. Her exposed hands were white as fine jade.

She tucked a loose strand behind her ear, and several young men forgot to breathe.

Half the square stared even though they couldn’t see her whole face.

Shi Feng was startled. He’d heard men compare beautiful women to descending immortals, and he’d always assumed they had never seen an immortal. Looking at her, he found he didn’t want to argue.

“Fairy Ling Qingzhu,” Fan Jun said, forgetting to lower his voice.

For once the scholar was useful. Lin Shuang’s carter on the road hadn’t been exaggerating. This was the first fairy of Great Liang, ranked above even the royal princess, and beauty like hers could stun a whole street.

Shi Feng thought: why is she first? Because she deserves it, or because the kingdom has no higher number to give?

The longer he looked, the better the question seemed. And she hadn’t even removed the veil!

Then a cart rattled up behind him, and he stepped clear of its wheel. Beauty was no reason to get run over.

Ling Qingzhu took a small parcel from her driver and turned toward Sky Pavilion. A young man near the steps hurriedly straightened his collar. Another pretended he was studying the stonework. She didn't glance at either of them.

Shi Feng put the price list in his sleeve. Pretty, he thought, but I can’t eat pretty. He’d seen the tower and the kingdom’s first fairy, and neither one made bone medicine cheaper. He started back toward Qingliu Lane.

The young man on the steps advanced with a folded poem in both hands. Kou Zhi had reached Qi Condensation and wore a fine sword at his waist. He looked as though every word of his greeting had been practiced in front of a mirror.

“Fairy Ling, this humble Kou Zhi composed a few lines—” Kou Zhi said.

A porter carrying a long crate squeezed past. The crate caught the poem and folded it across Kou Zhi's wrist. His greeting ended in a sharp squeak.

Ling Qingzhu stepped aside before the crate reached her sleeve.

“Be careful on the steps,” Ling Qingzhu said.

Kou Zhi stared at her. Then he stared at the crushed poem. By the time he decided which mattered more, she was already beyond him. His friends congratulated him on being spoken to, making the loss of his poem worse.

Shi Feng almost laughed. The kingdom's first fairy hadn't cast a single technique, yet men were losing their ability to walk around boxes.

A girl carrying a smaller parcel followed Ling Qingzhu from the carriage. Hongxiu kept a sensible distance from the poem's disappointed owner. She asked the driver to wait beside the awning and hurried toward the tower.

Ling Qingzhu stopped at the entrance to exchange a receipt. Her veil stayed in place even when the woman behind the desk leaned forward to speak with her. The crowd could admire her eyes, her hair and her bearing. Nothing in her manner promised it more.

Shi Feng looked away before he became another man waiting for a glimpse. He'd already spent more time watching her than he'd intended.

That annoyed him a little. His private cultivation could frighten a Foundation Establishment elder, but a strand of black hair tucked behind an ear had made him forget his sesame cake.

He finished the cake.

Near the fountain, Fan Jun closed his register without looking at Sima Lan's portrait again. His companion noticed and began laughing. The scholar refused to explain. A moment ago he had been defending royal bearing. Now his own bearing was struggling with a mouth that wouldn't close.

Shi Feng put his medicine receipt safely inside his robe. He checked that the little bottle hadn't knocked against his belt knife, then adjusted his pack. The room in Qingliu Lane was waiting, and Jiang Meilan had told him which stall sold decent greens.

Kou Zhi noticed Shi Feng's amusement and found someone safe to blame.

“A cripple should watch his own feet,” Kou Zhi said. “What are you laughing at?”

“Your friends congratulated you,” Shi Feng said. “I thought this was a happy occasion.”

Kou Zhi's friends stopped smiling. He could draw his sword over a poem, but the crate's owner was still watching from the steps. His hand stayed on the hilt without doing anything useful.

Shi Feng adjusted his pack and turned away. One ruined greeting was enough entertainment for a morning.

Hongxiu caught sight of his face and leaned toward her mistress.

“Young Mistress, isn't that the Qingshi youth from the royal review—” Hongxiu began.

“Hongxiu, lower your voice,” Ling Qingzhu said.

The maid immediately closed her mouth. Ling Qingzhu had heard the mockery and the calm reply. His circumstances had changed greatly. That composure had survived.

Ling Qingzhu's eyes moved toward him.

Shi Feng didn't know her, but he knew the expression of someone comparing a person with a story. The supposed cripple was standing straight, carrying a sword, and buying his own medicine. Those things always surprised people more than they should.

He wasn't about to explain his meridians in the middle of Sky Pavilion square.

Ling Qingzhu handed her parcel to Hongxiu and came down the steps. The people between them moved before she asked. Kou Zhi opened his mouth, saw where she was looking, and shut it again.

“You're Shi Feng, aren't you?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

Shi Feng stopped.

“That's my name,” Shi Feng said.

Up close, her eyes were clearer than he'd expected. A silver clasp held the pale fabric at her collar, and her black hair fell over one shoulder. He noticed all of that before reminding himself she had asked a question, not announced an exhibition.

Behind her, several admirers had gone completely still.

“She knows him?”

“The Shi clan's cripple?”

“How did he manage that?”

Shi Feng ignored them. Ling Qingzhu examined his face for a brief moment, then glanced toward the crowd. She could hardly discuss anything here without it reaching three teahouses before noon.

“May we speak somewhere quieter?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

Shi Feng looked at the tower, then at the waiting carriage. A woman arriving in that carriage probably didn't need to borrow his spirit stones.

That left many other possibilities, and not all were pleasant.

“About what?” Shi Feng asked.

“A proposal,” Ling Qingzhu said.

Kou Zhi dropped his ruined poem.

Ling Qingzhu heard the little sound and closed her eyes for a moment. Shi Feng looked past her, saw the man's face, and finally laughed.

“Somewhere quieter sounds sensible,” Shi Feng said.

chapters.title: A Proposal Without Flowers
chapters.html:
“Somewhere with fewer ears,” Ling Qingzhu said, with a glance at the surrounding stalls that made several curious men suddenly remember errands.

“Quiet costs money near this square,” Shi Feng said.

Her gaze went over the shouting medicine sellers, the stacked herb baskets and the cloth bag in his hand. Whatever she was about to say, she swallowed it.

“There’s a tea house across the street,” Ling Qingzhu said. “My treat.”

Shi Feng thought: a sensible way to start. The square watched them cross together, and the square was full of opinions.

“Fairy Ling is taking the cripple to tea!”

“Out of pity, surely.”

“…”

The attendant at the Cloud Mist Tea House recognised her before he even saw the spirit stones in her hand. His back bent so fast that Shi Feng wondered if the house taught a secret waist technique.

“Fairy Ling honours us! The east screen, open the east screen!” Luo Ping shouted, and three boys ran in three directions.

The screen closed behind them. Ling Qingzhu kept her veil on. This was a tea house, not her home. She shielded its lower edge with her hand when drinking, showing nobody her face. Her porcelain cup had painted clouds. Shi Feng’s had a crack beneath the handle.

He swapped them before Luo Ping finished pouring.

“Fairy Ling’s cup is damaged,” Shi Feng said calmly.

Luo Ping nearly dropped the pot. Both cups vanished and two new ones arrived. Through the gap in the screen, Shi Feng watched Luo Ping smack the boy who’d brought the cracked cup.

“A thousand pardons! The kiln sent us rubbish,” Luo Ping called through the screen.

“Then I hope you’ve stopped paying the kiln,” Shi Feng said, and the screen went very quiet.

Ling Qingzhu waited for it to stop shaking. Then she looked at Shi Feng, who took the chair facing the door. Up close, he was even better-looking. His ruined meridians were unfortunate, but there was nothing wrong with his face. At least she wouldn’t have to suffer every time she looked at her temporary husband.

“You took the seat facing the door,” Ling Qingzhu said. “Expecting trouble?”

“People usually ask what I want before they take me somewhere expensive,” Shi Feng said.

“Nobody dragged you here,” Ling Qingzhu said. “You walked in. On your own feet.”

“You offered to pay willingly,” Shi Feng said. “We’re off to a promising start.”

She lowered her eyes. A small red mark had appeared where her thumb pressed the cup, and she still hadn’t drunk. Shi Feng saw it, and her expression gave her away. He thought: the face that cost half the square their wits belongs to someone who hates what she’s about to say.

He waited. A good view didn’t mean he had to rescue its owner from silence.

“I need a husband,” Ling Qingzhu said.

Shi Feng glanced at the screen. It stayed shut, and no laughing young masters burst out to enjoy the joke.

“Then your carriage stopped at the wrong stall,” Shi Feng said, unmoved.

“A temporary one!” Ling Qingzhu’s voice didn’t waver, though her thumb pressed harder. “Real in public. A contract in private. You’d be paid, obviously.”

Outside, a vendor praised a miracle tonic that restored a man’s courage. Shi Feng briefly thought about asking whether the tea house allowed outside medicine.

“What does real in public mean?” Shi Feng asked.

“A registered marriage. Papers, witnesses, the whole thing,” Ling Qingzhu said. “Everyone has to believe it.”

“Everyone includes the man you’re refusing,” Shi Feng said. “Who is he?”

“Crown Prince Sima Yu,” Ling Qingzhu said. “His household is arranging the match. Nobody has asked whether I want it.”

“Sima Yu?” Luo Ping whispered from beyond the screen. “The crown prince? Impossible!”

On the other side of the screen, something hit a tray with a clang. Somebody had been listening, and now he was very sorry.

Shi Feng’s heart tightened. He turned his cup once and thought: some proposals make a man rich, and some make his funeral expensive. This one does both.

“You should have started with that,” Shi Feng said flatly.

“Would you have come if I had?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“I would have ordered better tea,” Shi Feng said.

For a moment she almost smiled. Then her gaze slid to his wrist, where a pale line from the splint still showed.

“I know how things stand with you,” Ling Qingzhu said, softer. “Nothing improper. So relax.”

There it was, the diagnosis, handed over with a kindness that assumed it had settled his future. Shi Feng put both hands on the table.

“You know what people say about my situation,” Shi Feng said. “You don’t know my price.”

Men had stared at her eyes, her waist and the veil they wanted her to remove. This one was pricing the trouble of burying himself.

“Then name it,” Ling Qingzhu said, a shade colder. “I’m not short on stones.”

“First tell me what the job is,” Shi Feng said. “A porter wants to know whether he’s carrying rice or a sleeping tiger before he agrees to the stairs.”

“It blocks a match I never agreed to,” Ling Qingzhu said. “There is no betrothal contract yet. I need time to leave their arrangements behind. Your future stays yours.”

“That part was already mine,” Shi Feng said.

The thumb mark on the cup got deeper. She took a breath and went on, short and precise. His courtyard was one room and a kitchen. She would take the bed, and he would take the floor. He would go out with her on certain occasions, call himself her husband and never contradict their story. Everything else would be in writing.

Shi Feng listened without cutting in. Not bad, he thought. She’s proud, and she’s still trying to be fair. She came looking for a shield, but at least she noticed a shield might have opinions.

“Can I leave the house?” Shi Feng asked.

“Of course you can,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Can I earn my own spirit stones?” Shi Feng asked.

“Earn all you like. I’d think less of you otherwise,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Can I turn down an invitation?” Shi Feng asked.

“As long as we talk about it first,” Ling Qingzhu said, after the smallest pause.

One of his brows rose.

“Then that’s a request, not a guarantee,” Shi Feng said. “Write it honestly when the time comes.”

Ling Qingzhu glanced at the screen. The shadow of a pair of shoes had been sitting under it for far too long.

“We asked for privacy,” Ling Qingzhu said, without raising her voice at all. “Is the floor so interesting?”

“Run!” Luo Ping gasped outside.

The shoes vanished with a squeak.

Shi Feng reached for the dish of roasted seeds. Whatever came of this, he meant to get his money’s worth out of the place. The first seed was hollow, so he put the shell beside the plate and picked another.

Ling Qingzhu watched. She’d prepared for a refusal born of humiliation, for anger over his broken engagement, even for some shameless demand. She hadn’t prepared to negotiate a marriage while the husband checked the tea house’s seeds one at a time. Her expression changed, and she was stunned into silence for a breath.

“You’re not even surprised,” Ling Qingzhu said. “Does everyone propose to you over tea?”

“I was surprised,” Shi Feng said. “Then you named Sima Yu. Now I’m wondering why you think I’d survive being picked.”

“My household would have obligations to you too!” Ling Qingzhu said, too quickly.

He met her eyes. There was no mockery in his face now.

“You answered fast,” Shi Feng said. “Promises are easy when the danger belongs to someone else. Tell me what’s backing yours.”

Ling Qingzhu put down her untouched cup, and Shi Feng left the seeds alone.

“And tell me,” Shi Feng said, “why a marriage would stop a royal household that has never asked what you think.”

Shi Feng thought: at last, this conversation is worth my time.

chapters.title: The Man Who Could Not Refuse
chapters.html:
“The consort sends gifts,” Ling Qingzhu said. “Silk for my aunts, medicine for an elder. Returning them insults the palace. Keeping them means remembering its kindness.”

“And the crown prince?” Shi Feng asked.

“He leaves the arrangements to his household,” Ling Qingzhu said. “He has never needed to chase anyone. His steward sends invitations. My relatives tell me how fortunate I am.”

“Then your relatives can accept,” Shi Feng said.

“One uncle's court appointment is waiting,” Ling Qingzhu said. “Our northern warehouse permit has been delayed twice. Another elder thinks becoming the crown prince's family will settle everything.”

Shi Feng stopped turning his cup. Nobody had threatened her with a sword. They had found enough other things to hold over her head.

“No decree or signed betrothal?” Shi Feng asked.

“Neither,” Ling Qingzhu said. “But the Grand Tutor's people have started congratulating my elders. Men who offered to help me refuse the palace have sons of their own.”

“Why can't your clan refuse together?” Shi Feng asked.

“The Sima clan has several early Golden Core experts,” Ling Qingzhu said. “The other great houses have one or two each. Even united, our elders would first argue about who takes the loss.”

“And the royal ancestor?” Shi Feng asked.

“He left after a powerful force beyond this region recruited him,” Ling Qingzhu said. “Nobody here knows his present realm, his position, or whether he still watches Great Liang. The uncertainty keeps people cautious.”

“Convenient for his descendants,” Shi Feng said.

“Less convenient in this case,” Ling Qingzhu said. “He forbade the royal house from taking a married woman. The rule is still in the kingdom register. A clerk cannot set it aside to please a steward.”

Shi Feng glanced at the screen. That was a better answer than hoping a prince would be embarrassed.

“A real marriage gives them a law they can't quietly forget,” Shi Feng said.

“And gives my own elders something to point to,” Ling Qingzhu said. “They can stop discussing bridal gifts without declaring themselves enemies of the palace.”

“For how long?” Shi Feng asked.

“I intend to enter a Great Sect,” Ling Qingzhu said. “Its disciples are outside the kingdom's marriage arrangements. Once a sect accepts me, a household invitation cannot call me home to be married off.”

“Those sects aren't frightened into obeying a missing ancestor?” Shi Feng asked.

“They avoid unnecessary trouble with the royal bloodline,” Ling Qingzhu said. “That doesn't make the Sima household their master. They choose and shelter their own disciples.”

“And if His Highness decides he'd rather have a widow?” Shi Feng asked.

Ling Qingzhu's fingers stopped against the cup.

“The rule protects the marriage,” Ling Qingzhu said after a moment. “It can't stop a knife. My household would have to protect you too.”

“Assassins don't usually introduce themselves,” Shi Feng said.

“Then put the protection in writing,” Ling Qingzhu said, lifting her chin. “I'm offering a bargain, not asking you to trust a pretty promise.”

He leaned back. Her plan could annoy a prince, and it would certainly buy her time. But neither result explained why she’d picked a man the whole capital believed couldn’t protect himself.

“You picked me because I can’t compete with him,” Shi Feng said.

“I picked you because you have no faction,” Ling Qingzhu said. “A powerful house would take one refusal as permission to arrange another. Another husband could give my clan to another faction. You’re the only man who wants nothing from me. Or so I thought.”

“And because you believe I can’t compete with him,” Shi Feng said again.

“…” Ling Qingzhu’s thumb went still against the cup.

She didn’t answer fast enough, and both of them heard it.

Shi Feng sighed in his heart, and his expression stayed flat. There were crueller reasons to pick him, and kinder ways to admit this one. But he preferred an honest ugly answer to a pretty one that cost him his neck.

He stood up.

“I’ll think about a deal,” Shi Feng said. “I won’t think about being your convenient idiot. Go find out what you’re asking me to risk.”

“Shi Feng! Sit down, I’m not finished!” Ling Qingzhu said, half rising herself.

“You’re finished deciding for both of us,” Shi Feng said. “When you’re ready to talk, send word.”

He left his cup untouched and walked out.

Ling Qingzhu stared at the empty chair. She had prepared for bitterness or eagerness. She had not prepared to be dismissed.

Luo Ping slid in with a fresh pot, saw the empty seat and froze.

“Fairy Ling, the young master… did he step out?” Luo Ping asked.

“Bring the bill,” Ling Qingzhu said, her eyes cold above the veil. “And don’t say one word.”

The tea house was stunned. By dinner, every attendant on the street knew.

“He walked out on her!”

“And she paid?”

“Impossible!”

“…”

At the western market, Shi Feng stopped outside the Hengyun permit office. Its board marked deep ravines where herbs that fed the marrow grew.

“How much for that ground?” Shi Feng asked.

“Forty spirit stones for ten days. Gathering costs extra,” Jia Wenlin said, glancing at his worn cuff.

“Your mountain understands business,” Shi Feng said.

A carriage stopped outside. Its servant presented a household pass. Jia Wenlin's voice softened, and no stones changed hands. The gathering slip covered every ground the common permit excluded.

Shi Feng remembered the seal, the boundaries and the clerk’s sudden new voice. He thought: so a household name opens what stones can’t. This was worth more than any purse.

He bought a cheap map at the next stall.

At home, Shi Feng practised the movements that tempered the unfinished stretches of his bones. The progress was real. So was the hunger that followed, and confidence couldn’t turn an empty pot into a spirit beast.

Rent, food, medicine, permits. On paper, by the lamp, his savings looked like a brave little army surrounded on every side. He could hunt, he could endure, and he could kill men who mistook him for easy prey. But he wouldn’t let Ling Qingzhu’s opinion of him become a term of the job.

A knock interrupted his counting. Bao Shun stood at the gate wearing the face of a man who’d just realised a beautiful woman and a fallen genius might both need his services.

“A message, young master! Bao Shun delivered it personally!” Bao Shun announced. “There’s usually a small service charge.”

“Charged to the sender or the receiver?” Shi Feng asked.

Bao Shun’s smile weakened. A promising business had just been inspected. “The sender was… generous, young master. It’s all been settled,” Bao Shun said.

“Then enjoy your evening,” Shi Feng said, and took the folded paper before the broker could find a charge for handing it over.

The handwriting was neat and calm. Ling Qingzhu would come to his courtyard tomorrow afternoon. She’d bring the tea herself. Below that, in smaller characters, she admitted that the dangers deserved clear terms.
