Shi Feng thought: she’s learned to ask. That was a small surprise. He read the last line twice and set the message beside his map.

He supposed this counted as progress.

He wrote a reply before the lamp burned low. Six months or sect entry, whichever came first, freely extended if both agreed. The ten thousand spirit stones would be due on registration. He added one condition the tea house hadn't settled: the Ling household would answer the Wei inquiry through the proper city office and refuse private surrender demands.

He didn't need the Ling household to fight Wei retainers for him. He needed people to stop turning every gate and permit desk into another ambush site. A legitimate household seal could protect his quiet days better than another corpse.

When Bao Shun returned for the reply, Shi Feng sealed it before opening the gate.

“Give it to Ling Qingzhu herself,” Shi Feng said. “These are terms for her to choose.”

chapters.title: The Crown Prince’s Gift
chapters.html:
Sima Yu read the grain report before looking at the returned gifts.

The pearl hairpin lay in its case beside two unopened invitations. Guo Zhen had also brought a letter from the consort's household. The letter received more attention than the pearl.

“Mother wants the next invitation sent through the Ling elders,” Sima Yu said. “Has the Grand Tutor agreed?”

“His secretary has already visited them, Your Highness,” Guo Zhen said. “Two elders favour the match. The northern warehouse permit is still waiting.”

“Then let them discuss it,” Sima Yu said, setting down the letter. “A willing clan will manage its own daughter better than a royal decree.”

There was no wounded sigh, no question about whether Fairy Ling had admired the hairpin. The match would bring a major household closer to the eastern residence. Her beauty made the arrangement pleasant. Neither required him to spend his mornings choosing jewellery.

By the pillars stood Cen Zhenli, waiting to report on the river district. Sima Yu beckoned him forward.

“The floods have taken enough,” Sima Yu said warmly. “Cut this season's tax by half. An empty granary can't feed loyalty.”

Cen Zhenli dropped to his knees, nearly losing his hat. “Your Highness is kind! The district will remember this for ten generations!”

The relief would reach the district. Sima Yu enjoyed gratitude when it was delivered before witnesses. He also knew how much grain remained in the palace stores.

After the magistrate withdrew, Guo Zhen opened the hairpin case.

“The Ling household returned this with thanks, Your Highness,” Guo Zhen said.

“Enter it back in the treasury,” Sima Yu said. “Don't send the same gift twice. It makes us look forgetful.”

An attendant carried it away with both hands. Sima Yu had already returned to the grain report.

“There is another matter,” Guo Zhen said. “Fairy Ling spoke privately with Shi Feng at a tea house.”

Sima Yu needed a moment to place the name. The Shi clan's genius had become a favourite warning in noble dining rooms: even splendid talent could collapse.

“The ruined one?” Sima Yu asked.

“Yes, Your Highness,” Guo Zhen said. “He refused this household once before, at the youth review. Now he has no cultivation and no position at court.”

“Has she asked us for something through him?” Sima Yu asked.

“Not that we know, Your Highness,” Guo Zhen said.

“Then find out what the meeting concerned,” Sima Yu said. “Give the household a useful report before it sends another invitation.”

He turned a page. Guo Zhen understood the dismissal and bowed.

“The screen is thick, honoured steward,” Luo Ping said, rubbing his hands on his apron. “We heard nothing.”

Guo Zhen looked toward the screened table. Marriage negotiations would matter. A casual meeting would merely make his afternoon longer. Guessing the wrong one would make the consort's steward unpleasant.

“Tell me what you saw, then,” Guo Zhen said.

“Fairy Ling paid. Two pots of tea, one dish of seeds,” Luo Ping said. “And he left first. Without finishing his tea!”

“He left first?” Guo Zhen asked.

Luo Ping nodded so hard that his apron string came loose.

Guo Zhen left the tea house without overturning a table or threatening its staff. He ordered inquiries into Shi Feng's lodgings and purchases. A fallen genius who walked out on Fairy Ling had either misunderstood an offer or refused it.

That was worth putting in the report.

Ling Qingzhu sat at her desk, veiled even with her maid present.

“That’s the fourth sheet, Young Mistress!” Hongxiu said, picking a crumpled ball from under the desk. “The whole eastern market says he walked out and left you the bill!”

“Keep the terms short. He’d find holes in long ones,” Ling Qingzhu said, not looking up from her brush.

Hongxiu smoothed the paper and read it, then grinned. “‘Ten thousand spirit stones.’ You wrote it and underlined it. Twice!”

“He likes clear numbers,” Ling Qingzhu said. “I could tell.”

Hongxiu perched on the chest by the window and swung one foot. “Is he really ugly, Young Mistress? He must be, to walk away from you!”

“No. He’s quite pleasant to look at,” Ling Qingzhu said.

Hongxiu’s swinging foot stopped.

“Young Mistress, that isn’t what the rumours say!” Hongxiu said.

“The rumours say he can’t cultivate. What does that have to do with his face?” Ling Qingzhu replied.

Hongxiu grinned. Ling Qingzhu lowered her eyes to the paper.

“He wears plain robes,” Ling Qingzhu added. “My cup was cracked. He swapped it with his. Then he tested the seeds one by one. Very thorough.”

“Was it?” Hongxiu asked.

“…One was hollow,” Ling Qingzhu admitted. “He announced it, too.”

Hongxiu burst out laughing, then clapped a hand over her mouth when the brush stopped. Ling Qingzhu’s eyes narrowed.

“He’s a convenient choice,” Ling Qingzhu said. “No faction, no prospects. That’s all.”

“Young Mistress said that very fast!” Hongxiu said.

“…Grind the ink, Hongxiu,” Ling Qingzhu said. “And stop grinning.”

Hongxiu ground the ink, still smiling. Then her smile faded. “Young Mistress, when the eastern residence hears about this…”

“It will,” Ling Qingzhu said, and kept writing. In her heart she knew the danger. “But a steward can ignore my refusal. A registry seal brings the ancestor’s rule into it.”

Hongxiu lifted two pale bags out of the open chest and set them beside the inkstone. Both had the same fine white stitching at the mouth. Ling Qingzhu moved one onto the folded travel robes and left the other beside her account book. Hongxiu cleared space for a fresh sheet, still watching her mistress with badly hidden curiosity.

“And the stones?” Hongxiu asked, nodding at the chest. “Should I fill a white bag from your savings?”

“No, I’ll do it myself,” Ling Qingzhu said. “If he counts it, I want it all there.”

The next morning, Shi Feng was buying onions.

The seller held up a fat bundle and praised how fresh it was to the whole lane. Shi Feng thought it looked good on the outside. He loosened the string and laid the soft ones in a row on the counter.

“Your onions are sick,” Shi Feng said. “Rotten in the middle.”

“They can still flavour soup!” Pan Liu cried, staring at the evidence like someone had planted it.

“Then keep them for your own soup,” Shi Feng said. “I’ll buy the healthy ones.”

The women behind him leaned in.

“Soft at the heart, every one!”

“He’s been selling those since spring.”

“…”

Pan Liu pulled a second bundle from under the counter, firm bulbs with clean green stalks. Shi Feng paid, took a knob of ginger, and refused to pay extra for the string.

He walked home thinking about the afternoon’s talks. Ten thousand stones from the first fairy of Great Liang, he thought, and he still had to check the onions himself. That, at least, was a problem he could solve.

chapters.title: Ten Thousand Stones
chapters.html:
“Ten thousand spirit stones,” Ling Qingzhu said, before she even sat down. “Don’t say anything yet. Let it sink in first.”

Shi Feng set the teapot on the table without spilling a drop.

She’d come on foot with a tin of fine tea. Bao Shun and Granny Qin watched from across the lane.

Shi Feng closed the gate on both of them.

Ling Qingzhu looked over the tidy courtyard. Through the open door she saw one room, one bed and a bare patch of floor beside it.

Shi Feng thought about the price of bone medicine, and then about the danger of a crown prince. Ten thousand stones was real money. The prince was a real risk. Only one of those two was easy to trust.

Ling Qingzhu drew a folded sheet from her sleeve and laid it between them. The terms were neat and short. He would appear as her husband when needed, keep up the marriage in public, and be paid on registration. The words “ten thousand” were underlined twice.

“You wrote six months or a sect. I accept,” Ling Qingzhu said, tapping the blank space beneath the payment clause. “Until I can leave the palace arrangements behind.”

Shi Feng read it, turned it over, and found the back blank.

“Where are your obligations?” Shi Feng asked.

Ling Qingzhu tapped the payment clause with one pale finger. “Here. It’s the biggest number on the page. How could you miss it?”

“The prince doesn’t get cheaper after I take the money,” Shi Feng said. “If your household announces tomorrow that I kidnapped you, do I get a second sheet explaining the misunderstanding?”

Ling Qingzhu frowned, then wrote that she entered freely and neither side could later accuse the other of forcing the marriage.

“Put the exact wording on the sheet: six months, or your entry into a Great Sect, whichever comes earlier,” Shi Feng said. “Either of us can end our private arrangement then. We can renew it only if we both agree.”

“People will ask questions if you leave after six months,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“So will marrying me,” Shi Feng said.

Ling Qingzhu added the term and a clarification: their private deadline would not cancel the legal registration.

Then she wrote the next lines slowly. One room. She takes the bed, he takes the floor. No intimacy owed. No touching each other’s belongings.

Ling Qingzhu glanced at the chest through the door.

“Are any of Lu Qingxue's belongings kept here?” Ling Qingzhu asked. “I should know what storage is available.”

“The engagement is over. Everything was returned,” Shi Feng said. “That chest holds my spare clothes.”

“Of course,” Ling Qingzhu said, bending over the paper.

She had asked too carefully about a chest in a courtyard he had only just rented. Her ears warmed. Shi Feng merely moved the inkstone within her reach.

“I’ve slept on worse floors,” Shi Feng said. “This one is even swept.”

Her ears turned faintly red above the veil’s ties, and her eyes narrowed. When she started listing the occasions where they might need to hold hands, Shi Feng reached for his tea.

The cup was empty. He put it down again.

“Appearances!” Ling Qingzhu said. “Only appearances. Don’t look so pleased.”

“I get it,” Shi Feng said. “Just warn me before we have to hold hands. I’d like to wash first.”

Her brush stopped and left a dark blot beside the clause. She covered it with a carefully drawn character and refused to look up. Shi Feng took the brush back and wrote one line: this agreement does not buy obedience.

“You expect me to make unreasonable demands?” Ling Qingzhu asked, reading it twice. “I don’t buy people, you know. Obedience wasn’t on my list.”

“You started with a crown prince,” Shi Feng said.

Something scraped outside the gate. Bao Shun had found his fourth urgent reason to stay in the lane. Shi Feng opened the gate and found him staring at a crack in the outer wall with deep professional worry.

“Walls this old need watching, young master! Bao Shun can arrange a repair, very cheap!” Bao Shun said.

Shi Feng put the empty tea tray into his hands.

“Then watch this on your way out,” Shi Feng said.

Bao Shun looked past him at the fairy, decided nothing worth selling could be overheard, and left with his dignity hurt.

“Young master! Young master! Sesame cakes!” Granny Qin shouted across the lane, waving her tongs. “Fresh and hot! For the guest! Is that her? Aiyo, so pretty! Too thin, though! She needs to eat! Take a cake! Take two!”

“I already made tea, Granny,” Shi Feng said, and shut the gate before the tongs could come over the wall.

When Shi Feng sat down again, Ling Qingzhu looked perfectly calm above her white veil, but amusement returned to her eyes. She wrote one more clause: neither side would invite the household’s enemies into the house.

He approved it without a word.

“One more thing,” Shi Feng said. “Not money.”

“Which is?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“A household gathering pass for the Hengyun grounds,” Shi Feng said. “This season, in my name, good whether or not I live under your roof.”

Her eyes dropped to his wrist. The old splint had left a faint mark, though the hand lay steady beside the paper.

“You’ll gather medicine yourself?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“Among other things,” Shi Feng said.

Ling Qingzhu pictured him searching deadly valleys for a cure every physician called impossible. Her heart softened.

“A pass won’t give you rank,” Ling Qingzhu said, more gently than she meant to. “And we can’t bail you out of every ravine. Come back in one piece. Explaining a dead husband is awkward.”

“I asked for access,” Shi Feng said. “I’ll do the walking.”

She agreed. Then she took out his reply, paused with her brush above the paper, and looked straight into his eyes over the veil.

“My Third Uncle checked the Southern Gate ledger before he signed off on this last condition,” Ling Qingzhu said sharply. “The Wei family of Yunze filed a gate inquiry over two dead men—one of them a Foundation Establishment elder. Why are Wei retainers hunting a supposed cripple across half the kingdom?”

Shi Feng met her gaze without blinking. “Their young master tried to rob me on a mountain path outside Yunze, and his father came after me when that failed. Their own witness saw who attacked first—which is why they’re using gate clerks instead of a magistrate’s warrant.”

Ling Qingzhu’s fingers tightened on the brush. She looked from his calm face to the plain sword leaning against the wall, clearly weighing how a man with ruined meridians walked away from a Foundation Establishment elder’s pursuit. He offered no more, and she didn’t press past what the contract required.

She dipped her brush and copied the condition: the Ling household would provide legitimate protection against private Wei demands while their marriage stood, requiring any formal accusation to go before a capital magistrate with witnesses and evidence.

“I won't ask your household to lie,” Shi Feng said. “I only want a court hearing before anyone talks about handing me over.”

“My uncle accepted that condition,” Ling Qingzhu said evenly. “He'll notify the Southern Ward office after we register.”

That was the shelter Shi Feng wanted. He could fight an attacker. Fighting every clerk would leave no time to cultivate.

He insisted the pass be in his hands before they registered. She searched his face for the shame he’d misplaced, found none, and wrote that condition down too.

By the end, the agreement covered both sides of the sheet. Ling Qingzhu flexed her fingers.

They made a second copy and signed both. Shi Feng sanded the ink, folded his copy, and laid it beside the rent receipt.

“Just so we’re clear,” Ling Qingzhu said. “I don’t love you.”

He looked up at the black hair beside her veil.

“You explained that very efficiently,” Shi Feng said.

This time she started to answer, stopped, and glared at the pear tree instead.

At the gate she stopped beside the pear tree and looked back. Two cups stood on the table, both properly filled. He’d refilled hers while she copied the agreement, and she hadn’t noticed.

“Tomorrow, then,” Ling Qingzhu said. “Try not to look so efficient.”

“Bring the pass,” Shi Feng said.

Her eyes softened in spite of herself. She checked her veil’s ties before leaving, and he watched her go.

Shi Feng collected the cups and looked at the blank place waiting for a seal. The deal was dangerous, he thought. It was also his own choice, and he wouldn’t get timid just because danger wore royal silk.

He’d come to the capital to find medicine.

Apparently he’d begin with a wife.

chapters.title: A Wife for the Price of a Seal
chapters.html:
Ling Qingzhu pressed the pass into his hand on the registry office steps.

“Hengyun grounds, every valley, this season, in your name,” Ling Qingzhu said, low and quick. “My household’s seal. Go on, check it. I know you want to.”

Shi Feng checked it. It was the same seal that made the permit clerk’s voice go soft and round, and the ink under it was dry. He tucked the pass inside his robe.

“Now we can get married,” Shi Feng said.

Ling Qingzhu adjusted her white veil and walked in ahead of him. Kong Wen had registered hundreds of marriages. Never once had he seen a queue go silent because the bride walked in.

The whole hall was stunned. The silence spread backward through the open doors. A groom holding a red sash forgot which end was his. A woman arguing over a household record lost three generations of evidence in the middle of a sentence.

“That’s… that’s…”

“Impossible! Not here! Not in the common hall!”

“Who’s the man?”

“Nobody. Look at his sleeves.”

“…”

Ling Qingzhu walked beside Shi Feng with her chin high. In her heart she was calm, and she didn’t hear the crowd’s gasps at all.

Behind the desk, Kong Wen recovered and brought out his finest certificate. It had a gold border, embossed clouds and two cranes with their necks twined together, meant to promise eternal devotion.

“Gold border,” Kong Wen said flatly, smoothing it out.

Shi Feng read the price printed under it.

“Does the plain paper make us less married?” Shi Feng asked.

Kong Wen glanced at the pile of ordinary forms by his elbow. “No.”

“Then plain, without the birds,” Shi Feng said.

Ling Qingzhu turned aside, but her eyes gave away her amusement above the veil.

“Do you haggle at your own funeral too?” Ling Qingzhu murmured. “Idiot.”

“The cranes aren’t signing,” Shi Feng said.

In the queue, the groom with the red sash looked down at his own expensive certificate. His bride saw him do it and stamped on his foot.

Kong Wen gave up the plain form. He checked their identities against the household entries and sent a runner for the register. The boy came back staggering under a book wider than his chest, and dust flew up when it opened.

At Shi Feng’s name, Kong Wen stopped turning pages.

There it was: the former genius of the Shi clan, the ruined meridians, the broken engagement, everything merchants told over wine. Kong Wen looked from the entry to Ling Qingzhu and back, and his expression went blank. He waited for the ink to fix itself. It didn’t.

“The previous engagement is recorded as cancelled,” Kong Wen said.

“Then there’s no previous engagement to register,” Shi Feng said.

Ling Qingzhu laid her household identification beside his. It was a small movement and a decisive one. Kong Wen straightened at once and examined the seal very carefully.

“Both parties must answer of their own free will,” Kong Wen said, looking at Shi Feng.

That earned him a steady look from the bride.

“I came of my own will,” Ling Qingzhu said, clear enough for the back row. “Nobody forced me. Write that down.”

The whole waiting room heard every word. Somebody near the door let out a small, sad sound.

Shi Feng answered just as clearly. Kong Wen wrote down their names, ages and families, blew the ink dry, and pointed to the spaces for their names.

This brush felt different from yesterday’s. Yesterday Shi Feng had bargained over every limit and written each one down where he could see it. This page had none of those terms. Husband. Wife. Two names under one household entry.

He signed without hesitation.

Ling Qingzhu took the brush from him, and their fingers touched. She fixed her sleeve before lowering the tip, so carefully that she was obviously annoyed at herself for noticing.

The seal came down.

For one breath the room held only that small, final sound.

Shi Feng had expected it to feel like buying another permit. It didn’t. He looked at the fresh red mark beside her name and thought: so that’s how it is. Whatever they promised each other in private, the whole world would read these lines one way.

“This is a registered marriage,” Kong Wen said, looking toward the listening queue. “Even a royal household must observe the ancestor's restriction. No servant can replace either party's consent with an invitation.”

A whisper ran through the waiting room. People who had been laughing at the plain certificate looked at its seal again.

Kong Wen waited until they’d studied the document, then pushed over a narrow red packet.

“Donation. For the lucky lamps,” Kong Wen said.

Shi Feng looked at the lamps. Both were unlit.

“Do they cost less because Heaven can see without them?” Shi Feng asked.

Ling Qingzhu made a small sound into her sleeve. Kong Wen took the packet back.

Outside, sunlight caught the edge of the certificate. Ling Qingzhu looked at it a moment too long, then slipped her arm through Shi Feng’s.

The queue began breathing again. An old visitor hurried to the doorway for a better view. A carriage driver nearly dropped his whip, and the fruit seller across the road forgot to lift his thumb from the scale until his customer followed his gaze.

By the corner, three versions of a secret courtship were already spreading in opposite directions.

“He saved her from a lake! At night! Under the moon!”

“Nonsense, they were promised as children, before his meridians broke, and she waited for him!”

“…”

None of the tellers knew anything, which made the stories very convenient. Ling Qingzhu heard enough to stiffen under her calm.

“Smile. You look like you’re being fined,” Ling Qingzhu murmured.

“Your veil makes your part easier,” Shi Feng said.

“My eyes are smiling,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

“Then mine can pay the clerk,” Shi Feng said.

Her shoulders shook. The crowd promptly mistook that for a bride leaning happily against her husband.

“You’re standing on my robe,” Shi Feng said.

She stepped back sharply, nearly catching her own heel in her hem. Shi Feng steadied her elbow, freed the cloth and offered his arm again. This time she took it more carefully.

At the carriage she reached for the certificate. He’d already folded it into a clean wrapper.

“I was sure you’d crease it,” Ling Qingzhu said, a little surprised.

“The clerk would sell us another blessing if we went back,” Shi Feng said.

She laughed then, briefly, without trying to hide it. The driver stared, and Shi Feng climbed in before the man could wonder about adding a charge.

They sat on opposite benches. With the curtains lowered, the public closeness disappeared and left an awkward gap that neither knew how to fill. Ling Qingzhu smoothed the cuff he’d steadied. Shi Feng tucked the certificate inside his robe, beside the pass and the agreement that explained everything the certificate didn’t.

From a doorway across the street, Guo Zhen watched until the carriage blocked his view.

The royal steward had expected a meeting, maybe an ugly rumour. He never expected a government seal! Now there were witnesses, records, and a bride who declared her consent before an entire office. Guo Zhen’s face turned pale, and he thought: The consort’s steward won’t like this.

He followed at a distance and didn’t approach.

In the carriage, Shi Feng felt a gaze settle on them and follow. Through the gap in the curtain he caught only a shape leaving, and the faint, heavy pressure of Foundation Establishment qi held in check. A Foundation Establishment cultivator, Shi Feng thought, sent to watch a married couple. The prince wasn’t subtle.

Ling Qingzhu noticed his glance.

“Let them stare. They’ll get bored in a few days,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Some people have way too much free time,” Shi Feng said.

He let the curtain fall. His hand rested near the plain blade at his waist, relaxed and calm.

The cranes, he suspected, wouldn’t have improved what came next.

chapters.title: Husband at the Gate
chapters.html:
“A married couple uses way more water!” Jiang Meilan shouted from the gate. “Two people, two buckets, two times the trouble!”

The landlady had come to inspect the new tenant before the new tenant had even unpacked. Ling Qingzhu stood under the pear tree with a small travel chest at her feet. Outside the gate, Bao Shun hovered around, and it was obvious he regretted renting out this courtyard so cheaply.

Jiang Meilan looked at the chest, then at Shi Feng, then at the well.

“What, you’re charging us by the bucket now?” Shi Feng asked.

“Every bucket wears out the well rope!” Jiang Meilan yelled, folding her arms. “Who’s going to pay for a new rope? Me?”

So she was even going to charge them for the rope wearing out.

“Fine. I’ll buy you a new rope,” Shi Feng said.

Her eyes moved to the kitchen chimney next. Apparently, being married also made way too much smoke.

Before she could get started on that, Bao Shun stuck his head through the gate. “And there are two people living here now, Auntie Jiang! That changes the price. The agreement was for one single man, it’s only fair.”

Ling Qingzhu’s fingers tightened on the handle of her chest. Royal invitations had never annoyed her this much. This broker’s oily smile made her want to draw her sword. How shameless, she thought.

Shi Feng’s expression didn’t change at all as he looked at Bao Shun.

“So you want extra because we’re married, and extra because there are two of us?” Shi Feng asked. “Isn’t that the same thing?”

Bao Shun suddenly found the gatepost very interesting. Jiang Meilan pulled out the rental agreement. Shi Feng already had his copy open, with his finger on the line that said the whole courtyard was his to use.

The landlady looked at his finger, then at Ling Qingzhu’s cold eyes above her veil. If she lost a quarrel in front of the number one fairy of Great Liang, half the lane would come running to watch. The extra rent wasn’t worth that much embarrassment.

“Just make sure it’s a good rope,” Jiang Meilan said, and stalked out, looking like she’d done them a huge favour.

“Auntie, my handling fee!” Bao Shun began.

“Handle yourself home!” Jiang Meilan snapped over her shoulder, and he followed her with nothing at all.

Ling Qingzhu waited until their footsteps faded and set down her chest.

“You enjoyed that,” Ling Qingzhu said. “Don’t deny it. You almost smiled.”

“He started enjoying it first,” Shi Feng said. “I felt obliged to join.”

She waited until he shut the gate. Then she untied her veil.

Shi Feng stopped looking at the latch.

Jade-white cheeks, a delicate nose, soft red lips. Her face was even more beautiful than he imagined. The veil had hidden far too much. No wonder the kingdom could find nobody to rank above her!

“What?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“I was checking whether the register exaggerated,” Shi Feng replied.

“And?” Ling Qingzhu asked, lifting her chin.

“It ran out of ranks,” Shi Feng said.

Her cheeks warmed. She folded the veil instead of answering.

“I wear it around everyone else,” Ling Qingzhu said. “At home, with only you here, I don’t need it.”

Shi Feng felt unexpectedly pleased. That wasn’t written in their agreement.

He showed her their only room. Her bed stood beneath the courtyard window, with space for her chest at its foot. A new folding screen stood beside it. His straw mat and rolled blanket lay against the opposite wall.

Ling Qingzhu looked at the bed, the screen, the mat, and the four steps between them. She said nothing.

The room was smaller than her dressing chamber, but clean and ready for her. Her heart eased a little.

“The bed’s yours,” Shi Feng said. “The screen is for changing. I’ll sleep on the mat, facing the wall.”

“Four steps,” Ling Qingzhu said. “That’s all between us? A border crossing?”

“I measured,” Shi Feng said. “The agreement doesn’t say how far.”

She turned away and became very interested in the table.

“You can move the table,” Shi Feng said. “The leg nearest the bed is short. Put the wedge back afterwards.”

She looked down and found the little wooden wedge exactly where he’d said.

“I could buy you a better table, you know,” Ling Qingzhu said. “It’s no trouble.”

“This one holds things,” Shi Feng said.

She couldn’t tell whether that was thrift or an insult to the whole furniture trade. Shi Feng would cultivate after she slept, or in the kitchen. She must never see it.

When she opened the chest at the foot of the bed, two pale storage bags lay among the wrapped clothes. She pushed them aside to reach a silver clasp, then frowned, because one drawstring was caught under the other. They were the same make, with fine white stitching across each mouth.

Shi Feng turned to face the wall and went out to heat water. He’d promised her privacy, he thought, and curiosity didn’t cancel a promise.

When he came back with the kettle, the bags were out of sight and her few things were laid out behind the screen. A sword lay within reach of the pillow. His own sword hung on a nail by the mat. He noted where hers was and asked nothing.

At dusk the public show began again.

At Granny Qin’s knock, Ling Qingzhu tied her veil before Shi Feng opened the gate. Granny Qin brought sesame cakes and her staring nephew.

“Aiyo, such a beautiful bride!” Granny Qin shouted. “Eat! Still hot! And if this courtyard’s too small, my nephew Qin Bao has a spare room. Very airy, east-facing, canal view…”

“Thanks, Granny,” Shi Feng said, taking the dish. “The cakes are very welcome.”

He shut the gate on the nephew. Ling Qingzhu removed her veil again. Ling Qingzhu stood by the kitchen door, her expression astonished.

“You could’ve let her finish,” Ling Qingzhu said, fighting a laugh. “She was just getting to the canal view.”

“She finished when she started describing a spare room in her nephew’s house,” Shi Feng said.

They split the cakes. He took the broken ones, and she noticed.

Before supper they had to decide what to call each other in public. She turned down every sweet nickname at once. He agreed so fast that her brows drew together.

“Just say ‘wife.’ That’s enough,” Ling Qingzhu said. “No honeyed names. I’ll laugh. Then we’re ruined.”

“That’s what the certificate calls you,” Shi Feng said.

“You don’t have to say it like it’s a cart registration!” Ling Qingzhu said.

He looked up from the kettle and actually thought about the complaint. Then he set her cup down beside her hand, instead of reaching across her.

“Then tell me when I do it,” Shi Feng said.

The straight answer took some of the edge off her face.

A royal messenger arrived before they ate.

He came in a lacquered sedan carried by four bearers, and every doorway in the lane emptied to watch.

“The eastern residence!”

“For the cripple’s courtyard?”

“For the bride, you fool! Nobody sends a sedan to a cripple!”

“That courtyard has one room. Where’s the husband going to sleep?”

“Granny Qin, your cakes are burning again!”

“Aiyo, my cakes!”

“…”

The invitation had an embossed border and a seal that made Bao Shun’s surcharges look cheap. Shi Feng took it at the gate. The messenger looked past his shoulder, failed to catch a glimpse of the bride, and left in an unseemly hurry.

Ling Qingzhu read it by the kitchen door.

“A celebration at the eastern residence,” Ling Qingzhu said slowly. “His Highness wants to congratulate me. How thoughtful of him.”

Shi Feng looked at the single name written on it.

“He forgot someone,” Shi Feng said.

The paper talked about flowers, music, and a small gathering of close friends. It said nothing about a husband. That was no accident, and Shi Feng sneered in his heart.

“You don’t have to go,” Ling Qingzhu said. “He only invited me. I can say you’re busy.”

She meant to give him a choice. To his ears it sounded like being shut out of a danger he’d accepted when he signed. He took the invitation and laid it beside the stove, safely away from the flame.

“You hired a husband,” Shi Feng said. “Let His Highness remember he invited a married woman.”

Ling Qingzhu looked at him in the firelight. His robe was plain, his blade undecorated, and every gossip in the capital claimed to understand his ruined cultivation. Yet even a crown prince’s rank didn’t change the shape of an insult to him.

For the first time since the tea house, she wondered whether she’d misjudged how difficult her harmless husband could become.

chapters.title: The Uninvited Husband
chapters.html:
“Only one name,” Guo Zhen said, holding the invitation up to the lantern.

The eastern residence had polished floors, flowering trees, and a steward with one main job that evening: keeping Shi Feng away from all of it. Ling Qingzhu wore pale sleeves over a fitted blue robe, her black hair pinned with the silver clasp from her chest. Her white veil stayed firmly tied.

Three men stopped talking when she stepped from the carriage. Only Guo Zhen cared more about the man beside her.

“What an unfortunate mistake,” Ling Qingzhu said. “You surely didn’t mean to leave out my husband. He’s coming.”

She said it without hesitation, and her fingers settled around Shi Feng’s arm.

Guo Zhen’s expression showed no surprise. It showed recognition. He had expected this. A shut gate might still salvage the household’s failed arrangements.

“The arrangements are limited,” Guo Zhen said.

“Then I won’t trouble them,” Shi Feng said, and turned toward the carriage.

Ling Qingzhu understood at once and turned with him.

“…Please enter,” Guo Zhen said, and stepped aside.

Shi Feng walked in without thanking him. Waste of breath, he thought. The man is only a gatekeeper.

Sima Yu waited beneath a carved canopy, the royal dragon dark on his robe, his smile easy, the smile of a man who rarely had to ask twice. Young nobles stood around him with cups in hand. Their laughter started before he finished speaking and died when Ling Qingzhu came near.

“A sudden marriage, Qingzhu,” Sima Yu said, using her given name without permission. “Your friends would have loved to celebrate it with you.”

“We came for Your Highness’s congratulations,” Ling Qingzhu said, her eyes cold above her veil. “So we brought the reason.”

She didn’t apologise. Shi Feng felt a slight pressure from her hand and wondered whether she meant to stop him from speaking, or just needed somewhere to put her fingers. The crown prince’s gaze finally moved to him.

“A man should know what he can provide,” Sima Yu said kindly. “Even beauty needs more than a roof.”

Shi Feng looked up at the expensive canopy.

“Then Your Highness has made a fine start,” Shi Feng said.

Several guests lowered their cups too carefully. Sima Yu smiled, but the smile didn’t reach his eyes, and his expression grew cold.

“And you?” Sima Yu asked.

“I brought the wife,” Shi Feng said.

Ling Qingzhu’s fingers tightened on his sleeve. Behind the prince, someone gasped at a bad moment and pretended it was a cough.

They received their congratulations. They also received a table as far from the canopy as the garden allowed, beside a pond where the mosquitoes had never been taught rank.

Shi Feng moved Ling Qingzhu’s chair out of the damp shade and set his own between her and the reeds. An attendant brought tea so pale that the leaves seemed to have run away before reaching the pot.

“Nobody to perform for here,” Ling Qingzhu said softly. “They seated us as far from him as possible. I’m almost impressed.”

“The mosquitoes haven’t noticed,” Shi Feng said.

She looked at his chair, then at his wrist, where one hungry insect was already getting to work on him.

For a while they sat without performing anything. Music drifted over the water. The tea was at least warm. Ling Qingzhu’s shoulders relaxed when she saw he wouldn’t complain about the distance or ask for a better seat.

Then Fan Yucheng arrived, wine cup first.

The Qi Condensation talent had drunk enough to be loud, and too much to notice he was unwelcome.

“Brother Shi!” Fan Yucheng boomed, loud enough for three tables. “Do you know who this young master is? Fan Yucheng, the best sword talent of my house! They say you once had talent too. Once!”

Shi Feng set down his cup.

“Then you’re finished talking about me,” Shi Feng said.

Fan Yucheng’s face went red to the ears. A cripple dared to brush him off in front of the first fairy of Great Liang! He yanked a narrow ceremonial sword from his sash, its silver tassel swinging in the lamplight.

“A friendly exchange of pointers, cripple!” Fan Yucheng declared. “Of course, nobody expects you to circulate qi. This young master will go easy on—”

The nearby tables turned in their seats.

“Fan Yucheng is going to make him dance!”

“Is that kind?”

“…”

Ling Qingzhu half rose from her chair. “Young Master Fan, you’re drunk,” Ling Qingzhu said. “Go and sit down.” Shi Feng touched the edge of the table, a small signal to wait.

“Are you teaching me, or asking me to teach you?” Shi Feng asked.

Fan Yucheng glanced toward the canopy, hoping His Highness had noticed his fine sword. Sima Yu watched with every sign of boredom.

“Teaching you is this young master’s honour!” Fan Yucheng said grandly.

Shi Feng looked at the ornamental blade, then at the young man’s soft silk boots, and thought: an amateur, and a drunk one.

“Your front foot is turned inward,” Shi Feng said. “Draw like that and your tassel will wrap around your wrist. Fix it before you ask an invalid for lessons.”

Fan Yucheng looked down in spite of himself. As he shifted his stance, the tassel swung across his sleeve and wound itself neatly around his wrist.

Shi Feng had neither risen nor touched his blade. He had simply pointed out an ordinary flaw.

“It wrapped! It actually wrapped!”

“He called it before it happened!”

“From a chair!”

“…”

Fan Yucheng jammed the sword into its sheath too fast and trapped two tassel threads under the guard. He tugged once, couldn’t free them.

“You… you!” Fan Yucheng spluttered. “This young master will remember this!” Then he stalked away with the tassel hanging crooked and his ears burning.

Around the pond, the whispers shifted at once. Two young gentlemen at the nearest pavilion quietly stood, cupped their hands toward Shi Feng’s table in genuine respect for his eye, and told an attendant to replace the pond table’s cold teapot with a silver flagon from the upper terrace. For the rest of the banquet, none of the nobles who had laughed at Fan Yucheng’s approach called Fairy Ling’s husband a cripple within earshot.

Ling Qingzhu sat down again.

“You could’ve turned him down more gently,” Ling Qingzhu said. Her eyes brightened above the veil anyway. “He might cry.”

“He came a long way to be corrected,” Shi Feng said.

Her laugh was quiet, but it carried across the pond. Beneath the canopy, Sima Yu set down his cup, and his expression darkened.

Afterward the gifts were displayed: jade cases, rare flowers, a comb carved from a spirit beast’s horn. An attendant offered a gold bracelet to Ling Qingzhu without once looking at Shi Feng.

She didn’t touch it.

“Your Highness has already honoured our marriage,” Ling Qingzhu said clearly. “We can’t accept more.”

Our marriage. The words landed harder than the bracelet would have. The nearby guests were stunned, and not one of them dared to look at the prince.

Shi Feng offered his arm when she stood, and they crossed the garden together, neither hurrying nor slowing down. At the gate, Guo Zhen bowed low enough to hide his face. In the carriage, Ling Qingzhu let go of Shi Feng’s sleeve and rubbed the place where the cloth had pressed her fingers.

“You weren’t scared,” Ling Qingzhu said. “Not even a little? My hands are still shaking.”

“There were six kinds of pastry and no supper,” Shi Feng said. “I was getting impatient.”

She stared at him, then laughed, though her chest was still tight. He let her laugh. She didn’t need to hear his other observations: the guards posted at the side gate, the exits, and the steward with a leather guard on his left wrist, who’d watched Shi Feng’s sword hand all evening.

Beneath the canopy, Sima Yu watched the gate close. Guo Zhen waited until the last nearby guests withdrew.

“The husband?” Guo Zhen asked.

“An ordinary man can have an ordinary accident,” Sima Yu said softly, and lifted his cup again. “Just keep it away from her.”

Guo Zhen bowed. Until tonight the prince had treated the match as household business. Now guests had honoured a nobody at his own banquet, and that nobody had walked away with the woman his courtiers had promised him. Sima Yu could not erase the registry without defying his ancestor's rule. He could remove the man who had made royal favour look cheap.

It was no longer the consort's arrangement. It was His Highness's wounded pride.

In the carriage, Shi Feng rubbed the swelling on his wrist, where the mosquito had won despite all his precautions. Ling Qingzhu saw the movement and silently held out a little pot of cooling balm.

He took it.

So that was royal hospitality. He’d remember it for a long time, mostly for the mosquito.

chapters.title: The First Feast
chapters.html:
The carriage rolled into Qingliu Lane long after the lamps should have been put out, and nobody in the lane had gone to bed. Granny Qin’s brazier still glowed opposite the gate. She stood beside it with a sesame cake in each hand, and her nephew Qin Bao stared over her shoulder.

“They’re back! And the husband walked home on his own two feet!”

“Look at his wrist. Did the crown prince bite him?”

“Mosquitoes, you fool! The pond was full of them!”

“Fairy Ling is holding a pot of balm! Fairy Ling!”

“…”

Shi Feng helped Ling Qingzhu down from the carriage. Her fingers left his sleeve at once, and he noticed she did it a little too fast.

“It’s late,” Ling Qingzhu said, a little too briskly. “Shouldn’t all of you be asleep?”

“Late? Young wife, a good cake is never late!” Granny Qin cried, pressing both cakes into Shi Feng’s hands. “A man who comes home from a rich feast with an empty stomach needs two! Burned a bit, but the burn is free!”

“How did you know I didn’t eat?” Shi Feng asked.

“The coachman’s cousin says there were six kinds of pastry and nobody dared touch them,” Granny Qin said proudly. “Bao, close your mouth. You’re letting the night in.”

Qin Bao closed his mouth. He kept staring. With the gate shut, Ling Qingzhu untied her veil and looked at the two black-edged cakes.

“You’ve been here five days,” Shi Feng said, “and we’ve eaten nothing but noodles from the corner stall.”

“The noodles were fine!” Ling Qingzhu said. “They were hot. Hot is the main thing.”

“Tomorrow I’ll cook,” Shi Feng said.

Ling Qingzhu turned her head. “You? Cook?”

“Badly,” Shi Feng said. “Eat first. Then judge.”

She took a cake and walked inside, too straight-backed. Shi Feng spared her another tease.

That night he spread his bedding on the floor in his corner while she changed behind the folding screen. The room was so small he could hear every rustle, so he stared hard at the ceiling beams.

The next morning, the silver spirit carp cost fifty-eight spirit stones. Shi Feng watched it flap against its basket. At that price, he thought, it should at least be able to perform a small miracle.

“Seventy was my price!” Peng Tao the fishmonger shouted. “Fifty-eight is robbery!”

“The left gill is bruised,” Shi Feng said. “Fifty-eight is generous.”

“A cripple who haggles like that…” a woman muttered behind him.

“…”

Peng Tao was stunned. His expression turned bitter, but he wrapped the fish. Shi Feng added lotus shoots, ginger, dried mushrooms, a parcel of sweet bean paste, and one duck, plucked and ridiculously expensive. He didn’t look at the total. Today he didn’t want to.

Ling Qingzhu came out of the room, drawn by the smell, just as he dropped everything on the kitchen table.

“Is someone visiting?” Ling Qingzhu asked. “That’s half the market on your table.”

“You moved in,” Shi Feng said. “This is the first meal.”

She looked at the ingredients. There was enough for a banquet, and the courtyard had one good table and a stool that tilted to the left. Her gaze finally settled on the lotus shoots. She wanted a job to do.

“Should I wash these?” Ling Qingzhu asked. “I can wash things. Probably.”

Shi Feng pointed to the basin. She rolled up her sleeves, showing pale wrists, and attacked the first shoot with the face she used for a difficult sword form. The shoot shot out of her hands, hit the bottom of the basin, and splashed water all over his robe.

Both of them looked down.

“It was slippery!” Ling Qingzhu said. “It jumped. You saw it jump.”

“It’s been here longer than you,” Shi Feng said. “It knows the house.”

Her expression stiffened. Her ears went pink. Shi Feng handed her a cloth and moved the basin further from the table.

She tucked a black strand behind her ear. Shi Feng forgot the carp in his hand.

“The fish is down there,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“I know,” Shi Feng replied, still looking at her.

“Then why are you scaling the air?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

He cleaned the carp himself. The knife slid under the scales, short and sure. After many days of cold roads and corpses, a steady hand felt surprisingly good. He steamed the flesh with ginger, crisped the skin on the side, and set the bones to simmer for a clear broth.

Three of her lotus slices were cut too thick. He dropped them into the pot first, so the extra time would soften them and she wouldn’t have to start again.

Steam fogged the window. Ling Qingzhu lingered by the kitchen door.

“You’ve cooked before,” Ling Qingzhu said. “That was not ‘badly’.”

“Bad cooking is expensive when you have to eat it yourself,” Shi Feng said.

That wasn’t a real answer. She decided, to her own surprise, that she was fine with it. Outside the gate, footsteps slowed and slowed again.

“Young master!” Bao Shun’s voice drifted through the wood. “The smell has reached the whole lane! Surely a host this generous will share with this humble Bao Shun—”

Neither of them moved.

“Want me to get rid of him?” Ling Qingzhu asked. “I’m very good at it.”

“He’s never paid a fee in this house,” Shi Feng said. “He won’t eat in it either.”

The footsteps shuffled away, offended.

The dishes were far too many for two people. Shi Feng knew it. After too many meals beside corpses, he wanted one where nobody ran away halfway through.

Ling Qingzhu tasted the broth, paused, and tasted it again. Shi Feng waited until she lifted her bowl before he took his own.

“This is good,” Ling Qingzhu said, and tasted it a third time. “Why am I surprised? You said ‘badly’.”

“Because you expected the duck to be raw,” Shi Feng said.

“I didn’t think that!” Ling Qingzhu said, and looked away. “…Not the whole duck.”

The duck vanished faster than either of them expected. When she picked a strip of bitter green out of her broth and set it on the rim of her plate, Shi Feng noticed. The next bowl he served gave her none, and gave himself double.

“You don’t have to eat my greens,” Ling Qingzhu said quickly. “I can manage a bitter leaf.”

“I like them,” Shi Feng said.

She stared at his face and couldn’t tell whether he was lying. He was already picking the fine bones from a piece of fish, and he didn’t look up.

After supper she went to the chest at the foot of the bed and came back with a pale storage bag, its mouth sewn with fine white stitching.

“Your payment,” Ling Qingzhu said. “Ten thousand, like we wrote.”

Shi Feng took it. The drawstring was neatly knotted. It seemed a small, innocent thing to set against a crown prince’s anger.

“Count it. I won’t be offended,” Ling Qingzhu said. “I’d count it too.”

“After the dishes,” Shi Feng said.

He set the bag on the high kitchen shelf, away from water and grease, and went to the basin. Ling Qingzhu stayed at the table with her cup in both hands and watched his back. She almost offered to help, then remembered the lotus shoots.

“What was Yunze Town like?” Ling Qingzhu asked instead.

He gave her the version without the quarry or the dead Foundation Establishment cultivator. It had bad inns, greedy merchants, and a kiln owner who thought a room didn’t need a door.

“A room without a door?! How does anyone sleep?” Ling Qingzhu asked, leaning forward until a strand of black hair fell over her shoulder.

“They tell you the roof is included,” Shi Feng said.

She laughed. He found that he liked the sound.

Later he wrapped the last two sweet cakes and left them by her cup. She picked up the parcel and carried it behind the screen without a word. It felt more intimate than walking arm in arm before a garden full of nobles, because nobody was there to applaud.

Behind the screen, she stopped. Ten thousand spirit stones, she told herself, was a generous price. Of course he wanted the arrangement to go smoothly. Good service meant nothing more.

The explanation settled easily. She didn’t look at it too closely.

In the kitchen, Shi Feng counted what was left in his own purse and frowned at the fishmonger’s receipt. He had overspent. The Hengyun pass would help, and the payment would refill the reserve as soon as he opened the bag.

He checked the latch and lowered the lamp. In the room, her breathing was already slow and even, a few steps from his bedding.

On the high shelf, the pale bag sat unopened.

chapters.title: An Ordinary Accident
chapters.html:
The message came folded around a dried root.

“A man left this at the gate,” Bao Shun said. “Grey hat. I thought he’d come to look at the courtyard.”

“Did he ask for me?” Shi Feng asked.

Bao Shun nodded, offended that the visitor hadn’t wanted a house. He described the man’s limp while Shi Feng unfolded the message. The dried root inside was fresh. Whoever sent it knew where he went gathering.

Bao Shun retreated like a merchant who’d just been refused his entire stock. Shi Feng broke a sliver from the root’s tip and smelled the fresh heart of it. It was genuine bone medicine, and good. Whoever sent it knew better than to offer rubbish.

The note was short. A merchant was closing his storehouse in the northern quarter. Old stock, low prices, cash before dawn.

Shi Feng read the lane’s name twice. A merchant with real medicine would sell it in daylight, he thought. Only a man who wanted no witnesses sold before dawn.

He put on his sword anyway. If the medicine was real, he’d buy it. If someone wanted him dead, it was better to walk in and meet him.

The northern lane was silent. Weeds pushed through the paving, and the neighbouring courtyards were tied shut with old rope. One lantern burned inside the storehouse. Whoever picked this place wanted every shout to die before it found an ear.

Shi Feng found the wire before he found the man.

It crossed the doorway at throat height, tied to a fresh nail in rotten wood. Behind it a broken plank lay under a reed mat. A careless visitor would stumble, raise his head, and hit the wire too late.

A trap for a cripple, Shi Feng thought coldly. How thoughtful!

He cut the wire with his knife and pushed the door open. He didn’t creep.

“You came,” Guo Zhen said from behind the crates.

“The note said cash before dawn,” Shi Feng said. “I’m early.”

Guo Zhen stepped out. The royal steward wore dark clothes now instead of his embroidered robe. The narrow leather guard still hugged his left wrist.

“Shi Feng,” Guo Zhen said, drawing his sword. “His Highness says a husband shouldn’t leave his wife alone at night.”

“I understand,” Shi Feng said. “You’re here without a signed order.”

Guo Zhen’s pupils tightened. “Dead man,” Guo Zhen said.

He charged.

Guo Zhen was at Foundation Establishment, one great realm above Bone Refinement. In Great Liang’s capital, that was the kind of gap men called a gulf. He swung his sword with the confidence of an executioner paid by the head.

The blow split Shi Feng’s wooden scabbard. Shi Feng turned with it instead of retreating and drove his shoulder under the steward’s breastbone.

Boom!

Guo Zhen crashed backward through a stack of crates. Rotten timber burst across the floor.

“You—” Guo Zhen coughed, scrambling up. “Cripples can’t do that!”

“Three physicians agreed with you,” Shi Feng said.

Guo Zhen’s face turned grim, and Foundation Establishment qi flared around him. His next stroke carried a pale edge that sliced two baskets in half without slowing. Shi Feng stepped inside its arc and rapped the man’s forearm with the flat of his blade.

Clang!

The sound rang through the storehouse. Guo Zhen’s expression changed.

He had come to murder a cripple. What stood before him had a body stronger than any physician’s report, and a hand that stayed steady under Foundation Establishment pressure.

“Impossible!” Guo Zhen snarled, gathering qi into a shield across his chest. “Your meridians are ruined!”

Shi Feng’s fist struck the shield. The pale light crumpled inward, and Guo Zhen slammed against the rear wall hard enough to bring dust down from the beams. His breath left him in a short, ugly sound.

Shi Feng didn’t give him time to find it again.

The steward thrust upward beneath the ribs. Shi Feng caught his wrist, turned the point aside, and drove a knee into the man’s thigh. Bone cracked.

He didn’t need a trap, a borrowed treasure, or luck. He only needed the gap between what Guo Zhen expected and what Shi Feng could do. In his heart, he marked it down: three hundred and sixty-five meridians and ten refined bones were more than any physician in the capital could see.

Outside, an ox cart rattled over the lane’s uneven stones. Shi Feng pressed the steward’s face into his sleeve before the scream could escape. He waited until the wheels passed and no one stopped.

“You were examined,” Guo Zhen gasped into the cloth, stunned. “The Pavilion’s own physician—”

“You should’ve hired a physician instead of buying wire,” Shi Feng said.

He broke the sword wrist.

Guo Zhen made a muffled sound, and Foundation Establishment qi stirred again, weak and scattered. Shi Feng tightened his grip until it stopped.

“Who ordered it?” Shi Feng asked.

Guo Zhen’s eyes slid toward the door. He’d rather run than tell the truth. Shi Feng brought the broken wrist closer to the edge of a crate.

“Sima Yu!” Guo Zhen shouted. “It was His Highness! The palace has guards! Royal elders! You’ll never pass the gate!”

“You passed mine,” Shi Feng said.

For the first time, Guo Zhen understood this wasn’t a threat meant to improve the bargain.

“Wait! I’ll pay! I know the men who carry the prince’s letters between his residences!” Guo Zhen said.

Nothing the steward offered changed the wire, the sword, or the choice that had brought them here.

“Brother Shi,” Guo Zhen whispered, “please—”

“This Shi has a wife who’s waiting,” Shi Feng said. “And I still have to make breakfast.”

He ended it with the man’s own blade.

The body settled against the broken boards. Shi Feng searched the clothes for orders and found none. There was no signed murder warrant, because Sima Yu knew that much about respectable accidents. He took only the unmarked spirit stones from the purse, left the Eastern Palace side-gate key and powder packet beside the corpse so the city watch would know whose man lay here, and pulled the throat-wire free from the doorframe, leaving only the freshly driven iron nail and a severed twist of wire in the rotten wood.

He wrapped the wire and the false note together to drop into the canal sluice on his way back, and tucked the genuine root sample into his sleeve. It was the only honest part of the invitation.

Before leaving by the rear courtyard, he wiped the blade and checked the edge. A small nick marked where Guo Zhen’s guard met it. That would cost money to repair.

The thought annoyed him more than the steward’s promises had frightened him.

So Sima Yu was on the list now, he thought. The prince himself wasn’t the problem. The royal family kept Golden Core powerhouses, two great realms above Shi Feng, and the palace never lacked defenders. He wouldn’t charge their gate because a dying man mentioned it. Sooner or later Sima Yu would walk out of those walls.

On that day, this Shi would be waiting.

At home, the courtyard was dark except for the lamp glowing in the window of the one room.

Inside, Ling Qingzhu had fallen asleep at the table over a half-read book, one hand beneath her cheek and the other still on the page. She hadn’t gone to bed. She’d been waiting up. The evening breeze lifted the corner of her sleeve.

Shi Feng closed the outer gate softly. He moved the book where falling wax couldn’t touch it and left a folded shawl within her reach, rather than wake her by draping it over her shoulders. His own bedding lay rolled in its corner. He didn’t unroll it yet.

In the kitchen he laid the broken scabbard on the table.

There had been an ordinary accident, exactly as the crown prince wished.

It had happened to the wrong man.

chapters.title: The Steward Who Didn’t Come Home
chapters.html:
Two mornings after the northern-quarter trap, Sima Yu was stopped at the foot of the court steps before the morning recess had even cleared.

Censor Lu Jing of the Directorate of Imperial Clan Affairs stood beside the bronze bell with a formal inquiry tablet in both hands, while half a dozen ministers and the Third Prince’s attendants slowed their steps to listen.

“Your Highness,” Lu Jing said clearly enough for the colonnade to hear, “at dawn the Northern Ward watch recovered the body of Guo Zhen, a registered fourth-rank steward of the Eastern Palace, from an abandoned timber storehouse near North Sluice Lane. His Eastern Palace key was still at his belt, and his chest had been crushed before his own sword ended him. Was Steward Guo acting on an Eastern Palace commission in the northern quarter?”

The surrounding officials went very still. A dead palace steward was a scandal. A royal commission would make it worse.

Sima Yu’s gentle smile did not flicker, though his fingers tightened inside his dragon-stitched sleeve. “Guo Zhen requested two days of private leave to settle a family debt, Censor Lu,” Sima Yu said smoothly. “The Eastern Palace had no business in North Sluice Lane. Still, since he served my residence for ten years, my household will pay the ward’s inquest fee and three hundred stones of bereaved stipend to the registry.”

“I shall record that statement,” Lu Jing said. “The ancestor's restriction binds every royal household. A registered marriage cannot be set aside by palace servants. If this death concerns one, the court must examine it.”

Two officials exchanged a look that made Sima Yu's jaw set.

Back inside the Eastern Palace, the doors had barely shut before Sima Yu swept a porcelain ink-rest off his desk. Two inner guards knelt by the shattered shards, holding up a rusted iron nail and a severed twist of wire pried from the northern storehouse doorframe.

“Guo Zhen hung a throat-wire inside the door to catch someone coming in before dawn, Your Highness,” Ge Fan reported in a low voice. “Whoever walked through cut the wire, broke Guo Zhen’s Foundation Establishment guard with bare hands, and left him with his own blade. The day before, Guo Zhen questioned the Cloud Mist Tea House about Ling Qingzhu’s new husband.”

Sima Yu stared at the cut wire. “A cripple from Qingshi Town didn’t shatter a Foundation Establishment shield with his fist,” Sima Yu said coldly. “Either the Ling household sent an expert behind him, or that marriage is hiding more than a shield. Put two quiet eyes on Qingliu Lane and the Hengyun pass office—and keep the Eastern Palace’s name out of it.”

In crowded shops, Ling Qingzhu’s admirers now kept their distance. Merchants greeted her husband politely and watched his purse.

At the eastern-market cloth shop, Bu Guang brought the expensive silk to the front before they entered.

“Newlyweds deserve a lucky price!” Bu Guang announced, bowing to Ling Qingzhu.

Shi Feng checked the good weave and the absurd price.

“What was the price before we got married?” Shi Feng asked.

Bu Guang’s face turned red.

“Look at him, asking about last year’s price!” a customer whispered from the corner.

“He’s right! That tag grew a zero!”

“…”

Ling Qingzhu’s eyes curved above her veil and fan. How refreshing, she thought. It was becoming a familiar pleasure to watch him say the awkward thing everyone else walked around.

She chose a length of darker cloth for a travel cloak. Bu Guang reached for it.

“My husband is carrying it,” Ling Qingzhu said. “I’m buying it. Look at his arms, Boss Bu. Does he look here to argue?”

“Of course!” Bu Guang said.

Outside, Ling Qingzhu took the parcel from him.

“You could let him win once, you know,” Ling Qingzhu said. “The poor man has a family.”

“He won when you bought the silk,” Shi Feng said. “He doesn’t need to win twice.”

Then Ling Qingzhu saw something past his shoulder, and her eyes turned cold.

Across the street, a royal carriage stood beside a tea house. The curtains were drawn. Two attendants waited by the wheels, and neither made any attempt to buy tea.

“That’s the crown prince’s carriage!” a vegetable seller muttered to his neighbour. “It’s been there since morning.”

Ling Qingzhu shifted the parcel into one arm and took Shi Feng’s hand with the other.

He looked down.

Her fingers were cool. This was no grand entrance, only two people walking side by side. It felt different.

Then he saw the carriage. Shi Feng understood, and his heart gave a short, annoyed twitch.

“An audience,” Shi Feng said quietly.

“An inspection,” Ling Qingzhu said, her voice low. “He dislikes people leaving his banquet with their heads up.”

He let his fingers close around hers.

They walked past without slowing. Ling Qingzhu tilted her veiled face toward him, her eyes warm as she hung on his every word. Shi Feng told her the pastry stall ahead was using yesterday’s oil.

She almost ruined the act by laughing at the wrong moment.

“Shi Feng! Be serious!” Ling Qingzhu whispered. “I’m trying to look in love! You’re talking about oil!”

“He can’t see your smile through the veil,” Shi Feng said.

“Then look at my eyes!” Ling Qingzhu replied.

Shi Feng did. Her fingers tightened around his, and for a moment she forgot the carriage.

“I am,” Shi Feng said. “That oil is really old.”

At the corner, beyond the carriage’s view, she let go. She did it as casually as putting down a fan she didn’t need anymore.

He’d known she would. Knowing didn’t make his suddenly empty hand feel ordinary.

Over the following days, their act turned into habits.

Ling Qingzhu called him “my husband” before people could ask. Shi Feng moved her chair, carried parcels, and refused prices that merchants thought a fairy’s beauty should raise. At the well, one gossip loudly wondered whether a fallen genius could keep such a fine wife happy.

Ling Qingzhu stepped close enough to brush his sleeve before she answered.

“My husband didn’t invite the lane’s judgment,” Ling Qingzhu said. “And I’m very happy. Thanks for asking.”

The gossips went quiet. A bucket rope slid through someone’s fingers and the bucket dropped with a splash. Behind the gate, Ling Qingzhu rubbed the space between her brows.

“Is the whole lane always this nosy?” Ling Qingzhu asked. “I wanted to drop that bucket on someone.”

“They were nosy before,” Shi Feng said. “Now they think the well entitles them to details.”

In private, they stayed careful. One room. She had the bed and he had the floor, and the folding screen stayed up whenever she changed.

He rolled his bedding every morning and waited for her answer before entering at night. Neither questioned the other’s errands.

She stopped moving the medicines on his corner shelf after he explained that two similar roots didn’t belong in the same jar.

One night she came back late from her household and found the kitchen table set for two.

The broth sat off the hottest part of the stove. A bowl was wrapped beside it to keep the rice from drying. The kitchen window was open a finger’s width to let out the steam.

“You didn’t have to wait up,” Ling Qingzhu said. “I said it might run late.”

Shi Feng looked up from the loose seam in his sword belt.

“I had to cook anyway,” Shi Feng said.

She untied her veil and sat. The greens she disliked were already missing from her bowl.

The first mouthful reminded her she hadn’t eaten since morning. The household meeting had dragged on for hours, an argument over which invitation could be refused without offending whom. Nobody asked whether she was hungry. Here, the spoon lay within reach of her right hand.

“You remembered,” Ling Qingzhu said, and tried to make it sound like nothing.

Shi Feng followed her gaze to the bowl.

“They’re easy to leave out,” Shi Feng said.

She ate slowly. With no audience outside, his ordinary care slipped past her guard.

For a moment she wondered if she should thank him some other way. Then she remembered the agreement. They had chosen the terms. He had chosen his price. Maybe this care was just a conscientious man doing what he was paid for.

Ling Qingzhu laid down her spoon.

“You take the arrangement very seriously,” Ling Qingzhu said. “Is the soup in the contract too?”

Shi Feng’s hand stopped above his own bowl. He’d never thought of the broth as an arrangement. She came home tired, so he saved her supper. The gap between those two explanations was small enough to ignore.

He chose to ignore it, for now. Why am I annoyed? he thought. It’s only soup.

“Does it need more salt?” Shi Feng asked.

She shook her head and reached for another spoonful.

chapters.title: What the Mountains Fed
chapters.html:
The Hengyun pass opened a gate that money alone had failed to move. Beyond it lay protected valleys, shaded pools where medicinal plants lived to full age, and beasts that hadn’t yet learned to run at the sound of a cart.

The gate clerk checked the pass twice. His eyes stayed on the issuing household’s seal, then slowly travelled to the ordinary sword at the visitor’s waist.

“Gathering is allowed inside the marked valleys,” Ke Song said. “Nobody promises you’ll come back safe.”

“Which marks?” Shi Feng asked.

Ke Song pointed to a red stake beyond the gate.

“Red stakes on both sides of each gathering valley,” Ke Song said. “Past the last one, you’re outside the permitted ground.”

Shi Feng checked the path and put the pass away. He came for resources, not a quarrel with the gate clerk.

“Ling household seal,” a burly gatherer muttered in the queue behind him. “On a cripple!”

“He’ll be back by dusk, crying,” another voice said.

“…”

Shi Feng took back the pass and went through. Ke Song was already calling for the next visitor, and he didn’t look up again.

For three days Shi Feng kept away from the beaten paths. He marked water sources, tested the ground by the streams, and picked his sleeping places more carefully than the capital’s innkeepers picked their roofs.

His injuries no longer ruled every movement. He no longer planned a sword stroke around the weakness in his shoulder, and his wrist held firm when he hung from a branch to cross a flooded gully. He was pleased. Better still, his enemies would go on expecting a man who needed help to stand.

On the fourth morning, a Blackhide Mountain Bear charged him beside a fallen pine.

Shi Feng drew before its second step. The first cut laid open the side of its foreleg. The bear kept coming, jaws wide enough to close around his head.

Roar!

He ducked under the sweeping paw and drove his shoulder into its chest. Needles rained from the dead branches. The beast staggered, and Shi Feng followed it, caught its weight as it turned, and broke its neck against the pine trunk.

Crack!

Silence returned. He stood over the carcass until the forest settled, listening for anything the noise might have drawn. Then he wiped the soil from his hands before touching the flesh.

Vitality poured in, thick and steady.

The first ten refined bones in his hands and feet no longer carried the whole load. New sections answered through his hands and forearms, then his ribs and legs. His meridians had already built the roads, Shi Feng thought. Now he just needed enough strength to build along them.

He stopped when the flow got heavier than the unsettled bones could use. Greed won’t help, Shi Feng thought. Power wasted through impatience stayed wasted, however many roads a man owned.

He looked at the carcass and sighed in his heart. The manual said such progress should take months. And still, the bear’s pelt was worth a few stones, and he was too poor to waste it.

He took the pelt.

A gatherer in a straw hat watched from the ridge with his mouth open, and ran before Shi Feng could turn. By nightfall the whole valley would know.

On the sixth day, a gatherer named Chai Hu found him washing roots at a pool and stood at a careful distance.

“Brother, was that bear on the ridge yours?” Chai Hu asked.

“It was in my way,” Shi Feng said.

“Sell me the claws!” Chai Hu said.

“Four stones,” Shi Feng said. “Talk less.”

Chai Hu paid and went off.

At the foothill market, Shao Jin pinched a medicinal root between two fingers and offered half the usual price.

Shi Feng took the root back.

“You should be grateful anyone buys from a cripple!” Shao Jin said.

“I’ll sell it elsewhere,” Shi Feng said.

Shao Jin’s expression turned sour. He snorted and leaned back in his chair, sure that Shi Feng would come crawling back. Two stalls down, the roots sold. Shao Jin shot upright.

“Hey! That buyer is ruining the market!” Shao Jin shouted.

The buyer ignored him and counted out the stones. That was the whole deal.

“First time I’ve seen anyone walk away from Shao Jin,” a trader beside the scales told his neighbour.

“The cripple?”

“The cripple. He carried a Blackhide bear pelt out of the valley!”

“A Blackhide Mountain Bear? That’s a Foundation Establishment beast!”

The traders were stunned into silence.

“…”

The sale paid for food, salt, and a new seam on his boot. Shi Feng stopped at a noodle stall afterwards. The pot was nearly empty, but the woman serving him scraped out a full bowl anyway.

“Eat,” Min Chun said, adding a spoonful of chili.

At night he practised the sword movements he remembered from Wei Renshan’s attack. He didn’t know the man’s art and wouldn’t pretend that seeing it once made it his. He remembered openings instead. Where did the point travel before the body turned? Which step announced the thrust? How much movement did a stronger man waste, because he expected others to retreat?

His blade grew shorter, cleaner. Less shoulder, more power at the point.

On the ninth day, heavy rain trapped him beneath a rock shelf. Water poured over the lip in a grey curtain. He could have gone on. Instead he dried the blade, rewrapped its grip, and spread out the roots that would spoil if left crowded.

At the bottom of his pack lay the parcel of cakes Ling Qingzhu had insisted he take. Most were broken. One survived, its bean filling pressed into a corner.

He ate the broken ones first.

It didn’t mean anything, he told himself in his heart. She saw him packing dry rations and put something better beside them. Still, he remembered how she pretended to be annoyed when he checked the wrapping.

When the rain eased, he folded the empty paper and put it away instead of dropping it among the stones.

By the end of half a month his boots had split at a new seam. His pack was heavier, his purse only a little better, and his bones had advanced much farther than his gathering profits suggested. Ling Qingzhu’s expression sharpened when she looked at the boots as he came into the courtyard.

“You were gone half a month,” Ling Qingzhu said. “Not that I counted. The lane kept asking where my husband went. I ran out of answers.” She pointed at his feet. “Those boots are a crime. Buy another pair.”

“These didn’t last as long as they promised,” Shi Feng said.

“Ten thousand spirit stones,” Ling Qingzhu said, shaking her head. “And you’re arguing with a boot.”

He put the gathered medicines away in his corner of the room and gave her a small packet of dried mountain mushrooms. His bedding had been aired in the sun while he was away. He didn’t mention it, and neither did she.

“They’re good in broth,” Shi Feng said.

She opened the packet, smelled it, and was already smiling before she remembered to ask a question.

“Were they expensive? Tell me honestly,” Ling Qingzhu asked. “I’ll know if you lie.”

“I found them,” Shi Feng said.

That answer seemed to please her more. She hurried to find a bowl, humming under her breath.

Later he went out for fresh ingredients. Another expensive fish joined the mushrooms in the kitchen. The marriage payment still waited on the high shelf to refill the reserve his own purse kept spending.

He’d count it before the next big purchase, Shi Feng decided.

After supper, when the lamp burned low, Shi Feng glanced up at the high kitchen shelf where the pale white-stitched payment bag had sat untouched since registration day. Tomorrow the rent was due, and his own pouch was nearly flat. He reached up, lifted the bag down by its cord—and frowned at how strangely light it felt in his palm.

chapters.title: A Bag Full of Air
chapters.html:
“Rent is due!” Jiang Meilan announced, stepping around the cloth on the table without even glancing at the medicines. “And your roof needs a tile!”

Shi Feng was sorting roots into three groups, checking each against the amounts the bone manual required. Some could be sold. Others would save more money if he used them himself. Every merchant called a root common when buying and rare when selling.

“Good morning, Auntie Jiang,” Shi Feng said without raising his head.

“Wind is a natural event,” Jiang Meilan declared. “Broken tiles are the tenant’s problem!”

Shi Feng counted out the rent in front of her and laid the receipt beside the rental agreement.

“The roof was included,” Shi Feng said. “You said so yourself when I paid.”

“One tile isn’t a roof,” Jiang Meilan said.

“Then you won’t mind replacing it,” Shi Feng said.

Jiang Meilan glared up at the tile from the courtyard, hoping to find proof that he’d climbed up and smashed it himself. She found none.

“Hmph. I’ll send someone when the weather gets better!” Jiang Meilan said, and took the rent.

The sky was cloudless.

“The weather’s been fine since spring!” Granny Qin shouted from across the lane, flipping a cake. “Auntie Jiang, that tile’s been waiting for months! The whole lane knows you’re stingy!”

“Old woman, mind your brazier!” Jiang Meilan shouted, and swept out.

Shi Feng smiled slightly. A sound came from the kitchen, Ling Qingzhu moving a bowl out of the sun. She was learning how to keep ingredients fresh, and nobody had told her it was a household duty.

He thought about the coming costs. Medicines, supplies, another trip to the mountains, and ordinary food that somehow stopped being ordinary once she arrived. It was time to open the payment bag.

He’d left it as a reserve for the next large expense. His own stones covered the daily purchases, and the Hengyun pass supplied what he couldn’t buy cheaply. That plan seemed sensible before the daily purchases multiplied.

Shi Feng took down the pale storage bag from the high kitchen shelf and loosened the knot. The stitching was clean, the cloth unmarked. He reached into the little space inside.

Nothing.

He looked inside.

Still nothing.

He turned the bag upside down over the table.

Air came out, free of charge.

Empty? Impossible, Shi Feng thought. Ten thousand stones can’t just vanish!

Maybe he’d missed something. He used storage bags often, and a well-made one could hide a fastening or an inner fold from a careless owner. He felt the seams. No damage. No broken clasp. No second chamber. The space opened properly, and held absolutely nothing.

He put one spirit stone inside. It vanished into the space exactly as it should. He took it out again without trouble.

The bag worked perfectly. Somehow that was worse!

Shi Feng sat down. His heart sank, and his hands went cold.

He’d registered a marriage. He’d offended the crown prince. He’d bought groceries for two people, paid for a fish that cost more than a sword, and killed the first man sent to settle the matter.

And the payment was an empty bag.

A mouthful of blood shot out over the table.

“Neighbour Shi,” Granny Qin’s voice floated over the wall. “Was that a cough? Do you need ginger?”

“Dust,” Shi Feng said hoarsely.

“Dust, in this weather,” Granny Qin said, and went back to her brazier, not convinced at all.

Shi Feng stayed seated and stared at the clean cloth. His face turned pale, then dark. Even with three hundred and sixty-five meridians, he couldn’t hold this one in.

Then he moved the rent receipt away from the drops.

Anyone in the capital would have been stunned to see it: the cripple who dropped Guo Zhen, beaten by a bag. There was no wound to treat. Pure fury had broken his calm more easily than a Foundation Establishment cultivator’s refined artifact.

He drew one steady breath, then another. I won’t let an empty bag finish what Guo Zhen failed to do, Shi Feng thought grimly. Calm down!

“Did you finish counting?” Ling Qingzhu called from the kitchen. “Count twice. I won’t be called a cheat.”

Shi Feng looked at the bag. He knew the total with perfect certainty. It was zero.

“Yes,” Shi Feng said.

“Put it somewhere safe!” Ling Qingzhu said. “You leave a fortune on a shelf. Careless.”

He closed his eyes, and his expression twitched. Careless with small things? She’d handed him an empty bag, and now she was telling him to keep it safe!

She knew. She had to know. Nobody packs ten thousand spirit stones and forgets to put them in. The first fairy of Great Liang wasn’t careless at all. She was a sadist, and she was enjoying every second of this.

He washed his mouth, wiped the table, and hung the cloth where she wouldn’t mistake it for a sign of injury. Then he counted his own stones.

It wasn’t ten thousand.

It wasn’t even close.

The money from the mountain roots, the rest of his reserve, and a purse from a man who’d tried to kill him made up the total. The royal steward, Shi Feng noted bitterly, had been more honest with this household than its supposed patron.

He opened the account paper. He kept every receipt, even through foolish assumptions, and now each slip meant something new. The household oil. The carpenter’s latch. The new rope. The fish. The duck. Another fish.

He laid them in a row. There were a lot of fish.

And she’d let him buy every one of them. She’d sat at his table, praised his fish and watched him spend his own savings on her, all while she knew the bag was empty. How cruel could one woman be?

It still didn’t put a single stone in the bag.

It did tell him what to say tomorrow. The promised payment wasn’t received. He didn’t need to invent anything more complicated.

She was in the kitchen washing the mushrooms he’d brought from the mountains. He could hear her tapping soil from a stem with small, determined taps. He’d put the bag in front of her when neither of them stood over supper, and let the facts speak.

On the stove, the day’s lavish ingredients waited.

Shi Feng looked at the fish.

The fish looked back, its expensive eye staring at nothing.

He felt like they’d both been tricked.

Ling Qingzhu appeared in the doorway with the clean mushrooms and stopped when she saw the receipts across the table.

“Was Auntie Jiang that bad today?” Ling Qingzhu asked. “You’ve got your landlady face on.”

“That roof tile is going to be a long fight,” Shi Feng said.

She smiled, relieved that his dark look was only about the landlady’s greed. He took the mushrooms from her and went to the stove.
