That evening, over supper, “This soup is dangerous,” Ling Qingzhu said. “I had three bowls. What’s the mountain like in autumn?”

“Wet,” Shi Feng said, “and full of things that want to be sold.”

“Like the capital,” Ling Qingzhu said, grinning.

“The capital charges more,” Shi Feng said, and she laughed.

Shi Feng watched her laugh. Look at her, he thought coldly. She’s enjoying this.

The fish was cooked as carefully as the first one, and there were no bitter greens in her bowl. She took both details as proof that the arrangement was going well.

On the shelf above the stove, the empty bag lay beside the folded agreement.

Tomorrow, Shi Feng would explain exactly how well.

chapters.title: The Unpaid Debt
chapters.html:
Shi Feng set the empty bag beside the breakfast bowls and waited for her to look up. The porridge was hot and the courtyard gate was shut. There were no visitors, so a plain quarrel could stay a plain quarrel.

“There wasn’t one spirit stone in this,” Shi Feng said calmly.

Ling Qingzhu’s spoon stopped halfway to her mouth. Her expression changed, and for a moment she looked truly startled. Then she remembered the savings she had counted herself, the expensive dinners of the past month, and his endless complaints about small prices.

So that’s it, she thought. He emptied it himself and now he wants to be paid twice!

“We agreed on a sum,” Ling Qingzhu said, and her chin came up. “I paid it. Don’t ask me twice.”

“I’m asking about the first payment,” Shi Feng said.

“The one I put in your hand,” Ling Qingzhu said. “You said ‘after the dishes.’ You were standing right there.”

“Open it,” Shi Feng said.

She snatched the bag and pushed her hand inside. It went in easily and came out empty. She checked the mouth, the seams and the stitching, and found nothing wrong. Her fingers tightened on the cloth.

Shi Feng watched her face settle into disappointment. He knew that look. She had reached her verdict before the evidence arrived.

“I thought we understood each other,” Ling Qingzhu said. “I really did. That’s the stupid part.”

That sentence nearly made him laugh. Yesterday he had been furious at the absurdity of it. Today, facing her certainty, it didn’t feel so funny. He could spread every receipt on the table and make her count each fish and each repaired latch. That would prove where his money went. It wouldn’t prove where her money never was.

“Ten thousand spirit stones were promised,” Shi Feng said. “You handed me this bag. It held none.”

“Not enough? Say that before we registered!” Ling Qingzhu said, eyes flashing.

Shi Feng looked at her steadily. What an actress, he thought. She hands me an empty bag, and now she’s the one who’s offended? Some arguments could be ended with a sword. This wasn’t one of them.

He took out his copy of the agreement. In the small space beside the payment clause, under both signatures, he wrote: bag received; ten thousand spirit stones promised, not received. Then he blew the ink dry and turned the paper toward her.

“My account will keep the debt,” Shi Feng said. “I won’t ask you to pay twice. I haven’t been paid once.”

Her expression hardened. “Hmph. Keep your debt, then,” Ling Qingzhu said. “Keep it where I can’t see it.” She didn’t touch the paper.

Shi Feng folded it and put it away slowly. She took the care for a show of hurt feelings, and he let her. In truth he just didn’t want to tear a page he meant to keep.

Breakfast went on badly. Ling Qingzhu ate half her porridge and walked out. Shi Feng washed both bowls and carried the bag back to the room, to his corner beside the rolled-up bedding.

Then he sat down on the floor and looked at the arrangement as it really stood.

The Hengyun pass was still valid. It had already given him mountain valleys that ordinary wages could never buy. Tearing up the agreement wouldn’t remove the danger of the marriage, and it wouldn’t make Sima Yu forget his name. It would only cost him a good bargain just to show he was angry.

I chose this for more than a purse, Shi Feng thought. Keep the terms, keep the debt, and make the rest profitable.

That was a decision, not a surrender. But the lavish dinners were over.

At the market, Shi Feng walked past the fish stall without slowing.

“Young Master Shi!” Peng Tao called, waving a silver carp by the tail. “The belly is still fresh! Young Master Shi!”

Shi Feng didn’t turn. Peng Tao stared after him, baffled.

“Is he sick?” the vegetable seller asked.

“He bought a duck three days ago!”

“A duck seven days ago and a bone today? The cripple’s wife must have found the purse.”

“…”

At the butcher’s, Shi Feng chose a cheap cut and asked for the bones. The butcher weighed them and tried to charge extra for the scraps of meat still stuck to them.

“Wrap them together,” Shi Feng said.

The butcher looked at the long queue behind him and did. At home Shi Feng blanched the bones, rinsed them and set them to simmer. He sliced the meat thin so it would cook fast, added greens near the end, and fried the morning’s rice for a second dish.

The meal cost a fraction of the carp. It still smelled wonderful.

Ling Qingzhu came in while he was scrubbing the chopping board. She stopped in the kitchen doorway and waited for another demand, or a speech about wounded pride.

“Move the clean bowls out of the steam,” Shi Feng said.

She did it without a word.

At supper the broth was rich and pale. Ling Qingzhu meant to eat in silence. Then she took a second spoonful, and the flavour made her feel that the household was carrying on as usual in spite of the morning.

“The soup is good,” Ling Qingzhu admitted, sounding like it hurt.

Shi Feng nodded. He’d spent the whole afternoon making sure of it.

She looked over the other dishes. There was meat, greens and rice. There was no silver fish with crisp skin laid along the edge of the plate.

“No fish?” Ling Qingzhu asked, before she could stop herself.

“No,” Shi Feng said.

One flat word, and she lifted her eyes to him in surprise. He ladled a second bowl and set it before her. There was no anger in it. There was also no offer to fix her disappointment by spending more.

Later, behind the folding screen, Ling Qingzhu opened her own purse. It held plenty for any supper she liked.

That’s not the point, she told herself. I paid for this arrangement already. Why should I reward a new demand?

She tied the purse shut.

In the courtyard, Shi Feng checked the Hengyun pass and counted his remaining medicine. Tomorrow he’d visit the warehouse notice board between mountain trips. Honest wages bought something that hidden strength couldn’t, which was a quiet reputation for being poor.

Beyond the wall, two neighbours were passing the lane and gossiping loudly.

“Did you hear? The cripple who married Fairy Ling!”

“What luck! A fallen genius, and now he eats from her table!”

“Heaven has no sense of justice.”

“…”

Shi Feng listened to the end, then closed the gate properly. Inside, he spread his bedding on the floor in the dark. On the other side of the screen, the bed creaked as she turned her back to him. Neither of them said goodnight.

My luck, he thought flatly, has remarkably complicated accounts.

Over the next week, fish became meat, then a small helping of meat among vegetables. He kept the bowls generous and the cooking careful. Ling Qingzhu still remembered the duck.

“Are we monks now?” Ling Qingzhu asked one wet evening.

“Monks cook less,” Shi Feng said.

A greedy dog, Ling Qingzhu thought, annoyed that the broth tasted good. He had been generous until he decided to ask for more. Yet the ginger in her bowl was still sliced thin the way she preferred. She noticed, and the neat explanation in her head became less comfortable.

After washing up, she moved his stool out from under the dripping eaves. Shi Feng found it dry when he came back. Neither mentioned it.

When the room went dark, Shi Feng counted the eight stones left in his pouch. Mountain trips took half a month, and his bones were hungry now. Tomorrow morning he would head to the commercial loading yards—and see who in the capital paid cash on the barrelhead.

chapters.title: Work for a Former Genius
chapters.html:
“Six spirit stones for a day of lifting,” Ke De said, tapping his work slate.

Then a porter by the cart whispered a name, and Ke De’s brush stopped.

“Four,” Ke De said.

Shi Feng looked at the stacked sacks. The nearest one was patched twice and already leaking grain from a seam.

“It was six a moment ago,” Shi Feng said.

“Then find someone paying six!” Ke De barked.

The porters waiting by the cart stared at the ground.

“That’s him, the Shi boy. Two hundred and thirty-seven meridians, they said.”

“Now he lifts sacks for four stones!”

“Quiet. Don’t get noticed.”

“…”

Shi Feng didn’t say another word. He lifted the first sack onto the cart. Then he lifted the second beside it, and held Ke De’s gaze the whole time.

Shi Feng used no visible qi, but Ke De’s expression changed. A cripple shouldn’t be able to carry two sacks without shaking! The porters were stunned.

“Eight,” Shi Feng said. “Or go find someone else’s arms.”

Ke De glanced at the loading yard. Two carts were late, and the owner had sent a runner three times already. The sacks wouldn’t carry themselves.

“Eight, if the loading is done before sunset!” Ke De said, scowling.

“That seam was already open when I got here,” Shi Feng said, pointing at the leaking sack.

Ke De scowled and made a mark on his slate.

The work only needed a steady pace, and the will to keep it while others rested. Shi Feng stacked the heavy sacks low and left room for the uneven ones. When a wheel sank into soft ground, the porters began shouting over who had chosen the spot. Shi Feng slid a board beneath it and told the driver to start when he said go.

The cart came free at once.

Ke De didn’t say a word of praise. He just bellowed at the other porters to keep moving.

Shi Feng kept the same pace through the next cart. There was no reason to throw sacks around to impress the yard. The work just needed finishing. Let them see a stubborn former cultivator who won’t admit his decline, he thought. It’s the safest face I can wear.

He had no plan to become a grain porter. The work filled the gap between mountain trips and brought in cash. It also gave the curious an easy answer. A cripple who hunted roots and carried sacks was easy to understand. A cripple who could kill Foundation Establishment cultivators was not.

At midday, Ke De waved a hand toward the last six sacks.

“Onto the front cart!” Ke De shouted.

The driver stopped Shi Feng before he lifted the first.

“Those are seed beans,” Tu Dali said. “The front cart goes to the mill.”

Ke De looked at the painted mark on the sacks. Then he looked at the merchant’s son standing beside the gate.

“I said the back cart!” Ke De barked.

“You pointed at this one,” Tu Dali replied.

“I was pointing past it!” Ke De shouted.

Shi Feng put the beans on the correct cart. Tu Dali tucked his head down and checked the load himself. Ke De strode away to find somebody who hadn’t heard the mistake.

A sack split as the last worker lifted it. Beans rattled across the yard. All three men froze.

“Not that seam,” Shi Feng said. “Catch it underneath.”

He lowered his end and spread the empty wrapping beneath the spill. Tu Dali caught the other side. They tipped most of the beans back in before Ke De returned.

The foreman opened his mouth, saw the seed mark, and shut it. This time, his shouting would bring the merchant’s son over. He found a broom instead.

Before the break, Tu Dali brought over a torn sack and a coil of string.

“Can you hold that corner?” Tu Dali asked. “If I lift it alone, the beans go everywhere again.”

Shi Feng held it while Tu Dali stitched a rough seam. The driver worked quickly and didn't ask why a fairy's husband needed loading wages. Shi Feng appreciated that more than he expected.

“My mother used to mend those,” Tu Dali said. “I never learned properly until the first load spilled.”

“This one will hold,” Shi Feng said.

Tu Dali tugged it twice, satisfied, and went back to his cart. The next sack reached the right place without shouting. For several quiet minutes the yard was just men doing work.

Shi Feng ate his packed rice under the eaves. A husk stuck to his thumb, and his water was warm. Beside the well, two porters argued about a wedding feast. One remembered the bride, and the other remembered only the pork.

At sunset Ke De tried to deduct money for sack damage that was there before the loading. Shi Feng pointed to the mark on the slate from that morning.

The foreman stared at his own handwriting, and his expression turned sour. Then he counted out eight stones in full.

Shi Feng counted them and left before Ke De found another cart. His arms weren’t tired. Spending a day listening to the foreman had been the harder work.

Walking back, he stopped at a pump to rinse the dust from his neck. Granny Qin’s nephew Qin Bao stared at the sword on his belt, then at the sack fibres clinging to his robe.

“Are you a swordsman or a porter, Big Brother?” Qin Bao asked.

“Today, a porter,” Shi Feng said.

Shi Feng walked on. He didn’t need a stranger’s understanding to eat supper. At the medicine lane he noticed a sheet pasted outside Fang’s Medicine House.

Pill testers wanted. Daily payment. Prior cultivation history preferred.

He read it twice.

Through the half-open door came the hot, bitter smell of a furnace being cleaned. On a side table lay a tray of dark pellets in uneven rows, several of them split along the surface.

Shi Feng’s stomach stirred. Beneath his sternum, the hunger woke up, quiet but very interested. A side door opened before he finished looking.

Fang Jingyuan looked him up and down. The alchemist’s gaze paused on the old shoulder scar under Shi Feng’s loosened collar, then moved to the travel paper in his hand.

“You were a cultivator,” Fang Jingyuan said.

“That’s what the notice asks,” Shi Feng said.

Fang Jingyuan took the paper, read the name, and his expression turned eager.

Ruined meridians, the alchemist thought. A former genius, now carrying grain, judging by the fibres on his sleeve. A desperate man like this would take a very low wage.

“Five stones a session,” Fang Jingyuan said, wringing his hands. “You swallow the test batch and I—I record the effect.”

“These are medicine?” Shi Feng asked, looking past him at the tray.

“Sinew nourishment, marrow support, circulation aid,” Fang Jingyuan said quickly. “Different preparations. You’ll be told what you need to know. Probably.”

“I’ll be told before I swallow,” Shi Feng said.

The alchemist gave a nervous laugh. Caution, he thought, was just a habit of people who couldn’t negotiate better terms.

“Of course, of course!” Fang Jingyuan said.

Shi Feng studied the pellets again. He didn’t know how they were refined or what mistakes had cracked them. But he could feel medicine still inside them, and his strange physique answered with a clear hunger.

“And you supply the pills?” Shi Feng asked.

Fang Jingyuan let out a shaky breath. The ruined genius was worried the pills might cost extra! Heaven had sent the perfect worker to a poor, struggling shop.

Shi Feng smoothed down the loose corner of the notice against the wall.

Both men, he thought, had just found a fool.

He decided he would return after the next hunt. Honest work and a quiet yard were useful.

chapters.title: The Tester's Wage
chapters.html:
“Payment comes after observation,” Fang Jingyuan said, wringing his hands.

“A written rate comes before the first pill,” Shi Feng said.

Fang Jingyuan was a Foundation Establishment alchemist with no Sky Pavilion Mark. A 1 Mark alchemist could make pills for Golden Core cultivators. Foundation Establishment was the minimum realm to even try for it, but almost everyone only got there after reaching Golden Core themselves.

Fang Jingyuan never would. His furnace made common pills, and not every batch came out right. A hundred failed attempts hadn’t made him stop trying.

They had made him willing to risk somebody else’s stomach. Shi Feng wanted the medicine inside those failures, but he wouldn’t mistake the man’s eagerness for goodwill.

On the table stood a narrow stool, a cup of water, and a paper saying Fang’s Medicine House wasn’t to blame if a patient died. The line for payment was an empty blank.

“Distrust makes medicine so difficult!” Fang Jingyuan complained.

Shi Feng pointed at the disclaimer.

Fang Jingyuan looked at his own handwriting, then at the tester, and reached for the brush. Five stones a session went onto the paper. Writing things down, they both agreed, was useful.

The first pill was meant to strengthen sinews. It split during cooling and showed a pale seam across its surface. Fang Jingyuan pointed out the flaw himself, watching to see if it would scare his tester into taking a lower wage.

“Does the batch number on the tray match the paper?” Shi Feng asked.

The alchemist fixed one character, very reluctantly.

Shi Feng swallowed the pill.

Warmth spread beneath his sternum. His strange physique caught the medicine and sent clean strength down the waiting pathways. Another body would have struggled to take it in. His took it as a feast.

He sat quietly.

Fang Jingyuan waited for a tremor, a flushed face, an upset stomach, anything to write beside the batch number. The tester’s calm was getting really annoying.

“How do you feel?” Fang Jingyuan asked.

“Warm,” Shi Feng said.

“Where?” Fang Jingyuan asked.

“Inside,” Shi Feng replied.

Fang Jingyuan put his brush down and fetched a drawing of the human body. He stabbed one finger at the stomach.

“Here?” Fang Jingyuan asked.

Shi Feng nodded. The alchemist marked it eagerly, then noticed that he was writing on the shop’s only clean anatomy chart. He snatched up the sheet before the ink spread.

The brush hovered over the paper. Fang Jingyuan’s expression twitched, and his face turned red.

“Can you be more specific?” Fang Jingyuan asked anxiously.

“I’m not a physician,” Shi Feng said. He wasn’t lying. And he didn’t owe a man who valued his possible death less than a good fish a description of what happened beneath his sternum.

Fang Jingyuan was stunned by the useless answer. He made a short mark and waited longer.

The second pill was badly bound. The third was overheated. The alchemist described each flaw as he picked it up, as if explaining his problems made it fine to have somebody else swallow them.

All of them gave strength! Fang Jingyuan scratched his head and found nothing to record.

Nothing poisoned Shi Feng, and he was secretly delighted. No burden gathered behind the comfort, and yesterday’s medicine didn’t dull today’s. His body treated every scrap of medicine as pure nourishment, free of the damage Fang Jingyuan expected another man to show. This must be the secret of my body, Shi Feng thought. Everything others throw away, I can eat.

The bitter taste was the only part he could do without. After the third observation period he stood up.

“The wage,” Shi Feng said.

Fang Jingyuan studied his sheet. “The result is… inconclusive!”

“The rate isn’t,” Shi Feng said, and stayed beside the stool until five stones appeared.

Outside, the street looked pleasantly bright. He’d earned money, taken useful medicine, and spent most of the session sitting down. Compared with carrying grain, this work had a lot going for it, Shi Feng thought with satisfaction!

He came back two days later. By the fourth session Fang Jingyuan was calling him an unusually suitable tester. By the fifth, the alchemist decided that being suitable was a reason to cut the wage.

“You recover faster than others, so the work is easier for you,” Fang Jingyuan said. “Three stones would be fair. I can’t afford more!”

Shi Feng rose from the stool.

Fang Jingyuan looked at the pills already arranged for the session, and at the pile of unfinished observation sheets. He was used to regular results now. He didn’t want to go back to the troublemakers who demanded payment before touching a single pellet.

“Five is fine!” Fang Jingyuan cried at once.

Shi Feng sat down again.

The terms stayed tight. Shi Feng took only medicine named beforehand. One day Fang Jingyuan brought an unmarked preparation from a back shelf, smiling nervously.

“A tester has to be adaptable,” Fang Jingyuan said, mopping his forehead.

“An employer must read his own agreement,” Shi Feng said.

The jar went back on the shelf. Shi Feng wasn’t afraid of poison. He refused because the alchemist had promised to explain the work and was trying to dodge it.

On another visit Fang Jingyuan dragged the observation stool to the shop’s open doorway, so buyers could watch a patient swallowing his pills.

A passing woman stopped to look.

“Is that the Shi boy? Fang is testing medicine on a cripple!”

“Look, he’s swallowing the cracked ones!”

“He must be desperate! Poor boy.”

“…”

Shi Feng carried the stool back behind the shop’s back curtain and sat down. He’d agreed to test pills, not to be a living advertisement for a cure that the alchemist never delivered. Fang Jingyuan sighed and left the stool where it was. Losing a handy display was cheaper than losing a tester who counted his wage so carefully.

When Fang Jingyuan later complained that ruined meridians made some observations worthless, Shi Feng calmly asked whether he wanted to hire somebody else. The alchemist suddenly remembered how valuable the diagnosis was.

No one examined his circulation closely. Fang Jingyuan believed the matter was settled, and he preferred recording what his pills did to an unlucky body over paying to learn that his assumptions were wrong. Shi Feng did nothing to correct him.

While waiting, he watched the furnace from a distance, but the gestures and tools meant little to him. The alchemist’s skill was the alchemist’s own business.

Shi Feng watched Fang Jingyuan pinch a pellet apart and reject it before it reached the tray. The man could recognize a failure. He simply cared less about the tester than about discovering which mistake caused it.

That evening Ling Qingzhu noticed the medicine-house stamp on the payment slip he laid beside the household account.

“That’s Fang’s stamp. You work there?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“Sometimes,” Shi Feng said.

Her gaze moved over his clean sleeves. That sounded right for a former genius, she thought: sorting roots, carrying jars, copying prescriptions he could no longer use. She felt an unexpected relief that he’d found something less degrading than lifting sacks.

Then she remembered the ten thousand stones and frowned.

“You count five stones like gold bars,” Ling Qingzhu said. “Dinner’s still greens. Where does it all go?”

“I keep careful accounts,” Shi Feng said.

“Oh, I can tell. Every stone, written down twice,” Ling Qingzhu said, her face turning cool.

He didn’t argue about the debt again. He’d stated it, written it, and she’d denied it. Repeating it wouldn’t make stones appear.

He bought rice and more greens, then made supper with mushrooms saved from the mountains. Ling Qingzhu ate enough to praise the flavour, though her eyes still drifted to the empty spot where another dish might have stood.

Later, when her breathing slowed behind the folding screen, Shi Feng sat cross-legged on his floor mat and drew the cracked pills’ medicinal heat down into his bones. Five spirit stones were only the visible part of his wage—and before he left the shop, he had seen an invitation card from the Marquis of Pingnan’s reception sitting on the lane’s delivery tray, addressed to Ling Qingzhu alone.

chapters.title: After the Performance
chapters.html:
“Brother Shi!” Zheng Wenbo raised his cup across the table, acting the generous elder, though he was only three years older. “Some men chase fortune their whole lives. You found yours sitting at your own table!”

Three hours into the reception, the hall was loud with wine. The host had invited half the idle young talents of the capital and called it an “intimate gathering.” Behind every screen, someone was looking for an excuse to walk past Shi Feng and Ling Qingzhu.

“Look at them,” a young noble whispered by the screen. “Fairy Ling is practically leaning on him.”

“It must be a show for the crown prince’s spies.”

“Then she’s a very good actress. Look at her hand!”

Ling Qingzhu heard every word. She kept her eyes pleasant above the veil and pressed her thumb against her cup. Shi Feng’s expression stayed calm as he drank a little water.

Zheng Wenbo was only a Qi Condensation cultivator. Shi Feng could have knocked him through the screen with one hand. But a stupid remark wasn’t worth spoiling supper, Shi Feng thought.

Zheng Wenbo, red-faced with wine, took the silence as an invitation.

“Don’t you worry you’ll wake up one morning and find it was all a dream?” Zheng Wenbo asked loudly.

“Is your wife imaginary too?” Shi Feng asked.

The woman seated beside Zheng Wenbo put down her cup. Slowly, she turned her head toward her husband.

Zheng Wenbo’s laugh died halfway out of his mouth. His wife’s expression was terrible. The nearby tables were stunned into silence, and nobody dared to laugh along and save him.

“He actually said that to a Qi Condensation cultivator’s face?”

“His wife is sitting right there!”

“Quiet! She’s looking this way!”

“…”

Ling Qingzhu knew she should scold Shi Feng. Instead she stared at her plate, grateful that the veil hid her grin. This is improper, she thought. Very improper. And I can’t make myself regret it.

Later a servant brought a cushion for her chair and none for Shi Feng’s. Shi Feng took the cushion, set it under her, and went back to listening. He acted like the insult didn’t exist.

“My husband needs a cushion too,” Ling Qingzhu said to the servant, her eyes sweet above her veil. “Now, please.”

Qin Song, the serving boy, turned pale. “Yes, Fairy Ling! Right away!” Qin Song stammered, and ran. Ling Qingzhu was angrier on Shi Feng’s behalf than Shi Feng was himself. He didn’t even seem to notice. That annoyed her even more!

In the carriage, Ling Qingzhu leaned her head back against the cushion.

“Did you hear what they called you?” Ling Qingzhu asked. “Fortune-seeker. Rice-eater. Fairy Ling’s pet. Pet! I should’ve tipped wine on his head.”

“The pet part is new,” Shi Feng said.

“You’re really not angry? Not even a little?” Ling Qingzhu asked, turning to look at him.

“Why would I be? Only people who matter can insult me,” Shi Feng said. “Those were just noises from a loud hall.”

Ling Qingzhu fell silent. Fool, she thought. What kind of man calls that noise?

By the time the carriage reached home, her silver hair ornament was digging into the same sore spot it had dug at all evening. Shi Feng opened the courtyard gate. The familiar pear tree rose out of the darkness, and Ling Qingzhu’s shoulders sank before she even stepped inside.

The little house had only one room, and tonight it felt like the best room in the world. She went in, removed her veil, unfastened a hair clasp and sat on her bed with a sigh.

“You could have been nicer,” Ling Qingzhu said, rubbing her neck as Shi Feng followed her in. “His father sits on the Board of Rites. Men like that hold grudges.”

“Neither will his wife,” Shi Feng said.

“That’s not an answer, and you know it,” Ling Qingzhu said, and turned away.

“Then here’s one. He should have been less interested in my bed,” Shi Feng said. He glanced at the bundle of floor bedding in the corner and added, “Not that it’s much of a bed.”

She laughed before she could stop herself.

It wasn’t the polite laugh she’d given the guests all evening. Shi Feng heard the difference, and he was glad they’d left early. That’s her first real laugh tonight, he thought.

He went to the kitchen. There was leftover rice, a little broth, and enough ginger to make something warm. The reception had served six fancy dishes and almost no real supper. He’d watched her push the wine aside and barely touch the platter nearest her.

While the pot warmed, a faint metal click came from the room, then silence.

“Is it stuck?” Shi Feng called, setting down the bowl.

“A little. Don’t laugh!” Ling Qingzhu said. One last ornament was tangled in her hair, and she refused to pull hard enough to make the knot worse.

He brought the small mirror from the shelf and held it where she could see the clasp. She found the twisted strand and freed it, looking far too pleased with herself for a woman just home from a banquet.

Black hair fell over her shoulders. Shi Feng stood holding the mirror long after she finished.

“Are you keeping that for yourself?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

He handed it over. She caught his foolish expression in the bronze and smiled.

Shi Feng put the mirror back before he could stare. What’s wrong with me, he thought. This is a contract!

When he came back from the kitchen with the bowl, she’d slipped off her outer silk robe. In plain sleeves, she made the little room feel quieter.

“No bitter greens,” Shi Feng said.

Ling Qingzhu looked into the broth.

“You remembered,” Ling Qingzhu said. “Fine, I’m touched. Don’t let it go to your head.”

“You pick them out every time,” Shi Feng said.

She ate. The ginger warmed her much better than the reception’s expensive wine ever could. He sat on his bedding across from her and loosened the knot at his cuff, where the stiff posture of the evening had rubbed his wrist raw.

For the time it takes to drink a cup of tea, neither of them was performing for anyone. Then Shi Feng stood up to wash the pot.

“You can stop being a statue now. Nobody’s watching,” Ling Qingzhu said, not looking at him.

His hand paused under the water.

“I’m washing a pot,” Shi Feng said calmly.

The answer made her feel foolish. She put down her spoon, unsure whether to apologise for something he never heard.

He heard it.

Shi Feng said nothing, but in his heart he understood. He liked seeing her back relax when the gate closed. He liked hearing what she really thought after a night of fake smiles. He’d saved the broth because she was hungry, and held the mirror because her hair was caught. Neither of those was written in the agreement.

That didn’t mean he’d explain himself tonight.

Ling Qingzhu carried her empty bowl to the basin. Their hands almost touched when he took it, and neither of them pulled away as fast as they should have.

“That man was rude,” Ling Qingzhu said. “Rude and boring. I counted his cups.”

Shi Feng glanced up. “Yes,” Shi Feng said.

“I wanted to say it earlier. Even a veil can’t hide how boring they are,” Ling Qingzhu said.

He nodded and didn’t make a big deal of it. She stayed beside him while he rinsed the bowl, then picked up the drying cloth. This time he let her use it.

Back in the room, the lamp burned low to save oil, and a cup of clean water stood beside the bed. His bedding was already unrolled on the floor in its corner, a careful distance from her chest at the foot of the bed.

When had all these little things become so familiar? She couldn’t remember when he started doing them.

He’s just careful, Ling Qingzhu told herself. He took a big payment, and he’s too proud to do the job badly. There was no reason to read anything more into plain diligence.

Her heart gave an odd little jump. She grabbed her nightclothes and ducked behind the folding screen a little too quickly.

“Don’t look! I mean it!” Ling Qingzhu said from behind it.

“I’m lying on the floor staring at the ceiling,” Shi Feng said. “The ceiling’s very interesting tonight.”

Silence. Then the faint rustle of silk, and one tiny snort that she tried to hide.

Just before the lamp went out, Ling Qingzhu spoke quietly from behind the curtain. “One of Sima Yu’s stewards visited the Hengyun pass office yesterday to ask how often our household pass had crossed the gate. Be careful on the mountain road tomorrow.”

Shi Feng’s eyes opened in the dark. Even as warmth lingered in his chest, he set his sword an inch closer to his mat.

chapters.title: The Hunter at the Narrow Pass
chapters.html:
He Zhong stood between the two boulders with somebody else's pack in his hand.

The woman in front of him kept reaching for its strap. He Zhong held it high enough that she couldn't get it without stepping within his reach. A spear floated beside his shoulder, turned sideways across the narrow path.

“Inspection fee,” He Zhong said. “You know the price.”

“I paid at the gate,” Lin Cai said. Her sleeve had torn along the seam, and loose leaves clung to her wrist. “That's my medicine money.”

He Zhong took a packet of red-veined roots and tossed the pack at her feet. Lin Cai dropped to gather the scattered bundles. Shi Feng stopped above the bend and watched. The hunter had been buying cheap roots at the gathering market that morning. Apparently fair prices hadn't satisfied him.

He Zhong saw the household pass at Shi Feng's belt and smiled.

“Go on,” He Zhong said to Lin Cai. “I've found a better fee.”

Lin Cai hurried downhill. As she passed Shi Feng, she glanced at his sword and shook her head. She didn't stop to ask a stranger to fight for her. Shi Feng couldn't blame her for that.

“Keep walking,” Shi Feng said. “Mind the loose stones.”

He Zhong set the butt of his spear against the opposite boulder. The shaft blocked the path at waist height. Its point faced away from Shi Feng, but the qi holding it steady was plain enough. Foundation Establishment, and comfortable using it to frighten gatherers.

Shi Feng stopped an arm's length from the barrier.

“Household pass,” He Zhong said. “Let me look.”

“You're not a clerk,” Shi Feng said.

“Clerks stay by the gate. I work up here,” He Zhong said. “Hand over the pass and that bag. I'll decide the share.”

The inner pocket of Shi Feng's cheap bag held his papers. The visible bundles were roots from a shaded ravine, wrapped to keep the fine fibres from breaking. He had spent most of the morning finding them. He wasn't going to give them away because a hunter preferred other people's work.

He set the bag carefully on a dry shelf of rock.

He Zhong grinned, taking that for obedience.

“Fairy Ling's husband,” He Zhong said. “They said you were sensible. A man who can't cultivate should borrow a good name and know when to use it.”

“The name on my pass isn't yours,” Shi Feng said.

“Then borrow mine for the way down,” He Zhong said. “You'll leave with your legs working. That's better than most bargains.”

The spear shaft swung toward Shi Feng's knees. He Zhong used the blunt part, aiming to knock him down and pin him against the slope. At the same time, the hunter reached for the pass.

Shi Feng caught the shaft.

He Zhong's fingers stopped short of the seal. His grin stayed for a moment, as though his face hadn't heard what his arm had discovered.

Then Shi Feng pulled.

The floating spear left He Zhong's control and struck the path. Shi Feng stepped across it and took the hunter's wrist before he could retreat. He turned the hand outward just far enough to fold He Zhong's arm behind his back.

He Zhong hit the boulder chest first.

“Let go!” He Zhong shouted.

Qi swelled around his shoulders. Shi Feng pressed harder, and the protective layer broke with a short crack. He Zhong's next breath came out as a wheeze. His face scraped the stone, leaving a thin red line.

That was the whole fight.

Shi Feng planted a foot on the spear shaft and held the hunter still. There was no need to bare his own qi. His strengthened bones and body did enough, and He Zhong had helped by reaching first.

“You collect fees with a spear?” Shi Feng asked.

“I was only holding you!” He Zhong said. “I didn't use the point!”

“I noticed,” Shi Feng said.

He Zhong twisted once. The movement stopped at his wrist. His face lost what colour it had left. He had chosen a supposed cripple because a bad reputation was easier to fight than a strong cultivator. Now he couldn't even turn his head far enough to see the man holding him.

“Take the roots back,” He Zhong said. “They're hers. Take them!”

Shi Feng looked toward the bend. Lin Cai had stopped well below them. She was watching from beside a scrub pine, too far away to hear the words.

“Come collect your packet,” Shi Feng called. “Stay on that side of the path.”

Lin Cai approached cautiously. Her gaze went from He Zhong's pinned arm to Shi Feng's plain robe. Shi Feng nodded toward the dropped roots. She picked them up and checked the binding with shaking hands.

“That's all?” Shi Feng asked.

“And two stones,” Lin Cai said.

He Zhong made an angry sound against the rock. Shi Feng raised his wrist a little. The sound changed.

“Left pocket!” He Zhong gasped. “Take two!”

Lin Cai took exactly two stones. She held the packet against her chest and backed toward the bend again.

“Thank you, young master,” Lin Cai said.

“Go before the gate closes,” Shi Feng said.

She went. Shi Feng waited until her footsteps had faded before easing his grip. He Zhong sagged, but Shi Feng kept him against the boulder until the hunter stopped trying to gather qi.

“Put the spear away,” Shi Feng said.

He Zhong obeyed. The weapon slid under a leather loop on his pack. His hand shook while fastening it.

“You could have said you were strong,” He Zhong muttered.

“You could have kept your hands to yourself,” Shi Feng said.

He took back the household pass from where He Zhong had dropped it, checked the seal and returned it to his belt. Then he lifted his bag. None of the medicine jars had broken. That mattered more than the hunter's opinion.

He Zhong stayed sitting beneath the boulder. There was blood on his cheek, dust on his robe and a swelling wrist tucked against his chest. He had tried robbery and restraint. Shi Feng left him alive with the lesson plainly visible.

That didn't mean he trusted him to remember it honestly.

Shi Feng didn't turn around to see what the hunter did next.

Half an hour later, at the foot of the pass beside the mule tether, He Zhong cradled his swollen wrist against his ribs and caught a passing fur broker by the sleeve.

“Brother,” He Zhong hissed through his teeth, his eyes still fixed on the trail Shi Feng had taken toward the gate, “people say the Eastern Palace hates that husband Fairy Ling married. Who in the capital pays spirit stones for real news about what that ‘cripple’ can do with his hands?”

“Pass and gathering slip,” Ke Song said at the gate.

Shi Feng handed them over, collected his stamped slip, and returned to Qingliu Lane before dusk. While Ling Qingzhu silently poured clean water into the yard basin for his scraped knuckle, a messenger boy slipped a handbill under the gate: a broker named Ma Zheng was recruiting an expedition into the newly opened Chiyun Ruins at dawn.

chapters.title: A Friend's Opinion
chapters.html:
Three-quarters of Shi Feng's ordinary bone refinement was finished by the time the next rain reached Qingliu Lane. He counted the remaining bones privately, checking each place where the qi still met resistance. Progress didn't make them vanish. He still had to refine every one.

A hunt supplied the last packet of medicine money for that week. He washed the mud off his boots before entering the room and tucked the cultivation notes beneath his rolled bedding.

“‘So?! What’s he really like?! Does he snore?! Does he talk in his sleep?! Tell me everything, everything, EVERYTHING!’” Ling Qingzhu read the letter aloud under the pear tree and frowned. “…This woman.”

Su Wanning’s letter had come with a box of scented cakes. Her friend wanted to know whether the “extraordinary marriage” was getting any less extraordinary. She wanted every little detail, and she’d underlined “everything” twice.

Ling Qingzhu looked around the little courtyard, at the repaired stove and the kitchen where Shi Feng was wrapping food for his trip. Details were annoyingly hard to come up with.

He was blunt. He was secretive about where he went. He could argue over the price of salt as seriously as another man studied a sword art. But he also kept the lamp turned low when she came home late. In their one small room, he always faced the wall when she changed behind the screen, and he never once peeked around it.

She began to write that he was useful company.

Then she crossed out “useful.” The correction left an ugly mark on the neat line. She turned the page, annoyed that picking one word was harder than facing a hall full of people waiting for her to regret the marriage.

In the kitchen, Shi Feng folded dry food into separate parcels, one for the trip out, one for emergencies. The cord he’d bought lay coiled beside his blade.

“So how much do you trust this expedition?” Ling Qingzhu asked from the doorway.

“I trust the route more than the broker,” Shi Feng said, testing his pack strap.

“That’s not very reassuring, you know,” Ling Qingzhu said, folding her arms.

“The broker isn’t going to reassure me for free,” Shi Feng said.

She wanted to tell him he didn’t have to chase every dangerous chance. The words got close, then stopped. He’d hear what was underneath: that a crippled future should be made small enough to fit other people’s pity. She hated it when others did that to her own choices.

Instead she set the cake box on the table.

“Who sent them?” Shi Feng asked.

“A friend,” Ling Qingzhu said. “Su Wanning.”

“Let me guess. She wants to know everything about me,” Shi Feng said.

Ling Qingzhu’s heart jumped. “How did you— how do you know that?” Ling Qingzhu demanded, hiding the letter behind her back.

“Friends who send cakes always want gossip,” Shi Feng said. “The cakes are the bribe.” He picked two broken pieces and left the whole ones where she could reach them.

Idiot, Ling Qingzhu thought, and she took a whole one.

At the market that afternoon, Shi Feng bought lamp wicks, clean cloth and enough sound cord for the descent. He checked the fibres, accepted the measured length and packed the coil where he could reach it without opening the whole bag.

He reached Ma Zheng’s meeting place before sunset. The broker looked over his pack with a practised eye, and Shi Feng saw the broker’s expression sour and thought: this one makes his living off other men’s mistakes. Badly equipped porters were a great source of emergency sales. Shi Feng’s preparations left no such opening.

“Ah, Brother Shi, please don’t bring bulky household things,” Ma Zheng said, bowing slightly. “The route is hard, very hard.”

“I wasn’t planning to carry the bed,” Shi Feng said.

Ma Zheng ignored that and repeated the common-chamber division. Shi Feng pointed to the written terms before the explanation could change. The broker repeated the entrance share twice and told him not to forget it at departure.

“I didn’t forget it the first time,” Shi Feng said.

A list of participants lay on the crate. Some men had sold their names dearly. Others gave them away so cheaply that Shi Feng suspected the names were fake. He read it all and didn’t ask Ma Zheng to make anybody more honest.

“We leave at dawn,” Ma Zheng said.

Supper was mushrooms with a little shredded meat, rice, and a warm bowl of broth. Shi Feng chose food that wouldn’t spoil while he was away. Ling Qingzhu looked at the table, then at the travel parcels stacked against the wall.

“We used to have four dishes,” Ling Qingzhu said. “Now it’s mushrooms and a bowl of broth.”

Shi Feng put down his chopsticks.

“You’ve mentioned that,” Shi Feng said.

“I paid you a fortune, and I get mushrooms,” Ling Qingzhu said.

His expression closed.

“The mushrooms are paid for,” Shi Feng said. “The fortune wasn’t.”

She hated what he was implying. She hated even more that it ruined the nice answer she’d almost written to Su Wanning. She was trying to describe the unexpected comfort of his company, and now the accounts crept back, stubborn and unwelcome, into the same old accusation.

Neither of them said more. He served himself more rice. She finished the broth, because the meal was too good to leave, and leaving it would look childish.

Later she added a line about his greed to the letter.

It was easier than explaining why a cheap supper could make her feel personally neglected. A bargain could be weighed. A feeling she never meant to have was harder to defend.

She folded the letter before changing anything else.

Shi Feng finished packing and never saw it. He left enough rice in the kitchen and told her which shop delivered water if the well rope caught. The spare key went where she could reach it. He checked the window latch and showed her how to lift the warped frame before it would close.

“I’m not a child. I can feed myself for three days,” Ling Qingzhu said. “I can even boil water. Usually.”

“Then surprise me,” Shi Feng said.

She almost smiled.

When he went out to bank the stove for the night, she knelt at the chest at the foot of her bed. She could send things that cost more than everything in his pack. But expensive medicine would only get another refusal or another account. Guards would make his private errand public and tell him she doubted he could manage it.

She took out clean wound cloth instead. If he’s hurt in that ruin, she thought, I don’t want to hear about it from a stranger.

It was plain, soft, and useful. She folded the lengths herself, small enough to fit inside his coat. Twice she retied the knot, because it seemed too tight to undo with one hand.

Then she shut the lid quickly, slid the chest back, and was lying very still behind the screen when he came in and quietly spread out his bedding. At the gate the next morning, she pressed the cloth into his palm.

“For the road,” Ling Qingzhu said. “Don’t make a face. It’s just cloth.”

Shi Feng looked down at the careful fold. There was no price on it. Nobody stood close enough to admire her concern.

“I’ll keep it dry,” Shi Feng said, and tucked it inside his robe instead of at the bottom of the pack.

He didn’t mistake the gesture for an apology, Shi Feng thought. He also didn’t pretend it meant nothing.

Behind him, Ling Qingzhu watched until the lane turned and took him out of sight.

On the table, the letter to Su Wanning still lay waiting, describing a man who was not quite the one she’d just watched leave.

chapters.title: The Men Who Divided Treasure
chapters.html:
“H-here’s your share of the equipment,” Ma Zheng said, pointing at a bundle under the eaves.

Beside a shrine where the statue of the god had lost both hands, Ma Zheng counted Shi Feng’s entrance stones into a leather pouch. Two iron stakes stuck out of the wrapping. The bundle looked heavier than the man standing next to it. From the broker’s face, even the god wouldn’t agree to carry it for free.

Shi Feng left the iron stakes where they lay and lifted only his own lamp. Ma Zheng looked toward Duan Kang, hoping the expedition leader would make him carry the rest.

“I came to search the ruin,” Shi Feng said. “Carry your own stakes.”

Laughter rang out from the steps.

“Hahaha! Listen to the cripple lecture the broker!” Pang Xun said, slapping the step. “Hey, Brother Shi, did you bring a coffin deposit too?”

Pang Xun was at Bone Refinement, the same realm as Shi Feng. That was where the similarity ended. Shi Feng could break his saber and the arm holding it with a single blow, he thought.

Pang Xun wore the saber at his waist and the face of a man who took every unanswered insult as a victory. His eyes moved from Shi Feng’s plain sword to the loose cuff hiding his wrist.

“Bring your own coffin,” Shi Feng said. “Mine would be wasted on you.”

The laughter stopped halfway through its second breath.

“What did you say?” Pang Xun demanded. His hand dropped to his saber. His expression turned vicious.

Shi Feng looked at him and didn’t move. Draw it if you dare, he thought coldly.

Pang Xun didn’t dare. Someone was walking up from behind the shrine.

“Enough!” Duan Kang said.

Duan Kang wore a dark travelling robe and an iron thumb ring. A narrow blade floated above his shoulder, turning slowly in the morning light. Foundation Establishment! The laborers were stunned and stood up straight at once, and Ma Zheng smiled like a man who wanted a commission just for standing near that realm.

“The hired men carry the common equipment,” Duan Kang said. “This leader’s participants save their strength for the chambers.”

He didn’t look at Shi Feng. He looked at the signed paper.

Shi Feng needed someone to show him the entrance. He didn’t need Duan Kang’s protection. He folded his copy and put it away.

“He won,” a laborer whispered.

“The broker lost face.”

They entered the hills before noon. The first day’s road ran through abandoned terraces and then climbed between slopes red with broken stone. Whenever mud got in his way, Duan Kang rode a short stretch on his flying blade. The laborers carried the tents, lamps, rope, and stakes, plus the bundles Ma Zheng couldn’t pass off on a cripple.

At the first stream, Pang Xun ordered the men across at the place where the water ran fastest.

“Faster water means shallower!” Pang Xun shouted. “Follow me!”

Shi Feng watched a leaf slide under a solid-looking shelf and vanish. Undercut bank, he thought. The water was eating the ground from underneath.

He walked twenty paces upstream.

“Afraid of wet feet?” Pang Xun called.

“Afraid of wasting time pulling fools out,” Shi Feng said.

The nearest laborer changed direction. Ma Zheng followed, pretending to check the weather. Pang Xun crossed at his original spot, and the shelf broke under him. He plunged in up to his waist.

“Help! Somebody help me!” Pang Xun roared.

Shi Feng didn’t offer a hand. Two laborers hauled their young master out, and he sat on the far bank pouring water from his boot. His saber was safe. His dignity was not.

“Did he know it would collapse?” a laborer whispered.

“Impossible!”

“…”

That evening, Duan Kang spread the ruin map beside the fire. Three passages were copied in clean lines. A fourth was just a smear under a greasy thumbprint.

“The marked entry chamber is common property,” Duan Kang said. “Anything found beyond it belongs to whoever finds it, as long as it doesn’t threaten the expedition’s safety.”

Shi Feng chewed his dried meat and waited.

“Dangerous objects will be held by me,” Duan Kang went on. “Objects that need special protection will also be held by me. Disputes will be settled when we get back.”

“By you,” Shi Feng said.

Duan Kang gave him a flat look. “By the leader,” Duan Kang said.

“And what do the participants hold?” Shi Feng asked.

Pang Xun held up the lamp he was cleaning. “These!” Pang Xun said, and burst out laughing.

Shi Feng glanced at the lamp, then at the contracts folded neatly beside Ma Zheng’s knee.

“Keep yours lit,” Shi Feng said. “You might want to see what happens to everything else.”

Nobody laughed. Ma Zheng gathered up the papers a little too fast. The leader will take everything valuable and call it safety, Shi Feng thought. And the broker knows it.

During the second watch, Shi Feng woke to the sound of cloth moving beside his pack. He opened his eyes without lifting his head. Ma Zheng’s fingers hovered over the buckle.

The point of Shi Feng’s knife touched the underside of the broker’s wrist.

“Wrong bag,” Shi Feng said.

Ma Zheng froze.

“I-I was only checking if you brought enough lamp oil!” Ma Zheng whispered.

“Ask in daylight,” Shi Feng said. “You’ll keep more fingers.”

Shi Feng pulled the knife away only after Ma Zheng crept off. There was no point starting a slaughter over a hand that reached for a buckle. The line between a thief and a murderer was thin, but it was still a line. Afterward he slept with the pack under his head.

By the second afternoon, the terraces were gone. Red cliffs crowded the path, and rainwater carried fine dust down the slopes and stained the scrub roots crimson. Above a gorge stood a shattered arch with three characters almost eaten away by moss.

Chiyun Ruins.

The old entrance was collapsed. A recent landslip had opened another way below it, showing steps that went down between the rock and the buried outer wall.

Shi Feng examined the fresh crack. The mountain hadn’t just crumbled. Something below was shifting and pulling the stone inward. He frowned in his heart.

Duan Kang sent a laborer ahead with a long pole.

The first step held. The second tipped under the pole and dropped into darkness. The man scrambled back on his hands, losing the pole as the last edge broke under his knee.

The pole fell, and no sound came back. Then, at last, it did. Ma Zheng stepped away from the opening, his complexion white.

“J-just a little damage from the rain,” Ma Zheng said, sweating.

“Then send the rain to test the next step,” Shi Feng said.

Duan Kang’s blade sank into the gap. Light flashed along its edge and showed a solid ledge below the broken stairs and several grooves cut into the wall. Old mechanisms. Some were rusted apart. Others had only been uncovered days ago.

“Tie a rope to an iron stake,” Duan Kang ordered.

Shi Feng checked the knot himself and tied a second loop around a rooted stump beside it. Pang Xun sneered at the extra rope, until Duan Kang tested the stake and found the soil under it hollow.

The stake pulled free. The second loop held.

“Good thing about that second knot,” a laborer breathed.

“…”

Cold air moved up from the opening, and somewhere below, stone scraped against stone.

Shi Feng raised his lamp and followed the rope down. He’d paid to enter a ruin, not to trust the other visitors.

Shi Feng checked the straps on his cheap bag before following. The household pass went into the inner pocket, away from the lantern oil. He hadn't joined this party to trust it. He'd joined because a known entrance saved a solitary hunter days of searching, and every man ahead of him seemed determined to arrive first.

chapters.title: Beneath the Red Stone
chapters.html:
The rope ended above a floor of dark red tiles. Shi Feng let go at the last arm’s length and stepped aside before the next laborer’s boots landed on his head. His lamp showed an empty pedestal, the lower half of a broken statue, and long scratches across the floor.

The scratches ran straight over the broken stone instead of stopping at its edge. Shi Feng frowned. Something passed through here after the collapse, he thought, and it didn’t bother with the door.

“Does anyone see anything alive?” Ma Zheng called from the rope, his voice thin and hopeful.

“Haha! Only the cripple, Broker Ma!” Pang Xun said, dropping to the floor with his saber already out. “Does he count?”

Duan Kang landed last. His flying blade circled the chamber once, stirring up dust, and nothing answered it.

“The room is safe,” Duan Kang announced. “Spread out. Remember the terms. Nothing past the entry chamber is common property.”

Duan Kang touched each red tile with his staff before putting his foot on it. Pang Xun marched across the row beside him and looked back with a grin.

“Too cautious, Leader!” Pang Xun said.

Duan Kang didn’t answer. He let Pang Xun reach the far wall first. The porters noticed and hurriedly stayed behind the staff.

Ma Zheng nodded eagerly, very pleased that someone else was checking the room for him.

A skeleton lay against the northern wall. Pang Xun reached it first and tried to pull a belt knife from its scabbard. Rust had welded blade and sheath together.

“Worthless!” Pang Xun spat, and flung it at the wall.

Shi Feng watched the dust rise from the impact. One thin stream of it drifted upward along a seam instead of falling. He raised his lamp, and the seam moved.

“Back,” Shi Feng said.

“What did he say?” the old porter Gu Tie asked.

Ma Zheng shouted another warning and dragged the old porter away by the collar.

Pang Xun turned to sneer, and a black mandible burst through the wall behind him. His sneer froze. The laborers were stunned into silence for one long breath.

He threw himself flat. A second mandible snapped through the air where his neck had been and cut his tied hair loose. Red stone exploded across the chamber, and a Stonehide Spirit Centipede uncoiled out of the hole, its armored segments scraping sparks from the tiles.

Its head was wider than the doorway it had come from.

“A spirit beast!” Ma Zheng shrieked. “N-nobody told me it was a spirit beast!”

Duan Kang’s flying blade flashed downward. The point struck a plate behind the skull and skidded away, taking only a thin sliver of armor. The centipede turned toward him.

Duan Kang turned toward the stairs.

“Fall back to the upper passage!” Duan Kang barked. “This leader will cover you! Everyone, fall back!”

He was already running before he finished the sentence.

The laborers stampeded after him. Ma Zheng snatched a dropped lamp and ran with them. Pang Xun scrambled behind a pedestal, then realized it wouldn’t protect him from a creature longer than a cart.

“Leader, wait for me!” Pang Xun wailed. “Leader!”

Nobody waited. Pang Xun’s face turned pale, and he stared after them in shock.

Shi Feng didn’t fight for the stairway. The centipede’s outer legs were already reaching it, and he saw no reason to die in a queue. Instead, he kicked the fallen statue under those legs and slid sideways into a broken doorway.

The beast followed the closer movement. Good, Shi Feng thought. It chases whatever is nearest, and the nearest thing is me.

The others’ lamps vanished around the upper bend. Shi Feng set his own lamp in a shallow niche in the wall and drew his sword. It was a plain blade, freshly sharpened. It would be enough if he hit the right places.

The centipede smashed headfirst into the doorway.

Shi Feng met it with his left palm. The impact shook dust from the roof and snapped the creature’s head sideways, crushing the doorjamb. He stepped inside the snapping mandibles and drove his sword into the soft fold under one armored cheek.

Dark fluid ran over his knuckles.

The centipede reared back with a hiss. Shi Feng pulled the blade free before its twisting body could trap it, planted a foot on the broken jamb, and struck again from above. The point sank in behind the skull, and this time he left the sword where it was.

Boom!

The beast rolled and smashed the pedestal behind him into three pieces. Shi Feng dropped under a scissoring leg, grabbed the ridge of the exposed neck plate, and drove his knee against the sword’s hilt. The steel sank deeper, and the head crashed to the floor.

He didn’t wait to see if it was finished dying. Both hands found the broken seam in the armor. His refined bones answered together, one strength flowing through all of them.

“Open,” Shi Feng said through his teeth.

He pulled, and the plate tore away.

The creature’s last thrash flattened the doorway. Shi Feng stepped over the wreckage and forced the head backward until the inner joint parted with a wet crack. Silence came slowly: first the mandibles, then the legs, then the last pieces sliding to a rest around his feet.

Shi Feng wiped his face with his sleeve. A Foundation Establishment cultivator decided this thing was somebody else’s problem, Shi Feng thought coldly. Duan Kang’s leadership was worth exactly as much as the contract’s safety clause.

He picked up his sword. There was one shallow chip near the point, but the blade was still sound.

Then he laid his hand on the exposed flesh. The All-Devouring Physique stirred and pulled the beast’s vitality inward in a great wave of heat. Duan Kang had barely scratched this armor. Shi Feng had faced its full strength and killed it himself, and the reward was his alone.

Heat flooded his chest and pushed into the stubborn places in his skeleton. He breathed until the first fierce rush grew steady, then stopped drawing. The rest could wait. A ruin with moving walls was a bad place to cultivate.

Voices echoed down from the upper passage.

“Is anyone still alive down there?” Duan Kang called.

Shi Feng didn’t answer.

“The cripple went down the lower passage, Leader!” Pang Xun shouted. “I saw him! The beast must have eaten him by now!”

“Th-then his entrance share is forfeit,” Ma Zheng said, and even through the stone his voice sounded relieved. “Write him down as lost.”

“Lost, then,” Duan Kang said. “We go around.”

Not one of them suggested going back for him. Shi Feng’s expression didn’t change as he listened to their footsteps fade. He only smiled faintly.

“Thanks for the funeral,” Shi Feng said to the empty dark. “Everyone is so generous with other people’s shares.”

He turned to the shattered doorway. The centipede had opened a route the map didn’t show, and cooler air flowed beyond it, under a hanging slab. His lamp showed tool marks along the lower edge and old wedges crushed under the weight.

Someone dug here before us, Shi Feng thought, and his eyes narrowed.

He crouched beside the opening. The ordinary fallen stones he could lift, but the slab itself was locked into dark grooves on both sides, and the carved lines inside them were fused into glass. An ancient trap once guarded this passage, and it had gone off right here.

He worked around the edge instead of putting his neck under it.

A strip of torn cloth appeared in the dust. Then a pale hand. Then a broken sword lying beside the hand, its edge ruined by something fiercer than rust.

The dead man hadn’t been laid out on an altar. He lay on his side with one shoulder pinned under the slab and digging tools scattered around him. No offering, no waiting disciple’s cushion. Just an explorer who met a danger he couldn’t escape in time.

Shi Feng raised his lamp.

A metal badge glinted at the dead man’s waist. He wiped the dust away with his thumb and read the four characters stamped into it.

Artificer Hall.

chapters.title: The Enforcer’s Last Entry
chapters.html:
The name on the badge was Xu Changhe.

Sect enforcer. Elder of Artificer Hall.

Shi Feng brushed the dust away with his sleeve. The characters were cut deep, and the collapse hadn’t erased them. On the back were several old sword nicks and a repair along one corner. So this elder used his badge more often than he polished it, Shi Feng thought, and he found himself liking the dead man a little.

A leather case lay under the body’s free arm. Shi Feng checked the seams before touching the clasp. No hidden needle, no trap left over. The case opened on folded papers wrapped in waxed cloth.

The first sheet was a shopping list: rope, oil, steel wedges, and food for a dig that was expected to last several days. Xu Changhe didn’t come here to die, Shi Feng thought. He came to work.

He looked back at the fused grooves. An ancient trap had failed while the elder worked beneath it. The cracked sword and the violent scars on the inner wall showed a man who fought to the end, not one who planned a gift for some lucky successor. Shi Feng eased the loose stones away from the shoulder and drew out the case without disturbing what the slab still held.

The final journal entry filled less than half a page.

Old passage opened. Southern support unsound. Examine central chamber before withdrawing. Do not strike the remaining anchor until the lower groove is clear.

The next page was blank.

There was no dying message written in blood, and no handy map to a treasure. Death had simply cut off a man who expected to keep working.

“Leader, I hear scraping below!” Pang Xun’s voice floated down through the stone, faint and nervous. “It’s a ghost! This ruin is cursed!”

“It’s the carcass settling, you idiot!” Duan Kang said sharply, his expression dark. “Keep looking for the bypass.”

“What if the cripple is still alive down there?” Gu Tie asked.

“Th-then he’s not our problem!” Ma Zheng said. “Hold the lamp higher, old man!”

“A cripple surviving a spirit beast? Ha! Impossible!” Pang Xun scoffed.

“Quiet, all of you!” Duan Kang snapped.

The porters were stunned by his sudden fury, and the chatter died. Shi Feng didn’t even look up. Let them search, he thought, and turned back to the journal.

The earlier pages were about roads, fugitives and troublesome cultivators. Xu Changhe escorted accused disciples, chased a murderer through three towns, and spent one wet afternoon looking for evidence that a merchant swore the river had swallowed.

The evidence was in the merchant’s pillow.

Shi Feng’s mouth twitched. The elder wrote down the merchant’s broken nose with much less anger than the wasted afternoon.

Between the travel entries were sword diagrams. Under a stain, Shi Feng found the title: Iron River Sword Art.

There were three main moves, followed by corrections taken from real fights. The pages showed no mountains splitting under a stroke. They showed feet, hands, and the places an enemy would strike if either moved wrong.

Piercing Current was a straight thrust with a short step, keeping the sword between the swordsman and the enemy. The elder drew three careless ways to do it, each marked with the spot where the swordsman got stabbed in return.

Turning Wave changed a missed thrust into a cut. The feet kept moving while the wrist turned, so an enemy who dodged the point met the edge. Returning Tide drew the blade back a short distance, inviting the enemy forward, then drove the point through the opening his attack left behind.

There were other cuts and steps, but these three were the heart of the art. They could be practiced with an ordinary sword. Using them later with a flying blade needed a realm Shi Feng didn’t have yet.

A real sword art, he thought, and his heart quickened. He was shocked by his own luck. Not a dead man’s stroke to copy, but a method I can learn.

He read the corrections twice and stood. The lamp threw his shadow across the opposite wall. He drew his sword and began with Piercing Current, and his first step carried him too far. The diagram made the exposed shoulder obvious.

He shortened the step and tried again.

Better.

Turning Wave gave him more trouble. He followed the imaginary enemy with the point before turning the edge, and that was too late. His wrist had to turn while his foot was still moving.

On the fifth try the change came smoothly. The straight thrust flowed into a short cut with no pause between them.

“Good!” Shi Feng said softly, and for once he allowed himself a real smile. His expression, usually flat, softened.

He won his fights through strength, quick judgment and painful experience. Now he had a swordsman’s method on top of that. It would make his overwhelming force much harder to avoid.

Returning Tide was the simplest to understand and the easiest to ruin by pulling back too far. He practiced until the sword withdrew only a palm’s width before striking forward again.

These were beginnings, not mastery. He’d have to repeat them until they belonged to his own hands. Shi Feng sheathed the sword and marked the three pages.

Above, footsteps crossed the upper chamber again. Nobody called his name now.

“Blocked again!” Ma Zheng’s voice complained. “Leader, this map is a joke!”

“Shut your mouth, Ma Zheng!” Duan Kang snapped. “This leader is thinking!”

Shi Feng ignored the noise and went back to the case.

The crafting papers were decent. A cracked weapon socket repaired. A damaged furnace fitting replaced. Notes on spotting cheap binding metal. Xu Changhe knew his equipment and made good repairs, but nothing suggested an elder who made wondrous artifacts. So he was no master artificer, Shi Feng decided. Just a practical man.

The sword pages were different. They were worth far more. He separated them with care.

At the bottom of the case were medicine notes, messy and stained. A wound wash shared a sheet with a reminder to replace three roof tiles. A recipe for strained tendons ended beside an angry sum: the difference between raw ingredients and finished medicine.

One root was underlined twice.

Do not buy from anyone who calls rot a sign of maturity.

“Wise man!” Shi Feng murmured. He agreed with that lesson right away.

The elder knew enough alchemy to write down useful recipes and complain about what others charged for them. These were a warrior’s practical notes, not the legacy of a supreme alchemist. Still, they beat paying a swindler to explain why a bottle smelled rotten.

Shi Feng wrapped them with the sword record.

The rest of the elder’s belongings were ruined. A crushed storage fitting lay split along its inner engraving, and cloth, metal scraps and spoiled packets lay tangled in the dust beneath it. Shi Feng picked out a good whetstone and a length of ordinary cord. The old medicines were long dead.

Nothing here looked like the untouched treasure Duan Kang had promised his paying participants.

The papers weren’t worthless, though.

Shi Feng cut a length from the elder’s outer robe and covered the exposed face. He couldn’t drag the whole slab away, but he could spare these remains the next scavenger’s rough search. From loose stone he built a low barrier across the opening.

It wasn’t a grand tomb. Xu Changhe probably liked a road out better when he was alive, so a practical barrier would have to do.

He copied the location into his own notes, held the scarred iron badge in his palm before the low stone cairn, and bowed once over the dead enforcer’s resting place.

“Elder Xu Changhe, I’ve taken your Iron River Sword Art and your notes,” Shi Feng said aloud into the quiet chamber. “I vow that I will carry this badge to Artificer Hall myself and return your name and record to your sect.”

He wrapped the badge carefully beside the journal and tucked both inside his robe.

The dead man didn’t answer.

No ghost rose from the badge, and no kindly old voice announced that Shi Feng had passed a test. The lamp flickered on the cloth, and the ruin stayed a ruin. Shi Feng preferred it that way.

He checked the narrow passage beyond the fallen support. Cool air moved through it, carrying the dry mineral smell of a room closed for a very long time.

At the far end, a thin line of darkness separated two unbroken doors.

Shi Feng lowered his lamp and followed the air.

chapters.title: The Ring in the Empty Room
chapters.html:
The doors were neither locked nor sealed.

One had settled deep into its lower groove. Shi Feng folded a strip of cloth between his palm and the edge, lifted, and pushed. Stone grated over stone, and dry air breathed across his face.

His lamp showed a low shelf. On it lay a black ring.

There were no heaps of spirit stones, no jade boxes sorted by rank, and no weapons waiting for a hero to claim his destiny. The chamber held a cracked vessel, a lot of dust, and that single small object.

Shi Feng stepped up to the shelf. Old scratches marked where a stand once rested, and whatever had brought the ring here was long gone. The ring itself showed no rust. When he moved the lamp, a faint line under the black surface caught the light and ran inward, deeper than the metal was thick.

A spatial ring, Shi Feng thought, and his eyes sharpened.

The plain storage bag Ling Qingzhu had given him was valuable for what it should have held. This was valuable even empty. A true spatial ring could carry a fortune without making a man hire three porters and invite a robbery.

He wrapped it in clean cloth and lifted it from the shelf.

“Cripple! Leave it!” Duan Kang said behind him.

Shi Feng turned.

Duan Kang stood in the doorway opposite, his flying blade hovering at his shoulder. Ma Zheng held a lamp behind him with a shaking hand, and Pang Xun’s saber was already out. They’d found another passage after all.

“Leader Duan,” Shi Feng said calmly. “You’re alive. I’m glad.”

“C-cripple?” Ma Zheng gasped, stunned, and his face turned pale. “You survived the beast?”

“That’s impossible!” Pang Xun shouted. “I saw the centipede go down that passage! It should have eaten him!”

“It tried,” Shi Feng said. He slid the ring inside his robe. “I found this outside the marked entry chamber, personally. You signed the terms.”

Duan Kang stepped into the room. His flying blade moved with him, its point turning toward Shi Feng’s throat.

“Dangerous objects belong in this leader’s keeping,” Duan Kang said.

“Then start with your mouth,” Shi Feng said.

Ma Zheng’s lamp trembled and his expression twisted with fear. The broker and Pang Xun were both shocked that a cripple dared talk to a Foundation Establishment cultivator this way. “You’re courting death!” Duan Kang roared, and attacked.

The flying blade crossed the chamber in a streak of winter light. Shi Feng knocked its flat aside with his sword and strode forward. The impact drove the weapon into the wall.

“Come back!” Duan Kang roared, and sent his qi after it. Too late. Shi Feng was already in front of him.

A Foundation Establishment cultivator could scare the porters outside, Shi Feng thought. He doesn’t scare me.

Duan Kang’s protective qi flared. Shi Feng struck the center of it with his fist.

Crack.

The shield shattered. Ma Zheng and Pang Xun stared in disbelief. Duan Kang flew backward into the doorframe, and his iron thumb ring hit the stone and flattened. The breath he tried to take came out red.

“Impossible! He’s a cripple! How did a cripple break a Foundation Establishment cultivator’s qi shield with his fist?!” Ma Zheng screamed. “Pang Xun, kill him! Kill him now!”

Ma Zheng himself stabbed at Shi Feng’s back. Shi Feng heard the sole scrape first. After fighting men who sent weapons through the air, he no longer trusted the empty space around anyone’s hands. He turned, caught the broker’s wrist, and pulled him across Pang Xun’s falling saber.

Steel cut deep into Ma Zheng’s shoulder.

The broker shrieked. Shi Feng broke the captured arm, seized the back of his neck, and drove his face against the stone edge. The shriek stopped.

Pang Xun recoiled, his saber stuck for a moment in the falling body. “Ma Zheng!” Pang Xun cried, staring at the dead broker in horror. “You idiot, you jumped right into my blade!”

Shi Feng’s gaze passed over him and returned to Duan Kang. The leader had dragged himself upright. His fingers shook as they formed a command, and behind Shi Feng the flying blade rose from the floor.

Shi Feng crossed the remaining distance in two steps. His heel smashed Duan Kang’s knee sideways, and his hand closed on the man’s throat and drove him against the shelf.

The returning blade slowed.

“Wait, wait,” Duan Kang rasped. “The ring, the ruin, all of it, take it! We can divide—”

“You already chose to divide my neck,” Shi Feng said.

He struck once more, and the blade fell across its master’s boots.

Pang Xun ran.

“Don’t kill me,” Pang Xun begged, scrambling into the narrow passage. “I was only following orders!”

Shi Feng drew his plain sword as he turned. The passage gave the fleeing man no room to swing, but Pang Xun tried anyway, hacking backward over his shoulder in panic.

Shi Feng changed the line of his thrust. The move from Xu Changhe’s notes carried forward without its empty shape. His point slid under the saber, entered Pang Xun’s back, and came out below the ribs.

Piercing Current, Shi Feng thought. It works.

Pang Xun struck the wall with both palms, and his knees folded.

“I can tell you where the other—” Pang Xun choked.

Shi Feng pulled out the blade and finished him. I don’t take directions from men who tried to kill me, he thought coldly. They all knew what steel at a throat meant when they started.

The silence afterward was complete.

Shi Feng stood still long enough to listen beyond the chamber. No porters coming. No fourth set of footsteps. Duan Kang had apparently decided a treasure room was too good to share with men hired to carry rope.

His greed did us one favour, Shi Feng thought, and wiped his blade.

He searched the bodies. Ordinary spirit stones went into his bag, and good medicine packets into a separate wrapping. Marked tokens, private letters and anything with the leader’s seals stayed behind.

He didn’t touch the corpses with any thought of devouring them. Killing an enemy was not the same as harvesting a beast.

Duan Kang’s flying blade was undamaged. Shi Feng wrapped it instead of trying to wield it. He had the strength to break the owner, but he didn’t have the realm to command the owner’s artifact. Those were two separate things, whatever Pang Xun believed at the end.

Only then did he look at the ring again.

A careful thread of qi met a smooth wall under the surface. There was no opening to the storage inside. When he pushed harder, only the pressure came back against his fingertips.

Shi Feng stopped.

Xu Changhe’s notes explained the difference between a simple storage bag and a sealed spatial ring. The inner seal of the latter needed Foundation Establishment qi to open. Smashing the metal would give him nothing but a broken ring.

“Storage can wait,” Shi Feng said to himself, and tucked it under his robe.

He went back through the lower passage. At the centipede’s carcass, he drew the last of its vitality until the armored shell lay slack on the floor, then let the heat settle before he moved on. The cooler air led through a crack above a dry drainage channel.

By dusk, Shi Feng climbed out onto the far side of the gorge.

Behind him, Chiyun Ruins kept three men who had divided the treasure before deciding whether its owner should live.

On the road ahead, one question remained. The ring was sealed, and only his own qi could open it, once he reached Foundation Establishment. The tournament notice would say the same thing, loudly, within seven days.

chapters.title: The Bones That Answered Gold
chapters.html:
Ling Qingzhu opened the gate before Shi Feng could lift the latch a second time. Her white veil was tied hastily, her hair pinned loosely, and flour marked one sleeve. She looked at his pack, his plain sword, and the dirt dried along the edges of his boots.

“Several days, you said. You lied. Or you can’t count,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“The passage was less convenient than the map,” Shi Feng said.

He stepped into the courtyard. The familiar pear tree threw its shadow across the water jar. After the dark, cramped ruin, even the crooked roof tiles looked almost fancy.

Ling Qingzhu didn’t move aside.

“So where’s the rest of your party?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“Some went home,” Shi Feng said. “Some decided to rob me.”

She studied his face. He spoke as bluntly as he did when he told a vegetable seller that the bottom of the basket held more mud than food.

“You just walked in. Like you’d fetched noodles,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Obviously,” Shi Feng said.

She should have found that irritating. Instead, the tension in her shoulders eased, and she was annoyed at herself for it.

Then she saw the blood in the fold of his cuff. He’d washed in a stream outside the capital, but the fold had escaped him.

“Is that blood? Is it yours?” Ling Qingzhu asked sharply.

“No,” Shi Feng said.

Her eyes stayed on the stain a moment longer. Then she turned toward the kitchen without another word.

“Aiya, young master, you’re back!” Granny Qin called over the lane wall, a sesame cake already in her hand. “Your wife stood at that gate three evenings in a row! Three! I told her the ruins eat people, and she said she was only checking the latch! Here, eat, you’re all skin and bones!”

“Granny Qin, stop making things up! I was checking the latch! It’s a bad latch!” Ling Qingzhu said from the kitchen door. Her ears went red.

“Oh, little wife, no need to be shy!” Granny Qin cackled, and pushed the cake over the wall.

Shi Feng said nothing. Only the corner of his mouth moved, and his expression stayed perfectly flat otherwise.

The meal was waiting: rice, vegetables, and a soup with the pieces cut in all different sizes. Shi Feng sat and ate. The rice was too soft. One piece of radish in the soup was bigger than the spoon, and he ate it without a word.

Ling Qingzhu watched his chopsticks.
