“Why do you look like you’re facing an enemy?” Ling Qingzhu said. “It’s just food.”

“I know,” Shi Feng said.

“I followed the instructions. The rice refused,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Rice does that when the fire goes out,” Shi Feng said.

She glanced toward the stove. He followed her glance and saw three damp sticks beside it, scorched at one end and still unburned in the middle. Shi Feng lowered his bowl to hide his smile, but Ling Qingzhu saw it anyway, and her expression stiffened.

Only after Granny Qin disappeared behind her brazier did Ling Qingzhu close the gate and remove her veil. Shi Feng raised his head again.

“Did the soup suddenly improve?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“The view did,” Shi Feng replied.

She snatched the ladle. His next helping contained almost no meat.

“Stop smirking! Fine. Chickens get it.” Ling Qingzhu said.

“I plan to finish eating first,” Shi Feng said, and took a second helping.

Afterward he washed the bowls while she sat under the pear tree. Neither of them mentioned how often she’d looked toward the lane while he was away. Shi Feng didn’t turn her clumsy meal into an apology she’d never offered, he thought. It was enough that she made it.

The next morning, he carried Duan Kang’s flying blade into a weapon counter near the Sky Pavilion square.

“Unclaimed salvage,” Shi Feng said, and laid the wrapped blade on the counter without naming Chiyun Ruins. Surviving porters like Gu Tie had seen Duan Kang’s group enter that gorge, and there was no reason to leave a trail connecting the dead leader’s weapon to his own name.

The counter keeper tested the cold edge with a brass ring, saw the clean spirit-channel engraving, and paid four hundred and sixty spirit stones after a single counter-offer. Most of the money went straight to the medicines listed in his bone manual, along with two plain wooden practice blades from a side stall.

When he returned at dusk, Ling Qingzhu picked up one of the wooden blades under the pear tree, tested its balance with a surprisingly steady wrist, and traded three slow footwork turns with him before supper—the first of the short courtyard sword lessons that neither of them wrote into the contract.

That night, he waited until Ling Qingzhu’s breathing slowed behind the screen. Then he gathered the new medicines and the ruin packets and slipped into the kitchen. The pills smelled strong, and he didn’t want her waking to it. Some were badly rounded. One cracked while cooling. Their maker might have refused to put them on a respectable counter.

Shi Feng swallowed them without a second thought.

The medicine turned into strength inside him. There was no creeping resistance, no pile of impurities waiting to punish him later. The All-Devouring Physique didn’t care whether a pill had embarrassed its maker.

But cultivation still meant guiding the benefit where it belonged. He settled his breathing and followed the response of his skeleton.

The centipede’s vitality gave the final push, and the medicines sustained it. The stubborn places past three quarters of refinement no longer gave in just because he owned a magnificent meridian network. Each one had to be reached, fed, and brought into harmony with the strength around it.

Shi Feng didn’t complain about the work. I’ve decided to finish, he thought, and that’s the end of it.

Days passed between ordinary meals and secret night cycles. By day he bought rice, replaced lamp oil, and mended the pack strap Chiyun Ruins had nearly torn off. Ling Qingzhu found his new quietness less annoying than his old absences, though she scolded him when he forgot the porridge pot on the stove.

“It’s burnt again! That’s twice in seven days!” Ling Qingzhu said, holding it up. “Are you planning to eat charcoal?”

“I’m planning to buy a new pot,” Shi Feng said.

He bought it that afternoon instead of arguing that burnt porridge could still fill a stomach. Each night, once her breathing slowed, he slipped away to the kitchen, and the pale gaps in his skeleton narrowed.

A small bone beneath the heel answered. Then the thin places along the ribs. Then the final stubborn section near the base of the spine, which resisted three cycles in a row and wasn’t the least bit ashamed of it.

Shi Feng sent another current through it.

This time the response ran outward instead of dying at the edge. He sat up straight, and his heart pounded. All two hundred and six bones answered together, one perfect structure.

Ordinary Bone Refinement: complete!

For several breaths nothing else happened. He let the strength settle, following every connection. Many cultivators would have called this a huge waste of resources and gone straight after Foundation Establishment.

Then something deeper stirred.

A speck of gold appeared beneath the finished surface of a finger bone.

Shi Feng froze.

A second speck answered from a rib. A third glowed inside the spine. They didn’t spread like an injury, and they didn’t replace the sound refinement above them. They lay beneath it, opening a depth that stayed locked while the outer work was unfinished.

Ancestral Bones! Shi Feng thought, stunned. The name from the cultivation record came back with a clarity no description could give.

All his labor so far hadn’t finished the road. It had only uncovered the next section.

He followed one golden trace carefully. It accepted the strength, brightened a little, and demanded more. The demand was enormous compared with the visible change.

Shi Feng opened his eyes. Empty medicine packets lay beside his knee, and the sealed ring rested on the folded journal. Neither gave any answer to the cost of turning a whole skeleton gold.

Outside the kitchen, gray dawn light was creeping over the pear tree. A soft knock sounded on the kitchen door.

“Your bedding’s empty again. Do you ever sleep?” Ling Qingzhu said through the door. “Are you eating, or should I put the rice away?”

“In a moment,” Shi Feng said.

He wrapped the ring and rose, every movement steadier than before.

Heaven gave him an extraordinary body. Now it expected him to pay for every inch of it.

chapters.title: The Minimum Requirement
chapters.html:
The selection notice drew a crowd before the paste dried. Shi Feng came to buy lamp oil and stopped, because three young men were arguing loudly enough to make a fish seller forget to cheat his customer.

“My family has lived in the capital for three generations! That should count!”

“Count for what? You’re still Qi Condensation, you fool!”

“Move aside, I can’t read the small characters!”

The royal Sima seal stood at the top of the notice. Beneath it, Great Liang announced the selection of representatives for the great tournament of the surrounding kingdoms. Registration would close in ninety days, at the end of the third month. Lineage and birth records would be checked. Cultivation would be verified.

Foundation Establishment was the minimum realm.

Shi Feng read that line twice.

At the mountain pass, a Foundation Establishment cultivator had tried to rob him and ended pinned to a rock. Beneath Chiyun Ruins, another found out that a flying blade didn’t protect its owner from a broken neck. Neither encounter changed Shi Feng’s own realm.

He was still in Bone Refinement, and the golden transformation made that gap far more expensive to cross. A clerk in a dark cap stood beside the notice with a register, and people were asking questions faster than he could write down his answers. Shi Feng waited until the argument about family places ended.

“Is the minimum decided by actual cultivation, or by fighting strength?” Shi Feng asked.

The clerk looked up. His name board read Yu Cheng.

“Actual cultivation,” Yu Cheng said. “Foundation Establishment and the age limit. Brawlers can watch from the street.”

Behind him, someone groaned about how few people in the capital reached Foundation Establishment before thirty.

“Few,” Yu Cheng said, and went back to writing.

Shi Feng pointed to the rolls being unrolled beside the register. “Are those the eligible birth years?”

“Yes,” Yu Cheng said. “Next.”

Shi Feng found it. Age wouldn’t stop him. Cultivation would, if he kept putting off the next realm.

He stepped aside so the next person could start explaining how important his grandfather was.

Lower on the notice were the names of the nearby Great Sects: Martial Palace, Hundred Flower Valley, Artificer Hall. The kingdom’s best young cultivators would be sent toward opportunities no ordinary household in the capital could buy. The notice spelled out the champion’s reward in careful detail: direct entry as an inner disciple into a Great Sect of his choice.

Shi Feng’s eyes rested on Artificer Hall.

Xu Changhe’s badge lay at home beside the sword record, tucked in the corner with his bedding. Shi Feng didn’t think the whole sect was like one dead enforcer. Every sect had its greedy men and proud fools, he thought.

But he respected the warrior who wrote the notes he’d carried out from under a fallen slab. Returning them there someday was a better reason to choose a destination than counting the embroidered robes in a procession.

First the kingdom selection. First Foundation Establishment.

Beyond the board, Ling Qingzhu had stopped beside her household carriage. Her white veil stirred in the breeze, but her gaze stayed on the sect names.

“Will accepted disciples return under the kingdom's orders?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“They answer to their sect after admission, Fairy Ling,” Yu Cheng said. “Their new elders arrange their journeys.”

Her fingers eased on the folded notice in her hand. Shi Feng noticed that small movement. The board promised more than cultivation resources to her. He hadn't realised how much of her plan rested on that one line.

Ling Qingzhu caught him watching, nodded once and returned to the carriage. He looked back at the minimum realm.

They had different reasons to want the same door open.

Laughter rose behind him.

“Look, it’s Brother Shi,” Bai He said, loudly enough for the whole crowd. She stood by the fish stall with two White Crane Pavilion juniors. “Reading the notice! How touching. Some people just can’t let go of old dreams.”

One junior giggled at the idea of him even knowing what Foundation Establishment meant.

A few onlookers glanced between them.

“Isn’t that the Ling family’s husband?”

“The cripple, yes.”

“…”

“Bai He,” Shi Feng said without turning around, “your sleeve is in the fish basket. The seller’s going to charge you for it.”

“What?” Bai He looked down and shrieked. Her silk cuff was trailing through a tray of silver carp!

“Ha! The White Crane is fishing!”

The fish seller demanded two stones for the tray. The crowd laughed, and the White Crane juniors edged away from Bai He’s fishy sleeve.

“Came to mock Fairy Ling’s husband and bought a basket of carp scales instead!”

“Look at the Shi boy—he didn’t even turn around and she’s paying the fishmonger!”

Bai He’s face burned crimson as she threw two stones into the basket and fled down the street with her cuff pinched between two fingers, while the men by the royal notice board stepped aside to clear a path for Shi Feng.

At the medicine street, the same preparations he’d bought seven days ago cost more than he remembered. He checked two counters before he accepted that his memory wasn’t the problem. The shopkeepers had read the royal notice too.

Fang Jingyuan stood behind the third counter, inspecting a delivery with the sour look of a man hoping to find a reason to charge less. When he saw Shi Feng, he straightened at once.

“Prices are up, I know, I know,” Fang Jingyuan called, wringing his hands. “Everyone’s buying! The young cultivators will empty these shelves, what can I do?”

“They haven’t emptied them yet,” Shi Feng said.

“It’s the demand!” Fang Jingyuan said. “I can’t help it!”

“Your medicine learned to see the future before you did,” Shi Feng said.

He asked the cost of the raw ingredients instead. Fang Jingyuan’s smile thinned. The gap between a packet of ingredients and the finished pill was big enough to make Shi Feng respect plain robbery for being honest.

“The skill costs too, you know!” Fang Jingyuan said, wringing his hands harder.

“So does being the customer who never asks that question,” Shi Feng said.

He bought nothing and left.

At home, Ling Qingzhu sat under the pear tree choosing between two lengths of silk for a torn lining. Shi Feng set the lamp oil down and began laying out his receipts beside a sheet of blank paper.

“You saw the tournament notice? The capital talks of nothing else,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“I did,” Shi Feng said.

She glanced at the receipts, and her expression turned sharp and suspicious.

“Don’t tell me you’re pricing out an entry fee. Seriously?” Ling Qingzhu said.

“I’m working out the cost of medicine,” Shi Feng said.

“Good. A sensible worry,” Ling Qingzhu said, and went back to the silk. Then she added, not looking up, “Bai He was at the fish stall. Hongxiu heard it from the baker. Ignore her. She’s been jealous since we were twelve.”

“I didn’t,” Shi Feng said. “She minded the fish.”

Ling Qingzhu’s needle paused. She bent lower over the silk, and her shoulders shook once.

In her mind, his ruined meridians made the tournament question silly before cost could even matter. She would have been shocked to learn the truth. She thought he was studying prices because the public excitement had made his errands more expensive. Shi Feng let her keep the mistake. He wasn’t asking anyone’s permission to cultivate.

The calculation took all afternoon. Hunting cost days of travel. Odd jobs covered meals and rent, then swallowed his training hours. Finished medicine cost enough to keep its maker far more comfortable than its buyer.

The golden traces in his bones demanded far more than the ordinary refinement ever did. He could give up the deeper transformation, rush Foundation Establishment, and aim at the entrance requirement like a starving dog lunging at the nearest scrap. Shi Feng put the thought aside.

I didn’t open three hundred and sixty-five meridians to choose a smaller future just because someone posted a deadline on a wall, he thought coldly. The problem needs more resources, not a weaker foundation!

He opened Xu Changhe’s medicine notes.

Beside one common preparation, the elder had written a blunt calculation of ingredient costs. Beneath it was a second remark.

Buy the ingredients separately. Finished medicine costs fools dearly. Shi Feng looked from the old handwriting to his own pile of receipts.

He’d been an excellent customer.

The achievement didn’t please him anymore.

He marked the ninety-day window on his paper. Three months remained. His next step would begin with a furnace.

chapters.title: The Old Master Who Chose the Wrong Body
chapters.html:
The ring had resisted Shi Feng's careful probe again. He had waited until Ling Qingzhu slept before taking it into the kitchen, well away from her bed. Xu Changhe's medicine cost notes lay beside the lamp; the elder's warning about finished pill markups had set him examining the sealed spatial ring he carried out of Chiyun Ruins.

A cold thread moved across his fingers. Shi Feng put the black metal down.

The laugh came from above the ring.

Shi Feng’s knife was already in his hand. He rose without scraping his chair and put the table between himself and the cold gathering over the black metal. The ring’s storage was still closed. Nothing opened under his qi. Whatever lived inside chose its own way out, through a hairline crack in the outer seal.

A thread of shadow climbed up from the crack and thickened into an old man’s face.

“At last,” Mo Tianheng said.

His features were almost transparent, but his eyes weren’t. They moved over Shi Feng’s shoulders, chest and throat with the hungry interest of a butcher inspecting a pig.

Shi Feng moved the knife point toward the ring. “Name,” Shi Feng said calmly.

“Brat! This master is Mo Tianheng of Sky Pavilion!” Mo Tianheng boomed. “Kneel. Meeting this master is the greatest luck of your pitiful life.”

“Then stay on your side of the table,” Shi Feng said.

“Hahaha, a brat with spine,” Mo Tianheng said, licking his thin lips. “Good. This master has waited a very long time for someone like you!”

Shi Feng’s scalp prickled. He thought: he doesn’t want to talk. He wants to move in.

Mo Tianheng laughed again, and pressure followed the sound, cold and enormous. The lamp flame bent flat. Shi Feng’s heart pounded. This was no Foundation Establishment cultivator. Even the Foundation Establishment cultivator at the mountain pass never pressed on him like this.

“A knife against this master’s spirit?” Mo Tianheng sneered. “Ridiculous. When this master stood at Profound Heaven, your ancestors were begging for pills!”

Shi Feng’s expression stayed calm. He didn’t know what Profound Heaven was, but he understood the pressure well enough. He thought: this old thing is a ghost that has waited a very long time for a body, and I’m the body.

He stabbed at the ring.

The shadow slid through the blade as if through smoke and entered his forehead. Cold flooded his skull. His hand missed the table edge, and his knee struck the floor hard enough to crack the paving tile.

“Stop struggling, brat!” Mo Tianheng’s voice roared inside his head. “Empty your mind and hand this master your body.”

“Get out,” Shi Feng gritted out, spitting blood from a bitten tongue.

He didn’t dare shout for help. Ling Qingzhu was asleep across the courtyard, and her sword couldn’t cut a spirit.

He couldn’t fight this enemy. There was no throat to seize, no arm to break, no weapon to snap. All his strength, which could crush men a full realm above him, found nothing to grip. Shi Feng felt real fear for the first time in months, and he despised it.

Mo Tianheng pushed deeper. Pictures tumbled through Shi Feng’s sight: a furnace larger than a house, a white flame held still between two fingers, a robe stitched with the Sky Pavilion emblem, rows of herbs with names he didn’t know. Then a greedy examination swept through his meridians.

“What a body,” Mo Tianheng whispered. “After all these years... what a body.”

Shi Feng’s fingers found the table, and the wood cracked under them. The spirit passed through one meridian, then another, and its delight grew sharper as the network went on past every number it expected.

“Three hundred and sixty,” Mo Tianheng said, and his voice shook. “That’s the limit of heaven and earth. How can it be?”

The first Epoch Meridian answered his probing. Then the second. Then the third, the fourth and the last.

“Five?” Mo Tianheng cried. “Impossible! Even in my age, no one reached this. Three hundred and sixty-five. This is the body of the age.”

The old man’s face froze in shock for an instant. Greed swallowed it.

“Mine!” Mo Tianheng roared. “This body is mine.”

The spirit gave up its careful pressure and hurled itself at the living centre of Shi Feng’s being. Shi Feng thought: I didn’t survive eighteen months as a cripple and fight my way out of Heilu Marsh only to become a coat for some dead stranger.

“Never,” Shi Feng said through his teeth.

Beneath his breastbone, the ancient hunger opened.

Mo Tianheng stopped moving.

“What’s this?” Mo Tianheng stammered. His voice dropped from triumph to terror. “This hunger... All-Devouring... Impossible.”

The cold recoiled, and then it began to slide downward. It wasn’t heading for the ring or any road of escape. Something inside the body he came to steal was pulling him in.

“No!” Mo Tianheng screamed. “Let go of me!”

The scream carried no air, but Shi Feng felt it tear through the invading will. The old spirit lashed out and scattered the pictures in his sight. The great furnace split. The white flame turned into a thousand pale threads, and the old man’s will tried to hide inside the knowledge it carried.

The hunger found it anyway.

“Wait! Wait!” Mo Tianheng begged. “Little friend! Young master... This master... no, this old man can teach you! Spare me, and I’ll make you the greatest alchemist in the kingdom!”

Shi Feng braced himself against the table. His expression was grim, and his arms were trembling.

“You should have asked before you came in,” Shi Feng said, hoarse but flat.

The spirit strained toward his forehead. The pull dragged it back so hard that the cold shrank to a single narrow point.

Then the point broke.

Mo Tianheng’s last cry ended without an echo.

Shi Feng lay on the floor and breathed through his teeth. His knife rested beside the cracked tile. The black ring sat on the table exactly where he left it.

No face rose from it. No old master remained to bargain for better terms.

It was over. A body thief had waited who knew how many years, and the body he chose had eaten him.

Then the gift arrived.

Names settled onto the strange herbs in his memory. Scents joined their properties. He knew why the white flame had narrowed at that moment, why one extraction needed stillness and another a sudden surge, why a brilliant colour could mean only an expensive failure.

It was more than recipes. A pair of hands that weren’t his own did these things ten thousand times. He remembered their judgement and their corrections, and the exact resistance of a mixture just before it changed. The memory of that whole lifetime lay open in his mind.

Mo Tianheng was a formidable man, Shi Feng thought. And he chose to be a body thief.

Both facts could sit in one mind. The Sky Pavilion emblem in those memories didn’t make every Sky Pavilion merchant a villain. This crime belonged to the man who committed it.

Shi Feng slowly stood up.

He checked his cultivation first. It didn’t leap to Profound Heaven. The golden traces in his bones were still unfinished, and his qi was still the qi of Bone Refinement, however remarkable the body that carried it.

He looked at the little clay furnace by the wall, and he knew its limits at once. He also saw the errors in his wound wash, including one small loss of useful substance that Xu Changhe’s notes never mentioned.

“So that’s how it is,” Shi Feng murmured.

He remembered techniques his body couldn’t possibly perform. He lifted a hand and traced one simple control movement. His fingers followed the shape. His qi didn’t follow the remembered response.

He lowered the hand and sighed. The knowledge and the experience survived the spirit’s death. The master’s realm and the master’s body didn’t become his.

He opened the kitchen door and looked across the courtyard. The window of the main room stayed dark. Ling Qingzhu hadn’t woken once. Beyond the wall the night watch struck its wooden clapper.

Shi Feng picked up the knife, checked the sealed ring and righted the chair. He was shaken, but he was also whole.

A lifetime of alchemy stood before him.

Now he only needed to find out what his own hands could do with it.

chapters.title: Knowing Is Not Doing
chapters.html:
Shi Feng slipped off his floor bedding before dawn, careful not to wake Ling Qingzhu, and lit the furnace in the kitchen.

He chose a simple strengthening pill from the knowledge that now belonged to him. The ingredients were common and the heat was modest. Mo Tianheng once refined it with one hand while watching three harder preparations with the other.

Shi Feng felt confident. I know the order, he thought. This will be simple! I know the changes, and I know the exact moment the medicine begins to bind. I can even remember how it feels under an old master’s fingers, as clearly as the grip of my own sword.

He laid out the ingredients and began.

The first extraction separated cleanly. The second needed less heat, and he lowered the fire before the smell turned sharp. Then he sent a thin thread of qi into the joined liquid and tried to hold its surface in the remembered pattern.

The thread surged.

The mixture leaped against the wall of the vessel. Shi Feng caught the heat, shifted his angle, and lost the pattern completely.

Crack!

Something split inside the furnace.

“Young man!” a cracked voice shouted over the wall. It was Granny Qin, who sold sesame cakes opposite the gate and never missed a noise in her life. “Aiyo, what was that? Is something on fire? Do I need to bring water?”

“Nothing is on fire, Granny!” Shi Feng called back.

“It sounded like a bone breaking!” Granny Qin cried. “Are you hurt? You’re too thin, you know. Come over later and I’ll give you a hot sesame cake!”

“It was only a pill, Granny,” Shi Feng said.

“A pill that breaks? Aiyo, what kind of pill does that?” Granny Qin called.

“A bad one,” Shi Feng said under his breath, and removed the lid.

Three ugly lumps clung to a skin of scorched residue. None of them deserved to be called a pill. Shi Feng was stunned. A pill this simple!

He stared at them for a while. In Mo Tianheng’s memory, this movement was as natural as lifting a cup. Shi Feng copied the direction, but he used far too much force at one point and too little steady pressure at another. He knew exactly what went wrong.

And knowing didn’t stop it. Shi Feng thought bitterly: a perfect map, and my own feet still walk off the road! How can this be so hard?

He cleaned the vessel and halved the next portion of ingredients. This time he drew his qi more slowly. The first breaths held. When the two extracts joined, his current thinned just where the remembered technique expected it to stay even.

He tried to compensate, but it was too late. The medicine broke into beads instead of gathering. One stuck to the lid and two collapsed into a greasy smear.

Shi Feng set the lid on the table very carefully. His expression was blank, but his heart was close to wailing. He could break Foundation Establishment cultivators with his bare hands, and the furnace didn’t care in the least.

Combat strength wasn’t refining control. His meridians gave him a frightening capacity, and his bones could carry force that no one at his realm could imagine. None of it turned his qi into the qi of a Profound Heaven master.

Some remembered techniques were wholly beyond him. Others could be simplified, but they still demanded a precision and steadiness that his present body must supply by itself.

Bone Refinement was a bottleneck, he thought. It was no use arguing that Mo Tianheng found the task easy. The hands at the furnace were Shi Feng’s, not Mo Tianheng’s!

Shi Feng took a blank sheet and drew columns. Portion of ingredients. Changes of heat. Length of steady control. Point of failure. Then he wrote down both attempts.

Mo Tianheng’s expertise let him recognize each mistake. Now Shi Feng needed to make his own hands stop repeating them. He scraped the failed medicine away and prepared the smallest portion his furnace could hold.

The third attempt used only a sliver of the usual portion, and he practised one stage alone. He held the extraction steady, released it before his control thinned, and repeated the motion with another small pinch.

Six breaths. Then seven.

“Seven!” Shi Feng muttered. “Real progress at last.”

It was also a real bill for ingredients.

By the time grey light touched the kitchen window, a tray held misshapen beads, scorched flakes and two failed mixtures that still smelled strongly of medicine. Shi Feng sorted them.

Shi Feng scraped the scorched residue into a bowl. The herbs’ qi was still there, even though the binding had failed.

The failed lumps held only the ingredients’ original strength. A sound pill would have multiplied it. Anyone else would be poisoned by this mess, but his physique could devour it safely.

Shi Feng swallowed one.

The All-Devouring Physique drew out what was left. Warmth flowed into the golden traces in his skeleton, and nothing dulled the benefit. No hidden poison or impure burden followed it. He ate the rest of the failures, residue and all, rinsed the vessel with warm water and drank that as well.

It wasn’t a successful refinement, but it wasn’t a total loss either. He wrote that distinction beneath the costs.

Practice still burned fuel, time and ingredients. Taking back some benefit from the waste softened the expense, but it couldn’t turn bad technique into good pills or give him anything he could honestly sell.

When Ling Qingzhu came out of the room into the courtyard, he’d already washed the vessels and hidden the failed residue. An ordinary ointment was warming over the small fire. She looked at the little tray of jars.

“You were up early,” Ling Qingzhu said. “I heard you sneaking. Tiptoeing isn’t your talent.”

“I tried to be quiet,” Shi Feng said.

Ling Qingzhu bit back a smile. “Granny Qin says you broke a bone. Want a bucket?”

“It was a pill,” Shi Feng said.

“And? Did it work?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“No,” Shi Feng said.

She made a small sound that might have been a laugh. He lifted the pot from the fire before he looked up.

“This one will,” Shi Feng said.

An ordinary ointment needed plain extraction, careful mixing and clean hands. It didn’t need the steady qi that ruined his pills, and Mo Tianheng’s knowledge cut the wasteful steps. Even with his cheap furnace, the result would be better than anything on the medicine street.

Shi Feng thought: the old master would have laughed at an ointment. Let him laugh, since he’s gone and the jars are mine.

Shi Feng finished the preparation, let it cool and filled the jars. Ling Qingzhu picked up a lid and read the label in his handwriting.

“Cracked skin?” Ling Qingzhu asked. “That’s it? The great alchemist’s debut is hand cream?”

“For cracked skin,” Shi Feng said.

“Nothing for meridians?” Ling Qingzhu asked, and her expression turned careful.

“None promised,” Shi Feng said.

Her face softened at his bluntness. She looked at the cheap furnace and the row of jars.

“Good. Don’t promise anybody immortality before breakfast,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Immortality requires a larger deposit,” Shi Feng said.

“Then Granny Qin keeps the bucket,” Ling Qingzhu said. She was laughing before she reached the gate. Shi Feng tightened the last lid. The salves and washes were worth selling, he decided. The pills weren’t, and would stay private practice until he could make them properly.

He wrapped the sealed ring and put it back in the box in his corner of the room. Its storage still waited for Foundation Establishment. The alchemy inheritance had come from devouring Mo Tianheng’s remnant spirit, while the ring’s inner storage space remained locked behind its Foundation Establishment seal.

On the table lay his new practice record. Beneath the morning’s failures, Shi Feng added a final line.

Smaller portions. Longer steady control. Don’t pay twice for the same mistake.

He counted the remaining herbs in his basket. At this burn rate, his savings would last four more mornings before the furnace went cold—unless the twelve jars of ointment on his tray started paying for his practice tomorrow at the silk-lane market.

chapters.title: The Medicine Peddler
chapters.html:
Shi Feng’s first customer wanted proof, a discount and credit.

Tao Laifu stood before the little board that served as a counter, turning an ointment jar in hands cracked white by lime. He inspected the lid, the bottom and the line of quantity on the side. Now he seemed to be searching for a fourth direction from which the price might improve.

“Two spirit stones?” Tao Laifu said softly. “That’s... a lot, young master.”

Shi Feng pointed to the marked line.

“For that much,” Shi Feng said calmly.

“The... the stall across the lane has a bigger jar,” Tao Laifu mumbled.

“Then compare what’s inside,” Shi Feng said.

Tao Laifu looked across the lane. The rival jar was certainly bigger. So was the amount of water sloshing under its badly fitted lid.

“Come over here, brother!” Hu Kang, the fat seller at that stall, shouted. “Bigger jar, lower price!”

Tao Laifu shuffled his feet. Then he put Shi Feng’s jar down, went red, and held out his hands.

“Will it mend these?” Tao Laifu asked.

Shi Feng studied the deep cracks without drawing qi or putting on any airs as a healer. Lime dust lay in the creases. One split was torn open again and again by lifting rough sacks.

“It’ll help the cracks close,” Shi Feng said. “Wash off the lime first and use a thin layer. Cover the worst split while you work, or the medicine will spend all its strength fighting the sack.”

“Will one jar last the season?” Tao Laifu asked.

“Not if you put it on your whole family,” Shi Feng said.

Tao Laifu nodded and looked at his hands. He seemed to have hoped for more.

A passer-by paused behind him and leaned over the jars. Shi Feng told him plainly that the other pot was a common wound wash. It couldn’t cure ruined meridians, it couldn’t grow back a limb, and no secret blessing came with it just because the buyer looked rich.

The passer-by laughed at such foolish honesty and walked on.

Tao Laifu watched the man go and leaned closer.

“Business is slow, young master,” Tao Laifu whispered. “Maybe... a little cheaper?”

“The first sale buys the next ingredients,” Shi Feng said.

They went back and forth until the market bell rang. In that time Shi Feng could have mixed another small batch. He thought of charging for the conversation, then decided the world already held enough men like Ma Zheng.

At last Tao Laifu counted out the stones with careful fingers. Then, very shyly, he asked for a spoon.

Shi Feng handed him a clean wooden sliver for spreading the ointment. Tao Laifu’s eyes slid to the full spoon lying beside the open sample jar.

“That one is better,” Tao Laifu said quietly.

“That one belongs to the stall,” Shi Feng said.

Tao Laifu bowed twice and left with his jar and his instructions.

“One jar since dawn!” Hu Kang crowed across the lane. “You’ll be selling your board for firewood by the new moon!”

“One jar, honestly sold,” Shi Feng said without raising his voice. “How many of yours came back to be returned?”

Hu Kang’s face went purple and his mouth shut with a snap. Shi Feng thought coolly: a man who waters his ointment fears only one thing, and that’s a customer who can read a line on a jar.

Across the lane, beneath a silk-shop awning, Ling Qingzhu lowered her eyes. Her veil hid her smile.

She didn’t come to watch him. She came to choose cloth for a new lining, and instead she found her husband seriously explaining cracked hands like a physician of thirty years. Ling Qingzhu was startled. She didn’t know he could speak so smoothly to strangers! Yesterday the dead swordsman’s notes were a pile of paper. Today they were a profession.

And the argument over the spoon! Her husband finally met a customer meaner than himself!

Ling Qingzhu’s heart gave a small, unwilling jump at the sight of him patiently wrapping the jar, and she was annoyed with herself. Her expression stayed perfectly composed. She bought her cloth and left before he could look up.

Shi Feng wrote down the sale. Two stones received. Ingredients, vessel, fuel and stall fee came off, and the margin that remained was small but real.

I made something useful, he thought, and a stranger paid for it without being lied to. This was a different kind of victory from a fight, and a cleaner one. That pleased him more than the stranger’s haggling annoyed him.

By late afternoon the other jars were still unsold. He wrapped each one, checked the lids and carried the board home under his arm. Ling Qingzhu sat beneath the pear tree, sewing with a concentration that suggested the needle personally offended her.

“So? How many did the great physician sell?” Ling Qingzhu asked, without looking up.

“One sale,” Shi Feng said.

“One,” Ling Qingzhu said, pulling her thread tight. “One whole jar. Should I light incense?”

Shi Feng put the jars in the shade and gave her a long look.

“Were you buying cloth, or counting my customers?” Shi Feng asked.

“I was choosing cloth,” Ling Qingzhu said, much too fast. “The silk shop is on that street. Streets are public.” She bent over her sewing, and her ears turned red.

Shi Feng went to cook supper. He didn’t mind her amusement. It only meant she was watching, and that was something. One real customer was worth more than a hundred imaginary admirers, he decided, even when one admirer was a beautiful wife who found his little board entertaining.

That night, once Ling Qingzhu’s breathing on the bed slowed into sleep, he slipped into the kitchen. He practised a short extraction beside his furnace, with Granny Qin’s brazier smoke drifting through the window. It failed when his qi thinned at the joining stage. He noted the point, swallowed the residue and washed the vessel.

The street business must pay for practice before practice could pay for a pill business. He wouldn’t mix up the two stages just because the knowledge in his head went so far beyond them.

Three mornings later, Tao Laifu came back.

Shi Feng saw him coming and reached beneath the board for the same ointment. The man held out both hands before he said a word.

The deep cracks were closing.

“Two jars,” Tao Laifu said, and bowed.

Shi Feng looked at the hands again. The cloth over the worst split was clean and freshly changed. He had followed the advice exactly.

“The same preparation?” Shi Feng asked.

Tao Laifu lowered his voice. “One is for my wife’s elbows,” Tao Laifu said.

“Cracked from work?” Shi Feng asked.

“Mostly,” Tao Laifu said.

Shi Feng explained the smaller amount she should use and wrote it on the second lid. Tao Laifu paid at once. His expression was almost respectful.

“Young master,” Tao Laifu added, almost shyly, “the men at the lime yard are asking where I got my hands back.”

“Tell them the board is by the silk shop,” Shi Feng said.

Tao Laifu nodded. Then, very shyly, he asked whether two jars earned him the spoon.

They didn’t.

From the silk-shop awning, Ling Qingzhu watched the familiar customer leave with both jars. A returning buyer was more convincing than a first one.

She wondered what it would cost to hire one.

The next buyer asked for medicine for an old limp. Shi Feng examined the description, then shook his head. The salve could help cracked skin; it could not repair a badly healed bone.

He directed the man to a physician and watched a possible sale walk away. Tao Laifu, waiting beside the awning, nodded to himself. When he returned to the lime yard, he repeated that refusal along with the story of his closing wounds.

Shi Feng learned about it when two more labourers came looking for the same small jars—while across the lane, a clerk wearing the green lapel of Zhou’s Medicine House stood beneath the tea awning, quietly copying down every price on Shi Feng’s board.

chapters.title: The Sign That Promised Heaven
chapters.html:
“Master Shi, it’s finished!” Wu Tong called, carrying the sign into the lane with both hands.

Shi Feng read it once.

HEAVEN-DEFYING MEDICINES. TEN THOUSAND AILMENTS DISPERSED. GOLDEN CORE NOT BEYOND REACH.

“I ordered my name and the word medicines,” Shi Feng said flatly.

The sign painter tapped the largest characters. “I added a border!” Wu Tong said.

He drew the last stroke again in the air with his finger. He was still pleased with it.

“I used my best brush,” Wu Tong said. “My teacher couldn’t have made that character larger.”

“The character isn’t the problem,” Shi Feng replied.

Wu Tong looked offended anyway. He turned the board toward the light, admiring the ink while the owner read the ridiculous promises beneath it.

Wu Tong’s expression fell.

“They need ointment,” Shi Feng said. “Remove the rest. You wrote what I’d be arrested for.”

A woman stopped at the words Golden Core and gasped. She looked at Shi Feng’s ordinary grey robe, looked at the four jars on his board, and walked away much faster than she’d come.

“Golden Core?! From a stall with four jars?”

“The magistrate’s runners flog men for lies this big!”

“…”

Shi Feng sighed in his heart, his face dark. The sign hadn’t even been up for a few breaths, and it had already frightened away one customer. At this rate it would bring the inspectors before it brought the buyers.

“Then every other seller may pay you for the truth,” Shi Feng said, pointing at the road. “Go.”

Wu Tong left with the board. He returned by noon with a modest one.

“A small dragon?” Wu Tong begged.

“No,” Shi Feng said, and handed over the agreed coins.

Across the lane, Ling Qingzhu had watched the whole performance from the doorway of the silk shop. She’d seen the first sign, too. It was large enough to offend Heaven from two streets away.

When she passed the stall again, the plain board hung under the awning.

“Oh, so you do have some sense,” Ling Qingzhu said. “I was worried. That first sign was visible from the capital.”

“Honest claims are easier to fulfil,” Shi Feng said, folding a clean cloth over the finished jars.

She read the board. His name, the word medicines, and below them the prices and uses, in characters big enough for a customer to read without leaning over the ointment. There wasn’t anything in it to laugh at. Ling Qingzhu felt strangely disappointed.

“Shame about the gold border,” Ling Qingzhu said. “I was getting attached. Why not keep it?”

“It cost more than the medicine in two jars,” Shi Feng said.

“...Miser!” Ling Qingzhu said. She looked away, but her lips curved. Shi Feng saw it and turned back to his work.

Not every wrong judgment is worth an afternoon of argument, he thought. Let her enjoy this one.

A father and son came to the stall before she could leave. The boy held one hand against his chest, and a strip of dirty cloth was wound around his forefinger. He kept lifting the corner to peek underneath.

“Show me the finger,” Shi Feng said.

The father, Cheng Shou, unwound the cloth. A shallow cut ran across the first joint, and its edges were red with grit.

“He keeps checking whether it has closed!” Cheng Shou said.

“You’ll know sooner if you stop reopening it,” Shi Feng said.

He showed the father how to wash out the grit and how little salve was needed. The cut didn’t need a grand name. It needed clean hands and an owner who left it alone. Cheng Shou paid, then asked whether a bigger jar would be better.

“Only if someone else cuts a finger,” Shi Feng said.

Cheng Shou bought the small jar.

Ling Qingzhu had stayed beside the stall, and she saw Shi Feng rinse the little spoon and put the used cloth into a separate basin. He didn’t return either to the clean supplies. That care was a cultivator’s habit, she thought. Strange, in a man who’s supposed to be ruined. The thought annoyed her less than she expected.

Cheng An came running back.

“Will it make me grow taller?” Cheng An asked.

“Not unless you stand on the jar,” Shi Feng said.

The boy considered this with great seriousness.

Ling Qingzhu laughed before she could hide it. Her expression changed at once, startled at herself, and she coughed into her sleeve. Shi Feng looked up at the sound, and for a moment the lane between them seemed much narrower than it was.

Then Cheng An set the jar on the ground and lifted one foot.

“Cheng An,” Cheng Shou called, catching his collar just before the experiment began.

Ling Qingzhu was still smiling when she walked on toward the cloth shops. Shi Feng found himself watching the turn of her head long after she passed the awning.

His own heart gave a small jump. He ignored it and put the lid on the sample jar.

The plain sign sold no miraculous number of jars that afternoon. It did save him from repeating the same prices until his mouth went dry. Three buyers read it, asked sensible questions, and left with exactly what they paid for.

A fourth demanded the advertised ointment at the advertised price in a jar twice the advertised size.

“The board says one measure for two stones,” Shi Feng said.

The man demanded a larger portion in the same indignant voice.

“Read it again,” Shi Feng said. The man was plainly able to read. That was the whole difficulty.

At home he hung the board in the dry corner of the kitchen and checked his ingredients. Ordinary medicine paid a little each day, but the finer work swallowed that profit before it could become savings.

Before supper, Ling Qingzhu noticed a splash of dried ointment on his cuff and brushed at it with her thumb. He looked down, unexpectedly pleased by the care. She noticed his expression and immediately became stern again.

“Wash it before it sets,” Ling Qingzhu said. “I refuse to be seen with a walking medicine shelf.”

Later that night, while Shi Feng logged another small binding practice in the kitchen and saw the sign board she had quietly straightened under the eaves, a neat man in a grey robe—the last customer who had bought a single jar before the market closed and asked three careful questions about its maker—passed through the side postern of the Eastern Palace.

In the study, Sima Yu turned the plain ointment jar between two fingers, then looked down at the copied ward-office slip the grey-robed searcher had laid beside it.

“So her ‘crippled’ husband mixes workman’s salve by day,” Sima Yu murmured, his eyes resting on the second document—the formal notice Third Master Ling Zhen had filed with the Southern Ward office barring private surrender on a Yunze Wei clan murder inquiry. “And the Wei family of Yunze says he killed a Foundation Establishment elder at a quarry before entering the capital. Send word to our friend in the Southern Ward: keep that Wei file warm. A marriage registry won’t shield him forever.”

chapters.title: The Neighbouring Medicine House
chapters.html:
“One more jar,” Zhou Mingde’s assistant Peng Jian said. “And how many can your master prepare in a month?”

It was the third day, and it was the same assistant. Shi Feng answered the question about quantity and charged for the jar. The questions about his suppliers and his recipe stayed unanswered.

“The ointment has no other name,” Shi Feng said. “Tell your master to buy it again if he wants to know more.”

The assistant bowed and hurried off. An hour later, the master came himself.

Zhou Mingde was a Bone Refinement cultivator. His medicine house filled three rooms on the next street, and its gilded sign promised everything Wu Tong was forced to scrape off Shi Feng’s. Yet customers now walked past his counter to buy from a cripple under an awning. He had come to end that.

“Hmph! So you’re the peddler,” Zhou Mingde said, his round face already red. “Do you know who runs this street?”

“Say what you came to say,” Shi Feng replied, closing the ointment jar.

Zhou Mingde laid two spirit stones on the board. He didn’t take a jar.

The customer beside them stared very hard at an instruction sheet. He didn’t intend to leave and no intention of looking curious.

“Supply is unreliable in this district!” Zhou Mingde said. “My house arranges ingredients for approved sellers. Sign under me, and no one touches you.”

“At what price?” Shi Feng asked.

Zhou Mingde named it. Shi Feng did the sum in his head. The price would swallow nearly all his profit, and the arrangement also demanded his recipes, the Zhou name printed on every jar, and every large customer sent to the Zhou counter.

Shi Feng thought coldly: this isn’t an offer. This is a leash with a sweet smell.

“What remains mine?” Shi Feng asked.

“Your labour is well paid!” Zhou Mingde barked.

“I already own that,” Shi Feng said.

The customer turned his instruction sheet over. Nothing was written on the back, but his interest in reading it hadn’t faded.

“He refused Zhou Mingde!” someone whispered.

“…”

Zhou Mingde was stunned for a breath, and his expression turned ugly as his face went from red to purple. “You dare? A new stall needs protection! Suppliers know which businesses last!”

“I’ve suppliers,” Shi Feng said.

“Suppliers change their minds!” Zhou Mingde roared. “Think it over, boy! You’ll regret it!”

He left the stones where they lay and stormed off, his threats still ringing down the street.

Shi Feng set one jar beside the stones. The assistant could collect it later. Paying for a conversation didn’t buy the man who answered.

By afternoon, two herb stalls claimed they had sold out. At the first, a delivery boy was carrying the supposedly exhausted stock through the back door. At the second, the owner covered a basket with his sleeve and described how impossible herbs were to find in the entire capital.

“Does a sleeve count as a shortage now?” Shi Feng asked.

The owner muttered about waiting customers and walked away.

At the third counter, delivery suddenly carried a special handling charge. It cost more than walking the same road with the herbs on his own back.

“A handling charge,” Shi Feng repeated. “For carrying a basket three steps.”

The clerk admitted that Zhou Mingde had told every counter to refuse him, then insisted that the handling charge stood.

“Then Zhou Mingde has told me where to shop,” Shi Feng said.

He left without buying. Scoundrels! He could have overturned every counter on the street. But he wanted herbs, and beating these men wouldn’t make their stock any better.

“Fine,” Shi Feng said quietly. “Then I’ll go where your master’s hand can’t reach.”

The longer road passed the grain warehouses, crossed a ditch on two narrow planks, and ended at stalls that served working people, who cared nothing for a medicine house’s dignity. He found one ingredient fresh, one dried, and a third that needed more work before it could be used.

Mo Tianheng’s knowledge supplied a substitute without a flicker of doubt. His purse supplied the irritation.

The cheaper herbs needed more careful washing and a slower extraction. That was within his ordinary heat. The great formula that would have wrung full value from them was still beyond his control.

He chose what his hands could actually use. The seller weighed the herbs and took the stones without a word.

Shi Feng carried his two parcels away, hungry and tired. This is a shorter road to the same place, he thought. Zhou Mingde has only shown me where his reach ends.

He got home late. Ling Qingzhu was standing under the pear tree with a cup in both hands.

“Rivals already?” Ling Qingzhu asked. “Granny Qin says an herb seller spat at you. She was very proud.”

“Every trade has people who prefer collecting to working,” Shi Feng said, sorting the herbs into lots.

Ling Qingzhu leaned against the pear tree and watched him. “Do you ever pick the quiet road? Just once? For my nerves?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“He may compete if he likes,” Shi Feng said. “I won’t disappear because he dislikes it.”

Her fingers tightened around her cup. The answer carried a force she associated with the man he once was, not with the harmless husband she hired. There was no bitterness in it. He simply refused to arrange his future around another man’s comfort.

This isn’t a cripple’s voice, Ling Qingzhu thought. She asked nothing more about abandoning the stall.

At the basin a stubborn root left a stain on his fingers. Shi Feng washed twice and reached for the sand soap.

Ling Qingzhu lifted the water ladle without being asked. “This business makes more washing than profit,” Ling Qingzhu said. She glanced at his face. He was tired and annoyed, but tomorrow still seemed worth trying to him. She poured the rest of the water in silence.

After supper he prepared the new extraction and compared it against a sample from the earlier lot. The scent was right. The thickness needed more time. He recorded the difference and sealed the jars.

The work would reach the stall tomorrow, but the larger margin he hoped for wouldn’t. He added the extra journey to his accounts anyway. If Zhou Mingde wanted to teach him dependence, his first lesson taught only the limit of the man’s influence.

Across the district, Zhou Mingde broke the seal on the second jar.

“The peddler came back with fresh stock, master,” Peng Jian reported. “Same price.”

Zhou Mingde rubbed a little ointment between his fingers. It spread cleanly. Nothing in it was thinned to make up for cheap herbs.

Zhou Mingde’s face darkened.

A bad medicine could be exposed. A foolish rival could be frightened. But this medicine was better than his own, and its maker had refused to take instruction.

“Impossible!” Zhou Mingde snarled, slamming the jar down. “A crippled nobody, better than my house?”

He wiped his hand on a cloth. Then he sent for a man who understood the less respectable kinds of complaint.

The next morning the assistant came back for the jar his master had paid for. Shi Feng handed it over without a sermon. The assistant checked the seal twice, as though Zhou Mingde might blame him for its quality.

“It is the same preparation,” Shi Feng said. “Keep the lid dry.”

The assistant nodded and left. Shi Feng watched him cross the road, then opened the stall. A rival's bad temper didn't excuse leaving his own customers waiting. He put the clean spoon beside the new jar and began work. Two labourers arrived together. Neither knew about the threats, and both needed medicine before their shift began.

chapters.title: The Customer with the Wrong Wound
chapters.html:
“Poison!” Liu Bao bellowed, thrusting a red, swollen forearm over the board. “This peddler’s ointment is burning my flesh!”

His voice carried across the whole market. Two porters stopped beside the next counter, and a woman weighing a jar of wound wash set it down without buying. Shi Feng calmly moved the open ingredient pot out of the man’s reach.

“Show me what you bought,” Shi Feng said.

Liu Bao raised his arm higher, then winced when his own sleeve rubbed it. His eyes darted toward the crowd.

A spectator nodded too eagerly.

“The whole forearm!” Liu Bao shouted, remembering his complaint. “Burning!”

Shi Feng moved the open jar behind him. The man wanted an audience angry enough to pay him before anyone examined the wound.

Liu Bao slammed a jar onto the board. Someone had forced its lid back after breaking the seal, and the paper still carried Shi Feng’s plain instructions.

“Pay for my treatment,” Liu Bao shouted. “Or I’ll carry this arm down every lane in the district!”

“A cripple selling poison!” a man in the crowd cried.

“Is that the peddler from the awning?”

“…”

Shi Feng opened the jar. A sharp green smell rose beneath the ointment’s usual scent, and he knew it at once. Mo Tianheng’s memory named the root, how it was prepared, and several uses that had nothing to do with cracked skin.

The swollen arm told him the rest. The red strip had straight, neat edges. Someone had painted an irritant across healthy flesh with a brush. Beyond the strip the skin was calm. A little dry powder still clung where Liu Bao’s sleeve brushed the lower edge.

This man didn’t use my ointment, Shi Feng thought. Someone used a blistering root on him and sent him here.

“Who applied the blistering root?” Shi Feng asked.

Liu Bao’s shout faltered.

Then he grew louder.

“Lies! Lies! He’s poisoning honest people,” Liu Bao yelled.

More people gathered. One man asked loudly whether ruined cultivators should be allowed to sell medicine at all. He never looked at the wound or the jar, but lack of evidence never stopped anyone from having an opinion.

Shi Feng took a clean spoon and spread a little of the mixture on a white cloth. The adulterated ointment left a yellow-green stain at its edge. Next he opened a sealed jar from his own stock and placed the same amount beside it. That patch stayed pale.

“Blistering root stains wet cloth,” Shi Feng said. “My preparation doesn’t. Anyone here who has bought it to clear old hide can smell the difference.”

One of the porters bent over the cloth and sniffed.

“That’s the green stuff the tanners use.”

“Then the jar was changed!”

“…”

The woman with the wound wash came back to examine both patches. Liu Bao snatched at the board.

“You swapped my sample,” Liu Bao screamed.

Shi Feng covered the suspect jar with its lid before the man could knock it over.

“Then let the Sky Pavilion tower test it,” Shi Feng said. “If it matches my stock, I pay for your treatment. If it doesn’t, you explain who changed it.”

The tower stood several streets away. Its test would cost a few stones and produce a finding far harder to shout down than a medicine peddler.

Liu Bao looked toward the tower and went pale. The road ahead of him seemed full of teeth.

“I’ve work,” Liu Bao said.

“You had time to visit every lane,” Shi Feng said.

A few people traded glances. Nobody laughed yet, but the smell of a better scandal made them patient.

Liu Bao lunged for the jar again. Shi Feng caught his wrist and stopped the hand above the board. The grip looked ordinary. It was exactly strong enough to end the argument.

“The evidence stays here,” Shi Feng said.

“Let go, you cripple!” Liu Bao howled, and wrenched his arm back. His sleeve slipped, and a folded slip of paper fell beside the stained cloth.

Shi Feng saw the mark before the man’s free hand could cover it.

Zhou’s Medicine House.

The porter nearest the board saw it too. He leaned in, and Liu Bao must choose between hiding the paper and saving what remained of his dignity. The crowd was stunned into silence for a breath.

“Zhou’s Medicine House?”

The question passed from one spectator to the next.

“The big one on the next street?”

“The one that offered to protect him?”

“…”

Shi Feng released the wrist and picked up the slip. It recorded a small payment for an errand. It didn’t announce a conspiracy, because Zhou Mingde wasn’t that stupid. But set beside the altered jar, it made the accusation very hard to repeat.

“An innocent delivery,” Liu Bao said quickly. His voice cracked. “I run errands for everyone.”

“Then the tower can say so,” Shi Feng said.

The crowd erupted across the lane.

“Zhou’s Medicine House paid him to paint blistering root on his own arm!”

“A grand shop on the main street hiring a runner to smear a two-stone stall—how shameless can Shopkeeper Zhou get?!”

“No wonder he wouldn’t go to Sky Pavilion—the peddler caught him with one spoon and a piece of cloth!”

Liu Bao’s face turned the colour of wet ash. As he bolted down the street without his jar, two market wardens blocked the corner to fine him for public fraud while shoppers pointed at his painted arm all the way to the main avenue. Back at the awning, the woman who had set down the wound wash bought two jars at once, and four buyers who had been walking toward Zhou’s Medicine House turned around and lined up in front of Shi Feng’s board instead.

Shi Feng wrapped the jar, the stained cloth, and the slip separately and wrote down the time. Then he wrote the names of those willing to testify. Most suddenly remembered urgent errands elsewhere.

Shi Feng expected nothing more.

A false complaint was fraud, he told himself. It wasn’t yet murder, however angry it made him. I’ll keep the evidence, and if Zhou Mingde needs another lesson, he’ll have it.

By evening every jar was sold. A crowd was no honest way to run a business, but today it bought what plain honesty would take a month to earn.

At home, Ling Qingzhu had already heard three versions of the story.

In the first, the cheat had fallen to his knees and begged. In the second, Shi Feng named the root from across the street. The third version came from a vegetable seller who swore he could now diagnose any poison with a wooden spoon.

“A spoon?” Ling Qingzhu asked. “The vegetable man swears you caught a poisoner. With a spoon. Tell me he’s lying. I bought his cabbage.”

“It was a small crowd,” Shi Feng said.

She let out a short breath that was almost a laugh. She helped him clear a space while he put the evidence away in the box in his corner of the room. Her eyes stayed on the two stains, now dried into separate patches on the cloth.

“They tried to ruin you,” Ling Qingzhu said. “On purpose. Over a few jars of ointment.”

“Yes,” Shi Feng said.

He didn’t sound surprised. That troubled her more than any complaint would have done.

When he left to prepare supper, she stayed beside the table and looked at the little jar. She thought his stall amusing. Someone else thought it dangerous enough to pay for a lie.

It was getting harder to call both judgments equally sensible.

He kept the altered sample apart from his clean stock. Tomorrow he would ask the tower what it cost to record its contents properly. An argument in a market faded quickly; a sealed finding could wait for the day it mattered.

chapters.title: Master Shen
chapters.html:
“Your hood’s caught,” Gao Yuan said around a yawn.

Shi Feng stopped. The cloth had hooked on a bent nail in the gate. He eased it free without exposing his face.

Gao Yuan watched from his stool. He wore one boot and held the other beneath his arm. A tenant behind him was shouting about a cold furnace.

“Lower vent!” Gao Yuan shouted back. “You shut the lower vent!”

The shouting stopped. Gao Yuan pushed a rental sheet across the table and finally put his boot on. Shi Feng read the room and fuel rates, paid the deposit, and waited for the key.

The yard stood behind a metalworking lane, and the whole place rang with hammers. Shi Feng had come in a plain hood and a face cloth, after changing the outer robe he wore at the medicine stall. The precautions were simple.

He knew no art of concealment and saw no reason to invent one. He only wanted the man at the stall and the man at the furnace to remain two separate people. No one in the capital—not Ling Qingzhu at home, not Gao Yuan at the furnace yard, and not a single customer in the market—knew that the medicine peddler Shi Feng and the hooded refiner Master Shen were the same man.

“Name?” Gao Yuan asked.

“Shen Mo,” Shi Feng said.

The false name went onto the sheet.

“Certification mark?” Gao Yuan asked.

“None claimed,” Shi Feng said. “I’m renting a furnace, not applying for an honour.”

Gao Yuan’s expression brightened as he weighed the deposit in his palm and decided that was answer enough. He was a Qi Condensation cultivator who owned furnaces, not an alchemy master, and a paying tenant interested him far more than a debate about marks.

“Fine, Master Shen,” Gao Yuan said. “Third room on the left. The furnace is... well loved.”

Well loved was the right phrase. The furnace was far worse than the price promised! Shi Feng found a blocked channel before he even set down his ingredients, and a crust of old metal residue clung to the inner wall.

Mo Tianheng’s knowledge named both faults at once. It didn’t make scraping them off any less filthy!

“Gao Yuan,” Shi Feng called through the door. “Come and look.”

Gao Yuan shuffled over, rubbing his eyes. Shi Feng showed him the residue before touching it.

“This was here when I came,” Shi Feng said. “Sign that, or you’ll find a damage charge the day I leave.”

“Too early for this!” Gao Yuan groaned, and signed without reading it.

Shi Feng shut the door. He cleaned the channel, sealed off the stained section, and tested the heat with no medicine inside. The furnace rose unevenly. He noted how long the chamber took to answer after he moved the lower vent.

Knowing was easy. Doing was another matter!

He chose a common recovery preparation, far below the refinements Mo Tianheng once performed without a second thought. The herbs were cheap and every change was clear in his mind. But his own qi failed at the joining stage.

His first two trial runs in the larger furnace broke apart at the joining stage whenever his Bone Refinement current surged too hard for the remembered method. Raw combat force did nothing for a pill that needed gentle, steady heat, so he split the process into smaller stages and adjusted one variable at a time.

“Slower, you fool,” Shi Feng said to himself in the empty room. “Slower!”

He split the work into stages. Extraction first. Then a steady thread over plain liquid. Then the joining movement, with just enough medicine to show whether the thread held.

At the familiar failure point he stopped chasing the master’s effortless pace. He changed one thing at a time and never two.

The process improved. It didn’t give him a finished pill.

When the session ended, the tray held useful failures, spent ash, and a short record of what his hands could carry today. He ate the failures that still held medicine and left the dead ash for the waste pot. The All-Devouring Physique took in the nourishment cleanly. No resistance dulled it, and no poison made the practice a debt against his future body.

Fuel, herbs, and rent were still debts against his purse. When he opened the door, Gao Yuan appeared at once. His eyes went to the covered containers.

“A share of product is customary,” Gao Yuan said.

Shi Feng held up the signed rental sheet.

“Then you should have written the custom,” Shi Feng said.

Gao Yuan read the sheet, and his expression fell. “Ah... too much trouble to fix now,” Gao Yuan muttered.

The second visit went little better. The third produced one round pellet with an unbound centre. Shi Feng cut it open, studied it, and put both halves among his own waste.

I won’t sell a shape just because someone can be persuaded to admire it, he thought.

He also stopped before exhaustion could make the next record meaningless. Practising while his qi was thin taught a different limit than practising fresh. Mo Tianheng’s memories let him see the difference, but only his own notes could show where it began in this body. He marked the resting time beside the failures. A dead man’s endurance was no excuse to lie about his own.

Between visits, the stall paid for the work. Ointments and washes needed skills he could already carry out, and pill practice ate a part of the profits, then returned something to his cultivation even when it failed.

It was slower than finding a master’s spirit and becoming rich overnight. It was also real.

“Master Shen,” Gao Yuan called one evening, stretching. “A hammer-man asked about the famous refiner in the third room.”

“There’s no famous refiner,” Shi Feng said.

“Hm. I told him there was,” Gao Yuan said, and wandered off, too lazy to argue.

Shi Feng corrected no harmless title, but he claimed no mark and showed no face. Private clients, if any came, would hear honest terms about what he could really make.

At home that evening, Ling Qingzhu wrinkled her nose.

“Why do you smell of furnace smoke?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“Because I was near a furnace,” Shi Feng said.

“That’s the most useless answer I’ve ever heard,” Ling Qingzhu said, frowning at him.

He thought it admirably accurate.

“Then hang that robe outside,” Ling Qingzhu said, pointing at the courtyard. “We share one room, remember? I’m not sleeping in a smithy.” She turned away.

“Fine. The pear tree can have it,” Shi Feng said.

She sniffed once more and went to the kitchen, and he heard the lid of a pot rattle with more force than the pot deserved. When he came back from washing, his bowl stood covered beside the stove. She had stopped waiting for him to explain his profession until the rice went cold.

Shi Feng lifted the lid and paused. She had even kept it warm!

Then he ate, wrote down another day’s limits, and planned the next attempt.

chapters.title: Twelve Pills and Four for Himself
chapters.html:
“The last pills I bought turned to powder in the bottle,” Zhu Shan said. “I won’t pay for another batch of dust.”

“Show me the ingredients first,” Shi Feng replied.

It was the twentieth day of practice, and Gao Yuan at last brought him a client. Zhu Shan was a Bone Refinement caravan guard who worked the Shuanghe Ferry freight road—one of the western convoys that had passed through right after Shi Feng’s trip—and was now preparing for a new season out of the capital. He carried a sack of ingredients and the empty bottle that had embarrassed him in front of his caravan captain.

The talks took place in the rented room behind a locked door. Shi Feng wore his hood and face cloth. Gao Yuan charged both men a fee for the introduction, then pressed his ear to the door.

Shi Feng quietly moved the chairs farther from the wood. Zhu Shan put the bottle down too hard. Grey dust jumped from its mouth.

“A refiner should know what he can make,” Zhu Shan said impatiently.

“Common recovery pills,” Shi Feng replied. “I’ll promise a number I can finish. Nothing more.”

Zhu Shan wiped the dust off his hand. He was still angry with the previous seller, but that man wasn’t in the room.

The change in him was small, and it would have looked pitiful beside Mo Tianheng’s memories. He could now complete one modest common recovery preparation often enough to count his failures instead of just suffering them. His records mattered more than his confidence. So he named that preparation and no other.

He laid out the quantities he inspected and his terms.

“You’ll receive at least eight usable pills,” Shi Feng said. “Your materials allow six small attempts. If the final yield reaches twelve, four pills belong to me. If it falls between eight and twelve, I’ll keep only what exceeds eight.”

“Fee?” Zhu Shan asked.

“A modest cash fee for room, fuel, and labour,” Shi Feng said. “You own the promised output. Failed material is mine only because this agreement says so. If fewer than eight pills result, I’ll make up the shortfall at my own cost before I collect the final fee.”

Zhu Shan read the shortfall term twice. Then he pushed the empty bottle aside. At least he would have a clear promise to bring back to his captain.

“Poor ingredients?” Zhu Shan asked.

“They’re your ingredients,” Shi Feng said. “We’ll settle their quality before I begin.”

He opened every packet in front of the guard. One dried root had lost half its strength. A bundle of leaves carried far too much stem.

“Hmph!” Zhu Shan grunted, and pulled out the poor portions with his own hands.

Replacements arrived the next morning. Shi Feng counted again before he accepted the commission.

Across six careful firings that afternoon, Shi Feng resisted the temptation to reach for Mo Tianheng’s advanced techniques and held strictly to the slower Bone Refinement adjustments his channels could sustain. After the first batch separated, the next five runs steadied, yielding twelve sound recovery pills in total—eight for Zhu Shan’s bottle, four for Shi Feng’s own bones, and a handful of scorched residue he set aside to devour later.

Four belonged to him under the agreement. Eight belonged to Zhu Shan. The usable waste was his too, but its nourishment didn’t make it a product he could honestly put in a customer’s box.

When the guard returned, all three piles lay apart beside the contract.

Zhu Shan held a pill up to the lamp. “Hm,” Zhu Shan grunted. Then he swallowed one from his own eight and waited for the promised warmth. His shoulders loosened.

It wasn’t a miracle. It wasn’t a great medicine in disguise. It was a common recovery pill that did what the agreement said.

“Next month,” Zhu Shan said, wiping his mouth. “Again!”

“Bring the ingredients earlier,” Shi Feng said.

Zhu Shan glanced at the cash fee. Shi Feng turned the agreement toward him and set one finger beside the line.

Zhu Shan paid.

At the door Zhu Shan stopped. “Your face,” Zhu Shan said.

“The room will be the same,” Shi Feng said.

Zhu Shan’s expression turned sour at the face cloth. He weighed curiosity against cheap and honest pills, and left.

“Master Shen,” Gao Yuan said from behind a pillar once the footsteps faded, yawning. “Bigger room. More rent. Good for both of us.”

“No,” Shi Feng said.

“A slightly bigger room?” Gao Yuan asked, without much hope.

“The room isn’t my limit,” Shi Feng said. “My control is. One good commission hasn’t made my qi any finer.”

He didn’t intend to rent a grander place so that he could fail more impressively.

Back home that evening, Ling Qingzhu was out in the courtyard watering the pear tree. Shi Feng slipped into the kitchen and swallowed the first pill he’d kept. The medicinal force flowed into the golden traces in his bones, clear and useful. The next worked just as well, with no resistance and no hidden poison.

Shi Feng smiled in his heart. Twelve pills! Four of them mine! The business could now pay twice: stones for food and supplies, and medicine for the enormous work inside his body.

It had also cost many days of practice, repeated failures, and a yield sheet too honest to resemble Mo Tianheng’s effortless memories. Shi Feng recorded all of it.

“Shi Feng!” Ling Qingzhu called from the courtyard. “Last bean curd! Want it? Or the pear tree gets it.”

He put away the account and went to supper. She saw the unusual satisfaction on his face and decided he’d won a petty dispute over money.

“You look pleased,” Ling Qingzhu said suspiciously.

“I am,” Shi Feng said.

“Did you win an argument or lose a tooth?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“Something like that,” Shi Feng said, reaching for the bean curd—though as he ate, he remembered Gao Yuan’s parting whisper at the yard gate: a woman who supplied a dozen Bone Refinement hunters was coming tomorrow, and Zhou Mingde’s clerks had just been seen visiting the district’s herb wholesalers.

chapters.title: The Household Discount
chapters.html:
The smell of the new cream reached the courtyard before Ling Qingzhu did.

It was a heavy floral stink. It crossed the pear tree, drowned out the smell of supper, and kept going toward the gate. Granny Qin’s sesame-cake brazier stood across the lane, and the old woman’s voice carried over the wall.

“Heavens! Who’s boiling flowers in Qingliu Lane? Ai ya, my nose.”

Ling Qingzhu came through the gate holding a little porcelain jar between two fingers, as far from her body as her arm could reach. She shut the gate before untying her veil. Even that silk had caught the dreadful scent.

“The shop changed the recipe,” Ling Qingzhu said. “Smell it. No, don’t. Someone’s boiling a flower garden.”

“Is it that bad?” Shi Feng asked, looking up from his account book.

She put the jar down at the far end of the kitchen table, as far from her own seat as she could get it.

“It stinks,” Ling Qingzhu said. “And greasy. My teacup slid right out. I paid real silver!”

Shi Feng read the label without touching the cream. The jar was expensive, the seal was fancy, and six lines praised the beauty it would supposedly keep. The medicine itself got half a line.

A fool’s price for a fool’s cream, he thought. He also remembered how she rubbed the backs of her hands after cold mornings at the basin, and how she hid it whenever anyone looked.

She noticed his glance right away.

“Don’t offer to sell me ointment,” Ling Qingzhu said. “I know that look. That’s your customer look.”

“I wasn’t going to,” Shi Feng said.

“Good,” Ling Qingzhu said. She turned her face away. “I’m your wife. Wives get the household discount, and the household discount is free.”

Shi Feng’s heart gave a small, unexpected jump, and his expression went blank with surprise. She meant the public arrangement, of course. He closed the account book anyway, faster than usual.

He had faced refined artifacts without a flutter, he scolded himself. One sentence about a wife shouldn’t rattle him!

The next afternoon, after he finished the stall’s stock, he set aside a handful of plain ingredients.

Mo Tianheng’s memory held a dozen grand formulas for skin and bone, and Shi Feng sneered at every one of them in his heart. Showy recipes were useless to him. His Bone Refinement qi would fail halfway through the extraction, and a gift ruined by ambition was no gift at all. He chose the simplest one. It needed careful mixing but no pill technique.

He warmed the base on the kitchen stove and strained it twice. The first sample came out too heavy, so he changed the amounts and made a smaller batch instead of wasting the pot. The second batch went on smoothly and left no perfume behind.

Granny Qin peered over the wall, sniffing like a hound.

“Young man, that smells like honest herbs!” Granny Qin shouted. “Not like that flower-boiling from yesterday! Who’s it for? Eh? Eh?”

“A customer who doesn’t pay,” Shi Feng said.

“Ha! That’s called a wife!” Granny Qin cackled so loudly that the pear tree shook. “Feed her well, young man! Feed her well!”

Shi Feng ignored her. Old women see too much, he thought.

He filled a plain jar, wiped the rim, and left it on the shelf beside her cup. He didn’t mention it. Their one room had no place to hide a gift, and he wanted her to find it herself.

Ling Qingzhu found it after washing her hands. There was no fancy seal and no proud name claiming to come from an immortal valley.

“What’s this?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“For you,” Shi Feng said, not raising his head from the table.

She opened the lid. The lack of any smell surprised her after yesterday’s jar. She held it closer and waited for a sting under the plain scent, but there wasn’t one.

“Is it for sale?” Ling Qingzhu asked. “I don’t pay for stink.”

“There’s no bill,” Shi Feng said.

She rubbed a little on the back of her hand. It felt wonderful! Her first thought was to ask which shop sold it. Then she saw the empty jars drying beside his work table.

“You made this?” Ling Qingzhu asked. Her voice was very short. “Yourself? At the kitchen stove?”

“Yes,” Shi Feng said.

She was startled, and her fingers slowed. She remembered complaining. She didn’t remember asking him to do anything about it.

For a moment she looked at him in a way he couldn’t name. It pleased him more than any customer’s praise. Nobody was haggling, and nobody was trying to push the price down.

Then her expression turned bright and innocent, and she smiled so sweetly that it hurt.

“Even the capital’s cosmetic houses leave oil on the skin,” Ling Qingzhu said slowly, testing the smooth salve on her knuckle. “Where did a Qingshi Town sword student learn to blend a base this clean?”

“Old notes and a cheap pot,” Shi Feng said calmly.

She looked at him for a moment longer, as if realizing how little of his day fit inside the six-month contract she had written.

“Don’t leave it in the sun,” Shi Feng said calmly.

Ling Qingzhu nodded and carried the jar inside, still pleased and totally unaware of what she’d done.

She came back out with the fashionable cream and held it at arm’s length.

“Can the stink come out?” Ling Qingzhu asked. “It was expensive. Throwing it away admits I was cheated.”

Shi Feng sniffed it and shook his head. “Pulling the scent out would ruin the medicine,” Shi Feng said. “It’s a lost cause.”

“Then it’s not your fault,” Ling Qingzhu said, and for once she didn’t call him useless. “I’ll be gracious about it.”

That small trust pleased him too, against his better judgment.

“Give it here,” Shi Feng said. “I’ll wrap it so it stops stinking up the house.”

She held the paper steady while he tied the cord. Their hands met at the knot, and hers stayed there a moment after the cord was tight.

Neither of them mentioned it.

Footsteps scraped outside. Ling Qingzhu caught up her veil and tied it before Granny Qin peered over the wall again. “Young people! Holding hands in the courtyard in broad daylight!” Granny Qin shouted happily.

“Granny Qin!” Ling Qingzhu snapped, her ears turning pink. “We were tying a parcel! Go mind your customers!”

Granny Qin cackled and ducked back behind the wall while Ling Qingzhu picked up her wooden practice sword by the pear tree and demanded ten minutes of footwork drills just to stop thinking about the parcel.

That evening a drop of cooking water splashed her hand and slid off more easily than she expected. She turned her wrist under the lamp, studying her skin with the seriousness of someone who’d found a small private treasure.

Shi Feng saw her looking. He bent over the vegetables before she could catch him smiling.
