At bedtime he spread his bedding on the floor in the corner, as always, and she went behind the screen to change. When she came out, the plain jar was standing beside her mirror, and the costly jars had been pushed to the back. Their fancy lids fought uselessly for a spot she could reach.

He saw it when she called him over to trim the lamp wick. His gaze stayed on that jar a heartbeat too long. Being useful is reason enough to be glad, he told himself.

He wasn’t quite convinced.

Then she drew the bed curtain, and he lay down on the floor and looked at the ceiling.

Behind the curtain, Ling Qingzhu used the cream once more and remembered how quietly he’d said for you. No crowd had demanded that gesture. No prince’s carriage waited outside the wall.

She wanted to ask whether he made it because of her complaint, or because he’d noticed her hands himself. But he was lying three steps away, and she could hear him breathing.

Either answer would make her ask why she wanted to know. Her heart was uneasy, and she didn’t like it. She closed the jar and set it carefully beside the mirror.

The marriage had grown some comfortable routines, she decided.

Comfortable was a safe word. It took far less courage than the words waiting underneath it.

chapters.title: The Woman Who Brought Ingredients
chapters.html:
A woman was waiting outside Gao Yuan’s yard with three sealed ingredient boxes and a chair of her own.

Yan Meizhen planted her chair where it blocked Gao Yuan’s favourite place to stand. One leg was tied with string. She tested it, shrugged, and sat again. She’d rather bring a broken chair than spend another morning listening to the landlord boast about his rooms.

“Master Shen?” Yan Meizhen asked, rising with a bright laugh. “You’re late! I’ve waited an hour. Is this how you treat a lady?”

Her name was Yan Meizhen. She wore a dark green traveling robe and dusty boots, and she was a Bone Refinement cultivator. Her clear eyes stayed on the boxes, not on the hood hiding his face. She didn’t beg for miracles.

“Twelve hunters come back in nine days,” Yan Meizhen said. “Some will be wounded. All of them will have full purses. I need medicine before they spend it all on wine and women!”

“You sell to your own company?” Shi Feng asked.

“At a discount. Hunters are men, and men are never satisfied,” Yan Meizhen said. She laughed loudly.

She managed supplies for a private hunting company. Her last supplier missed two deliveries and then told her Heaven decided whether any furnace succeeded. Yan Meizhen decided Heaven wasn’t getting any more deposits. Zhu Shan had given her Master Shen’s name, and she planned to take the introduction fee off the final price if she could.

Shi Feng opened the first box. The roots inside were properly dried and cut. The second held leaves packed too tight. The third smelled faintly of cellar stone.

He snapped one stem and showed her the dark rot at its center.

“This lot goes back,” Shi Feng said.

Yan Meizhen examined it without flinching.

“That slippery supplier swore it was natural moisture!” Yan Meizhen said, her expression darkening.

“Then pay him in naturally damp spirit stones,” Shi Feng said.

She burst out laughing. “Ha! I like you, Master Shen! Cold as a block of ice, and funnier than you look!” Yan Meizhen said.

Gao Yuan, listening at the gate, was stunned for a moment. Then he yawned and wandered off.

The two good lots would make plain wound ointment and a few common recovery pills. Shi Feng laid out his terms. The ointment gave a steady yield, the pills didn’t, and his present control was only good enough for small work. It couldn’t support a promise written just to flatter a customer. Better to say so now than to pay for it later, he thought!

He offered a trial run, a minimum he could cover from his own checked stock, and an open split of anything above it. Failed waste would be his. Any bad material would be recorded before firing.

Yan Meizhen tapped the fee line with one fingernail.

“You want to get paid even if the furnace fails?” Yan Meizhen asked, leaning forward with a smile. “So mean, Master Shen!”

“You want me to pay for your experiment with a new supplier?” Shi Feng asked.

She studied the hood and found nothing soft under it.

“…Fine! Men are even stingier than women!” Yan Meizhen said at last. “A small deposit for room and fuel. The balance after inspection. A pill share for you.”

“Agreed,” Shi Feng said. “If your hunters come back early, the furnace won’t hurry for them.”

She struck out a clause that allowed pointless delay. He struck out her attempt to demand a refund after using the goods. The brush passed between them seven times.

This woman is as stingy as I am, Shi Feng thought, with respect.

Eventually the paper was signed.

Yan Meizhen came back the next morning with dry replacement herbs and an angry note from the supplier. Shi Feng took the herbs and ignored the note. He rented the furnace by the hour, and reading someone else’s rage wouldn’t improve the batch.

The first firing gave four good pills and two collapsed lumps.

At the binding stage his qi faltered for less than a breath. Mo Tianheng’s memory showed him exactly how to catch it. But his channels answered too coarsely, and force could bring back heat without fixing a shape that was already broken.

Shi Feng wrote down the pulse he’d used and weakened it for the next run.

The second firing was better. The third wasn’t. He finished with enough approved pills for the trial, plus several useful failures that cost him time, herbs, and profit.

He ate one failure while checking the tray. The medicine entered his body without a fuss. The furnace didn’t care that his body could use whatever his hands spoiled.

Next time he’d need better control, Shi Feng thought. Much better.

Yan Meizhen’s inspection was practical. She weighed the ointment jars, checked the texture, and paid a company attendant to test a recovery pill on a tired day. The man left with his fee and a short, honest report, exactly what she wanted.

She paid the balance without asking for any favors. Now I see why merchants talk so warmly about customers who pay on time, Shi Feng thought.

“What about cheaper medicines for the road?” Yan Meizhen asked.

“A peddler named Shi Feng stocks ordinary road medicine,” Shi Feng said in the low, clipped cadence he kept behind the hood. “Leave a note at his stall. Those jars are a separate business.”

She understood and didn’t push. Shi Feng kept his hood and face cloth on until she left; when Yan Meizhen stopped by the street stall three days later to order ordinary road ointment in bulk, he kept the exchange to two plain sentences over the receipt so she never connected the quiet peddler to the hooded refiner at Gao Yuan’s yard.

From the ribbon stall across the street, Ling Qingzhu caught a single glance of the brisk woman in green laughing as she handed Shi Feng a deposit pouch. Ling Qingzhu lingered a beat beside the awning before turning away without saying a word—while at the corner of the lane, a runner from Zhou’s Medicine House watched Yan Meizhen’s porters load the ointment crates and hurried back to report that the peddler was now taking bulk company orders.

chapters.title: The Second Offer
chapters.html:
“Master Zhou has raised his offer,” Peng Jian said, setting a folded sheet beside the medicine jars.

Shi Feng pressed a seal onto a lid and didn’t look up. “Read them to me,” Shi Feng said.

Peng Jian cleared his throat. “Close the stall. Name the private refiner who makes your medicines. Never sell medicine in this district again. The payment is bigger,” Peng Jian said.

Shi Feng read the sheet twice himself. Zhou Mingde no longer feared a false complaint, he thought. He feared real medicine, and he was willing to pay for its silence.

He pushed the paper back unsigned.

“Which term—” Peng Jian began.

“All of them,” Shi Feng said. “Take it back.”

Peng Jian bowed and left.

Before noon, three men who usually bought one small jar each came to the stall together.

“All of it!” Hou Ping said, slapping a purse on the board. “Every jar!”

“At the stated prices,” Shi Feng said.

“And the batch in seven days too. Promise us,” Hou Ping said.

“No,” Shi Feng said, and counted the jars into their baskets.

They left down the same alley, whispering. The noodle seller next door leaned over his pot.

“Three men emptied the cripple’s stall?”

“Since when do they have that much money?”

“Those are Zhou’s Medicine House shoes!”

“…”

The whole row of stalls was stunned. Nobody had ever seen the cripple’s little board so empty.

Shi Feng watched the baskets go. So that was the first half of the scheme, he thought. If he sold out and promised more, he’d be tied to a delivery he couldn’t make. If he refused, Zhou Mingde would learn that he couldn’t make another batch quickly. Either way the man was spending good stones to measure him.

He closed the empty box and went to the suppliers. There he found the second half.

One merchant claimed the Dryleaf was sold.

The jar seller claimed every jar was reserved.

The furnace clerk claimed no room was free until next month.

Not one of them could meet his eyes. Shi Feng thanked them. He bought a different herb for ordinary wash and bigger jars he could divide at the stall, then pulled up his hood, covered his face, and went to Gao Yuan’s furnace yard as Master Shen.

Gao Yuan was posting a new rate notice on the gate when Shi Feng arrived in his hood. Every furnace room in the yard had gone up by five stones.

“Maintenance?” Shi Feng asked from beneath his face cloth.

“Demand,” Gao Yuan said, scratching his neck sheepishly. “Zhou’s Medicine House sent clerks to every furnace yard in the metalworking quarter this morning, paying five stones to close uncertified rooms until they find out which private refiner is supplying that Qingliu Lane peddler. They don’t know who works here, Master Shen—I didn’t give them a single name!—but since half the street shut its doors for the bribe, my remaining rooms cost extra today.”

Shi Feng took back his unsigned booking slip. Zhou Mingde was firing blind at every furnace yard in the district, and Gao Yuan was using the blanket squeeze to pad his own rent.

“Enjoy it,” Shi Feng said, and left.

Across the metalworking lane he rented a smaller furnace. Its owner demanded a deposit for the lid and charged separately for fuel. Shi Feng paid after checking both. The room was narrow and hot, but the air channel was clear and nobody’s awkwardness was written into the agreement.

The smaller furnace spoiled his usual timing. The first trial portion caught on one side, because the base held heat unevenly. Shi Feng saved the residue, shifted the supports under the vessel, and tried again. This time the liquid thickened correctly.

By evening he had ordinary medicines for the stall, and he’d lost most of a working day. He wrote the extra cost in his account, right under Zhou Mingde’s earlier interference. His hand was steady. That didn’t mean he’d forgiven anything.

At home, Ling Qingzhu found him cutting vegetables far more carefully than vegetables needed.

“Did your rich customer complain?” Ling Qingzhu asked. “Or did he cry about the price like everyone else?”

“The rich customer paid,” Shi Feng said. “Other men don’t like that.”

She leaned on the kitchen doorpost and watched him lay the knife down. She’d expected a boast or a complaint. His bluntness gave her nothing to tease.

“So selling medicine isn’t peaceful,” Ling Qingzhu said. “I thought it was jars and yawning.”

“Only to people who don’t sell medicine,” Shi Feng said. “Want broth with supper?”

“Yes,” Ling Qingzhu said, and she hung around while he added water to the pot.

Shi Feng noticed these small visits to his kitchen, and he no longer took each one for a request connected to their public act. She stood there without deciding how long to stay, and he was pleased, though he told himself it was only the stove. When he went back to put away the display box, he found a folded note pressed under the wooden divider.

A private buyer wanted several jars. Cash in advance. An afternoon meeting, at a hired room behind a disused preparation house. In the corner was a stamped medicinal leaf, its stem bent exactly like the design on Zhou Mingde’s packaging.

Careless, or on purpose? Shi Feng held the paper under the lamp. The buyer named no medicine and no amount. No sensible customer paid in advance without naming either one.

A trap, he thought coldly. Good. Let me see who set it.

He slipped the note into his sleeve, picked his ordinary knife up from his corner of the room, tucked it under his outer robe, and locked the stall account in its box. His own affairs didn’t need to follow him into another man’s snare. Ling Qingzhu looked up from her book, where she sat on the edge of the bed, as he crossed the room.

“Another buyer?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“Someone willing to spend stones,” Shi Feng said.

“You sound thrilled,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“I want to find out what they want,” Shi Feng said.

Her book shut harder than it needed to.

At the gate Shi Feng stopped. “There’s broth in the pot. Keep the heat low and add water if it thickens,” Shi Feng said.

Her expression stayed polite. She gave him the look she saved for merchants who thought she couldn’t count.

“I can watch a pot,” Ling Qingzhu said. “Easily.”

Shi Feng left before he could say what he thought of that.

Across the district, Zhao Sheng checked the hired room's window latch. Zhou Mingde wanted preparation notes or sound medicine, taken without an injury that would bring the Ling household down on his shop. Zhao Sheng had half the fee already. A buyer's invitation and a quick hand should earn the rest.

chapters.title: The Buyer’s Hidden Hand
chapters.html:
Before Shi Feng left for the late-afternoon meeting, the smell of scorched soup reached him from the kitchen door.

Ling Qingzhu stood by the stove with a wooden spoon in her fist, glaring at the pot. The broth had shrunk to a dark crust around the vegetables, and bright coals glowed under it.

“You said low heat!” Ling Qingzhu said. “I gave it low heat! It chose violence!”

Shi Feng looked at the coals. “They didn’t listen,” Shi Feng said.

She stepped back, offended on behalf of herself and the stove. Shi Feng lifted the pot off the fire, moved the unburned part into a clean pot without scraping the bottom, and added water. Ling Qingzhu watched with the reluctant interest of a proud woman learning that a chore beneath her notice had several hard steps.

“I added water,” Ling Qingzhu said stiffly.

“When?” Shi Feng asked.

“After it started to smoke,” Ling Qingzhu admitted.

“So you added it late,” Shi Feng said.

Ling Qingzhu’s ears turned red. “The smoke should have said something sooner,” Ling Qingzhu muttered at the wall.

A dark mark showed on the back of her hand where she’d touched the hot lid. Shi Feng took the scentless cream from the shelf and spread a little on it.

“It’ll fade,” Shi Feng said. “Leave the lid on while I meet this buyer.”

At the hired room behind the disused preparation house, Zhao Sheng offered tea before he offered a name.

“Sit, young master, sit!” Zhao Sheng said warmly, pushing a cup across the table. “Have some tea!”

Shi Feng remained by the door. The hired room had one shuttered window and a table wide enough for the sample case Zhao Sheng had asked him to bring. According to the invitation, a travelling company wanted ordinary medicine in bulk. So far Shi Feng had seen no company mark and no order list.

“The advance?” Shi Feng asked.

Zhao Sheng patted his robe, then looked toward the empty passage outside.

“My partner has it,” Zhao Sheng said. “Let me call him. Please look over the sizes we need.”

He laid a sheet on the table and moved toward the door. Shi Feng read the first line. Ointment, wound wash, twelve jars of each. Nothing about that list needed a private room.

A soft scrape came from the case.

Shi Feng looked up. Zhao Sheng's hand had slipped through the half-open lid. He was lifting the small notebook wrapped beside the samples.

Their eyes met.

For a breath, Zhao Sheng tried to keep the friendly smile. Then he threw the notebook toward the window, caught it in his other hand and ran.

Shi Feng blocked the door.

Zhao Sheng reached for the latch over his shoulder. Qi gathered around the thief's ankles, Foundation Establishment force preparing a short burst of speed. He meant to jump through the shutter if he couldn't pass the door. He didn't draw a weapon or strike at Shi Feng's throat.

Shi Feng caught his wrist and turned it.

The notebook fell onto the table. Zhao Sheng followed it halfway, bent at the waist, his trapped hand against his own shoulder.

“Let go!” Zhao Sheng shouted.

He shoved at the table with his free hand to upset it between them. Shi Feng stepped around the sliding leg and pinned him against the wall. The thief's qi scattered under the pressure. His free hand stopped moving.

“You're hurting me!” Zhao Sheng said.

“Stop pulling,” Shi Feng said.

Zhao Sheng stopped. He stared at the hand holding his wrist as though it belonged to a spirit beast. The information he had bought described a cripple who sold common medicine. It hadn't mentioned this strength.

Shi Feng retrieved the notebook. Its first pages held prices and customer instructions. The actual preparation notes stayed at home. A thief who never asked what he was stealing had found the wrong book.

“Who wants it?” Shi Feng asked.

“It's a misunderstanding,” Zhao Sheng said.

“Then explain why my notes are in your hand,” Shi Feng said.

Shi Feng brought him away from the wall, sat him on the floor and used the sample case's binding cord to secure his wrists tightly behind him, pressing a thumb against the shoulder meridian so he couldn't gather another qi burst.

A folded slip showed beneath the thief's loosened collar.

Zhao Sheng saw Shi Feng notice it and shut his eyes.

The paper carried Zhou Mingde's private seal. Half the fee had been paid. The remainder was due after delivery of preparation notes or sealed medicine from the peddler's stock. The last line specified that there should be no injuries and no damage traced to the medicine house.

He flattened the payment slip beneath the clean lid so spilled tea couldn’t blur Zhou Mingde’s seal. Then he checked that the torn invitation still named this room and tucked it beside the slip.

He placed the notebook beside them and checked the samples. One jar had cracked when Zhao Sheng tipped the case. The others remained sound.

“Zhou Mingde said you wouldn't notice,” Zhao Sheng muttered. “He said you were desperate for a customer. I can pay for the cracked jar!”

“Keep your stones,” Shi Feng said. “Zhou Mingde owes you the second half of your fee. It would be rude not to let you collect it at his front counter.”

Zhao Sheng’s face went white. “You’re taking me to his shop door?!” Zhao Sheng said.

Shi Feng called the lodging keeper from the passage. The keeper arrived with a lamp, stared at his bound tenant on the floor, and looked at the sealed commission slip in Shi Feng’s hand.

“Bar this shutter until the morning bell,” Shi Feng told the keeper, placing two spirit stones on the table. “And send your boy to the district watch post at dawn. Tell Senior Runner Deng that a hired thief with a shopkeeper’s private seal is ready to be delivered to Zhou’s Medicine House when the morning market opens.”

On the floor, Zhao Sheng closed his eyes in despair. Across the district, Zhou Mingde was still waiting for his stolen notebook.

chapters.title: The Wrong Kind of Jealousy
chapters.html:
“Two empty baskets, a big order, and a smaller price!” Yan Meizhen announced with a loud laugh as she walked through the courtyard gate. “Master Shi, did you miss me?”

Shi Feng was fixing a cracked lid and didn’t look up. “Not particularly,” Shi Feng said.

“Cruel!” Yan Meizhen said, delighted.

He’d arranged the pickup at home, because the stall’s narrow counter couldn’t hold so many full baskets. Ordinary wound medicines needed no secret furnace meeting, and he saw no reason to pay a porter extra to carry fragile goods downhill.

Across the lane, Granny Qin leaned over her stall counter, craning her neck.

“A woman in green, carrying baskets, going through that gate!” Granny Qin shouted to her nephew Qin Bao. “Go and look, boy! Go and look!”

Qin Bao stared, stunned, and didn’t move.

Inside, Ling Qingzhu tied her veil and appeared at the pear tree before Yan Meizhen set down the second basket. The visitor’s perfume was light, expensive and instantly annoying.

Yan Meizhen looked at the white robe, then at Shi Feng, then back at the robe. Her expression changed as recognition crossed her face. Then came the more useful thought of a merchant wondering if knowing this woman might get her a better deal.

“Oh! Your wife?” Yan Meizhen asked.

“Yes,” Shi Feng said.

There was no pause, and no remark about papers or private arrangements. Ling Qingzhu felt a small, unreasonable satisfaction.

Yan Meizhen bowed with a bright smile. “Fairy Ling! What a lucky man you are, Master Shi. I’d have married him myself, but he’s far too stingy!”

Shi Feng said nothing.

“He counts every spirit stone twice,” Ling Qingzhu said, her eyes perfectly pleasant above the veil. “Count your change, Miss Yan.”

Yan Meizhen laughed loudly and went back to the jars.

“A big order should cut your packing costs,” Yan Meizhen said.

“It did,” Shi Feng said. “You brought the baskets.”

Ling Qingzhu watched them count the sealed jars. Their back-and-forth was quick, almost comfortable. Yan Meizhen knew which medicines needed dark storage, which lids had to stay dry, and how long her company could keep a reserve without paying for more than it needed.

She also knew when Shi Feng was joking. That last discovery was especially irritating, Ling Qingzhu thought, and her thumb pressed hard against her sleeve.

“Can the next delivery come two days earlier?” Yan Meizhen asked.

Shi Feng checked his written schedule and shook his head. “I won’t promise work I can only finish by shorting another order.”

“I’ll add a fee!” Yan Meizhen said.

He considered the number, considered the furnace room he could actually book, and refused again. Ling Qingzhu’s opinion of the perfume improved a little. Before leaving, Yan Meizhen looked at the cracked lid on the table.

“You should make the jar maker pay for that,” Yan Meizhen said.

“I plan to,” Shi Feng said.

“Good! Don’t be soft!” Yan Meizhen said. She paid the balance, tied up her baskets, waved cheerfully at Ling Qingzhu, and walked out without leaving an invitation or any other sensible reason for jealousy.

“She’s gone already!” Granny Qin complained across the lane. “Boy, what kind of watching was that?”

The whole lane was disappointed that there was no scandal. Ling Qingzhu was jealous anyway.

Shi Feng carried the broken lid to the shelf. Behind him, she picked up a spare jar and turned it in her fingers, hunting for a flaw in the glass to explain her mood.

“You’re awfully attentive to her needs,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“She pays on delivery,” Shi Feng said.

The answer hit more than one target. Ling Qingzhu set the jar down very carefully.

“I was talking about how you treat customers,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“So was I,” Shi Feng said.

“She visits a lot,” Ling Qingzhu said, picking at the jar’s label.

“The medicine leaves every time,” Shi Feng said. “That’s usually the point.”

Her eyes narrowed and her expression cooled. He could’ve asked whether she disliked the color green, and he would’ve enjoyed her answer far too much.

With the visitor gone, she removed her veil. He looked at her face properly. Under the irritation was real discomfort, and Shi Feng thought: this isn’t one of her public performances. He knew how to answer an insult. A question she couldn’t bring herself to ask took more care.

“She buys supplies for hunters,” Shi Feng said. “They use them on the road, and she comes back when they need more. That’s all our business is.”

“I didn’t ask what your business was!” Ling Qingzhu said.

“You’ve been talking about it for a while now,” Shi Feng said.

Her cheeks went warm. She walked to the middle of the courtyard.

The practice blade still stood beside the hanging cord. Their short lessons had grown irregular whenever a commission took his mornings. Ling Qingzhu picked it up, tested its weight, and made the turn he’d shown her.

Her point passed the cord without touching it.

Shi Feng watched her reset her feet. She picked up a correction faster than most people understood the explanation. There was no qi in the movement and no declared realm, only an ease that made an ordinary gesture look inevitable. A real talent, Shi Feng thought. She was concealing practice, perhaps more than practice. He had no evidence for an exact realm or any right to name her talent from a wrist movement.

“Like this?” Ling Qingzhu asked, and a smile escaped her.

“Yes,” Shi Feng said.

“Good,” Ling Qingzhu said. “Then your green customer didn’t need the whole morning, did she?”

He almost laughed. “Want another lesson?” Shi Feng asked.

“If you haven’t sold the time to someone else,” Ling Qingzhu said, turning away.

He took the second practice blade.

They worked until the sun crossed the courtyard wall. Once he fixed the angle of her wrist with two fingers beneath it, and Ling Qingzhu stood perfectly still for a moment after he let go. Her heart beat a little faster, and she blamed the sword.

The lesson cost no spirit stones. Shi Feng didn’t enter it in his accounts.

At supper she moved her stool closer, because a cold draft was coming from the other side of the room. The window there was shut. Shi Feng served the rice and mentioned neither fact.

Her sleeve brushed his wrist. Neither of them moved away.

The silence felt different from a pause in conversation. He found himself listening to the small sound of her spoon against the bowl, happy just to have her there. Then Ling Qingzhu asked, very casually, whether going with her to a household visit in seven days would clash with his profitable customers.

The word going was harmless. The reminder of their arrangement under it was not.

“I’ll make time,” Shi Feng said. He was surprised at how quickly he said it.

“Good. Without you I’d smile at three aunts for two hours,” Ling Qingzhu said, brightening, and started describing the occasion right away. He listened, enjoying her pleasure, while the unfinished account beside the lamp waited for him.

Later she went behind the screen to change, then drew the bed curtain. Before spreading his bedding in the corner, Shi Feng set her cleaned bowl upside down on the little table beside her bed and placed Zhou Mingde’s sealed commission slip beside the cracked sample jar by the door, ready for the district watch at the morning bell.

Across the district, Zhou Mingde counted out a thief’s remaining payment on his counter and wondered why Zhao Sheng still hadn’t knocked on his back door.

chapters.title: The Unpaid Balance
chapters.html:
Senior Runner Deng Shun met Shi Feng at the lane corner at the morning bell and marched the bound Zhao Sheng straight to Zhou's Medicine House as the market shutters opened.

Shi Feng walked behind the two runners, carrying the cracked sample jar and the signed slip from his threshold. After sitting trussed in the firewood shed until dawn, Zhao Sheng looked even less like a travelling merchant than he had the night before.

Zhou Mingde saw the group through his open shop door.

His brush stopped above a customer's receipt.

“Move those people away from my entrance,” Zhou Mingde said. “Customers have business here.”

The senior runner, Deng Shun, stepped beneath the shop sign and opened his register.

“Zhou Mingde, we're asking about a payment bearing your seal,” Deng Shun said. “Answer here, or come to the office.”

Two customers turned around. The apprentice at the herb drawer closed it very slowly. Outside, a woman who had meant to pass the shop stopped to adjust a sandal that needed no adjusting.

Zhou Mingde looked at Zhao Sheng, then at Shi Feng.

“A peddler's complaint?” Zhou Mingde said. “I've sold medicine in this district for twenty years. He has a board and four jars. Perhaps somebody should inspect him instead.”

The customer nearest the counter nodded uncertainly. Zhou Mingde had a large shop, a proper sign and a familiar name. Shi Feng's robe still carried a mended cuff.

“That's Fairy Ling's husband.”

“The one from the little stall?”

“What has he done now?”

Shi Feng set the cracked jar on the step. Deng Shun showed the payment slip without handing it over.

“This seal,” Deng Shun said. “Is it yours?”

“Seals can be copied,” Zhou Mingde said.

“Then we'll compare it with the supplier receipts in your shop,” Deng Shun said.

The apprentice took a half step back from the ledger. Zhou Mingde saw the movement and glared at him.

Shi Feng kept quiet. He hadn't come to win a shouting match. The runner had a simpler way to test the lie, and Zhou Mingde had supplied it himself.

Deng Shun laid the invitation beside the payment record. Both named the same hired room. Zhao Sheng had given its location before the guard found the invitation in Shi Feng's bag. The lodging keeper's statement recorded who rented it and who asked for the extra shutter latch.

“Speak,” Deng Shun said to Zhao Sheng.

Zhao Sheng swallowed.

“Zhou Mingde hired me to take the notes or the prepared medicine,” Zhao Sheng said. “Half before, half after. I was to offer a large order so Shi Feng would bring the samples.”

“Liar!” Zhou Mingde shouted.

Zhao Sheng flinched, then looked at the shopkeeper with sudden resentment.

“You told me he'd be easy to fool,” Zhao Sheng said. “You said a cripple would be pleased somebody wanted his stock.”

Several people looked at Shi Feng's hands. One knuckle was scraped. Zhao Sheng was bound, sore and alive. Whatever had happened in the room, the easy part hadn't gone as expected.

“Did he order you to injure anyone?” Deng Shun asked.

“No,” Zhao Sheng said. “He said not to. He wanted the preparation, not trouble with the Ling household.”

“Then put that down as well,” Shi Feng said.

Deng Shun's brush moved. Zhou Mingde stared at Shi Feng, thrown by the correction. He had expected an accusation to grow as it reached the street. This one was becoming exact.

The woman by the doorway straightened from her sandal.

“Isn't this the shop that sent the man with the swollen arm?”

“Blistering root, wasn't it?”

“He offered protection first!”

The crowd turned toward Zhou Mingde's sign. A moment ago its size had proved his importance. Now everyone could read it while asking what kind of business stood underneath.

“That complaint was nothing to do with me,” Zhou Mingde said.

Shi Feng took out the earlier sealed sample and the tower's finding on its contents. The altered ointment remained separate from his clean stock. He gave the papers to Deng Shun.

“That evidence belongs with this complaint,” Shi Feng said. “The witnesses' names are inside.”

He didn't claim the paper proved every thought in Zhou Mingde's head. It established what had been added to the ointment and where the errand payment came from. Alongside the new theft commission, it was enough to make the guard ask further questions.

Deng Shun called for the supplier ledger.

Zhou Mingde put his hand on it.

For an instant Shi Feng thought the shopkeeper might try to tear out a page. Deng Shun's second runner stepped beside the counter, and the hand lifted again. Zhou Mingde hadn't lost his mind. He was still choosing which disgrace cost less.

The apprentice opened the book. There were notes beside several suppliers: refuse the peddler, reserve all usable roots, inform the house if new stock arrived. Some were in Zhou Mingde's own handwriting.

The customer waiting for his receipt slowly pushed his unpaid medicine back across the counter.

The customer muttered that he would return later.

He didn't wait for an answer. The other buyer followed him out. Nobody needed their names to remember the empty places they left.

Zhou Mingde's face turned dark red.

“You came to destroy my business,” Zhou Mingde said to Shi Feng.

“I came to sell mine,” Shi Feng said. “You made that difficult.”

Deng Shun closed the ledger. He would take Zhou Mingde's statement at the office, along with the receipts and the seal. The charge concerned theft and commercial interference. The result would be decided there, where customers couldn't shout over the clerk.

Zhou Mingde walked between the runners without chains. Zhao Sheng went behind him, still bound. Their positions were different, but neither walked away from the complaint.

The apprentices stayed in the shop. One began putting lids back on open jars with hands that wouldn't quite steady.

Shi Feng picked up his cracked sample and returned to his own awning.

People followed at a distance. By the time he laid out the clean stock, Tao Laifu was waiting with a question about sore palms. Shi Feng explained the ordinary salve and its limits. He didn't raise the price because a crowd had arrived.

Across the street, two apprentices lifted the carved signboard down from Zhou's Medicine House and pulled the heavy shutters closed under the ward clerk's seal. A murmur ran through the morning market.

“Zhou Mingde tried to steal the peddler's formula and lost his own signboard before breakfast!”

“No wonder his shop feared that little awning—the peddler's salve is the real thing.”

“Give me two jars before the line reaches the corner!”

“Will Zhou's house reopen?” Tao Laifu asked, peering past the crowd now pressing up to Shi Feng's board.

“That's for the guard and Zhou Mingde,” Shi Feng said, handing the next buyer a sealed jar at the usual price. “Keep this lid dry.”

By mid-morning his sample tray was empty and three new buyers had left deposits for tomorrow's batch.

chapters.title: The Tower's Receipt
chapters.html:
The first supplier who’d refused to sell to Shi Feng yesterday now hurried out to greet him. Shi Feng looked behind him for a rich customer.

The street was empty.

“Master Shi, this way,” Sun Ke said, pointing at a crate of herbs.

Shi Feng checked the sample, paid the price written on the lid, and took the parcel. Someone has decided the cripple has a powerful patron, he thought. And this merchant is too scared to ask who.

By midday, two more merchants found out that the shortage wasn’t so bad after all. One even offered credit.

“No credit,” Shi Feng said. “I’ll pay now.”

The merchant said that extending credit would be an honour.

“This lot will do,” Shi Feng said. He paid for the good herbs and left before the merchant could finish another compliment.

Fear isn’t loyalty, he thought. A good discount is just a good discount, and I’ll take it without pretending to be grateful.

Rumors of Zhou Mingde’s disgrace brought crowds to the stall, though curiosity didn’t always bring a purchase.

“That’s the cripple! His little jars ruined Zhou’s House!”

“Did he catch the thief himself?”

“Look at him! He can’t even lift a sword!”

“Then who makes his medicine?”

“…”

Shi Feng answered questions about use, storage and price. He told no story about a secret patron who’d avenged him. Other people were inventing plenty of stories already.

One honest customer hesitated over a sealed jar until the shadow of the awning crossed his hand. Shi Feng knew that look. The man wanted to believe, and he was afraid to.

The man admitted he had heard that it worked, but worried whether a peddler might change the mixture whenever a cheaper herb came along.

Shi Feng wasn’t offended. He’d met enough peddlers to share the worry. That afternoon he closed the stall early and carried a sealed sample to Sky Pavilion.

The capital tower rose above the roofs, and its upper windows caught the light long after the shops below were in shadow. Merchants passed under its gate and nobody bowed to them like lords. Well-dressed cultivators waited their turn beside men who’d come to pay for the examination of a single object.

Shi Feng went to the product assay hall. The clerk behind the counter wore a plain name token: Ji Wenzhao. He asked what Shi Feng wanted tested, not which grandmaster praised the medicine.

Shi Feng set down the jar.

“Medicine stability, stated ingredients and proper use,” Shi Feng said.

Ji Wenzhao checked the seal and handed over a printed list of charges.

“One tested sample doesn’t certify future batches,” Ji Wenzhao said. “It doesn’t certify the maker, and it definitely doesn’t give you a Mark.”

“That’s not what I’m buying,” Shi Feng said.

“Then write the batch description here,” Ji Wenzhao said.

Nobody needed to argue the point. Up a separate staircase, a notice listed the certification appointments. A 1 Mark alchemist made pills for Golden Core cultivators.

2 Marks meant pills for Nascent Soul, 3 Marks for late or peak Nascent Soul, and so on up the ladder to the legendary Heavenly Mark. Candidates had to be at least Foundation Establishment. A Bone Refinement cultivator couldn’t even sit for the first test, Shi Feng thought.

Fine. A merchant’s jar belonged at a different counter anyway.

Shi Feng found the arrangement refreshing, and for the first time in the capital his heart felt light. He wrote down the medicine, its intended use and the lot of the sample. Ji Wenzhao sealed the entry, took the fee, and named the day the report would be ready.

No pulse check. No demand to prove he could refine. No insistence that a man who sold useful medicine must first prove every rumor about his body false.

While the assay ran, Shi Feng went back to the smaller furnace.

A private practice run was waiting. He tried the same common pill twice, changing the pace of the final joining stage. The first run produced two usable pills. The second produced one, and several crumbled pieces.

He compared the residue, swallowed it, and wrote down the difference.

Sky Pavilion can check a finished medicine, Shi Feng thought. It can’t lend me the qi quality I lack. His ordinary medicines were reliable because they stayed within what his present hands could do. Finer pills needed practice and honest limits, no matter how much expertise he remembered. He wouldn’t hang a receipt over a furnace and expect the receipt to do the work.

The report came before the evening bell.

Correct preparation. Stable properties. Ingredients matching the stated formula. The handling instructions and the sample’s limits were laid out clearly under the result.

“Show the whole statement,” Ji Wenzhao said.

Shi Feng read them and nodded. “If anyone dislikes them, he can bring his own sample,” Shi Feng said.

Ji Wenzhao handed back the leftover material. His expression stayed flat, and he said nothing more.

The next morning Shi Feng put the complete report up beside the tested lot. He kept that lot apart from his newer stock and matched the seals to the record.

“The Sky Pavilion tower tested it!” an old woman read aloud from the board. “It really works!”

“Real medicine from a cripple?” a young man said, stunned.

“The paper says so!”

Three customers bought without repeating the old argument about whether a cripple had any right to sell medicine. A fourth demanded the same price for a bigger jar. The tower’s receipt did nothing to stop the bargaining.

Gao Yuan heard about the assay by noon and showed up, yawning.

“Congratulations, Master Shi,” Gao Yuan said. “You should rent a better furnace room. Mine, maybe.”

Shi Feng knew that pitch well. Gao Yuan had already tried the same offer on Master Shen under his hood. He showed Gao Yuan the booking he’d already paid at the other yard.

The congratulations stayed free.

At home, Ling Qingzhu found the report on the table beside his accounts. She read the title first, then the findings, then the small print under them. Shi Feng watched from the kitchen doorway with a bowl in his hand, wondering what she’d decide.

“So the medicine is real,” Ling Qingzhu said, tapping the stamp. “Even the tower agrees with you.”

“It was real before the receipt,” Shi Feng said.

She looked up.

He didn’t sound offended enough for her to write his answer off as wounded pride. He sounded certain. The cream beside her mirror had already worked, and his explanations were already clear. Yet it was the tower’s ink that convinced her, she realized, and not either of those.

“That’s not what I meant,” Ling Qingzhu said, chin up, her expression daring him to argue.

“What did you mean?” Shi Feng asked.

She couldn’t find a graceful way to say her original sentence again. At last she handed him the paper and asked if the assay had been expensive. He named the fee.

“You should’ve bargained,” Ling Qingzhu said at once. “They’d have knocked off a fifth.”

Shi Feng looked at the tower’s fixed charges, then at her.

“…Fine, it’s a tower. They don’t bargain,” Ling Qingzhu said, and laughed in spite of herself. “They should, though.” It eased the moment, but not completely.

That night she drew the bed curtain and opened the scentless cream. Shi Feng lay on his bedding in the corner, pretending to count the ceiling beams, while she used a little before bed. The jar had no fancy seal. He’d made it because she disliked the smell of another cream, and it worked from the first evening.

How many other things have I waited for someone important to confirm? she wondered, in the dark, a few steps from the man on the floor.

Then she told herself that a wife couldn’t be expected to understand every detail of her husband’s trade.

The explanation was comfortable enough to keep.

chapters.title: One More Month
chapters.html:
“Seven bundles of charcoal, not nine,” Shi Feng muttered, and struck out Gao Yuan’s figure with his brush.

He fixed two more quantities, checked the total against the chit, and pulled the household account book toward him. The marriage agreement lay underneath in its narrow folder. At the top, in handwriting that now felt like it belonged to another life, it said: six months.

Under it were the house rules. She takes the bed, he takes the floor, no intimacy owed, no touching each other’s belongings.

He looked at the almanac on the wall and his brush stopped.

Today was the last day.

Shi Feng set the accounts aside. The registered marriage was still valid, because the registry didn’t care about private terms. But the private term was over. The ten thousand stones also stayed unpaid in his notation. He didn’t rub it out to make the months more comfortable. He just stopped arguing with a woman who kept acting as if that matter was closed long ago.

Ling Qingzhu stopped at the courtyard threshold. She saw the folder, the brush and the chit under his hand, and for a moment the little house seemed to hold nothing but things that could be packed. His floor bedding was already rolled up in the corner of the room. She noticed it for the first time in days.

“You can leave now,” Ling Qingzhu said.

Shi Feng looked up.

That came out way too sharp! She meant to honour the agreement with dignity, and instead she sounded sharp and rude, a woman throwing out a guest.

“I know,” Shi Feng said.

Ling Qingzhu rested one hand on the back of an empty chair. Her heart was pounding, and she hated it.

The consort's household still sent gifts to her elders. Court clerks still delayed answers, and certain relatives still called the royal match sensible. The ancestor's rule barred taking a married woman; it hadn't taught her family to stop bargaining.

The marriage was still useful. She could say all of that, and it was reasonable and clear. It was also the same excuse she’d been giving herself for six months.

“Would one more month kill you?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

Shi Feng looked at her calmly. A corner of the paper lifted in the morning breeze, and he set the empty inkstone on it before he answered.

“Either of us can end it,” Shi Feng said. “No duty to stay.”

Ling Qingzhu nodded much too quickly, and her ears turned pink. Then she straightened and her expression turned stern, annoyed at her own haste.

“Of course,” Ling Qingzhu said. “We’re only keeping what’s convenient. Don’t read anything into it.”

He drew out a clean sheet, and they wrote the extension in plain words. Staying was voluntary. Either side could end it with no second locked period. The bed and the floor stayed exactly as they were. The old unpaid claim stayed on record, and no new paper would quietly cancel it.

Ling Qingzhu read that last line and pursed her lips.

Typical, she thought, annoyed. This man haggled over herbs and beamed at every customer who paid on time. He wanted every spirit stone to answer to its name. She let the line stand, because she didn’t want to spoil the morning arguing about something she thought was settled.

She signed. Shi Feng watched her brush move.

There were practical reasons to stay, he told himself. The furnace yards were close. The courtyard suited his work. Moving in the middle of a run of orders meant lost days and deposits he could spend on ingredients. Every reason was true! The cold floor was not one of them, and Shi Feng’s expression stayed flat all the same.

None of them explained why he felt so relieved when she pulled out the chair and sat.

“So. What do you want for supper?” Ling Qingzhu asked. “Don’t say vegetables.”

He thought about this question harder than he’d thought about the extension.

“Something you didn’t burn,” Shi Feng said.

Her hand came down on the folded paper. “Keep talking and I’ll change my mind about the whole month,” Ling Qingzhu said.

He laughed.

The sound startled them both. Ling Qingzhu stood very still for a moment, and then she walked out of the gate toward the market without another word. In her heart she kept repeating one thought: he laughs so rarely. She wanted to hear it again.

“A fish like this only comes once in a hundred years, Fairy Ling!” Hu Da cried, waving a carp above his tub. “You’ve got a master’s eye!”

She was pleased, and she didn’t ask herself why.

“How much?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“Three spirit stones,” Hu Da said.

“Three stones for one fish!” someone gasped.

“Fairy Ling never haggles…”

“…”

Ling Qingzhu paid at once and carried the carp home in a covered basket, very proud. Shi Feng took one look inside and asked the price. She told him.

He closed his eyes.

“The seller said it was fresh,” Ling Qingzhu said, lifting her chin. “It looked at me. Very alive.”

“At that price, it should jump into the pan by itself,” Shi Feng said.

She reached for the basket. He moved it out of her reach and started scaling the fish.

“Well, it’s bought,” Shi Feng said. “We might as well eat it before the price goes up again.”

Ling Qingzhu stood beside him, insulted for half a breath and amused for the rest. When he handed her the vegetables, she took the knife with great confidence. Her slices came out thick, thin, and wedge-shaped.

“Those aren’t slices,” Shi Feng said. “They’re a rumour of slices.”

“…How dare you!” Ling Qingzhu said, her face flushing. “Fine. Show me how, Master Chef.”

He turned her thickest piece on its side and curled his fingers over hers on the handle. She watched the angle of his knuckles and copied it exactly on the next one.

Shi Feng was a little astonished at how fast she learned. Worse, he noticed how easily he could picture this again tomorrow.

Not for visitors. Not to give the registered names a convincing home. Just her hair loosely pinned after the market, her sleeves tied back, and some small question carried across the room. A whole life of ordinary mornings was starting to look like something he wanted.

His chest tightened slightly. For months he had treated the courtyard as a rented shelter with clear boundaries and an end date written in ink. Now the end date had arrived, and the thought of packing his rolled bedding and walking out of this kitchen felt colder than the stone floor ever had.

He didn’t name the feeling over a board of crooked vegetables. He only knew he wanted tomorrow morning to look just like this one.

Ling Qingzhu reached for the salt jar. He caught her wrist before she added enough to preserve the fish for ten years.

“You’ve interfered at every step!” Ling Qingzhu said. “It’s my fish!”

“I’d like to survive supper,” Shi Feng said.

She laughed and let him take the jar.

They ate under the courtyard lamp. The fish was excellent, though Shi Feng refused to say so. Ling Qingzhu insisted that his complaints hid gratitude, and for once he let her keep the victory without a sharper answer.

Later she sat on the edge of the bed, took the extension out of its folder and looked at the two names.

He’d agreed quickly. Maybe the house was useful for his trade. Maybe the marriage gave him a little dignity and shelter. Maybe a man who counted stones so carefully just hated moving. Maybe he even liked the floor.

She asked him to stay, and he stayed. That was the simplest explanation, and the one she most wanted to avoid.

Ling Qingzhu put the paper away and told herself that a comfortable arrangement didn’t need examining.

Outside, Shi Feng washed the last bowl and set it down beside hers.

chapters.title: The Prince Who Waited
chapters.html:
“Your stall board is eleven inches too long!” Mei Qian announced, flapping the permit form at the whole market.

Shi Feng looked at the board. Then he looked at the measuring cord, which the clerk stretched from the far end of the handle.

“The handle isn’t part of the board,” Shi Feng said.

“A stall includes everything attached to it!” Mei Qian said, his face turning red.

“Then write that down and sign it,” Shi Feng said, offering the brush. “Today’s date, your name, your reason.”

Mei Qian’s expression froze. His mouth opened, then shut. The neighbouring stallkeepers leaned closer.

“He wants the clerk to sign it!” someone whispered, stunned.

“Nobody signs anything here…”

“…”

“Inspection takes the whole morning!” Mei Qian said stiffly.

“Then inspect,” Shi Feng said. “Don’t waste the morning telling me you might.”

He waited beside his closed stall while the other shops opened. By the time the clerk finally stamped the form, two regular customers had walked away and bought elsewhere. The fee was legal. The delay was on purpose. Shi Feng wrote both facts in his account book, on separate lines.

At the furnace yard, another clerk demanded an irrelevant household guarantee. Shi Feng checked the old rule, found it concerned stored fuel, and refused to lend the delay a respectable excuse.

He moved the long booking to another yard and kept only one short session, already paid. None of these men drew a blade, Shi Feng thought. Killing a stupid clerk wouldn’t bring back a lost morning. It would only give the men behind him something better than an irregular form.

An inconvenience wasn’t an assassination. He knew the difference.

But Sima Yu is testing me, Shi Feng thought, and he’s patient. First the clerks, then the knife. A prince can afford to buy both!

The thought didn’t trouble him much. It only made him watch his steps more carefully on his walk home.

That afternoon his first firing failed at the joining stage. Irritation made his qi follow the wrong rhythm before he caught it, so he scraped out the residue and sat by the furnace until he stopped thinking about Mei Qian. The next attempt gave two small pills.

Mo Tianheng’s whole art was complete in his memory, but his current qi needed slow, steady handling at this scale. He didn’t need a clerk sharing control of the flame.

“Master Shen, the room’s yours for the hour,” Gao Yuan called through the door, yawning. “The other tenants say clerks were asking about you. Not my business, eh?”

“Then the other tenants should mind their own fires,” Shi Feng said, wiping his hands.

Gao Yuan yawned and shuffled off. Even a lazy landlord could tell when a customer was in trouble.

Across the capital, He Zhong left the eastern residence holding a small purse and nursing a wrist that still ached.

He had told Sima Yu about the mountain pass. He had claimed a hard fight, but under questions the useful facts became smaller: Shi Feng had caught a spear shaft, broken a qi shield with physical force and left him alive. He Zhong knew nothing about a restored meridian network or a concealed refiner. The prince paid for the limited account anyway.

After the hunter left, Sima Yu received another visitor in a room emptied of servants.

The old man wore a plain grey robe and carried no fancy weapon. When he sat, the prince waited for the cup to reach his hand before he spoke. Cao Wenshu had served the royal house for forty years.

He stood at mid Foundation Establishment. Decades of palace service had sharpened his killing methods, and he didn’t need an expensive robe to make lesser cultivators nervous.

“Guo Zhen has vanished,” Sima Yu said softly. “And a certain medicine peddler still goes into Hengyun. It’s a pity, with the mountains so dangerous these days.”

Cao Wenshu lifted the lid of his cup. “A medicine peddler?” Cao Wenshu said. “You summoned this old man for a peddler?”

“Someone searched Hengyun,” Sima Yu said gently. “They found nothing worth bringing me.”

Cao Wenshu looked faintly amused. Finding nothing could mean many things, especially to a prince who disliked every explanation on offer. Sima Yu laid a thin sheet on the table: gathering routes, late returns, a private refiner, and a link to the stall that nobody could explain.

“I’m told accidents are common in the mountains,” Sima Yu said.

“Hmph. So they are,” Cao Wenshu said.

“I would only ask that the palace’s name stay out of it,” Sima Yu said.

Cao Wenshu set the cup down. His fee went up when discretion was required, and went up again if the body had to stay outside the city. He named the total without apologising for either part.

“Agreed,” Sima Yu said.

A few stones lost to inspections hadn’t scared the cripple off, he thought coldly. The fool mistook a shopkeeper’s troubles for real pressure. Cao Wenshu would teach him a plainer lesson.

The old man folded the sheet and slid it into his robe.

At Qingliu Lane, Ling Qingzhu sat on the edge of the bed and watched Shi Feng pack, since in a house with only one room there was nowhere else to look. Knife, food packet, binding cord and root cloth went into his bag from his corner, in their usual order. He’d rolled up his floor bedding and tucked it against the wall.

“Have prices gone up again?” Ling Qingzhu asked. “Say yes. I’ll buy the whole lane. Nobody raises anything.”

“They never apologise and come back down,” Shi Feng said.

“Don’t. Ruining a lane is a hobby, not a plan,” Ling Qingzhu admitted. “I’ll buy vegetables if you’re back before the market closes.”

“Don’t pay extra for freshness just because a fish looked at you,” Shi Feng said.

“Also,” Shi Feng added at the gate, “if the fishmonger calls you a master of fish again, walk away.”

“He didn’t say master of fish!” Ling Qingzhu protested. “He said I had a good eye. I do have a good eye!”

“He said master’s eye,” Shi Feng said. “It’s the same fish.”

She picked up the nearest folded cloth and threw it at his head.

He caught it, tucked it into the bag, and went out smiling. Ling Qingzhu stared at the empty gate and her cheeks warmed. “Shameless!” Ling Qingzhu muttered. She didn’t know why he was smiling. Neither did he, really.

All those difficult bookings made gathering his own herbs worthwhile. Hengyun’s inner ground still held the roots he needed, and a clean lot would lower the cost of Yan Meizhen’s next order. Shi Feng worked through the afternoon, rejecting damaged stems and taking only what he could use or sell.

Before heading back he sat under a rock shelf and took out the sealed storage ring.

It was still sealed. Foundation Establishment was the threshold, he thought. All of Mo Tianheng’s knowledge couldn’t convince the ring that its owner had crossed it.

Shi Feng put the ring away and started down. Near the abandoned signal fort, the birds stopped singing.

He set down the root bundle and looked up. A man stood on the broken parapet. There was no scrape of footsteps, and no effort to balance on the narrow stone. A breath later the pressure reached the path, so thick that the air under the man’s feet felt strangely still.

Shi Feng’s heart tightened. His pupils shrank. Mid Foundation Establishment. This was a stage beyond the opponents he could dominate.

He drew his ordinary sword slowly. The path behind him offered distance, not safety, and against an opponent like this, turning his back would only choose the place where he’d be struck.

“Sima Yu sent you?” Shi Feng asked.

Cao Wenshu looked down at him.

“A mere ant, and this old man must climb a mountain for you,” Cao Wenshu said. “Be glad it will be quick, boy.”

Shi Feng shifted his feet and let the bag slide where he could drop it.

“Then he should’ve saved his stones,” Shi Feng said calmly.

He had no intention of dying politely just because a prince had bought a powerful hand.

chapters.title: At the Limit
chapters.html:
Cao Wenshu raised one finger.

Boom! The parapet exploded beside Shi Feng’s head.

Stone flew into his cheek. He rolled with the blast, crossed the fallen blocks and thrust at the old man’s wrist. Piercing Current! The short step carried him close without throwing his weight forward, and against an ordinary early Foundation Establishment cultivator it would have forced a desperate retreat.

Cao Wenshu didn’t retreat.

A thin shield of qi met the blade. The ordinary steel bent, then snapped in the middle. Shi Feng turned his shoulder, but the palm behind the shield still landed on his chest.

Bang! The world flew backward. He crashed through the inner doorway of the fort and slammed into the far wall, and old plaster burst around him. The air left his lungs. His ribs groaned but held, because his Bone Refinement was complete, and the unfinished gold beneath them took the rest of the blow.

Shi Feng was on his feet before Cao Wenshu crossed the threshold.

“Bone Refinement,” Cao Wenshu said, surprised. “Guo Zhen was a fool.”

Shi Feng spat blood on the stone.

“He wasn’t alone,” Shi Feng said.

The old man’s expression turned cold. He advanced with his palm open, and qi filled the room. The pressure bore down on Shi Feng’s shoulders and knees, heavy as a mountain. Mid Foundation Establishment, Shi Feng thought. Early Foundation Establishment opponents couldn’t withstand him, but this old man was another stage higher. This fight would take everything he had.

Cao Wenshu no longer thought of this as an execution. Now he treated it as a real danger.

Shi Feng moved before the gathering hand could close. He thrust the broken sword at the wrist again, and Cao Wenshu turned the hand aside, certain the short blade would pass harmlessly by.

Turning Wave!

Shi Feng’s wrist turned while his foot was still moving. The thrust became a cut. The jagged edge slid under the old man’s elbow, exactly where his shield was thin from meeting the first attack.

Blood ran down Cao Wenshu’s sleeve.

“What?” Cao Wenshu said, and his face changed.

Xu Changhe’s lesson had found what raw strength alone would’ve missed. Shi Feng’s heart leapt. A mid Foundation Establishment cultivator was bleeding from the hand of a boy still in Bone Refinement!

The old man looked at his arm once. His next attack carried no contempt at all.

Qi filled the ruined chamber. A window frame cracked outward. Shi Feng felt the pressure clamp around his limbs, and he forced every meridian in his body to carry the strength rising through him.

Three hundred and sixty-five pathways answered.

The five Epoch Meridians carried what ordinary cultivation couldn’t. No borrowed power came from the ring. No dead master appeared to save him. Every current belonged to the battered body standing against the wall.

I can still move, Shi Feng thought. That’s enough.

Cao Wenshu struck at his chest. Shi Feng stepped aside, let the palm slide past his shoulder, and drew the sword fragment back by the width of one hand.

Returning Tide!

The point shot forward beneath the attacking arm. Cao Wenshu twisted sharply and the fragment missed his throat, but it opened the side of his neck.

“Impossible!” Cao Wenshu roared, his expression twisted.

His return blow caught Shi Feng across the ribs. Something tore, and warmth ran beneath his robe. Shi Feng’s legs nearly folded. He caught the broken doorway with one hand, forced himself upright, and met the next palm with his own.

Crack! Stone broke under both men.

Cao Wenshu’s supporting foot slipped. Shi Feng stepped into him, seized the wounded arm and drove his knee under the old man’s ribs. The shield held. He struck the same place again, and this time it trembled.

Then Cao Wenshu caught him by the throat.

The air vanished. The old man’s fingers tightened and lifted him against the jagged doorway. Stone dug into his back. Shi Feng stabbed again with the broken blade, but Cao Wenshu knocked it aside with his good arm and hit his wounded side.

Pain turned the room white. The blade fragment fell from his fingers.

Shi Feng knew he couldn’t win by pretending the wounds didn’t matter. His golden bones were unfinished. The First Extreme was still far away. No Foundation Establishment breakthrough would come to rescue him, and nobody else would finish this fight.

So he’d finish it as the man he already was. Both hands closed around the wrist at his neck. His right heel found a fallen block, and he planted it and put his whole body into the turn.

Snap! The wrist broke.

Cao Wenshu’s fingers opened. Shi Feng dragged the old man forward and drove his forehead into the face above the strained shield. The protective qi shattered between them. Pain burst behind Shi Feng’s eyes, and Cao Wenshu’s nose collapsed with a wet crunch.

“You little beast!” Cao Wenshu screamed, staggering, one ruined wrist hanging while his other arm drew back for a killing blow.

Shi Feng saw the shoulder move.

He drilled Returning Tide every single day, until retreating no longer meant retreating. Now he stepped back just far enough, let the blow pass, drew the knife from his belt and came back along the same short line.

A knife has less reach than a sword. At this distance, it doesn’t need any, Shi Feng told himself, and the thought was almost calm.

The point entered the unprotected throat. Cao Wenshu’s eyes went wide, shock frozen on his face, and he tried to speak. Shi Feng followed the knife in, caught the back of the old man’s head and pinned him to the stone. Qi gathered under his hand, fierce enough that another breath might still kill.

Shi Feng pushed the knife deeper.

The gathering force broke apart. Only then did he let go. He stepped backward and almost fell beside the body.

Mid Foundation Establishment, and the old man lay dead at his feet. This was the limit of what Shi Feng could handle now, not another easy victory. Shi Feng stared down at him, stunned by his own survival. The gap was real, he thought. So was the corpse.

His strength kept him alive long enough to fight, and Xu Changhe’s sword art opened wounds, spoiled blows and carried his last weapon to the throat. Neither one alone would’ve been enough.

He pressed a folded cloth to his side. His hands shook so badly he had to start the binding again, and he pulled it tight with his teeth while blood from his mouth darkened the cloth. Then he sat against the broken wall and swallowed a healing pill.

It worked cleanly, but the wound was still there. For a long while he counted breaths instead of victories.

When he could stand without the chamber tilting, he searched only what was safe to search. Under Cao Wenshu’s robe lay a sealed royal pouch, its identifying jade pulsing faintly as the body cooled.

Shi Feng left it where it was.

That jade will call someone, he thought. Or it’ll tell someone where this man died. Either way, I don’t want it near my gate.

Carrying unknown royal objects home would only bring the next assassin to Ling Qingzhu’s door, he thought. And no vitality rose from this human corpse. He’d repair himself with his own supplies.

He fetched the root bundle from the path and went down the dry ravine, one hand pressed to his side. At the lower slope he washed his face in the stream and closed his collar over the marks on his throat. He’d promised to be back before the vegetable market closed.

Shi Feng looked toward the distant roofs of the capital.

What a terrible detour. He was going to be late for the vegetables.

chapters.title: The Bandage She Tied
chapters.html:
“Aiya! Young man, you’re bleeding on my lane!” Granny Qin shrieked from behind her brazier. “Heaven help us, sit down, sit down! Have a sesame cake!”

Shi Feng looked down. A dark drop soaked through his outer cloth and landed on the stones outside his gate.

He’d washed at the lower spring and changed the cloth. That hid the worst of it, until the long walk through the capital pulled fresh blood through the binding. Now the whole lane was staring.

“The medicine peddler is hurt!” a woman gasped, stunned.

“That’s a lot of blood…”

“Quiet! Fairy Ling is coming!”

“…”

The gate flew open. Ling Qingzhu stood with her veil hastily tied and her fingers white around the latch. Her eyes widened at the blood before he crossed the threshold.

“Sit down,” Ling Qingzhu said.

Shi Feng sat. For once neither of them could find an argument.

She shut the gate and pulled off her veil. Only then did he see how pale she was.

She brought clean water, a folded towel and the little box of household medicines. He’d already cleaned the wound and swallowed a healing pill outside the city. What he needed now was a fresh dressing and time for the torn flesh to knit.

Ling Qingzhu knelt beside the stool and reached for the binding.

A strand of black hair fell beside her cheek. She tucked it behind her ear and bent closer. Shi Feng watched her instead of lifting his arm.

“Your arm,” Ling Qingzhu said.

He obeyed, still staring.

“Did you hurt your head too?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“No,” Shi Feng replied. “You’re just very close.”

Her fingers paused. Then she pushed his chin away with the clean towel, her ears red.

“Cut the edge first,” Shi Feng said. “Don’t pull it.”

She obeyed. Her hands were steady until the cloth came away, and then they stopped.

The tear was ugly. Bruises spread past it and darkened toward the ribs. His collar hid most of the marks on his throat, but when he moved to take the towel she saw enough of those as well. Her heart seized, and her whole body went still.

“The mountains?” Ling Qingzhu asked, her voice shaking.

“On the road home,” Shi Feng said.

Her gaze rose to his face. He couldn’t tell her about a dead mid Foundation Establishment cultivator, Shi Feng thought. She still believed his meridians were ruined and he was just a man who sold ointment from a board. To explain the truth, he’d have to give up far more than an attacker’s name.

So he guided her through the dressing instead. She tied it too tightly. He showed her where to loosen it, and she fixed it without one sharp reply. Then she sat back with the spare strip of cloth twisted between her fingers.

“You could’ve sent word,” Ling Qingzhu said. “A runner. A note. A rock through the window.”

“I got home,” Shi Feng said.

“Idiot! That’s not the same thing!” Ling Qingzhu said.

He looked at her. She was angry, but there was no contempt in it, no demand for payment, and no complaint about the trouble he caused. There was fear under the anger. Shi Feng was shaken. He was grateful, and he found he had no answer at all!

That night, she wouldn’t let him lie on the floor. She dragged the spare quilt off her bed and stacked it under his bedding herself, and then she lay down behind the bed curtain without a word. Shi Feng stared at the ceiling. A few steps away, her breathing stayed too quiet and too even to be asleep. She was listening to him.

The next morning he cancelled his furnace session.

Gao Yuan kept the deposit anyway and sent a note very fast. The room was reserved, he wrote. A sick tenant didn’t make a furnace owner any less responsible for his maintenance.

Shi Feng sent back a correction to the sum and an order that the remaining materials stay sealed. Then he told his buyers about the delay, one by one. Yan Meizhen accepted a later delivery and sent back a laughing note, teasing him for getting hurt without her. Zhu Shan sent his messenger twice with the same question: “Done yet?”

“Not yet,” Shi Feng told the messenger, both times.

He didn’t try to refine from his floor bedding. Mo Tianheng’s memories told him how the work should be done, and his wounded body told him why today was the wrong day.

For several days he used healing medicine from his own reserve. His physique took each dose cleanly. There was no pill resistance, and no impurity built up to turn the cure into another injury. But torn flesh still needed time to repair, and no pill could make the signal fort unhappen. The cost went into the account book beside the lost deposit.

Ling Qingzhu took over supper.

The rice improved after Shi Feng explained that lifting the lid again and again didn’t help it cook. The broth was less successful. She got impatient with floating scraps and added so many greens that the spoon stood upright.

“Is it edible?” Ling Qingzhu demanded, glaring at the pot. “Say yes.”

“It’s a forest,” Shi Feng said, and took a second helping.

She watched him eat it, and her shoulders loosened and the hard inspection was over. On the fourth evening she found him writing by the lamp, and she took the brush out of his hand.

“It can wait,” Ling Qingzhu said. “Your accounts have waited years. They won’t die tonight.”

“The furnace owner disagrees,” Shi Feng said.

“Then let him disagree by himself!” Ling Qingzhu said.

She capped the ink and moved the paper out of reach. He could have taken it back. Instead he watched her set a fresh cup beside him and adjust the lamp so its smoke stopped drifting into his face.

Nobody was watching them in the room. Nobody would praise her for a convincing marriage. It was concern, plain and simple, Shi Feng thought, and the thought pleased him so much that he let the account wait.

In the eastern residence, Sima Yu received a report that didn’t comfort him.

“Cao Wenshu hasn’t returned, Your Highness,” Ge Fan said, kneeling. “Our private searchers reached the old signal fort before the mountain patrol. His throat was pierced and his wrist broken in a close fight.”

“And the appointment slip?” Sima Yu asked sharply.

“Burned on the spot, Your Highness. Our men left the body before the road patrol climbed the ridge, so only his official royal service jade remained at his belt,” Ge Fan said. He swallowed. “We can’t tell who killed him.”

Sima Yu’s expression went cold, and his fingers trembled on the paper. A forty-year royal servant at mid Foundation Establishment, killed by someone nobody could name! And once the mountain patrol carried that service jade down to the palace, the King would demand to know why the eastern residence had borrowed him from active duty.

He read the report once more and held the unsigned appointment note over a candle. If anyone started investigating, it would begin by asking why he’d secretly paid a mid Foundation Establishment cultivator to enter mountains frequented by the crippled husband who had humiliated his household before the banquet guests. It might end by discussing the killing of a royal servant in terms he couldn’t control.

“The dead can keep the first question with them,” Sima Yu said.

The paper curled into black ash.

At Qingliu Lane, Shi Feng stood in the courtyard for the first time without stopping halfway across it. His side still ached, but the dressing stayed clean.

Ling Qingzhu came out carrying the basin.

“You’re not going out!” Ling Qingzhu said.

“I’m standing beside the tree,” Shi Feng said.

“You were looking at the gate,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“The gate is beside the tree,” Shi Feng said.

She narrowed her eyes. He let the argument end there and sat on the bench.

For the next dressing her hands didn’t hesitate. She loosened the binding before he asked and passed the clean cloth under his arm without touching the tender edge. Shi Feng watched the top of her bowed head. A loose strand of black hair slipped from its pin and lay against her cheek, and she ignored it until the knot was done.

“Better?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“Yes,” Shi Feng said.

She looked relieved. Then she scolded him: if he was going to ruin clothes in the mountains, he could at least wear the cheaper ones. He took the scolding without pointing out that she’d never bought a single robe he owned.

The bandage lay warm and neat against his side, and he thought that no physician’s work had ever felt so careful.

For this evening, that was enough.

chapters.title: A Dead Man of the Royal House
chapters.html:
Cao Wenshu's identifying jade reached the palace before his body did.

An hour after Sima Yu's private searchers slipped away from the ridge, a mountain patrol had found the ruined signal fort after noticing fresh stone scattered across the lower path. The officer recognised the official royal service jade at the corpse's waist and sent a runner down at once. By evening the jade lay on a tray outside the council chamber, still carrying the dead servant's name.

Sima Yu heard about it while choosing which robe to wear to court.

He dismissed the attendant and stared at the empty doorway. Guo Zhen could be missing on an errand. Cao Wenshu had served the royal house for forty years. His death required an answer that a household clerk couldn't bury.

The next morning, Sima Yu found the jade beside the King's hand.

The King asked why Cao Wenshu had been outside the capital.

The assembled officials lowered their eyes. They had come expecting a dispute about grain carts. Nobody reached for the grain report now.

Sima Yu bowed.

“He accepted a private commission,” Sima Yu said. “I heard he intended to inspect the mountain roads.”

The King turned the jade over. A narrow paper lay beneath it, copied from the royal service book.

The King pointed out that the eastern residence had requested Cao Wenshu's release from duty. The commission money came from Sima Yu's private account. He wanted to know what the prince had sent the servant to inspect.

Sima Yu's expression stayed respectful. Inwardly his thoughts moved quickly. The service office had copied the payment before giving him a chance to explain it. Someone had decided this was worth the King's attention.

“The hunting roads have become unsafe,” Sima Yu said. “Guo Zhen vanished there. I wanted a trustworthy man to inquire.”

The King observed that this trustworthy man had been sent alone, without notice to the patrol office. Now he was dead and the office that could have supported him knew nothing.

Sima Yu lowered his head farther.

“The omission was mine,” Sima Yu said.

He could admit carelessness. He couldn't tell the chamber that a medicine peddler had killed two men sent to murder him. He still had no witness to Cao Wenshu's last fight and no explanation that would survive those words being spoken aloud.

The King watched him for several breaths.

The King removed the eastern residence's authority over auxiliary road appointments and returned it to the patrol office. He also ordered Sima Yu's household to pay the burial grant owed to Cao Wenshu's family.

A clerk began writing.

Sima Yu felt the attention of every official who pretended to study the floor. The authority had been small compared with succession to the throne. It had still put several useful posts in his hands. Those men would answer to another office by tomorrow.

“Your son accepts the correction,” Sima Yu said.

The King ordered an inquiry into the royal servant's death. Another unexplained private errand would not be accepted as an accident.

Nobody accused Sima Yu of murder in that chamber. Nobody had proof of the order he had given. That absence didn't make the censure less public. The clerk read the removal aloud, and three officials stepped forward to acknowledge their new duties.

Sima Yu stayed in place until dismissed.

Outside, the corridor seemed much longer than usual. A junior official who normally hurried over to greet him stopped to inspect a pillar. Sima Yu passed without looking at the man. Kindness was easy when people wanted something. He remembered its absence just as clearly.

Ling Qingzhu learned the news that afternoon from Ling Zhen.

Her uncle came to Qingliu Lane without a carriage, carrying a small household packet. Ling Qingzhu tied her white veil before opening the gate. Shi Feng was at the furnace yard, finishing a short booking.

“Your name isn't in the order,” Ling Zhen said after they sat. “Neither is his. I checked.”

“Then why tell me?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“Because Cao Wenshu died in Hengyun,” Ling Zhen said. “Because Guo Zhen is still missing. And because the prince has just lost authority he enjoyed using.”

Ling Qingzhu looked toward Shi Feng's empty stool.

She remembered the marks on his throat. He had called the mountain trip troublesome. She had tied the bandage and disliked how little he said about the wound. Now an old royal servant was dead near the road he used.

“The patrol found him?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“At a broken signal fort,” Ling Zhen said. “That's all the report gives us.”

She asked nothing about Cao Wenshu's realm. She knew enough of the palace to understand what his presence meant. But the man she had bandaged was supposed to have ruined cultivation. Those two facts would not fit together just because she stared at them.

Ling Zhen set the household packet on the table.

“The Wei matter stays with the city office,” Ling Zhen said. “No retainer has the right to take your husband out of this courtyard. If anyone tries, send for me.”

Ling Qingzhu nodded. The condition Shi Feng had insisted on now seemed less like one more demand and more like a sensible boundary.

After Ling Zhen left, she sat beside the cooling kettle. The gate remained shut. She removed her veil, folded it carefully and found that she had no interest in the book beside her chair.

When Shi Feng came home, she looked first at his side.

“Does it still hurt?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“A little when I turn too quickly,” Shi Feng said.

“Then stop turning quickly,” Ling Qingzhu said.

He set down his bag. She had warmed water and laid out fresh binding cloth. He saw both before she could pretend they had been left there by chance.

Shi Feng sat and let her check the bandage. Her fingers were careful where they had once been impatient. He wanted to touch her hand and didn't.

“Cao Wenshu is dead,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“I heard,” Shi Feng said.

She waited. He offered nothing more. After a moment she smoothed the new cloth and tied the end where it wouldn't press when he lay down.

Across the capital, Sima Yu received the same report for the third time. The fort was broken. Cao Wenshu was dead. A root gatherer matching Shi Feng's description had passed the lower gate that evening.

It wasn't proof. Sima Yu no longer needed proof to know where his suspicion belonged.

chapters.title: The Payment That Was a Root
chapters.html:
“Don’t throw that away,” Zhu Shan said, catching the empty lid. “My daughter painted it.”

Shi Feng looked at the red animal on the wood. Its four legs were different lengths.

“A tiger?” Shi Feng asked.

“A horse,” Zhu Shan replied stiffly.
