Shi Feng wrapped the root in clean cloth and returned the box without another comment. The guard fitted the lid carefully. He looked far happier with it than with the little animal’s resemblance.

The completed order from Master Shen sat wrapped on the stall board, delivered by the peddler as far as Zhu Shan knew. The payment sat beside them, wrapped in cloth: a Golden Vein Root, knotted and crooked, with fine golden lines still clear beneath its skin. Shi Feng had asked for it himself before the pills were made.

Zhu Shan found it on the road while guarding a caravan, and it was a fine ingredient for the work Shi Feng was doing on his bones. A medicine shop would charge far more.

Zhu Shan pocketed his pills and left without another word. Ling Qingzhu happened to be standing beside the board. She watched the knotted root stay behind, and her expression turned puzzled.

“He paid you with that gnarled thing?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“Partly,” Shi Feng said.

“So someone finally out-bargained you,” Ling Qingzhu said, and the neighbouring stallkeepers perked up their ears.

“He paid a root and kept the box…”

“…”

Shi Feng unwrapped one end. The cut surface was clean, the golden veins hadn’t darkened, and Zhu Shan hadn’t swapped in a cheaper root after fixing the price.

“I asked for it,” Shi Feng said.

“Instead of spirit stones?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“Instead of buying it with more spirit stones,” Shi Feng said.

She fell silent. He checked the other end and wrapped it again. A root this good was hard to find, and he could use it himself without paying three merchants to pass it along. To her, a careful buyer was a greedy buyer. Yet the thought that he knew exactly what he was doing kept coming back, in small, annoying ways.

“It looks like something a dog dug up,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Lots of useful things do,” Shi Feng said.

She glanced at the little jar of cream in her sleeve. Then she hid it before he could see. Shi Feng saw anyway. He said nothing at all, though the corner of his mouth moved.

A man in a rich brown robe pushed through the crowd by the stall, holding out a paper.

“You’re the peddler who knows a private refiner?” Shao Fu demanded. “I’m Shao Fu. My uncle needs this pill. Can you get it?”

Shi Feng took the list and read it from top to bottom. The heavy herbs on it made his eyebrows lift.

“I can’t supply that,” Shi Feng said, and handed it back.

“I can pay!” Shao Fu said.

“That doesn’t change what I can supply,” Shi Feng said.

The ingredients weren’t the problem. Shi Feng knew the formula well, and Mo Tianheng’s experience showed him how to make far better pills. But his current qi couldn’t hold that preparation steady until it finished, and he refused to pretend otherwise. A good price wouldn’t turn a failed pill into medicine for anybody’s uncle, he thought.

Shao Fu’s face went red, and he doubled his offer. The crowd drew a sharp breath.

“Double!” someone whispered. “For one list!”

“He’ll take it. Anyone would.”

“Look at his face. He’s not taking it.”

Shi Feng shook his head and pointed Shao Fu toward the established medicine counters. The man left cursing, and the market stared after him, stunned. Ling Qingzhu turned to her husband, her expression astonished.

“He was willing to pay more,” Ling Qingzhu said, almost offended on the man’s behalf.

“He wanted something I can’t provide,” Shi Feng said.

“You didn’t even try to bargain,” Ling Qingzhu said. “Who are you, and what did you do with my husband?”

“Would that make his uncle any better?” Shi Feng asked.

She laughed, then shook her head. It was hard to call a man a swindler when he turned money away. She didn’t take back her earlier thought, but she stopped suggesting that he’d been cheated over the root.

At home, Shi Feng tucked the root into his corner of the room, under his rolled-up bedding, where it was out of her sight. His side had healed enough that a day of ordinary work no longer reopened the wound, though he still avoided any movement that pulled hard on the new flesh. He was powerful, he told himself, and that didn’t make rest foolish after fighting a mid Foundation Establishment cultivator.

Before sunset he took his plain wooden practice blade into the courtyard. The good sword was broken at the signal fort. For now, wood was enough to work through Xu Changhe’s teachings.

He thrust, turned the thrust into a short slash, and brought the point back toward the same opening. The first stroke was fast. The return was faster.

An enemy who dodged the first strike would meet the next before finding his footing. That was what the enforcer meant. Shi Feng repeated it until he no longer had to think about the turn of his wrist. He could crush many opponents with strength alone, he thought. Learning to use that strength properly would make the hard fights easier.

Ling Qingzhu was out collecting a letter, and nobody stood in the courtyard to ask why a cripple’s wooden blade sounded so sharp in the air.

That night, he prepared the root.

He waited on his floor bedding until Ling Qingzhu’s breathing slowed behind the bed curtain. Then he slipped out to the kitchen with the root, his cups and a single candle stub, and shut the door.

He didn’t try the impressive pill that Mo Tianheng might once have made from it. A simple medicinal preparation would give his body what it needed. He cut a small portion, added two cheaper ingredients and heated them slowly.

The first extraction came out too thin. He changed the water for the next portion instead of pretending it was good enough because the root was costly.

The second was right.

He drank the medicine and took a pill from his own stock. Warmth flowed through his body, and the golden traces in his bones grew brighter. More of the skeleton answered than before.

Not all of it.

Shi Feng thought: the golden bones are still unfinished, and the First Extreme is waiting beyond them. Only after finishing both could he enter Foundation Establishment. The tournament notice gave him a deadline, but he wouldn’t wreck his future by rushing toward it.

He opened his eyes and counted the root that remained. There was enough for more preparations. He wrapped it carefully, pleased with Zhu Shan’s payment, even though it added little to the purse he could spend tomorrow. Then he crept back to the floor without a sound and lay still. The bed creaked once. He held his breath until it stopped.

The next morning, in the kitchen, Ling Qingzhu opened Su Wanning’s latest letter. The ink was smudged and every line ran into the next.

Her friend was coming to the capital!

Su Wanning wanted to meet the husband properly, because letters weren’t enough. Did he really argue over rope?! Did he smile?! Had the cheaper meals gotten better? Did Qingzhu like him?! Was she blushing right now? She’d better be blushing!

“Bring the man to dinner,” the letter finished, “and I’ll decide whether he’s a treasure or a swindler!”

Ling Qingzhu’s ears went warm. A swindler. She couldn’t remember why that word had once seemed so reasonable.

Ling Qingzhu frowned at the other line. She remembered writing it. Somehow it sounded far worse when someone else repeated it.

From the courtyard came the soft clink of Shi Feng rinsing his cups at the well.

Ling Qingzhu looked toward it, and her heart began to turn over a plan: one evening that would prove something she hadn’t yet decided how to name.

chapters.title: The Friend at the Door
chapters.html:
“Honoured guest, honoured guest, there’s a far wider courtyard standing empty just two lanes over!” Bao Shun cried, trotting beside the carriage with both sleeves flapping.

The black carriage filled Qingliu Lane. Granny Qin forgot her brazier and burned a tray of sesame cakes watching its gold-thread curtains.

“Who owns that carriage?”

“It must be for Fairy Ling.”

“Nobody visits the cripple. Of course it’s for her…”

“…”

The gate opened, and Ling Qingzhu walked out, white veil in place, before Bao Shun reached the carriage door.

“My friend came to visit me,” Ling Qingzhu said with her broker smile. “She didn’t come to buy the lane.”

Bao Shun laughed awkwardly, bowed twice and backed away.

The curtain lifted. A young woman in apricot silk stepped down, a jade bell at her waist ringing softly. Su Wanning, a salt merchant's daughter, was bouncing before her feet touched the ground.

“Qingzhu, Qingzhu, Qingzhu!” Su Wanning cried, and threw both arms around her friend. “Look at you, you’ve gotten thin! Is the capital starving you? Is this really the lane? It’s so narrow, and where’s your husband, is he hiding, did he get scared?”

“The capital feeds me fine,” Ling Qingzhu said, prying herself loose. “I’m not thin. You’re squeezing me. Come in. Stop eyeing the lane.”

Su Wanning looked at the lane anyway. Then she looked at the gate, the pear tree, and the plain table beneath it, and she pointed at all of it.

“Why doesn’t that roof tile match? Why is a cord holding your window? Is that the whole kitchen? It’s tiny, it’s so cute,” Su Wanning said.

Through the open door of the only room, she also saw a single bed, a chest at its foot, and a neat roll of bedding on the floor in the far corner.

“One bed?” Su Wanning whispered, eyes huge. “And that’s his bedding on the floor, Qingzhu, really?”

Ling Qingzhu looked at the sky.

Shi Feng came out carrying a tray. He set down three cups without a sound.

“So you’re the husband, the famous husband,” Su Wanning said, leaning toward him. “Qingzhu’s letters say you argue over rope. Is it true?”

“So this is the famous friend,” Shi Feng said.

Su Wanning laughed loudly, then peered at him. He sounded polite, and that worried her more than rudeness would have.

Ling Qingzhu took a cup before he could finish setting it down. Then her gaze dropped to the hand he kept resting against his side.

“Does it still hurt?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“Not much,” Shi Feng said.

“Don’t carry the heavy water jar,” Ling Qingzhu said at once.

“I wasn’t going to,” Shi Feng said.

“You were,” Ling Qingzhu said.

Su Wanning’s eyes lit up. That question came far too fast for an introduction. Ling Qingzhu watched the man’s movements before she thought to watch her own words.

So the contract wife already counts his wounds, Su Wanning thought. Ooh, interesting.

Su Wanning waited until the kitchen doorway was empty.

“Still wearing the veil with me here?” Su Wanning asked.

“You’re a guest,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

“But your husband isn’t?” Su Wanning asked.

Ling Qingzhu’s hand stopped on her cup. Su Wanning grinned. That answer was much better than another denial.

“The Qingshi boy at the royal youth review,” Su Wanning said. “You were sixteen. Remember?”

“His eyes stayed so calm when—” Ling Qingzhu said.

“EYES, Big Sis Qingzhu!” Su Wanning whispered. “I asked about the review!”

“I meant his composure,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“And your jealousy of a tenth-ranked fairy?” Su Wanning asked. “Our First Fairy, jealous!”

“Have some tea,” Ling Qingzhu said.

Su Wanning leaned forward, delighted. Ling Qingzhu's ears burned above the ties of her white veil.

“One more word and you can eat your own carriage curtains,” Ling Qingzhu said.

In the next room, Shi Feng knocked two medicine jars together while sorting a crate. Through the rattle, he caught something about eyes, sixteen, and a tenth-ranked fairy. Another story about their friends, probably. He shifted the crate and heard nothing more until Su Wanning raised her voice again.

Ling Qingzhu checked the doorway. Su Wanning followed her glance and finally lowered her voice. Whatever she remembered, it stayed between the women.

“But you paid him so generously!” Su Wanning whispered loudly. “I hope he keeps you comfortable. Does he? Is he nice, is he a little handsome?”

Ling Qingzhu glanced toward the kitchen.

“He isn’t difficult to live with,” Ling Qingzhu said, a little too fast. “That’s all I said.”

“Isn’t difficult?” Su Wanning squealed. “That means yes, that means so much yes!”

Ling Qingzhu pressed her thumb hard against the cup. “He cooks for me,” Ling Qingzhu muttered. “He also insults my knife work. It balances out.”

“He cooks? How useful, you always hated waiting for the household kitchens,” Su Wanning said.

That was true. It didn’t explain why Ling Qingzhu’s heart warmed each time she came home and found supper waiting.

Back in the kitchen, Shi Feng finished a label. He'd heard the payment talk clearly enough.

Ten thousand spirit stones, he thought. Paid generously. Taken care of.

The money had never crossed the table, and he was sure she knew it. He sneered in his heart. She could tell her friends whatever story she liked. He’d written the truth into the account with his own hand. He wouldn’t stand at his own gate begging to be judged more kindly.

He rinsed his hands and carried out a plate of sliced pear.

“So what do you sell? Does it earn much? Do I get a discount?” Su Wanning asked, taking a piece.

“Enough to keep going,” Shi Feng said.

“How peaceful,” Su Wanning sighed. “A quiet life.”

Shi Feng looked at the blade resting beside the kitchen door. A quiet life? Not long ago he’d killed a mid Foundation Establishment cultivator. He didn’t correct her.

Su Wanning ate her pear. Then her gaze fell on a strip of plain cloth tied around Ling Qingzhu’s wrist.

“What’s that cloth on your wrist?” Su Wanning asked. “It doesn’t match your robe, you never wear things that don’t match.”

“It protects my skin from the new sleeve,” Ling Qingzhu said. “It’s useful. Very practical.”

Ling Qingzhu looked down. The cloth matched nothing. Shi Feng had tied it there himself after noticing the red mark, and she’d forgotten it was even there.

Ling Qingzhu’s ears reddened above her veil’s ties as she stared at the cloth in shock. Su Wanning clapped both hands over her mouth, eyes shining.

“…Don’t,” Ling Qingzhu said. “Don’t say it. Not one word.”

Shi Feng passed her another piece of pear. Ling Qingzhu accepted it while glaring at Su Wanning, who took the glare as another excellent answer.

By late afternoon the two women had worked through household gossip and visiting relations, and then two stories Shi Feng had no wish to understand. He came back when Ling Qingzhu called him in to ask about supper.

“We could eat here,” Ling Qingzhu said. “It’s quiet, and nobody stares.”

“There’s enough for three if I make another dish,” Shi Feng said.

“Nonsense!” Su Wanning cried, clapping her hands. “Yuelan Terrace! I just arrived, and everyone says the music there is amazing! We’re going, all three of us, a proper evening! Qingzhu, say yes!”

Ling Qingzhu turned to Shi Feng with bright, open hope.

She wanted her friend to see them outside this little courtyard. She wanted an evening with him as well. The two wishes tangled together before she could separate them.

“A proper one,” Ling Qingzhu said. “I’ll even let you read the prices out loud. Will you come?”

Shi Feng thought, She isn’t performing.

That was the dangerous part. He knew Yuelan Terrace by name and reputation, and he knew what its menu cost. A man could refuse an outing without losing face. No contract forced him to buy a pleasant evening for a woman who believed she already owned his company.

But the hope in her eyes was real, and he wanted to be the reason it stayed there.

“Yes,” Shi Feng said.

Ling Qingzhu’s eyes brightened at once. Su Wanning began choosing dishes aloud, naming three different fish.

Shi Feng went back to the kitchen and finished the labels. Only after the last jar was sealed did he open the account book beside it and count his reserve: two hundred and nineteen spirit stones, saved coin by coin across weeks of furnace smoke, plus a note from Gao Yuan warning that Eastern Palace clerks had been asking which herb stalls sold Hengyun mountain roots.

Sima Yu was still looking for the man on the signal-fort path, and tomorrow night Yuelan Terrace was going to take almost every stone in his purse.

chapters.title: Not Hired Work
chapters.html:
“You noticed that?” Ling Qingzhu asked, stopping beneath the eaves with her sleeves still dusty from the road.

Shi Feng stood on a stool beside the room’s only window, tying the loose cord of its screen. It had knocked against the frame all through the previous night.

“It kept making the same noise,” Shi Feng said.

“I thought you’d slept through it,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Did you?” Shi Feng asked.

She shook her head. He pulled the knot tight, tested the screen, and climbed down. Ling Qingzhu leaned past him to push the frame herself, and a loose strand of black hair brushed his wrist. The screen held.

She looked pleased in the simple way he liked best. There was no polite smile for guests and no distant look for men hoping to win her favour. She was just glad that something bothering her was fixed.

She swept the loose hair behind her ear. Shi Feng kept his hand on the chair and forgot to move it.

“Must I pay you to stop staring too?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“You couldn’t afford it,” Shi Feng replied.

She laughed, taking it as a joke. He smiled back despite the first half of her question.

“You’re very thorough, for a hired husband,” Ling Qingzhu said, trying to sound casual.

Shi Feng’s hand stopped on the back of the chair. For once he couldn’t brush off a phrase with a joke.

“Don’t call this hired work,” Shi Feng said.

Ling Qingzhu turned in surprise. He wasn’t smiling, and he wasn’t arguing about money. He looked at her calmly, and the calm was heavier than any shout.

“I was only teasing,” Ling Qingzhu said. “Since when do you bite?”

“The agreement covers what we do in public,” Shi Feng said. “Remembering whether you’ve eaten isn’t a performance.”

Her gaze fell on the bowl set upside down on the table, still warm from the stove. She had no answer, and her expression went blank. Over the garden wall, a grey head popped up.

“Aiya! He fixed the window and she called him hired!” Granny Qin whispered loudly to nobody. “Qin Bao, come and look, the husband is angry! Somebody take a sesame cake over there!”

“Granny Qin,” Shi Feng said without turning around, “your cakes are burning.”

“They are not!” Granny Qin cried, and vanished with a clatter.

Ling Qingzhu bit her lip. Her cousin said that very word at the Ling household this morning, she thought, and I carried it home like a stone in my sleeve!

The kitchen was familiar to her now, and so were all the small things he did without asking her to notice. A cup moved out of the sun. Broth kept warm. The vegetables she disliked quietly missing from her bowl.

She knew he was considerate. She never thought that naming the arrangement could hurt him. Then she found an explanation that was easier to understand, and her heart ached for him.

His cultivation was ruined. The whole capital mocked his marriage. He took this work for money, but being called hired still stung the pride of the genius he used to be. I should’ve been more careful, she thought.

“Fine,” Ling Qingzhu said softly. “I won’t say it again.”

Shi Feng studied her face. She looked sincere. Did she understand what I meant, he wondered, or has she found a kinder way to misunderstand it?

He moved the stool aside.

“Eat before it gets cold,” Shi Feng said.

They sat at the table, and he uncovered her bowl first. There was rice, a little meat, and vegetables bought that morning. Ling Qingzhu asked about his day, and she asked with unusual patience.

“A customer wanted one jar to cure his sore hands and his wife’s nagging,” Shi Feng said.

“Both?” Ling Qingzhu asked, putting down her chopsticks.

“He was very disappointed to hear the second problem needed no medicine,” Shi Feng said. “Only better manners.”

She laughed.

“Did you tell him that?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“He asked twice,” Shi Feng said.

“And then?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“His wife showed up,” Shi Feng said. “The problem got better right away. He stopped talking.”

Ling Qingzhu laughed so hard she had to cover her mouth with her sleeve. He found himself smiling too, though the sting by the window hadn’t quite gone.

“Will the buyers pay tomorrow?” Ling Qingzhu asked, picking out a green bean.

“Two of them promised,” Shi Feng said.

“Then you’ll be rich and unbearable by evening,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Promised,” Shi Feng repeated. “I’ve learned not to trust that word.”

She laughed again, and he thought, Money can wait one more night.

The evening slowly grew warm again.

After supper she gathered the bowls before he could stop her. One loose sleeve trailed through the leftover broth. Shi Feng caught her wrist, folded the cuff back, and let go once it was secure.

She stared at his hand, and her expression went strangely soft. An ordinary touch! It shouldn’t have made her forget where the basin stood.

At the kitchen door she turned the wrong way. He stepped aside without a single joke, and that somehow made it worse.

“Don’t,” Ling Qingzhu muttered.

“I said nothing,” Shi Feng said.

“You were going to,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Yes,” Shi Feng admitted.

They washed the bowls together. She dried them, and this time none slipped.

Afterward the pear tree’s shadow lay across the bench, and the courtyard lamp made a small gold circle on the stones. Ling Qingzhu sat down.

“Mind hearing about a ridiculous family fight?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“Will I have to settle it?” Shi Feng asked.

“No,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Then go ahead,” Shi Feng said.

Two relatives fought over who deserved the better seat at a banquet neither one meant to attend. By the end, their servants were shouting about cushions over the whole family’s honour, which they claimed was stuffed inside.

“And the servants?” Shi Feng asked.

“Worse,” Ling Qingzhu said. “The cook threatened to quit. The steward fainted. Nobody knew if he meant it. I took a bun and left.”

“Third Uncle said, ‘My grandfather’s cushion was embroidered with cranes!’” Ling Qingzhu said, puffing out her chest and dropping her voice low. “And Fifth Aunt said, ‘Your grandfather also sat on the floor!’”

Shi Feng burst out laughing. He knew exactly how hard that floor was.

She stopped, astonished at herself. She never meant to act so foolishly in front of anyone. Yet the joy of hearing him laugh drowned the embarrassment in a moment.

For a while neither of them mentioned the agreement.

I love her, Shi Feng thought.

The knowledge needed no great discovery. He wanted her company after tiring days. He listened for her footsteps at the gate. Her careless words could hurt because her opinion mattered.

He wasn’t waiting to be paid for any of it. Nor was he keeping an account of each kindness, hoping she’d finally owe him affection.

He only wanted her to understand the difference. That was all, and it was proving much harder than a mid Foundation Establishment cultivator.

Ling Qingzhu leaned back against the bench. The window screen above them stayed quiet.

“It’s much quieter,” Ling Qingzhu said. “Three nights that cord kept me up. I never said a word.”

Shi Feng followed her gaze.

“Yes,” Shi Feng said.

“Thank you,” Ling Qingzhu said.

The words were plain. He accepted them plainly.

Later she stopped at the door of the room and looked back. He was checking the gate latch before he put out the lamp. It was nothing impressive. No poet would recite it at a royal banquet.

Yet she wanted it to happen again tomorrow, and the thought made her draw the screen around the bed more slowly than usual.

A whisper floated over the wall.

“Did you hear that?” Granny Qin hissed. “She laughed! The cripple’s wife laughed, Qin Bao, and the husband laughed too!”

“…” Qin Bao said from somewhere behind her.

“Good night, Granny Qin,” Shi Feng called calmly.

“Good night, husband! Eat more!” Granny Qin answered, delighted, and the wall fell silent at last.

Shi Feng waited until her lamp was out and the rustle behind the screen had stopped. Then he went in quietly and spread his bedding on the floor in his corner. He laid the practice blade beside Xu Changhe’s notes and opened the account book by the dimmed lamp.

Tomorrow he would collect two payments and take her to Yuelan Terrace before Sima Yu’s quiet inquiries reached the southern furnace yards.

Tonight, listening to her breathing behind the screen, he knew why he had stayed.

chapters.title: A Proper Husband
chapters.html:
“Welcome to Yuelan Terrace, honoured guests!” Cao An, the attendant, sang, bowing so low that his topknot nearly brushed the floor.

Lanterns hung above an ornamental pond, and their light trembled on the water. Music drifted from an upper gallery, soft enough that guests could talk without raising their voices. The attendants wore clean robes and smiled with a care that was surely included in the prices.

Shi Feng read the menu before he sat down. The fish on it seemed to have a noble title.

Su Wanning chose a table beside the pond. Ling Qingzhu sat next to Shi Feng in her pale violet sleeves, arranging them so they wouldn’t trail across the dishes, and looked toward the musicians with open delight. Shi Feng decided that the view, at least, was worth the walk.

“The Three-Cloud Carp, honoured guest,” Cao An said. “From the Cold Peak springs.”

“What does it taste like?” Shi Feng asked.

The attendant told him.

They ordered rice, vegetables, a meat dish and the expensive carp. Su Wanning added a specialty she was curious about. Ling Qingzhu added another and told the attendant, “My husband likes savoury. Nothing sticky.”

Shi Feng turned to look at her.

She remembered! He’d never told her as a useful fact for their public act. They’d simply eaten enough meals together for her to notice, and that small pleasure made the bill harder to resent.

The attendant repeated the order and its price. Shi Feng checked that the room and ordinary music were still included, then nodded. Nobody was cheating him. He knew exactly what he’d agreed to buy.

“Master Shi, Master Shi,” Su Wanning said while they waited, “Qingzhu writes that you sell medicines, so how’s business, do you make lots of money, do you have apprentices, do you get tired of people asking?”

“Common ointments sell well,” Shi Feng said. “Some customers come back so often that I know their jars before they speak. Big orders need more planning than a street sale.”

“Oh, how practical,” Su Wanning said. “An ordinary life is so peaceful!”

“It gets better when people stop explaining it,” Shi Feng said.

Ling Qingzhu lowered her eyes, the veil already hiding her smile. Su Wanning laughed a moment later, deciding the answer was funny and not rude. Shi Feng did nothing to help her decide more firmly.

At the next table, two men noticed Ling Qingzhu.

“That’s Fairy Ling!” one whispered.

“The cripple beside her is the husband…”

“…”

One of the men, a plump youth in an embroidered robe, couldn’t resist. He walked over with a wine cup raised.

“Fairy Ling! This Hu Jian pays his respects!” Hu Jian declared, lifting his jade cup before looking Shi Feng over from collar to cuffs. “So this is the cripple husband? That robe’s washed to rags. Tell me, peddler, have you ever smelled Cold Peak spirit wine before your wife brought you upstairs, or do you need the waiter to read the price to you slowly?”

Laughter started at Hu Jian’s table. Ling Qingzhu’s expression turned to frost, her hand rising from her sleeve, but Shi Feng set his teacup down first.

“That isn’t Cold Peak spirit wine,” Shi Feng said calmly. “Cold Peak is sealed in red clay and smells of pine resin. You’re drinking last autumn’s valley press, which Yuelan Terrace serves to tables running a ninety-day credit slip.”

Hu Jian’s smile froze. The attendant standing beside the pillar coughed and looked painfully at the lanterns.

“I paid in coin before sitting,” Shi Feng continued, pouring Ling Qingzhu’s tea with a steady hand. “If Young Master Hu wants to compare purses, ask the counter to bring out your father’s credit ledger first.”

“He smelled the vintage from three paces away?” an older merchant at the rail murmured.

“And Hu Jian has been boasting about that jug for half an hour on house credit!”

“Look at Young Master Shi’s composure—he didn’t even raise his voice.”

“Hu Jian!” Su Wanning cried, springing up with delighted fury. “Your father buys his salt from MY father on credit too! Should I tell him you’re waving unpaid valley wine at Qingzhu’s husband, should I, should I?”

Hu Jian’s face went from red to chalk-white. “I… I was only joking!” Hu Jian stammered, backing away so fast he left his jade cup on the rail.

“Your cup, Young Master Hu,” Ling Qingzhu called after him, sweet as syrup. “Have the house put it on your ninety-day tab.” Around the pond, several guests raised their cups toward Shi Feng with open respect. It was the first time in months anyone in a capital hall had looked at him and seen a young master instead of a cripple.

Su Wanning suddenly got very interested in the pond when her friend turned her head. Ling Qingzhu shifted her chair closer to Shi Feng’s.

It could have been part of the public act. Yet her sleeve resting against his hand didn’t feel so simple, and Shi Feng thought, This isn’t the act.

The first dishes arrived. Ling Qingzhu reached across him for the serving spoon, but Shi Feng took it first, picked a piece without the bitter garnish and set it in her bowl before he served himself.

She accepted it without surprise.

Su Wanning watched much more carefully than she watched the food.

“Ooh, you two look so married,” Su Wanning said, leaning in. “Qingzhu, you like him, don’t you?”

Ling Qingzhu’s head came up at once.

“We are married,” Ling Qingzhu said, much too fast. “Eat your rice, Wanning.”

The certainty startled all three of them, each for a different reason. Su Wanning expected a blush. Ling Qingzhu didn’t mean to sound offended. Shi Feng found that four plain words could make him forget the menu completely.

He put down the spoon.

Beneath the table, her fingers touched his wrist. She didn’t pull them back when he looked at her. Instead Ling Qingzhu asked, with great dignity, “Tried the dish I ordered? Or still reading prices?”

“Not yet,” Shi Feng said.

He tried it. It was excellent, which made the price much harder to complain about.

For a while the talk ran easily. Su Wanning described a young master who sent the wrong poem to two women, then blamed his servant for copying it badly. Ling Qingzhu knew one of the women and filled in the part Su Wanning left out.

“Did both women return the gifts?” Shi Feng asked.

“Neither, can you believe it?” Su Wanning said. “They both kept the gifts and said the poem was terrible!”

Shi Feng laughed. Ling Qingzhu leaned closer as she joined him, and her black hair slipped over one shoulder.

Su Wanning’s doubts began to ease. Whatever strange private bargain lay behind this marriage, her friend didn’t look miserable. The man was blunt, and his robe was clearly worn, but Ling Qingzhu watched him more often than she watched the expensive room.

That, she thought, was never in the letters.

The carp arrived with its crisp skin laid neatly beside it. Shi Feng knew enough about cooking to respect the work. He separated a portion from the small bones and placed it in Ling Qingzhu’s bowl.

She tasted it, then looked up.

“Yours was better,” Ling Qingzhu said. “Don’t tell the chef.”

Su Wanning raised her brows.

Shi Feng knew exactly which meal she meant. He remembered her fighting the lotus shoots, the splashed water, and her laughter when he put the thick pieces into the pot first.

“Mine had fewer witnesses,” Shi Feng said.

Ling Qingzhu’s eyes curved above her veil.

The warmth in her eyes above the veil was worth far more to him than winning an argument about which fish deserved its price. She ordered one last dish to share. Shi Feng saw the attendant write it down, heard the sum, and accepted it.

He still had enough. It wasn’t enough to do this again tomorrow, and it wasn’t enough to ignore the days ahead. But it was enough to choose this evening without turning his feelings into a fight over food.

Afterward Su Wanning suggested a walk past the pond. Ling Qingzhu rose, then waited for Shi Feng instead of hurrying after her friend.

He offered his arm.

She took it.

At the railing, small fish gathered under the lantern reflections wherever guests dropped crumbs. Su Wanning declared that even the fish here ate better than most people.

Shi Feng glanced at the kitchen door.

“At least they have the right address,” Shi Feng said.

Ling Qingzhu laughed softly beside him.

When they got back to the table, the bill had arrived. Shi Feng took it before either woman could reach the tray.

The total was written in a beautifully steady hand.

He read it, and his heart sank.

chapters.title: The Last Eleven Stones
chapters.html:
Two hundred and eight spirit stones.

Shi Feng read the bill a second time. Reading it twice didn’t make a single dish any cheaper.

The prices matched what the attendant promised. The room and ordinary music were included. There was no fake charge for a spoon, no hidden fee for looking at the pond, and no convenient mistake he could expose with one steady finger.

The evening simply cost that much. He thought, A fish with a noble title should at least cost less than a sword!

Beside him, Ling Qingzhu was telling Su Wanning about the replacement well rope. “Half the afternoon,” Ling Qingzhu said. “He measured it twice. I wanted to push him down the well.” Her voice was warm. She told the story with affection now.

Su Wanning laughed.

“He argued over a rope?” Su Wanning gasped, then laughed, patting Ling Qingzhu’s hand. “Oh, he’s so careful, that’s wonderful, a husband who counts is a husband who keeps your money!”

Shi Feng counted out the payment.

At the next table, the plump youth from earlier was gone, but his friend stayed behind, and the attendants stopped to stare.

“Two hundred and eight, in coin!” an attendant whispered.

“The cripple paid that?” a guest muttered, stunned.

“…”

The household fortune now stood at eleven spirit stones.

Shi Feng kept his expression level while the attendant carried away enough money to make his old clay furnace look like a gift from Heaven. Eleven stones, he thought bitterly. Eleven! I survived a mid Foundation Establishment cultivator, and a carp did this to me.

Ling Qingzhu turned toward him, and her expression was full of hope.

“Well? Was it good?” Ling Qingzhu asked. “Be honest. I’ll know if you lie.”

She meant the meal. Or maybe the evening. The hope in her eyes above the veil made either answer worth giving honestly.

“Yes,” Shi Feng said.

It was true! That was exactly why the bill hurt in such an absurd place.

Outside, Su Wanning’s carriage waited beneath the lanterns. Bao Shun somehow appeared at the carriage door with an offer of a better inn for the lady.

Ling Qingzhu dismissed him with one look. The broker bowed three times and disappeared.

“Qingzhu, you must write to me every day!” Su Wanning said, hugging her friend, and then she whirled to Shi Feng. “And you, take good care of her, Brother Shi, or I’ll come back and ask every day!”

“I’m trying,” Shi Feng said.

Ling Qingzhu glanced at him quickly. He wasn’t smiling the sharp way he did at dishonest merchants. He was just answering.

Su Wanning looked satisfied. She climbed into the carriage, convinced that her friend found an odd but useful husband. Ling Qingzhu waited until the wheels turned the corner, then took Shi Feng’s arm again.

They walked home.

The night was clear. Shops were closing along the road, and the smell of hot oil lingered beside a stall where the owner had finally stopped claiming the oil was fresh. Ling Qingzhu talked about the music, then the fish, then the ridiculous poem Su Wanning told.

Shi Feng listened.

At a narrow crossing he stepped to the outside of the path so a cart wouldn’t brush her sleeve. She moved closer without thinking and stayed there after the cart passed.

He liked that more than he should.

Beneath a lantern, she stopped to fix a loose clasp in her hair and couldn’t find its edge. Shi Feng raised the lantern higher. She settled it herself with a small, triumphant breath.

“Better,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Yes,” Shi Feng said.

She looked up and smiled. No audience was waiting to approve. For a few breaths, he nearly told her everything that mattered.

Then she started wondering aloud whether Su Wanning liked the evening, and the moment passed. At the courtyard Shi Feng opened the gate. The pear tree’s shadow lay across their familiar table, and the little house smelled faintly of the herbs he’d dried that afternoon.

Ling Qingzhu paused at the door of their one room.

“I’m glad you came,” Ling Qingzhu said warmly. “Even if you glared at every price tonight.”

Shi Feng looked at her in the lamplight.

“So am I,” Shi Feng said.

She went inside, and the door closed softly behind her. A moment later came the rustle of the folding screen being drawn across.

He stood a moment longer in the courtyard. Then he went into the kitchen and emptied his purse onto the table.

Eleven stones clicked onto the wood. He lined them up.

His All-Devouring Physique had swallowed the spirit of a Profound Heaven alchemy master. His mind held knowledge rich households would fight to buy. His sword was improving. He’d killed a mid Foundation Establishment cultivator and walked home alive.

And right now he was calculating how much rice was left in the kitchen.

Shi Feng began to laugh.

Quietly at first, and then so hard that he had to cover his mouth so he wouldn’t wake her through the wall.

What a magnificent husband! He could survive the killing blow of a man who pushed him to his limit, yet three people eating fish had nearly finished his purse!

When the laughter faded, he drew a clean sheet of paper toward him.

The cure wasn’t hard to name. He needed to earn more and keep some of it. For too long, every useful pill and rare root went straight into cultivation, while his daily expenses waited for the next customer to pay.

That would change.

He listed the buyers who paid promptly. Yan Meizhen came first. Zhu Shan came next, as long as the guard paid the full balance before collection.

Regular orders. Smaller batches he could make reliably. Enough advance payment for ingredients and furnace time. Clear collection dates. Cash set aside before he touched the retained pills.

He’d still take his agreed share for cultivation. His physique could use that medicine without resistance or harm, and his golden bones needed a great deal more of it. But a good commission should leave him able to buy breakfast afterward.

Then he turned to his practice notes. There were pills he knew how to make but couldn’t yet refine with his own qi. He struck them from the offer. Promising impossible goods wouldn’t make him rich. It would only make him a fool with angry customers waiting outside.

The common pills he could handle were enough to begin. Foundation Establishment would lift part of the limit later. Until then, he’d use what he had properly, instead of complaining that it wasn’t everything he remembered.

“I’ll become rich!” Shi Feng said aloud, then clapped a hand over his mouth and listened for the room. No sound came back.

The vow lacked the grandeur of splitting mountains or overturning the heavens. Shi Feng figured the heavens never paid his furnace rent anyway.

He wrote the first offer before sleeping.

In the room, Ling Qingzhu lay awake behind the screen, remembering how naturally he’d served her the fish. Her friend’s approval pleased her. His plain answer at the gate pleased her even more. Across the room, his floor bedding lay empty and flat, and she noticed that she was waiting for him to come lie down on it.

She thought the evening proved how well their arrangement worked.

Out in the kitchen, the table held eleven spirit stones and a new business proposal. Shi Feng paid for an evening he truly wanted. She still didn’t understand which parts of it were never for sale.

In the eastern residence, a grey-robed retainer knelt on the polished floor.

“Your Highness, the cripple dined at Yuelan Terrace tonight,” Ge Fan reported. “The bill was two hundred and eight spirit stones, paid in full and in coin.”

Sima Yu set down his cup.

“From a board of ointment jars?” Sima Yu asked softly.

“Yes, Your Highness,” Ge Fan said.

“Cao Wenshu is dead, and no one has found the man who killed him,” Sima Yu said. “A cripple with no meridians pays two hundred stones for fish, and a hooded refiner nobody has seen sells pills to hunters across the capital.” His smile didn’t reach his eyes. “Do you believe in so many coincidences?”

Ge Fan lowered his head. “This servant doesn’t, Your Highness!” Ge Fan said.

“Then do bring me the refiner’s customers,” Sima Yu said gently. “And, if it’s no trouble, that purse.”

At that very hour, in a courtyard in Qingliu Lane, the whole purse of the man he hunted lay on a kitchen table, and it held eleven stones.

Sima Yu didn’t know it yet, but the hunt had just become expensive for both of them.

chapters.title: A Customer Who Paid
chapters.html:
“Three of my men came back before the others,” Yan Meizhen said. “They’re asking for medicine already.”

“Did the wounds reopen?” Shi Feng asked.

Yan Meizhen shook her head and pushed the delivery paper across the table. Morning light entered the rented furnace room. Shi Feng kept his hood and face cloth in place. Her green robe still carried dust from the road, and the three ingredient boxes beside her looked newer than her boots.

The Bone Refinement buyer read his offer again. Twelve common recovery pills each delivery, three deliveries across nine days. He'd take a small cash fee and an agreed share of any extra usable pills. The customer received her twelve before he kept anything.

“They want to go back out,” Yan Meizhen replied. “The first trip paid well. Now they all think the next one will be better.”

“Not if they spend it with an open wound,” Shi Feng said.

“That’s what I told them!” Yan Meizhen said.

She took a creased list from her sleeve. There were twelve names on it, with little marks beside the men who were still away. Her jokes faded while she checked them.

Shi Feng read the quantities. They agreed on three deliveries across nine days, with the first ready that evening.

“I’ll inspect each batch,” Yan Meizhen said.

“Of course,” Shi Feng replied. “Keep the first box dry. Those men won’t wait to reach your store.”

Yan Meizhen nodded and folded the list. She was thinking about the hunters now, rather than another way to reduce his fee.

Yan Meizhen tapped the nearest ingredient box. He opened it and examined the contents. The herbs were dry this time. She'd apparently finished arguing with her supplier.

The room and fuel deposit was paid in advance, with the balance due on collection under the signed division.

Shi Feng put the advance in a separate pouch. His own eleven stones stayed untouched.

At last, he thought. The furnace wouldn't be eating his breakfast money today. Yan Meizhen stood, then turned back at the door.

“My hunters like larger pills,” Yan Meizhen said. “They think a small one isn't worth much.”

“Bring one here when he comes back,” Shi Feng replied. “He can try a small pill before ordering a large one.”

“He’ll claim he needs three to be sure,” Yan Meizhen said.

“Then bring the captain,” Shi Feng replied.

Yan Meizhen laughed. That would settle the experiment faster than any explanation she gave them.

Yan Meizhen stared at him before laughing again. She left without securing an improvement in pill size.

Shi Feng checked the furnace before lighting it. The air passage was clear, the lid sat evenly, and nobody else's residue remained in the bowl. Once those things were right, he stopped looking for tricks and began working.

His first mistake was his own.

During the joining stage, he fed in qi too quickly. The medicinal liquid gathered at the center, but the outer layer thickened before the inside settled. One pill cracked as soon as it cooled.

Shi Feng broke the remaining pills open. Two were sound. He set those aside and put the cracked one in his own jar.

“Too eager,” Shi Feng muttered.

Mo Tianheng's memories showed the proper movement clearly. Knowing it didn't mean his fingers would always follow it. The dead master's hands controlled far stronger qi. Shi Feng needed a smaller flow and a slower turn.

He repeated the movement with an empty spoon before beginning again. It looked foolish, but foolish practice was cheaper than ruined herbs.

The second attempt gave four usable pills.

On the third, he kept the flame steady even when the liquid thickened. Four more emerged. He didn't speed up to chase a grand yield. The last attempt produced five.

Fifteen common recovery pills lay on the clean tray.

Twelve belonged to Yan Meizhen. Three belonged to him. He inspected every one before sealing the customer's box, then ate the failed pill and loose medicinal crumbs.

The failed medicine fed his golden bones without harming him. He swallowed a sound pill next and felt the stronger, multiplied effect. Those three successful pills were worth the extra care at the furnace.

He sat until the warmth settled through his skeleton. The next portion could wait until evening. His remaining furnace time belonged to cleaning the vessel and sealing Yan Meizhen’s medicine properly.

That much medicine, and only this much progress!

Shi Feng wasn't discouraged. He finally had a way to keep feeding it.

Yan Meizhen returned before sunset. She checked the seals, opened the box, and chose a pill from the middle herself.

“Don't say I picked your best one,” Yan Meizhen said.

“Take one from the bottom too,” Shi Feng replied. “They were cooled together.”

She snorted, examined the pill, and counted twenty-four spirit stones onto the table. The transaction ended without a single plea for a discount. Then she reached for the empty ingredient boxes.

“The boxes are mine,” Yan Meizhen said quickly.

“Take them,” Shi Feng replied.

Yan Meizhen stacked the boxes beneath her arm and hurried out. A company runner was waiting beside the gate. She asked which hunters were back before he could offer to carry them.

After paying the session's eighteen-stone costs from the advance, the twenty-four-stone balance joined the eleven stones in his pocket for thirty-five stones in all. Before leaving the market lane, he bought a plain mortar and a finer sieve so Yan Meizhen's next batch wouldn't settle into coarse grains on the road.

One completed commission hadn't made him rich. It had left him with medicine and money at the same time. That was already an improvement.

At the rice stall, he bought grain, greens, and two eggs for three stones. He didn't buy a spirit fish to celebrate surviving a spirit fish. The remaining thirty-two stones could stay alive for another day.

“Only two?” Ling Qingzhu asked when he set the eggs beside the stove.

“Would you like to hatch them?” Shi Feng asked.

Ling Qingzhu gave him a cold look. Her black hair was tied loosely behind her, and one sleeve was rolled higher than the other. She'd been washing a cup. Water still clung to her fingers.

“I meant eggs for tomorrow,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Tomorrow's chickens haven't been consulted,” Shi Feng replied.

“Your business must be doing wonderfully,” Ling Qingzhu said. “You're even arguing with chickens now.”

“Customers are harder,” Shi Feng said.

He washed the vegetables while she dried her hands. She stayed in the kitchen doorway instead of going back into their room. When he reached for the salt, she passed it before he asked.

He looked at her.

“What?” Ling Qingzhu asked. “You've put it in the same place every day.”

“Then remember where the rice bowl goes too,” Shi Feng said.

“I know where it goes,” Ling Qingzhu replied. “Into your hands.”

Shi Feng laughed and turned back to the stove. Her answer was shameless, but he liked hearing it. There was nobody here to impress, and she wasn't using the careful voice she wore before strangers.

He fried the eggs with chopped greens. When he divided them, her bowl received the crisp edges she liked.

Ling Qingzhu noticed. She took a bite, then glanced at the money pouch hanging from his belt.

“Did someone finally buy your medicine?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“Someone paid for an order,” Shi Feng replied.

“So don't glare at the lamp tonight,” Ling Qingzhu said. “You make it look guilty whenever I turn it up.”

“The lamp burns oil,” Shi Feng said.

“I burn oil too,” Ling Qingzhu replied. “Are you going to glare at me?”

“You'd charge me for looking,” Shi Feng said.

Ling Qingzhu almost smiled before lowering her head. He saw it anyway.

After supper she stayed beside the courtyard table, talking about Su Wanning's departing carriage. Shi Feng listened while cleaning a bowl. His business notes could wait a little.

Later, behind the folding screen, she heard him spreading his bedding on the floor.

“Shi Feng, tomorrow I don't want the egg burnt,” Ling Qingzhu called.

“The crisp edge?” Shi Feng asked.

“Yes,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

“You ate all of it,” Shi Feng said.

Ling Qingzhu pulled her blanket higher and didn't answer.

In the corner, Shi Feng smiled before closing his eyes. Tonight there were thirty-two stones in the house and two pills put away—yet Gao Yuan's parting whisper at the furnace gate stayed with him in the dark: a clerk wearing the Eastern Palace badge had visited two neighbouring furnace yards that afternoon, asking which private refiners paid their bills in clean spirit coin.

chapters.title: Strength Wasn’t Enough
chapters.html:
“Another crack,” Shi Feng said.

He lifted the lid and watched the half-formed pill crumble. A bitter smell filled the rented furnace room. This was his own practice batch, bought with his own spirit stones, and nobody stood outside waiting for an explanation.

That didn't make the result less irritating. The ingredients for today's practice cost eight spirit stones. He used the last of his previously booked furnace hours. He could afford them now without touching a customer's advance, which was why he dared make the attempt.

The preparation was meant for cultivators approaching Foundation Establishment. Mo Tianheng's memories held the entire process. Shi Feng knew the temperature, the order of extraction, and the exact point when the final herbs should bind.

His qi couldn't hold them together.

He pressed two fingers against the furnace rim, checking the heat before withdrawing his hand. The furnace wasn't the main problem. Neither were the herbs. At the final stage, his Bone Refinement qi couldn't keep the medicinal forces separated and then join them cleanly.

His reserves were enormous. Their quality still belonged to his current realm.

Shi Feng thought, I can kill someone stronger. That doesn't mean my qi becomes theirs.

He could force a heavier stone off the ground. He couldn't force an unstable medicinal mixture to become a sound pill just by being stronger than it!

The second attempt confirmed the same limit. This time he slowed the binding and used more qi. The liquid stayed steady longer, then separated into dark grains before it could take shape.

Shi Feng stopped there. Repeating the same failure ten more times would only make the furnace richer.

He scraped out the cooled residue and swallowed it, letting the unrefined herb qi sink into his golden bones. When he opened his eyes, he was still annoyed.

Benefiting from a mistake didn't make it less of a mistake.

Gao Yuan found him wiping down the tray, still hidden beneath his hood and face cloth. Smoke from the shared flue had begun entering the doorway. The landlord pressed a wet rag over the crack and succeeded only in moving the leak upward.

“You said it was repaired,” Shi Feng said.

“It was sound yesterday,” Gao Yuan said.

Shi Feng moved his ingredients away from the smoke. Gao Yuan hurried to open the room at the back. Inside stood an ordinary copper furnace, with a dry flue and a lid that didn't sit properly.

“This is the wrong lid,” Shi Feng said.

Gao Yuan brought another from storage. It settled evenly into place. Shi Feng checked the seams and booked a short run of sessions. The copper would hold heat more steadily, but it couldn't improve Bone Refinement qi.

Before leaving the doorway, Gao Yuan lowered his voice. “Two clerks from the Crown Prince's household came down the lane an hour ago asking who refines for the hunting companies. I told them my rooms only rent by the hour and nobody signs a real name, so they went to watch the front herb shops instead.” Shi Feng nodded once and noted the side alley exit.

The furnace owner finally went away. Shi Feng returned to the common recovery formula and made a small comparison batch. The result wasn't spectacular, but the herbs joined correctly. His qi could sustain every stage without being dragged beyond its limit.

That was the difference. He didn't lack expertise. He lacked a body at the realm needed to use all of it.

Foundation Establishment would open the next step. Before that, the First Extreme had to be finished. He wouldn't abandon his chosen path just because a pill refused to cooperate.

Five common pills lay on the tray. He compared one with the sample saved yesterday, checking its middle rather than judging the round shell. The new batch was evenly bound. His earlier practice was working.

He didn't need to keep proving that an advanced formula could defeat him. First he'd improve the medicine he could actually sell. Then he'd use its profits to reach the realm that stopped him today.

He sealed the sound pills and wrote one short note beside the failed formula: wait until the next realm.

At home, Ling Qingzhu intercepted him beside the kitchen door.

“Don't come closer,” Ling Qingzhu said.

Shi Feng stopped. “What's wrong?” Shi Feng asked.

“Your sleeve,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

A black streak ran from his wrist toward his elbow. He rubbed it once and discovered he'd only spread the soot.

“It's from work,” Shi Feng said.

“I didn't think you fought the stove for amusement,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

She brought a basin and set it on the courtyard table. When he reached for the cloth, she slapped his fingers aside and pointed at the water instead.

“Wash your hands first,” Ling Qingzhu said. “You'll make it worse.”

“Yes, Lady Ling,” Shi Feng replied.

“Don't call me that,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Madam Shi?” Shi Feng asked.

Ling Qingzhu pressed the wet cloth onto his sleeve much harder than necessary.

Shi Feng laughed. She was embarrassed, and that pleased him far more than teasing a furnace owner. He held still while she scrubbed the worst patch, then took the cloth before the cold water soaked through his whole robe.

“Did you sell anything?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“Not today,” Shi Feng replied.

“Then why were you burning things?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“Practice,” Shi Feng said.

She looked at him with mild surprise. His medicine business still seemed odd to her. She could understand simple ointments, but his determination to meddle with pills looked like another stubborn effort to fix ruined meridians.

“You shouldn't believe everything an alchemist tells you,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“I rarely do,” Shi Feng replied.

“Especially if he takes your spirit stones first,” Ling Qingzhu added.

“That part I noticed,” Shi Feng said.

She nodded, satisfied with her warning. Shi Feng didn't tell her whose memories were inside his head. He wrung out the cloth and hung his robe near the kitchen wall.

Ling Qingzhu glanced at his bare forearm before looking away. The skin showed no trace of the injuries she'd bandaged after his dangerous absence. He recovered well, at least. That pleased her, although she didn't say it.

“There's rice left,” Ling Qingzhu said. “I didn't eat it all.”

“You boiled rice?” Shi Feng asked.

“I said there's rice left,” Ling Qingzhu replied. “Don't invent things.”

It was yesterday's rice, covered carefully with a plate. She'd moved it away from the window so the afternoon sun wouldn't spoil it.

Shi Feng felt unexpectedly happy. It was a small thing, but she didn't need to do it. He took the bowl inside and began chopping vegetables.

Behind him, she continued rinsing the soot from the cloth instead of going back to her bed.

That night, Shi Feng lay on his floor bedding until Ling Qingzhu's breathing grew even. Then he slipped into the kitchen and shut the door.

He swallowed two retained recovery pills. Their medicinal force passed through him and entered the golden traces within his bones. His body accepted both as cleanly as the first pill he'd ever taken. There was no growing resistance to reduce the benefit.

He also used a small portion of the Golden Vein Root left from Zhu Shan's earlier payment. The simple preparation suited his present qi. Its warmth joined the pills and slowly strengthened another stretch of golden bone.

Shi Feng watched the change inwardly. He wasn't at the end yet, but he could reach it. Paid commissions would give him enough medicine if he kept producing and improving.

From the room came a sleepy voice.

“Shi Feng, are you cooking?” Ling Qingzhu called.

“Preparing medicine,” Shi Feng replied through the door.

“It smells better than supper,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Then I'll feed you roots tomorrow,” Shi Feng replied.

“Don't you dare!” Ling Qingzhu snapped.

Shi Feng smiled and covered the remaining root. Sima Yu's clerks were already sniffing around the furnace lanes, and Bone Refinement wouldn't keep them outside the door much longer.

chapters.title: A Night Without a Private Room
chapters.html:
“There's no private room,” Shi Feng said.

Ling Qingzhu stopped beside the courtyard gate. She wore a pale violet robe and a white veil, and her black hair fell from a silver clasp. Beneath the evening light, even the plain lane looked brighter around her.

“I haven't asked for one,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

“I'm telling you beforehand,” Shi Feng said.

She understood immediately. Her expression turned cold.

“Are you still thinking about Yuelan Terrace?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“I remember my own name too,” Shi Feng answered. “Neither takes much effort.”

Ling Qingzhu wanted to refuse the outing just to annoy him. Instead, she stepped past him and held the gate open.

“Then stop talking about it,” Ling Qingzhu said.

Shi Feng followed. He'd finished his commissions early and bought enough ingredients for the next day's work. For once, he didn't have to choose between an evening outside and an unfinished batch.

He wanted to spend that evening with her. That was all.

The streets near Qingliu Lane were still busy. Several young cultivators hurried toward the richer quarter, boasting about a visiting elder. Shi Feng turned toward the river instead.

Ling Qingzhu glanced behind them.

“The lantern fair is that way,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“The crowds are that way,” Shi Feng replied.

“And the lanterns,” Ling Qingzhu added.

“They'll still be visible from here,” Shi Feng said.

She gave him a doubtful look but kept walking.

At the river, red lanterns hung along the opposite bank. Their reflections trembled in the water. The path on this side held only a few food stalls and scattered walkers.

Ling Qingzhu stopped complaining.

Shi Feng noticed and smiled slightly. He thought, Good. The river hasn't asked for a room fee yet.

A boy ran past carrying a paper kite. Behind him, a tired father shouted for him to watch the water. Ling Qingzhu stepped aside, and Shi Feng caught the loose kite string before it wound around her sleeve.

He handed it back without breaking his stride. The boy thanked him loudly and ran back to his father.

Ling Qingzhu looked at Shi Feng's fingers.

“You're quick when there's no work involved,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“You should see me leave a bad shop,” Shi Feng replied.

She laughed softly. There was no one here whose opinion she needed to manage. Nobody was asking whether her husband deserved her or whether the Crown Prince would be offended.

She walked a little closer.

“Two bowls,” Shi Feng told the stall owner.

A broad-shouldered man stood behind a steaming pot. His thin Qi Condensation aura was weaker than most guards in the capital. He looked at Ling Qingzhu, then hurriedly wiped an already clean stool.

“Fresh sesame dumplings!” He Shun said. “Young lady, I make them myself.”

“That sounds less reassuring when you shout it,” Shi Feng said.

He Shun glared at him before remembering who was paying.

“They're good,” He Shun said stiffly.

Ling Qingzhu sat down. Shi Feng took the stool opposite her. The bowls were plain, the spoons didn't match, and nobody appeared to announce the history of the sesame.

She tried one dumpling and paused.

“It's good,” Ling Qingzhu admitted.

He Shun brightened at once.

“Of course! My wife taught me,” He Shun said proudly.

“Then your wife deserves the praise,” Shi Feng replied.

Ling Qingzhu lowered the spoon, her eyes laughing above her veil. He Shun nodded without arguing and returned to his pot.

Across the path, a silk-robed young man noticed her. He checked his own sleeves before approaching. A pair of servants followed, both carrying wrapped boxes.

The young man's Qi Condensation cultivation was ordinary, but his belt buckle was large enough to announce his family's money first.

“Miss Ling?” Kou Liang asked eagerly. “I didn't expect to meet you here!”

Ling Qingzhu put her spoon down. Her warmth disappeared.

“Then you've met me,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

Kou Liang faltered. His gaze moved to Shi Feng, and recognition made him bold again.

“You brought her here?” Kou Liang asked. “There are better places across the river. My family's booked a pavilion.”

“Go there,” Shi Feng said.

Kou Liang's face reddened.

“I wasn't inviting you,” Kou Liang snapped.

“Neither was I,” Shi Feng replied.

Ling Qingzhu picked her spoon up again. She didn't even turn toward Kou Liang.

“I'm eating with my husband,” Ling Qingzhu said. “You're blocking the path.”

Kou Liang's servants stared at the ground. Their young master stood still for two breaths before turning away.

One of his boxes caught the edge of a stool. He jerked it free and walked faster.

He Shun watched him leave with great satisfaction. A customer who ordered nothing had nearly knocked over his furniture.

“Another bowl?” He Shun asked.

“No,” Shi Feng said.

“Half a bowl?” He Shun tried.

Ling Qingzhu finally laughed aloud.

They walked farther along the bank after eating. Shi Feng paid the ordinary price. He didn't spend the next ten steps looking pained, and Ling Qingzhu found herself strangely pleased about that.

“Did you like it?” Shi Feng asked.

“The food?” Ling Qingzhu replied.

“The shouting,” Shi Feng said.

She bumped his arm with her sleeve.

“The dumplings were good,” Ling Qingzhu said. “Your taste isn't completely hopeless.”

“High praise,” Shi Feng replied.

“You should treasure it,” Ling Qingzhu said.

Her praise pleased him, even with the proud way she gave it.

Ling Qingzhu saw his expression before he turned toward the river. Her heart beat faster. She lowered her gaze and pretended to straighten a fold in her robe.

Why did he have to look at her like that?

He was usually so irritating that she knew exactly what to say. Now she couldn't think of a single useful insult.

They reached a stone crossing with a shallow step beside it. Ling Qingzhu's hem caught under her shoe. She stopped, annoyed, and Shi Feng held out his hand.

She looked at it.

“I can walk,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Then walk,” Shi Feng replied, leaving his hand there.

She took it anyway.

Her fingers were cool. Shi Feng led her down the step without tightening his grip. Once the path was level, she didn't let go immediately.

Neither did he.

A lantern seller passed on the far bank, shouting prices. Ling Qingzhu watched the coloured lights drift between the people and suddenly wanted one. Then she looked at the joined hands and kept quiet.

She didn't need to carry anything else.

They passed an old woman selling embroidered purse strings. Ling Qingzhu glanced at a violet one, then at the plain knot on his purse.

“That one's coming loose,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“It still holds,” Shi Feng replied.

“One day it won't,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“You sound hopeful,” Shi Feng replied.

She pulled him to the stall and bought the string herself. It cost little, and she didn't make a show of paying. Shi Feng let her replace the worn knot.

Her fingers worked carefully. He watched her bowed head, feeling pleased in a way a full purse hadn't managed.

“I won't charge for the work,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“I was waiting for the price,” Shi Feng answered.

She tightened the last knot harder than necessary. Near home, Shi Feng finally released her hand to lift a loose branch from their path. Ling Qingzhu's fingers curled into her sleeve.

“Next time, we can try the other stall,” Ling Qingzhu said.

Shi Feng glanced back.

“Next time?” Shi Feng asked.

“If you're not busy,” Ling Qingzhu added quickly.

“I'll see,” Shi Feng said.

She immediately regretted sounding so eager.

“Don't make yourself too important,” Ling Qingzhu said coldly. “There are other people I can ask.”

“Then I'll be busy,” Shi Feng replied.

Ling Qingzhu stared at him. The small smile at his mouth made her understand that he was teasing her. She caught his sleeve and pulled him toward the gate.

“You've already promised,” Ling Qingzhu declared.

“I haven't,” Shi Feng said.

“Then promise now,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

chapters.title: The Crooked Silver Clasp
chapters.html:
“Don't touch it,” Ling Qingzhu said.

Shi Feng stopped with his hand over the kitchen table. A silver hair clasp lay beside the lamp. Its pin bent sharply near the middle.

“I was moving the bowl,” Shi Feng replied.

“Then move the bowl,” Ling Qingzhu said.

He moved it. She stood in the doorway with her black hair loose around her shoulders. Without the clasp, she'd tied the upper strands with a strip of violet silk. One stubborn lock kept falling across her cheek.

She pushed it behind her ear. Shi Feng’s hand stayed over the bowl.

“Move it, then,” Ling Qingzhu said.

He moved the clasp instead.

“The bowl!” Ling Qingzhu said.

Shi Feng looked down. She turned away, but not quickly enough to hide her smile. Shi Feng looked at the bent pin again.

“Did it offend you?” Shi Feng asked.

“It caught in the screen,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“And you defeated it,” Shi Feng replied.

Ling Qingzhu's expression cooled. The clasp wasn't precious, but she liked its shape. She'd pulled too hard when it snagged and bent the pin herself.

She didn't need him to sound pleased about it.

“I'll buy another,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Leave this one here,” Shi Feng replied.

“Why?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“I'll have a look after work,” Shi Feng said.

She studied him doubtfully. She knew he made medicines. That didn't mean he could repair ornaments.

“Don't turn it into a hook for drying herbs,” Ling Qingzhu warned.

“I already have hooks,” Shi Feng said.

That didn't reassure her at all.

A strip of soft copper wire and a pair of small pliers rested beside the silver clasp that evening. Shi Feng sat beneath the lamp and checked the bend before applying pressure.

Xu Changhe's notes covered ordinary repairs alongside the care of weapons. The dead elder was a swordsman and sect enforcer, not some legendary crafting grandmaster. Still, he knew how to work a simple piece of metal without ruining it.

That much was enough here.

Shi Feng protected the silver with cloth, eased the pin straight, and checked its movement. The fastening loop had loosened as well. He closed it carefully and polished away a small scratch.

No qi entered the clasp. This wasn't a refined artifact. He didn't need a realm breakthrough to repair a bent hairpin.

Ling Qingzhu came out from behind the folding screen and stopped beside his stool.

“You really fixed it?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“Try it,” Shi Feng said.

She tested the catch twice. It held firmly.

Her surprise pleased him more than it should. Shi Feng leaned back before she could notice.

“It hasn't turned into a herb hook,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Not yet,” Shi Feng replied.

She put it in her hair and tried to check its position in the small bronze mirror. The lamp stood at the wrong angle. Shi Feng moved it closer before she asked.

Ling Qingzhu's fingers slowed.

“Is it straight?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“A little left,” Shi Feng said.

She adjusted it.

“Now?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“Now it's crooked the other way,” Shi Feng replied.

Ling Qingzhu turned and glared at him. He was smiling.

“You're doing that on purpose!” Ling Qingzhu said.

“It was straight the first time,” Shi Feng admitted.

She hit his shoulder with the folded cloth. He didn't move, and she didn't use strength. For a moment, she stood close enough that the loose edge of her sleeve rested against his wrist.

Shi Feng wanted to reach for her hand again. He remembered how she'd held his sleeve by the gate. He could still feel the coolness of her fingers from the river path.

Before he decided, Ling Qingzhu stepped toward the kitchen.

“I'll make tea,” Ling Qingzhu said.

Shi Feng watched her go. He was disappointed and a little amused with himself. He could face a killing blow without hesitation. A woman standing beside his stool was making him think too much.

The tea arrived darker than usual.

He tasted it. Ling Qingzhu waited with the serious expression of someone awaiting an alchemist's verdict.

“You used too many leaves,” Shi Feng said.

“Then add water,” Ling Qingzhu replied immediately.

He did. She took the other cup and sat opposite him.

Ling Qingzhu glanced at the paper beside his cup. Two collection dates were circled, and another line reminded him to buy charcoal.

“You're going out early tomorrow?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“Before the streets fill,” Shi Feng replied.

“Wake me first,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“What for?” Shi Feng asked.

“I want breakfast,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

“You can sleep. I'll leave yours covered,” Shi Feng said.

She looked at the paper again and drew it away from the damp edge of his cup. Then she put a dry saucer beneath it.

It was such a small thing that he nearly missed it. She'd never bothered about his work notes before.

The clasp shone faintly above her black hair. Shi Feng looked at it once, then looked at her face.

“Thank you,” Ling Qingzhu said quietly.

He was so surprised by the simple words that he forgot his next teasing reply.

Ling Qingzhu noticed. Her smile grew.

“So you can be quiet,” Ling Qingzhu said.

Shi Feng raised his cup.

“The tea's frightened me,” Shi Feng replied.

Rain woke them before dawn. Water ran through the roof above Shi Feng's bedding. He lifted the wet roll and moved a basin beneath the drip. Ling Qingzhu came out from behind the screen, frowned at the dark patch and took the blanket from him.

“Put it by the kitchen fire,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Your sleeve will get wet,” Shi Feng said.

“Then stop discussing it,” Ling Qingzhu said.

She hung it herself. When he returned from fetching Jiang Meilan, she had turned the damp side toward the warmth and spread the mat where the water couldn't reach it.

A hired tiler arrived carrying a tile basket and a short ladder. He was a Meridian Opening tiler Jiang Meilan hired for repairs, more interested in the cracked gutter than in either tenant. He climbed up, replaced two broken tiles and poured water over the patch to check it.

Ling Qingzhu tied her veil while he worked. Once the tiler and the grumbling landlady had gone, she removed it and helped Shi Feng clear the wet floor. She held the screen high enough that his broom could pass without soaking the cloth.

“You're sweeping toward my slippers,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Move one step,” Shi Feng said.

She took the broom instead. Her first stroke sent a line of water against his ankle. He looked down, then at her carefully composed face.

“I moved the water,” Ling Qingzhu said.

He laughed. She turned away, pleased enough that she forgot to hide it. By evening his bedding was dry and the roof held. She checked the middle of the blanket herself before allowing him to roll it again.

Shi Feng laid it in its usual corner, four steps from her bed. Outside the dry eaves, a night runner’s gong sounded down the street—fifteen days remained until the royal tournament’s standing list went up on the capital square, and his final golden bones were nearly ready to close.

chapters.title: Three Moves in the Forest
chapters.html:
“He caught the sword with his sleeve,” Ling Qingzhu said, tapping the open book. “Then all seven enemies fell to their knees.”

Shi Feng tied his pack shut beside the kitchen door. She sat at the courtyard table, reading the passage she promised him yesterday.

“A good sleeve,” Shi Feng said. “Did the book name the tailor?”

Ling Qingzhu lowered the book and stared at him.

“You're supposed to admire the swordsman,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Seven men admired him already,” Shi Feng replied. “The tailor got nothing.”

She laughed, then tried to hide it behind the page. Her black hair slipped over one shoulder, and morning light caught the clasp he'd repaired.

He wanted to stay a little longer. Instead, he checked the wooden practice blade beside his pack. Wanting something didn't mean the day had more hours.

“Where are you going with that?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“Outside the capital,” Shi Feng said. “I'll be back before evening.”

She glanced at his wooden sword. He could almost hear what she wanted to ask.

“The men outside might not kneel,” Ling Qingzhu said at last.

“Then I'll leave my sleeves at home,” Shi Feng replied.

He slipped a knife into his pack and went out while she was still deciding whether to be annoyed.

His hunting pass carried him through the Hengyun checkpoint without trouble. Beyond the road, thin mist hung between dark trunks, and rainwater gathered in shallow hollows.

A broad-faced hunter named Shao Sheng sat beside the path, replacing the cord on a crossbow. He was at Bone Refinement, with fewer than half his bones refined. He glanced at the wooden sword and laughed.

“Going to frighten rabbits?” Shao Sheng asked.

“If they're easily frightened,” Shi Feng replied.

“There's a tusked boar near the old lime pit,” Shao Sheng said. “Its hide stopped my bolt. Don't wander that way.”

Shi Feng thanked him for the warning and left the main path. The hoofprints were plain enough to follow without turning directions into another bargain.

He left the main trail and followed the slope until the voices disappeared. At an empty clearing, he stopped beneath a pine and opened Xu Changhe's notes.

The elder's corrections were short and useful. A careless foot went too far. A wrist turned too late. A retreat opened the chest when it should have drawn the enemy forward.

Shi Feng placed the journal on a dry stone and raised the wooden blade.

Piercing Current.

His point passed beneath a hanging branch without touching it. The short step followed, keeping his shoulder covered. He withdrew and repeated the thrust twenty times, then moved the target lower.

His strength was already far beyond most Bone Refinement cultivators. The unfinished golden refinement made the gap even wider. But strength didn't place the point where he wanted it. That depended on his own practice.

Mo Tianheng's spirit gave him alchemy expertise. It never taught his feet this step.

Shi Feng thought, Xu Changhe wrote the mistakes down because someone would make them. Better here than in front of an enemy.

He changed to Turning Wave. The first thrust missed a leaf by design. His wrist turned while his foot kept moving, bringing the wooden edge across the space beside it.

The leaf fell. The branch stayed whole.

Better.

He repeated the change until he could stop the point at the same place every time. Then he practiced Returning Tide, withdrawing just enough to create an opening before thrusting back into it.

The wooden blade weighed less than his broken sword. He couldn't pretend the feeling was identical. He shortened his movements and corrected the difference instead of adding force.

From beyond the clearing came a hard snort.

Shi Feng looked up. A Black-Tusk Boar moved between the trees, low and broad, with pale points curving beside its mouth. Old mud covered its shoulders. A snapped crossbow bolt stuck in the thick hide.

The boar found him first.

“You've saved me some walking,” Shi Feng said.

It charged.

He stepped aside and thrust the wooden point toward its eye. The boar jerked its head, and he turned his wrist without chasing the target. Turning Wave struck the side of its jaw.

Crack!

The beast staggered. The wooden blade stayed intact.

Shi Feng was pleased. A boar of this strength could injure an ordinary Bone Refinement cultivator with half his bones refined. He'd used only enough force to test the change of direction.

The beast squealed and swung back. Its tusk tore through his outer sleeve without reaching his skin. He didn't retreat in panic. He drew the blade back a palm's width, then drove it into the open mouth.

Returning Tide.

The thrust broke through the upper jaw. He released his strength for a breath, and the boar's heavy body stopped as if it struck a wall. Its legs folded beneath it.

Shi Feng withdrew the wooden sword. The tip was split. He looked at the dead beast, then at the damage.

“Still cheaper than a sleeve that catches flying swords,” Shi Feng said.

There wasn't a scratch on his body. His durability already made attacks from beasts of this level almost useless. The exercise proved something better than that. He could direct his force through the sword art instead of simply battering everything in reach.

He thought, Next time, the point shouldn't split. Enough force to kill isn't the same as wasting force.

He kept his devouring power still. The carcass was worth more to him today as meat and hide.

He took the useful tusks, hide, and meat, then cleaned his knife. Ordinary hunting work didn't need a hidden treasure or a dying enemy's storage bag to pay.

Before leaving, he wrote down the flaw in his last thrust. His wrist was steady, but he'd pushed too much strength through the tip after the jaw broke. Against an enemy behind the first, that wasted effort could delay his next strike.

He read the correction once and shut the journal. There was no shame in writing down a mistake. Xu Changhe's own pages were full of them, and that elder actually lived by his sword.

Shao Sheng looked up when Shi Feng returned carrying the wrapped hide over one shoulder. His gaze stopped on the broken bolt still lodged in it.

“That boar's dead?” Shao Sheng asked, suddenly eager.

“This part certainly is,” Shi Feng replied.

The hunter stood. He didn't see the kill, and the wooden sword didn't convince him of anything. He looked toward the trees, searching for the stronger hunter Shi Feng must be carrying it for.

“Remember who warned you!” Shao Sheng said. “You must have found a powerful hunting partner.”

“A hungry one,” Shi Feng replied.

“So you did have help,” Shao Sheng said.

“I heard the boar first,” Shi Feng said.

He continued toward the checkpoint. Shao Sheng followed for several steps, then stopped when Shi Feng didn't even turn around.

The hunter looked at the hide once more. Next time, he decided, he'd demand payment before giving directions.

By the time Shi Feng reached the capital, most of the meat was sold. He kept a small parcel for home and enough payment to replace his outer robe when it finally wore through.

Ling Qingzhu met him at the kitchen door. Her gaze dropped to the torn sleeve.

“Did the rabbits fight back?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“One of them had tusks,” Shi Feng replied, setting down the parcel.
