Returning Tide drew the blade back along his wrist and guard line in a tight counter-cut without his fingers ever leaving the grip. He'd rather keep a reliable sword in hand than overextend a thrust to impress a crowd and lose the next exchange.

He thought, Win with what's needed. Keep the rest until someone earns it.

His early Foundation Establishment qi stayed smooth through the exercises. The immense foundation beneath it was still far from filled. He'd gained stability and control over the past days, not another stage.

That was enough for Great Liang's qualification.

He arranged three targets close together and stepped between them without swinging. Footwork first. A sword exchange could end in the first movement, but he still wanted a clean answer if an opponent changed direction.

On the next pass, he added the blade. The first target marked the opening attack. The second forced a turn before his point reached it. The third stood where an enemy might retreat after losing the exchange.

Shi Feng stopped the final thrust short of the wood. A defeated competitor didn't need a hole in his chest to prove who won. He repeated the halt until it came as easily as finishing the strike.

Xu Changhe's enforcer training included taking people alive when the sect required it. That wasn't mercy for someone trying to murder him. It was control over what his sword actually did. He wanted the same choice in his own hands, rather than letting excess force choose every ending.

He cleaned the blade and put the targets aside. The practice was finished before he grew tired.

On the way back, he stopped at the furnace yard to collect a finished medicine sample. Gao Yuan waited near the gate with his hands tucked into his sleeves.

“No one came back,” Gao Yuan said quietly.

“Who?” Shi Feng asked.

The landlord glanced at his hood and lowered his voice. “The Eastern Palace steward, Zheng Jian! The canal watch dragged his waist plaque and three bodies out of the west-canal timber sluice at dawn. Because the canal watchman saw Zheng Jian chain the alley gate himself, the Censorate made the Eastern Palace pay two hundred stones in sluice-clearing fines, and His Highness's clerks haven't dared set foot in our lane since!”

“Then you've had a peaceful week,” Shi Feng replied.

Gao Yuan looked uncertain whether he was allowed to enjoy that. Eventually, profit overcame fear.

“Would you like to keep the better room booked?” Gao Yuan asked.

“For short sessions,” Shi Feng replied. “Don't promise all of them to someone else after taking my payment.”

“I wouldn't do that,” Gao Yuan said.

Shi Feng looked at him.

“Not again,” Gao Yuan added.

He paid only for the sessions he intended to use. Some buyers still waited to see whether royal pressure returned. He wasn't going to fill a month with hopeful orders and then discover the customers had stopped coming.

His own ingredients, pills, and cash reserve could carry him through the interruption. When he entered the qualification arena under his real name, the capital would have something else to discuss. Gao Yuan watched him leave with the expression of a man trying to decide whether a difficult tenant was worth more than an easy one.

Shi Feng left him to count.

At home, Ling Qingzhu had placed a small medicine bottle beside his work notes.

“What's this?” Shi Feng asked.

“For ordinary injuries,” Ling Qingzhu replied. “A clan physician prepared it.”

He opened the lid and checked the scent. It was a sound external medicine, useful for cuts and bruises. It didn't promise to rebuild meridians or change his realm.

She'd chosen something practical.

“Thank you,” Shi Feng said.

“Don't sound surprised,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

“I'll practise sounding grateful more often,” Shi Feng said.

“Practise being careful first,” Ling Qingzhu answered.

He smiled and put the bottle with his supplies. He might not need it tomorrow. That wasn't why he was pleased to receive it.

Ling Qingzhu looked relieved when he didn't refuse. She'd expected him to become stubborn over accepting medicine before a fight.

“Keep the bottle,” Ling Qingzhu said. “Don't sell it.”

“I wasn't going to,” Shi Feng replied.

“You sell everything,” Ling Qingzhu complained.

“Not everything,” Shi Feng said.

He looked at her when he answered. She lowered her eyes too quickly and began arranging papers that were already straight.

The quiet between them felt warm. He wanted to reach for her hand, but she turned toward the kitchen before he moved.

“Supper,” Ling Qingzhu said. “Unless your preparations include starving.”

“Only if you cook,” Shi Feng replied.

She spun back with a furious look. He was already laughing.

That night, Shi Feng laid out what he would carry. Birth record. Registration payment. Ordinary sword for the road. Refined artifact inside the ring. Returning Breath Pills and the external medicine Ling Qingzhu gave him.

He didn't fill the table with every treasure and memory he owned. Qualification wasn't an expedition into an unknown ruin. He knew the objective: defeat tenth, claim third, and keep the place.

Sima Yu remained first on the standing list. His name still brought anger, clear and steady.

The men he sent died. The orders behind them didn't disappear with the bodies. Shi Feng intended to settle that debt, but he wouldn't turn tomorrow's qualification into a palace battle on the prince's chosen ground.

For now, the prince could watch someone he called a cripple take a place beside him. Behind the screen, Ling Qingzhu turned a page, then stopped.

“Shi Feng,” Ling Qingzhu called.

“Yes?” Shi Feng replied.

“Wake me before you leave,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“You'll want breakfast?” Shi Feng asked.

“I'll want to know whether you've gone,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

He smiled at the screen.

“I'll wake you,” Shi Feng said.

He kept that promise in mind while putting the last bottle away.

Tomorrow, the crowd would finally need a new name for him.

chapters.title: The Name on the Slip
chapters.html:
“Shi Feng?” Yu Cheng said.

The clerk read the birth record again, then looked at the man standing before his table. Behind Shi Feng, several waiting applicants leaned sideways to see what caused the delay.

“Yes,” Shi Feng replied.

“Qualification registration,” Yu Cheng said, tapping the table.

“I can read the sign,” Shi Feng replied.

A laugh rose from the line. Someone recognized his face and whispered his name. By the time Yu Cheng checked the clan seal, three people were openly staring.

“The Shi family's cripple?” one young man said.

“He's registering?”

“Maybe he wants a seat to watch.”

Shi Feng waited without turning. The registration ground stood beside the capital arena. Ten tall boards displayed the standing candidates, and a separate awning sheltered the officials.

The ranked names were the same as the notice. Sima Yu first. Ling Qingzhu second. Han Zong third.

Gao Zhen tenth.

Yu Cheng checked the birth year against the eligible list. Everything matched. He couldn't reject the paper merely because the face beside it was famous for the wrong reason.

“Your age is eligible,” Yu Cheng said. “Your clan seal is sound. Cultivation must meet Foundation Establishment before the first challenge proceeds.”

“It will,” Shi Feng replied.

The clerk's brush stopped.

“Don't make me repeat the condition,” Yu Cheng said.

“Then don't,” Shi Feng replied.

A young man in a pale gold robe stepped out from beneath the next awning. A refined artifact sword hung at his waist, and early Foundation Establishment qi spread openly around him.

The crowd made room at once.

Gao Zhen looked at Shi Feng, then at the plain scabbard by his side.

“So this is the famous husband,” Gao Zhen said. “I thought Lady Ling kept you at home.”

“I left through the gate,” Shi Feng replied.

Gao Zhen's smile sharpened. He was twenty-one and proud of reaching Foundation Establishment before most of his clan cousins. Being tenth already made him important in the capital's younger circles.

A cripple answering him casually in front of applicants wasn't amusing for long.

“Do you know which rank you'll have to challenge?” Gao Zhen asked.

“Tenth,” Shi Feng said.

“Mine,” Gao Zhen added.

“That's why I'm looking at you,” Shi Feng replied.

The people nearby went quiet. Then someone laughed too loudly and stopped when Gao Zhen turned his head.

Yu Cheng sighed. He'd expected an argument about paperwork, not a young genius finding a reason to become offended before noon.

“Registration first,” Yu Cheng said firmly. “Challenges go through the official board. Not beside my table.”

Gao Zhen looked back at Shi Feng.

“If you can show Foundation Establishment, I'll accept,” Gao Zhen said. “Don't expect your wife's name to make me gentle.”

“I didn't bring it on the slip,” Shi Feng replied.

Yu Cheng looked down. Only Shi Feng's own name stood there.

A man in a dark official robe approached from the arena steps. The surrounding guards straightened. His mid Foundation Establishment aura was steady, and a narrow scar marked his chin.

Wen Shou stopped beside the registration table.

“What's the delay?” Wen Shou asked.

“An eligible record and an unlikely applicant,” Yu Cheng replied.

Wen Shou read the slip, then looked at Shi Feng. His expression didn't become friendly, but neither did he laugh.

“Do you understand the rules?” Wen Shou asked.

“Unranked candidates challenge tenth first,” Shi Feng replied. “Once ranked, I may challenge higher. The first three places at the close represent Great Liang.”

“Correct,” Wen Shou said. “Your realm will be verified on the platform before the fight. If you fail the condition, you lose the challenge payment and leave.”

Shi Feng nodded.

“Then register him,” Wen Shou told Yu Cheng.

The clerk pressed the seal onto the slip. The small sound carried much farther than it should have.

A cripple's name entered the qualification list.

Gao Zhen watched the seal dry with a cold smile. In his mind, the official merely gave a fool enough room to embarrass himself properly.

Shi Feng accepted the slip and paid the required sum. He didn't release qi at the desk, explain his meridians, or ask anyone to believe him in advance.

They'd have proof when the challenge began.

Ling Qingzhu arrived before he left the registration ground. Her violet robe, white veil and black hair drew attention at once. Conversations lowered, and several young men moved aside without waiting for a guard to tell them.

Second on the standing list. First among Great Liang's beauties.

She walked straight to Shi Feng.

“You registered?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

He held up the slip.

She looked at the seal, then at Wen Shou near the steps. Her expression became serious.

“I told you I wouldn't ask for an exception,” Ling Qingzhu said quietly.

“I haven't received one,” Shi Feng replied.

Her eyes searched his face. He remained calm, without the reckless anger she expected from someone trying to silence mockery.

“Do you really know what you're doing?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“Yes,” Shi Feng replied.

She didn't look satisfied, but she stopped arguing in front of the crowd. That pleased him. She could question him privately without helping strangers laugh at him.

Gao Zhen approached again, bowing more carefully to her than he spoke to Shi Feng.

“Lady Ling, your husband wants my place,” Gao Zhen said.

“Then speak to him,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

Gao Zhen straightened, embarrassed. She didn't ask him for mercy or explain away the registration. His prepared generous answer became useless.

Shi Feng glanced at her. She looked back coldly, as if warning him not to mistake silence for approval.

He smiled anyway.

Kou Tao stopped them on the way to the challenge board. The Bone Refinement buyer carried two empty ointment jars beneath his arm and looked more annoyed than astonished.

“You closed the stall,” Kou Tao said.

“I registered here,” Shi Feng replied.

“Then when can I buy medicine?” Kou Tao asked.

“After tomorrow's challenge,” Shi Feng replied.

Kou Tao glanced at Gao Zhen, then at Ling Qingzhu. He clearly decided his questions about the fight weren't worth asking in front of her.

“Same price?” Kou Tao asked.

“Same medicine,” Shi Feng replied.

“Good,” Kou Tao said. “People become famous and forget what a jar costs.”

He moved away, clutching the empty containers. Gao Zhen looked irritated that someone discussed ordinary ointment while he stood there. Shi Feng found the interruption pleasant. Kou Tao didn't suddenly believe he could win. The man simply valued medicine that worked more than a chance to laugh at its seller.

Ling Qingzhu watched the buyer leave and glanced at Shi Feng. She seemed surprised anyone came looking for his goods rather than his wife. He didn't explain. There would be time for plenty of explanations after tomorrow.

At the challenge board, Yu Cheng wrote the first pairing on a fresh strip.

Shi Feng, unranked. Gao Zhen, tenth.

The appointed time was the next morning. Gao Zhen accepted with a sharp stroke of his brush, then handed it over without looking at the applicant.

Shi Feng signed beneath him.

A small crowd gathered to read the names. By the time he stepped away, the whisper had already become a story. The cripple would challenge a Foundation Establishment genius.

Someone claimed Ling Qingzhu arranged it. Another pointed out that she was second and could've asked for something less humiliating. Neither bothered asking Shi Feng himself.

He left the noise behind and walked toward the gate with her beside him.

“You're smiling,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Should I cry?” Shi Feng asked.

“You should be careful,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

“I will,” Shi Feng said.

His answer was plain enough that she believed that much, even if she didn't know what else to believe.

Behind them, the challenge strip fluttered beneath Gao Zhen's rank.

Tomorrow, Shi Feng would give the capital a better subject than his ruined meridians.

chapters.title: The Tenth Name
chapters.html:
“Shi Feng challenges Gao Zhen,” Wen Shou announced.

Laughter spread around the stone arena. Several people stood to see whether the name belonged to the same cripple they remembered. When Shi Feng walked through the gate, the laughter grew louder.

Gao Zhen waited beneath the tenth name on the ranking board. He wore a bright green robe, his refined artifact sword hanging at his waist as early Foundation Establishment qi flowed around his shoulders without restraint.

“Did you get lost?” Gao Zhen asked.

Shi Feng stepped onto the platform.

“Your name's tenth,” Shi Feng said. “I'm in the right place.”

Gao Zhen looked toward the official, expecting him to remove the fool. Wen Shou checked the challenge token against his register and nodded.

“The application is valid,” Wen Shou said. “The challenger accepts the risk. Intentional killing after surrender is forbidden.”

“Then I surrender on his behalf,” Gao Zhen said, drawing another burst of laughter.

Wen Shou didn't smile.

“Only he can do that,” Wen Shou said.

At the edge of the audience, a seller lowered his tray of sunflower seeds. His neighbour leaned forward so far that the bench creaked.

The capital's famous cripple actually intended to fight!

Shi Feng glanced at the ranking board. Three places qualified for the Great Kingdom Tournament. The tenth place was only a step toward what he wanted.

There was no reason to stand here arguing all morning.

“Begin whenever you're ready,” Shi Feng said.

Gao Zhen's expression darkened. Being treated casually by a cripple wasn't amusing when the entire audience could see it.

“You've learned a few tricks from your wife?” Gao Zhen sneered. “I'll teach you how far tricks go against Foundation Establishment!”

Across the arena, Ling Qingzhu stood beside the second-ranked candidates' waiting area. Her fingers tightened around the rail. She couldn't understand Shi Feng's calm. He'd refused her warning that morning without even giving her a convincing explanation.

Now Gao Zhen was drawing his refined artifact.

Ling Qingzhu shifted forward. She could stop a fatal blow if the official failed, but intervening would humiliate Shi Feng before the capital. Her heart was filled with anger and worry.

Why couldn't he have told her what he was planning?

Wen Shou raised his hand. “Realm verification on the first exchange. Begin!”

Gao Zhen lunged immediately, intending to sweep the cripple off the stone before Wen Shou could call a halt. Green light flared along his blade as he slashed toward Shi Feng's shoulder.

Shi Feng didn't draw his sword.

He raised one hand, caught the flat of the incoming blade between two bare fingers, and let his early Foundation Establishment aura roll cleanly across the platform.

The green blade stopped dead.

Around the arena, the laughter died in a single breath. Beside the waiting rail, Ling Qingzhu's hand froze on the stone balustrade—he wasn't crippled; he had broken through to Foundation Establishment!

Gao Zhen jerked his arm. The steel didn't budge. His expression twisted from contempt to stunned disbelief.

“Let go!” Gao Zhen shouted.

Wen Shou's eyes widened slightly before he gave the verification nod. Genuine early Foundation Establishment qi—and dense enough to stop a refined artifact between two fingers!

Gao Zhen's heart trembled. He pulled harder, but the sword remained trapped. Shi Feng stepped inside the reach of the broad blade and pressed his free palm against Gao Zhen's chest.

He pushed.

The green-robed candidate flew backward, crossed the boundary, and landed on his backside outside the platform. His sword left his grip and stayed between Shi Feng's fingers.

For a moment, Gao Zhen sat with both hands raised. He couldn't understand why he was no longer standing.

Wen Shou lowered his arm slowly.

“Gao Zhen is outside the boundary,” Wen Shou declared. “Shi Feng wins.”

The whole fight took less time than Gao Zhen's boast.

“He caught a refined artifact!”

“Foundation Establishment! That's real Foundation Establishment!”

“Wasn't he crippled?”

“Then what does that make Gao Zhen?”

“…”

Gao Zhen scrambled to his feet. Shame burned across his face. Losing would've been bad enough. Losing without making the opponent draw a weapon was unbearable.

“You hid your cultivation!” Gao Zhen shouted.

“I didn't ask you to announce yours,” Shi Feng replied.

A few people laughed before covering their mouths. Shi Feng turned the broad sword around and held it by the blade. Gao Zhen stared at the offered hilt, then at the fingers holding the metal.

“You want it?” Shi Feng asked.

Gao Zhen snatched it and stepped away. He had no desire to test the strength of those fingers again.

Wen Shou inspected the platform and the defeated candidate. Gao Zhen wasn't badly injured. His pride suffered far more than his body.

That made the result harder to dispute.

“Your name will replace the tenth position,” Wen Shou told Shi Feng. “You can wait for the next challenge period.”

“How long?” Shi Feng asked.

“Until the next bell,” Wen Shou said.

Shi Feng nodded and stepped off the platform. He didn't bow toward every section of the audience or explain how his meridians recovered. He'd come to qualify, not tell his life story.

Ling Qingzhu waited near the passage. The moment Shi Feng approached, she caught his sleeve.

“Foundation Establishment?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“Yes,” Shi Feng said.

“How long?” Ling Qingzhu demanded.

“Not long,” Shi Feng replied.

Her eyes stayed fixed on his face. She thought of the medicine jars, the late nights, and his refusal to abandon the qualification. None of those things looked quite the same now.

“Why didn't you tell me?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“You told me not to get myself killed,” Shi Feng said. “I haven't.”

“That isn't an answer!” Ling Qingzhu snapped.

“It was your main concern,” Shi Feng replied.

She wanted to hit him. She also wanted to smile. The two feelings made her grip tighten on his sleeve instead.

At least he was safe. At least he wasn't forcing himself into a fight he couldn't survive. Then she remembered how easily he'd caught Gao Zhen's sword.

That wasn't just being safe.

Wen Shou approached with a wooden ranking token. Ling Qingzhu released the sleeve before he reached them, but her expression remained troubled.

“Keep this,” Wen Shou told Shi Feng. “Anyone challenging the tenth rank must challenge you now.”

Shi Feng accepted it and looked toward the higher names on the board.

First, Sima Yu. Second, Ling Qingzhu. Third, Han Zong.

His gaze stopped at the third name.

A familiar face hurried toward the passage before Wen Shou could speak. Kou Liang stopped several steps away, his expensive belt buckle shining beneath the sun.

He looked at Shi Feng's token and swallowed. The riverside encounter was still fresh in his mind. He remembered offering Ling Qingzhu a better place to eat while treating her husband as an annoyance.

“Young Master Shi,” Kou Liang said stiffly. “Congratulations.”

Shi Feng glanced at him.

“Your pavilion was comfortable?” Shi Feng asked.

Kou Liang's face reddened immediately.

“Very comfortable,” Kou Liang replied.

“Good,” Shi Feng said.

There was no threat in the answer. Kou Liang still hurried away. He didn't want another question about that evening.

Ling Qingzhu watched him leave, then looked at her husband, her eyes smiling above the veil. At the river, she dismissed Kou Liang because she wanted Shi Feng beside her. Now everyone would call that decision wise.

She suddenly disliked the difference.

Shi Feng didn't bother following the youth with his eyes. A rich fool wasn't worth interrupting his plans.

He thought, Third place, then I can go home. He wasn’t interested in standing beneath a ranking board all day while strangers guessed at his meridians. There's still a batch waiting for collection.

Wen Shou noticed.

“Don't rush,” Wen Shou advised. “Gao Zhen only recently entered Foundation Establishment. Han Zong is already at mid Foundation Establishment.”

Shi Feng considered that for a breath.

“Does the third place qualify?” Shi Feng asked.

“Yes,” Wen Shou replied.

“Then I'll challenge him next,” Shi Feng said.

chapters.title: You Let Me Believe It
chapters.html:
Ling Qingzhu waited until Wen Shou had sent the challenge to Han Zong. Then she took Shi Feng away from the crowded passage.

An empty waiting room stood behind the south wall. Its door opened onto the arena corridor, and voices carried through the upper shutters. She left the door ajar. Her white veil stayed tied.

Shi Feng stood beside the window. He had expected questions. He hadn't expected the careful way she kept her hands at her sides, as though holding his sleeve again would make her anger harder to state.

“You let me believe you were crippled,” Ling Qingzhu said.

He looked at her.

“Yes,” Shi Feng said.

She had prepared for one of his dry answers. The direct admission made her pause.

“How long?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“Foundation Establishment is recent,” Shi Feng said. “The recovery began before I came to the capital.”

Her fingers tightened. Before the tea house. Before the marriage papers. Before she stood over his bedding and wondered whether he could survive another mountain trip.

“You could cultivate when we made the agreement,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Yes,” Shi Feng said.

She turned toward the open door, then back again. Outside, someone laughed about Gao Zhen's fallen sword. She wanted those voices farther away.

“I told you what I believed,” Ling Qingzhu said. “I explained the danger and why the arrangement suited me. You heard it and said nothing.”

“You chose a man with no faction and a ruined reputation,” Shi Feng said. “The reputation was real. The condition wasn't.”

“That distinction mattered to me,” Ling Qingzhu said.

Her own words caught at her. She had explained the permits, her elders and the marriage rule. She hadn't explained why she had stopped to look at this particular man before asking him to bargain. He still thought she had met a convenient stranger.

Ling Qingzhu looked at the open door. That withheld reason didn't make his concealment painless. It did make it harder to speak as though she had placed everything honestly between them. She said nothing about it.

“I know that now,” Shi Feng said.

He had known it earlier too, if he was honest. He had simply preferred the safety of letting the world be wrong. At first she had been another person in that world. Somewhere between shared meals and her fingers straightening his work notes, that had changed without either of them agreeing what it meant.

She watched him, waiting for more.

“My recovery was mine to protect,” Shi Feng said. “Wei people were asking questions. The prince already disliked my name. I wanted time to cultivate before anyone decided what I should do with it.”

“So you couldn't trust me,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“At the tea house, I didn't know you,” Shi Feng said.

The answer hurt because it was reasonable. She remembered arriving with a neat paper on which his obligations filled the page. She had been offended that he asked about hers. Trust hadn't been among the things either of them offered that afternoon.

“And afterward?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

He didn't answer at once.

Afterward she had saved his rice, dried his blanket and stood close enough for him to forget what he was saying. Afterward he had wanted to tell her many things. Wanting hadn't made the words easy, and every quiet day made another quiet day seem sensible.

“I let it continue,” Shi Feng said. “That part was my choice.”

Her eyes shone above the veil. She was relieved by his acknowledgment and still angry enough to dislike the relief.

“I bandaged you,” Ling Qingzhu said. “I thought you were trying to survive with a body that couldn't carry qi. You stood there and let me worry about that.”

“The wound was real,” Shi Feng said.

“I know the wound was real,” Ling Qingzhu said. “I'm talking about what you allowed me to think while I tied it.”

He lowered his gaze to his own hand. She was right about that. He could defend the reason for keeping his cultivation secret without pretending the secrecy had cost her nothing.

“I should have answered more clearly when you asked,” Shi Feng said.

She drew a slow breath. It wasn't a full explanation, and she knew it. There were things behind his calm that a recent breakthrough couldn't explain. She didn't ask him to put every one on the table because she had finally noticed the first.

“Are you going to be safe against Han Zong?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“Yes,” Shi Feng said.

“You said that about Gao Zhen without telling me why,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Then here's why,” Shi Feng said. “I'm at early Foundation Establishment. My strength is greater than the ordinary measure of that realm. Han Zong is at mid Foundation Establishment. I'll need to pay attention. I won't need you to rescue me.”

She searched his face. He spoke without contempt for either her concern or Han Zong's cultivation. That helped more than another joke would have.

“I wasn't ashamed to stand beside you before today,” Ling Qingzhu said.

Shi Feng's chest tightened.

“I know,” Shi Feng said.

He remembered her taking his hand before the prince's carriage. Part performance, part something he had never managed to name. He remembered the day she carried his bowl without being asked. He hadn't mistaken every kindness she gave him.

“Don't say it as if I only wanted a useful husband,” Ling Qingzhu said.

He looked up sharply. She hadn't meant the words to sound so personal. Now they hung between them, and neither knew how to finish what they began.

“I won't,” Shi Feng said.

The bell keeper tested the bronze rim outside. A low note passed through the shutters. Their remaining time was shrinking.

Ling Qingzhu moved toward the door, then stopped.

“You don't have to tell the whole capital how it happened,” Ling Qingzhu said. “I understand that. I just don't want to learn everything about you from a crowd.”

Shi Feng felt the force of that simple request. He could promise care. He couldn't promise to hand over the physique, the ring's dead spirit and every enemy he had killed because one hidden fact had finally become public.

“I'll speak for myself,” Shi Feng said. “Where I can.”

She nodded slowly. It wasn't the easy answer she wanted, but it was one he meant. She accepted that much without claiming the hurt was settled.

At the corridor, he paused to let her pass first. Her sleeve brushed his wrist. Neither reached for the other.

Han Zong waited at the far end with his spear upright beside him. The crowd's talk had changed from whether Shi Feng belonged on the platform to how far he could climb.

Ling Qingzhu returned to the rail. Shi Feng went toward the official, carrying his own secrets and one honest answer more than he had brought into the room.

chapters.title: Three Moves Are Enough
chapters.html:
Han Zong accepted the direct challenge to third place. Wen Shou checked both tokens beneath the ranking board, then called the candidates onto the platform. Shi Feng drew his plain refined artifact sword. Across from him, Han Zong lowered his spear into a steady two-handed guard. Mid Foundation Establishment qi gathered along its shaft.

“Catching Gao Zhen's blade doesn't put you in the top three,” Han Zong said coldly, resting his thumb against the spear's iron collar. “Step down to tenth now, or leave the platform with a broken wrist.”

“The board says third is open to challenge,” Shi Feng replied calmly. “Point your spear whenever you're ready.”

From the front benches, two of Han Zong's clan cousins laughed aloud, calling out that three spear thrusts would send the peddler back to his ointment stall.

Wen Shou gave the signal.

The spear struck before the last echo of the announcement faded.

Han Zong drove forward with both hands on the shaft. His mid Foundation Establishment qi gathered behind the steel point. There was no wild shouting, only a straight thrust aimed at taking the centre.

Shi Feng moved half a step.

His sword touched the side of the spearhead and turned it past his robe. He didn't meet the whole force head-on. The simple movement left Han Zong's first strike pointing at empty stone.

Han Zong's expression tightened. He pulled the shaft across his body and swept at Shi Feng's waist. A worried shout rose from the front benches.

Shi Feng lowered his sword and stopped the sweep.

A sharp ring echoed across the arena. The spear trembled. Shi Feng's wrist remained steady.

Han Zong felt the force travel into both arms. His confidence shook immediately. He'd expected the lighter sword to give way, but the clash nearly broke his own grip.

Early Foundation Establishment? What kind of early Foundation Establishment was this?

Shi Feng pushed the spear away and stepped forward. Han Zong retreated without thinking. The movement saved his sleeve from being cut, but it gave Shi Feng the centre he'd meant to control.

Three exchanges. The crowd could see who was advancing.

“This isn't like Gao Zhen's fight!”

“Han Zong's being pushed back!”

“He hasn't used his real spear art yet!”

“Then he'd better hurry!”

Han Zong heard that last shout and felt anger rise beneath his shock. He didn't need a fool in the stands to tell him how to fight.

His qi surged through the shaft. A pale yellow light wrapped the spearhead.

“Stone-Splitting Spear!” Han Zong shouted.

He stamped down and thrust with enough force to crack the stone beneath his rear foot. The attack was stronger than the first two. Even Wen Shou moved closer to the platform's edge.

Shi Feng watched the spear come.

He thought, Too much force in one direction. He can't change it now.

His sword slid along the shaft instead of striking the point. The Iron River Sword Art's Turning Wave converted the short movement into a cut across Han Zong's grip.

Han Zong let go with one hand before his fingers met the edge. His spear dipped. Shi Feng withdrew half an inch, then returned the sword point beneath the opponent's chin.

Returning Tide.

The cold tip stopped against skin without drawing blood.

Han Zong froze.

His spear remained in one hand. He could still lift it, but lifting it wouldn't stop the sword already at his throat.

Shi Feng's breath was even. His early Foundation Establishment aura hadn't grown brighter. He hadn't been forced to reveal the strength of his foundation or his completed golden bones.

Only a little qi and three familiar sword movements were needed.

“Do we continue?” Shi Feng asked.

Han Zong looked at the blade. Anger, shame, and disbelief passed across his face. Then he slowly lowered the spear.

“I surrender,” Han Zong said.

Shi Feng stepped back at once.

Wen Shou stood beside them and raised his hand toward the ranking board.

“Shi Feng wins the challenge,” Wen Shou declared. “The third position changes hands.”

The audience erupted.

Gao Zhen slapped his own knee in relief. His servant jumped and nearly dropped the cloth.

“I told you!” Gao Zhen said loudly.

The servant stared at him. Gao Zhen hadn't told him anything useful since being thrown out of the arena.

“You saw it,” Gao Zhen insisted. “Han Zong couldn't stop him either!”

At least people now had another match to discuss.

Han Zong checked his spear before leaving the platform. A thin mark ran along the shaft where Shi Feng's sword passed. He traced it with one finger, then looked at the plain weapon in the winner's hand.

“That sword art,” Han Zong said. “Where did you learn it?”

“From someone who used it well,” Shi Feng replied.

Han Zong understood that he wouldn't get a name. He nodded stiffly and put the spear away.

“I lost,” Han Zong said. “But don't expect everyone at the Great Kingdom Tournament to leave an opening like mine.”

“I won't,” Shi Feng said.

There was no sneer in his answer. Han Zong felt a little less humiliated by that. Losing to a stronger opponent was bad enough without being lectured afterward.

He left the platform under his own strength. Wen Shou watched him go before turning to Shi Feng.

“You can challenge the second position after the required interval,” Wen Shou said.

“No need,” Shi Feng replied.

Wen Shou paused.

“You're certain?” Wen Shou asked.

“The first three qualify,” Shi Feng said. “I'm third.”

The official looked toward Ling Qingzhu, then toward Sima Yu's pavilion. Several nearby spectators followed his gaze and immediately formed their own explanations.

“He won't challenge his wife!”

“Of course not. Would you?”

“The Crown Prince is still first.”

“Third is enough. He's already qualified!”

Shi Feng returned his sword to its scabbard. Let them guess. He wasn't interested in arranging an extra fight just to correct strangers.

Ling Qingzhu approached him as he stepped down.

“You stopped,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“I got what I wanted,” Shi Feng replied.

Her gaze rested on his sword. He'd used it exactly as he promised, then beaten someone at a higher stage without looking strained.

She felt proud of him. The feeling came so quickly that she didn't have time to hide it.

“That last move was good,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“It worked,” Shi Feng replied.

“You don't have to sound so casual!” Ling Qingzhu said.

“You'd rather I shout?” Shi Feng asked.

Her eyes curved above her veil despite herself. Across the arena, Sima Yu stood at the pavilion rail. His expression remained pleasant, but Shi Feng didn't mistake it for goodwill.

He looked back without bowing.

The prince's gaze dropped briefly to the sword, his fingers tight on the carved rail. Guo Zhen had been found dead, Cao Wenshu had died on Hengyun Mountain, and Zheng Jian and Peng Zhao had died in the west-canal timber yard, and now the public cripple stood calmly in the third position.

Keep looking, Shi Feng thought. At Qingyun City, your rank won't stand between us.

He turned away first.

Wen Shou called for the next challenge. Several candidates glanced toward the third position, but none stepped forward. Han Zong was wiping sweat from his face beneath the far awning.

Nobody wanted to discover that they could lose even faster.

A familiar ointment buyer waited at the edge of the passage. Kou Tao bowed awkwardly when Shi Feng noticed him. His Bone Refinement cultivation wasn't enough to qualify, but he'd come to watch the stronger candidates.

“Young Master Shi, your medicine,” Kou Tao began.

“Did it fail?” Shi Feng asked.

“No! It worked very well,” Kou Tao replied. “I only wondered whether you'd still sell it.”

Shi Feng looked at the man's worried expression. A qualification token apparently made people think he'd forgotten how to open a medicine jar.

“The stall's still there,” Shi Feng said.

“The price?” Kou Tao asked carefully.

“Also still there,” Shi Feng replied.

Kou Tao smiled in relief and hurried back to his companions. He immediately began telling them that he bought medicine from the third-ranked candidate before anyone else believed it worked.

Shi Feng didn't interrupt that version of events. Kou Tao paid promptly. A little harmless boasting wouldn't empty his purse.

Shi Feng took a seat beside the waiting area and accepted a cup of water from an attendant. Ling Qingzhu stood beside him, her eyes still warm above her veil. For the first time since arriving, he relaxed his grip on the scabbard.

“Hungry?” Shi Feng asked.

“We're at a qualification competition!” Ling Qingzhu replied.

“That doesn't feed us,” Shi Feng said.

She looked at him for a moment, then glanced toward the food sellers outside the gate.

“A little,” Ling Qingzhu admitted.

chapters.title: Three Places for Great Liang
chapters.html:
One challenge remained before the final bell closed the board.

Fourth-ranked Qian Heng, a mid Foundation Establishment swordsman who had spent the afternoon watching third place slip out of reach, stepped forward and called a desperation challenge against Ling Qingzhu for second.

Ling Qingzhu walked onto the stone platform in her white veil, her slim scabbard still at her waist. When Wen Shou gave the signal, Qian Heng drove forward with a whistling three-step thrust that split the air across ten paces.

Ling Qingzhu drew and sheathed her sword in a single breath.

A line of pale frost ran across the flagstones. Qian Heng's blade stopped an inch from her sleeve, coated in rime to the hilt, while a clean cut parted the silk tie of his shoulder guard before he could take a second step. Even Wen Shou straightened in shock: she had released only enough qi to freeze the strike, hiding her true ceiling so cleanly that not one spectator could tell whether she stood at late or peak Foundation Establishment.

Watching from the third-place post, Shi Feng's eyes brightened. Her courtyard pointers hadn't shown a tenth of that speed.

“Second and third places confirmed,” Wen Shou announced as Qian Heng bowed and stepped down.

The final challenge period ended beneath a clear afternoon sky. Shi Feng stood beside the ranking board while an attendant replaced the temporary token with a carved jade plate. His name sat beneath Sima Yu and Ling Qingzhu.

Three names. Three representatives for Great Liang.

Wen Shou handed him the plate without ceremony. Shi Feng turned it over. The kingdom's crest was carved on the back, with a small identifying seal beneath it.

“Keep it until Qingyun City,” Wen Shou said. “The regional officials will check the seal against our list.”

“Can I travel separately?” Shi Feng asked.

“Yes,” Wen Shou replied. “As long as you arrive before registration closes. You'll receive the route and dates with the other representatives.”

Shi Feng nodded. He didn't need the court choosing every inn along his road.

Ling Qingzhu received her own plate nearby. Sima Yu accepted his from another official and walked toward them beneath the shade of two royal attendants.

The surrounding candidates stepped aside. Late Foundation Establishment cultivation was impressive among Great Liang's young generation. The royal crest made it more impressive still.

“Congratulations, Brother Shi,” Sima Yu said warmly.

Shi Feng looked at him.

“Your Highness,” Shi Feng replied.

No smile followed. The prince's warmth didn't change the men he'd sent or the killing intent behind their blades. Sima Yu glanced at Ling Qingzhu, then back at Shi Feng's plate.

“Great Liang needs capable representatives,” Sima Yu said. “I look forward to seeing what you can do beyond our borders.”

“So do I,” Shi Feng replied.

Wen Shou felt the coldness beneath the ordinary words. He quickly cleared his throat and lifted the departure notice.

“The Great Kingdom Tournament isn't this qualification,” Wen Shou said. “There will be candidates from every surrounding kingdom. Don't assume today's ranks will mean anything there.”

“How many will the Great Sects recruit?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“The top ten,” Wen Shou replied. “Martial Palace, Hundred Flower Valley, and Artificer Hall will send representatives. The champion can choose direct inner-disciple entry among the nearby Great Sects.”

Several defeated candidates listened from a few steps away. Their expressions were filled with envy. Even an ordinary outer-disciple place in a Great Sect was far beyond what their families could buy easily.

Shi Feng thought of Xu Changhe's worn notes. The dead sect enforcer's sword art brought him to the third position today. Artificer Hall remained his intended destination.

He didn't need to explain that to the Crown Prince.

“Arrive on time,” Wen Shou continued. “A kingdom's recommendation won't reopen closed registration.”

Sima Yu smiled and left with his attendants. Ling Qingzhu waited until the royal group moved away before looking at Shi Feng.

“You don't like him,” Ling Qingzhu said quietly.

“No,” Shi Feng replied.

She didn't ask him to pretend otherwise. That pleased him more than the qualification plate in his hand.

By evening, the capital seemed to have recovered his meridians on his behalf.

At one tea stall, Shi Feng heard that a mysterious elder healed him. At the next crossing, someone insisted that Ling Qingzhu gave him a priceless pill. Outside a fabric shop, two women confidently agreed that he'd never been crippled at all.

Shi Feng passed them without stopping.

Ling Qingzhu listened beside him, her expression growing stranger with every version.

“Apparently, I'm a wonderful physician,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“You should charge,” Shi Feng replied.

“Don't tempt me,” Ling Qingzhu said.

A silk merchant nearly walked into them while carrying two sample bolts. He recognised Ling Qingzhu first, then looked at her husband and hurriedly moved aside.

The silk merchant bowed in greeting.

Shi Feng nodded and continued walking.

He wasn't especially interested in the change. People who once looked past him were now afraid of standing too close. Their opinion had followed his visible strength, just as he expected.

Ling Qingzhu noticed the indifference and felt a little ashamed of her own excitement. She was proud of him. She also liked seeing people acknowledge that he belonged beside her.

Those weren't quite the same feeling.

At Qingliu Lane, Jiang Meilan was waiting outside the gate. The landlady carried a broom, but her smile was much too bright for someone cleaning.

“Third place!” Jiang Meilan exclaimed. “I always said this courtyard had good fortune.”

“You said the roof leaked because I hung herbs too near it,” Shi Feng replied.

Jiang Meilan's smile faltered for one breath.

“Small things!” Jiang Meilan said. “The roof's fixed now. Very good courtyard. A fine young couple.”

Ling Qingzhu coughed to hide a laugh. Shi Feng opened the gate before the landlady could discover a qualification fee among the fallen leaves. Ling Qingzhu waited until the gate shut before removing her veil.

Inside, nothing had changed. The pear tree stood beside the table. The kitchen was too small for all his trays. His bedding was still rolled in the corner of their one room.

He liked that more than the cheers outside. Ling Qingzhu set her plate on the table beside his. She looked at the two carved names for a while.

“We qualified together,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Yes,” Shi Feng replied.

“You could look pleased,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“I am,” Shi Feng answered.

She turned toward him. He wasn't looking at the plates anymore.

Her cheeks warmed. She picked hers up quickly and went inside to put it away.

Shi Feng made a simple supper after washing the arena dust from his hands. He didn't arrange a banquet to celebrate defeating Gao Zhen and Han Zong. There were ingredients to inspect later and a collection promised for the following day.

Ling Qingzhu sat at the table with her sleeves tied back. She took a bowl from him before he could place it down.

“Are you injured?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“No,” Shi Feng said.

“Not even your hand?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

He held it out. She looked at the fingers that caught Gao Zhen's sword and found no cut.

“That really was a refined artifact,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“I noticed,” Shi Feng replied.

She gave him an annoyed look and returned his hand. For a moment, he wanted to tell her how much stronger he was than the platform showed. Then he saw the genuine relief in her expression and decided she didn't need another reason to worry about his judgment.

He'd tell her things when they mattered.

Ling Qingzhu took the first bite of supper and smiled. The food tasted familiar. After the noise at the arena, that familiarity made her strangely happy.

She reached for the vegetables and noticed the plain sword leaning beside the doorway. Tomorrow, people would probably offer him much finer ones.

“Will you change your sword?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“Not unless I find a reason,” Shi Feng replied.

“Half the capital will want to give you something now,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“And ask for something afterward,” Shi Feng answered.

She considered that and nodded. Her clan received gifts too. Rarely did the giver forget to mention a cousin seeking employment or a shop needing protection.

“Don't let them disturb your work,” Ling Qingzhu said.

Shi Feng smiled slightly. Hearing her care about his work pleased him. He still remembered how she once looked at his medicine board as though the ink was the most valuable thing on it.

“I'll shut the gate,” Shi Feng said.

Outside the gate, somebody shouted his name.

Shi Feng paused with his chopsticks raised.

A second voice joined the first. Then came a knock and the rustle of several people arguing over who arrived earlier.

Ling Qingzhu looked toward the gate.

“Your customers?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

Shi Feng put his chopsticks down with a sigh.

“My cultivation's recovered,” Shi Feng said. “Apparently, everyone else's memory has too.”

chapters.title: An Old Friend at Every Gate
chapters.html:
“Young Master Shi, surely you remember me!” Bao Shun called through the gate.

Shi Feng looked at the steaming supper, then at Ling Qingzhu. She lifted her bowl with an expression that clearly told him this was his problem.

He opened the gate a hand's width.

Bao Shun leaned forward immediately. Behind the broker waited a thin merchant with a wooden gift box and a plump man carrying a jar of wine.

“I've come to congratulate you!” Bao Shun said.

“Done,” Shi Feng replied, and began closing the gate.

Bao Shun caught the edge before it shut.

“Wait! I've also brought two friends,” Bao Shun said.

“I’m eating,” Shi Feng replied. “Speak from there.”

The thin merchant, Luo Fang, coughed. His Qi Condensation cultivation barely showed beneath his fine clothes. He lifted the box quickly.

“Young Master Shi, a small gift,” Luo Fang said. “My shop sells excellent sword cloths.”

Shi Feng glanced at the box. A folded strip of silk rested inside. It was good silk, but hardly worth visiting someone's home over supper.

“What do you want?” Shi Feng asked.

Luo Fang looked relieved. He preferred someone who understood the purpose of a gift.

“My nephew hopes to serve a promising cultivator,” Luo Fang said. “Just a little guidance. He's hardworking.”

“No,” Shi Feng replied.

“You haven't met him,” Luo Fang protested.

“I'm not looking for a nephew,” Shi Feng said.

The plump man, Peng Lu, pushed forward before Luo Fang could continue. He wore a Bone Refinement waist token and smelled faintly of the wine he carried.

“I don't have a nephew,” Peng Lu announced.

“Congratulations,” Shi Feng said.

Bao Shun pressed his lips together. He couldn't decide whether laughing would improve his chances or ruin them.

Peng Lu lifted the wine jar.

“I run a small guard business,” Peng Lu said. “We could use your name. Nothing more! You won't need to fight. We'll pay a little every month.”

“And if your guards rob someone?” Shi Feng asked.

Peng Lu's smile stiffened.

“We wouldn't,” Peng Lu said.

“Then you don't need my name,” Shi Feng replied.

He closed the gate. Bao Shun removed his fingers just in time. Inside the courtyard, Ling Qingzhu was laughing into her sleeve.

“No nephew?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“An excellent qualification,” Shi Feng replied.

He sat down and found his bowl covered with another plate to keep it warm. Ling Qingzhu pretended not to notice his glance.

The next morning brought three more old friends. Shi Feng recognised none of them.

One claimed to remember his father. Another announced that their grandfathers once drank together. The third waited until the other two left before admitting he only wanted to buy medicine.

That one got a price instead of a closed gate.

“Can I have a discount?” Wu Gan asked.

The man was a Qi Condensation cultivator with thick hands and an honest expression. Shi Feng had already learned that an honest expression didn't prevent bargaining.

“For what?” Shi Feng asked.

“Being direct,” Wu Gan replied.

“The price is direct too,” Shi Feng said.

Wu Gan scratched his head, paid for the jar, and left. Shi Feng liked the transaction more than the previous visitors' speeches. At least he knew what the man wanted.

A familiar food seller arrived after Wu Gan left. He Shun carried a covered bowl and looked almost as nervous as the men with expensive gift boxes.

“Two portions,” He Shun said. “For you and your wife.”

Shi Feng recognised the sesame scent.

“What do you want?” Shi Feng asked.

He Shun scratched his ear.

“Could I say you ate at my stall?” He Shun asked.

“I did,” Shi Feng replied.

“And liked it?” He Shun added hopefully.

“My wife liked it,” Shi Feng said. “Don't turn it into medicine for reaching Foundation Establishment.”

He Shun looked horrified.

“They're dumplings!” He Shun said.

“Then we agree,” Shi Feng replied.

He paid for both portions before accepting them. He Shun tried to refuse, but the spirit stones were already in his hand. He left pleased enough with an honest claim to make outside his stall.

Shi Feng carried the bowl inside. Ling Qingzhu immediately put her book down.

She remembered the evening too.

Then Jiang Meilan appeared with a broom and an empty basket.

“The neighbours are asking whether you'll hold a celebration,” Jiang Meilan said.

“No,” Shi Feng replied.

“They'd all come,” Jiang Meilan added.

“That's why,” Shi Feng said.

The landlady sighed. She looked toward the medicine trays and lowered her voice.

“You won't leave immediately, will you?” Jiang Meilan asked.

Shi Feng glanced at her.

“The regional registration isn't tomorrow,” Shi Feng said.

“I meant the courtyard,” Jiang Meilan explained. “A Foundation Establishment cultivator usually wants more space.”

“And pays more rent,” Shi Feng replied.

Jiang Meilan's expression became innocent.

“The roof's fixed,” Jiang Meilan said.

“I remember paying rent before it was fixed,” Shi Feng replied.

She lifted the broom and discovered something urgent to sweep beside the gate. Shi Feng watched her for a moment, amused. His cultivation apparently made the courtyard better without moving a single wall.

Ling Qingzhu returned from the cloth shop before noon carrying a small parcel and a look of restrained annoyance. She tied her veil before answering another knock. A woman with a gift box asked whether Shi Feng received visitors who weren't customers.

“Madam Shi,” Luo Fang said quickly, arriving behind the caller, “we only hoped for a proper introduction.”

“Then ask him at the stall,” Ling Qingzhu said. “He decides whom he sees.”

The visitors left. She shut the gate, removed her veil and looked at Shi Feng over the parcel.

“Some of your old friends haven't met you yet,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Those are my favourite,” Shi Feng said.

She laughed despite herself. Then she pushed back her hair to show him the finished cloth, and he lost track of the explanation halfway through.

“Did you hear the price?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“No,” Shi Feng admitted.

She tapped his forehead with the folded silk. He caught her wrist, grinning, and she let him hold it for a moment before drawing away.

At the furnace yard later, he changed into Shen Mo's covered robe before entering by the side lane. Gao Yuan saw the familiar hood and asked about the next booking. He did not greet Great Liang's third representative, because Shi Feng hadn't given him the connection yet.

Inside, the copper furnace waited in its ordinary place. Neither the charcoal nor the medicine needed an old friendship to work. Shi Feng lit the fire and was glad of that.

chapters.title: The Man Under the Hood
chapters.html:
“Ask Master Shen to meet me,” Yan Meizhen said.

Shi Feng set her ingredient box on the furnace-room table and removed his hood.

“You're meeting him,” Shi Feng replied.

Yan Meizhen's hand stopped above the chair. Her Bone Refinement aura stirred as surprise broke through her usual calm.

She looked at the hood, the face cloth, and the familiar tools on the table. She already knew Shi Feng carried messages and medicines for Master Shen. She never suspected that the supposed intermediary was the alchemist himself.

“You?” Yan Meizhen asked.

Shi Feng nodded.

“All this time?” Yan Meizhen asked.

“Since your first order,” Shi Feng replied.

She sat down slowly. For a while, the only sound came from someone splitting charcoal outside.

Then Yan Meizhen laughed sharply.

“I offered you a delivery fee,” Yan Meizhen said.

“You wanted a delivery,” Shi Feng replied.

“And the refiner's fee too,” Yan Meizhen added.

“You wanted pills,” Shi Feng said.

She shook her head. The arrangement was irritating only because she hadn't seen it. The medicines arrived, the terms were honoured, and nobody forced her to pay for imaginary work.

Still, she wanted to complain.

“Why the hood?” Yan Meizhen asked.

“People argue less with a hood than a cripple,” Shi Feng replied.

Yan Meizhen looked at the sword at his waist. After the qualification, nobody could mistake his public strength again.

“And now?” Yan Meizhen asked.

“Now I'd rather work without covering my face,” Shi Feng said.

That was all the explanation he intended to give.

“The Eastern Palace steward who threatened our road permits had his plaque dredged out of the west-canal sluice three mornings ago, and his body was found behind the chained gate of the timber yard,” Yan Meizhen added quietly, opening her ingredient box and pushing it across the table. “When the ward constables questioned Gao Yuan and the sluice watchman, both testified that Zheng Jian had threatened Master Shen here, followed him into the yard with two armed retainers, and locked the chain from the inside. The ward office recorded it as an extortion ambush gone wrong and closed the file. His clerks vanished from the herb market the same day, and Duan Li already sent his runner ahead of me to rebook his Returning Breath Pill order.”

“Duan Li's slip arrived an hour ago,” Shi Feng said.

“Then Master Shi,” Yan Meizhen said, tapping the neat packets inside her box, “tell me what you can make from these.”

The argument outside began before they finished.

Zhu Shan stood in the courtyard with Cheng Huan beside him. Gao Yuan blocked the furnace-room door, looking unusually troubled.

“Master Shen's inside?” Zhu Shan demanded.

“Yes,” Gao Yuan said.

“Then why did Shi Feng go in?” Zhu Shan asked.

“He booked the room,” Gao Yuan replied.

“Which one?” Cheng Huan asked.

Gao Yuan opened his mouth, then shut it. He'd charged both names for different sessions and never looked beyond the hood when the spirit stones were correct.

The furnace-room door opened.

Shi Feng stood there without the face cloth. Yan Meizhen sat at the table behind him, checking her commission terms.

Zhu Shan stared.

Cheng Huan looked from Shi Feng to the hood hanging beside the door.

Gao Yuan's expression became painful.

“Master Shen?” Zhu Shan asked weakly.

“Shi Feng,” Shi Feng replied. “The medicine hasn't changed.”

“You were both?” Cheng Huan asked.

“No,” Shi Feng said. “I was one person.”

Yan Meizhen laughed behind him. Zhu Shan didn't find it funny yet.

He remembered his complaints about the alchemist's stubborn terms. He also remembered telling Shi Feng that his mysterious master should be more generous.

All those complaints reached the same ears.

Gao Yuan rubbed his forehead.

“Why didn't you say so?” Gao Yuan asked.

“You didn't ask,” Shi Feng replied.

“I introduced customers to you!” Gao Yuan protested.

“And collected the fee,” Shi Feng said.

The landlord had no answer to that.

Zhu Shan finally stepped into the room. He looked at the familiar pill boxes and checked one of the small written labels.

The handwriting was the same. The arrangement was the same. Even the plain cloth beneath the pills was familiar.

He suddenly felt foolish for caring about the face more than the medicine.

“You still make the common recovery pills?” Zhu Shan asked.

“Yes,” Shi Feng said.

“Same terms?” Zhu Shan asked.

“For the same order,” Shi Feng replied.

Zhu Shan immediately put his ingredients down.

“Then this conversation was unnecessary,” Zhu Shan declared.

Cheng Huan laughed so loudly that two tenants peered around the courtyard wall.

By noon, the tenants knew. By afternoon, the neighbouring shops knew. Gao Yuan made certain everyone heard that the rising alchemist rented his furnace room, although he wisely stopped short of painting Shi Feng's name on the gate.

Shi Feng ignored the gossip until Fang Jingyuan appeared. The unmarked Foundation Establishment alchemist stood in the doorway with his sleeves tucked behind him. His gaze moved over the furnace and the sealed medicine boxes before settling on Shi Feng.

“So you're the hooded one,” Fang Jingyuan said.

“I was,” Shi Feng replied.

Fang Jingyuan stepped inside. He remembered the medicine peddler who once accepted paid pill-testing work. Seeing the same man with a kingdom representative's sword annoyed him more than he expected.

“Foundation Establishment doesn't make an alchemy master,” Fang Jingyuan said.

“Then we agree,” Shi Feng replied.

The easy answer spoiled the lecture Fang Jingyuan prepared. He picked up a sealed pill bottle, then paused when Shi Feng held out a hand.

“That's a customer's,” Shi Feng said.

“I can inspect it,” Fang Jingyuan replied.

“Buy one of mine,” Shi Feng said.

Fang Jingyuan's expression darkened. Two waiting customers watched from outside, clearly interested in whether the older alchemist would pay.

He paid.

Shi Feng opened a separate bottle and handed over one pill. Fang Jingyuan examined the colour, scent, and smooth surface. He scratched a tiny piece from it and tested the medicinal force carefully.

His expression changed.

The refining was sound—cleanly bound, free of scorched sediment, and steadier than half the marked bottles sold along South Pill Street.

“The binding is clean and the fire held evenly,” Fang Jingyuan admitted aloud before catching himself in front of the watching doorway crowd. He cleared his throat stiffly. “Still only common medicine.”

“That's what you bought,” Shi Feng replied.

A laugh came from the doorway. Fang Jingyuan turned sharply, and the nearest customer became interested in his own shoes. Fang Jingyuan put the pill away and left without another lecture.

Shi Feng didn't chase him with a boast. He had no Sky Pavilion Mark, and he didn't need to pretend otherwise. Today's commissions paid for medicine within his actual ability.

That ability was growing.

Yan Meizhen returned to collect her written terms before sunset. She looked at the now-open doorway and shook her head again.

“The hood would've been worth something,” Yan Meizhen said.

“To whom?” Shi Feng asked.

“Gao Yuan,” Yan Meizhen replied. “He'd charge tenants to look at it.”

Shi Feng glanced outside. The landlord was already staring at the hook beside the door.

He took it down before leaving.

At home, Ling Qingzhu was standing beside his medicine board in the fading light. The gate was shut, and her veil lay folded on the table untouched. Two women outside the lane had been excitedly repeating the news from Gao Yuan's furnace yard when she walked home.

“Master Shen,” Ling Qingzhu said. Her voice was flat.

Shi Feng paused with his hand on the strap of his bag. “Not anymore,” Shi Feng said.

“Three days ago, in the arena waiting room, I asked you for one thing,” Ling Qingzhu said, looking straight at him. “I told you I didn't want to learn everything about you from a crowd. And you looked at me and said you would speak for yourself.”

Shi Feng's smile faded. “The furnace yard was business—” Shi Feng began.

“Yan Meizhen knew before noon. Zhu Shan knew. Half of South Pill Street knew before I walked past Granny Qin's brazier,” Ling Qingzhu said quietly. “You stood in that waiting room after hiding your cultivation for six months, promised you would speak for yourself, and walked back to a hooded room you didn't bother to mention.”

“Keeping the hood separate kept the Eastern Palace's errands away from this gate,” Shi Feng said.

“You always have a practical reason,” Ling Qingzhu said. Her fingers rested briefly on the edge of the table, then withdrew. “And every time I believe we've stopped performing, I find another curtain behind the one you just opened.”

She didn't shout, and she didn't reach for the supper bowls waiting by the stove.

“The rice is under the cover,” Ling Qingzhu said evenly, turning toward the inner room. “Eat when you like.”

The door closed behind her, followed by the quiet scrape of the folding screen. Out in the courtyard, Shi Feng stood alone beside the basin as the water cooled, knowing a joke about washing dishes wouldn't cross that threshold tonight.

chapters.title: Madam Shi Has a Seat
chapters.html:
“The seat beside me is taken,” Shi Feng said.

The servant stopped with a cushion in his hands. Behind him, a smiling merchant looked from Shi Feng to Ling Qingzhu and hurriedly pointed toward another table.

“Of course,” Cen Hao said. “Madam Shi, please sit.”

Ling Qingzhu sat beside her husband without waiting for another invitation. They had exchanged barely three sentences over breakfast after last night's chill beside the medicine board, yet she had still tied her veil at the gate when Yan Meizhen's carriage arrived.

Her white veil stayed tied. Cen Hao could see only her eyes as she acknowledged him. She placed her sleeves neatly against the table and gave the merchant a cool nod.

Cen Hao withdrew. His early Foundation Establishment cultivation didn't help him understand why arranging one room became harder every time a new guest arrived.

The gathering occupied the upper floor of Qinghe House. Merchants and cultivators sat around six low tables, with samples of weapons and herbs displayed along one wall.

Yan Meizhen invited Shi Feng because several buyers wanted to discuss medicine. She invited Ling Qingzhu because bringing the kingdom's first beauty made any gathering look grander.

She didn't pretend those reasons were charity.

“I told them you might accept new orders,” Yan Meizhen said. “Not that you'd agree to all of them.”

“Good,” Shi Feng replied.

“And I told Cen Hao to provide decent tea,” Yan Meizhen added.

“Then he has work to do,” Ling Qingzhu said after tasting it.

Yan Meizhen laughed. Cen Hao heard from the next table and immediately waved for a fresh pot.

Shi Feng looked at his wife. Her expression was perfectly calm. She was much better at frightening merchants than he was.

The second buyer knew what she wanted.

Ning Hong was a woman in her thirties with early Foundation Establishment cultivation and a thin scar beneath one ear. She supervised guards for several trading houses and asked about ordinary recovery medicines rather than legendary pills.

“How long will they keep in a warm climate?” Ning Hong asked.

Shi Feng answered, then asked where the guards would travel. She named a southern route and showed him the kind of medicine boxes she used.

He checked the lining.

“Change this,” Shi Feng said. “It holds damp.”

Ning Hong frowned.

“The seller promised it was suitable,” Ning Hong said.

“For dry roots,” Shi Feng replied. “Not finished pills on that road.”

She tested the soft inner cloth with her fingers and nodded.

“Can you supply the boxes too?” Ning Hong asked.

“I can tell you which ones to buy,” Shi Feng said.

Ning Hong accepted the advice and went to examine a different lining. Ling Qingzhu remained beside Shi Feng, making the occupied seat very clear without saying another word.

Pei Rong arrived with a cup of tea and the same unhurried expression Shi Feng remembered from the ferry road.

“You kept the plain sword longer than I expected,” Pei Rong said.

“It still had uses,” Shi Feng said.

“So did the one with the Wei maker's mark,” Pei Rong said quietly.

Ling Qingzhu was speaking to Yan Meizhen a few steps away. Shi Feng looked at the merchant. Pei Rong recognised provenance, not a fight. He hadn't been at the quarry and knew better than to pretend otherwise.

“Good metal travels,” Shi Feng said.

“Naturally,” Pei Rong said, lowering his voice over the rim of his cup. “And Jade Scale Trading House has naturally forgotten which crate held that Yunze blade when Officer Cheng held your permit at the Southern Gate. Though my factor did mention that a Wei household rider passed through the gate yesterday asking after a quarry witness named Gao An—and after an audience at the Eastern Palace.”

Shi Feng's gaze stayed level. “Name your term, Master Pei.”

“First call on two batches of your Returning Breath Pills before the tournament road opens, at ten spirit stones below the South Pill Street rate,” Pei Rong said smoothly. “In return, my house's Southern Gate surety stays sealed, and my southern herb carts remain open to your orders.”

That was discretion with a concrete price attached, not friendship. Shi Feng weighed the twenty-stone concession against an unhurried supply line and nodded once. Pei Rong raised his cup, Shi Feng returned the gesture, and each kept his own reasons.

Cen Hao found Shi Feng beside the displayed tools after the discussion ended. The merchant lifted a small silver scoop from a velvet-lined box.

“For measuring medicinal powder,” Cen Hao explained. “Excellent work. Very suitable for a kingdom representative.”

Shi Feng took it and checked the bowl. The metal was clean. The handle carried an elaborate dragon pattern that served no purpose.

“How much?” Shi Feng asked.

Cen Hao named a price.

Shi Feng put it back.

“The ordinary one,” Shi Feng said.

Cen Hao's smile became strained.

“Young Master Shi, surely your standing—” Cen Hao began.

“Doesn't measure herbs,” Shi Feng interrupted.

Ling Qingzhu lowered her eyes, letting the veil hide her smile. The merchant took a plain copper scoop from beneath the table. Its bowl was properly shaped, and its handle was strong enough for years of use.

Shi Feng paid the ordinary price.

“Anything else?” Cen Hao asked without much hope.

“A clean wrapping,” Shi Feng replied.

Cen Hao found one.

They left Qinghe House before the larger banquet began. Shi Feng had no reason to spend another evening listening to people explain why being powerful meant paying more for everything. Ling Qingzhu walked beside him with her hands folded into her sleeves.

“You were patient today,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“I was buying something,” Shi Feng replied.

“With Ning Hong,” Ling Qingzhu added.

“She was buying something,” Shi Feng said.

“You answered all her questions,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Would you buy medicine from someone who wouldn't?” Shi Feng asked.

She had no good reply. Of course she'd want clear answers. That didn't make her irritation disappear.

Shi Feng looked at her lowered lashes and felt pleased despite himself. Jealousy wasn't an apology or a confession, but it meant she cared where his attention went.

He thought, Don't push too hard. She's already annoyed enough.

“Your questions are harder,” Shi Feng said.

Ling Qingzhu glanced up.

“Which questions?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“Whether I should go back to meet someone's niece,” Shi Feng replied.

Her cheeks warmed behind the veil at once.

“You knew what answer to give,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“I did,” Shi Feng replied.

She stayed quiet for several steps. Then her sleeve brushed his arm deliberately rather than by accident.

At the courtyard, Shi Feng opened the gate and let her enter first. She stopped beside the table and turned toward him. Once he shut the gate, she untied her veil.

“You didn't have to leave early,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“I wanted to,” Shi Feng replied.

“Because the merchants were annoying?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“Partly,” Shi Feng said.

She waited.

Shi Feng put the wrapped scoop on the kitchen table and looked back at her.

“The walk home was better,” Shi Feng added quietly. “And I shouldn't have let South Pill Street tell you about Master Shen before I did.”

Ling Qingzhu paused with her hand on the veil's knot. The stiffness that had lingered since the previous evening eased by a fraction.

“Don't make a habit of apologizing after the street finishes talking,” Ling Qingzhu said, though she moved one of her own small boxes aside in the gate-side cupboard to make room for his wrapped scoop.

Before he could answer, a breathless boy from the southern herb market rapped on the outer latch with a slip from Mu An: Qian Bo and two armed guards had locked the warehouse lane and were seizing every southern root cart booked under Shi Feng's name.

chapters.title: Who Sold You My Herbs?
chapters.html:
“Who sold you my herbs?” Qian Bo demanded.

Shi Feng stood beside a handcart loaded with sealed root packets. The question interrupted Mu An's explanation of the last two bundles.

The young herb seller turned pale. His Qi Condensation cultivation wasn't enough to stand against the Bone Refinement merchant blocking the warehouse entrance.

Qian Bo wore a brown robe and three heavy rings. Two guards stood behind him. One carried a short staff. The other's early Foundation Establishment aura was strong enough to make several workers step away.

Shi Feng looked at Mu An.

“Are they his?” Shi Feng asked.

“No,” Mu An said quickly. “I bought them from the southern growers. You checked the whole lot yesterday!”

Qian Bo snorted and slapped the cart's side.

“Every bundle from that district passes through my trade,” Qian Bo said. “You don't get to avoid my share because a young master wants cheap medicine.”

Mu An's fear turned to anger.

“You stopped buying from them!” Mu An protested. “You said the roads made the price too high!”

“And now I've changed my mind,” Qian Bo replied.

Shi Feng understood immediately. The merchant didn't want to pay the growers when the harvest arrived. Once someone else bought and carried the goods into the capital, he wanted his profit anyway.

There wasn't a hidden rule to study. Qian Bo simply expected people to be afraid of his guards.

Shi Feng thought, Good. This won't take long.

He picked up the cart handles.

Luo Hu stepped in front of him. His Bone Refinement aura rose as he tightened his grip.

“Didn't you hear Master Qian?” Luo Hu snapped.

“I heard enough,” Shi Feng replied.

Qian Bo pointed toward the warehouse.

“Leave the goods inside,” Qian Bo ordered. “We'll settle the price after I've inspected them.”

“No,” Shi Feng said.

The flat refusal made the merchant's face redden. Several workers stopped pretending not to watch.

“You think a qualification token lets you steal my trade?” Qian Bo asked.

“I paid the owner,” Shi Feng said. “You're neither the owner nor interesting. Move.”

Qian Bo looked toward the stronger guard.

“Du Jiang,” Qian Bo said. “Explain things.”

The early Foundation Establishment cultivator stepped forward. A long scar marked his forehead, and his belt held a curved refined artifact blade.

He recognised Shi Feng. Everyone near the market knew about the third-ranked candidate. Du Jiang also heard that Shi Feng only recently reached early Foundation Establishment.

He'd spent seven years at the same stage. That gave him confidence it shouldn't have.

“Young Master Shi, don't make trouble,” Du Jiang said.

“Then don't stand in front of my cart,” Shi Feng replied.

Du Jiang placed a hand on the handles. His qi flowed into his palm, pressing the wood downward.

The cart didn't move.

Shi Feng lifted the shaft with one hand and sent a measured pulse of early Foundation Establishment force through the oak frame.

The flagstone beneath Du Jiang's front boot cracked down the middle. Du Jiang's arm numbed to the shoulder; he lost his grip and staggered three paces backward into Qian Bo's tally table, spilling ink and weight-stones across the cobbles.

Around the warehouse arch, a dozen southern growers and herb carriers stopped unloading their baskets.

“That's Shi Feng—the third representative who beat Han Zong in three moves!”

“Du Jiang couldn't even hold the cart down against one hand!”

“Qian Bo refused the southern harvest last month and now wants a toll from Master Shi?”

“Why are we paying Qian Bo's gate cut at all if Master Shi buys direct?”

Du Jiang cradled his numb wrist, his face grey as he stepped behind Qian Bo instead of reaching for his curved blade. Qian Bo stood ankle-deep in scattered tally slips, his three heavy rings trembling against his sleeve as two southern growers walked straight past his overturned table to hand their sample packets to Mu An.

“What are you waiting for?” Qian Bo hissed at his guard.

“Find another guard if you want to test his sword,” Du Jiang muttered, refusing to meet Shi Feng's eyes.

Shi Feng turned the cart cleanly around the ruined table and started toward the furnace lane while the crowd parted with respectful nods.

Luo Hu shifted as though he might block them again. Shi Feng looked at the staff, then at its owner.

Luo Hu stepped aside.

Qian Bo shouted after them, but Shi Feng didn't turn. An angry merchant wasn't enough reason to miss the morning's furnace session.

Mu An helped unload the herbs in the yard before Gao Yuan could invent a fee for using the gate.

“Young Master Shi, I didn't know he'd come,” Mu An said.

“I know,” Shi Feng replied.

“He tries that whenever someone's goods sell well,” Mu An continued. “Usually they give him a little to make him leave.”

“Then he comes back,” Shi Feng said.

Mu An looked embarrassed.

“Yes,” Mu An admitted.

Shi Feng opened the last packet and checked the roots against the sample. They were fresh enough for Ning Hong's trial order and two smaller commissions. He paid the balance without deducting anything for the delay.

Mu An accepted the spirit stones carefully.

“If he bothers you again, I'll tell the market overseer,” Mu An said.

“Sell your herbs,” Shi Feng replied. “I'll handle my own trouble.”

The young seller nodded and left quickly. He wasn't a brave companion, and Shi Feng had no reason to demand that he become one. Gao Yuan peered around the doorway once the cart was gone.

“A dispute?” Gao Yuan asked.

“Someone wanted my ingredients,” Shi Feng replied.

“Will he come here?” Gao Yuan asked nervously.

“He can knock,” Shi Feng said.

The landlord didn't look reassured.

Shi Feng shut the furnace-room door and began sorting the roots. His anger faded as soon as he had useful work in front of him. Qian Bo tried to take what he bought, failed, and embarrassed himself.

If the merchant left matters there, that would be the end of it.

The first roots needed slicing rather than grinding. Shi Feng laid them across a board and cut away the dry ends. This medicine required the inner pulp and outer skin to soften together. Grinding everything first would bring the bitterness out before the useful parts joined.

He tested one small portion before opening the rest. The paste held evenly beneath his qi, and the familiar medicinal scent filled the room.

A knock came from outside.

“Your wife sent this,” Gao Yuan said through the door.

Shi Feng opened it and found a covered lunch bowl in the landlord's hands. A folded cloth rested beneath it.

“How much did you charge for carrying it?” Shi Feng asked.

Gao Yuan looked offended.

“She brought it to the gate herself!” Gao Yuan replied.

“Then why didn't she knock?” Shi Feng asked.

“She said not to interrupt the fire,” Gao Yuan answered.

Shi Feng looked down at the bowl and smiled. His irritation with the morning's merchant disappeared completely.

He put the lunch somewhere clean and returned to the furnace. Ning Hong's first order would be ready on time.

When Shi Feng stepped out at dusk to empty the cooled ash tray, Mu An stopped by the lane gate with two fresh southern contracts already signed at grower rates—and word that Qian Bo had been seen hurrying toward the Eastern Palace's outer steward office, boasting that a Yunze murder petition was about to strip the third representative of his token before the caravans ever left Great Liang.

chapters.title: The Price of a Useful Pill
chapters.html:
“Enough for the first route,” Ning Hong said.

Shi Feng placed the last box beside the others. Each held the same recovery medicine, sealed against damp and packed for the southern journey.

Ning Hong opened one. Her early Foundation Establishment qi entered the pill lightly, testing its stability. Then she checked the boxes themselves.

“You changed the lining,” Ning Hong said.

“You asked me which kind to buy,” Shi Feng replied.

“And you actually bought it,” Ning Hong said.

“The rough cloth sheds threads,” Shi Feng replied. “One caught under a lid last time.”

Ning Hong opened a second box and ran her thumb along the clean lining.

“Good,” Ning Hong said. “My men stack everything under the heaviest sack they can find. I don’t need loose threads in the medicine as well.”

She smiled. She was used to merchants promising small things during a discussion and forgetting them once paid.

The furnace room smelled faintly of fresh medicine. Outside, Gao Yuan kept passing the doorway without finding a convincing reason to enter.

Ning Hong counted the customer's share and set her payment on the table. Shi Feng didn't touch the spirit stones until she finished inspecting the last box.

“Those are yours?” Ning Hong asked, pointing to the separate bottle.

“The agreed share,” Shi Feng replied.

She nodded. Four successful pills remained beside a little failed medicine from the practice portion. The customer received what was promised, and his own cultivation gained resources alongside his purse.

He liked business that ended clearly.

Ning Hong took one pill from her box and swallowed it. Its medicinal force spread evenly through her body. The effect was modest for her realm, but it was clean and steady.

Her guards at Bone Refinement would benefit more.

“This will do,” Ning Hong said.

Shi Feng accepted the payment.

“Let me know how they keep after the southern crossing,” Shi Feng said. “If the lining gets damp, I’ll change it for the next order.”

Ning Hong laughed.

“I'll make the guards listen,” Ning Hong replied.
