She called for a porter to carry the boxes. The man waiting outside was at Qi Condensation and stared openly at Shi Feng's sword before remembering the task. He picked the boxes up with both hands and left without dropping one.

That was all the respect Shi Feng needed from him.

By noon, the final balance from two smaller commissions arrived. Shi Feng put the ingredient money aside first, paid for the next furnace sessions, and kept a real reserve after both expenses. There was no need to count whether buying rice would delay charcoal.

He felt a quiet satisfaction at that. The vow made over eleven spirit stones was finally producing something he could hold onto. Gao Yuan found him checking the next ingredient list.

“Business is good,” Gao Yuan said.

“Yes,” Shi Feng replied.

“Then perhaps a larger room,” Gao Yuan suggested.

“No,” Shi Feng said.

Gao Yuan sighed. He'd prepared three reasons for the larger room and got no chance to use any of them.

“The current one has limited space,” Gao Yuan said stubbornly.

“Your doorway's usually full of you,” Shi Feng replied.

The landlord stepped aside before remembering that it was his doorway.

Shi Feng returned to his notes. More work didn't mean accepting every order. He still had sword practice, cultivation, and a regional journey ahead. He wanted useful income, not a yard full of angry people waiting for promises he couldn't keep.

Once alone, Shi Feng spent a short practice portion on the Golden Core formula. The first joining held longer than before. The final turn still broke it. He wrote down the improvement and kept the failed medicine separate from every customer's stock. More income gave him time to practice; it didn't certify an unfinished pill.

That evening, Shi Feng bought fresh fish, rice, and a bundle of good vegetables. Nothing had a noble name. Everything was fresh enough that the seller didn't need to explain away the smell.

He also bought a thicker mat for the floor. The mat amused Ling Qingzhu more than the food.

“You're finally tired of the old one?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“My back's been tired of it longer,” Shi Feng replied.

“You never said,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“You've never offered to exchange,” Shi Feng replied.

She glanced toward her bed and immediately raised her chin.

“The terms were clear,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“I remember,” Shi Feng replied.

He wasn't asking for the bed. She understood that after a moment and looked slightly embarrassed by her quick answer.

He unrolled the thicker mat beside the old bedding. It fit without reaching beneath the folding screen or blocking her chest. Ling Qingzhu watched him smooth the edge with one hand.

“You could've bought it earlier,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“I bought it now,” Shi Feng replied.

She accepted that answer easily. In her mind, his new success explained the better purchase. It didn't occur to her to question the original payment she still believed he received.

A folded dark robe lay beside his bedding. He recognised the cloth bought with her violet silk.

“The seamstress sent it,” Ling Qingzhu said.

Shi Feng put it on before cooking and checked the cuffs. They sat properly against his wrists. The stronger lining made them feel firmer without becoming stiff.

“Better?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“Yes,” Shi Feng replied.

She stood up to check the collar. It needed no adjustment, but her fingers rested there for a moment anyway.

“Don't burn this one immediately,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“I'll tell the furnace,” Shi Feng replied.

“Tell yourself,” Ling Qingzhu said.

He looked down at her hand. She noticed and stepped back, trying to sound annoyed as she ordered him to change before cooking fish in a new robe.

Shi Feng changed with a smile. He folded the garment carefully instead of hanging it over the nearest chair. Someone had spent time making it fit him.

Shi Feng went to cook. She followed him and took the vegetables before he reached for them.

“I can wash these,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“I didn't say you couldn't,” Shi Feng replied.

“You were about to,” Ling Qingzhu said.

He wisely left her the basin.

They ate after sunset. The fish was ordinary and well cooked. Ling Qingzhu took another piece without commenting on the price.

Shi Feng watched her enjoy it and felt pleased. He could provide a better meal without emptying his purse. He could keep pills for his foundation without leaving the next day's ingredients unpaid.

That was the kind of wealth he wanted first.

Later, he swallowed his retained pills one by one and guided their strength through his foundation. The effect didn't weaken with repeated use. His physique absorbed each portion cleanly, leaving no poison or hidden cost.

His foundation grew steadier, but it demanded far more medicine before the next stage. Shi Feng didn't mind. He now had a way to obtain it.

From behind the screen, Ling Qingzhu called his name.

“The new mat?” Ling Qingzhu asked. “Is it comfortable?”

Shi Feng stretched out and looked at the ceiling.

“More than the old one,” Shi Feng replied.

“Good,” Ling Qingzhu said softly.

The travel notice came the next morning. Ling Qingzhu tied her veil before opening the gate to Lu Sen, who checked both names on the delivery slip.

“Either spouse can acknowledge it,” Lu Sen said.

Ling Qingzhu signed. The ordinary word pleased her. She put the notices together until Shi Feng returned, then handed him his own. They checked the reporting dates and the identification plates before discussing where they might go afterward.

“Artificer Hall,” Shi Feng said. “An elder's lessons helped me. I'd like to see the place.”

“Hundred Flower Valley interests me,” Ling Qingzhu said. “I'll listen before choosing.”

He smiled at that, though as he folded the travel notice he noted the red magistrate's endorsement stamped in the margin: the pre-departure representative briefing had been moved up, and any pending household petitions from the provinces were to be heard before the reporting tokens were issued.

chapters.title: The Boat Beyond the Willows
chapters.html:
“You're standing on my sleeve,” Ling Qingzhu said.

Shi Feng looked down and moved his foot. The violet silk slipped free without damage.

“You wore a long one,” Shi Feng replied.

“You said to wear it,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“I said it suited you,” Shi Feng answered.

“Then watch where you stand,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

The boatman waiting beside the landing looked away to hide a smile. His name was Old Su, and his Qi Condensation cultivation earned him enough to handle the small passenger boat without struggling against the river.

Shi Feng paid for an ordinary circuit beyond the willow bank. Old Su offered a longer journey toward a famous waterside restaurant.

“No restaurant,” Shi Feng said.

Ling Qingzhu laughed before the boatman could ask why.

They stepped aboard. Shi Feng held the edge steady while she settled onto the narrow bench. Then he sat opposite her and put the small food parcel between them.

The boat moved away from the landing. Within a few breaths, the shouting merchants behind them became difficult to hear.

Ling Qingzhu relaxed.

“You prefer this side?” Shi Feng asked.

“No one follows us here,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

“There's a boatman,” Shi Feng said.

“He's useful,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

Old Su nodded solemnly from the stern.

“Very useful, young lady,” Old Su agreed.

Her eyes curved above her veil, then turned toward the landing shrinking behind them.

“At a clan gathering, someone always wants me to meet another elder,” Ling Qingzhu said. “Or smile at a guest. Or hear what a guest's son achieved.”

“Should I describe my qualification?” Shi Feng asked.

“You should fall into the river,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

He laughed. She liked the sound and turned toward him again.

“Here, I can sit quietly,” Ling Qingzhu said.

Shi Feng nodded and stopped teasing. He hadn't thought the simple journey would matter so much to her. For a while, he let her enjoy the river without another question.

The river widened beyond the willows. Low stone walls bordered several gardens on the far side. A few birds rested on the roof of an empty pavilion.

Shi Feng looked at his wife instead.

The new silk suited her, just as he expected. Her black hair was fixed with the silver clasp he repaired, leaving a few loose strands beside her white veil. When she turned toward the breeze, he had trouble remembering the gardens at all.

Ling Qingzhu caught him looking.

“What?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“The clasp's straight,” Shi Feng replied.

She raised a hand to it before recognising the excuse.

“You've become very fond of that clasp,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“It hasn't insulted me once,” Shi Feng replied.

She laughed and shielded the lower edge of her veil with her hand to eat a plum slice from the parcel. He bought the sweeter kind this time. She noticed immediately.

“Better,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“I'll tell the plums,” Shi Feng replied.

Old Su brought the boat beside a small landing beyond the busiest gardens. A low pavilion stood nearby, with a tea seller beneath one corner and an old painter arranging paper under a stone weight.

“Half an hour?” Old Su asked.

Shi Feng looked at Ling Qingzhu. She nodded.

“Half an hour,” Shi Feng replied.

The painter noticed them before they reached the pavilion. His name was Bian Zhuo. He was an elderly Meridian Opening cultivator with ink on two fingers and an expression that became enthusiastic when he saw Ling Qingzhu.

“Young lady, a painting?” Bian Zhuo asked.

“No,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

“Just the landscape,” Bian Zhuo added quickly.

“You were looking at her,” Shi Feng said.

“A fine person improves a landscape,” Bian Zhuo replied without shame.

Shi Feng picked up a sample painting. The river was good. The distant roof looked a little crooked, but the willows were better than he expected from the man's hurried pitch.

He named a fair price for one small painting.

Bian Zhuo immediately agreed. That annoyed Shi Feng briefly. He could probably have named less.

Then Ling Qingzhu sat beneath the pavilion and looked at him with open amusement.

“Regretting it?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“The roof in his sample leans,” Shi Feng replied.

“The roof in his sample is mine!” Old Su called from the boat.

Bian Zhuo pointed at the real leaning roof across the landing. Shi Feng looked at it and said nothing. Ling Qingzhu laughed until she had to turn away.

For once, the seller hadn't lied about anything.

Bian Zhuo arranged his paper and began sketching the river. Shi Feng sat beside Ling Qingzhu without being told. The old painter nodded as though that solved a difficult part of the composition.

“Don't make me look foolish,” Ling Qingzhu warned.

Bian Zhuo looked at her, then at Shi Feng.

“I can manage half of that,” Bian Zhuo said.

Shi Feng decided the old man was charging enough already.

The painting took longer than promised. Neither of them complained. Ling Qingzhu watched the brush move, and Shi Feng enjoyed having nothing urgent to do for a little while.

There was no furnace waiting to be opened. No prince stood at the next table. No guest needed persuading that the marriage looked convincing.

They were simply there together.

Shi Feng wanted more days like this.

On the return journey, Ling Qingzhu held the rolled painting carefully above the river spray.

“It's paper,” Shi Feng said.

“I noticed,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

“You're holding it like a precious sword manual,” Shi Feng said.

“It might become one if you keep talking,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

He smiled and passed her the food parcel again. She took the last plum, then broke it in half and offered him a piece.

Shi Feng accepted it.

Old Su kept his eyes on the river. He'd ferried many couples, but most young masters spent their journey trying to impress a woman with stories about their own cultivation. This one seemed content to let her threaten him with a painting.

At the landing, Shi Feng helped her step onto dry stone. Her fingers remained around his for two extra breaths.

Neither mentioned it.

They stopped at a small tea stall on the way home. Ling Qingzhu drank half her cup, then began describing the crooked roof in Bian Zhuo's sample again. Shi Feng listened while pretending to regret the purchase.

He didn't regret it.

At home, they unrolled the painting across the table. Ling Qingzhu removed her veil and tucked her hair behind her ear. Shi Feng’s gaze followed her hand and stayed on her face.

“The painting is down here,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“He left out the best part,” Shi Feng replied.

“He painted exactly what he saw,” Ling Qingzhu said, folding the silk beside her. Her voice grew softer. “He doesn’t live here.”

Shi Feng grinned so foolishly that she pushed the painting beneath his nose. Bian Zhuo captured the distant willows and the small boat neatly. Beneath the pavilion, two figures sat close enough that their sleeves touched.

Ling Qingzhu studied the painted woman first. Then she looked at the man beside her.

“He made you look too serious,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“I was considering his price,” Shi Feng replied.

“You were smiling,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“You watched?” Shi Feng asked.

Her bare cheeks warmed. She bent closer to the painted willows.

“The river's good,” Ling Qingzhu said.

Shi Feng let her change the subject. He looked at the two figures again and felt a quiet happiness.

He could remember when sharing a room meant making careful rules about the bed, the screen, and each other's belongings. Now she'd spent the afternoon beside him without needing a reason beyond wanting to go.

That was enough for today.

Ling Qingzhu rolled the painting before a loose drop from the kettle could reach it.

“Where should it go?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“The wall,” Shi Feng replied.

“Which wall?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“Not the one that leaked,” Shi Feng said.

She laughed, then glanced toward their shared room.

“Above the table,” Ling Qingzhu decided.

He brought a strip of clean cord and helped her hang it. She adjusted the lower edge twice before stepping back.

The room was still small. His bedding still rested on the floor, and her chest still stood beside the bed.

The painting made her smile anyway—even when a late message from Ling Rong arrived under the gate warning that a witness from Yunze had been quartered in the Eastern Palace's outer hostel ahead of the representative briefing.

chapters.title: One Stroke Was Enough
chapters.html:
“Young Master Shi, that sheath will make your sword look ordinary,” Weng Qi said.

“It is a sheath,” Shi Feng replied.

The weapon seller held up a red one covered in brass studs. Its mouth was too wide, and the stitching bulged near the bottom. Ordinary blades hung behind him above a row of polished cases.

“This one shows your status!” Weng Qi insisted.

“Does it hold the sword better?” Shi Feng asked.

“People will recognize you from across the street,” Weng Qi said.

“They can walk closer,” Shi Feng replied.

Weng Qi put it down. His early Foundation Establishment cultivation did nothing to improve his expression. He recognized the kingdom's third qualifier immediately and hoped the young man would spend like someone important.

Instead, Shi Feng examined the plain goods.

His refined artifact sword needed something that wouldn't catch the edge when he drew it. The current sheath loosened after repeated practice. Buying another was easier than adjusting it every morning.

He selected a black one and tested the fit. The blade slid free smoothly.

“That one has no history,” Weng Qi warned.

“Good,” Shi Feng replied. “I won't have to listen to it.”

Weng Qi named a price. Shi Feng bargained briefly, paid, and left the red sheath behind.

Outside, a shop runner waited with two ingredient baskets. Shi Feng checked the White Marrow Grass, paid the carrying fee, and put the baskets away once he reached a quiet corner.

Those herbs were for commissions. His afternoon belonged to himself.

The deeper slopes of Hengyun were quieter than the hunting paths near the road. Shi Feng passed abandoned snares, climbed a ridge, and followed a narrow ravine toward the shaded ground below.

Blue Vein Leaves grew there. He'd seen the plants during earlier practice, but the leaves weren't ready to pick then. Their pale veins needed to darken before they held the medicinal force he wanted.

Now several were ripe.

Shi Feng crouched beside the first patch and examined the stems. He needed the leaves for his own medicine, not another customer's order. Buying everything saved time, but sometimes gathering a useful ingredient himself was worth an afternoon outside.

He cut only the ripe leaves and left the younger growth alone. The thin layer beneath each leaf held much of its useful medicine. Pulling them off roughly would tear it, so he used the small knife from his gathering kit. The first few settled inside a clean cloth without losing their sap.

A low scrape sounded beyond the rocks.

Shi Feng stood before the loose stones began falling. Something heavy moved through the ravine, rubbing against both sides as it approached.

A thick bronze-scaled python lifted its head from the shade. Its body filled the narrow passage. Yellow eyes fixed on him, and a forked tongue flickered above two long fangs.

The pressure it released matched a peak late Foundation Establishment cultivator on the verge of the next threshold, heavier and more ferocious than Peng Zhao's saber aura. Shi Feng glanced at the gathered leaves, then at the beast.

“So you live here,” Shi Feng said.

The python didn't appreciate the greeting.

Its tail struck first. The heavy body twisted, driving a slab of bronze scales across the ground toward Shi Feng's waist.

He stepped inside the sweep instead of retreating down the ravine. The tail smashed through the rock where he stood. Broken stone struck his sleeve and fell without hurting him.

The python's head dropped immediately.

Its jaws opened wide enough to swallow him whole. A dark stream of foul breath rushed before the fangs, scattering the loose leaves across the ground.

Shi Feng drew the sword.

No frantic dodge, no desperate attempt to find a weak spot while the beast chased him. He could see the attack clearly, and his body could move faster than it.

The refined artifact answered his Foundation Establishment qi. Force passed along the blade without making the steel bend.

Turning Wave.

Shi Feng's wrist turned. The sword crossed the python's lowered neck in a short, clean arc.

Bronze scales split.

The great head struck the ground. Its open jaws snapped shut against stone, and the body thrashed once before collapsing along the ravine. Shi Feng stepped clear of the falling weight and lowered his sword.

One stroke.

He checked the blade and found no damage. His robe was dusty, but there wasn't a wound beneath it. He hadn't needed to reveal every bit of his strength or exhaust his qi.

The difference from his battle with Cao Wenshu was enormous. Back then, a mid Foundation Establishment opponent forced his Bone Refinement body into a dangerous fight and broke his ordinary sword.

Now the First Extreme was complete. His foundation was established. The weapon finally supported the force he could use.

A peak Foundation Establishment beast with iron-hard scales no longer made victory uncertain. Shi Feng felt satisfied. This was why he'd refused to leave the golden refinement unfinished just to enter Foundation Establishment sooner.

He thought, Strong enough isn't a reason to stop preparing. It's the result of preparing properly.

The python's last movement faded. Shi Feng waited, then checked that it was dead before approaching. He didn't put his hand beside a living mouth merely because he'd won the first exchange.

Its hide might fetch a good price, but skinning such a large body would take time. He had money coming from commissions. Today, he preferred the cultivation resource.

He touched the dead beast and let the All-Devouring Physique act.

The flow entered steadily. Shi Feng sat beside the body and guided the gathered strength inward instead of letting it rush without direction.

This was his own nonhuman kill. His physique could use it. The human attackers he'd killed offered nothing like this, and he never expected them to.

The python's strength wasn't a finished realm he could wear. It was a resource his body still needed to absorb and refine.

Warmth spread through his meridians. He drew it through his established foundation, letting each circuit settle before beginning another. The enormous capacity beneath his early Foundation Establishment realm accepted the gain without being filled.

He remained at the same stage.

There was no sudden leap to mid Foundation Establishment and no excuse to stop taking cultivation seriously. However, the progress was substantial enough to please him.

After a while, the flow weakened. He finished the assimilation slowly and opened his eyes. Sunlight had shifted across the ravine wall.

Shi Feng stood, stretched his fingers, and tested a short circulation. The new strength moved cleanly with the rest.

“Useful afternoon,” Shi Feng said.

He returned to the herb patch before leaving. Several ripe leaves remained outside the damaged ground. He gathered those carefully, brushed the dirt from their veins, and packed them apart from the commissioned White Marrow Grass.

He folded the clean cloth around the leaves and tied it loosely. Crushing them now would spoil the whole trip. With the herbs packed safely, he climbed back toward the capital road before sunset.

He passed Weng Qi's stall on the way home. The seller noticed the dust on his robe and looked eagerly at the black sheath.

“Still pleased?” Weng Qi asked.

“It held,” Shi Feng replied.

“The red one would've looked better,” Weng Qi said.

“The python didn't complain,” Shi Feng replied.

Weng Qi opened his mouth, then decided not to ask. Instead, he offered sword cloth at a slightly lower price.

Shi Feng bought one. A useful seller could remain greedy without needing to become an enemy. At home, Ling Qingzhu looked up from the courtyard table.

“You're dusty,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“I noticed,” Shi Feng replied.

“Then don't lean on my chair,” Ling Qingzhu said.

He stopped his hand just above the backrest. She smiled triumphantly and pushed the washbasin toward him.

Shi Feng laughed, set his gathered leaves in the kitchen, and washed before touching anything else—though as he set the black sheath beside his bedding, he remembered the Eastern Palace carriage he had passed outside the magistrate's side gate at dusk, and the Yunze travel dust clinging to its rear step.

chapters.title: A House Too Small for Fame
chapters.html:
“Two spirit stones to see the courtyard?” Shi Feng asked.

Bao Shun immediately lowered his hand. Three strangers waited behind the broker, peering past his shoulder toward the pear tree.

“Not to see it,” Bao Shun said. “To hear its history.”

“I rent it,” Shi Feng replied. “Its history is a leaking roof.”

The three visitors looked at one another. Bao Shun laughed too loudly and stepped closer to the gate.

“Young Master Shi, you've misunderstood,” Bao Shun said. “People admire your rise. A little account of your cultivation would inspire them.”

“Tell them to refine pills until their sleeves smell of charcoal,” Shi Feng said.

“That's not very inspiring,” Bao Shun replied.

“Neither is sleeping beneath a leak,” Shi Feng said. “Did you mention that part?”

Bao Shun's smile weakened. A woman behind him examined the roof with growing disappointment. She seemed to expect a glowing formation or a hidden immortal sitting on the tiles.

Shi Feng pointed down the lane.

“Return their money,” Shi Feng said. “You won't be bringing people through my gate.”

“I haven't brought them through it yet,” Bao Shun protested.

“Keep it that way,” Shi Feng replied.

The broker bowed and led his customers away. His explanation became quieter with every step. Shi Feng shut the gate before another listener could decide that the conversation deserved an entrance fee.

Ling Qingzhu untied the veil she had put on at the knocking. Their home was theirs again. Ling Qingzhu stood behind him with folded sleeves.

“You could've charged Bao Shun,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Then he'd sell tickets to collect his losses,” Shi Feng replied.

“He'd sell tickets to watch you chase him,” Ling Qingzhu said.

Shi Feng looked at the gate. That was probably true.

Her laugh followed him across the courtyard.

Clothes covered half the bed. Ling Qingzhu's chest stood open at its foot, and a folded traveling cloak lay on the chair. There was nowhere left for her book.

Shi Feng stopped beside his own rolled bedding.

“Are we moving?” Shi Feng asked.

“I'm deciding what to take,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

“To the tournament or to establish a new clan?” Shi Feng asked.

She picked up a folded robe and threw it at his chest. He caught it before it fell.

“Put that on the chair,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Which chair?” Shi Feng asked.

She looked at the cloak, the washbasin, and the little stack of books occupying every available seat.

“Hold it,” Ling Qingzhu said.

Shi Feng held it. He was pleased enough by her ridiculous difficulty that he didn't immediately remind her about storage bags.

She noticed his expression anyway.

“Don't say it,” Ling Qingzhu warned.

“I haven't said anything,” Shi Feng replied.

“You look ready to,” Ling Qingzhu said.

He put the robe across a clean section of the bed. She checked the edge, then started sorting again. Most of the things in her chest were ordinary clothes. Some were carefully wrapped, and he didn't reach for them.

Their agreement still meant something. Living together didn't make every private belonging his to inspect.

Ling Qingzhu lifted a small silk pouch and paused. The old violet ribbon beneath it was badly creased.

“That one's useless,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Then leave it,” Shi Feng replied.

She put it into the traveling pile.

He smiled. She immediately covered it with another robe.

For a while, they worked without arguing. She sorted her clothes while he tied fresh cords around the books. The little room filled with the smell of sun-dried cloth.

Shi Feng liked this more than he expected. He thought, Everyone outside wants the kingdom's third qualifier. In here, she just wants somewhere to put a sleeve.

That was easier to understand.

“Your cloak's too thin,” Ling Qingzhu said suddenly.

“It's not cold yet,” Shi Feng replied.

“It will be on the road,” Ling Qingzhu said.

She pointed at the folded cloak on the chair. It was dark blue, plainly cut, and large enough for his shoulders.

“That's yours,” Ling Qingzhu said. “Don't leave it behind.”

Shi Feng picked it up. The stitching near the neck was new. She'd chosen something without patterns or bright borders.

“No silver beasts?” Shi Feng asked.

“You'd complain they were heavy,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

He felt warm despite standing with a cloak he didn't need yet.

“It suits me,” Shi Feng said.

Ling Qingzhu looked satisfied. Then she noticed that she looked satisfied and turned back to the chest.

“Naturally,” Ling Qingzhu said. “I chose it.”

She told him to stand. He put the cloak around his shoulders, and she walked behind him to check the length.

“Too long?” Shi Feng asked.

“Don't move,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

He stood still while she straightened the collar. Her fingers brushed his neck, and he felt strangely pleased about obeying such a small instruction.

“Now move,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“A difficult inspection,” Shi Feng replied.

She came around to look at the front. The cloak fitted well. Its hem stayed clear of the floor, and his sword hand had plenty of room.

Ling Qingzhu looked openly proud of that last detail.

“You checked the sleeve,” Shi Feng said.

“I watched you practice,” Ling Qingzhu replied. “I'm not blind.”

He touched the fastening once, then folded the cloak carefully himself.

By afternoon, the bed was clear again. Shi Feng carried the books outside and set them on the courtyard table. A breeze moved the pear leaves overhead.

Ling Qingzhu followed with tea. This time, the liquid wasn't dark enough to resemble a medicinal extract.

He took a sip.

“Better?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“You remembered the water,” Shi Feng replied.

“Give it back,” Ling Qingzhu said, reaching for the cup.

He moved it out of reach and drank again. She sat down with an irritated expression that didn't last.

The neighbors talked beyond the wall. Someone mentioned the three representatives. Another person claimed Shi Feng spent every night meditating on a bed of precious jade.

Ling Qingzhu looked toward the room.

“Your floor must be very valuable,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Jiang Meilan will hear that,” Shi Feng replied. “Then we'll have to pay more.”

She laughed into her tea.

It still surprised him how easily she could make him forget the people outside. His strength changed their manners. Her laugh changed his whole afternoon.

He was in love with her. There was no point pretending otherwise to himself.

The thought no longer frightened him. It simply made him want this quiet courtyard to remain part of his life after the tournament.

Ling Qingzhu opened the top book and noticed a loose page inside. It was one of his short refining records, tucked away the previous evening.

“This isn't mine,” Ling Qingzhu said.

She passed it back without reading further.

Shi Feng accepted it. She understood the same boundaries he did, at least in small things.

“Have you finished your own practice today?” Shi Feng asked.

“Enough,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

He didn't ask to inspect her cultivation. Her Foundation Establishment cultivation—left unmeasured beside her second-place rank on the royal board—already put her among Great Liang's finest young cultivators. Whatever else she chose to keep private belonged to her.

She didn't ask about his foundation either.

That quiet understanding pleased him.

A knock sounded at the gate. Both of them looked toward it. Ling Qingzhu reached for her veil before going to answer.

“If it's Bao Shun, I'm charging him for knocking,” Ling Qingzhu said.

Shi Feng went to answer. A delivery boy held out a sealed envelope, collected his carrying fee, and hurried away. The envelope bore the mark of Ling Qingzhu's clan.

He brought it to the table unopened.

Ling Qingzhu broke the seal, read the first few lines, and sighed.

“Another family gathering?” Shi Feng asked.

“Several,” Ling Qingzhu replied. “Apparently qualifying means every elder needs to see me eat.”

“A dangerous responsibility,” Shi Feng said.

She folded the letter and looked at him over it.

“They'll ask about you too,” Ling Qingzhu said.

He leaned back beneath the pear tree. The blue cloak lay across his knees, still warm from her room.

“Then tell them I eat without instruction,” Shi Feng replied.

Ling Qingzhu's smile faded slightly as she read the postscript at the bottom of the page. “Uncle Ling Zhen says Sima Yu has added a formal petition from the Wei household of Yunze to tomorrow's briefing before Wen Shou.” She looked up at him closely. “The same Wei summons from the Southern Gate?”

“The same one,” Shi Feng said calmly. “Let him bring the witness into the light.”

chapters.title: The Prince’s First Place
chapters.html:
“Third place seems to satisfy you,” Sima Yu said.

Shi Feng took the empty seat beside Ling Qingzhu. Three cups waited on the long table. Behind the Crown Prince, two guards stood beneath the royal banner, their early Foundation Establishment auras carefully restrained.

“It qualifies,” Shi Feng replied.

“That wasn't what His Highness meant,” Ge Fan said sharply.

Shi Feng glanced at the guard.

“Then His Highness can explain,” Shi Feng said.

Ge Fan's expression changed. Sima Yu raised a hand before the guard could speak again. The prince wore pale gold robes without a single loose fold. His late Foundation Establishment qi was steady, and his smile was just as controlled.

He looked every bit like Great Liang's finest young cultivator. Shi Feng knew what that appearance was worth.

“A young man should aim higher,” Sima Yu said. “Some might think you were afraid to challenge the next two places.”

“Then let them challenge you,” Shi Feng replied.

Ling Qingzhu lowered her cup. Her expression remained calm, but Shi Feng noticed the slight movement at the corner of her mouth.

Sima Yu noticed it too.

His fingers tightened around his own cup before relaxing again. Wen Shou cleared his throat from the end of the table. The mid Foundation Establishment official unrolled a route map and put two small weights on its corners.

“The three representatives may travel with the royal convoy,” Wen Shou said. “Separate travel is also permitted. All three must report in Qingyun City before the final bell on the stated day.”

“The convoy provides lodging and guards,” Sima Yu said. “There's no reason to refuse.”

“I have work to finish,” Shi Feng replied.

“My people can handle your little business,” Sima Yu said.

“No,” Shi Feng said.

The answer came without hesitation. Wen Shou kept his eyes on the map. Ge Fan looked furious, but nobody asked him a question.

Shi Feng thought, His people already tried to handle me. They won't be touching my furnace next.

He didn't need the prince's food, guards, or carriage. He needed to arrive on time. Those were different matters.

“Master Shi values independence,” Sima Yu said lightly. “I hope it remains useful outside the capital.”

“It's been useful inside it,” Shi Feng replied.

For a moment, neither man touched his cup.

Ling Qingzhu looked from one to the other. She knew the banquet had made Sima Yu resent the marriage as a public challenge to his household's control. The coldness in Shi Feng's eyes was different from ordinary annoyance, though.

He rarely looked at anybody like that.

Wen Shou moved one of the weights.

Before Wen Shou could distribute the report tokens, Sima Yu laid a second paper on the table.

“A matter from Yunze,” Sima Yu said. “The Wei household requests judgment before a man accused of killing its head represents Great Liang.”

Ge Fan opened the side door. Gao An entered wearing a borrowed formal robe, his hands held tightly together. Shi Feng recognised the steward from Bian Cui’s gate. So Gao An was the witness mentioned in the Wei demand. The distant watcher had finally acquired a room full of listeners.

Ling Qingzhu's cup stopped above the table.

Wen Shou took the accusation and read it. The household seal was genuine. It named Wei Renshan, repeated the old demand for surrender and offered Gao An as a witness.

“You saw the fight?” Wen Shou asked.

“Yes,” Gao An said. “From the upper path. I followed Elder Wei.”

“Why?” Wen Shou asked.

“He was looking for his son,” Gao An said. “He said Shi Feng knew what happened.”

Sima Yu sat back. The room had become quiet enough to hear the paper move. A household killer wasn't a suitable representative. The prince didn't need a perfect crime if the accusation kept Shi Feng at the city office until departure closed.

“What happened first?” Wen Shou asked.

“Elder Wei ordered him to kneel,” Gao An said. “He refused. Then Elder Wei struck.”

Wen Shou looked up.

“Struck whom?” Wen Shou asked.

“Shi Feng,” Gao An said. “He was entitled to question him. A Foundation Establishment elder doesn't need a boy's permission.”

Shi Feng said nothing. Gao An had seen enough to tell the truth and understood it badly enough to believe the truth served his employer.

“Was Shi Feng attacking when the first blow came?” Wen Shou asked.

“No,” Gao An said. “He was standing by the quarry wall.”

“Was there a city warrant?” Wen Shou asked.

“The household demand,” Gao An said, pointing at the paper.

“That isn't a warrant,” Wen Shou said.

Sima Yu's smile thinned.

“A man's death deserves more than a few questions,” Sima Yu said.

“It deserves the correct ones,” Wen Shou said. “This witness describes a private attack, answered by the man attacked. That doesn't establish the crime alleged here.”

Gao An stared at the official. He had expected someone important to recognise Wei Renshan's authority. Instead he was being asked why the elder had attacked a traveller without a lawful order.

“He killed him,” Gao An said.

“I heard you,” Wen Shou said. “Did he pursue a surrendering man?”

“No,” Gao An said after a pause.

“Then I won't remove a qualified representative on this accusation,” Wen Shou declared, his voice carrying clearly through the open hall doors to the Ministry of Rites clerks and merchant factors waiting in the outer gallery. “The city office will retain Gao An's signed testimony as a lawful defense on the road, and the Southern Gate inquiry filed by the Wei household is hereby discharged.”

The clerk brought a fresh page. Gao An looked desperately toward Sima Yu, found only cold stone in the prince's face, and signed with a shaking brush.

A low murmur rippled across the outer gallery:

“The Eastern Palace brought a Yunze witness all this way and proved Shi Feng was defending himself!”

“Wait—Elder Wei Renshan was a Foundation Establishment clan head! Shi Feng killed a Foundation Establishment elder before he even entered the capital?”

“And the Southern Gate inquiry is discharged too—Sima Yu handed him a clean docket in front of the whole office!”

Ge Fan slammed the side lattice shut, his neck dark red, while Sima Yu's knuckles turned white against his jade belt clasp.

Ling Qingzhu set down her cup and looked across at Sima Yu.

“Shi Feng asked my household to leave the Wei demand to the proper office rather than our family seal,” Ling Qingzhu said clearly. “It seems His Highness saved us the trouble of summoning the witness.”

Sima Yu couldn't object without defending an unlawful ambush Wen Shou had just dismissed. He rose stiffly and left the hall without waiting for his attendants to announce his carriage.

Shi Feng accepted his reporting token and the stamped discharge slip that freed Pei Rong's Southern Gate surety.

On the quiet flagstone path outside the ministry gate, Ling Qingzhu stopped beneath an old locust tree and turned to face him.

“You said Foundation Establishment was recent,” Ling Qingzhu said quietly. “What realm were you in when you fought Wei Renshan?”

Shi Feng met her eyes above the veil. “Bone Refinement,” Shi Feng said. “He came after me over his son’s ambush on the western hill path. If I hadn’t killed him at that quarry, I wouldn’t have reached the capital.”

She stared at him. She had known the dead elder’s realm since their contract talks. What she hadn’t known was that Shi Feng had defeated him while still an entire major realm below him. His calm in the courtyard took on a different meaning.

“You asked for a hearing, not our seal to settle the accusation,” Ling Qingzhu said slowly. “You wanted proper evidence, and you didn’t want anyone looking closely at how a Bone Refinement cultivator killed Wei Renshan.”

“Both,” Shi Feng said honestly. “Until I had a rank of my own, a provincial clan's accusation was still a rope Sima Yu could pull.”

She let out a quiet breath and walked beside him toward Qingliu Lane. At the corner, Shi Feng glanced once toward the gold-fringed Eastern Palace carriage rolling toward the palace ward. Guo Zhen, Cao Wenshu, Zheng Jian—Sima Yu would never stop reaching for knives in the dark so long as he breathed. At Qingyun City, on the tournament platform, royal guards wouldn't be allowed to step onto the stone.

chapters.title: A Fish Cooked at Home
chapters.html:
“Don't tell me its ancestors were famous,” Shi Feng said.

Peng Tao looked down at the fish in the wooden tub. Its silver scales flashed beneath a thin stream of water. He'd brought it from a relative's pond and spent the morning telling customers how fresh it was.

“It's a fish!” Peng Tao said. “What ancestors should it have?”

“Good,” Shi Feng replied. “I'll take it.”

The fishmonger counted out the price twice, suspicious that the purchase went so smoothly. His Qi Condensation cultivation couldn't make a fish more valuable, and Shi Feng wasn't paying for anyone's reputation today.

“You're not bargaining?” Peng Tao asked.

“You named a fair price,” Shi Feng replied.

Peng Tao looked troubled. He clearly wondered whether to remember a second, less fair price. Shi Feng picked up the covered tub before that thought could finish.

At the vegetable stall, he added green leaves, fresh ginger, and a little lotus root. The whole purchase cost less than the wine at Yuelan Terrace. This time, it also left enough money in his purse for everything already planned.

That pleased him greatly.

He thought, I should've bought a fish and kept the other two hundred stones. Unfortunately, the restaurant wouldn't have let me cook it on their table.

He went home smiling.

Ling Qingzhu lifted the cover before he could stop her. The fish jumped, splashing water onto her fingers.

She stepped back at once.

“It's alive!” Ling Qingzhu said.

“I was told it's fresh,” Shi Feng replied.

“Don't look so pleased,” Ling Qingzhu said, shaking water from her hand.

He passed her a cloth and carried the tub into the kitchen. She followed, keeping a respectful distance from the fish.

“What's the occasion?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“I finished an order,” Shi Feng said.

“You finish orders every week,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

“Then I've been neglecting the fish,” Shi Feng said.

She leaned against the doorway and watched him work. He cleaned the fish quickly, washed the board, and set water to heat. There was no secret pill formula involved. He wanted a good supper with her, and he could afford to make it properly.

That was enough reason.

Ling Qingzhu reached for a knife. Shi Feng moved the lotus root toward her before she could attempt anything involving scales.

“Thin pieces,” Shi Feng said.

“I know how to cut a root,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

Her first piece was thick enough to stand upright. He looked at it. She looked at him.

“It'll be thinner after cooking,” Ling Qingzhu said.

Shi Feng took the knife and cut the piece in half. She watched closely, then held out her hand again.

The next slice was better. The one after it was almost the same thickness.

“There,” Ling Qingzhu said, satisfied.

“A great victory,” Shi Feng replied.

“You'd better eat every piece,” Ling Qingzhu said.

He promised that he would. She took the task seriously after that, although she still left him the difficult end of the root.

The little kitchen grew warm. Her violet sleeve kept slipping down, so he found a clean strip of cloth and tied it above her wrist. Ling Qingzhu held her arm still while he worked.

He didn't hurry to let go.

She didn't ask him to.

When the knot was finished, she lowered her eyes to the board. Shi Feng turned toward the stove with a smile he couldn't hide.

He was happy. There was no audience outside and no public appearance to maintain. They were simply making supper in a kitchen too small for two people who both insisted on standing near the board.

“Move your elbow,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Move the root,” Shi Feng replied.

She moved the root.

They ate beneath the pear tree. Shi Feng served the fish with a shallow dish of clear sauce. Ling Qingzhu tried it before commenting on anything else.

Then she tried another piece.

“Well?” Shi Feng asked.

“It's acceptable,” Ling Qingzhu said.

He moved the serving dish toward himself. Her chopsticks immediately stopped him.

“I didn't say I was finished,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“I didn't say it was all yours,” Shi Feng replied.

She gave him a cold look and took another piece. Her smile appeared the moment she lowered her head.

Shi Feng ate one of her thick lotus slices. She watched until he swallowed it, then looked pleased with herself.

The evening breeze cooled the courtyard. Beyond the wall, carts rattled over the lane. Nobody knocked at their gate.

Ling Qingzhu tucked her hair behind her ear and leaned over to choose another piece of fish. Shi Feng watched the movement with his chopsticks raised.

“You’ll get hungry eating like that,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“I’m not hungry,” Shi Feng replied.

“Then why cook so much?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“So you’ll sit here longer,” Shi Feng said.

Her fingers slowed over the plate. This time she didn’t call him foolish. She chose a smaller piece and ate it very slowly.

“You mentioned Artificer Hall,” Ling Qingzhu said. “What was the elder's name?”

“Xu Changhe,” Shi Feng replied.

She set her chopsticks down. He rarely volunteered anything about the things he practiced alone. Earlier, he only mentioned that an elder's teachings helped him. She wanted to know a little more about the man who taught him swordsmanship.

“What did he do there?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“He was a former elder and sect enforcer,” Shi Feng replied. “He enforced the sect's rules with his sword.”

“Was he a great artifact crafter?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“He was a swordsman,” Shi Feng said. “The ordinary repairs in his notes are useful. The sword art matters more.”

She looked toward the plain sheath hanging near the door. That explained the movements she'd seen him repeat long before the qualification.

“You want to follow him there,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“I want to see the place,” Shi Feng replied. “His teachings helped me. I haven't forgotten that.”

“Artificer Hall is weaker overall than the other two,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Then its disciples should practice more,” Shi Feng replied.

She laughed before pressing her lips together.

“You make it sound simple,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Choosing somewhere isn't difficult,” Shi Feng replied. “Getting there takes work.”

He didn't assume the regional tournament would hand him an inner disciple's place. He intended to earn the choice. His sword, cultivation, and alchemy were all things he could keep improving before then.

Ling Qingzhu turned her cup slowly.

“Hundred Flower Valley still interests me,” Ling Qingzhu said. “But I haven't decided.”

“What do you want there?” Shi Feng asked.

She took a little time before answering.

“People who speak to me about cultivation first,” Ling Qingzhu said. “Not my face, my family, or somebody who wants to marry me.”

Shi Feng nodded. That was a better reason than choosing whichever carriage looked grandest at the tournament.

“Then make them pay attention,” Shi Feng said.

“You think I can't?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“I think you're still holding your chopsticks,” Shi Feng replied. “Don't waste good fish proving it.”

She looked down at them, then laughed. Her seriousness didn't disappear, though. He liked seeing it. Her life extended beyond their little courtyard, just as his did.

He wanted to hear what she'd choose when she was ready to say it.

“You have time,” Shi Feng replied.

She studied his face. He didn't tell her which sect would suit a woman or insist that she follow his choice. The decision remained hers.

That pleased her more than a flattering promise would've.

“Finish the fish before planning to conquer a sect,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“You took the best part,” Shi Feng replied.

She looked at her bowl, hesitated, then placed an untouched piece in his.

“There,” Ling Qingzhu said. “Don't complain.”

Shi Feng ate it without teasing her.

Afterward, she helped clear the table. He washed the dishes while she dried them, checking the chipped plate before putting it away.

There were still commissions to finish and pills he wanted to practice. He would do those things. But tonight, he didn't feel any need to rush away from her.

Ling Qingzhu untied the cloth from her sleeve. Instead of leaving it beside the stove, she folded it neatly and put it away.

Shi Feng watched for a moment, then returned to the bowls. He wanted to cook for her again tomorrow—before the thirty-day road to Qingyun City tested how much of this quiet kitchen could survive outside the gate.

chapters.title: Before the Road
chapters.html:
“You're leaving customers behind?” Yan Meizhen asked.

“I'm leaving the capital,” Shi Feng replied. “The customers can stay.”

The Bone Refinement buyer sat in Gao Yuan's yard with her own chair. Her latest order rested between them. She checked the seals while he put away the last of his tools.

“You could stay and earn,” Yan Meizhen said. “Hunters don't stop getting injured because there's a tournament somewhere.”

“Then buy from somebody else until I return,” Shi Feng replied.

Yan Meizhen looked offended by the suggestion. She also looked as if she'd already made a list of other suppliers.

He didn't mind. Their business worked because his medicine was useful and she paid for it. Neither needed to pretend that a few completed orders made them sworn friends.

“If your prices rise after you join a sect, I'll complain,” Yan Meizhen said.

“You've been practicing,” Shi Feng replied.

She laughed and counted out the balance. Then she picked up the largest container and shook it lightly.

“All here?” Yan Meizhen asked.

“Open it,” Shi Feng said.

“I trust you,” Yan Meizhen replied.

She opened it anyway.

Shi Feng finished tying his tools while she counted. No hidden yield, missing pills, or promised stock remained between them when she left.

Gao Yuan arrived as the gate closed. He examined the cleared workbench with growing alarm.

“Master Shen, you aren't taking the room with you, are you?” Gao Yuan asked.

“Would you charge for carrying it?” Shi Feng replied.

“Naturally,” Gao Yuan said, then stopped. “That's not the point!”

Shi Feng showed him the final paid booking. He'd finish the remaining sessions before the reporting deadline. After that, Gao Yuan could rent the room to someone else.

The landlord tried to look relieved. His early promises of a grateful long-term tenant hadn't survived Shi Feng's habit of checking the furnace. Still, a tenant who paid on time was useful.

“I can hold it,” Gao Yuan offered. “For a small fee.”

“Rent it,” Shi Feng replied.

“You might come back,” Gao Yuan said.

“Then I'll knock,” Shi Feng replied.

Gao Yuan sighed as if someone had stolen a season's rent from his pocket.

Ling Qingzhu had the route map open when Shi Feng returned. A folded letter lay beside it, marked with her clan's seal. She glanced up at his empty carrying frame.

“Finished?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“The larger orders,” Shi Feng said. “A few collections remain.”

“Then you can rest a little,” Ling Qingzhu said.

He sat across from her. The map showed the road toward Qingyun City and several smaller towns along the way. A note marked the final reporting day.

“Thirty days,” Ling Qingzhu said, touching the note. “We shouldn't leave everything until the last morning.”

“I wasn't going to,” Shi Feng replied.

“You say that while carrying three bundles at once,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“They're herbs,” Shi Feng replied. “They won't complain about the road.”

“You would hear them if they did,” Ling Qingzhu said.

He smiled and took the map. The ordinary caravan road was longer than the path he could travel alone. There was no reason to spend every remaining day sitting in a carriage.

“I'll finish my work, then go separately,” Shi Feng said.

Her fingers stopped on the edge of the letter.

“Separately?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“That's permitted,” Shi Feng replied.

“I know it's permitted,” Ling Qingzhu said. “I meant from me.”

He looked up. Her question pleased him more than the map deserved.

“Do you want to come with me?” Shi Feng asked.

Ling Qingzhu glanced away first. She could've answered simply. Instead, she straightened the letter and moved her cup onto its saucer.

“My clan has arrangements,” Ling Qingzhu said. “There are people to meet before we leave. They expect us to appear together.”

“Before we leave,” Shi Feng repeated.

“And when we arrive,” Ling Qingzhu added.

He set the map down. That wasn't quite the answer he expected. He'd asked about traveling with her, not about arriving at a gate in front of people who needed convincing.

Still, she looked more embarrassed than calculating.

Shi Feng thought, She makes asking for company harder than challenging a ranked candidate.

“If you want company, ask,” Shi Feng said.

“I'm asking,” Ling Qingzhu replied quickly.

“You're discussing arrangements,” Shi Feng said.

She looked at him, then at the map again. A faint flush reached her ears.

“Can't both be true?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

That answer made him soften. He wanted them to be true. He wanted the shared evenings and the quiet care in this courtyard to mean more than a convenient public marriage.

“They can,” Shi Feng said.

Ling Qingzhu looked relieved. She drew the clan's letter closer and started explaining the first gathering.

He listened. There was no reason to spoil a pleasant afternoon over a question she found difficult to answer.

She asked which towns had decent inns. He knew two from his earlier travels and marked them on the map.

“Not every room needs a view,” Shi Feng said.

“It needs a roof,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

“That tiler from the ferry road could travel ahead of us,” Shi Feng suggested.

She laughed at the memory of their dripping room, then examined the little marks he'd drawn. One road passed close to the river.

“That way,” Ling Qingzhu said. “If there's time.”

“There's time if we leave early enough,” Shi Feng replied.

She nodded and kept the map open between them. For a little while, he let himself imagine the journey as something they'd enjoy together, without anyone waiting to judge their marriage at the next gate.

Later, Shi Feng checked the supplies he intended to carry. Medicine for his own cultivation went into separate containers from the last customer orders. He checked the seals and left the open ones for immediate use.

His physique still accepted every useful pill without resistance. Weeks of steady intake strengthened his early Foundation Establishment cultivation, but his foundation demanded far more medicine than an ordinary one.

He wasn't going to call that a defect. A foundation capable of supporting greater strength should need more to fill it.

The ring made carrying supplies easy. Finishing every promise before leaving took more care.

Ling Qingzhu sat on the bed with a list of her own. She crossed out two lines, added another, then watched him wrap his sword cloth.

“You don't have to make every decision alone,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Neither do you,” Shi Feng replied.

She nodded, apparently satisfied, and set the red clan invitation beside his work ledger without opening it yet. Shi Feng put the final medicine container away, glad to have one last stretch of unhurried work before the Ling residence called on them both.

The room was small enough for him to hear her turn the page of her book. He set the blue cloak on top of his traveling bag.

“Wake me before you go out tomorrow,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Another invitation?” Shi Feng asked.

“No,” Ling Qingzhu replied. “I want to eat with you.”

He looked up from his bag. She was already turning another page, but she hadn't read the one before it.

His bedding stayed rolled in its familiar corner.

chapters.title: The Ling Clan's Invitation
chapters.html:
“The invitation includes you,” Ling Qingzhu said, putting the red envelope beside Shi Feng's cup.

“I can read my name,” Shi Feng replied. “I'm wondering why they wrote it larger than yours.”

She leaned over the table. The two names were the same size. He watched her realize that, and her cold gaze immediately returned to him.

“You have too much time,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Not enough for everything people invite me to,” Shi Feng replied.

The Ling clan wanted its two young Foundation Establishment cultivators at a family gathering before the journey. One was its own daughter. The other was the son-in-law many relatives preferred not to discuss before Great Liang's qualification.

Now they discussed him a great deal.

He turned the envelope over. Beside the family seal was a second, smaller note about preparing medicines for the road.

“Are they inviting a guest or booking a furnace?” Shi Feng asked.

“A guest,” Ling Qingzhu replied. “They can ask about medicine separately.”

“Good,” Shi Feng said. “I'm more expensive when someone tries to mix the two.”

Her mouth curved. She took his untouched cup, drank from it without noticing, and began explaining the gathering. He noticed. The little act pleased him enough to distract him from the invitation.

Three days later, relatives leaving with other trading parties would meet at the Ling residence. Ling Qingzhu needed to settle her own travel supplies and speak to an elder about Hundred Flower Valley. Nobody could promise her entry. Even Great Liang's second-ranked candidate still needed to compete against the surrounding kingdoms.

“Will you come?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“For the gathering,” Shi Feng said. “Don't promise anyone my medicine.”

“I heard you the first time,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

He let the subject go. She sounded annoyed, but she didn't withdraw the invitation. He thought, Perhaps she wants me there even when nobody needs a husband to stand in front of a prince. He wanted that to be true.

Ling Rong arrived before noon with two servants carrying packed travel cases.

Ling Qingzhu put on her veil before admitting them. The thin steward was at early Foundation Establishment. He bowed to Ling Qingzhu, then gave Shi Feng an equally careful greeting.

“Young Master Shi, the clan would like to know your departure date,” Ling Rong said.

“After my last orders are finished,” Shi Feng replied. “I've already given the travel office my route.”

“You won't use our carriage?” Ling Rong asked.

“I haven't decided how much of the road I'll ride,” Shi Feng said.

The steward glanced at Ling Qingzhu. She immediately looked displeased.

“Ask him,” Ling Qingzhu said. “He's sitting in front of you.”

Ling Rong bowed again and changed the subject. The cases held a cloak, dry provisions, and several jars chosen for her. She opened the cloak, checked its lining, and rejected two jars because the sealing wax smelled too strong.

Ling Rong set a sealed permit beside the cases.

“The northern warehouse finally has its approval,” Ling Rong said. “The court office signed it three weeks after your wedding.”

“After keeping it unsigned for half a year,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

“The elders would rather discuss the result,” Ling Rong said.

Shi Feng looked at the seal. The marriage had changed the court's leverage. It hadn't made her relatives forget how comfortably they could bargain with someone else's future.

Then Ling Rong opened a third paper.

“Several relatives would like advice from Young Master Shi,” Ling Rong said. “Nothing difficult. A few old injuries and some cultivation concerns.”

“How many?” Shi Feng asked.

“Eleven,” Ling Rong replied.

Shi Feng looked at him. Ling Qingzhu lowered the cloak.

“That's not a few,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“They only wish to make his acquaintance,” Ling Rong said quickly.

“Then they can introduce themselves,” Shi Feng replied. “Their old injuries can stay at home.”

The steward's smile stiffened. Ling Qingzhu looked away, hiding amusement. Shi Feng wasn't angry. These relatives saw an alchemist appearing in the family and immediately developed ailments that required free attention.

Eleven sore knees didn't need to become a great conspiracy.

“Should I tell them you're unavailable?” Ling Rong asked.

“Tell them I'll attend as a guest,” Shi Feng replied.

Ling Qingzhu nodded. The steward rolled up the paper and finally took it away.

After the visitors left, Shi Feng carried one empty case into the room. Ling Qingzhu untied her veil again. Ling Qingzhu stood beside her chest, looking between the case and the folding screen.

“Where should it go?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“Outside,” Shi Feng said.

“It's going to rain,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

“Then we'll tell Jiang Meilan we need a second room,” Shi Feng said. “She'll charge us for imagining one.”

She laughed and moved the case beneath the bed. Her cloak followed it, folded into a much smaller bundle than the servants managed.

His own belongings needed little space. With the storage ring open, he could keep the furnace tools and most ingredients safely out of the way. He still slept on the same floor bedding. Neither improved cultivation nor more money changed that arrangement without her consent.

Ling Qingzhu looked at the rolled blanket, then at his travel pack.

“You're taking everything?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“I'll need my things,” Shi Feng replied.

“We might come back,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“We might enter a sect,” Shi Feng replied.

She fell quiet. That possibility was the point of qualifying, yet the room suddenly felt different when he said it aloud. He watched her fingers move over the edge of the chest.

“You want Artificer Hall,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“If I earn a choice,” Shi Feng replied.

“Hundred Flower Valley suits me better,” Ling Qingzhu said. “Its sword methods aren't all gentle flower dances, despite what people in the capital say.”

“Good,” Shi Feng replied. “I'd hate to see you attack someone with a flowerpot.”

She picked up the little empty pot beside the window.

“Don't be so sure,” Ling Qingzhu said.

He held up his hands. She put it down with a satisfied smile. Her gaze moved to the leather-wrapped journal and the dark iron enforcement badge resting beside his pack.

“The elder's sword notes and his sect badge?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“Yes,” Shi Feng replied, touching the engraved Artificer Hall mark on Xu Changhe's iron badge. “I swore over his cairn to return his badge to the Hall myself once I finished studying the last corrections.”

She sat beside him and looked at the worn iron token. He opened a page of the journal and showed her the correction beside Returning Tide.

“When you return his badge to Artificer Hall, can you show them where he fell?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“I marked the chamber,” Shi Feng replied. “They can choose what to do with it.”

She nodded. He wasn't promising service to an entire sect because one dead elder taught him useful swordsmanship. He was returning a name and an account.

She let him close the notes. The next morning she appeared at the kitchen door holding another clan letter.

“Tomorrow afternoon,” Ling Qingzhu said. “Ling Rong is bringing two elders. I said you'd show them the pills before we go.”

Shi Feng set down his pestle.

“I've promised that hour to a customer,” Shi Feng said. “Did you ask whether I was free?”

“It's only a look,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Don't promise my time without asking,” Shi Feng said.

Her expression changed. She folded the letter more tightly, embarrassed enough to become sharp.

“Fine,” Ling Qingzhu said. “I'll tell them you're busy.”

He nodded and returned to the roots. Giving a clear answer wasn't a quarrel unless someone insisted on making it one. Still, the kitchen felt less pleasant after she left.

He finished the promised order the next day. When he returned, Ling Qingzhu stood at her mirror fastening the repaired clasp. She had told Ling Rong not to bring the elders. Shi Feng thanked her, and she looked annoyed by his relief.

He gave her a small warming wash for the shoulder she had complained about after practice. It wasn't part of the clan's request. She looked at the parcel, pleased and puzzled.

“You remembered?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“You mentioned it three times,” Shi Feng said.

“Two,” Ling Qingzhu said.

He smiled. She put the parcel beside her own medicines and handed him the dark robe she wanted him to wear. For him, the disagreement had a sensible ending. She asked too quickly, he refused, and she changed the plan. He still wanted to go because she would be there.

Behind the screen, Ling Qingzhu considered another explanation: he was proud of his new work and disliked relatives inspecting it. That seemed reasonable. She never asked whether it was true.

When she came out, he waited by the gate. She tied her veil, took his arm and told herself she would make sure the clan treated him properly.

chapters.title: He Came for Her
chapters.html:
“Young Master Shi, this way!” Ling Rong called at the gate.

Ling Qingzhu walked beside Shi Feng, her white veil tied beneath her black hair. Two rows of lanterns lit the Ling residence. Servants carried dishes through the courtyard, and relatives stopped talking when Ling Qingzhu entered on Shi Feng's arm.

He felt their attention move from her veiled face to his sword, then back to the hands resting together. A month ago, some of these people would've looked only at the marriage certificate and wondered how quickly it could be forgotten.

Now an early Foundation Establishment alchemist stood beside their most celebrated daughter. The change made everyone very welcoming.

“Our family's good fortune!” Ling Jian said, stepping forward with a cup.

The broad-shouldered relative was at Bone Refinement, with most of his bones refined. He looked at Shi Feng's hands before greeting his own cousin.

“I've wanted to meet you for a long time,” Ling Jian said.

“We've met,” Shi Feng replied. “You wanted to know whether I delivered ointment.”

Ling Jian's smile froze. Ling Qingzhu gave him a cold glance.

“Find your seat,” Ling Qingzhu said.

The cousin found it at once.

Shi Feng followed her to the table, leaving the old insults where they belonged.

An older woman, Ling Shufeng, greeted them from the head of the table. Her late Foundation Establishment presence was restrained, and her hair was almost entirely white. Ling Qingzhu bowed to her with real respect.

“You've become difficult to see,” Ling Shufeng said. “The whole capital gets a glimpse before your family does.”

“The whole capital doesn't ask me eleven questions before tea,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

Ling Shufeng laughed and waved them down. Shi Feng found himself liking the reply more than the wine set before him.

The first disagreement came from Elder Ling Guoli, seated two places below Ling Shufeng.

“The consort's people still ask after our household,” Ling Guoli said. “Royal kinship would have served us better than this delay.”

Ling Qingzhu's fingers tightened beside her cup.

“I'm married,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“I can read the register,” Ling Guoli replied. “They're asking about a younger daughter in the western branch now. We should receive the messenger properly.”

“Ask the girl before you prepare her answer,” Ling Shufeng said.

Ling Guoli drank instead of replying. The elder faction hadn't abandoned its profitable match. It had found another woman to discuss.

Ling Qingzhu moved her untouched cup away from the table edge. Shi Feng shifted the dish nearer her without pretending a quiet meal could settle that argument.

Other relatives began discussing which kingdom would send the strongest candidates.

Ling Jian declared Great Liang's crown prince would take the championship.

Shi Feng ate a piece of fish.

“You've fought in the qualification,” Ling Jian said to him. “You must know how great the gap is.”

“I know how large a plate is,” Shi Feng replied. “Move your elbow.”

The cousin looked down. His sleeve rested in the sauce.

Several people laughed. Ling Qingzhu’s eyes brightened above her veil, and the conversation moved away from Sima Yu before it could become unpleasant.

Later, Ling Shufeng asked Ling Qingzhu about Hundred Flower Valley. Her questions were practical. What sword method attracted her? What would she do if another sect offered better resources? Did she want instruction, or only a famous name?

Ling Qingzhu answered clearly. Shi Feng listened without interrupting. She wasn't only a beautiful woman caught in a court faction's marriage plans. Her ambition was real, and she understood why she wanted a different path from the capital's sheltered young ladies.

He felt proud of her. There was no reason to hide that from himself.

“And if you enter different sects?” Ling Shufeng asked, looking between them.

Ling Qingzhu's fingers stopped beside her cup.

“We'll decide when there's a choice to make,” Shi Feng said.

“A marriage isn't a road you choose at a crossing,” Ling Shufeng said.

“Neither is a cultivation path,” Shi Feng replied calmly. “She shouldn't give up a useful teacher just to make our route look tidy.”

Ling Qingzhu looked at him. Her expression softened before she remembered the people watching.

“I can answer for myself,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Then answer,” Shi Feng replied, smiling.

“I agree with him,” Ling Qingzhu said.

Ling Shufeng laughed again. The cousins looked disappointed.

After the meal, Ling Qingzhu led him into a smaller courtyard. A stone pond stood beneath an old pine. The music from the main hall sounded distant here.

“You didn't have to say that,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“You don't want a useful teacher?” Shi Feng asked.

“About my choice,” Ling Qingzhu replied. “I didn't ask you to defend it.”

“You don't need to ask for every small thing,” Shi Feng said.

She went quiet. He rested one hand on the low stone wall and watched a fish turn beneath the water.

“Did I make things difficult for your work?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“No,” Shi Feng replied. “I finished what I promised.”

“You could've taken another order,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“I could've done many things,” Shi Feng replied. “I'm here.”

She looked at his face. The plain answer pleased her, but it also left her unsure what to say. She reached for a loose strand of hair instead.

A servant hurried into the courtyard and asked whether Ling Qingzhu would return. Her younger relatives wanted to see the sword she used in the qualification. Ling Qingzhu's expression turned impatient.

“Go,” Shi Feng said. “I'll wait.”

“They'll talk for ages,” Ling Qingzhu warned.

“Then don't let them,” Shi Feng replied.

Her eyes curved above the veil before she left. He remained beside the pond, enjoying the quiet until Ling Jian appeared with another cup.

“You have a good wife,” Ling Jian said. “Very generous too.”

“You want something,” Shi Feng said.

“Only some advice,” Ling Jian replied. “There's a pill that helps refine the last bones. Perhaps you could arrange a few at the family price.”

“The family price is the price after you pay,” Shi Feng replied.

The cousin stared, then laughed uncertainly. Shi Feng didn't join him.

Ling Jian left after a few more useless words. Shi Feng returned his attention to the fish. He didn't attend this gathering to become the Ling clan's free furnace.

A little later, Ling Shufeng came through the side door and stopped beside the wall. She watched him for a moment before speaking.

“Ling Jian has already complained,” Ling Shufeng said.

“He works quickly,” Shi Feng replied.

“He complains quickly,” Ling Shufeng corrected. “His work takes longer.”

Shi Feng smiled. The elder looked toward the hall, where Ling Qingzhu's voice briefly rose above the others.

“She doesn't like being told what to do,” Ling Shufeng said.

“I noticed,” Shi Feng replied.

“And you aren't easy to push either,” Ling Shufeng said. “I wondered whether you'd spend the whole evening fighting.”

“You invited me to eat,” Shi Feng replied. “The dishes weren't bad enough to fight over.”

The elder laughed. She didn't offer him a position or ask for a promise of lifelong service. She simply told him which side gate opened toward the quieter road, then returned to the hall.

Shi Feng stayed beside the pond. He was glad Ling Qingzhu had someone in her family who could speak without turning every sentence into a request. It didn't make the whole clan his responsibility. It did make the evening easier to enjoy.

When Ling Qingzhu came back, she carried a little paper bundle. Inside were two warm cakes she saved from the hall.

“They took too long,” Ling Qingzhu said, handing him one.

“You came back,” Shi Feng replied.

“Where else would I go?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

The question was careless. It still made him happy.

They ate beside the pond before leaving. On the way home, she leaned lightly against his arm. He didn't mention Ling Jian's request. She didn't need to answer for every greedy relative.

He thought, I chose this evening. I would've chosen it without an invitation seal or a marriage certificate. At their gate, she stopped him before he reached for the latch.

“I was glad you came,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Then it was worth coming,” Shi Feng replied.

Her eyes smiled, and he believed they both understood the warmth between them. At home, with the gate shut and her veil removed, she called him to help with the stubborn clasp.

He freed it. She tucked the loosened hair behind her ear, and his hand stopped in midair.

“Again?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“I’m checking for another knot,” Shi Feng replied.

“On my face?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

He grinned. She pushed his hand down, laughing, then asked him to stay while she combed her hair. He sat without another excuse.

chapters.title: What Had Changed
chapters.html:
“Ling Rong sent the caravan schedule for the eastern road,” Ling Qingzhu said, setting the folded sheet beside Shi Feng's commission ledger.

Shi Feng glanced up from his notes. “He still wants me sitting in the clan carriage for two full days of farewell calls?”

“Only the final morning at the residence,” Ling Qingzhu said. “I already told him you had furnace commitments for the rest.”

He looked at her with genuine appreciation. “Thank you.”

“You don't need to sound surprised,” Ling Qingzhu replied, though she lingered by the table instead of returning to her book. “If you want to check the road provisions with me, we can go after your last order.”

“We don't need Ling Rong's clerks for that,” Shi Feng said warmly. “We can go ourselves.”

She folded the schedule away, yet a quiet crease remained between her brows. He thought the matter of his hours was settled; she was still wondering why every clan request lately seemed to press against a wall he hadn't named.

At the furnace yard, Gao Yuan waited beside a pile of unused charcoal sacks. His Qi Condensation cultivation didn't keep him warm enough to stop complaining about the wind.

“A man asked whether your furnace would be free after you leave,” Gao Yuan said.

“It isn't my furnace,” Shi Feng replied. “Rent it to him.”

“He wants the same price you pay,” Gao Yuan said.

“Then charge him the same price,” Shi Feng replied.

Gao Yuan looked genuinely disappointed. He apparently expected Shi Feng to explain why the next tenant should pay more.

“He also wants your supplier's name,” Gao Yuan said.

“You can give him the shop's name,” Shi Feng replied. “The herbs won't become good because he knows me.”

“You've become very difficult to earn from,” Gao Yuan complained.

“You've become very willing to tell me,” Shi Feng said.

Gao Yuan grumbled and left. Shi Feng went inside without a hood. The capital already knew who refined here. Hiding his face wouldn't make his personal life any simpler now.

Today's order used a larger portion of the same dependable recovery formula. He divided it into smaller runs instead of filling the furnace beyond what he controlled comfortably. The extra firing took time, but it kept the medicine even.

He thought, I don't need to impress a customer by using the whole furnace. I need every promised pill to work.

The first run finished cleanly. He let the copper cool before wiping the inner lip, then began the next. Between runs, he prepared the agreed share for himself and marked the delivery boxes.

His early Foundation Establishment cultivation was settling. The qi moved readily through all his meridians and answered his hands with far less delay. There was still a vast difference between this and the cultivation Mo Tianheng remembered.

That didn't bother him today. He could see his own progress clearly, and he wasn't short of work that suited it.

After collecting the payment, he stopped at the travel office to confirm his route. Xu Wen, the clerk at the side desk, checked his representative's token and unfolded a map.

“The main party leaves through the eastern gate,” Xu Wen said. “You're expected at Qingyun City's registration hall before the final bell on the appointed day.”

“Must I ride with the party?” Shi Feng asked.

“No,” Xu Wen replied. “Your place belongs to your name, not your carriage. Arrive on time with the token.”

The clerk pointed out the safer roads and two stretches without reliable inns. He was at Bone Refinement and spoke with the bored patience of a man answering the same questions all morning.

“What happens if someone loses the token?” Shi Feng asked.

“They report it here before leaving,” Xu Wen replied. “Please don't test whether falling into a river makes it disappear.”

“Someone did?” Shi Feng asked.

“Someone claimed he did,” Xu Wen said. “Then tried to sell it.”

Shi Feng took the marked route and put it away. He wasn't planning to separate from Ling Qingzhu, but having a clear route meant they could choose their own pace instead of following every official stop.

Near evening, he left the office and bought two packets of tea on the road home. One was for travel. The other was the sort Ling Qingzhu drank without making a face.

He remembered her overly strong first attempt and smiled.

Ling Qingzhu was writing when he came in. He placed the tea beside her paper, and she immediately reached for it.

“This one?” Ling Qingzhu asked, reading the wrapper.

“The seller says it's impossible to ruin,” Shi Feng replied.

She hit his hand with the packet.

“Your tea was worse last week,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Because you made it,” Shi Feng replied.

She stared at him, then laughed despite trying not to. He was glad to hear it. The awkward exchange from morning wasn't worth losing the evening over.

They drank the tea together. She said the seller lied about ruining it. He said she hadn't tried hard enough yet. For a while, she leaned over the table to read his notes and asked which pills he planned to carry.

He explained the ordinary travel medicines without naming what his physique could do. She knew enough cultivation to follow their uses, and her questions were good.

“You've become much busier,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“There's more demand,” Shi Feng replied.

“And your time is worth more now,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“To a customer,” Shi Feng replied.

She looked at him, waiting for more. He thought the distinction was obvious and went back to packing the medicines.

The silence left her thinking. When she first asked him to marry her, the whole capital called him a cripple. He sold little jars, argued over a few spirit stones, and slept on a rented floor. Now he was one of Great Liang's three representatives and a successful alchemist.

His circumstances changed. Of course he might dislike the old terms.

Ling Qingzhu felt she finally understood the awkwardness. He had pride, and she kept acting as if nothing needed adjusting. Perhaps he didn't want to be the one to bring it up.

She looked at the tea packet. He still remembered her preferences. He still came home with something she liked. Whatever troubled him didn't mean he wanted to stop living together.

“I'll speak to Ling Rong,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“About the afternoon?” Shi Feng asked.

“About the arrangements,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

He nodded, relieved she wasn't insisting. She felt relieved for a different reason.

Later, when he sat in the kitchen to cultivate, she opened the travel list again. Beside the supplies, she wrote a short reminder to ask about a more suitable agreement.

She thought, It should be fair to him too. She wanted him to agree readily, the way he smiled when she asked him to attend the gathering. She didn't consider that he wasn't asking to sell more hours. She put the reminder away carefully, satisfied she had finally found something useful to do.
