In the kitchen, Shi Feng swallowed his retained pills and let their medicine strengthen his foundation. Tomorrow's work was already planned. He wanted enough free time afterward to ask her about the road again.

chapters.title: A New Quilt
chapters.html:
“It won't fit,” Shi Feng said.

Ling Qingzhu stood in the middle of their room holding a rolled quilt nearly as wide as the folding screen. She looked at his bedding corner, then at the quilt.

“You can fold it,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

“Three times?” Shi Feng asked.

“Then you'll be warm,” Ling Qingzhu said.

He took one end before it knocked the mirror from the table. Together they spread it across the bed. Soft cotton filled the dark blue cloth, and the stitching was neat. It was much better than the blanket he used through the rainy months.

“Why buy it now?” Shi Feng asked.

“The old one is thin,” Ling Qingzhu replied. “You're taking it on the road too, aren't you?”

He looked at her face. She tried to look annoyed at the question, but he could see she wanted him to like the gift.

“Thank you,” Shi Feng said.

Her expression softened. She smoothed one corner of the quilt and immediately began explaining how the seller tried to charge extra for the darker cloth.

“I told him the cotton didn't know what colour it was,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“A strong argument,” Shi Feng replied. “Did he ask the cotton?”

She pushed the quilt into his arms.

He laughed and folded it smaller. When it finally fit the corner, she looked far more satisfied than the simple purchase required. He felt happy too. Whatever bothered them yesterday could still be talked through.

That afternoon, Shi Feng took his refined artifact sword outside the capital. His cultivation wasn't hidden anymore, but the full strength of his body and foundation still belonged to him alone.

At a weapon stall near the gate, Ren Bo tried to sell him a silver sword tassel. The middle-aged seller was at Qi Condensation and spoke as if he personally instructed every famous swordsman in Great Liang.

“It steadies the sword's flight,” Ren Bo said. “All the young masters use one.”

“How?” Shi Feng asked.

“It improves the balance,” Ren Bo replied.

Shi Feng held the tassel between two fingers. An uneven iron weight hid beneath the silver thread.

“It improves your balance of spirit stones,” Shi Feng said, putting it down.

Ren Bo's smile disappeared. Shi Feng left before the seller could develop a second explanation.

Beyond the Hengyun trail, he found an empty stretch of rock above a dry stream. He checked the approaches, set his pack down, and drew the sword.

His qi entered the refined artifact. The blade lifted from his palm and stopped a few steps away. Its movement was light, but that didn't mean he could stop paying attention.

He placed three broken sticks upright between the stones. The first stood straight ahead. The others were on either side, close enough that a careless turn would hit the wrong one.

His blade passed the first and curved toward the second. He stopped it before the edge struck, then drew it back through the narrow gap.

Too much movement. The third stick shook in the blade's wake.

He tried again with less force. This time the sword turned in a shorter arc and stopped cleanly beside the second target. He brought it back to his hand and stepped into Piercing Current.

The thrust stopped at a pale mark on the rock. He didn't strike through it. Precision was the purpose today.

Turning Wave followed. His wrist and foot changed together, moving the blade across a second mark. Then Returning Tide pulled the point back just enough before the next thrust.

The three movements were becoming familiar in his own body. He could use overwhelming strength whenever he needed it. He preferred having the choice to use less.

A small Stone-Eating Lizard climbed onto a nearby boulder and stared at him. It wasn't strong enough to threaten an ordinary Qi Condensation cultivator.

“You're not a teacher,” Shi Feng told it. “Stop looking so disappointed.”

The lizard snapped up a beetle and disappeared.

He practiced until the blade could turn between all three sticks without disturbing the wrong one. Then he increased the distance by a few steps and began again. Flying the sword farther was easy. Placing it exactly where he wanted while moving himself needed more practice.

That difference mattered against anyone worth fighting.

A shadow crossed the streambed just as he prepared to sheathe the sword. Shi Feng looked up and saw a Greywing Spirit Hawk drop from the cliff.

Its hooked beak opened. The beast's strength matched a Bone Refinement cultivator with more than half his bones refined. An ordinary hunter would've reached for cover before the talons arrived.

Shi Feng lifted two fingers.

The sword turned upward and passed through the hawk's chest. Its wings folded at once. He guided the falling body away from his pack, then brought the blade back into his hand.

The whole exchange took less than a breath. His early Foundation Establishment cultivation already put a refined artifact's power within easy reach. Combined with his foundation and sword control, a beast of this level couldn't force him to take a step.

“An unfortunate place to hunt,” Shi Feng said.

He touched the carcass and let the devouring flow begin. The useful qi entered his body, and the remains dried beneath his fingers. He sat long enough to assimilate the gain before leaving. He didn't need to rush home carrying unrefined beast qi just because the kill was easy.

When he finally sheathed the blade, the sun was low. He sat beside the streambed and let his qi settle. His early Foundation Establishment foundation felt firm, with room for far more medicine than he'd already assimilated.

The tournament would give him opponents beyond Great Liang's young cultivators. He looked forward to testing his sword against them. Sima Yu would be there too, without a kingdom's rank deciding whose life mattered more.

Shi Feng's gaze turned cold for a moment. He hadn't forgotten Guo Zhen or Cao Wenshu. Stopping at third place didn't erase an attempted murder.

He put the thought away and headed home. His cultivation remained at early Foundation Establishment, steady enough that the hawk's medicine caused no disturbance.

Ling Qingzhu sat in the kitchen peeling a pear when he returned. She cut one piece, tasted it, and frowned.

“Sour?” Shi Feng asked.

“Very,” Ling Qingzhu replied, holding it out to him.

He took the piece. It was sweet.

She smiled before he could speak.

“A fairy's judgment can't be questioned,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Then I'll eat the rest to protect your reputation,” Shi Feng replied.

She pulled the pear away at once. He took a chair beside her, feeling the earlier strain ease again.

She asked about his practice. He marked three dots on the table with one finger, showed her the sword's path between them, and explained the change in his qi. Her questions were precise. He didn't mistake her for a helpless beauty after watching the qualification.

“You turn it before drawing it back,” Ling Qingzhu said, tracing a short line on the table.

“Too early and it exposes the edge,” Shi Feng replied.

“Then don't turn so much,” Ling Qingzhu said.

He considered the suggestion. It was useful.

“I'll try it,” Shi Feng said.

Her pleasure was immediate. She hid it by cutting another pear slice and claiming she was only tired of hearing about broken sticks.

After supper, they moved the table to make room for his newly folded quilt. She insisted its edge shouldn't touch the wall. He pointed out that the room hadn't grown since morning.

They argued for half a dozen sentences, then found a position that suited them both.

That night, he lay beneath the warmer quilt and listened to her turn a page behind the screen. He thought, I'll ask her properly tomorrow. Not about dates or carriages. About us.

He didn't know she was planning a different sort of conversation.

chapters.title: Because He Wanted To
chapters.html:
“Is this mine?” Ling Qingzhu asked, touching the little case beside her chest.

“Unless you've hidden another wife behind the screen,” Shi Feng replied.

She looked at him coldly, but opened the lid. Travel medicines rested inside, each wrapped separately. A folded instruction sheet lay across the top.

“I know how to use recovery pills,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“The sheet isn't for those,” Shi Feng replied. “It's for the other jars. You dislike the smell of the usual insect wash.”

She picked up the smallest bottle and opened it. There was almost no scent. Her expression softened at once.

“You remembered that too,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“You threaten every mosquito that enters the room,” Shi Feng replied. “It's difficult to forget.”

She laughed and put the bottle back. He watched her arrange the case's contents, pleased with how much she liked them. Nothing inside was beyond his ability or expensive enough to trouble his business. He made them because he knew her habits.

That should've been simple.

He lifted a narrow packet from the lower layer and put it beside the wash.

“Don't open this until you camp,” Shi Feng said. “Keep it near the entrance, not beside your face.”

“Another insect medicine?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“For the smaller biting flies,” Shi Feng replied. “The wash works on your skin. This keeps them out of the bedding.”

She turned the packet over. Its cloth was plain, and the cord was tied tightly enough that the contents wouldn't scatter if she dropped it.

“You've thought of everything,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Not everything,” Shi Feng replied. “If you insist on sleeping in an ants' nest, move before complaining.”

She laughed and nudged his arm. He let himself enjoy the contact.

He showed her the remaining bottles one by one. The little warming wash needed only a few drops. The eye rinse belonged away from the stronger ointment. None were rare treasures, but they were chosen for her, not copied from a shop's travel bundle.

“Was this troublesome?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“Less troublesome than hearing you curse every insect between here and Qingyun City,” Shi Feng replied.

She pretended to be offended. He could see her pleasure clearly. Her fingers moved carefully over each wrapper, and she kept turning the case toward the light to read his notes.

He thought, She'll use them and remember I made them. It was a small, selfish wish. He wanted some part of their ordinary life to travel with her even if their paths later separated.

She found the little jar of scentless cream last. Its lid carried no shop seal. He prepared it separately, leaving out the ingredient that made the ordinary formula smell too sweet for her.

“My cousin asked about this,” Ling Qingzhu said. “Can you give Ling Shuyun the recipe? She wants the women at the residence to try it.”

“They can buy the ordinary cream,” Shi Feng replied.

“They dislike its scent too,” Ling Qingzhu said. “Just write down what you changed.”

He hesitated. The request wasn't difficult. It was the way she made it, turning something prepared for her into another item her family could claim without asking him.

“Did you promise them?” Shi Feng asked.

“I said it should be fine,” Ling Qingzhu replied. “It's only a cream.”

He closed the empty outer wrapping and put it aside.

“Then tell them you should've asked first,” Shi Feng said.

Her smile faded. He didn't sound angry, but he wasn't teasing either.

“I wasn't giving away your pill formulas,” Ling Qingzhu said. “You made this for me.”

“Yes,” Shi Feng replied. “For you.”

“And I've already paid for that,” Ling Qingzhu said. “I thought you wouldn't mind.”

Shi Feng went still. The room was quiet enough that he heard the porcelain lid click against the jar when she set it down.

“Paid for what?” Shi Feng asked quietly.

She frowned, confused by the edge in his voice.

“The things you do for me under our agreement,” Ling Qingzhu replied. “I didn't mean every pill you refine for South Pill Street.”

Shi Feng looked at her across the open medicine case. “First, you haven't paid the agreement. The pale bag you handed me the morning after we registered had not a single spirit stone inside it, and when I showed it to you, you told me to keep the unpaid line out of your sight.”

Ling Qingzhu's posture stiffened at once. In her mind, the old claim from their second morning in the courtyard was resurfacing only because he was now a famous alchemist who felt the original sum was beneath him.

“You're bringing that up again?” Ling Qingzhu said, her voice cooling. “I counted those ten thousand stones myself before we moved in. And even if you feel the original terms were too small for what you do now, you don't need a separate commission for every small jar.”

He remembered the actual terms. A registered marriage, temporary protection from a forced royal match, a bed for her and floor bedding for him. No intimacy owed. No right to the other's things.

None of it required him to remember how she liked her tea. He thought, Ask clearly. Don't turn one careless answer into something worse than it is.

“When I waited for you beside the pond,” Shi Feng asked, “did you think I was doing work?”

Ling Qingzhu's expression changed. The question sounded too serious for a little jar of cream.

“You were being a good husband,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“That's not what I asked,” Shi Feng replied.

She looked away first. He couldn't see whether she was embarrassed or annoyed, and for once that uncertainty frightened him more than an enemy's threat.

“You accepted the arrangement,” Ling Qingzhu said. “Of course I expected you to take it seriously.”

He nodded slowly. She still believed she was explaining something they both understood.

“And the evenings we spent here?” Shi Feng asked.

“What about them?” Ling Qingzhu replied.

“The things nobody outside this room saw,” Shi Feng said. “Did you think those belonged to the agreement too?”

She glanced toward the kitchen. There were the cups they used yesterday and the tea packet he brought home. She thought of his work, his growing reputation, and the way he kept refusing extra demands.

Perhaps this was the conversation he'd been avoiding. Perhaps he wanted her to recognize how much he did beyond standing beside her in public.

“I know you've done more than the bare minimum,” Ling Qingzhu said. “I've never said you haven't.”

It was an answer someone might give a worker asking whether his work was satisfactory. Shi Feng felt a dull ache in his chest. He could take a sword strike without stepping back, yet he suddenly wanted to turn away from her face.

He didn't.

“I didn't do those things because I had to,” Shi Feng said.

“I didn't force you,” Ling Qingzhu replied quickly.

“I know,” Shi Feng said. “I'm telling you why I chose them.”

She went quiet. He looked at the case he prepared for her and felt foolish for needing to explain something he thought she could see.

“I like spending time with you,” Shi Feng said. “When you asked me to come to the gathering, I came because you wanted me there. Not because your family's seal was on a letter.”

Her heart beat faster. For a moment she almost smiled. Then she remembered the dispute over his time and thought she understood the complaint beneath the words.

“I didn't know you felt the terms were unfair,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“I'm not discussing terms,” Shi Feng replied.

His voice stayed calm. That cost him more effort than she knew.

Outside, someone crossed the lane calling a vegetable seller. An ordinary morning continued beyond the gate. He looked at her and wanted one ordinary answer from the woman he'd come to love.

“You don't need to call every kindness a duty,” Shi Feng said. “I cared because I wanted to.”

She held his gaze. The warmth in his words reached her, but she still tried to fit it inside the arrangement that made their shared life safe and understandable.

“Then why does the agreement trouble you now?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

His hand stopped beside the medicine case.

It wasn't the agreement that troubled him. It was realizing she couldn't hear him without returning to it.

He drew his hand back and waited. He loved her enough to give her another chance to understand.

chapters.title: A Higher Price
chapters.html:
“I'll increase the payment,” Ling Qingzhu said.

Shi Feng didn't move. She mistook his stillness for calculation and continued before he could speak.

“Your circumstances changed,” Ling Qingzhu said evenly. “You're Master Shen now, and one of Great Liang's three representatives. If ten thousand spirit stones feels too little for the time you've spent on me, I'll add more—you don't have to pretend the first bag was empty just to renegotiate.”

She sounded completely sincere. That was what made the words cut to the bone.

He looked at the little medicine case. The lids were still open, and the scentless cream sat beside her hand. A moment ago he had spoken to her about love, and she had heard a merchant lying about an old receipt to drive up his fee.

“That's your answer?” Shi Feng asked.

“It's fair,” Ling Qingzhu replied. “I don't want you to feel I've taken advantage.”

He could've laughed. He almost did. Instead he stood quietly, afraid that if he said the first thing in his mind it would make the room uglier than it already felt.

She believed fairness meant paying more for the same willing care. He told her his feelings were real, and she heard a price that hadn't been settled.

“I didn't ask for more spirit stones,” Shi Feng said.

“I know you didn't ask directly,” Ling Qingzhu replied. “You don't have to.”

His expression changed. She noticed that and finally stopped speaking.

“Directly?” Shi Feng repeated.

Ling Qingzhu felt a sudden unease. She thought she was sparing his pride. Now he looked at her as if she'd insulted something he hadn't allowed anyone else to touch.

“I didn't mean you were begging,” Ling Qingzhu said quickly.

“Then don't answer as if I was,” Shi Feng replied.

The words were quiet. She flushed, embarrassed and annoyed at once. He never needed to raise his voice to make her feel she'd answered badly.

“What would you have me say?” Ling Qingzhu asked. “That I should keep asking things of you without making the arrangement fair?”

“That you heard me,” Shi Feng replied.

She looked at him. His face wasn't cold the way it became when a merchant lied. He looked hurt. Seeing that frightened her, but she still didn't know where the mistake lay.

“I heard you say you wanted to do those things,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“For you,” Shi Feng replied.

“And I'm grateful,” Ling Qingzhu said. “That's why I'm willing to change the payment.”

He turned his face toward the open window. His chest felt tight, and he hated how much he still wanted her to stop speaking and reach for him instead.

Ling Qingzhu pushed a loose strand behind her ear. He used to follow that little movement as though she had performed some peerless sword art. She would call him foolish, and he would grin without shame.

This time he didn’t turn back. Her hand stayed beside her ear for a moment before falling.

Shi Feng thought, She isn't trying to wound me. She simply believes this. That left him with nobody easy to hate.

He could crush an enemy who meant to kill him. There was no useful sword stroke for this.

“Keep your spirit stones,” Shi Feng said.

Her mouth tightened. She heard rejection of her effort to be reasonable, not the exhaustion beneath it.

“Don't make it sound dirty,” Ling Qingzhu said. “We agreed from the beginning. I didn't deceive you about what I wanted.”

He looked back. She was right about the beginning. That didn't make everything afterward part of the same bargain.

“I know what you wanted at the beginning,” Shi Feng replied. “I thought something changed.”

She fell silent. The words struck nearer to her own hidden feelings than she expected. She remembered his arm beneath her hand on the road home and the pleasure of hearing him return early.

Something did change. She hadn't decided what to call it.

“Things don't become simple just because you say that,” Ling Qingzhu said at last.

“I didn't ask for simple,” Shi Feng replied.

He waited another moment. She couldn't give him an answer she wasn't prepared to name, and she resented feeling pressed to do so.

“Let's speak when you're calmer,” Ling Qingzhu said.

He lowered his eyes. It was the sort of sensible sentence people used when they wanted an uncomfortable conversation to disappear.

“I've got work,” Shi Feng replied.

He picked up his pack. The movement was ordinary, but she immediately looked alarmed.

“You're going now?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“The customer is still waiting,” Shi Feng said.

He didn't slam the door. She listened to the gate close and looked at the medicine case again. For the first time, its neat little labels made her uncomfortable.

The furnace yard was loud with carts when Shi Feng arrived. Gao Yuan tried to ask about renewing the room after the tournament, saw his face, and decided to discuss charcoal with someone else.

Shi Feng put down his pack and checked the prepared herbs. He didn't light the furnace immediately. His hands were steady, but his attention kept returning to a room across the capital.

He could hear her voice clearly. I'll increase the payment.

She offered it to keep him content. She thought the things he treasured could be continued by settling the right sum.

He closed his eyes once, then opened them and read the order from the start. There were ingredients, a quantity, and a delivery date. This was actual work. He owed the customer a proper result, not a batch spoiled by his private hurt.

Shi Feng thought, Finish one thing at a time. He set the copper furnace heating and began.

The first stage went well. The second needed a slower fire, and he made the adjustment without delay. The pills formed evenly beneath his qi. For the length of the refining, there was no room for anything else.

Afterward, the room grew quiet. He stared at the finished tray and felt the ache return exactly where he'd left it.

A successful batch didn't make him feel better. It only proved he could still do his work.

He cleaned the mixing spoons and checked the ingredients remaining in his own boxes. The practical work was simple. Each herb went back into its proper wrapping, each finished pill into a dry container.

One small packet was hers. He bought enough for her scentless wash and kept the unused leaves apart from the commission stock.

His fingers stopped over it.

Throwing the leaves away would be childish. Selling them wouldn't prove he no longer cared. He put them in the box with the other useful ingredients and shut the lid.

Gao Yuan passed the open doorway and glanced inside.

“More charcoal tomorrow?” Gao Yuan asked.

“One sack,” Shi Feng replied.

“The larger sort?” Gao Yuan asked. “It's better value.”

“The sort I ordered,” Shi Feng said.

Gao Yuan nodded and moved on. He didn't ask why a successful young alchemist sat staring at a closed herb box. There wasn't a fee for the answer, so it didn't interest him.

Shi Feng stood and opened the shutters. Late sunlight fell across the clean table, and the ordinary noise of the yard returned. Somewhere outside, a porter complained about carrying a chest that weighed more than its owner admitted.

He heard the complaint and remembered his own paid loads. The memory didn't make him feel ashamed. He worked because he needed money. There was honesty in that.

What hurt was having a different part of his life treated as if it worked the same way. Near sunset, Yan Meizhen collected a separate order. The Bone Refinement merchant checked the jars and paid promptly.

“You look tired,” Yan Meizhen said. “Don't charge me extra for noticing.”

“Then don't ask for a discount because of it,” Shi Feng replied.

She laughed and left. He packed his retained pills carefully, then sat alone until the furnace cooled. He didn't swallow them in anger or try to force his cultivation forward. The medicine was useful, and his body would take it without harm. None of that answered the question waiting at home. He wished she hadn't offered such an easy answer to it.

He didn't want to return home. He wanted, desperately, to return to the home he thought he had yesterday.

Those were no longer the same wish. He put out the furnace lamp and walked back through the familiar streets.

chapters.title: The Same Room
chapters.html:
“Will you eat?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

Shi Feng stood at the kitchen door with a bowl in his hand. He came home after dark and found two places set at the table. She'd bought food from the stall at the lane's entrance.

“Yes,” Shi Feng replied.

He sat across from her. She pushed the warmer dish toward him, then looked annoyed when he noticed.

“The seller gave too much,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Then he made a mistake,” Shi Feng replied.

The familiar answer should've made her laugh. Instead she lowered her eyes and began eating.

He ate because he needed food and because refusing it would turn the evening into another accusation. He didn't want to punish her with an empty bowl. The dish was good. He could taste it without feeling much pleasure.

For a while they spoke only about the next day's weather. She said the mornings were colder. He said the roads should stay dry. Both knew they weren't discussing what mattered.

Finally, she put down her chopsticks.

“Ling Rong asked whether you'd attend the last meeting,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“I've already said I would,” Shi Feng replied.

“You don't have to come if you're angry,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“I gave my word,” Shi Feng replied. “I'll settle what I promised.”

The answer hurt her. She wanted him to say he wasn't angry, or that he'd come because she wanted him there. Yesterday, he offered that freely. Tonight, he spoke of settling a promise.

“I didn't mean to insult you,” Ling Qingzhu said.

He looked at her. She sounded sincere again. He wished sincerity alone could undo what they now understood about each other.

“I know,” Shi Feng replied.

“Then why are you still looking at me like that?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

He didn't know what she saw. He wasn't trying to look cold. He was trying not to keep asking for an answer she didn't have.

“Like what?” Shi Feng asked.

She couldn't explain it without sounding frightened. He looked like someone sitting beside a road after deciding not to take it, though his feet hadn't moved yet.

“As if I've become a stranger,” Ling Qingzhu said.

He lowered his chopsticks.

She had removed her veil when he came home, as always. He hadn’t paused at the sight of her. When she brushed the hair from her cheek, his eyes stayed on the bowl.

Once, she couldn’t get through supper without telling him to stop looking. Now she wanted to hear one of his ridiculous excuses.

None came.

“You haven't,” Shi Feng replied. “That's why it hurts.”

She went still. His bluntness left her nowhere to hide behind an argument about schedules.

“I like living here,” Ling Qingzhu said. “I like the time we spend together. Isn't that clear?”

His chest tightened. There it was, close enough that he wanted to believe it answered everything.

“Then why did you answer me with money?” Shi Feng asked.

“Because you said the things you did weren't covered by the agreement,” Ling Qingzhu replied. “I wanted you to know I valued them.”

“You wanted to pay for them,” Shi Feng said.

“Does being paid make every feeling false?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

He was quiet. She wasn't asking an entirely foolish question. They started with an arrangement. He couldn't pretend he never accepted one.

But she still thought his feelings belonged inside a service she could keep purchasing.

“No,” Shi Feng replied. “But my feelings weren't what I offered to sell.”

She looked at his face, confused and hurt by the distance that remained even after she admitted enjoying their life together.

“I didn't know you separated it like that,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“I thought you could see the difference,” Shi Feng replied.

He remembered the little moments he chose not to name. Her hand on his arm. Her waiting at the gate. The tea made too strong. He took those as signs she wanted him, not simply a convenient husband doing his work well.

Perhaps some of them were. That uncertainty was worse than a clean rejection.

“Would you have agreed to marry me without the payment?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“At the beginning, I agreed for ten thousand spirit stones, a hunting pass, and a name that kept the Yunze Wei inquiry from detaining me at the gate without a hearing,” Shi Feng said evenly. “You gave me an empty bag, called me a liar when I showed you the seams, and I stayed anyway because the pass was real—and later because I cared for you. We're not at the beginning anymore, Ling Qingzhu, yet yesterday you still thought I was lying about the first bag to bargain for a second.”

Her lips parted. She couldn't deny that. She couldn't easily abandon the explanation she'd trusted for months either.

He stood and began clearing the table. She reached for a dish at the same time, and their fingers touched. Usually he'd tease her or let the contact last. Tonight he simply passed it over.

“I'll wash these,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“All right,” Shi Feng replied.

He didn't stop her. She carried the bowls into the kitchen and stared at them as if she'd never seen their shapes before.

He went into the room and opened his order book. Three deliveries remained. None required more than the time he already reserved. After those, he could leave the capital without owing anyone unfinished work.

The marriage certificate lay wrapped beneath a spare robe. He didn't take it out. A legal name on paper wasn't the thing hurting him tonight.

Shi Feng thought, She doesn't owe me feelings because I have them. He understood that clearly. He only wished she hadn't mistaken his for another thing her payment secured.

He set the book aside and checked the sword beside his bedding. The blade needed no repair, but wiping it gave his hands something ordinary to do.

When the cloth passed over the hilt, his thumb brushed a familiar worn patch. He remembered practicing beside the dry stream, guiding the sword between marked targets while the forest stayed quiet.

That problem was easier. There was a movement to correct and a clear result when he corrected it. If he worked carefully, the blade went where he intended.

Here, being alive and strong didn't tell him what to do next.

He sheathed the sword and leaned it against the wall. No enemy's blade forced him to remain in this room. Neither did a contract require him to keep hoping every night.

Shi Feng thought, I can leave. The thought didn't make him feel free. It made him realize how much he'd wanted to stay.

Behind the kitchen wall, the dishes stopped moving. She remained there for a little while before returning. He didn't call her. If she needed a quiet moment, she could have one without explaining herself to him.

He folded the cleaning cloth and put it away. The little mirror beside her bed caught the lamp's light. He looked away from it before remembering another evening in which her reflection smiled at him.

Ling Qingzhu returned after washing the dishes. She stood beside the screen and looked at him.

“Are you going to keep sleeping there?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

He glanced at his bedding corner. The new quilt lay folded above the old blanket.

“Tonight,” Shi Feng replied.

She heard the word and felt uneasy. She wanted to ask about tomorrow, but pride and fear made her hesitate.

He closed the book and put it into his pack. Then he took the medicine he retained from the day's work and went to the kitchen to cultivate.

His qi answered readily. His foundation remained firm. His cultivation path was still his own, and the tournament still waited. He hadn't forgotten either just because another part of his life was breaking. The pills strengthened him without resistance, and the process required enough attention to keep him still for a time.

Afterward, he sat with the empty wrapping in his hand.

He still loved her. Discovering a painful difference didn't switch that off. He wanted to hear her call him back into the room, then hated that he was waiting for it.

No call came.

When he returned, the lamp burned low beside the screen. Ling Qingzhu was awake, but her breathing became careful when he spread the bedding.

He lay down without saying anything. Four steps remained between them, the same as on the first night.

He never noticed the distance so much before. Behind the screen, the lamp stayed lit until long after the lane outside became quiet.

chapters.title: A Room of His Own
chapters.html:
“No more orders before the tournament,” Shi Feng said, setting the final boxes on Gao Yuan's table.

The furnace owner looked at the seals and immediately began worrying about empty rooms.

“You could take one more,” Gao Yuan said. “I know a buyer with good herbs.”

“Then introduce him to someone else,” Shi Feng replied.

“Someone else will want a fee,” Gao Yuan complained.

“So will I,” Shi Feng said.

Gao Yuan sighed. Shi Feng paid the last room charge, collected his own tools, and left the rented furnace clean. He didn't owe the yard anything except the normal mess Gao Yuan somehow considered part of its charm.

At the gate, Yan Meizhen waited with two empty carrying cases. She inspected her last order, checked the quantities, and handed over the balance.

“You'll return at a higher price,” Yan Meizhen said.

“If I return with better pills,” Shi Feng replied.

“Men always promise the improvement after naming the increase,” Yan Meizhen said.

“You're planning to resell these at a higher price tomorrow,” Shi Feng replied.

She laughed without denying it. Their business ended with paid balances and no promises of lifelong friendship.

That suited him. He couldn't bear another arrangement pretending to explain things it never touched.

Shi Feng thought, Don't bring her into every conversation. Yan Meizhen didn't know his private hurt, and it wasn't her responsibility to cure it. He put away the spirit stones and carried the empty cases toward the main street.

He rented a small room at Yonghe Inn beside the canal, paid for several nights and accepted Kang Fu's key. One bed, one table, one chair. Choosing it wasn't the same as moving into it. He still had belongings at home and a decision Ling Qingzhu deserved to hear.

That evening he told her he would move the next morning. She asked for how long. He couldn't answer honestly, so he didn't give her a date.

Shi Feng rolled his bedding after sunrise.

Ling Qingzhu sat behind the screen, listening to the cloth move. Usually he folded the blanket, washed, and began heating water. This morning he tied the bedding shut.

“You're taking the new quilt,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“You gave it to me,” Shi Feng replied.

She looked at him through the space beside the screen. He wasn't discarding her gift. Somehow that made his decision harder to dismiss as anger.

He put the bundle away in the storage ring. The ring's space made packing simple. It couldn't make deciding what belonged to him pleasant.

His clothes, sword notes, medicine tools, and remaining ingredients went first. The knife followed. He left her bottles on the kitchen shelf, clearly marked, and took only the jars he'd kept for his own use.

She came out when he lifted the last pack.

“You don't have to hurry,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“There's no hurry,” Shi Feng replied.

He checked the floor once. The little pale storage bag lay beside the folded private agreement. He picked up the paper and left the bag on the table.

“You forgot that,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“It's yours,” Shi Feng replied.

He didn't offer another explanation of the payment. He already gave one when the debt began. Repeating it now wouldn't tell her why he was leaving.

She looked at the bag, then back at him. He thought she would say something about it, but her attention moved to the sword at his waist.

“Where are you staying?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“Yonghe Inn,” Shi Feng replied. “Until I leave for Qingyun City.”

There was no secret destination. He wasn't hiding so she would have to chase him across the capital. He needed a different room and the space to decide his own next step.

She nodded slowly, as if learning the address made this an ordinary change of plans.

“The inn's food won't be as good,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Then I'll eat elsewhere,” Shi Feng replied.

Her attempted smile disappeared. He saw it and felt the familiar urge to make the moment easier for her. He didn't know how to do that without pretending nothing had changed.

Shi Feng thought, Don't stay because leaving hurts. That isn't a reason to keep doing this.

He lifted the empty carrying box he still used for the street stall. She moved aside at the door, then stopped him with a hand on his sleeve.

“We haven't ended the marriage,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“I know,” Shi Feng replied.

“People will talk,” Ling Qingzhu added, frightened by how little the first answer secured.

“They've talked since the first day,” Shi Feng said. “This isn't for them.”

She let go. He waited a moment, hoping she would ask about what he actually felt instead of what others might say.

She couldn't find the words quickly enough.

He went through the courtyard and opened the gate. The pear tree's shadow lay across the same little table. One cup sat near the edge, where she liked it in the morning.

He looked at it once and left.

Jiang Meilan intercepted him near the lane's entrance. She looked at the carrying box, then toward the gate behind him.

“You're moving?” Jiang Meilan asked.

“My things,” Shi Feng replied.

“And the courtyard?” Jiang Meilan asked, immediately worried about losing rent.

“Paid until the agreed date,” Shi Feng said. “Ling Qingzhu is still there.”

The landlady looked relieved, then curious. He didn't wait for the second feeling to become a question.

“Don't add charges because one tenant leaves,” Shi Feng said. “You already tried charging because one arrived.”

Jiang Meilan shut her mouth. He walked on without discussing his household with the lane.

At Yonghe Inn, Kang Fu offered to carry the box for an extra spirit stone. Shi Feng carried it himself. The innkeeper then offered hot water, which was included in the room price, and looked annoyed when Shi Feng remembered.

“You've got a good memory, Young Master Shi,” Kang Fu said.

“Try giving me less to remember,” Shi Feng replied.

He shut the door and put the box beside the table. His things were moved. There was nothing left to delay the quiet.

He sat on the bed but didn't unfold the quilt. For months, his place was a corner on someone else's side of a screen. Now he had a whole bed, and he would've traded it for the evening before she spoke about payment.

The wish made him angry with himself. He couldn't purchase yesterday either.

After a while, he stood and checked his road provisions. He sharpened the ordinary knife, inspected the sword's sheath, and put the representative's token where he could reach it easily.

His hands knew the work. They helped him continue when his thoughts didn't.

Ling Qingzhu stayed by the gate after his footsteps faded. The bowls still stood in pairs. His cup remained because he had bought it for the household, not because he needed an excuse to return.

At noon she bought enough food for two before remembering. By evening the second bowl had cooled beneath its cover. She warmed it, then stopped before calling his name.

The pale bag lay on the table where he left it. She pushed it aside without opening it. Neither had filed to end the marriage. The corner opposite her bed was empty all the same.

chapters.title: Ten Thousand Spirit Stones
chapters.html:
“Did you hand over the ten thousand spirit stones from your cedar trunk yet?” Ling Zhen asked.

Ling Qingzhu looked up from the untouched cup on the table.

Her white veil was in place for her uncle’s visit. The silk hid her mouth, but not the sleeplessness in her eyes. Her uncle stood beneath the pear tree carrying the clan's departure ledger. He was at late Foundation Establishment, with a square jaw and the brisk manner of someone who disliked unfinished accounts.

“What do you mean?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

Ling Zhen looked around the small courtyard before answering. The table stood beneath the pear tree, and the kitchen door stood half-open onto an unlit stove.

“Still living here?” Ling Zhen asked. “Your standing is secure now. There's room at the residence until the carriages depart.”

“I don't need another room,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

Ling Zhen heard the sharpness and waved the suggestion aside. “I didn't come to drag you home. I'm closing the quarter's accounts before the Qingyun road. When you registered the marriage in the autumn, you refused the clan's contribution, had the vault steward release ten thousand of your own stones, and counted them into one of my pale bags yourself. Since Young Master Shi is travelling to Qingyun City separately, I came to ask whether you'd already handed it over.”

Ling Zhen glanced toward the quiet kitchen. “Where is he?”

“Out,” Ling Qingzhu said too quickly. “And I paid him the morning after we moved here. There's nothing left to settle.”

Ling Zhen frowned slightly, sitting down opposite her. “The morning after you moved? I remember the porter carrying your locked cedar trunk into the bedroom last. Which pale bag did you give him?”

She pointed to the bag Shi Feng left on the table. Its fine white stitching was familiar, and one end of the drawstring had a little extra knot.

“That one,” Ling Qingzhu said. “The spare you gave me. I had two alike.”

Ling Zhen picked it up and laughed.

“That bag was empty!” Ling Zhen said. “You asked for a spare to carry your little travel things. Don't tell me you paid your husband with air!”

His laughter stopped.

The blood drained from Ling Qingzhu’s face behind her veil. Her fingers went cold. She stared at the bag as if she no longer understood what it was.

“Qingzhu?” Ling Zhen asked.

She didn't answer. The extra knot. The matching mouths. Her own counted stones, packed away while she chose which clothes to bring.

She stood so suddenly that the chair scraped the tiles.

“Wait here,” Ling Qingzhu said.

She went into the room and opened her chest. Her hands moved too quickly, pushing cloth aside, then catching on the edge of a folded robe.

Beneath it lay the other pale bag.

She opened it.

The spirit stones were inside.

She reached in and pulled out one wrapped bundle. The cord was tied the way she always tied it, with the shorter end tucked beneath the knot. She remembered counting it herself and being pleased that she could settle the arrangement without waiting for the clan.

She never gave that bundle to him.

Her fingers loosened. Several stones rolled across the bed before she caught them. The small sound made her flinch, and she stared at the stones resting against her quilt.

She'd been so certain. Certain enough to be angry when he asked. Certain enough to call his careful account another attempt to take advantage of her.

Not a few forgotten stones. The sum she counted for the arrangement, still separated from her everyday purse. She didn't need to count them again to recognize the wrapping around the bundles.

Her knees weakened. She sat on the edge of the bed, holding the full bag in both hands.

Ten thousand spirit stones. All here.

The courtyard seemed very far away.

Ling Zhen stopped at the room's doorway. He saw the second bag and immediately understood enough to stop asking foolish questions.

“You mixed them up,” Ling Zhen said quietly.

Ling Qingzhu looked at him. The veil stirred with her breath, but no answer came.

He didn't tell her what Shi Feng bought or how the household lived. He didn't know. He could only look at the two bags and the stunned eyes above his niece’s veil.

“It wasn't deliberate,” Ling Zhen said. “Give him the payment and explain.”

The simple advice struck her harder than his laughter.

Explain. Shi Feng already explained.

There wasn't one spirit stone in this.

His voice returned with terrible clarity. He sat across from her over breakfast, holding the very bag now dangling from her uncle's fingers.

She opened it then. She saw it was empty. She decided he spent the money and wanted another payment.

He told her the truth, and she called him greedy. Ling Qingzhu bent forward, unable to draw a steady breath. Her uncle moved toward her, but she raised a hand before he reached the bed.

“He told me,” Ling Qingzhu said.

Ling Zhen stopped.

“I didn't believe him,” Ling Qingzhu said.

She wasn't defending herself or asking her uncle to explain the mistake away. She heard what she was admitting, and there was nothing he could say that would make it smaller.

He put the empty bag on the table beside the full one. Two pieces of pale cloth. Months of certainty between them.

“Where is he?” Ling Zhen asked.

“He moved out yesterday,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

Her uncle's expression changed. He finally looked at the empty corner across from the bed, then at the single pair of slippers near the screen.

“Because of this?” Ling Zhen asked.

“No,” Ling Qingzhu said, and the answer frightened her. “Not only this.”

“I didn't choose him only because the court—” Ling Qingzhu began.

She stopped. Explaining the choice to her uncle wouldn't explain how she had treated Shi Feng afterward. Whatever private feeling she'd kept safe, she had still refused to believe him about an empty bag.

She remembered offering more money. She remembered his face when she said it, and how certain she was that fairness could settle what troubled him.

She didn't even pay the first sum.

Ling Zhen remained silent. His earlier laughter felt cruel now, although he never meant it that way.

He closed his ledger quietly and said he'd wait at the residence until she was ready to speak. Ling Qingzhu barely heard him. She sat beside the two pale bags—one empty, one holding the ten thousand stones she had sworn he stole—until the gate closed.

Then she went to the kitchen.

The shelf was tidy. Her medicines stayed where Shi Feng left them. The rice jar stood beside the clean bowls. There was no forgotten note explaining everything, because he never expected her to need one.

She touched the lid of the jar and remembered the first expensive meal he prepared here.

She praised it. He looked pleased.

For months, she believed she knew what bought that expression. Ling Qingzhu covered her mouth. The first sob escaped before she could stop it.

He told her. She heard him. She looked at the evidence with her own eyes.

And she still chose not to believe him.

chapters.title: He Already Told Her
chapters.html:
“Shi Feng,” Ling Qingzhu said.

Only the empty kitchen answered her.

She stood beside the rice jar with one hand over her mouth. His name slipped out before she remembered there was nobody behind the wall to hear it.

She couldn't blame him for leaving without explaining. He explained. He put the empty bag beside her breakfast and asked her to open it.

She remembered her own fingers searching the seams. Nothing was broken. Nothing prevented her from seeing the truth. She simply decided the truth was a trick because she trusted her own certainty more than his words.

The memory made her ashamed enough to sit down. On this same table, he wrote that the promised payment hadn't been received. She told him to keep the debt where she couldn't see it.

He did. He stopped putting it in front of her. She took his silence as proof that he knew she was right.

Ling Qingzhu pressed her hands against her knees. She wanted to find a different explanation, one that left some part of her judgment intact. The full bag in the room refused to provide it.

The fish disappeared first.

She remembered that clearly. There were still two dishes and soup, but no silver carp laid carefully along the plate. She asked why. He said no fish and gave her another bowl of broth.

She thought he was punishing her for refusing a second payment.

Now she saw the butcher's bones differently. He bought them, carried them home, and spent the afternoon making something good from what he could afford. She ate it and complained about what wasn't there.

He didn't owe her expensive meals after being paid nothing. Yet the cheaper food still suited her tastes. He reduced the chili when she complained. He kept the greens from cooking too soft because she disliked them that way.

Those things didn't cost ten thousand spirit stones. They required him to remember her.

Her eyes filled. She wiped them impatiently, but the next memory came before her hand fell.

She watched him count a few spirit stones and called him stingy. She opened her own purse that night. It held enough to buy anything she wanted for supper.

She closed it because she wouldn't reward his greed.

Ling Qingzhu bent forward. The shame hurt worse now that it had somewhere exact to land. It wasn't a vague mistake between two people. She had the means to help, saw his need, and decided her suspicion mattered more.

He still set her bowl down first.

She remembered the well rope. He measured it twice, argued over the price, and made sure it would hold before letting her use the bucket. She told Su Wanning the story as a joke about a husband who counted everything.

Her friend laughed. Shi Feng paid for their evening while she laughed too.

Now she remembered carrying a bucket without worrying whether the rope would break. She treated that small comfort as something the courtyard naturally provided. Someone chose it, bought it, and checked it first.

Not every practical thing was proof of love. She understood that. But she couldn't keep calling the whole person greedy just because he cared whether a merchant cheated him.

She was wrong about his actions before she was wrong about his feelings.

Her gaze moved to the doorway. During the rain, she dried his bedding and pretended she only wanted it out of the kitchen. He thanked her with a smile instead of forcing her to admit the kindness.

He allowed her pride to keep its little excuses. When his own heart finally needed a plain answer, she gave him a bargain.

Ling Qingzhu closed her eyes. She couldn't remember what she paid for the purse string, but she could remember how she wanted him to look when she gave it to him. Why did she imagine his wishes were simpler than hers?

She covered her face. She didn't know when her quiet tears became sobbing.

Later, she went out because she couldn't stay beside the cold stove. The lane looked unchanged. Granny Qin's brazier smoked near the corner, and someone argued over the price of cabbages.

Peng Tao saw her near the fish stall and immediately lifted a fresh carp.

“Young Mistress Ling! Good timing,” Peng Tao called. “I've kept the best one.”

“Did you keep it, or just pick it up?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

The fishmonger laughed without embarrassment. She almost heard Shi Feng answering him instead, calm and unwilling to pay for a story.

“Your husband used to buy these often,” Peng Tao said. “Then he stopped. I thought I'd offended him.”

She looked at the fish and couldn't speak.

“Shall I wrap it?” Peng Tao asked.

“No,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

She stepped away before he could ask another question. Buying an expensive fish wouldn't undo the meals she insulted. It wouldn't bring Shi Feng into the kitchen to cook it.

At the street corner, she remembered Yuelan Terrace.

Su Wanning laughed. Music drifted over the pond. Shi Feng read the bill, then read it again.

Two hundred and eight spirit stones.

She saw him count them out and thought he cared too much about money. She never asked whether the payment she'd given him covered the evening, because she believed it did. She wanted her friend to approve of their life, and he made room for that wish.

He could've refused. He could've chosen a cheaper table and let her be disappointed. Instead he came, listened, and honestly said he enjoyed himself.

On the road home, she took his arm. She told him she was glad he came.

He said he was too.

Ling Qingzhu stopped walking. She remembered the exact warmth of his voice. There wasn't an audience to fool on that quiet road. He wasn't proving anything to a prince or a clan elder.

He was answering her.

She wanted to hear that answer again so badly that her chest hurt.

Before returning to the courtyard, she went to the warehouse street. Ke De recognised her and boasted about paying Shi Feng eight stones for a full day loading carts. She saw the sacks, remembered dust on his sleeves and understood where another part of his time had gone. She left before the foreman could ask for an introduction.

Fang Jingyuan recognized her before she entered his medicine shop. The unmarked Foundation Establishment alchemist immediately straightened his robe and moved a cracked bowl beneath the counter.

“Fairy Ling!” Fang Jingyuan said. “Looking for medicine for the journey? Your husband knows my quality well.”

“That's what I came to ask about,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

His smile faltered. He looked toward the back room, then at the empty doorway behind her.

“Young Master Shi and I always dealt fairly,” Fang Jingyuan said.

“What did he do here?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

The alchemist hesitated. Her expression turned cold enough that he decided a simple answer was safest.

“Pill testing,” Fang Jingyuan replied. “Paid sessions. Nothing hidden.”

“Failed pills?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“Test batches,” Fang Jingyuan said quickly. “Sometimes flawed. He agreed to the terms before swallowing anything.”

She remembered the smell from the kitchen. A chipped jar stood behind the rice sack. Shi Feng ate from it when she thought he was wasting money on a ridiculous medicine trick.

Her heart shook.

“You paid him to swallow your failures?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“Five spirit stones a session,” Fang Jingyuan replied. “He insisted on the written rate. I paid it.”

“Did he become ill?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“He never complained,” Fang Jingyuan replied. “He was unusually suitable. Kept coming back.”

“Did you know what the failed pills would do?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“That's why I paid for observation,” Fang Jingyuan replied. “I wrote down the ingredients. He knew what he was taking.”

She imagined him hiding discomfort in their small kitchen so he could still cook supper for her without a word of complaint.

“He also bought some waste,” Fang Jingyuan added, eager to show everything was voluntary. “I didn't force it on him. He bargained very hard.”

Ling Qingzhu stared at him. The alchemist finally stopped speaking.

She left without buying anything. Fang Jingyuan watched her go and wondered whether he should offer Shi Feng a lower price next time, just in case.

At home she set the two bags beside the agreement. She took out a sheet to explain why she'd first noticed him, then put it away. A pleasant beginning wouldn't repay the months when she had heard his care as hired work.

He had wanted to care for her. She had heard a price complaint. Even now she was imagining damage without asking whether it was real. Tomorrow she would bring the stones to Yonghe Inn and listen to his answer. She couldn't repair the first refusal by making another one sound kinder.

chapters.title: The Debt and the Heart
chapters.html:
“The bag was empty,” Ling Qingzhu said.

Shi Feng stood beside the open window of his room.

Ling Qingzhu kept her veil tied. This inn room wasn’t their home, however much she wanted him to return there. She sat at the table, with the payment between them. For a moment he couldn't answer.

“I know,” Shi Feng replied.

“I mixed up the two bags,” Ling Qingzhu said. “The stones I counted were still in my chest.”

He looked at the bag she brought. There was no satisfaction in finally hearing the truth admitted. He wanted this conversation months ago, before the little debt became part of so many other things.

“You told me,” Ling Qingzhu said. “I didn't believe you.”

He nodded once. She didn't explain that the bags looked alike again. The mistake was one thing. Her certainty afterward was another.

“I thought you'd spent it and wanted more,” Ling Qingzhu said. “That was wrong.”

“Yes,” Shi Feng replied.

The simple answer made her eyes fill. He didn't soften it, and she didn't ask him to.

She pushed the bag toward him.

“Ten thousand spirit stones,” Ling Qingzhu said. “The original payment. I checked it.”

He opened the bag and confirmed the sum. This time there was something inside. He closed it, put it on his side of the table, and took out the old private agreement.

Beside the unpaid line, he wrote the date and the amount received. Her shoulders trembled. Watching him settle the debt properly hurt, because she remembered telling him to keep the account where she couldn't see it.

“It's paid,” Shi Feng said.

He folded the agreement and put it away. He didn't smile or move his things toward the door. She knew then that he could accept the money without accepting the life she wanted back.

“I didn't come only for that,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Then say the rest,” Shi Feng replied.

He poured water into a clean cup and set it within her reach. She took it with both hands, but didn't drink at once.

“Thank you,” Ling Qingzhu said.

He nodded. The courtesy didn't mean he was ready to go home. It meant she was sitting in his room and looked as if she needed water. She let it remain that simple.

She looked at his face. He gave her the attention she refused to give him when the truth first sat between their breakfast bowls.

“Before we met at the tea house, I—” Ling Qingzhu began.

The full payment lay beside his hand. She stopped. Telling him now that she had a better reason for choosing him might sound like another offer: take this older feeling and come home. He had already heard her try to settle his hurt with a larger sum.

“The money isn't an answer to the rest,” Ling Qingzhu said instead.

“No,” Shi Feng replied.

“I learned about the warehouse,” Ling Qingzhu said. “And Fang Jingyuan.”

His expression changed slightly. He wasn't embarrassed by either job, but he didn't expect her to arrive with them.

“You worked and paid for everything,” Ling Qingzhu said. “I complained about the meals while you were swallowing those pills.”

She stopped, unable to keep her voice steady. He saw where her thoughts were going and shook his head.

“The pills didn't harm me,” Shi Feng said.

She looked up quickly.

“You don't need to say that to make me feel better,” Ling Qingzhu said.

His face became serious.

“Listen to me,” Shi Feng replied. “Don't decide my answer is false because you've already chosen another one.”

She went pale. The words struck exactly where they should.

“They were useful to my cultivation,” Shi Feng said. “I could take them safely. That's why I accepted the work and bought the waste.”

He didn't explain his physique's deepest secrets. She didn't need them to stop imagining an injury he never suffered.

“No damage?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“None,” Shi Feng replied. “No poison, no hidden cost. The flaws didn't give me the multiplied effect of good pills, but the ingredients still helped.”

She drew a shaky breath. Relief came first, then shame at how quickly she'd turned him into another story she didn't ask him to confirm.

“I thought you endured it because I didn't pay,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“I chose useful work,” Shi Feng replied. “I wasn't helpless.”

She nodded. He wasn't the poor cripple she believed at the beginning. He wasn't a wounded saint sacrificing his body for her either. He was Shi Feng, strong and practical and capable of making his own choices.

She needed to apologize to him, not to a person her guilt invented.

“Did you think I knew?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“About the empty bag?” Shi Feng replied. “Yes.”

She stared at him. He looked at the window before answering the next question she hadn't yet spoken.

“I told you and you refused to believe me,” Shi Feng said. “I thought you meant to keep the money.”

“And you stayed,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“The hunting pass was useful, and your household's name on the Southern Gate slip kept the Wei inquiry off my back until I was ready to answer it before Wen Shou,” Shi Feng replied. “The arrangement still had value. I made my own decision.”

He didn't turn the beginning into a grand sacrifice. She needed the truth, even where it was less flattering than the story her guilt invented.

“When did that change?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

He looked back at her. There wasn't one day he could point to, one meal or smile that neatly explained months of choosing to return.

“Not all at once,” Shi Feng replied.

She thought of the rain, the ordinary outings, and his expression when she made the tea too strong. There were enough memories that she couldn't honestly ask him to name one for her.

He didn't owe her a perfect account of how his affection grew. She already treated too much of him as something that should fit an account.

She lowered her eyes and let the question go. If they ever spoke of those days again, she wanted him to choose to remember them, not feel pressed to justify why they mattered.

“But the expenses were yours,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Yes,” Shi Feng replied.

“And the time,” Ling Qingzhu added.

“Yes,” Shi Feng said.

She looked down at her hands. The true wrong didn't become smaller because he wasn't poisoned. She ignored his words, mocked his work, and called his personal affection another part of what she bought.

“I'm sorry,” Ling Qingzhu said.

He looked away. He wanted to hear it. Hearing it still hurt.

“I know why you're saying that now,” Shi Feng replied.

“I should've said it before,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“You didn't know before,” Shi Feng replied.

“Because I wouldn't listen,” Ling Qingzhu said.

He didn't contradict her. She wiped her eyes and forced herself to continue without making him comfort her for admitting his hurt.

“When you showed me the empty bag, I decided you only cared about spirit stones—and when you told me two days ago that you cared for me because you wanted to, I still treated you like a man bargaining for a second bag of stones,” Ling Qingzhu said, her voice breaking slightly. “I thought increasing the payment would show I valued you.”

“I know,” Shi Feng replied.

“I understand how that sounded,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“It wasn't only how it sounded,” Shi Feng replied. “You believed it.”

She couldn't deny that. His voice was quiet, and there was no anger she could argue against.

“I did,” Ling Qingzhu said.

The admission left the room silent. Outside, a cart rolled along the canal road. She watched him rest his hand on the window ledge and wanted to cross the space between them.

She stayed seated. Touching him because she was afraid he wouldn't return would be another choice made only for herself.

“I want to do better,” Ling Qingzhu said.

He looked back. He believed she meant it. That didn't erase the exhaustion of trying to explain something he thought they shared.

Shi Feng thought, I don't know how to go back. Even if she understood now, he couldn't make himself forget the moment she named a higher payment.

“I don't have an answer for that today,” Shi Feng said.

She nodded, though disappointment hurt. He wasn't refusing to hear her. He heard her, and the hurt remained.

When she stood, he opened the door for her. She paused beside him, close enough to touch his sleeve.

“May I speak to you again?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

He looked at her hand, then at her eyes above the veil.

“Tomorrow,” Shi Feng replied.

She left without asking him to promise anything else.

chapters.title: My Heart Is Tired
chapters.html:
“Leaving tomorrow?” Kang Fu asked.

Shi Feng put the last room charge on the counter. The innkeeper counted it, looked toward the stairs, and sighed over a bed that would stop earning.

“Tomorrow morning,” Shi Feng replied.

“Qingyun City?” Kang Fu asked.

“Yes,” Shi Feng said.

“My cousin has an inn there,” Kang Fu said quickly. “If you mention my name—”

“Will he charge more?” Shi Feng asked.

Kang Fu coughed. The introduction suddenly became less urgent.

Shi Feng left the counter and went to the travel office. Wen Shou confirmed that his token and route were in order. The official didn't demand he sit behind a royal carriage to prove loyalty to Great Liang.

“Arrive before the reporting deadline,” Wen Shou said. “The three places are yours to defend, not ours to replace at the last moment.”

“I'll be there,” Shi Feng replied.

“And keep your token,” Wen Shou added.

Shi Feng touched it through the cloth at his waist. That much was simple. Qualification belonged to him because he won it. The next tournament would ask him to win again.

He looked forward to something that clear.

Outside, the capital was already preparing to cheer the departing candidates. A man painted Sima Yu's name on a hanging board. Another argued that Ling Qingzhu's name should be higher because more people came to look at her.

Shi Feng walked past without correcting the order. His name could be written third. He still intended to get what he wanted.

Ling Qingzhu waited in the inn's small courtyard when he returned. She didn't bring another bag of spirit stones. Her hands rested empty in her lap.

He stopped beside the bench. The sight of her still made him want to sit closer than he should.

“May I?” Ling Qingzhu asked, touching the space beside her.

He sat, leaving a small distance. She noticed it and didn't move into it.

“I heard you're leaving tomorrow,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“I told the office this morning,” Shi Feng replied.

She nodded. Her family would leave separately. They could travel the same road without sharing the journey, and the thought frightened her more now that she knew what staying beside him actually meant.

“I went back to the courtyard after seeing you,” Ling Qingzhu said. “I thought I could prepare the room and ask you to return.”

He looked at her. She stared at her empty hands.

“Then I realized I was still deciding what you needed before asking,” Ling Qingzhu said.

He didn't answer immediately. The admission mattered. He could hear her trying to speak without arranging an easy ending for herself.

“So I'm asking,” Ling Qingzhu continued. “What do you want me to do?”

His chest ached. For months, he wanted something as simple as that question. Now it arrived when he didn't trust himself to answer without reaching for what already hurt him.

“Don't turn this into another task,” Shi Feng said quietly.

She looked up, alarmed.

“I didn't mean it that way,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“I know,” Shi Feng replied. “There isn't a list you can finish tonight.”

She nodded slowly. Her fingers loosened. She'd spent the morning thinking of repairs, but his feelings weren't a room she could tidy before he inspected it.

Kang Fu appeared carrying a kettle. He stopped at the courtyard door, saw Shi Feng’s expression and Ling Qingzhu’s reddened eyes above her veil, and suddenly became very careful with his steps.

“Tea,” Kang Fu said. “Already included in the room charge.”

Shi Feng nodded. The innkeeper put it down and left without offering another cousin's address.

Ling Qingzhu reached for the kettle. The handle was hot, and she drew her fingers back. Shi Feng wrapped a cloth around it before pouring.

“Wait a moment before drinking,” Shi Feng said.

She looked at him over the cup. The ordinary warning nearly broke her composure. He didn't say it to show what she'd lost. He simply remembered that she often drank before the tea cooled.

He put the kettle down and moved his own cup farther from the edge. Neither spoke for a little while. The innkeeper closed the courtyard door behind him, leaving only the ordinary sounds from the front hall. For once, nobody tried to fill the silence with a useful arrangement.

She held the warm clay between her hands. She wanted to use the moment as proof that everything could return to normal. Then she looked at the distance he left beside her and stopped herself.

A remembered habit wasn't a promise. His care didn't become hers to claim just because it survived the argument.

She drank when the tea cooled. It was cheap tea, weaker than the kind they kept at home. She didn't complain about it.

“I miss you,” Ling Qingzhu said.

The words came without an excuse. He felt them more sharply because of that.

“Not only the cooking,” Ling Qingzhu added. “Not the medicines or the things you did. I keep wanting to tell you something and remembering you aren't there.”

He looked toward the courtyard wall. She kept speaking, afraid that if she stopped she would return to the safer words that ruined everything.

“I bought the purse string because I wanted you to keep something I chose,” Ling Qingzhu said. “I didn't think about any agreement when I gave it to you.”

He touched the purse beneath his robe before he could stop himself. She saw the movement, and her eyes filled.

“You kept it,” Ling Qingzhu whispered.

“Yes,” Shi Feng replied.

There was no reason to lie. He didn't throw away every reminder of her to prove that leaving was real.

“I should've understood you could want the same thing,” Ling Qingzhu said. “That when you remembered what I liked, it wasn't something I bought.”

He drew a slow breath. She understood more than yesterday. He couldn't deny it just to make remaining hurt easier.

“You hear it now,” Shi Feng said.

“Too late?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

He didn't know how to answer that. Saying yes would be simpler than the truth. Saying no would give her a promise he couldn't keep.

“I don't know,” Shi Feng replied.

She looked down. A tear fell onto her hand, and she wiped it away before asking him to do it for her.

“I'm not asking you to pretend,” Ling Qingzhu said. “I know paying the debt doesn't settle this.”

He believed her. That hurt too. If she remained blind and cruel, leaving would let him be angry. Instead she was trying, and he still couldn't find the ease he once felt beside her.

Shi Feng thought, I still want her. Wanting isn't the same as being able to trust the next kindness.

He remembered her saying she'd pay more. The memory came between her hand and his before either moved.

“I can't return as if nothing happened,” Shi Feng said.

“Then don't,” Ling Qingzhu replied quickly. “Let it be different. Let me learn.”

Her urgency made him look at her again. She was proud, talented, and used to deciding her own path. Asking like this cost her something. He didn't enjoy seeing the cost.

“You can learn without me living on that floor,” Shi Feng said.

She lowered her head. He stood before the wish to comfort her made him promise what he couldn't honestly give.

She rose too. Her fingers caught his sleeve, very lightly, then released it when he looked down.

“Stay a little longer,” Ling Qingzhu said. “Please. Give me another chance.”

He looked at the woman he loved. He wanted the home she was asking him to return to. He couldn't bear another evening of wondering which part of himself she thought she'd paid for.

“My heart is tired,” Shi Feng said.

Ling Qingzhu's hand fell to her side. He went inside without adding anything else.

chapters.title: The Eastern Road
chapters.html:
“A fine horse for a fine young master!” Ma Shun said, patting the animal's neck.

The horse turned and tried to bite his sleeve. Shi Feng looked at the seller. Ma Shun was at Qi Condensation, with yellow teeth and a smile that survived almost anything except a reasonable price.

“It agrees with half of that,” Shi Feng said.

“High spirits,” Ma Shun replied. “A very useful quality on the road.”

Shi Feng checked its legs, teeth, and breathing. The dark horse was healthy, ordinary, and strong enough for the journey if he didn't ride it foolishly. That was all he needed.

He paid a fair sum. Ma Shun tried to add a blessing charm for safe travel. Shi Feng pointed at the same charm hanging above three broken wheels in the yard.

The blessing stayed with its owner.

By the time Shi Feng reached the eastern gate, people crowded the road beneath Great Liang's banners. The official party gathered beside the guardhouse, with carriages, hired escorts, and more luggage than several families could use in a month.

He guided his horse around the edge. His own supplies rested in the ring, leaving only a plain saddlebag where others could see it.

Wen Shou checked his name and token.

“Independent travel confirmed,” Wen Shou said. “The reporting date hasn't changed.”

“Neither has my answer,” Shi Feng replied.

The official nodded and handed back the token. Behind him, a servant began arguing that a fifth trunk wasn't really luggage because it only held clothing. Shi Feng left them to settle that profound question.

The eastern residence's carriage arrived with six mounted guards. Two were at Foundation Establishment. Their presence cleared a path before anyone saw the crown prince's face.

“His Highness!”

“The first-ranked candidate!”

“Great Liang's pride!”

The cheers rose quickly. Sima Yu stepped from the carriage in pale gold robes, smiling as if the whole road belonged to his morning walk.

His late Foundation Establishment cultivation was stronger than most young candidates in the kingdom. That wasn't what made Shi Feng watch him carefully. A man who sent others to kill could smile just as pleasantly after they failed.

Sima Yu saw him beside the gate and approached within the guards' view.

“Young Master Shi travels lightly,” Sima Yu said. “No place with the Ling clan?”

“I have a horse,” Shi Feng replied.

“A useful substitute for good company,” Sima Yu said.

“Sometimes an improvement,” Shi Feng replied.

The prince's smile tightened. The nearest guard looked angry but kept his hand away from his weapon. This was a public departure, not a quiet place to carry out an order.

Sima Yu stepped half a pace closer to the stirrup, pitching his voice beneath the rattle of the baggage carts so only Shi Feng could hear.

“Guo Zhen was careless in a storehouse, Cao Wenshu was old, and Zheng Jian never knew when to wait,” Sima Yu said, his smile never leaving his lips. “The mountain passes to Qingyun City cross three borders, Brother Shi. Men who ride alone don't always reach the registration hall.”

Shi Feng looked straight into the prince's eyes. Guo Zhen's wire, Cao Wenshu's sword at the signal fort, Zheng Jian's crossbow in the timber yard—every shadow wore the same gold crest.

“Send whoever you can spare on the road, Your Highness,” Shi Feng said quietly. “What doesn't finish me in the mountains, I will settle with you in person on the Qingyun City platform—where your household guards can't step onto the stone.”

Sima Yu's smile turned to ice for a single breath before he smoothed his sleeve and turned back toward the royal carriage.

“Then ride carefully, third representative,” Sima Yu said.

The prince walked away. Shi Feng didn't mistake the exchange for peace, and he didn't chase him through an official escort to stage a fight on someone else's terms. The regional arena would give them a different place to stand.

He intended to use it.

Ling Qingzhu waited beside the Ling carriage, with Ling Rong checking the last provision boxes. Her violet robe, white veil and black hair drew as much attention as the royal banners.

She saw Shi Feng and stopped speaking.

He looked at her. The words from yesterday returned before either greeted the other. His heart still felt exhausted, and seeing her didn't make it less so.

She came a few steps toward him, then stopped instead of reaching for his sleeve.

“You're leaving now?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“Yes,” Shi Feng replied.

“We'll leave after the official party,” Ling Qingzhu said.

He nodded. She was a qualified candidate too. Her journey didn't end because their home emptied, and he wouldn't ask her to abandon it to prove remorse.

“Take care on the road,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“You too,” Shi Feng replied.

She looked at the horse, searching for something else to say. Then her eyes caught the violet purse string when he shifted his robe.

He didn't hide it. He didn't make it an invitation either.

Ling Rong approached and bowed. His face was carefully neutral, but he didn't ask Shi Feng to ride in the carriage again.

“The clan will report its arrival through the Qingyun City office,” Ling Rong said. “If your route changes, the same office can carry a message.”

“I'll remember,” Shi Feng replied.

The steward withdrew. Ling Qingzhu remained for one more breath, then stepped aside to let him pass.

That small act cost her more than arguing would've. Shi Feng saw it and felt the ache return. He mounted and guided the horse through the gate.

Outside the capital, the road widened between dry fields. The cheers faded behind him. For the first stretch, he listened to the horse's hooves and didn't look back.

He wanted to. That was the truth. He imagined her standing beside the carriage, watching until he disappeared.

Looking back wouldn't tell him what to do with that image.

Shi Feng thought, Keep going. Not because he stopped caring, and not because the tournament would conveniently erase it. He had a place to reach and a cultivation path that didn't end at a rented courtyard.

A few miles beyond the gate, the horse shied at a cart carrying clattering iron pots. Shi Feng loosened the reins instead of dragging its head around. The animal settled once the cart passed.

It was a horse, not a refined artifact. Pouring his qi into it wouldn't turn it into a flying sword or make a foolish pace sensible. He let it find a steady rhythm and saved the faster stretches for open road.

At a low bridge, two men argued over whose cart should cross first. One claimed his master's goods mattered more. The other said his master's mother was waiting and surely outranked a box of wine.

Shi Feng rode through the shallow stream beside them. The water barely reached the horse's knees.

The men stopped arguing long enough to watch him reach the other bank. Then one began explaining why he'd intended to do the same thing.

Shi Feng didn't turn back to listen. Once, he would've enjoyed telling Ling Qingzhu that story over supper. The thought arrived without warning and left the next stretch of road painfully quiet.

He let himself miss her. Pretending he didn't would be another lie, and he had no audience to satisfy out here.

When the horse slowed, he dismounted and walked beside it for a while. His own body needed less rest than the animal. The change gave him something simple to attend to besides memory.

At the first crossing, a tea seller pointed toward the main eastern road. Shi Feng paid for water, checked the horse's saddle, and studied the mountains ahead.

Qingyun City lay beyond them. Candidates from many kingdoms were already travelling there, each convinced that their own name deserved to be heard.

He checked the medicine case in his ring, then tightened the saddle strap and mounted again. Enough recovery pills, sound equipment, and a clear reporting date. He could take care of the journey without borrowing anyone's protection.

Great Liang was behind him. Far back along the dust cloud of the eastern road, two unbadged outriders detached themselves from the royal convoy's rear guard to keep his trail in sight—and Shi Feng rested one hand lightly on his scabbard, welcoming the first stretch of mountain stone where he wouldn't have to hold back.

chapters.title: The River Did Not Wait
chapters.html:
“Lead it from the left,” Tao San said. “Keep its head away from the gap.”
