Shi Feng guided the dark horse down the landing. It was the third morning since leaving Great Liang’s capital. The nearest bridge stood half a day’s ride north, and this flat-bottomed ferry carried horses across the river each morning.

The horse stopped at the plank. Shi Feng loosened the rein and waited rather than dragging it forward.

“Doesn’t like the water?” Tao San asked.

“It doesn’t like that loose board,” Shi Feng replied.

The ferryman checked beneath his foot. One end lifted. He swore, wedged it down, and beckoned again.

This time the horse crossed. Tao San’s Qi Condensation qi steadied the rail while Shi Feng tied the bridle where the animal could keep its footing.

The crossing cost five spirit stones for horse and rider. Shi Feng paid and sat near the bow. Tao San tested the board once more before pulling the plank aboard. He wasn’t about to spend the morning recovering a horse from the river.

A mushroom peddler sat opposite him with two baskets of dried mushrooms. The man's Meridian Opening cultivation wasn't strong enough to hide how nervously he watched the water.

“Does this boat leak?” the peddler asked.

“Only when it rains,” Tao San replied.

The peddler looked up at the clear sky, then down through the gaps beneath his shoes. Shi Feng smiled faintly. For a moment, he wanted to turn and tell Ling Qingzhu what the boatman said.

The empty place beside him stopped the thought.

He looked toward the opposite bank instead.

Tao San pushed them away from the landing. The river moved quickly beyond the reeds, carrying the boat downstream while he guided it toward the far bank.

Shi Feng sat with one hand near his sword. The horse stood quietly behind him. the peddler checked the basket lids twice, then asked whether Qingyun City's mushroom prices really rose when tournament candidates arrived.

“Ask at the western gate,” Tao San said. “The cooks buy there before the crowds wake up.”

The peddler glanced toward the sun. He began counting how many hours of walking remained after the crossing. His mushrooms might reach the city at exactly the wrong time.

Shi Feng watched a broken branch drift past. He'd travelled alone before marrying Ling Qingzhu. There was nothing difficult about deciding when to eat, where to sleep, or which road to take.

The difficulty came when he forgot he was alone. At the morning stall, he'd nearly ordered the kind of vegetables she liked. Last night, he took the blue cloak out and remembered her checking that it wouldn't catch his sword hand.

He still used it. Throwing away a useful gift wouldn't make him stop loving the person who chose it.

Shi Feng thought, Keep going. The road won't shorten because I stare at it.

The horse snorted sharply.

He looked toward the reeds.

A dark head rose beside the boat. Hard ridges covered its jaws, and a yellow eye fixed on the moving horse. The water bulged around a broad shell beneath the surface.

Tao San's face turned pale.

“Black-Armoured River Turtle!” Tao San shouted. “Don't move!”

The peddler immediately moved. He scrambled away from the side and nearly knocked a mushroom basket overboard.

The beast's head struck the rail. Wood cracked. The horse pulled back against its rope, terrified by the sudden noise.

Shi Feng stood and caught the bridle before the animal could rear.

“How strong?” Shi Feng asked.

“Foundation Establishment!” Tao San cried. “This one shouldn't be here! They stay upriver!”

The turtle didn't care where it should've stayed. It opened its jaws and lunged toward the horse again.

Shi Feng drew his sword.

He stepped across the narrow deck and thrust beneath the beast's lower jaw. Piercing Current drove through the soft seam before the shell could turn toward him.

The beast shuddered.

Shi Feng held the sword steady and released a short burst of qi. The force tore through the head from inside. The jaws stopped a hand's width from his sleeve.

Then the beast collapsed against the side of the boat. Water splashed across the deck. Shi Feng pulled the sword free and caught the broken rail before it fell on the peddler's foot.

Tao San stared at him.

One strike. A Foundation Establishment river beast died before the ferry could even turn.

An ordinary early Foundation Establishment cultivator would've struggled against that shell. Shi Feng's strength and control made the exposed seam enough.

“Keep steering,” Shi Feng said.

Tao San jerked back to his pole.

“Yes, Senior!” Tao San replied.

The peddler stared at the dead eye beside the boat. Then he carefully moved his mushrooms farther away from it.

At the far landing, Shi Feng led the horse onto dry ground and checked its legs. It was frightened but uninjured. The horse dealer sold him a healthy animal, and it settled after a little water and fresh grass.

Tao San stood beside the broken rail, looking from it to the carcass floating against the bank.

“I can't pay for the beast,” Tao San said.

“I didn't offer to sell it,” Shi Feng replied.

The ferryman swallowed.

“And the repair?” Tao San asked.

“Ask the turtle,” Shi Feng said.

The peddler laughed once, then stopped when Tao San looked at him.

Shi Feng kept the devouring flow still and put the carcass into his spatial ring after checking that the useful shell remained intact. He'd decide what to keep later. There was no reason to leave a valuable kill in the river.

Tao San untied the boat from the landing and hesitated.

“The crossing fee,” Tao San began.

“You brought me across,” Shi Feng said.

“I nearly fed your horse to a beast,” Tao San replied.

“You didn't invite it,” Shi Feng said.

The ferryman looked relieved. Shi Feng wasn't interested in turning every incident into a debt of gratitude or a claim against someone else's purse. He took the reins and continued toward the road.

The peddler called after him before he mounted.

“Senior, are you entering the tournament?” the peddler asked.

“Yes,” Shi Feng replied.

“Which kingdom?” the peddler asked.

“Great Liang,” Shi Feng said.

The merchant nodded eagerly. He already looked forward to telling his buyers that he crossed the river with a kingdom representative. Shi Feng didn't offer to carry his baskets too.

That evening, he stopped beside a sheltered rise and let the horse graze. The road was quiet enough to hear wheels approaching from a long way off.

He took out the carcass and separated the useful shell from the soft parts. Then he touched the remaining flesh and allowed the devouring flow to begin.

The beast's qi entered his body. He assimilated it patiently before packing the shell away. His foundation absorbed the gain without difficulty, but the medicine was only a small addition to what it needed.

Early Foundation Establishment remained his realm. He wasn't going to mistake one easy kill for another breakthrough.

He checked the horse's water before sitting down. The animal nosed his sleeve, looking for more grain, and he moved the bag out of reach.

“You've already eaten,” Shi Feng said.

The horse tried again.

He gave it a small handful and tied the bag shut. An ordinary horse didn't care about Great Sects, qualification ranks, or unhappy marriages. It wanted feed and a dry place to stand.

Tonight, he found that simple appetite easier company than another concerned question from a stranger. When he finished, he opened his provisions and ate beside a small fire.

He had food, money, and the strength to keep going without asking anyone to take him in. The road ahead wasn't beyond what he could manage alone.

Shi Feng banked the embers with a flat stone, checked the perimeter where the two royal outriders had lost his trail before the ferry, and pulled the blue cloak over his shoulders without looking back toward Great Liang.

chapters.title: Qingyun City
chapters.html:
“Candidates to the left,” Pan Zhi called.

Shi Feng guided his horse out of the line of loaded carts. Qingyun City's eastern gate rose above three broad roads, each crowded with arrivals. Beyond it, roofs climbed toward a high stone ridge beneath banners bearing the marks of the three Great Sects.

He'd spent several more days on the road. Dust covered his boots, and the blue cloak lay folded across the horse's back.

A guard named Pan Zhi checked the plate in his hand. The man's early Foundation Establishment cultivation was enough to command respect at an ordinary kingdom gate. Here, two dozen equally strong young cultivators waited for him to finish reading.

“Great Liang, third qualifying place,” Pan Zhi said. “Reporting hall at the end of the western avenue. Don't sell the plate or lend it to a friend.”

“I haven't found a buyer,” Shi Feng replied.

Pan Zhi looked up sharply, then noticed his calm expression.

“Don't look for one,” Pan Zhi said.

He returned the plate and waved him through.

Inside, Shi Feng stopped beside a horse trough and looked along the avenue. A Golden Core cultivator crossed above the roofs on a flying refined artifact. Nobody knelt or shouted his name. Most people didn't even stop bargaining.

In Great Liang, an early Golden Core expert could make a whole street fall quiet.

The difference was clear enough.

Shi Feng thought, Good. There's more to see here than another royal banner. He watered the horse and continued toward the reporting hall.

A Bone Refinement clerk named Kang Shu checked his name against Great Liang's list. The process took less time than the ride from the gate.

“Age?” Kang Shu asked.

“Nineteen,” Shi Feng replied.

The clerk checked the birth entry and nodded. Shi Feng's birthday passed during the journey without a feast or an announcement. He'd remembered the date while buying feed and gone on with his day.

“Early Foundation Establishment,” Kang Shu said after a brief verification. “Report here again on the opening morning. Your lodging is your own affair.”

“Any area I should avoid?” Shi Feng asked.

“The ones with signs saying they're full,” Kang Shu replied.

Shi Feng smiled slightly. The clerk already reached for the next candidate's plate.

There was no royal greeting, no speech about being Great Liang's hope. Here, his qualification made him one entry among many.

That suited him.

Outside, an inn runner hurried toward the horse before Shi Feng mounted.

“An excellent room, Young Master!” Fu Shen said. “Close to everything!”

“How close?” Shi Feng asked.

“A short walk,” Fu Shen replied.

“To the arena?” Shi Feng asked.

“To the road that leads there,” Fu Shen said.

Shi Feng looked at him. The runner's Qi Condensation aura was weak, but his smile survived the inspection.

“The room's clean,” Fu Shen added.

“Show me,” Shi Feng said.

The inn wasn't close to the arena. It wasn't especially far either. A quiet side street led to its gate, and the stable had water, feed, and enough room for his horse.

The owner, Kang Liu, was at Bone Refinement. He showed Shi Feng a plain upstairs room with a bed and one table.

“The window overlooks our courtyard,” Kang Liu said proudly.

Shi Feng opened it. Below, a servant was washing a large cabbage in a basin.

“A fine cabbage,” Shi Feng said.

Kang Liu coughed.

“The room has good light,” Kang Liu said.

Shi Feng checked the lock, bedding, and roof. Nothing leaked. There was no smell of old damp beneath the clean cover.

He asked the total price, including the horse. Kang Liu named it and waited hopefully.

“And the courtyard view?” Shi Feng asked.

“Included,” Kang Liu said.

“Keep it included,” Shi Feng replied.

They settled the fee without another description of the cabbage. Fu Shen received his introduction payment from the owner and left pleased.

Shi Feng unpacked only what he needed. His sword stayed within reach. The travel medicines remained in his ring, with the thicker quilt folded beside his clothing.

He didn't stand staring at the empty chair this time.

He had work to do outside.

Qingyun City's medicine street began beneath the shadow of the Sky Pavilion tower. Its lower halls were larger than the tower Shi Feng used in Great Liang, and the certification staircase held a steady line of cultivators. Two men argued beside the entrance about whether a visiting alchemist would sit for a second Mark.

Shi Feng listened for a moment before walking past. Pills for Nascent Soul cultivators belonged far beyond his present hands, no matter how much Mo Tianheng's expertise remained in his mind.

He wanted to see local ingredients first.

At a materials shop, Wang Tong examined the turtle shell he brought from the river. The Qi Condensation merchant tapped its edge and announced that the colour was poor.

“Then don't buy it,” Shi Feng said.

Wang Tong immediately stopped tapping.

“It still has uses,” Wang Tong said.

“So does my time,” Shi Feng replied.

The merchant named a better price. Shi Feng compared it with a similar shell displayed behind the counter and accepted after a short bargain.

He didn't need to sell everything he owned for a few spirit stones. He had no immediate use for the shell, and the fair payment could buy ingredients suited to his current practice. Wang Tong noticed the representative's plate while wrapping the purchase.

“Which sect are you hoping for?” Wang Tong asked.

“Whichever one still looks worth choosing after the bracket,” Shi Feng replied.

The merchant chuckled.

“Most young swordsmen name Martial Palace before they even find an inn,” Wang Tong said. “Though Artificer Hall's elders have been buying up every crate of good metal and broken mechanisms along this street since yesterday.”

“To repair?” Shi Feng asked.

“To learn from,” Wang Tong replied. “Cheap mistakes, they say. A shopkeeper's best customers.”

Shi Feng smiled. Xu Changhe's notes contained enough ordinary repairs that he could believe it.

“The Great Sects' senior experts really are Nascent Soul?” Shi Feng asked.

Wang Tong lowered his voice despite the noisy street outside.

“Late Nascent Soul at their highest,” Wang Tong said. “Not people who come here to bargain over a turtle shell. Today's Golden Core visitors already make the city officials careful.”

Shi Feng nodded. The kingdom was one step, and the Great Sects were another. He didn't mistake a qualifying plate for the strength to stand at their summit.

He bought two small packets before leaving. There were rarer things on the shelves, but he wasn't going to fill his ring with herbs he couldn't yet use properly.

Outside, a group of candidates passed in matching dark robes. Their Foundation Establishment auras drew attention without emptying the street. One wore a kingdom plate bearing an unfamiliar crest.

Shi Feng watched them head toward the arena district.

The surrounding kingdoms were arriving.

At the inn, Kang Liu offered a table near the front so other guests could see his sword and plate. Shi Feng chose the back corner instead.

Dinner arrived at the stated price. That improved his opinion of the owner considerably.

He ate, checked the opening notice, and returned upstairs before the hall grew louder. The window let in sounds from three different streets, none familiar. For a moment, he remembered Ling Qingzhu asking whether the room on their route had a roof.

This one did.

He wondered which room she'd choose when she arrived, then closed the shutters before the thought carried him farther. On the table, his qualifying plate lay beside the new ingredient packets.

Shi Feng sat down to cultivate. The city was larger, the opponents were stronger, and the tournament was nearly here.

The opening was still several days away. He would use them properly instead of sitting beside the window waiting for familiar footsteps.

Over the next two days, Shi Feng cultivated with the pills retained from his commissions. He had been strengthening his foundation since the breakthrough, through medicine, hunting and steady practice. Now the accumulated qi filled the remaining gap.

On the second night, his qi grew denser and flowed through his foundation with renewed force. He steadied it until the change settled.

Mid Foundation Establishment.

Shi Feng opened his eyes and clenched his hand. His strength had increased again. No pill resistance slowed him, and no medicinal impurities needed clearing. The gain belonged to the work he had already done.

He put away the empty medicine wrapping and heated his small practice furnace. The simple Golden Core formula he had tried in Great Liang still demanded care. This time, the joined medicinal streams held together through the difficult turn. He lost the pill during cooling, but he knew exactly where his hands had failed. Tomorrow, he would confirm his registration. Tonight, he recorded the correction.

chapters.title: Three Names Again
chapters.html:
“Great Liang's other two representatives have arrived,” Kang Shu said.

Shi Feng stood beside the reporting counter with his plate in hand. The clerk checked the seal once more and placed it beside two others.

First, Sima Yu. Second, Ling Qingzhu. Third, Shi Feng.

The names hadn't changed during the journey. A great deal else had.

“Final kingdom list,” Kang Shu explained. “Check the entry, sign, and take your plate. When the opening bell rings, enter by the arena's eastern gate.”

Shi Feng checked his name and signed. His mid Foundation Establishment qi remained steady beneath his robe. The breakthrough at the inn had settled fully. He was ready for the opening rounds.

Behind him, several newly arrived candidates argued over where they should stand. None wore Great Liang's crest.

One young man leaned past him to examine the list. His name was Duan Yichen, a mid Foundation Establishment cultivator from Great Zhao. He wore a dark robe without ornaments and carried a heavy sabre.

“Third?” Duan Yichen asked.

Shi Feng looked at him.

“That's what it says,” Shi Feng replied.

“Mid Foundation Establishment takes third place in your kingdom?” Duan Yichen asked.

“It sent three qualifiers,” Shi Feng said.

Duan Yichen studied him for a moment. There was no offence in his expression, only a direct attempt to judge an opponent.

“Don't expect the arena to be gentle,” Duan Yichen said.

“Then you should stand carefully,” Shi Feng replied.

The sabre user laughed once and moved toward the next counter. Neither needed to become a lifelong enemy over a few words. Kang Shu handed the plates back to their proper tray and called for the remaining Great Liang names.

Sima Yu entered from the side passage.

The Crown Prince wore pale gold robes and a jade belt. Two servants followed him until a hall guard pointed at the waiting area outside.

“Candidates only,” Pan Zhi said.

One servant looked offended. Sima Yu raised a hand, and both stopped immediately. There was no point making a scene beneath the Great Sects' registration banners.

“Brother Shi,” Sima Yu said pleasantly. “A safe journey?”

“Yes,” Shi Feng replied.

The prince looked at the plain sword and travel-worn boots. His late Foundation Establishment cultivation drew a few interested glances from nearby candidates, but nobody bowed because of his robe. Here, he was another young cultivator with a qualifying plate.

“Great Liang's representatives should stay together,” Sima Yu said.

“The clerk has the three names,” Shi Feng replied. “That should be enough.”

Sima Yu's smile cooled.

“I meant we should share what we learn,” Sima Yu said.

“Then learn something useful,” Shi Feng replied.

Pan Zhi glanced toward them. The Crown Prince noticed and returned his attention to the counter.

Shi Feng didn't press further. He hadn't forgotten the killing orders, and he hadn't come to argue about them in a queue. The arena would give them a clearer place to settle their grudge.

Kang Shu checked Sima Yu's signature without calling him Your Highness.

The prince completed it with controlled patience.

Then Ling Qingzhu entered.

Shi Feng heard her steps before turning. His fingers stopped on the bottle's cork. He pressed it firmly into place, then looked toward the stair.

Her white veil covered her face, and her black hair was pinned with the repaired silver clasp. The violet robe beneath her travelling cloak was familiar too.

She stopped when she saw him.

“Shi Feng,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Fairy Ling,” Shi Feng replied.

Sima Yu looked between them. The space they left was too noticeable for him to miss, but neither offered an explanation.

Ling Qingzhu went to the counter and completed her registration. The clerk confirmed her eligibility without announcing her exact cultivation. Her qi remained restrained, giving the watching candidates little to judge.

She took her plate and turned toward Shi Feng again.

“May I walk out with you?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“I'm only going as far as the notice board,” Shi Feng said.

They left Sima Yu standing beside the list.

Outside, the avenue was crowded with cultivators heading toward the arena district. A tall notice board listed the opening time and the candidates' entrance.

Ling Qingzhu stopped beside it. Shi Feng kept two full paces between them, his attention on the posted bell schedule rather than her veil.

“Have you found a room?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“Yes,” Shi Feng said.

“I'm near the southern avenue,” Ling Qingzhu said, her fingers tightening briefly around her reporting plate when he didn't offer his inn's name. “If there's anything important about the tournament, I'll send word through the reporting hall.”

“The notice board will have the draws,” Shi Feng replied evenly.

She wanted to ask where he stayed. She wanted to ask whether he'd eat with her, whether he still woke before dawn, whether he used the warmer quilt. She didn't ask all those questions at once simply because she missed knowing the answers.

“Do well in the opening round,” Ling Qingzhu said quietly.

“You too,” Shi Feng replied.

Ling Rong came out of the reporting hall and stopped a few steps away. The steward's early Foundation Establishment aura was familiar, but his careful greeting was quieter than it used to be.

“Young Master Shi,” Ling Rong said. “The clan's lodging is near—”

“I've told him,” Ling Qingzhu interrupted.

The steward stopped. She didn't sound angry, but the firmness in her voice made him wait.

“Don't arrange visits for me,” Ling Qingzhu said. “I'll ask for what I want myself.”

Ling Rong bowed and moved toward the carriage waiting farther down the avenue. He didn't understand every part of the couple's disagreement. He understood an instruction clear enough to follow.

Shi Feng inclined his head once—polite, unhurried, and no warmer than he had been to Duan Yichen at the counter.

She stepped aside first. He walked toward the medicine street without asking her to follow.

Ling Qingzhu watched him go until the crowd hid his dark robe. Then she turned toward her own lodging.

At the inn, Shi Feng checked the sword and the medicine he intended to carry. There was no need for a great pile of treasures. He knew the weapon, knew his own strength, and had enough pills to recover between matches.

He took one from his own bottle and swallowed it. Its force entered his foundation without resistance. The process steadied his attention while the hall below grew louder with arguments about tomorrow's favourites.

Sima Yu's name appeared once among them. So did several names Shi Feng hadn't heard before. He wasn't interested in deciding a winner from a dinner table.

Kang Liu knocked before the lamps were lit.

“Early breakfast tomorrow?” Kang Liu asked.

“Yes,” Shi Feng replied.

“The plain one?” Kang Liu asked. “There's also a candidate's strengthening meal.”

“What's different?” Shi Feng asked.

“More meat,” Kang Liu replied.

“Then call it more meat,” Shi Feng said.

The innkeeper sighed and wrote down the order. After he left, Shi Feng opened the shutters. Beyond the rooftops, great banners moved above the arena walls.

For months, he'd worked toward this gathering. He completed the Extreme, established his foundation, and earned a qualifying place. None of those things depended on anyone else.

He still wanted to win.

Shi Feng shut the window and set the plate beside his sword. When the opening bell rang, he would enter the arena for himself.

chapters.title: The Old Man Who Bought Broken Tools
chapters.html:
The small bronze puppet had only one arm, and that arm kept slapping the stall.

Shi Feng stopped because the third slap knocked a pin out of its shoulder. The seller, Chen Lu, caught the pin, looked at the watching crowd, and put it behind his back.

An old man in a patched brown robe scratched his chin. His beard needed trimming. A straw basket at his feet held two cracked furnace lids and what looked like the handle of a shovel.

“Show me the core,” Li Changyuan said.

Shi Feng waited. Before the seller answered, a neighbouring merchant leaned over the partition.

“Li Changyuan, you've been asking that since breakfast,” Jin Sheng said. “Buy it or let him eat.”

“Then he should stop feeding it qi,” Li Changyuan replied. “He'll crack the seat before he sells anything.”

Chen Lu snorted. He was a Bone Refinement cultivator with blackened fingers and the patient anger of someone who repaired other people's mistakes all day.

“You want a working puppet at scrap price,” Chen Lu said.

“I want scrap that knows it's scrap,” Li Changyuan replied.

Shi Feng smiled despite himself. He had come out to stretch his legs after practising medicine, and the puppet was more interesting than another banner advertising tournament champions who hadn't fought yet.

Chen Lu lifted the puppet's chest plate. Three bronze channels led into a round stone seat. A crack crossed the casing beneath it.

Shi Feng leaned slightly closer.

“The crack isn't the only problem,” Shi Feng said.

Both men looked at him. Li Changyuan's eyes dropped briefly to the sword at his waist, then returned to the puppet.

“Go on,” Li Changyuan said.

“The shoulder pin was replaced,” Shi Feng said. “It fits the hole, but the arm catches before it finishes turning. The core keeps driving against it.”

Chen Lu brought the pin from behind his back. He didn't look pleased, but he didn't try to conceal it again.

“The old pin was gone,” Chen Lu said. “I used what I had.”

“That doesn't make the new one fit,” Li Changyuan said.

Li Changyuan turned the puppet on its side. Shi Feng pointed to a bright crescent where the metal had rubbed against the shoulder socket.

He recognized the fault because Xu Changhe had drawn almost the same crescent beside a gate-hinge repair. The notes had included measurements, failed replacements and a short complaint about disciples who thought force could substitute for filing.

Nothing about the little puppet required a miraculous inheritance.

Chen Lu fetched a narrower pin from a drawer. Li Changyuan rolled it between his fingers and shook his head.

“Too thin,” Li Changyuan said. “It'll walk out under load.”

Shi Feng looked through the drawer after Chen Lu moved it toward him. There were several pins, three washers and a spring bent into a useless hook. He selected a straight pin with a rough collar.

“The collar needs shortening,” Shi Feng said. “The shaft looks close.”

“Looks close isn't a measurement,” Li Changyuan replied.

He passed over a pair of worn calipers.

Shi Feng accepted the correction. He measured the socket, then the pin. The difference was small enough to repair with a thin sleeve. He said so, and Chen Lu took a strip of bronze from beneath the counter.

Li Changyuan watched without offering praise. That suited Shi Feng. A stranger didn't need to declare him a genius because he'd noticed a rubbing mark.

They fitted the sleeve and shortened the collar. Chen Lu did the filing; his practiced hands were faster than Shi Feng's would have been. The arm moved freely when he turned it by hand.

Then Chen Lu sent a thread of qi into the chest.

The arm rose, paused, and slapped the stall again.

Jin Sheng laughed from the other side of the partition.

“Good repair,” Jin Sheng said. “Now it hits without squeaking.”

Chen Lu glared toward the partition. Shi Feng crouched to watch through the open chest instead of looking at the arm.

A faint light travelled through the upper bronze channel. It faded before reaching the return junction.

“The qi isn't coming back properly,” Shi Feng said.

Li Changyuan's beard shifted with a small smile.

“That's a different fault,” Li Changyuan said. “Can you tell which part?”

Shi Feng studied the exposed channels. The simple loop resembled the return passages used to keep heat even around a small pill furnace. Resembled didn't mean identical. He wouldn't pretend to know the puppet's whole design.

He pointed to the darkened junction.

“Somewhere here,” Shi Feng said. “I can see where the flow fails. I can't tell whether the plate underneath is broken without opening it.”

“Then don't claim more,” Li Changyuan replied.

Chen Lu folded his arms.

“If you open that seat, you're buying it,” Chen Lu said.

Li Changyuan named a fair scrap price. Chen Lu accepted at once, looking relieved that the puppet would become somebody else's problem.

The entire bargain took two sentences.

Li Changyuan moved to the stone bench beside the market well. Shi Feng helped carry the puppet because its remaining arm caught on the basket handle every few steps.

Children watched until Li Changyuan placed the arm facing the wall. Disappointed that it wouldn't slap anything, they ran after a cart selling warm buns.

The old man loosened the core seat. Beneath it, a thin bronze plate had split along an old repair.

Shi Feng looked at the break and exhaled.

“So both faults were real,” Shi Feng said.

“Usually are,” Li Changyuan replied. “People like finding one mistake. Makes them stop looking.”

He wrapped the damaged plate in cloth. He didn't reveal a hidden treasure inside it or ask Shi Feng to swear secrecy. He simply set it aside and checked whether the casing could still be used.

“Do you make puppets?” Li Changyuan asked.

“No,” Shi Feng said. “I've read some ordinary repair notes. I make medicine.”

“Medicine has pots, pipes and men who overheat things,” Li Changyuan said. “You'll find plenty to repair.”

Shi Feng laughed. It came easily, which surprised him a little. Most of the morning had passed without his mind returning to the room in Great Liang.

Li Changyuan looked at the tournament plate hanging from his everyday bag.

“Going to fight?” Li Changyuan asked.

“Yes,” Shi Feng said.

“Don't carry that loose knot onto a platform,” Li Changyuan said.

Shi Feng checked the tie. One end had worked free while he crouched beside the stall. He tightened it and put the bag strap firmly over his shoulder.

It was sensible advice. Nothing more needed to be made of it.

Li Changyuan began gathering his purchases. Shi Feng passed him the missing washer before it could roll into the gutter, noticing as their fingers neared that he couldn't sense a trace of qi from the old man—not Bone Refinement, not Foundation Establishment, not even the faint heat of an ordinary meridian circuit. Yet when two hurrying Foundation Establishment swordsmen barrelled down the well lane behind them, their footsteps drifted half a pace aside around the old man's straw basket without either youth realizing he had yielded the path.

“Which notes taught you to check rubbing marks?” Li Changyuan asked.

“An enforcer's repair journal,” Shi Feng replied. “He also used a sword.”

Li Changyuan nodded as though that was an ordinary answer. He didn't demand the journal or press for the dead man's name in the street.

Shi Feng liked him a little better for it.

At the end of the lane, Shi Feng stopped to buy two buns. He offered one to Li Changyuan when the old man caught up with his basket.

Li Changyuan accepted without ceremony and bit into it while it was still too hot.

“Bad choice,” Li Changyuan muttered.

“Wait for it to cool,” Shi Feng said.

“I know that now,” Li Changyuan replied.

They stood beside the wall until the crowd thinned. Above the market roofs, the arena bells sounded a practice sequence. Porters were still hanging banners near the northern avenue.

Li Changyuan brushed crumbs from his beard and went back toward the tool stalls. There was apparently another broken thing he wanted to examine.

Shi Feng returned to the inn.

His furnace waited where he'd left it. The next practice batch would demand steady hands and a clean cooling turn. He sat down, checked the heat passages, and found a small piece of ash lodged beside the air inlet.

Yesterday, he would probably have increased the flame first.

Today, he cleared the passage.

The flame settled evenly beneath the furnace. Shi Feng placed the first measured ingredient inside and began again—knowing that at dawn the arena gates would open on one hundred and eight contenders, and that Sima Yu's name was on the same list.

chapters.title: One Hundred and Eight
chapters.html:
“One hundred and eight candidates,” Lu Yong declared.

Shi Feng walked through the eastern gate beneath three great banners. Beyond the passage, the arena opened into a broad circle of stone platforms surrounded by crowded stands.

Thirty-two kingdoms sent three representatives each, and twelve recognized lesser sects held independent places. Their crests hung along the inner wall, where attendants checked the final names against the reporting lists. Great Liang's banner occupied one space among many.

No larger than the others.

Shi Feng stopped at the assigned entrance and handed over his plate. A Foundation Establishment attendant named Zhou Ke checked the seal, then pointed toward the waiting area.

“Your draw will appear on the board,” Zhou Ke said. “Don't enter a platform before your name is called.”

Shi Feng nodded and took the plate back. He was nineteen, at mid Foundation Establishment, and carrying a plain sword beside a plain dark robe. Several nearby candidates glanced at him before looking toward opponents with stronger visible auras.

He didn't correct their choices.

Let them watch whoever they wanted.

The stands quieted when the Great Sects' representatives arrived. Wei Chengyuan of Martial Palace walked first. His late Golden Core pressure spread briefly across the front rows, and even several visiting royal officials stood to greet him.

Behind him came Mu Shuyun from Hundred Flower Valley, a mid Golden Core cultivator with a pale green sash. She looked over the candidates without slowing her steps.

Artificer Hall's He Zhen followed carrying a short wooden case. His early Golden Core cultivation drew less noise, but the guards at the entrance bowed just as carefully.

Three delegates. Each represented a sect whose senior experts stood far above any kingdom's strongest cultivator. For many candidates, being noticed by one of them would change an entire family's future.

Shi Feng looked toward He Zhen's wooden case. A small tool mark crossed its clasp. He remembered Xu Changhe's ordinary repair notes and the sword movements practised in a narrow ruin passage.

He didn't know this delegate. Holding a dead elder's teachings didn't make the whole sect his family. It gave him a reason to look at Artificer Hall more closely.

That was enough for now.

A thin young man standing nearby followed his gaze. The stranger wore the crest of Great Wu and a late Foundation Establishment aura.

“Choosing a sect before the draw is even up?” Lu Ting asked.

Shi Feng looked at him.

“Looking at the wooden case,” Shi Feng replied.

“Martial Palace is the only seat worth watching,” Lu Ting said.

“Then watch them,” Shi Feng replied.

Lu Ting frowned, unsure whether the answer was rude or sensible. He turned toward Wei Chengyuan instead.

The conversation ended there. Shi Feng didn't need to defend a sect he'd never entered.

The presiding official stepped onto the central platform. Lu Yong wore a dark robe and a simple jade badge. His late Golden Core aura made the remaining private conversations die away.

“Representatives of the kingdoms and independent sects,” Lu Yong said. “Your local qualification earned the right to stand here. It earned nothing beyond that.”

Several candidates straightened. Others held their weapons more tightly.

Sima Yu stood beneath Great Liang's banner with a controlled expression. His late Foundation Establishment cultivation remained impressive, but he wasn't the only candidate at that stage. Shi Feng saw him glance toward Martial Palace's seats.

Let him look. The Crown Prince's household wasn't standing on the fighting platform beside him.

Ling Qingzhu waited farther along the same row. Her qi was calm and restrained. Nearby candidates watched her, unable to judge her depth. She gave them no help. The repaired silver clasp shone against her black hair above the white veil.

She looked toward Shi Feng once.

He met her gaze, then turned toward the central platform.

Shi Feng checked the number on his plate again and stepped forward when the attendant called it. Ling Qingzhu's name remained farther down the register.

Lu Yong raised one hand toward the three sect banners.

“The top ten will earn recruitment by the Great Sects,” Lu Yong announced. “The champion will receive direct inner-disciple entry and may choose among the nearby Great Sects.”

The stands erupted.

“Direct inner disciple!”

“Choose any of the three!”

“Even a royal clan can't buy that place!”

“One hundred and eight people for ten places!”

Lu Yong waited until the noise fell.

“Your birth, beauty, and kingdom rank won't replace a victory,” Lu Yong said. “Neither will a complaint from your elders.”

Mu Shuyun smiled faintly in her seat. Wei Chengyuan looked bored by the warning, as though he'd heard every complaint before. He Zhen opened the wooden case and took out a writing brush.

Their interest would have to be earned.

Shi Feng liked that better than another official asking him to bow toward a prince.

Zhou Ke brought the first draw slips to the long board beside the waiting area. Two attendants placed the names in matching columns while Lu Yong explained the opening round.

One hundred and eight candidates. Fifty-four matches. Winners would advance, with the following rounds arranged under the announced rules.

Crossing the boundary meant defeat. A clear surrender ended the match. Deliberately attacking after surrender would bring the officials onto the platform.

The warning was delivered without a threat about anyone's family. The Golden Core cultivators seated above the arena were enough to make its meaning clear. Shi Feng checked the position of his sword.

He'd kept promises, earned medicine, and refined every bone before establishing his foundation. He practised until his own hands could use what the inherited notes taught him. His strength wasn't something this morning's crowd granted.

Their opinion couldn't take it away either.

He thought, Top ten first. Then the championship.

In Great Liang, third place gave him everything he needed. Here, first place offered the choice he'd travelled to earn. He wouldn't settle for less simply because some candidates looked impressive.

The first names appeared.

Duan Yichen of Great Zhao leaned forward to find his match. The sabre user from the reporting hall saw Shi Feng and nodded once before returning his attention to the board.

Lu Ting muttered something about an unlucky draw. Several other candidates began arguing about opponents they hadn't even met. Shi Feng waited until the attendant moved clear of his row.

Great Liang, Shi Feng.

Opposite his name stood White Crane Pavilion's chief disciple, Xie Wenyuan. Mid Foundation Establishment, according to the registration entry.

Near the sect waiting area, Han Zheng saw the pairing and spoke to a young man in white. Xie Wenyuan listened without looking hurried. He carried a slim sword and wore his hair neatly tied.

Farther down the line, an old man presented a dark sect token. Zhou Ke compared its worn seal with the official register before accepting it.

“Lone Spear Peak's independent place is confirmed,” Zhou Ke said.

The one-eyed youth beside the old man grinned. Gu Zhan rested his spear against his shoulder and started looking for whoever had drawn him.

Lu Yong raised his voice before the waiting candidates dispersed.

“Burst pills that imitate a higher realm are forbidden,” Lu Yong said. “If one is used, the referee halts the match and activates the platform barrier. Do not strike through an official halt. Protection is enforced while the offender is removed. The violation will be recorded publicly.”

At his gesture, pale light rose around the central platform. The barrier carried the combined support of the arena formations and the officials above it. Shi Feng watched its edges settle into the stone.

“A surrender ends the fight at once,” Lu Yong added. “For a violation, the warning precedes the halt seal. The four beams joining make that seal binding. Our timing crystals record whether a blow landed before or after it.”

This was a tournament under other people's rules. He needed to remember exactly where their protection began.

A bell rang above the arena.

The sound carried over the stands, across the stone platforms, and out beyond the city walls. People rose from their seats as the first candidates moved toward the marked passages.

Ling Qingzhu watched Shi Feng walk past Great Liang's banner. She wanted to call something to him and didn't. He knew where she stood. He didn't need to turn back to make her feel less afraid of the distance.

Sima Yu's eyes followed him too. There was no welcome in that gaze. Shi Feng didn't look toward either of them again.

Now there was a sword in his hand and an open platform ahead.

Lu Yong's voice rang across the arena.

“The Great Kingdom Tournament begins!” Lu Yong declared.

Shi Feng stepped toward his assigned platform.

chapters.title: White Crane's Chief Disciple
chapters.html:
Xie Wenyuan bowed from the opposite side of the platform.

“White Crane Pavilion, Xie Wenyuan,” Xie Wenyuan said. “Please advise me.”

“Great Liang, Shi Feng,” Shi Feng replied.

Shi Feng returned the courtesy and looked at the stone beneath his boots. A white line marked the boundary three steps behind Xie Wenyuan. Beyond it stood the referee, Zhou Ke, and a short stair leading into the candidates' passage.

There was no need to break anything expensive.

Xie Wenyuan drew his sword. Its narrow blade carried a pale green gleam, better workmanship than Shi Feng's plain weapon. His stance was balanced, with the left foot light enough to turn in either direction.

A proper swordsman. Shi Feng could acknowledge that without pretending they were evenly matched.

In the White Crane seats, Han Zheng leaned toward the railing. Lu Qingxue sat beside two other disciples, hands resting together over her knees. She recognized the simple sword and the face above it. The cultivation beneath that face still seemed difficult to accept.

The boy dismissed at Qingshi stood at mid Foundation Establishment.

Zhou Ke lowered his hand.

“Begin,” Zhou Ke said.

Xie Wenyuan stepped forward. His blade drew three green lines through the air, each aimed to force a different response. The first threatened Shi Feng's sword wrist, the second his shoulder, and the third the space he would enter if he retreated to the left.

Shi Feng didn't retreat.

He caught the first line on the lower half of his sword and turned his wrist. Turning Wave guided the narrow blade across his body. Xie Wenyuan felt the contact change, tried to recover, and found that his arm was already travelling too far to the right.

A quiet push of qi reached him through the blades.

His stance broke.

Xie Wenyuan stepped back to regain balance. Shi Feng followed one pace, keeping the swords joined, then let the pressure turn outward. It lifted the chief disciple cleanly from the stone and carried him over the white line.

Xie Wenyuan landed on both feet outside the platform.

His sword was still in his hand. His robes weren't torn. The next breath he took was the first one he had found time to take since attacking.

Zhou Ke looked at the boundary, then at Shi Feng.

“Shi Feng wins,” Zhou Ke announced.

The first cheering came late.

“Already?”

“That was White Crane's chief disciple!”

“Wait—Shi Feng of Great Liang? Isn't he the Qingshi boy whose meridians White Crane Pavilion declared ruined when Lu Qingxue broke off their marriage?”

“Ruined? He just threw White Crane's chief disciple over the boundary with one turn of his wrist!”

“Look at Steward Han Zheng's face in the White Crane row!”

Xie Wenyuan looked down at his sword. A small tremor ran through the blade before he steadied it. His right wrist hurt slightly, but nothing had been damaged.

That made the result clearer, rather than easier to bear.

Shi Feng had chosen where he landed.

Xie Wenyuan sheathed his sword and bowed again.

“I lost,” Xie Wenyuan said. “Thank you for controlling the last push.”

“Your opening was clear,” Shi Feng replied. “I found the return before you completed it.”

Xie Wenyuan nodded slowly. He had expected an insult or a smug explanation. The short answer gave him something useful to check later.

Zhou Ke opened the exit passage. Shi Feng put away his sword and stepped down. There was no wound to treat and no need to stand in the middle while people decided what they thought of him.

In the White Crane seats, Han Zheng's hand tightened around the rail.

“Wenyuan was careless,” Han Zheng said.

Lu Qingxue looked at the platform, where the attendants were already checking the next pair's names.

“He wasn't careless,” Lu Qingxue said. “He was moved.”

Han Zheng turned toward her. The other disciples suddenly found the empty platform very interesting.

“Everyone can make a mistake,” Han Zheng said.

Lu Qingxue didn't argue further. A mistake didn't explain why Shi Feng could place another mid Foundation Establishment swordsman beyond the boundary without hurting him.

White Crane had called him finished. Han Zheng had made that judgment sound certain before half a town.

The cheering below reached their seats again.

Certainty had become a difficult thing to hold.

Duan Yichen waited near the drinking water when Shi Feng returned. The sabre user had already won his own match, judging by the attendant's fresh stamp on his plate.

“That was quick,” Duan Yichen said.

“I had a clear boundary,” Shi Feng replied.

Duan Yichen looked at him, then laughed.

“I watched your feet,” Duan Yichen said. “You didn't need the boundary.”

Shi Feng took a cup of water. He didn't explain how much less he had needed it than the other man imagined.

“You're through?” Shi Feng asked.

“My opponent kept trying to knock the sabre aside,” Duan Yichen said. “It weighs more than he thought.”

The man's tone held satisfaction without a demand for admiration. Shi Feng found it easy enough to stay beside him while the next contestants entered.

A porter arrived with a basket of clean cups. Duan Yichen shifted his heavy weapon out of the narrow path before the porter asked. Shi Feng noticed the small movement. Manners showed more clearly there than in a bow made before crowded stands.

Xie Wenyuan appeared at the passage entrance with a White Crane attendant. He paused when he saw Shi Feng, then raised his hand in brief acknowledgment.

Shi Feng returned it.

The chief disciple went to his sect without inventing a grievance over a fair loss.

“He looks less angry than his steward,” Duan Yichen said.

“He's the one who actually fought,” Shi Feng replied.

From the delegates' seats, He Zhen wrote a short line beside Shi Feng's name. Mu Shuyun watched the next contestants approach, while Wei Chengyuan continued speaking to a visiting official.

One clean first-round win hadn't stopped the tournament.

Shi Feng preferred that. He could sit beneath the awning and watch how the remaining candidates moved. He wanted to know the common standard here, how the officials handled close boundaries, and which weapons the better fighters trusted.

Lu Qingxue came down the steps with a folded cloth in her hand. She paused beside the drinking water until Shi Feng looked toward her.

“You left this beside your cup,” Lu Qingxue said.

Shi Feng recognised the plain furnace cloth.

“Mine,” Shi Feng replied, his voice softening with quiet courtesy as he accepted it. “Thank you for bringing it down. The glare off the lower rail is sharp this afternoon—keep to the shaded row if you're watching the next pair.”

“I will,” Lu Qingxue said, pausing a breath longer. “Wenyuan said he landed exactly where you wanted. He's gone to check the first turn again.”

“He fought properly,” Shi Feng said mildly. “He'll find something useful in it.”

Lu Qingxue nodded and went back toward White Crane's seats. Shi Feng put the cloth away, glanced across the steps where Ling Qingzhu stood, gave her only a brief, silent nod, and turned to the next platform.

Ling Qingzhu had seen all of it.

She stood beneath the opposite stair with her white veil in place. He had offered Lu Qingxue an easy, unguarded warmth, yet when his eyes met hers across the passage, he had spared only a cool nod.

She remembered how evenly he now said Fairy Ling. He could speak gently to a former fiancée because no recent mistrust stood between them, while the quiet care Ling Qingzhu remembered from their home in Qingliu Lane was gone. She couldn't stop wondering whether the same calm distance explained his manner toward her.

The thought frightened her more than anger would've.

She lowered her eyes before he turned toward the stands.

The bell rang for another completed match.

Shi Feng rested his hand on his ordinary sword and watched a one-eyed youth retrieve his spear from the broken stone. The youth looked delighted.

That might be worth watching.

chapters.title: The Names Everyone Bet On
chapters.html:
The betting board outside the northern entrance put Yuan Kuang's name in the largest characters.

Great Qin's crown prince wore black armour with a red sash. His peak Foundation Establishment qi spread over his platform as he lowered a broad spear toward his opponent. Behind him, the Martial Palace seats had grown attentive.

The match lasted longer than Shi Feng's, mostly because Yuan Kuang enjoyed making the difference visible.

His first thrust shattered his opponent's guard. His second sent the man sliding backward with both heels scraping stone. The third stopped beside the throat.

The opponent surrendered before the point moved another finger's width.

Yuan Kuang turned toward the stands. The cheers rose exactly when he expected them to.

“Great Qin's finest!”

“Martial Palace has already chosen him!”

“Put another hundred stones on the prince!”

Shi Feng watched Yuan Kuang lower the spear. The man's control was sound, although the turn after his second thrust left an unnecessary opening. An ordinary opponent at the same stage might never reach it.

Gu Zhan would probably enjoy reaching it.

The one-eyed youth entered the next platform with his spear balanced across his shoulder. His robe was clean but patched at one elbow. He looked around the stands as though searching for someone to share a good meal.

An old man seated in the independent sect section was peeling a pear with a small knife.

“Master, this one uses a halberd,” Gu Zhan called.

“I can see,” Nie Wufeng replied.

“It's longer than my spear,” Gu Zhan said.

“Then stand closer,” Nie Wufeng replied.

The halberd user frowned. He was a late Foundation Establishment cultivator from Great Chen, with two successful kingdom tournaments behind him. Being discussed like a piece of inconvenient furniture hadn't improved his mood.

Zhou Ke gave the signal.

The halberd swept sideways with enough qi to make the platform edge hum. Gu Zhan moved directly into the sweep. His spear butt tapped the shaft, his shoulder turned, and the halberd's blade passed behind him.

The spear point stopped against the other man's breastplate.

Gu Zhan pushed.

Metal buckled with a blunt crack. The halberd user flew backward and hit the platform outside the boundary, sliding another yard before he stopped.

Gu Zhan lowered his spear and peered after him.

“Can you get up?” Gu Zhan asked.

The defeated man raised a shaking hand. Zhou Ke went over to check him, then announced the result.

Gu Zhan looked almost disappointed.

Nie Wufeng finished peeling his pear.

By midday, the betting hall's runner was climbing a ladder to add Lone Spear Peak beneath the favourites.

His brush dripped ink over the old odds. The crowd yelled competing suggestions until the manager, Yu Cao, ordered everyone away from the ladder.

“Yesterday you wouldn't give him a price!”

“Yesterday he hadn't put a spear through Great Chen's armour!”

“Lone Spear Peak has two people. Two!”

“Perhaps that's all they need!”

Shi Feng passed the board with Duan Yichen. He had bought a bowl of cold noodles from the stall beside it and was trying to eat before the afternoon matches began.

Duan Yichen studied the fresh odds.

“I should've bet before he fought,” Duan Yichen said.

“You'd have needed someone to take it,” Shi Feng replied.

“True,” Duan Yichen said. “Yu Cao told me to find the sect on a map first.”

Yu Cao heard his name and pretended to inspect a crack in the ladder.

Shi Feng finished the noodles. The betting didn't make Yuan Kuang stronger or Gu Zhan weaker. Still, it explained where the public's attention had been, and how quickly it could move.

His own name had gained a smaller line below the established favourites.

He didn't stop to read his price.

Ling Qingzhu's opponent used paired short blades. She approached carefully, clearly aware that nobody had measured the veiled woman's depth from a glance.

Ling Qingzhu drew her sword and waited.

The first blade came low. She stepped outside it without spreading her qi across the whole platform. Her sword touched the second blade near its guard and turned it across the wielder's body.

The woman recovered faster than Xie Wenyuan had. Ling Qingzhu gave her room to finish the turn, then placed the sword point against her sleeve.

A pale thread of force cut the cloth without touching skin.

The opponent stopped.

For three breaths, both women stood still. Then the paired blades lowered, and the woman surrendered.

The crowd applauded the clean result. Some called Ling Qingzhu strong; others complained that the short exchange told them too little. Neither group gained an answer from the white veil.

Shi Feng watched her put away the sword.

Her restraint was familiar, but familiarity didn't give him a precise measure of everything beneath it. He had reasons to think she held much more than she showed. Those reasons remained guesses.

Ling Qingzhu looked toward the waiting area. He gave a brief nod, acknowledging the victory, and returned his attention to the next match.

Ling Qingzhu rested her hand over the sword hilt for a moment before leaving.

Earlier, he'd spoken gently with Lu Qingxue when she returned a cloth, yet for her own victory he had spared only a silent nod. Ling Qingzhu caught herself comparing the two and felt a sharp sting beneath her ribs.

She wanted her victory to earn something different from him because she was his wife. But the difference she missed had never been something a title could demand.

She lowered her hand and left the passage without asking him for another word.

Sima Yu won late in the afternoon. His royal palm technique drove his opponent to the boundary in six exchanges. The Crown Prince's smile returned when the referee declared the result.

He reached the exit first and found an attendant blocking the passage while an injured candidate was carried through.

“Make room,” Sima Yu said. “I am Great Liang's crown prince.”

The attendant, Zhou Ke, looked at the stretcher and didn't move.

“Then you should understand waiting for the wounded,” Zhou Ke replied.

Two candidates nearby laughed. Sima Yu's smile froze.

He could force a servant to kneel in the capital. Here, a single arena official could make him stand beside a wall while strangers carried a bleeding man past his gold-trimmed sleeve.

Shi Feng saw the exchange from the water table. He didn't add a word. Sima Yu had heard the laughter well enough.

Once the passage cleared, the prince left with measured steps. His servants hurried after him outside the candidates' gate.

Duan Yichen lifted his cup toward Shi Feng.

“Your kingdom seems lively,” Duan Yichen said.

“It gets tiring,” Shi Feng replied.

Across the arena, Nie Wufeng had fallen asleep with the pear core balanced on his knee. Gu Zhan stood behind him, quietly practising the same close step he had used against the halberd.

Shi Feng watched that step twice.

Of everything he'd seen that day, it was the thing most worth remembering.

chapters.title: The Princess Who Left
chapters.html:
The last group of first-round candidates entered while the stands were beginning to empty for dinner.

Shi Feng stayed because the next platform faced the shaded steps where he sat. He had no urgent reason to return to the inn, and the woman in pale blue robes carried an unusual short sword.

A crescent-shaped guard covered the backs of her fingers. The sword wasn't flashy, but the grip suited close turns.

“Moon Lake Sect, Sima Lan,” Zhou Ke announced.

Sima Yu stopped walking.

Shi Feng noticed because the prince's servants nearly collided with him. The gold sleeve lifted, then lowered without giving the command waiting behind it.

On the platform, Sima Lan bowed to her opponent. She was beautiful in a cool, composed way, with dark eyes and a small mark beside her left brow. Her late Foundation Establishment qi remained close to her body.

Shi Feng had heard the name before. Great Liang's younger princess, the court's second beauty, and a topic people lowered their voices to discuss.

Nobody had mentioned Moon Lake robes.

Her opponent attacked with a long staff. Sima Lan gave up the centre, letting its reach carry him forward. She moved twice around his left side, measuring how quickly he could shorten his grip.

On the third turn, her sword guard caught the staff just above his hand.

She pulled down and stepped behind his heel. The staff hit the stone, and the opponent's knee followed it. Her sword rested beside his neck before he could rise.

The surrender was immediate.

Sima Lan withdrew her blade and offered the man room to stand. She neither helped him up nor turned toward the crowd for applause.

Sima Yu's face had gone pale.

Shi Feng left through the eastern passage after the result was recorded. The corridor split around a storage court, and he stopped beside the open water jar to rinse the dust from his hands.

Sima Yu's voice came from the covered walkway beyond it.

“You should have sent word,” Sima Yu said.

“Moon Lake submitted its list on time,” Sima Lan replied. “The officials found no difficulty reading it.”

Shi Feng could see them through the square opening above the jar. He didn't step closer. Sima Yu had dismissed his servants to the far gate, but he had chosen a public corridor for a family conversation.

“You know which word I mean,” Sima Yu said.

Sima Lan adjusted the cord at her wrist. A small Moon Lake seal hung there, worn enough to show it had travelled with her for some time.

“The court used to read my letters before I did,” Sima Lan said. “I thought it would manage.”

“Those arrangements concerned more than you,” Sima Yu replied.

“They always do,” Sima Lan said. “Someone signs a household paper, and the rest of us are meant to call it our wish.”

Sima Yu glanced toward the gate. One servant immediately looked away.

“Father will want an explanation,” Sima Yu said.

“Then he can ask for one,” Sima Lan replied.

Her voice wasn't loud. That made the prince's effort to lower his own more noticeable.

“You left without permission,” Sima Yu said.

“I left,” Sima Lan replied. “The other part is something we disagree about.”

Shi Feng dried his hands and picked up his bag. He knew enough now to understand that the reunion wasn't going to improve either person's afternoon.

Before he reached the turn, Sima Lan looked through the opening and met his eyes.

She had known he was there.

“Brother's fellow representative,” Sima Lan said. “Shi Feng, isn't it?”

“Yes,” Shi Feng replied.

Sima Yu turned sharply. For a moment, the polite expression he used in public didn't return.

“An unfortunate place for a private conversation,” Shi Feng said.

Sima Lan looked at the open walkway, then back at her brother.

“So it seems,” Sima Lan replied.

Sima Yu straightened his sleeves.

“My sister has been away from home,” Sima Yu said. “There are matters to settle.”

“Then settle them,” Shi Feng replied.

He continued toward the exit. He wasn't interested in becoming a tool in a royal family's argument simply because the prince disliked being watched.

Sima Lan walked with him for several steps before Sima Yu could speak again.

“Did you enjoy the first round?” Sima Lan asked.

“It was brief,” Shi Feng said.

“I heard,” Sima Lan replied. “White Crane's seats were quieter afterward.”

She said nothing about the old cripple or the marriage. That restraint seemed deliberate. Shi Feng couldn't decide whether it was good manners or careful study, and didn't need to decide immediately.

At the gate, Sima Lan stopped beneath the Moon Lake banner.

“Perhaps we'll meet on a platform,” Sima Lan said.

“Perhaps,” Shi Feng replied.

She gave him a small nod and returned toward the independent sect court. Sima Yu followed until a Moon Lake elder came to meet her, then stopped.

The elder spoke quietly to Sima Lan and guided her inside. Nobody invited the Crown Prince to join them.

Shi Feng walked into the street.

Behind him, a servant hurried to bring Sima Yu's carriage nearer the gate. The prince entered it without looking toward the Moon Lake banner again.

Duan Yichen found Shi Feng at a stall selling skewered fish. He ordered three and ate the first before the seller had finished wrapping the others.

“You know Sima Lan?” Duan Yichen asked.

“I know who she is,” Shi Feng said.

“Half the people under the awning are pretending they always knew she'd enter,” Duan Yichen said. “The other half want to know which court official failed to stop her.”

“Moon Lake had a legitimate place,” Shi Feng replied.

“That's less entertaining,” Duan Yichen said.

Shi Feng accepted the skewer the seller handed him. The fish was hot, salted heavily and cooked through. For a few moments, that was all the attention it needed.

Duan Yichen finished the second skewer and looked down the street.

“My family would've followed me if I'd vanished like that,” Duan Yichen said. “Mostly to ask who was going to carry the winter grain accounts.”

“Can you count grain?” Shi Feng asked.

“Better than my cousins,” Duan Yichen replied. “That's the problem.”

Shi Feng laughed. He liked hearing a complaint that didn't conceal a threat.

The evening bells began. Officials would post the next draw tomorrow after checking injuries and completing the first-round records. Until then, every surviving candidate had a night to decide how impressive the others had looked.

Shi Feng returned to the inn with no interest in adding to the stories about Sima Lan.

She had won her place fairly. Her brother's expression suggested that the rest of her story belonged to a less orderly contest.

chapters.title: White Crane's Steward
chapters.html:
Han Zheng chose the medicine street for his complaint because there were enough people to hear him.

Shi Feng had just left a shop with cooling sand for his practice furnace. He saw the White Crane steward beside a tea stall and would have continued walking if Han Zheng hadn't stepped into the middle of the lane.

“The boy who wouldn't kneel,” Han Zheng said. “You remember how to bow now, after all.”

Several shoppers stopped. Two White Crane disciples stood behind Han Zheng, looking as though they wished they had chosen another errand.

Shi Feng put the sand packet in his everyday bag.

“I bowed to Xie Wenyuan,” Shi Feng said. “He was courteous.”

Han Zheng's mouth tightened.

“Wenyuan underestimated you,” Han Zheng said.

“He accepted the result,” Shi Feng replied. “You should ask him how.”

Someone beside the tea stall laughed into a cup. Han Zheng turned toward the sound, and the man became very interested in the tea leaves.

Shi Feng didn't draw his sword or release pressure. A steward's wounded pride wasn't a reason to damage a busy street.

Han Zheng clearly wanted anger. He was less comfortable with a man who had errands to finish.

“White Crane is attached to Martial Palace,” Han Zheng said. “A first-round victory doesn't put you above a Great Sect's judgment.”

“Then let Martial Palace judge what it sees,” Shi Feng replied.

The answer reached the nearby shoppers. White Crane's connection sounded less impressive when the steward had to announce it after losing.

Shi Feng stepped around him.

Han Zheng didn't reach out.

Lu Qingxue waited outside the White Crane lodging until Han Zheng returned. She had sent the younger disciples to the arena notice board, leaving no audience for what she wanted to ask.

The steward saw her expression and slowed.

“You shouldn't linger in these streets alone,” Han Zheng said.

“I want to see the old treatment correspondence,” Lu Qingxue replied.

Han Zheng's hand stopped on the door latch.

“That matter is closed,” Han Zheng said.

“The internal report described dormant meridians,” Lu Qingxue said. “The public account said destroyed. Who approved the change?”

A cart rattled past behind her. Neither spoke until its wheels had faded.

Han Zheng looked toward the empty stairwell.

“Your elders wanted the engagement ended cleanly,” Han Zheng said.

“That's not what I asked,” Lu Qingxue replied.

The steward frowned. He had given the same sort of answer for years and seldom needed a second one.

Lu Qingxue kept looking at him.

“I signed the public copy,” Han Zheng said at last. “A dormant network with no remedy was of no practical use to anyone. You had a future in the sect.”

“And he had a future in the town,” Lu Qingxue said.

Han Zheng's patience broke.

“He stood on a platform today because he found something elsewhere,” Han Zheng said. “Would a different word have healed him then? Did I hide a medicine that could restore him?”

“No,” Lu Qingxue replied. “You hid the difference between not knowing how and knowing it was impossible.”

Han Zheng opened the door.

“Don't make an enemy of your own sect over an old marriage arrangement,” Han Zheng said.

Lu Qingxue didn't follow him inside.

She found Shi Feng near the public furnace suppliers. He had stopped to inspect a stand for a small cauldron, measuring its height against his own hand.

Lu Qingxue waited until the seller moved away.

“Han Zheng signed the destroyed-meridians account,” Lu Qingxue said.

Shi Feng looked up. He set the stand back where he'd found it.

“Did he admit that to you?” Shi Feng asked.

“Yes,” Lu Qingxue replied. “He said there was no remedy, so the distinction didn't matter.”

Shi Feng remembered the courtyard in Qingshi. His aunt had stood between him and people who felt entitled to decide what remained of his life. The report might not have cured him. That didn't make its concealment harmless.

Lu Qingxue held a newly sealed note alongside the original clinic record she had sent him in Qingshi.

“I wrote what he said while I still remembered it exactly,” Lu Qingxue said. “I put my seal on it.”

Shi Feng accepted the signed note and read the short account, then gently pressed the older clinic copy back into her hand.

“Keep the record. You were the only one who sent it,” Shi Feng said quietly. “It doesn't matter now. It mattered then.”

Lu Qingxue lowered her eyes, her fingers closing around the paper.

“I know,” Lu Qingxue said.

He folded the new note into his bag, his manner easy and unguarded.

Lu Qingxue watched his hand leave the bag.

“You don't have to be kind to make me feel better,” Lu Qingxue said.

“I'm not saying it to make you feel better,” Shi Feng replied gently. “You sent the truth when nobody else in that hall did.”

She nodded, a faint warmth touching her eyes. When Shi Feng turned back toward the counter and saw Ling Qingzhu beneath the awning at the end of the row, his expression cooled at once; he gave her only a brief nod before facing the seller again.

Ling Qingzhu saw them from the other end of the suppliers' row. She had come for a practice medicine and stopped beneath the awning when she recognised Lu Qingxue.

She had heard the quiet warmth in his voice when he told Lu Qingxue to keep the record, and she had felt the immediate distance when his eyes met hers and offered only a nod.

A sharp, unmistakable jealousy stung her chest.

He had kept a small, genuine kindness for the girl who had sent him one honest report in Qingshi, while for his wife he left only polite stone. Ling Qingzhu turned back to the medicine counter with her throat tight.

The furnace seller returned with the price of the stand. Shi Feng paid, and Lu Qingxue moved aside so the man could wrap it.

There was no reason to stretch their conversation into a walk through the city.

“I'll return to the lodging,” Lu Qingxue said.

Shi Feng nodded. She left without asking whether he blamed her, forgave her, or remembered how they had once spoken. He appreciated that more than he could have appreciated another apology made to win an answer.

At the corner, two White Crane disciples were reading the betting board. One saw Lu Qingxue and hurried to tell her Xie Wenyuan had been invited to observe a Martial Palace training session.

Life in the sect would continue. Her chief disciple's defeat would become a lesson, then a story, then something younger disciples exaggerated after dinner.

The judgment made in Qingshi had stayed with Shi Feng much longer.

He lifted the wrapped stand and headed back to the inn.

On the way, he passed Han Zheng again. The steward stood beneath a Martial Palace notice, speaking to a clerk in respectful tones entirely unlike those he had used in the lane.

Shi Feng didn't stop.

He had the report and the acknowledgment. He also had a furnace that needed a level base before tomorrow's practice.

Of those things, the furnace was the one still capable of improving his evening.

Upstairs, he set the stand beneath the cauldron and locked Han Zheng's signed admission beside the Pavilion physicians' copy inside his ring—a complete docket ready for the day he returned to Qingshi Town.

chapters.title: A Pill on the Doorstep
chapters.html:
The bottle stood beside his room door when Shi Feng returned from breakfast.

It was wrapped in a clean square of cloth, with a narrow paper strip under the stopper. He recognized the handwriting before he read the words.

For recovery between matches. No need to answer.

Ling Qingzhu's name appeared at the bottom.

Shi Feng stood in the corridor with one hand on his key. The window at the far end was open, letting in the smell of steamed grain from the kitchen. Someone downstairs argued over whether the tournament gate would admit a child without charging full price.

Ordinary morning sounds. They made the little bottle harder to look at.

Kang Liu came up the stairs carrying a folded quilt. He saw what Shi Feng held and slowed.

“Your wife came early,” Kang Liu said. “She didn't ask me to wake you.”

“Fairy Ling left this?” Shi Feng asked.

The innkeeper heard the change in address and shifted the quilt against his chest.

“Yes,” Kang Liu replied. “I told her you were eating in the back court. She said the bottle could wait here.”

Shi Feng nodded and unlocked his room.

Kang Liu hesitated by the stairs. He had the expression of a man with a helpful observation pressing against his teeth.

“The broth was good this morning,” Shi Feng said.

“It was,” Kang Liu replied after a pause. “I'll tell the cook.”

He carried the quilt away.

Shi Feng set the bottle on the table and checked the stopper. The seal was unbroken. Inside lay three pale pills suitable for recovering Foundation Establishment qi after a demanding fight.

Good medicine, properly stored.

He didn't invent a fault with them because they came from her.

His first match hadn't left anything to recover. He had used less qi than a short furnace practice and taken no injury. Even if he needed medicine later, he had his own supply.

He held the paper strip between two fingers.

No need to answer.

Shi Feng folded the note around the unopened bottle, placed it in the back corner of his ring untouched, and took out his own refined pills to cultivate.

The pills carried warmth into his foundation. He guided it through the restored meridians at an even pace, keeping the devouring flow quiet. Nothing about the medicine hurt him. The remembered fears about failed pills belonged to another person's misunderstanding, not his body's reality.

That had been true in Great Liang too.

He opened his eyes when the gain settled and reached for his practice notes.

At the southern lodging, Hongxiu found Ling Qingzhu sitting beside an unopened breakfast tray.

The white veil remained over her face. Her travelling cloak lay folded across the other chair, and the repaired silver clasp still held her black hair.

“Did you see him?” Hongxiu asked.

“No,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

Hongxiu moved the porridge bowl nearer her hand.

“You went all that way,” Hongxiu said.

“I took medicine,” Ling Qingzhu replied. “I didn't take a reason he had to open his door.”

Hongxiu didn't immediately answer. She had expected anger, perhaps tears, perhaps another question about what Shi Feng was thinking. Ling Qingzhu's quiet made those prepared comforts useless.

Ling Qingzhu lifted the bowl.

The porridge had cooled. She ate it anyway.

“I used to think he would tell me if something truly mattered,” Ling Qingzhu said.

Hongxiu sat on the edge of the other chair.

“He did tell you some things,” Hongxiu replied.

“I know,” Ling Qingzhu said.

There was no argument left to hide behind. He had told her about the promised money. He had told her when work ran late. He had made room for her bed and kept eating smaller meals without turning each one into an accusation.

She understood the separate moments now. Together, they were harder to bear.

Outside, Ling Rong spoke to the carriage driver. The clan wanted a short report about the first round and the next draw. Ling Qingzhu set the bowl down and reached for paper.

Her family still had business to conduct. Missing Shi Feng didn't remove it.

Shi Feng spent the middle of the day at the arena's open practice court. Candidates were allowed to use the ordinary stone lanes until sunset, provided they kept their techniques inside the marked spaces.

At the practice gate, an attendant checked the sword's wrapping before allowing the sword into the marked lane. A loose grip had sent another candidate's blade over the wall that morning. Shi Feng tightened the final knot, tested a short, controlled cut and presented it again. The attendant nodded. He entered without needing anyone to fetch his weapon from a neighbouring roof.

Duan Yichen was practising short sabre cuts. He stopped after the seventh and shook out his wrist.

“Too much watching yesterday,” Duan Yichen said. “My hand kept trying somebody else's angle.”

“Was it better?” Shi Feng asked.

“No,” Duan Yichen replied. “That's why I'm annoyed.”

Shi Feng drew his sword. Returning Tide brought the edge back along his forearm before turning it outward. The weapon's balance was familiar, though the grip had worn smooth beneath his thumb.

He would need to replace the wrapping soon.

Duan Yichen watched one sequence, then returned to his own cuts. Neither interrupted the other to explain what a useful friendship they might become.

After practice, they sat on the wall to drink water. A young candidate hurried through the court with a fresh notice from the officials.

The second draw would be posted before evening.

Duan Yichen stood immediately. Shi Feng finished his water first.

He had no preference strong enough to make the names change by reaching the board sooner.

At the inn, the little recovery bottle remained untouched inside his ring. The paper wrapped around it had gained a crease where his thumb had held it too long.

He remembered that crease while tightening the new cloth around his sword hilt.

Then he tested the grip and went to see the draw.

chapters.title: The Draw of Fifty-Four
chapters.html:
The second draw went up under a yellow awning because the afternoon rain had begun.

Fifty-four names remained. Each had a fresh seal beside it, confirming that the first-round result had been entered and the candidate could still fight. The attendants carried the discarded first-round sheets away in a covered basket.

Shi Feng waited beside a stone pillar while Zhou Ke fastened the last corner. Rain rattled against the canvas above him. Duan Yichen arrived with his sabre wrapped in oiled cloth and water dripping off his nose.

“I chose the wrong gate,” Duan Yichen said.

“You found the board,” Shi Feng replied.

“After finding every puddle in Qingyun,” Duan Yichen said.

He shook the water from his sleeve and began reading. The crowd pushed closer before the attendant had stepped off his stool.

Shi Feng found Great Liang's crest in the third column.

Shi Feng against Sima Yu.

For a moment, the rest of the board stopped mattering.

He read the name once more, making sure there was no similar character mistaken in the rain-darkened light. There wasn't.

Duan Yichen saw where he looked.

“Your crown prince,” Duan Yichen said.

“Yes,” Shi Feng replied.

“Is that troublesome?” Duan Yichen asked.

“The platform will be simple,” Shi Feng said.

He meant it. The trouble came from everything that had happened before they reached it.

The first shout came from the back of the crowd.

“Great Liang eats itself!”

“First place against third!”

“That leaves the veiled fairy to carry their banner!”

“Or the man who threw White Crane's disciple out in one turn!”

A kingdom officer tried to quiet the jokes. Nobody listened. Other kingdoms had drawn their own countrymen before; the crowd enjoyed the same unpleasant surprise every time.

Sima Yu reached the awning from the covered passage. His attendants cleared no path for him inside the candidate area. He had to wait while a man carrying an umbrella argued about a Great Zhou pairing.

Then he saw the third column.

His expression didn't change immediately. Shi Feng watched the effort required to keep it that way.

The Crown Prince turned toward him.

“Brother Shi,” Sima Yu said. “An unfortunate draw for our kingdom.”

“Only one of us needs to lose,” Shi Feng replied.

The words were calm enough that several nearby candidates smiled. Sima Yu returned a smile of his own, too measured to be natural.

“Of course,” Sima Yu said. “We should speak before the match.”

“You can find me at the inn,” Shi Feng replied.

He didn't mind hearing what the prince thought could still be said. Listening wouldn't make the previous killing orders disappear.

Sima Yu nodded and moved away from the board. He stopped beneath the covered passage where the rain couldn't reach his robe.

Shi Feng saw his fingers press once against the ornament at his belt.

Ling Qingzhu read the draw after the main crowd thinned. Her white veil moved slightly with her breathing as she found Shi Feng's name.

She knew Sima Yu's anger. She also knew the prince had resources he didn't display in ordinary exchanges. The thought of a hidden weapon made her look toward the officials' seats rather than toward Shi Feng.

Lu Yong's earlier rules had been clear. Officials would halt violations, and the platform barriers weren't decorations.
