That didn't make her entirely easy.

Shi Feng passed beside the awning on his way to the exit. Ling Qingzhu took one step toward him.

“Sima Yu won't fight cleanly if he's pressed,” Ling Qingzhu said.

Shi Feng paused for a single breath without turning fully toward her.

“I know how he fights, Fairy Ling,” Shi Feng said evenly, and walked out through the gate before the next shower began.

Ling Qingzhu watched only until he reached the street. Then she turned back toward the board to read the time of her own match.

Sima Lan stood beneath the far end of the awning. She had arrived quietly enough that Shi Feng hadn't noticed her in the first crush of candidates.

The younger princess looked at her brother's pairing and smiled slightly.

Not a happy smile. More like the expression of someone who had finally seen a door open where she expected a wall.

A Moon Lake disciple beside her pointed to their own names. Sima Lan listened, nodded and said nothing about Great Liang.

Sima Yu saw the smile from the passage.

His jaw tightened.

At the inn, Kang Liu had moved the outdoor tables beneath the eaves. A travelling family huddled around one of them, counting the dry spaces left in their luggage.

Shi Feng helped the youngest child retrieve a shoe that had rolled under a bench. The boy took it without noticing the tournament plate on his bag.

That was pleasant.

Upstairs, Shi Feng laid his sword across the table and checked the new grip. The cloth sat firmly. The blade carried several small marks from the road, but nothing that would affect tomorrow's use.

Sima Yu was late Foundation Establishment. A better royal artifact might make his techniques sharper or conceal an attack from an awkward angle. It wouldn't close the distance between them.

Shi Feng didn't need to imagine a desperate battle to take him seriously as an enemy.

He remembered Guo Zhen's attempt to kill him. Cao Wenshu's attack. The later men sent to finish what earlier servants had failed to do.

Those were decisions, not misunderstandings.

A knock sounded below. Kang Liu spoke to someone at the entrance, then sent a runner up the stairs with a message.

The Crown Prince wished to visit after dinner.

Shi Feng set the sword down.

“Tell him he can come,” Shi Feng said.

The runner hurried away. Shi Feng closed his practice journal and put the medicine aside.

Tomorrow's draw had given him an opponent.

Tonight would tell him how much fear the prince could hide beneath the words Brother Shi.

He copied the match time from his plate onto the inn's message board. Kang Liu would know when to expect the room empty and when to keep callers downstairs. Then Shi Feng put the sword within reach and lay down. The draw had given him the opponent he wanted. Staying awake to stare at the name wouldn't bring morning any sooner.

chapters.title: Brother Shi
chapters.html:
Sima Yu arrived without a royal carriage.

He wore a plain pale robe, although the material cost more than most of Kang Liu's furniture. One servant remained at the gate. The Crown Prince came upstairs carrying a narrow wooden box.

Shi Feng left the door open and moved the second chair away from the table. There was enough room to sit without either man's sleeve touching the other's.

Sima Yu looked at the modest furnace, the notes beside it and the sword within reach.

“You're still working tonight,” Sima Yu said.

“The furnace hasn't entered the tournament,” Shi Feng replied.

Sima Yu gave a brief laugh. It didn't survive long enough to warm the room.

He placed the box on the table. Shi Feng didn't reach for it.

“Brother Shi,” Sima Yu said. “There have been many unpleasant things between us.”

Shi Feng waited.

The prince looked toward the open doorway, where the corridor was empty.

“This gathering matters to Great Liang,” Sima Yu said. “Two representatives fighting each other in the second round is a waste. I have arrangements with people who can help our kingdom once I enter a Great Sect.”

“Say your conditions,” Shi Feng said.

Sima Yu lifted the lid. Inside lay a jade document seal and a small purse.

“I can clear the Ling family's outstanding court obligations,” Sima Yu said. “Their supply duties, the disputed land levy, the delayed appointment your wife's father wants settled. All of it can be made simple.”

Shi Feng looked at the seal. The prince's personal authority had been reduced after his misuse of royal service, but enough connections remained to inconvenience a clan that depended on court approval.

Sima Yu hadn't come offering something entirely imaginary.

“What would I do?” Shi Feng asked.

“Concede tomorrow,” Sima Yu replied. “A strained meridian, a problem after refining medicine, anything dignified. You don't even need to appear on the platform.”

“And the purse?” Shi Feng asked.

“A token of goodwill,” Sima Yu said. “You won't leave without compensation.”

Shi Feng closed the box.

“No,” Shi Feng said.

Sima Yu sat very still.

“You haven't asked how much,” Sima Yu said.

“It doesn't change the condition,” Shi Feng replied.

The prince's fingers moved against his knee. He had clearly prepared several stages to the offer and disliked losing the first before completing it.

“The Ling clan will remember who made life easier for them,” Sima Yu said.

“Then make it easier,” Shi Feng replied. “You don't need my defeat to do that.”

Sima Yu leaned back. The friendliness left his face in small, careful steps.

“You know your wife has been under pressure,” Sima Yu said. “You could remove some of it.”

Shi Feng felt the old hurt stir, but it didn't pull his judgment aside.

He and Ling Qingzhu were separated. They were still married. Neither fact entitled Sima Yu to use her family's difficulties as a handle on his throat.

“If you have an official debt to collect, collect it lawfully,” Shi Feng said. “If you invented it to reach me, keep your box.”

Sima Yu's gaze sharpened.

“People with no place at court sometimes misunderstand how obligations work,” Sima Yu said.

“I understood Guo Zhen,” Shi Feng replied.

The room became quiet.

Outside, Kang Liu called down to the cook that a guest wanted more hot water. The ordinary voice carried clearly through the open door.

Sima Yu didn't look toward it this time.

“Guo Zhen acted badly,” Sima Yu said.

“He tried to kill me,” Shi Feng replied.

“Servants can exceed their orders,” Sima Yu said.

“And Cao Wenshu?” Shi Feng asked.

The prince's answer took a little longer.

“The court already addressed that matter,” Sima Yu said.

“The court addressed your use of an office,” Shi Feng replied. “I'm speaking about the man who came for my life.”

Sima Yu reached for the box. The jade seal clicked against the wood as he closed it properly.

He hadn't brought an apology. Even now, he seemed offended that Shi Feng could distinguish between lost court privileges and a dead assassin.

“You may regret making everything personal,” Sima Yu said.

Shi Feng stood. The movement was unhurried, but Sima Yu's hand stopped beside his belt.

“You sent it to my door,” Shi Feng replied.

For a moment, the prince looked at the sword. Shi Feng didn't touch it. An attack in the inn would endanger ordinary guests and give officials a reason to intervene before the lawful match.

Tomorrow was close enough.

Sima Yu rose with the box under his arm.

“Then we meet on the platform,” Sima Yu said.

“Yes,” Shi Feng replied.

The Crown Prince walked out. His steps remained measured until the turn in the stairs, where they grew faster.

Shi Feng closed the door after the gate below had opened and shut. He moved the second chair back against the wall.

The room looked exactly as it had before the visit.

He found that steadiness useful. No threat, promise or royal seal had changed what he intended to do.

Kang Liu came up later with the requested hot water. He set the kettle on the table and glanced at the empty chair.

“The important guest left early,” Kang Liu said.

“He finished speaking,” Shi Feng replied.

Kang Liu seemed satisfied with that. The prince had paid for no room and broken no furniture, which was about all an innkeeper could ask of an unexpected royal visit.

“Will you eat before the morning matches?” Kang Liu asked.

“Yes,” Shi Feng said. “The same breakfast.”

“More meat?” Kang Liu asked.

“More meat,” Shi Feng replied.

The innkeeper left to write it down.

Shi Feng poured the hot water and washed the cooling sand from his fingers. Sima Yu had looked at the furnace and seen another possible excuse for surrender.

Shi Feng looked at it and saw work he would continue after the prince was gone.

He put the kettle aside, sat down and steadied his qi before sleep. The night didn't require a speech to himself about courage.

He had already said no.

chapters.title: A Visitor from Moon Lake
chapters.html:
Sima Lan arrived while Shi Feng was cleaning his furnace.

Kang Liu announced the Moon Lake candidate from the stairs with obvious relief. He had begun treating the upper corridor as though every visitor might carry a national dispute in a wooden box.

Shi Feng set the brush down and opened the door.

Sima Lan stood with her hands folded beneath her sleeves. No attendant waited behind her. The crescent guard of her short sword showed beneath the edge of her blue robe.

“You receive a great many royal visits,” Sima Lan said.

“More than I asked for,” Shi Feng replied.

“May I add one?” Sima Lan asked.

He stepped aside. She took the chair without inspecting the room as though its cheap furniture offered a useful judgment of him.

Shi Feng returned to the table. He left the furnace lid off so the remaining damp could dry.

“Your brother was here,” Shi Feng said.

“I expected that,” Sima Lan replied.

“Did you come to improve his offer?” Shi Feng asked.

“No,” Sima Lan said. “I came because he won't fight honestly if he begins losing.”

Sima Lan placed a finger against her own left wrist.

“The jade ornament under his sleeve contains a refined artifact,” Sima Lan said. “Three narrow darts. He can guide the first openly and send the other two from lower angles.”

Shi Feng noted the placement.

“Poison?” Shi Feng asked.

“Not in the practice version I saw,” Sima Lan replied. “The darts return through the same wrist channel. Breaking the return will make them difficult to recall.”

“Is it forbidden?” Shi Feng asked.

“No,” Sima Lan said. “The officials allow declared personal artifacts. He declares the ornament, then lets people think it's defensive.”

A hidden use wasn't the same as an illegal weapon. Shi Feng stored the distinction. He wouldn't rely on an official to stop something the rules permitted.

Sima Lan rested her hand in her lap.

“There's also a burst pill,” Sima Lan said. “The royal house keeps a small number for emergencies. The qi change is violent. Someone at late Foundation Establishment can briefly show something like early Golden Core force.”

“Briefly,” Shi Feng repeated.

“And badly,” Sima Lan said. “It isn't a Golden Core. It drives what he already has until the channels can't keep up.”

Shi Feng looked at her. She spoke with the ease of someone who had listened carefully when adults thought she was merely standing nearby.

“Those pills are forbidden here,” Shi Feng said.

“Yes,” Sima Lan replied. “He heard the announcement too.”

The furnace gave a soft click as its metal cooled. Sima Lan glanced at it, then at the ink on Shi Feng's thumb.

“You were working after he left,” Sima Lan said.

“Yes,” Shi Feng replied.

“He would've found that insulting,” Sima Lan said.

“I didn't invite him to stay and supervise,” Shi Feng replied.

She smiled faintly. It was the first expression that looked her age rather than like a carefully chosen court response.

Then it disappeared.

“You don't seem surprised by the pill,” Sima Lan said.

“People who send assassins don't become fair because a crowd watches,” Shi Feng replied.

The princess's gaze held his for a moment.

“No,” Sima Lan said. “They usually become more careful about witnesses.”

Shi Feng sat back. There were several questions he could ask about her departure from Great Liang, her standing in Moon Lake, and why she wanted her brother exposed. Asking them wouldn't guarantee truthful answers.

He chose the useful one.

“Why tell me?” Shi Feng asked.

“I'm not helping you,” Sima Lan said. “I'm watching what you do with it.”

“That sounds inconvenient for your brother,” Shi Feng replied.

“He has survived inconvenience before,” Sima Lan said.

She didn't claim to be kind or ask him to trust her. Shi Feng appreciated the absence of a performance while remaining aware that information could still serve a purpose she hadn't named.

“Anything else?” Shi Feng asked.

“He touches his belt before using the darts,” Sima Lan replied. “Not because he has to. Because he likes feeling ready.”

Sima Lan stood and adjusted her sword strap.

“Don't mistake a habit for certainty,” Sima Lan said. “He knows people watch his hands.”

“I won't,” Shi Feng replied.

She reached the door, then paused.

“Did he offer the Ling family's obligations?” Sima Lan asked.

“Yes,” Shi Feng said.

“My brother never wanted her. The court wanted her for him,” Sima Lan said.

Shi Feng looked at her.

“The Ling match?” Shi Feng asked.

“The consort's household and the court elders,” Sima Lan replied. “He was content to let them arrange a useful favour. Until you answered his guests at the banquet and affirmed the marriage in front of them.”

“And his answer was murder,” Shi Feng said.

“His pride doesn't improve when it's embarrassed,” Sima Lan replied. “Don't mistake that for affection.”

Shi Feng had no intention of doing so. A different motive didn't make the men sent to kill him less dead or the orders less deliberate.

“That was a large box for such small promises,” Sima Lan added.

She went down the stairs without explaining further.

Shi Feng didn't follow. He remained at the open doorway until her steps faded, then returned to the furnace.

The artifact was useful information. The burst pill explained the prince's likely answer to public defeat. Neither changed the difference in their actual strength.

A false early Golden Core burst sat comfortably within what Shi Feng could dominate. It might astonish the crowd. It wouldn't force him to reveal his full reserves.

The officials' barrier mattered more.

He recalled where the pale light had risen, how it joined the platform stones, and Lu Yong's warning about striking through a halt. If Sima Yu broke the rules, the officials would take control of the platform.

Shi Feng couldn't pretend he hadn't heard that part.

Below, Sima Lan stopped in the courtyard to let a maid carry a water bucket past. Kang Liu waited beside the gate, politely resisting the urge to ask which important person would visit next.

“The inn is comfortable?” Sima Lan asked.

“For those who like quiet,” Kang Liu replied.

Sima Lan looked up at the second-floor window.

“Then perhaps stop announcing every visitor quite so loudly,” Sima Lan said.

The innkeeper looked embarrassed. She left before he could make a promise he'd probably forget at the next royal arrival.

Upstairs, Shi Feng replaced the furnace lid and put the notes away. There would be no more medicine practice tonight.

He drew the sword once, tested the edge against the light, and sheathed it. The grip sat firmly beneath his hand.

Tomorrow, he would watch Sima Yu's left wrist.

He would also watch the people who could keep the prince alive.

chapters.title: The Crown Prince's Hidden Hand
chapters.html:
Sima Yu wore the royal colours again.

Gold thread crossed his shoulders, and a jade belt held the pale robe close enough for fighting. His left sleeve covered the wrist ornament Sima Lan had described.

Shi Feng stepped onto the central platform in the same dark robe he had worn yesterday. He carried one inexpensive refined artifact sword. The contrast pleased the stands before either man spoke.

“Great Liang's own crown prince!”

“Will the third-place man bow?”

“He didn't bow to White Crane's steward!”

Zhou Ke checked their plates and withdrew beyond the fighting lines. Above the platform, Lu Yong sat beneath the official canopy with a clear view of both men.

Sima Yu looked at Shi Feng's sword.

“You could still avoid an ugly result,” Sima Yu said.

“Begin when the referee tells you,” Shi Feng replied.

The Crown Prince's jaw shifted. Zhou Ke raised his hand, made sure both contestants were ready, and lowered it.

Sima Yu moved first.

His palm gathered a broad gold glow. Royal Mountain Palm, a technique built to overwhelm another Foundation Establishment cultivator's guard through concentrated qi.

Shi Feng knew the kind of attack. The name didn't make it mysterious.

He turned half a step and let the palm pass beside his chest. Its force struck the stone behind him, leaving a shallow impression in the surface. The stands roared at the noise.

Sima Yu followed with a second palm, lower this time, and brought his knee toward Shi Feng's waist.

Shi Feng placed two fingers against the prince's forearm and redirected it. The knee went wide when Sima Yu's balance turned with his shoulder.

He could have ended the exchange there.

Instead, he let the prince recover.

Shi Feng wanted the hidden hand used where everyone could see it. Sima Yu had spent enough months letting other men carry his threats into dark places.

The prince mistook the room he'd been given for hesitation.

“You've learned some tricks,” Sima Yu said.

Shi Feng drew his sword.

Sima Yu's next palm met the flat. The contact rang across the platform. Shi Feng guided the force downward, and the prince's boots scraped two lines through the dust.

The gold qi broke apart before reaching Shi Feng's sleeve.

Sima Yu stopped smiling.

From the Great Liang section, Ling Rong leaned forward with both hands on his knees. He had watched the qualification matches, but a royal technique made the officials around him sit differently.

On the platform, it made no useful difference at all.

Ling Qingzhu remained still beside him. The white veil hid her mouth. Her eyes followed Shi Feng's feet rather than the bright palms, seeing the deliberate space he left between each exchange.

Duan Yichen watched from the candidates' awning.

“He's letting him show everything,” Duan Yichen muttered.

Sima Lan stood several paces away. She heard and gave no reply.

Sima Yu raised both hands. Two palm shadows formed above his shoulders, then closed toward Shi Feng from opposite sides.

Shi Feng stepped through the narrow centre before the shadows joined. His sword tapped the prince's right wrist.

A sharp pain made Sima Yu pull back.

Another step carried Shi Feng past the outer elbow. He stopped with the sword angled toward the prince's shoulder and waited.

The Crown Prince turned too quickly, almost exposing his back.

Laughter rose from the lower stands.

Not admiration. Laughter.

Sima Yu's left hand touched his belt.

Shi Feng saw it. So did Sima Lan.

A green dart slipped from beneath the prince's sleeve. It travelled low enough to vanish against the pale stone, heading toward Shi Feng's calf while a new palm shadow drew the crowd's eyes upward.

Shi Feng brought his sword down.

The dart struck the blade with a bright click. A second dart curved toward his ribs from the left. He turned the same movement into Returning Tide and caught it near the guard.

The third came from behind his right shoulder.

Shi Feng leaned forward a fraction. The dart passed over his collar and met the sword as he lifted it behind him.

Three clicks.

The crowd saw three green lines suddenly hanging in the air around his weapon.

“An artifact!”

“Inside the wrist!”

“He attacked from behind!”

“Personal artifacts are allowed. Watch the referee!”

Zhou Ke hadn't raised his hand. The jade ornament had been declared, and no forbidden use had yet been proven.

Shi Feng didn't need a ruling.

He sent a short thread of qi along the blade and turned all three darts toward their owner. Sima Yu tried to recall them. The return flow caught against Shi Feng's pressure and shuddered visibly.

The prince's left sleeve tore.

The jade housing lay exposed beneath the ruined cuff. Sima Yu closed his fist, forcing more qi into its channels.

Shi Feng let the darts go.

They shot back too quickly. One struck the ornament at the wrong angle and snapped its outer rim. Another hit the stone beside Sima Yu's foot. The third buried itself in his belt fitting.

The Crown Prince stumbled backward.

Shi Feng advanced one pace and stopped the sword tip beside the broken jade.

“You should repair that before using it again,” Shi Feng said.

The plain advice drew another burst of laughter.

Sima Yu's face flushed darkly. He ripped the damaged ornament from his wrist and threw it aside. His servants stood near the passage with helpless expressions, unable to enter or change what the stands had seen.

Above them, Wei Chengyuan finally looked directly at the platform.

Shi Feng noticed without taking his eyes off the prince.

The displayed royal palm was spent. The hidden weapon lay broken. Sima Yu had not landed one clean touch.

That was the public result so far.

Shi Feng's breathing hadn't changed.

Sima Yu slid his hand beneath his robe. It was a small movement, sharper than the ones that had drawn the darts.

Shi Feng knew what came next.

He kept his sword low and gave the prince enough space to make his decision in full view.

chapters.title: The Forbidden Pill
chapters.html:
Sima Yu crushed the wax seal with his thumb.

A dark red pill fell into his palm. He swallowed it before Zhou Ke could finish the first warning.

The effect was immediate.

Gold qi burst from his shoulders and climbed above his head. His robe snapped outward. The torn sleeve pulled tight against a swelling forearm, and the veins at his neck rose like cords.

Several spectators stood.

“Golden Core?”

“He broke through?”

“No lightning! What did he swallow?”

Shi Feng watched the unstable force gather. It had the breadth of an early Golden Core attack without a true core's steady support. Each new surge dragged more violently against the prince's existing foundation.

The pill did what Sima Lan had said it would.

He didn't step back from fear. He shifted left to keep the prince between himself and the nearest crowded stands.

“Stop the match,” Zhou Ke shouted. “Forbidden burst medicine!”

Sima Yu lunged before the referee's raised arm had fully straightened.

His palm struck where Shi Feng's chest had been.

The platform shook. Dust rose around their ankles, and a crack ran through the stone surface under the attack. The pressure made the nearest protective screen brighten above the front rows.

Shi Feng stood beside the prince's extended arm. His sword had turned flat against Sima Yu's wrist, guiding the worst force into the ground.

He took care because he didn't want the weapon damaged by a careless collision.

Sima Yu swung his other fist toward Shi Feng's head. Shi Feng leaned inside the arc and pressed the heel of his free hand beneath the prince's elbow.

The fist shot upward instead.

Gold qi burst harmlessly into the open air. Sima Yu staggered, dragged forward by the excess force he couldn't properly guide.

His eyes were bloodshot.

“Stand still,” Sima Yu snarled.

Shi Feng looked at him.

“No,” Shi Feng replied.

The single word reached the front rows. Someone laughed nervously, then stopped as another violent surge spread from the prince's body.

Lu Yong rose beneath the canopy.

The official's late Golden Core aura settled across the arena, firm and unmistakable. He pointed toward the central platform, and attendants at four stone posts pressed their hands against the formation plates.

“Activate the halt protection,” Lu Yong ordered.

Pale light began climbing from the platform's edges.

The protection had been demonstrated on the opening day. It didn't depend on Sima Yu agreeing that he had violated a rule. It belonged to the tournament and the officials responsible for clearing its platform.

Shi Feng saw the light rise.

He also saw Sima Yu reach for him again.

The prince wasn't thinking about surrender or removal. The pill had given him one last thing that looked like superiority, and he refused to recognize how little it changed.

Shi Feng turned his sword flat to meet the incoming forearm. The blade slid along Sima Yu's sleeve and guided his hand past Shi Feng's collar.

Sima Yu's own force dragged him sideways. His wrist ornament struck the sword guard and broke with a sharp crack. Shi Feng stepped clear rather than follow with another blow.

The broken jade scattered across the stone. The prince's fingers closed on empty air.

Sima Lan watched from beneath the awning. Her fingers tightened once around her own sleeve, then relaxed.

Ling Qingzhu had risen from her seat. She wasn't looking at Sima Yu's growing pressure now. She was watching the official light and Shi Feng's sword.

Wei Chengyuan spoke quietly to the official beside him.

“The boy is still fighting,” Wei Chengyuan said.

“The offender is still attacking,” Mu Shuyun replied from the next seat.

He Zhen kept his eyes on the platform. His brush had stopped moving.

Lu Yong didn't answer either delegate. His attention remained on the formation posts and the two men inside them. The protective light had reached waist height, too low to separate the fighters completely.

“Clear the approach,” Lu Yong ordered.

Zhou Ke waved the candidates away from the central stairs. Two stronger arena guards moved into position with a carrying board and restraint bands.

At the passage mouth, a Great Liang servant tried to cross the cleared line. Pan Zhi stopped him with a hand against his chest.

“His medicine is in our carriage,” the servant, Gao Rui, said.

“Give it to the healer when requested,” Pan Zhi replied. “Stay outside the platform approach.”

Gao Rui looked toward his master and obeyed. He had carried messages in the capital that made officials hurry to open gates. Here, his household badge didn't get him past one guard. He pressed the medicine case against his ribs and waited beneath the arch.

The officials were preparing to remove Sima Yu alive.

Shi Feng understood that as plainly as he understood the prince's failed attacks.

His jaw tightened.

At the nearest formation post, an attendant moved the red warning flag aside so both fighters could see the growing light. Zhou Ke repeated the halt warning from the stairs. Sima Yu turned his head toward neither man. He dragged his foot across the broken stone and tried to regain his balance before attacking again.

Sima Yu forced another surge through his injured arm. The pill's qi flickered where the damaged channels failed to carry it evenly.

He cried out, then drove forward with both palms.

Shi Feng met him at close range.

His sword stayed beside his own leg. He didn't need its edge for what came next. His left hand caught the prince's wrist, turned it outward and exposed the centre of his chest.

Sima Yu tried to wrench free.

Nothing moved except the cloth at his shoulder.

For the first time, the prince felt the difference without a technique or an artifact between them. The borrowed force roared through his body. Shi Feng's hand remained steady.

“You used it,” Shi Feng said.

Sima Yu's gaze darted toward the formation posts. The pale barrier light stood at waist height. Only moments remained before the four corners joined overhead to seal the platform and enforce the halt.

Sima Yu opened his bloodied lips to shout his surrender before the barrier finished rising.

Shi Feng didn't wait for the word or the wall. Inside his body, all three hundred and sixty-five meridians answered at once.

chapters.title: Guo Zhen Was a Fool
chapters.html:
Shi Feng struck Sima Yu four times at close range before the word of surrender could leave the prince's throat.

Each short blow fell from less than an arm's length, driven by all three hundred and sixty-five meridians and the unyielding frame of his completed golden bones, and Shi Feng's voice carried clearly above the formation's hum to the front rows with every strike.

“One for the ordinary accident you promised in the capital,” Shi Feng said, his first palm shattering the prince's right shoulder guard.

“One for Guo Zhen's wire in the northern storehouse,” he continued, his knuckles crushing the left collarbone channel where the pill's surge gathered.

“One for Cao Wenshu at the Hengyun signal fort,” he said as the third strike caved in the side of Sima Yu's rib guard, choking the cry in his throat.

“And one for Zheng Jian in the west-canal timber yard.”

The fourth palm landed squarely in the centre of Sima Yu's chest, shearing straight through the gold qi to the exact node where the burst pill's false Golden Core pressure met his foundation.

The borrowed strength folded inward with a deep, muffled crack. Gold light shattered across Sima Yu's shoulders in uneven strips as the pill's violent force tore backward through channels that could no longer hold it together.

Shi Feng caught the prince by the front of his gold-threaded robe before he could drop to the stone, holding him upright while the formation light climbed past their waists.

Sima Yu coughed blood across his own collar, his late Foundation Establishment qi fracturing along the foundation he had tried to force into a higher realm.

“You—” Sima Yu wheezed, his fingers clawing weakly at Shi Feng's wrist as he tried to draw breath enough to cry yield.

Sima Yu's bloodshot eyes widened in terror as he realized none of his murderous orders had stayed buried.

“Guo Zhen was a fool,” Shi Feng said clearly as the pale barrier light reached shoulder height between them. “He thought a prince's order could kill me without a receipt.”

One breath before Sima Yu's trembling lips could form “I yield,” and a heartbeat before the four formation beams locked overhead to seal the halt, Shi Feng opened his hand and stepped back.

The pale wall of the official halt snapped shut between them as Sima Yu hit the flagstones on his knees.

Shi Feng stood on his own side of the light with his sword already lowered at his side, untouched by the barrier. He hadn't struck through an official halt; he had finished the exchange inside the legal window while Sima Yu was still lunging under the forbidden pill's surge.

Lu Yong descended beside the platform at blinding speed, his hand settling on the formation post as he inspected the boundary and the timing crystal.

The crystal showed the final blow had landed before the halt seal closed.

Inside the barrier, Sima Yu collapsed onto his side, coughing blood over his broken wrist ornament while Zhou Ke and the arena guards hurried forward with a carrying board and restraint bands.

“The final strike preceded the halt seal,” Lu Yong declared after checking the post. “Remove the offender to the medical court.”

For several breaths, Shi Feng watched the guards strap Sima Yu onto the board.

The prince could no longer lift his head properly. His qi leaked in ragged wisps from his cracked foundation, his tournament run ended in public disgrace, and every breath dragged across ruined channels. He was alive only because killing him after the barrier closed would have forfeited the championship Shi Feng came here to win.

Zhou Ke guided the carrying board toward the central stairs. The protected band travelled with it until the guards reached the cleared passage.

Sima Yu's eyes opened briefly as they passed.

Shi Feng didn't look away.

The prince saw no mercy waiting there.

The stands erupted when the carrying board vanished beneath the arch.

“He used the forbidden pill!”

“And still lost!”

“That wasn't a breakthrough!”

“Did you hear the crack?”

“Great Liang's crown prince is being carried out!”

The front rows repeated the names Shi Feng had called out. Guo Zhen. Cao Wenshu. Zheng Jian. A Great Liang officer shouted for silence, then stopped when several spectators asked whether he could answer for those men. He couldn't. The herald recorded the forbidden pill and the final timing; the accusations would remain part of what the crowd had heard.

Several Great Liang officials stood helplessly beneath their banner. They couldn't call the loss an ordinary injury, and the broken wrist ornament still lay on the platform where thousands had watched it fail.

Sima Lan remained beneath the awning. She didn't move toward the medical passage.

Ling Qingzhu gripped the edge of her sleeve, then let it go. Shi Feng stood alone beside the light while the attendants cleared the broken jade and checked the cracked stone.

He hadn't been hurt. That didn't make his expression easy to watch.

Lu Yong returned to the centre.

“Victory to Shi Feng,” Lu Yong announced. “Sima Yu used forbidden burst medicine and is disqualified. The violation and its consequences will be entered in the public record.”

The announcement carried to the highest seats.

No royal title followed the prince's name.

Zhou Ke opened the ordinary exit after the barrier lowered. Shi Feng sheathed his sword and stepped down.

The referee looked at the blood on his sleeve.

“Are you injured?” Zhou Ke asked.

“No,” Shi Feng replied.

Zhou Ke nodded and let him pass. There was no congratulatory pat on the shoulder and no lecture about how fortunate the prince had been.

Shi Feng washed Sima Yu's blood from his hand at the water basin. The red thinned, circled once and disappeared through the drain.

Duan Yichen stood nearby, silent for longer than usual.

“Do you want company?” Duan Yichen asked.

“Not yet,” Shi Feng replied.

The sabre user nodded and moved aside.

Shi Feng dried his hand carefully. The officials had ended a match. They hadn't ended what Sima Yu had begun in Great Liang.

He left the arena with that difference intact.

chapters.title: Eliminated in Round Two
chapters.html:
By noon, Sima Yu's violation had been posted at all four arena gates.

The notice carried Lu Yong's seal. Forbidden burst medicine, immediate disqualification, no eligibility for the sect trials or the later placement bracket. The medical report remained private, but the cause of removal didn't.

Shi Feng read the notice outside the eastern gate.

A Great Liang officer stood nearby with two servants. He had brought a prepared explanation about an emergency medicine taken in error. The official clerk pointed to the seal and refused to replace a single line.

The officer folded his explanation and left.

The crowd remembered which way he went.

“Taken in error? He crushed the seal himself!”

“Perhaps the pill jumped into his mouth!”

“He wanted Golden Core force and got a carrying board!”

Shi Feng checked the stamped result beside his own name. His entry remained valid, with no injury delay requested. Then he moved past the gate. The jokes did nothing for the old grievance. He didn't need the crowd to understand that.

Sima Yu woke in the medical court with both wrists secured to the bed frame.

One restraint held his injured arm still. The other prevented a second burst of unstable qi from damaging the channels the healer was trying to settle.

Gao Rui stood beside the door with the royal medicine case. A court officer named Jin Jian sat near the window, his fine robe crushed from too many hours on an uncomfortable stool.

The healer, Luo Wen, checked the prince's pulse and frowned.

“Don't circulate qi without instruction,” Luo Wen said.

Sima Yu tried anyway.

Pain drove a sharp breath through his teeth. Something deep in his foundation refused to join the flow. The medicine's backlash had left a fracture he couldn't simply push closed.

“How long?” Sima Yu asked.

“Before I can judge the damage properly?” Luo Wen replied. “Days. Before you can cultivate normally? I won't promise what I don't know.”

Jin Jian looked away from the bed.

“The notice must be removed,” Sima Yu said.

“It bears the presiding official's seal,” Jin Jian replied.

“I am the crown prince,” Sima Yu said.

Luo Wen lifted the prince's uninjured wrist, checked the pulse again and put it down.

“That didn't protect your foundation,” Luo Wen said. “Rest.”

Outside, Sima Lan received a written request to attend her brother.

She read it in the Moon Lake courtyard while the sect's younger disciples ate beside the training steps. The messenger waited with his hands folded, expecting a carriage order.

Sima Lan handed the paper back.

“Tell Jin Jian that the arena has capable healers,” Sima Lan said.

“His Highness asked for family,” the messenger, Gao Rui, replied.

“Then write to Father,” Sima Lan said.

Gao Rui hesitated. She watched him until he understood that no softer answer was coming.

He bowed and left.

Sima Lan returned to her sword practice. The first cut was a little sharper than intended. She stopped, adjusted her grip and repeated it correctly.

Her brother's defeat hadn't won her own match. She still had a second-round opponent waiting that afternoon.

Shi Feng watched Duan Yichen's fight from the candidates' awning.

The sabre user faced an agile swordsman who kept circling toward his left shoulder. Duan Yichen allowed two turns, then shortened his grip and struck across the man's escape path.

The sword bent under the contact. Its owner wisely surrendered before it broke.

Duan Yichen returned with a shallow cut across his upper arm and a pleased expression.

“He made me work for the angle,” Duan Yichen said.

Shi Feng handed him a clean strip of cloth.

“He kept showing you the same step,” Shi Feng said.

“Yes,” Duan Yichen replied. “I was almost grateful by the third time.”

He tied the cloth around the cut without asking Shi Feng to admire his endurance. The wound was shallow and already closing under his qi.

For a few moments, they watched the attendants sweep another platform.

“People are going to ask you about the prince,” Duan Yichen said.

“They can read the notice,” Shi Feng replied.

Duan Yichen nodded. He didn't ask whether Shi Feng regretted the sword stroke stopped by the barrier.

He had seen enough to understand the answer.

The betting hall removed Sima Yu's name before the afternoon bell.

A space remained where the gilded characters had been. Yu Cao ordered the board washed rather than leave a blank that every passing customer would point at. Even the wash drew a crowd.

Great Liang's remaining names were Shi Feng and Ling Qingzhu.

Sima Lan appeared beneath Moon Lake, entirely separate from the royal entry. Several onlookers argued that the princess should be counted as a fourth Great Liang representative. The betting clerk told them to argue with the tournament register.

Shi Feng walked past without stopping. He bought a fresh water bottle and returned to the shade.

The crowd wanted the day's result to explain a whole kingdom. He wanted the next match to begin on time.

Those interests didn't need to meet.

At the medical court, Jin Jian wrote the report home.

He began with injury, crossed it out, and wrote disqualification. Lu Yong's public notice left no useful way around the word. Royal messengers would arrive before the tournament ended, and the emperor would ask why his son had needed forbidden medicine against a man one substage below him.

Sima Yu watched from the bed.

“Don't send it yet,” Sima Yu said.

Jin Jian looked up.

“The court requires a report,” Jin Jian replied.

“One evening won't change that,” Sima Yu said. “There is someone I need to see first.”

The officer's brush hovered over the page.

Sima Yu closed his eyes. Every attempt to circulate qi brought pain, and the image of Shi Feng's steady hand returned whenever he tried to sleep.

Defeat hadn't made him less angry.

It had only taught him that his own household was no longer strong enough to finish the matter.

He turned toward the open shutters. Beyond them, the evening bells announced another completed match. The sound reached every bed in the medical court, including his.

chapters.title: The Crown Prince's Visitor
chapters.html:
Wei Chengyuan came to the medical court after the evening meal.

No procession announced him. The Martial Palace delegate walked through the gate with one attendant, handed his badge to the guard and entered before Jin Jian had finished straightening his robe.

Sima Yu tried to sit up.

Pain stopped him halfway.

“Stay where you are,” Wei Chengyuan said.

He took the chair beside the bed. His late Golden Core cultivation filled the small room without any deliberate release of pressure. Gao Rui lowered his eyes and carried the empty medicine bowls outside.

Jin Jian waited at the door.

“You requested a private visit,” Wei Chengyuan said.

“Yes,” Sima Yu replied. “It concerns the Wei branch in Yunze.”

The delegate's gaze sharpened.

Jin Jian understood the glance that followed and stepped out. The door closed quietly behind him.

Sima Yu had prepared the order of his words while the healer worked. He began with names rather than accusations.

“Wei Renshan,” Sima Yu said. “His son Wei Kuo. Their disappearance, the later investigation, and a sword brought into Great Liang's capital.”

Wei Chengyuan rested one hand on the chair arm.

“What do you know?” Wei Chengyuan asked.

“Shi Feng travelled through Yunze,” Sima Yu replied. “He had dealings with the Wei household before he reached us. A maker's mark on his sword was recognized later.”

“By whom?” Wei Chengyuan asked.

“Pei Rong,” Sima Yu said. “That recognition doesn't prove the killing. I understand the difference.”

Wei Chengyuan's expression suggested he preferred the qualification to a confident lie.

Sima Yu continued.

“There was also a private witness account in the Wei inquiry,” Sima Yu said. “Gao An. I don't possess his original statement. I can give you the route by which it was reported.”

“Then give me that,” Wei Chengyuan said.

The prince pointed toward the drawer beside his bed. Wei Chengyuan opened it and took out the prepared paper.

Sima Yu had written only what he could support. Adding a false detail might interest the delegate for one evening and destroy the usefulness of the rest tomorrow.

He wanted a lasting problem for Shi Feng.

Wei Chengyuan read the page twice.

The Yunze branch was distant. A Great Sect contained more Wei relatives than any one elder could keep close to his own table. Distance didn't make the deaths pleasant, especially if a nineteen-year-old had carried a dead clansman's sword through markets where the maker's mark could be recognized.

“Why didn't your court send this earlier?” Wei Chengyuan asked.

Sima Yu kept his breathing shallow.

“The evidence was incomplete,” Sima Yu replied. “My authority over the relevant offices was also reduced.”

“Because you used royal service against this same man,” Wei Chengyuan said.

Sima Yu said nothing.

The delegate folded the paper.

“I watched your match,” Wei Chengyuan said.

The prince's face tightened despite the medicine dulling his pain.

“He concealed what he could do,” Sima Yu said.

“Everyone conceals something,” Wei Chengyuan replied. “You concealed a pill badly.”

Sima Yu looked down at the bandage across his chest. There was no useful answer to that.

Wei Chengyuan rose.

“I'll verify what you've given me,” Wei Chengyuan said. “If you have facts, send facts. Keep your embarrassment out of them.”

He left with the paper inside his sleeve.

Jin Jian returned after the delegate passed through the outer gate.

“Will Martial Palace intercede?” Jin Jian asked.

“Not over the notice,” Sima Yu replied.

The court officer looked disappointed, then relieved that he wouldn't need to delay the report again.

He set fresh water beside the bed. Sima Yu didn't drink it.

His thoughts followed Wei Chengyuan instead. A private account would need checking. Pei Rong would need questioning. Someone would trace the sword, the road, and the dead men whose absence had first made the Wei household search.

Shi Feng had survived royal servants.

Let him explain himself to Martial Palace.

Sima Yu closed his eyes and found no comfort in the thought. The crack in his foundation remained where it was. Revenge imagined from a bed couldn't repair it.

At his inn, Shi Feng was eating a bowl of noodles when a Martial Palace attendant entered the common hall.

The man asked Kang Liu which room belonged to Great Liang's Shi Feng. His voice was polite, and he carried no written summons.

Kang Liu pointed toward the back table instead.

Shi Feng put down his chopsticks.

The attendant, Meng Qi, approached and bowed slightly.

“Delegate Wei Chengyuan asks whether you possessed a sword acquired in Yunze,” Meng Qi said.

Shi Feng looked at him for one quiet breath.

“Yes. I sold it to Pei Rong at Shuanghe Ferry,” Shi Feng replied.

“May I ask how it came into your hands?” Meng Qi said.

“You may ask,” Shi Feng replied. “I'll discuss it with the person who wants to know.”

Meng Qi's expression barely changed. He had enough training to recognize an answer that wouldn't improve through repetition.

“I'll report that,” Meng Qi said.

He left without touching the table or raising his voice.

Shi Feng resumed eating. The noodles had begun to soften, but they were still warm.

He didn't need much time to guess where the inquiry had begun.

Sima Yu had spent the day in a medical bed. His servants couldn't kill Shi Feng, and his own strength had failed before the stands. Information was one of the few weapons left within reach.

Wei Chengyuan's surname supplied the rest.

Shi Feng finished the bowl and paid. Upstairs, he took the sale note from his everyday bag and checked Pei Rong's seal. The merchant owned Wei Renshan's old sword now. His current blade was the plain refined artifact he'd purchased after entering Foundation Establishment. He remembered Wei Renshan advancing on him, certain that a dead son entitled him to another person's life.

That memory hadn't become less clear with distance.

Shi Feng folded the sale note again and put it beside his travel papers.

Tomorrow, twenty-seven people would emerge from the second round. He intended to be ready for the trials after that.

Martial Palace could bring its questions when it was ready to ask them directly.

He checked the practice appointment once more and set it beneath the lamp. Questions from a sect delegate could wait; his own work still required steady hands in the morning.

chapters.title: What the Fairy Kept Private
chapters.html:
The Great Yue swordsman kept his blade low while Ling Qingzhu stepped onto the platform.

He was a late Foundation Establishment cultivator with a narrow scar across his chin. His first-round match had ended in a clean surrender after he'd cut through the opponent's weapon guard.

He studied her white veil without making a joke about it.

Shi Feng watched from the upper end of the candidates' awning. The broken stone on the central platform had been replaced overnight, and the officials had moved the afternoon matches to the two side platforms while the formation posts were checked.

Everything had continued.

Ling Qingzhu drew her sword.

The swordsman began with three probing cuts, each returning close enough to protect his chest. She met the first, allowed the second to pass, and stepped inside the third without changing her breathing.

Their blades touched for a heartbeat.

The man's wrist turned inward. He recovered before losing his grip and pushed harder, sending a thin sword light toward her shoulder.

Ling Qingzhu inclined her head. The light crossed the edge of her sleeve without cutting it.

Shi Feng's gaze sharpened.

That small movement left more room than it appeared to. She had chosen the exact amount of qi needed to disturb the sword light while keeping the rest beneath her own control.

A strong cultivator could do that.

A much stronger one could do it without concern.

He couldn't tell from one exchange exactly how deep her reserve went. He suspected that the answer lay beyond what the spectators had guessed, perhaps far beyond it. His own foundation gave him reasons to notice the distinction, not a magical measurement of hers.

He kept the thought to himself.

The swordsman changed methods. His blade rose vertically, drawing a bright arc over his head before descending toward her guard.

Ling Qingzhu moved one step sideways. Her sword struck the flat near his tip, guiding it past her, then returned toward his chest.

He caught the return and retreated.

She didn't chase with an overwhelming burst. She advanced at the same measured pace, letting him spend effort on the distance between them.

By the ninth exchange, his breathing had grown audible. By the twelfth, desperate to break her rhythm, the Great Yue swordsman poured his full late Foundation Establishment reserves into a heavy overhead cleave.

Ling Qingzhu didn't step aside. For the first time since entering the arena, she let her restrained aura unfurl for a single breath.

Cold, crystalline sword qi at peak Foundation Establishment flashed along her narrow blade and met the descending cleave mid-arc.

The Great Yue swordsman's sword light shattered like thin ice. His blade was knocked wide, his boots skidded three feet across the stone, and Ling Qingzhu's point stopped a hair's breadth from his throat before her aura vanished back beneath her veil.

The man stared at the steel tip and lowered his weapon.

Zhou Ke announced the victory, and the stands broke into an uproar.

“Peak Foundation Establishment! Great Liang's veiled woman is at peak Foundation Establishment!”

“Wait—if she's at peak Foundation Establishment, how was Sima Yu ranked first in Great Liang when he was only at late Foundation Establishment?”

“She never challenged him at home! She let the Crown Prince keep first place so she wouldn't have to bother with the palace!”

“Great Liang's first and second places were backwards the whole time!”

Above the arena, Mu Shuyun leaned forward in the Hundred Flower Valley seat, her brush pausing over Ling Qingzhu's sheet as genuine interest lit her eyes.

Shi Feng left the awning after the next bell. He had planned to visit Sky Pavilion before dinner and ask which rest-day examinations were available.

Ling Qingzhu caught up with him beside the western stair.

“May I speak with you?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

He stopped at the landing. People passed above and below them. It was a public place with enough room to avoid blocking anyone's path.

“You fought well,” Shi Feng said.

“Thank you,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

Her eyes moved briefly to his sleeve. The blood was gone, and he carried the sword as easily as before. She knew he hadn't been wounded in the prince's match. The knowledge didn't answer what she had seen in his face afterward.

“I hid peak Foundation Establishment during the capital qualification,” Ling Qingzhu said quietly. “I didn't want the court or my clan using first place to bind my sect choice before Qingyun City.”

Shi Feng looked at her without surprise.

“You don't owe me an explanation, Fairy Ling,” Shi Feng said evenly.

The formal title made her fingers tighten on the stone rail.

“I wanted you to hear my reasons from me rather than guess from the stands,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“I heard it on the platform,” Shi Feng replied. “It was a clean match. Excuse me—I have an appointment at Sky Pavilion before the desk closes.”

He gave her a brief, courteous nod and walked down the steps without pausing.

Ling Qingzhu stayed beside the rail until the next group of spectators passed. Then she returned to the candidates' court to collect the result stamp on her plate.

The official didn't ask why she had taken so long. He pressed the seal beside her name and pointed out the rest-day schedule.

Twenty-seven names would remain when the round ended.

She had earned one of those places. Her peak Foundation Establishment cultivation was public now. The depth beneath it remained her own, and Shi Feng hadn't asked her to measure it for him.

At the result desk, a younger candidate made room for Ling Qingzhu without being asked. He had heard the crowd's judgment and now watched her sword instead of her veil. She accepted her plate and walked away. The newly revealed realm had changed how strangers stood around her. It hadn't changed the formal title Shi Feng had used.

That should have been a relief.

Instead, she remembered how he used to stare when she tucked loose hair behind her ear at home. He had been terrible at pretending he wasn't looking. Calling him out had once been the easiest way to make a quiet evening warm.

Today he had watched her sword carefully and given her every courtesy.

She had no reason to tell him that was what hurt.

chapters.title: Twenty-Seven
chapters.html:
The last second-round match ended with a staff lying broken across the boundary.

Twenty-seven winners remained beneath the awning. The others had left by choice, injury or the officials' order. Sima Yu's name carried a red disqualification mark on the public sheet rather than an ordinary line through it.

Lu Yong waited until the attendants finished checking every result.

“The next stage consists of three trials,” Lu Yong announced. “Pressure, illusion and a measured puppet array. Their combined scores select the sixteen candidates for the main bracket.”

A murmur crossed the court. Several candidates had prepared for continuous duels and looked less pleased by the change.

“The three trials test your physical and cultivation foundation under pressure, your heart-temperament in the Illusion Garden, and your combat discernment in the Puppet Array,” Lu Yong continued. “Only the top sixteen combined results enter the main bracket.”

Shi Feng listened carefully. That distinction suited him.

Lu Yong indicated a second sheet.

“If a qualifying candidate withdraws before the draw of sixteen, the next eligible trial rank takes the place,” Lu Yong said. “The rule applies before the bracket is sealed. Afterward, withdrawals count as losses.”

Zhou Ke fastened the sheet where everyone could read it.

Sima Lan stood near the back, drying a shallow cut beside her collarbone.

Her own second-round opponent had made her work harder than the staff user now leaving the platform. She had won by holding her line after losing the advantage of reach, choosing a close exchange that left both contestants bleeding.

Shi Feng looked at the cloth.

“Does it need a healer?” Shi Feng asked.

“No,” Sima Lan replied. “It needs me to stop touching it.”

She moved her fingers away from the edge.

Duan Yichen laughed once. He had made the same mistake with his arm twice that morning.

Across the court, Yuan Kuang spoke to two kingdom princes about the coming trials. Xiahou Lie stood beside him, thick arms folded over a sleeveless robe. The body cultivator looked as though pressure stairs had been invented to save him the trouble of finding a heavier training stone.

Bai Chenxi listened alone beneath the far pillar. Her peak Foundation Establishment qi was cold and controlled. She checked the edge of her pale sword while the other candidates talked.

Gongsun Ce held a small jointed wooden bird. The late Foundation Establishment prince adjusted one wing with a pin, apparently more interested in its movement than in the crowd.

Gu Zhan approached him and pointed at it.

“Does it fight?” Gu Zhan asked.

“No,” Gongsun Ce replied.

Gu Zhan lost interest immediately.

Outside the candidates' gate, Han Zheng was explaining the trials to a circle of White Crane supporters.

A first-round defeat had cost him an easy argument. The new stage offered another.

“Throwing a man over a boundary is one thing,” Han Zheng said. “Three sect trials require more than brute force. The cripple won't make the sixteen.”

The tea seller beside him raised his brows. His name was Qiao Ping, and he'd sold enough cups to hear the steward's earlier certainty about Xie Wenyuan.

“Would you put stones behind that?” Qiao Ping asked.

Han Zheng looked at the watching faces.

“How many?” Han Zheng said.

“Twenty,” Qiao Ping replied. “Paid here when the scores are posted.”

It was not a ruinous sum. That made refusing it look worse.

Han Zheng placed the money on the tea table. Qiao Ping matched it and asked the neighbouring stallkeeper to witness the terms.

People nearby began smiling.

Shi Feng heard the last part while passing with Duan Yichen. He didn't stop to place a counter-bet. Han Zheng had found a way to make his own embarrassment more expensive without any help.

Sky Pavilion's examination desk occupied a quiet side hall above the ordinary medicine counters.

A clerk named Wen An checked the rest-day schedule. She was a Bone Refinement cultivator with neat cuffs and ink stains on the side of one finger.

“One Mark requires Foundation Establishment at minimum,” Wen An said. “You'll produce a Golden Core-serving medicine under an examiner's observation. Ingredients are sealed until the examination begins.”

“I understand,” Shi Feng replied.

“Which of the listed formulas have you practised?” Wen An asked.

He selected Clear Spring Pill, the simple recipe whose cooling turn had occupied his recent nights.

Wen An marked the choice.

“The examiner checks your preparation, control and finished medicine,” Wen An said. “Knowing the formula won't substitute for a pill.”

“It shouldn't,” Shi Feng replied.

She looked up briefly, then handed him the morning appointment.

The fee and ingredient allowance occupied one line on the receipt. Shi Feng paid, folded it and left. He wasn't going to spend the rest day imagining the badge instead of preparing his hands.

At the inn, Duan Yichen stopped outside Shi Feng's door with a bundle of fruit.

“You're examining tomorrow?” Duan Yichen asked.

“Yes,” Shi Feng said.

“Then these are congratulations if you pass,” Duan Yichen said. “Otherwise they're breakfast.”

Shi Feng accepted the bundle with a small smile.

“Efficient,” Shi Feng replied.

“I dislike carrying things back,” Duan Yichen said.

He left without asking to watch the practice. Shi Feng ate one piece of fruit, set the others aside and unpacked his furnace.

He didn't attempt a stronger recipe to prove he could. He practised the same joining stage, then the cooling turn, stopping after each failure to note what his own hands had done.

Mo Tianheng's remembered experience gave him a clear method. It didn't move his fingers for him.

When the last flame died, the room smelled of warm herbs and clean sand.

Shi Feng washed the furnace and went to bed early.

He placed the examination receipt inside the everyday bag, beside his tournament plate. One belonged to the arena and one to the tower. Neither could stand in for the other.

Twenty-seven candidates remained in the tournament. Before he faced the trials, he had a different piece of work to finish.

Before lying down, he checked the furnace lid for cracks and packed the cleaned tools in their proper order. Searching for a brush during an examination would be a foolish way to lose concentration.

chapters.title: The Staircase in the Tower
chapters.html:
The certification staircase had shallow steps and no pressure formation.

Shi Feng appreciated that. Enough people waited below it without the tower inventing a second tournament for alchemists carrying their own furnaces.

He reached the examination landing shortly after sunrise. Wen An checked the receipt and directed him to the third room, where a middle-aged examiner was arranging three sealed trays beside a clean furnace base.

“Zheng Hui,” the examiner said. “I'll observe your practical work today.”

“Shi Feng,” Shi Feng replied.

Zheng Hui wore a one-Mark badge. His early Golden Core cultivation supported a calm, steady presence, and the tools on his desk were arranged for use rather than display.

He checked Shi Feng's registration and measured his current realm through the standard verification plate. Mid Foundation Establishment met the minimum requirement. The plate recorded nothing about hidden meridian counts or foundation grades.

“Clear Spring Pill,” Zheng Hui said. “Tell me what the finished medicine serves.”

“Restoring qi for Golden Core cultivators after sustained expenditure,” Shi Feng replied. “It doesn't repair a cracked core or replace proper treatment for injured channels.”

Zheng Hui nodded.

“Then make one that does what you claim,” Zheng Hui said.

They opened the ingredient trays together.

Shi Feng checked each herb for age, moisture and damage. One root had a thicker centre than the examples he had bought in Great Liang. The leaf beside it retained slightly less water than yesterday's practice material.

He adjusted the cuts accordingly.

Zheng Hui watched without speaking. The examination allowed preparation time because preparation was part of making medicine, not a courtesy before the important part.

Shi Feng weighed the dried portions, laid the tools where he could reach them and tested the furnace's air inlet.

He remembered Li Changyuan examining the puppet return channel. One found fault didn't mean the next fault had vanished.

The inlet was clean. The base sat level. He began.

A thin flame grew beneath the furnace. Mid Foundation Establishment qi carried it steadily through the first heating stage, allowing him to preserve the leaf's gentler essence while the harder root softened in the separate preparation cup.

He had known the proper temperature for months.

His hands had only recently become reliable enough to hold it without correcting every few breaths.

That difference mattered now.

The first medicine stream gathered at the furnace centre. Shi Feng fed in the root essence slowly, letting the heat join them without scorching the lighter leaf.

Mo Tianheng's remembered experience showed him the expected colour and density. His own eyes checked what was actually in front of him.

The thicker root required a longer joining turn.

He gave it one.

Zheng Hui made a small mark on his sheet.

Sweat formed at Shi Feng's temple, mostly from the furnace heat. His qi expenditure remained manageable. He hadn't suddenly become capable of every Golden Core recipe merely because this one held together.

Clear Spring Pill used a direct sequence with few violent conflicts between ingredients. He had chosen it because he had trained it, because the ingredients were available, and because its demands fit his present control.

A stronger formula could still outrun his hands or his cultivation.

This one didn't.

He closed the upper vent by a finger's width and began the difficult turn.

The joined essence tried to spread as the temperature fell.

Shi Feng had lost two practice batches at exactly that point. Once, he'd held the flame too strongly and dried the outside before the centre settled. The second time, he'd cooled too fast and let the medicinal streams separate.

He recognized the beginning of the second mistake now.

His wrist paused. Instead of forcing the whole mass inward, he gave the weaker edge a small supporting thread of qi and reduced the air from below.

The spread stopped.

A pale bead formed above the furnace floor.

Zheng Hui leaned forward slightly. He could see the correction, and he could see that it belonged to the candidate rather than a lucky collapse into shape.

Shi Feng held the bead steady through three slow breaths.

Then a hairline tremor crossed it.

Too much support at the edge.

He released the extra thread before it could draw the medicine off centre. The bead settled again, smaller and denser.

His fingers had done what his mind asked.

That simple fact pleased him more than the badge waiting somewhere in the tower.

The furnace timer rang softly.

Shi Feng didn't lift the lid at once. The final settling period remained part of the process, and opening too soon would waste the work already completed.

Zheng Hui checked the timer and let him continue.

Outside the room, footsteps passed along the landing. Someone in the next examination chamber cursed, then apologized to an examiner. A furnace lid clanged against stone.

Shi Feng kept his attention on the quiet bead inside his own furnace.

When the surface stopped shifting, he reduced the last heat and waited for the pill to cool enough to handle.

Only then did he lift the lid.

One pale pill rested in the cup.

It had no spectacular light and sent no medicinal cloud through the roof. Its importance lay in the stable essence contained inside it.

Shi Feng placed the cup before Zheng Hui.

The examiner smelled the medicine, checked its weight and cut a tiny sample from the edge with a clean blade.

He placed the sample on an assay plate. Three shallow channels carried the released qi into separate measuring stones. The first confirmed the formula's character. The second showed the retained potency. The third tested whether the joined medicine stayed stable as it was released.

Shi Feng watched the last stone.

It brightened evenly.

Zheng Hui looked at the record he had made during the cooling turn.

“Your correction was timely,” Zheng Hui said. “It also cost some final yield.”

“I held the outer edge too long,” Shi Feng replied.

“Yes,” Zheng Hui said. “You noticed before the medicine split.”

He wrote the measured result beside the practical notes and turned the sheet toward Shi Feng.

The pill existed. It was stable. It served the realm the formula claimed to serve.

Now the tower would decide whether the entire performance met its standard.

chapters.title: One Mark at Nineteen
chapters.html:
Zheng Hui placed the assay sheet beside the furnace record.

“Pass,” Zheng Hui said.

Shi Feng let out a breath he hadn't realized he was holding quite so carefully. He had known the pill was sound when the last measuring stone brightened. Hearing the tower's judgment still felt different.

The examiner stamped both sheets.

“Your medicine clears the minimum potency by a useful margin,” Zheng Hui said. “The stability is good. The cooling correction kept it that way, though you should practise doing it with less loss.”

“I will,” Shi Feng replied.

Zheng Hui took the remaining pill from the assay cup and sealed it in a small bottle.

“The practical sample stays with the certification record,” Zheng Hui said. “You'll receive the written result below. Don't describe this as mastery of all Golden Core medicine. It certifies that you've met the first Mark's practical standard.”

Shi Feng nodded.

He had no desire to promise clients recipes his own hands couldn't finish.

Wen An was checking a stack of receipts when he returned to the lower desk.

She looked at the examiner's stamp, then checked the age entry again.

“Nineteen,” Wen An said.

“Yes,” Shi Feng replied.

“The birth record was already verified,” Zheng Hui said from the stair behind him. “Enter it as written.”

Wen An straightened and completed the certificate. A second clerk brought a small badge with one clean mark across its surface.

Shi Feng held it in his palm.

He remembered the first smoke-filled batches in Great Liang. He remembered wrists that couldn't maintain the flame and ingredients ruined because remembered expertise wasn't the same as physical control.

The badge represented those failed attempts as much as the successful pill upstairs.

Wen An passed over the certificate.

“Your purchase register now has the certified alchemist's terms,” Wen An said. “You may request Golden Core ingredient lots and accept appropriate tower commissions. Availability and your own capacity still govern the work.”

“Understood,” Shi Feng replied.

She indicated where he should sign. The improved terms took one paragraph. He read it, signed and stored the certificate carefully.

News travelled down the staircase before he did.

At the medicine counter, two assistants stopped sorting boxes. A customer looked from the badge to Shi Feng's face, then asked whether the young man was someone's disciple taking an introductory assessment.

“One Mark,” Wen An answered from the desk. “Practical certification completed this morning.”

The room quieted briefly.

“Nineteen?”

“At Foundation Establishment?”

“That's the Great Liang swordsman!”

“Master Shen? The one people talked about from the capital?”

Shi Feng hadn't hidden that identity since its public reveal. He also didn't need to answer every customer whose memory arrived one breath late.

He thanked Zheng Hui once more and moved toward the ingredient counters.

The examiner stopped him with a raised finger.

“Keep the notes from your failed cooling turns,” Zheng Hui said. “Don't replace them with a cleaner account of today's success.”

Shi Feng smiled.

“They're already written,” Shi Feng replied.

“Good,” Zheng Hui said. “A surprising number of people forget how useful their mistakes were as soon as somebody gives them a badge.”

He bought only enough ingredients for several familiar batches.

The new terms made the total better than yesterday's estimate. It was a real improvement, and there would be more valuable commissions available after the tournament. None of that changed the months when he had worked with too little sleep and eaten what remained after other needs were covered.

Success didn't reach backward and put money into an empty bag.

Shi Feng tucked the receipt away without following that thought farther.

Outside, Duan Yichen waited beside the tower steps. He had apparently finished his own practice early enough to watch for the result.

The sabre user looked at the badge.

“So the fruit was congratulations,” Duan Yichen said.

“It was good breakfast too,” Shi Feng replied.

Duan Yichen grinned and caught his arm, careful of the furnace case.

“Then lunch,” Duan Yichen said. “You can explain why one little line makes the tower assistants stand straighter.”

“They trust what it means,” Shi Feng replied.

“Good answer,” Duan Yichen said. “Still buying lunch.”

They ate in a small courtyard behind the medicine street. Duan Yichen ordered too much fried bean curd, admitted it halfway through and finished it anyway.

Shi Feng laughed when the sabre user tried to blame the size of the bowls.

For once, recognition arrived without a demand that he humiliate someone first. Zheng Hui had judged the work. Wen An had entered the result. Duan Yichen had waited because he wanted to hear it.

Shi Feng found he enjoyed that more than the startled crowd below the stairs.

On the way back, a tower assistant brought him a sealed copy of the assay. The assistant bowed politely and addressed him as a certified alchemist.

Shi Feng accepted the sheet and put it beside his practice journal.

He would compare them later, while the corrections remained clear.

Ling Qingzhu heard the news from Hongxiu that afternoon.

She was checking her sword belt before the next day's trials. Her white veil lay properly across her face, and the little clasp held every loose strand except one beside her ear.

“He passed,” Hongxiu said. “The tower confirmed it.”

Ling Qingzhu's hand stopped on the belt.

“One Mark,” Ling Qingzhu said softly.

Hongxiu nodded. She looked ready to suggest a congratulatory visit, then thought better of it.

Ling Qingzhu understood the silence.

She wrote a short note wishing him success in the coming trials. After reading it, she set it aside. He had already thanked her for the same wish yesterday. Another paper didn't need to arrive simply because she wanted to feel present at his good news.

She finished checking the sword belt.

Across the city, Shi Feng put the one-Mark badge in his everyday bag, where the certificate wouldn't crease beneath it. Tomorrow's arena entry would still depend on his tournament plate.

He checked that too.

The new badge rested beside the old plate for a moment. He looked at both, then packed them separately and turned out the lamp. Each had been earned through different work.

chapters.title: The Pressure Stair
chapters.html:
The stair stood beneath an open-sided hall north of the arena.

Forty broad steps rose toward a blank wall. Each had a numbered plate set into its edge, and the formation posts beside them carried pressure down toward anyone who climbed.

Lu Yong waited at the bottom while the twenty-seven candidates gathered.

“Your score is the highest step held for three breaths,” Lu Yong said. “You may descend when you choose. Falling below your last completed step does not erase that score. The protective formation prevents a failed attempt from crushing you.”

He pointed to the measuring plates.

“They record position and duration. Nothing more,” Lu Yong said.

Shi Feng looked up the stair. Good. He could decide what result he wanted without giving the apparatus access to anything beneath it.

A small board displayed the previous gathering's highest score: thirty-seven.

Xiahou Lie grinned when he saw it.

“Solid enough?” Xiahou Lie asked, tapping the first step with his heel.

“Try climbing before you break my floor,” Lu Yong replied.

The body cultivator laughed and took his place.

Yuan Kuang went first among the favourites.

He climbed twenty steps without pausing. His black armour creaked as the pressure rose, and a thin gold light gathered close to his shoulders. At twenty-eight, he shortened his stride. At thirty-two, he stopped long enough for the crowd to begin counting his breaths aloud.

He reached thirty-eight—one step beyond the previous tournament's standing record of thirty-seven.

The third breath came through clenched teeth as the stone beneath his boots groaned. When the thirty-eighth plate flashed gold, the hall erupted in cheers for Great Qin's crown prince.

Xiahou Lie followed.

His broad shoulders rolled once beneath the crushing weight. He advanced with less grace than Yuan Kuang, planting each foot flat until he reached thirty-seven—tying the old record for second place before coming down with sweat pouring along his jaw.

“Good floor,” Xiahou Lie said, grinning at Yuan Kuang.

Bai Chenxi reached thirty-four with her face pale and her breathing steady. Gongsun Ce completed thirty-two, studying the formation posts at each tier. Duan Yichen held thirty and descended rubbing both knees.

Gu Zhan took the steps two at a time until Lu Yong reminded him that the three-breath count was mandatory. The one-eyed youth slowed, completed thirty-six, spotted Nie Wufeng holding up a parcel of steamed buns in the gallery, and came straight down for breakfast.

Ling Qingzhu climbed next. Her white veil stayed still as she rose smoothly to thirty-five, held for three calm breaths without a tremor in her shoulders, and descended to an approving nod from Mu Shuyun.

Shi Feng's turn came near noon.

Nineteen candidates had already climbed; eight remained. He ascended the first twenty-five steps at an ordinary walking pace. As the array pressure multiplied past the thirty-second tier, a faint, unseen hum answered inside his frame—all two hundred and six completed golden bones and three hundred and sixty-five meridians bearing the load as if it were a spring breeze.

He passed Ling Qingzhu's thirty-five. He passed Gu Zhan's thirty-six and Xiahou Lie's thirty-seven without his stride shortening.

The hall went quiet.

At thirty-eight—Yuan Kuang's new record—Shi Feng didn't pause. He lifted his boot and stepped cleanly onto thirty-nine, a single step below the fortieth summit.

Yuan Kuang's hand tightened on his spear shaft. Up in the sect pavilion, Wei Chengyuan and He Zhen both leaned forward.

Shi Feng stood on the thirty-ninth step for three unhurried breaths. His back stayed straight, his breathing didn't quicken, and when the plate blazed gold to mark a new record across the thirty-two kingdoms, he glanced once at the fortieth step, left it untouched, and walked down the stair.

An astonished roar broke across the hall:

“Thirty-nine! A mid Foundation Establishment cultivator took thirty-nine!”

“He passed Great Qin's prince and stopped one step from the wall!”

“He wasn't even shaking—why didn't he take the fortieth step?”

The last suggestion amused him. The crowd had no way to distinguish a chosen stop from an inability to continue, and he wasn't responsible for helping it guess.

He had taken first on the stair and still kept the fortieth step in reserve.

Duan Yichen handed him a water cup at the bottom.

“You looked comfortable,” Duan Yichen said.

“The steps were level,” Shi Feng replied.

Duan Yichen looked back at the stair, then at his own knees.

“I'll remember that comfort next time they make me climb something,” Duan Yichen said.

Sima Lan completed twenty-nine later in the session. She needed the full allowance between attempts and descended with one hand braced against her thigh. Her result left little room for error in the remaining trials.

She read the board twice, made no complaint and asked an attendant when the illusion garden would open.

That seemed more useful than blaming the stair.

By afternoon, every candidate had a first score.

Han Zheng stood outside the barrier with his arms folded. Qiao Ping had left the tea stall under his nephew's care and come to see whether the steward's twenty stones were becoming an easier debt to collect.

Thirty-nine blazed at the top of the column beside Shi Feng's name.

Han Zheng pointed toward the two unfilled trial columns.

“One result,” Han Zheng said.

Qiao Ping nodded pleasantly.

“One result,” Qiao Ping replied. “I'll keep the money dry.”

Shi Feng heard them while returning his cup. He didn't look back.

Two attendants inspected the thirty-ninth plate after Shi Feng descended. Neither found a fault. Lu Yong waited for their nod before entering the score in ink. Yuan Kuang watched the brush finish, then turned toward the next court without disputing it. Xiahou Lie rubbed his shoulders and laughed. Someone stronger had climbed the same steps; complaining wouldn't make his own result higher.

The line moved again. A candidate behind Sima Lan asked to repeat an attempt, but the attendant pointed to the completed score and the posted rule. He went down to wait with everyone else.

The next trial would ask for a different kind of control.

chapters.title: The Illusion Garden
chapters.html:
The gate opened into a room Shi Feng knew.

A screen stood beside the bed. His floor mat lay in the corner, folded too narrowly because there had been little space between the chest and the wall. A bowl waited on the table with less food than he remembered being hungry for.

On top of the chest lay the promised spirit-stone bag.

He stopped inside the doorway.

The illusion had been built to catch at things a candidate carried, not to search and record hidden cultivation. Outside, the judges would see whether he emerged within the allotted time. They would not see this room.

That didn't make it pleasant.

Shi Feng walked to the chest and picked up the bag.

Empty.

The weight felt exactly right.

Ling Qingzhu stood beyond the screen in a familiar violet robe. Her face was uncovered because this was the home they had shared, at a moment when nobody else should have been present.

“You should have told me,” the image of Ling Qingzhu said.

Shi Feng looked at her.

He knew it wasn't her. The real woman had begun to understand that he had told her. This image used the old words because those were the ones he still carried easily enough for an illusion to reach.

“I did,” Shi Feng said.

The figure's expression softened.

“Then stay,” the image of Ling Qingzhu said.

That hurt more than the accusation.

For a breath, he wanted the room to be real in a different way. Food on the table, warmth without suspicion, a place beside her where his work didn't need defending before it could be accepted.

Wanting it didn't make the empty bag full.

He set it down.

The floor mat shifted, trying to pull his thoughts back into the old bargain.
