Shi Feng didn't linger over the mat or the phantom beside the screen. He had already walked out of this room in Great Liang.

He turned toward the door. When the phantom Ling Qingzhu reached for his sleeve and whispered, “Don't go,” his hand didn't hesitate.

“That room is closed,” Shi Feng said evenly, and stepped straight through the threshold.

The gravel path of the outer garden reappeared around him before the second timing bell had finished its ring.

The exit attendant stamped his plate.

No one asked what he'd seen.

He was grateful for that part of the rules.

Ling Qingzhu entered later through the western gate.

The white veil remained across her face as the garden darkened around her. She heard footsteps in a corridor, then the quiet sound of a door closing.

Shi Feng's inn door.

She stood outside with a bottle in her hand. This time, the paper beneath the stopper was blank.

She knocked.

No answer came.

The illusion didn't need to invent shouting. A closed door was enough.

Ling Qingzhu pressed her fingers against the wood and found herself wanting to explain everything at once. The missing money. The meals she'd failed to count. The work she'd treated as an excuse. The way she'd heard his confidence and thought it could protect him from needing trust.

The door remained closed.

She lowered her hand.

An apology could be offered. It couldn't force someone else to receive it when she wanted relief.

She set the bottle beside the threshold and stepped back.

The corridor dissolved.

Outside, the bronze exit bell chimed after only nine breaths—the fastest clearance of all twenty-seven candidates in the Illusion Garden.

In the upper pavilion, Mu Shuyun rose to her feet, her hand resting on the rail as the recording stone flashed with the top mark of the second trial.

Yet when Ling Qingzhu stepped out beneath the exit arch, her face was pale behind the white veil and her fingers were cold against her cuff. She walked down the gravel path where Shi Feng stood waiting for the third-trial call. As she passed within an arm's length of him, her eyes lifted to his face—and Shi Feng met her gaze calmly, held it for a single unhurried breath without speaking, and looked away last toward the Puppet Array court.

Sima Lan came out with her lips pressed together.

Duan Yichen, waiting his own turn, glanced at the sleeve she had twisted tightly around her wrist.

“Unpleasant?” Duan Yichen asked.

“Predictable,” Sima Lan replied.

Inside, she had seen a throne waiting beneath Great Liang's roof. The steps were empty. No brother barred the way, and nobody told her which marriage could be exchanged for another clan's favour.

She had walked past it.

The throne had followed her voice through the hall, promising that power would make the rest worthwhile.

She knew too many people who had believed exactly that.

At the exit, she loosened her sleeve and checked the time. Better than the pressure stair. Not enough to relax.

Shi Feng remained beneath the tree until Duan Yichen returned. The sabre user looked annoyed rather than shaken.

“Grain accounts,” Duan Yichen said.

Shi Feng stared at him, then laughed once.

“All winter,” Duan Yichen added. “Numbers changing every time I finished a column.”

“Terrifying,” Shi Feng replied.

“It was,” Duan Yichen said. “Don't laugh until you've met my uncle with a missing receipt.”

The ordinary complaint loosened something in Shi Feng's chest. He stood, put the plate away and went with the sabre user toward the water tables.

Zhou Ke collected the stamped plates beside the water tables. A candidate tried to ask which visions had caught the other competitors. The official returned his own plate and refused. The trial ranked their answers to its illusions; it hadn't bought their private memories. Shi Feng put his plate away without joining the questions.

Across the court, Ling Qingzhu watched the second result appear beside her name. Mu Shuyun spoke briefly to an attendant above her, but no image from the garden appeared on the recording stone. Only the time and score were written. Ling Qingzhu straightened her sleeve and went to the next waiting line.

He had only needed to keep walking when the path opened.

At the water table, he filled one cup, then paused before reaching for a second. Duan Yichen took it from him and filled it himself. The small mistake passed without a question.

chapters.title: The Puppet Array
chapters.html:
Six wooden puppets waited inside the final trial circle.

Their arms held padded poles, and small bronze plates covered the joints. Lines cut into the stone joined each puppet to the control post at the centre. A clear crystal on the outer desk counted valid strikes and completed targets.

He Zhen supervised this trial himself.

“You have twenty breaths,” He Zhen said. “Disable the marked joints or reach the central post. Striking the same target twice earns nothing. Breaking the floor earns a repair bill.”

Xiahou Lie looked disappointed.

Gongsun Ce smiled for the first time that morning.

The prince entered with three small discs tucked between his fingers.

He didn't throw them immediately. He watched the first puppet turn, stepped outside the pole and tapped a disc against its elbow plate. A soft click locked the joint for half a breath.

That was enough to move behind it.

The next disc caught another puppet's knee. Gongsun Ce used the resulting stumble to cross between two overlapping poles, turning his shoulder at exactly the right moment.

He reached the central post with seven breaths remaining.

The crystal brightened, recording a strong result.

He Zhen checked one disc after the prince left and nodded at the ordinary construction. It used permitted personal tools and precise timing, not a hidden attack on the trial machinery.

Gongsun Ce put it away with obvious satisfaction.

Yuan Kuang chose a more direct route and broke four marked joints with his spear. Bai Chenxi completed five before the last pole forced her to change position. Xiahou Lie shattered one entire arm, was told it counted as one joint rather than three, and grumbled without arguing.

The trial gave everyone a clear number.

Shi Feng watched the control lines while the attendants replaced the broken arm.

The simple qi loop was visible whenever a puppet moved. Force travelled from the post to a shoulder joint, split toward the elbow and returned through the line beneath the heel.

He understood the principle from furnace formations. A controlled supply, a directed task, a returning flow. Xu Changhe's journal contained modest diagrams for gate mechanisms and practice dummies built on similar loops.

That didn't mean he could construct these six puppets.

It meant he could recognize where one movement stopped supporting the next.

He drew his sword when He Zhen called his name and entered the circle.

The first pole came from his right.

Piercing Current touched the marked wrist plate before the swing finished. Shi Feng moved past the disabled hand and turned his blade toward the second puppet.

The low pole tried to catch his knees.

Turning Wave guided it upward. He didn't stop the whole puppet by force. He let its own motion lift the pole away while he stepped across the line beneath its feet.

The return channel flashed.

There.

Shi Feng struck the marked ankle plate during the brief change in supply.

The second puppet stopped with one foot raised. Its body blocked the third puppet's approach, giving him an open path toward the centre.

He could have smashed directly through the rest. That would make the trial a demonstration of strength rather than a useful check of the sword method he'd been practising.

He chose the method.

A pole swept across his back. Returning Tide brought his sword around from beneath his elbow, caught the wooden shaft and carried its tip into the fourth puppet's shoulder plate.

A bright click sounded.

He Zhen straightened at the desk.

Shi Feng didn't notice the movement. He was watching the next return channel, counting the breaths without moving his lips.

Two puppets remained active. Their poles crossed in front of the control post.

He sent one short sword stroke between them, touching the marked plate on the post without cutting the supply lines buried beneath it.

The crystal lit.

Four breaths remained.

He Zhen looked at the sword before looking at the result.

“That returning movement,” He Zhen said. “Who taught you?”

Shi Feng stepped out of the circle and sheathed his blade.

“Xu Changhe's notes,” Shi Feng replied.

The delegate's face changed.

It was a small change, but clear enough that the nearest attendant lowered his brush and waited.

“Where did you find them?” He Zhen asked.

“In a ruin passage,” Shi Feng said. “He died there. I have his badge and journal.”

He Zhen glanced at the waiting candidates. There were still scores to record and a trial to finish. Whatever the name meant to him, he kept those duties in place.

“Will you bring them after the session?” He Zhen asked.

“Yes,” Shi Feng replied.

He Zhen nodded and called the next candidate.

Shi Feng left the circle with the result stamp still damp on his plate.

Duan Yichen waited beside the tool table.

“You made the puppets hit each other,” Duan Yichen said.

“They were standing close,” Shi Feng replied.

“I also stood close,” Duan Yichen said. “They hit me.”

Shi Feng looked at the padded mark on his friend's sleeve and smiled.

“Different timing,” Shi Feng said.

Duan Yichen rolled his shoulder and glanced toward He Zhen.

“That name mattered to him,” Duan Yichen said.

“Yes,” Shi Feng replied.

He didn't explain the ruin in the crowded trial court. Xu Changhe's journal deserved a quieter place than a water table surrounded by people comparing scores.

Sima Lan entered the circle as they spoke. She disabled three joints and touched a fourth just before the time ended. The last pole struck her shoulder hard enough to make her wince.

She waited for the recording crystal to settle, then bowed to the desk and left.

Her score would be close.

When all twenty-seven candidates had finished, He Zhen sealed the trial sheets and sent them to Lu Yong's clerks.

Only then did he approach Shi Feng.

“I have a room beside the equipment court,” He Zhen said. “We can speak there.”

Shi Feng nodded. He checked that his everyday bag remained secure, then followed the delegate through the side gate.

The old journal waited in his ring beside a plain badge that had travelled farther than its owner ever would.

It was time to return both.

chapters.title: The Enforcer's Badge
chapters.html:
He Zhen's room contained a repair bench, three stools and a shelf crowded with spare puppet joints.

The delegate cleared a space by moving two cracked elbow plates onto the floor. He didn't summon attendants or ask Shi Feng to stand while he remained seated.

“Show me the badge first,” He Zhen said.

Shi Feng took it from his ring.

The metal had darkened around its edge. One corner carried the mark of a hard impact, and the reverse bore a number beneath Artificer Hall's old seal.

He Zhen picked it up with both hands.

For several breaths, he said nothing.

Then he turned it over, touched the damaged corner and let out a quiet breath.

“Xu Changhe always caught this against his belt hook,” He Zhen said. “He kept promising to change the hook.”

Shi Feng set the journal beside it.

“He left these in the passage where he died,” Shi Feng said.

He Zhen opened the journal near the middle. Ordinary handwriting crowded the page, with a repair diagram squeezed into one margin and a correction crossing half the next line.

The delegate's thumb stopped beside the note about filing.

“He wrote this after a disciple jammed the western gate,” He Zhen said. “I remember the shouting.”

There was affection in the complaint. It made Xu Changhe seem less like a dead man beside a dangerous passage and more like someone who had once annoyed living people for ordinary reasons.

Shi Feng found he preferred that.

He gave a brief account of the place: the excavation, the trapped passage, the remains and the things left within reach. He described what he had personally seen without pretending he knew Xu Changhe's final thoughts.

He didn't mention Mo Tianheng's ring or the possession attempt. Those belonged to another part of the ruin and another secret.

He Zhen listened without interrupting.

“Was there enough left to bury?” He Zhen asked.

Shi Feng answered honestly about what he had been able to do there.

The delegate bowed his head for a moment.

“Thank you for telling me plainly,” He Zhen said.

“I practised the sword method,” Shi Feng said. “The repair diagrams helped me understand some ordinary mechanisms too. I copied what I needed before bringing the original.”

He Zhen nodded.

“You didn't pretend the return movement was yours,” He Zhen said. “That's enough for me to begin with.”

“Was he a sword elder?” Shi Feng asked.

“An enforcer,” He Zhen replied. “A good swordsman. He could repair the tools disciples actually broke and make sound equipment without wasting half the storehouse. People forget how useful that is when they start talking about legendary refiners.”

Shi Feng looked at the journal. Nothing in it had claimed otherwise.

The skill had been practical, tested and written by a man who corrected his own mistakes. That had made it useful long before anybody in Qingyun recognized the name behind it.

“Iron River Sword Art,” He Zhen said. “Piercing Current, Turning Wave, Returning Tide. He liked people who could bring the sword home without making a second opening.”

Shi Feng remembered the puppet pole turning into the next target.

“He explained the return carefully,” Shi Feng said.

“He had to,” He Zhen replied. “Most young men only wanted the first strike.”

The delegate closed the journal and placed the badge on top.

“Are you returning these to the Hall?” He Zhen asked.

“Yes,” Shi Feng replied.

“Any condition?” He Zhen asked.

“No,” Shi Feng said. “They belong with people who knew him.”

He Zhen studied him, then bowed from his stool.

Shi Feng returned the bow.

There was no burst of hidden power, no second inheritance awakening from the metal, and no sudden declaration that the whole sect owed him its future. The badge had done what a badge should do. It had carried a name home.

He Zhen wrapped it and the journal in clean cloth.

“I'll enter the return in the Hall record,” He Zhen said. “The report of his death too. You won't need to repeat it for every clerk who asks.”

“That would help,” Shi Feng replied.

The delegate smiled faintly.

“I know our clerks,” He Zhen said.

A knock came at the door. An attendant brought the preliminary trial sheets and asked for He Zhen's confirmation of the puppet scores.

The delegate checked the numbers in front of him. Shi Feng looked away while the other candidates' entries were visible, giving the official room to complete the work properly.

He Zhen sealed the sheet and handed it back.

“The final list will be posted shortly,” He Zhen said.

Shi Feng stood.

“Then I won't keep you,” Shi Feng replied.

At the door, He Zhen paused with a hand on the wrapped journal.

“Whatever sect you eventually choose, keep practising the method honestly,” He Zhen said.

“I intend to,” Shi Feng replied.

That answer required no larger pledge. He had learned from Xu Changhe because the method suited him. The return of the badge didn't turn every Artificer Hall disciple into a trusted friend.

It did give him a clearer reason to look at the Hall with interest.

Outside the equipment court, Li Changyuan sat on a low wall eating roasted beans from a paper cone.

He looked at the repaired puppet joint in Shi Feng's hand. He Zhen had given him the discarded piece to examine, with no claim that it was valuable.

“Another broken thing?” Li Changyuan asked.

“A shoulder joint,” Shi Feng replied.

“Does it slap?” Li Changyuan asked.

“Not anymore,” Shi Feng said.

The old man looked disappointed, then offered the cone. Shi Feng took a few beans and sat beside him until the bell for the posted results sounded.

They didn't discuss the badge. Li Changyuan asked whether the furnace inlet had been cleared, and Shi Feng told him the flame had steadied afterward.

“Usually helps,” Li Changyuan said.

Shi Feng finished the beans and went toward the notice court.

Behind him, the old man folded the empty paper and put it in his pocket rather than dropping it on the ground.

chapters.title: Sixteen
chapters.html:
Sima Lan reached the notice court before the officials carried out the final board.

She stood beneath Moon Lake's small banner with the cut beside her collarbone freshly covered. The puppet strike had left one shoulder stiff enough that she kept the arm close to her side.

Shi Feng arrived with Duan Yichen as Zhou Ke lifted the board onto its hooks.

No one cheered immediately.

Three score columns stood beside the names, followed by the final order. A heavy line separated the sixteenth candidate from the seventeenth.

Shi Feng found his own name near the top. All three measured performances had placed him comfortably within the qualifying group. He didn't need to claim the highest result in each trial to get what he wanted.

Then he looked lower.

Fourteenth: Lu Ting, Great Wu.

Fifteenth: Duan Yichen, Great Zhao.

Sixteenth: Sima Lan, Moon Lake Sect.

Seventeenth: Cen Ruchen, Great Wei.

The difference was narrow enough to make both names draw a crowd.

Sima Lan read the three columns carefully.

The pressure stair had cost her. The illusion garden had brought her back into reach. The fourth puppet joint, touched just before the final breath, had carried her over the line.

She hadn't been inserted by a royal request. The officials' numbers showed every piece of the route.

Cen Ruchen stood beside the board with his arms folded. He was a late Foundation Establishment swordsman, neat in grey, with dust still caught along one boot from the pressure stair.

“Close,” Cen Ruchen said.

“Yes,” Sima Lan replied.

“I should have taken the fourth joint first,” Cen Ruchen said.

“I almost missed it,” Sima Lan replied.

He looked at her shoulder, then back at the board.

“Almost isn't the score,” Cen Ruchen said.

He gave her a short nod and moved away. Disappointment remained on his face, but he didn't ask the officials to turn it into a new rule.

Sima Lan watched him go before allowing herself a slow breath.

Duan Yichen had qualified without needing the final few points.

He read his line, checked the seal and grinned toward Shi Feng.

“No grain accounts in the main bracket,” Duan Yichen said.

“Only swords,” Shi Feng replied.

“And spears,” Gu Zhan added from behind them.

The one-eyed youth leaned between their shoulders to read the board. He found his own name, nodded as though the result confirmed that lunch would be served, and began looking for the next draw time.

Gongsun Ce stood farther down, comparing the puppet column with the other trials. His technical result had been among the best. Yuan Kuang looked displeased that his pressure score hadn't put him above everyone, while Xiahou Lie was asking a clerk whether they kept the stair open for ordinary training.

Bai Chenxi read the list once and left.

Ling Qingzhu remained nearby with her veil in place. Her completed results had earned a clear qualification. Nothing beside her name identified what she had withheld.

Shi Feng gave her a brief nod when she looked toward him.

She returned it and stepped away from the board.

The loudest noise came from the tea stall.

Qiao Ping had brought the witnessed bet to the notice court in a small wooden tray. Han Zheng stood beside him with two White Crane disciples and no useful objection left to make.

“Shi Feng qualified,” Qiao Ping said.

“I can read,” Han Zheng replied.

“Then we agree on the result,” Qiao Ping said.

The neighbouring stallkeeper checked the sealed purse and counted the forty stones in front of them. Twenty returned to Qiao Ping from his own stake. Twenty came from the steward.

A crowd gathered close enough to see every stone.

“He said the cripple wouldn't make it!”

“Perhaps he meant some other cripple!”

“White Crane's steward has paid for two lessons now!”

Han Zheng's ears reddened.

He reached for his empty purse, then realized it looked worse to snatch it away. He accepted it slowly and tucked it beneath his sleeve.

Qiao Ping bowed with maddening politeness.

“Thank you for settling promptly,” Qiao Ping said.

Han Zheng left before the stallkeeper finished putting away the tray.

Shi Feng watched from the edge of the court.

He hadn't asked for the bet, won any part of it or promised Qiao Ping a favour. The tea seller had listened to a public claim and made a public wager. The result belonged to the man who had insisted certainty was worth twenty stones.

Duan Yichen looked amused.

“Will he try a third bet?” Duan Yichen asked.

“He may run out of purse first,” Shi Feng replied.

They moved aside to let an official carry a fresh notice through the crowd.

Lu Yong's seal marked the draw schedule and the placement rules. Every round-of-sixteen loser would enter an eight-person placement bracket. Four would advance, then two. Those two would secure the remaining recruitment places and fight to decide ninth and tenth.

Sima Lan stood close enough to read over Shi Feng's shoulder.

“So a first loss doesn't end the top-ten route,” Sima Lan said.

“For any of the eight,” Shi Feng replied.

She nodded. The rule offered no private advantage to a princess. It offered the same hard path to everyone who would fall in the next round.

At sunset, the candidates' gate closed behind the final scores.

Shi Feng put his plate into the everyday bag beside the tower badge. The little shoulder joint from the equipment court sat wrapped below them, waiting for a quiet hour when he could study how it had broken.

He had qualified, passed his examination and returned a dead man's belongings. The day had contained enough useful work.

At the inn, Kang Liu asked whether he wanted his usual table.

Shi Feng nodded and sat near the back.

Outside, people argued over the sixteen names until the kitchen shutters closed. Upstairs, a lamp remained lit over the small practice furnace.

Before the draw, candidates had to confirm that they would remain in the field. Zhou Ke had repeated the deadline twice. Shi Feng marked it beside the appointment in his bag, then returned to checking the sword edge.

Tomorrow would bring the draw.

chapters.title: The Champion's Reward, Given Early
chapters.html:
Before the twenty-seven candidates could disperse from the notice court, Mu Shuyun stepped down from the sect pavilion onto the central dais.

Every conversation around the score board died at once. Shi Feng stopped beside Duan Yichen near the eastern pillar as the Hundred Flower Valley delegate held up a jade recruitment token stamped with the Valley's inner-court seal.

“Ling Qingzhu of Great Liang,” Mu Shuyun said, her voice carrying clearly across the packed court and spectator galleries. “Your peak Foundation Establishment sword control, your thirty-five steps on the Pressure Stair, and your first-place clearance of the Illusion Garden have met our inner court's standard ahead of the bracket.”

A sharp gasp ran through the candidates and the watching kingdom delegations.

“By right of the Three Sects Charter,” Mu Shuyun declared, “Hundred Flower Valley offers you direct inner-disciple entry today—the same standing granted to the tournament champion.”

Ling Qingzhu's fingers tightened together beneath her sleeve.

It was the privilege the champion would earn through the bracket, offered through a sect's separate recruitment judgment. Hundred Flower Valley could make such an invitation without declaring her champion or inventing a final placing.

The choice came with a condition.

“Our returning party leaves in the morning,” Mu Shuyun said. “You would withdraw before the draw and travel with it. Your place goes to the next eligible trial rank under the announced rule.”

“Why leave before the tournament ends?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“The teaching elder for your sword course returns with that party,” Mu Shuyun replied. “I remain to finish our recruitment here. If you accept this offer, I'd rather you begin with the proper teacher than wait in the audience for several more days.”

Ling Qingzhu nodded slowly.

Mu Shuyun didn't speak about secret grades or an extraordinary foundation she couldn't have identified. She described the training available, the entry terms and the conduct she had personally observed.

That made the opportunity easier to trust.

It didn't make leaving easier.

“May I have a little time?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

“Until the withdrawal desk closes tonight,” Mu Shuyun replied. “Enough to think. Not enough to hold a place you don't intend to use.”

Ling Qingzhu walked back through the court with the written offer folded in her hand.

Ling Rong met her at the gate. When he read the seal, his first reaction was open relief.

“Inner court,” Ling Rong said. “The clan will be pleased.”

“I know,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

“The court can't arrange a Great Sect disciple's marriage as if she were still waiting in our capital,” Ling Rong added. “The consort's people will have to leave those papers unanswered now.”

She looked at him.

The steward stopped. His relief wasn't false. Neither was hers.

This was the road she'd intended to find beyond the registered marriage. Once she entered the Valley, her clan's tempted elders and the royal household couldn't simply resume the old matchmaking through delayed permits and obligated gifts.

The political shield had done its work.

She'd once imagined how freely she would breathe when that happened. Now she held the offer and wanted to go back to a small courtyard whose gate he no longer opened for her.

Winning her escape hadn't kept the home she came to want.

“I want to learn there,” Ling Qingzhu said.

Ling Rong bowed his head.

“Then I'll arrange the luggage,” Ling Rong replied.

“After I confirm,” Ling Qingzhu said.

She wanted one decision left in her own hands until she had actually made it.

The offer reached the delegates before it reached the betting halls.

Wei Chengyuan set his cup down with a small click.

“A direct inner place before the bracket,” Wei Chengyuan said. “You value your discretion generously.”

Mu Shuyun remained calm.

“She demonstrated what we need for the available training,” Mu Shuyun replied. “The Valley's rules permit the offer.”

“She didn't win the trials,” Wei Chengyuan said.

“I didn't give her a trial victory,” Mu Shuyun replied.

He Zhen looked between them and returned to the puppet component he was repairing.

“Then the seventeenth candidate gets work tomorrow,” He Zhen said.

That plain consequence ended the useful part of the argument. Wei Chengyuan could dislike the choice. He couldn't make another sect's invitation count as a false tournament result.

Around the notice court, the crowd erupted in disbelief:

“Direct inner-disciple entry before the round of sixteen even begins!”

“That's the champion's reward, handed out in public before a single bracket match!”

“Great Liang lost its crown prince in disgrace and still produced Hundred Flower Valley's top recruit!”

Across the court, Ling Qingzhu looked past the congratulating officials toward the eastern pillar where Shi Feng stood with Duan Yichen. Shi Feng gave her a single composed nod of acknowledgment—no warmer and no colder than any fellow contender's—and turned with Duan Yichen toward the exit gate before the crowd could press around him.

At the withdrawal desk, Ling Qingzhu read the declaration before signing.

No final placing. No place in the remaining bracket. Her qualification acknowledged, her withdrawal voluntary, the replacement determined by the posted trial order.

She signed her name.

Zhou Ke checked the Valley offer, pressed the official seal beside her signature and gave her a copy.

“Your plate remains a travel record,” Zhou Ke said. “It no longer admits you to the fighting passage.”

“I understand,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

She took it back and stood outside the desk for a moment.

The choice was made.

She checked the departure time once more, then asked the clerk where her clan steward should send the luggage list. There were still ordinary arrangements to finish. Choosing a teacher had not packed the cases or told Hongxiu which carriage would carry them.

At the reporting table, an attendant removed Ling Qingzhu's name plate from the bracket tray. The empty position was marked for the next eligible trial result, and the candidates crowded closer to see which name would replace hers. Zhou Ke kept one hand over the tray until the withdrawal seal dried.

“Read the replacement notice before arguing,” Zhou Ke said.

The nearest youth shut his mouth. He had already begun calculating whether the new opponent would be easier. The announcement changed more than one person's hopes, and none of them had asked Ling Qingzhu what the choice cost her.

There was still someone she wanted to speak with before morning.

She put the folded declaration beside the offer and turned toward the inn street, keeping her white veil in place as the first lamps brightened over the road.

chapters.title: What She Asked Before Leaving
chapters.html:
Sima Lan visited the inn shortly after dinner.

She stayed in the corridor because Shi Feng was packing his practice furnace and the room had little space left around the case. Her Moon Lake robe caught the light from the stair lamp.

“My brother leaves for Great Liang after the healers permit travel,” Sima Lan said. “Jin Jian has written the report.”

“Good,” Shi Feng replied.

“He had a visitor before the report went,” Sima Lan said.

“Wei Chengyuan,” Shi Feng replied.

She looked at him, then nodded.

“So you heard,” Sima Lan said.

“An attendant asked about Yunze,” Shi Feng replied.

Sima Lan rested one hand on the railing.

“I don't know exactly what he gave the delegate,” Sima Lan said. “Don't assume the public notice made him quiet.”

“I haven't assumed that,” Shi Feng replied.

She accepted the answer without trying to turn the warning into a debt. After a brief pause, she stepped toward the stairs.

“We'll have the draw tomorrow,” Sima Lan said.

“Yes,” Shi Feng replied.

She left just as footsteps sounded below.

Ling Qingzhu saw the pale blue Moon Lake robe before she saw Shi Feng.

Sima Lan paused on the stair to give her room. The younger princess's eyes moved once over the white veil and the folded papers in Ling Qingzhu's hand.

“Fairy Ling,” Sima Lan said.

“Princess Sima,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

The greetings were faultlessly polite.

That made the tightness in Ling Qingzhu's chest seem even less reasonable. Sima Lan had done nothing more than visit a fellow candidate. Shi Feng had no obligation to explain who stood in his corridor.

Knowing that didn't prevent the feeling.

Sima Lan continued downstairs. Ling Qingzhu watched the Moon Lake robe disappear around the turn, then looked toward the half-open door.

Shi Feng stood inside it with a furnace cloth in his hand.

“Fairy Ling,” Shi Feng said.

“I accepted the Valley offer,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“I heard about it,” Shi Feng replied. “Congratulations.”

“Thank you,” Ling Qingzhu said.

She held the papers more tightly than they needed. The written declaration had felt simple at the desk. Here, one step from a room he had chosen without her, every part of it seemed difficult to place in words.

“Our party leaves in the morning,” Ling Qingzhu said.

Shi Feng nodded.

He didn't ask whether she had arranged luggage or food. Once, he would have checked both before she remembered to worry. She knew why he didn't now, and missed it anyway.

“I wanted to ask you something,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Go on,” Shi Feng replied.

She looked past him at the small room. One bed. A table. His sword beside the wall. The furnace case nearly packed.

No screen between a bed and a floor mat.

“Should I refuse it?” Ling Qingzhu asked. “Stay until the end, and follow you to whichever sect you choose?”

Shi Feng's hand stopped on the cloth.

He looked at the Valley seal in her hand.

“Don't give up a good teacher,” Shi Feng said.

His voice was flat, like advice to someone he had only recently met.

Ling Qingzhu lowered her eyes.

He hadn't asked her to leave. He hadn't asked her to stay. She had offered to place her next road beside his, and he had returned the choice to her own cultivation.

It was fair.

She wished fairness didn't feel so cold.

“I see,” Ling Qingzhu said.

Shi Feng folded the furnace cloth once and set it on the case. He didn't fill the silence with a gentler sentence that would make the first one untrue.

Below them, Kang Liu called to the kitchen for a clean cup. A door opened farther down the corridor, then closed again.

Ling Qingzhu glanced toward the stairs where Sima Lan had passed. Shi Feng picked up the furnace cloth and checked a worn corner. He offered no account of the princess's visit.

She slipped the papers beneath her sleeve.

“I hope your next match goes well,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“Thank you,” Shi Feng replied. “Travel safely.”

She nodded.

Her hand lifted a little, then lowered before reaching the doorframe. There was no reason to touch the wood merely because he stood on the other side of it.

She went downstairs.

Shi Feng remained by the open door until he heard the gate.

Then he closed it halfway, as it had been before she arrived, and sat beside the furnace case.

He didn't call after her on the stairs. The choice was hers, and his own road tomorrow started on the fighting platform.

He checked the outer clasp twice and left the open case beside the table.

Kang Liu passed the open doorway carrying a lamp. He stopped when he saw the furnace case still across the floor.

“Is that leaving tomorrow too?” Kang Liu asked.

“Not tomorrow,” Shi Feng said. “The fittings need checking before I take it on another road.”

The innkeeper nodded and moved on. Shi Feng unpacked the top tray, separated the cracked spacer from the sound ones and wrote its size on a scrap. Remembered alchemy experience could guide his flame. It couldn't keep a loose furnace fitting in place. He would buy the small replacement before the draw.

He returned the sound pieces to their slots and tied the tray down. When he lifted the case again, nothing rattled. He set it beneath the table and washed the dust from his hands before putting out the lamp.

In the courtyard, Hongxiu waited beside the carriage.

Ling Qingzhu stopped before entering it. The night air shifted the edge of her white veil, and she held it steady with two fingers.

Hongxiu didn't ask whether he had invited her to stay. The papers were still in her sleeve, and the answer showed in the way she stood.

“The luggage is ready,” Hongxiu said.

“Thank you,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

She climbed into the carriage and sat with both hands in her lap.

After a while, she took out a narrow violet ribbon from the small inner pocket beside her belt.

She smoothed it once over her fingers.

There was one thing she hadn't asked yet.

chapters.title: The Violet Ribbon
chapters.html:
The Valley carriages gathered at the southern gate before the shops opened.

A teaching elder checked the travel list beneath a lantern while disciples loaded the final cases. The early air was cool enough for breath to show beside the horses' noses.

Shi Feng arrived on foot.

He wore the blue cloak Ling Qingzhu had chosen for him. Its fastening stayed clear of his sword hand, exactly as she had intended when she checked it on the road. The plain refined artifact sword hung at his waist, its grip newly wrapped and its scabbard worn along the lower edge.

Ling Qingzhu saw the cloak first.

For a moment, she forgot the folded travel declaration in her hand.

Then Hongxiu moved aside, and there was no one between them.

“Fairy Ling,” Shi Feng said.

“Shi Feng,” Ling Qingzhu replied.

Her white veil remained across her face. The repaired silver clasp held her black hair, and a travelling robe lay beneath the cloak she had drawn close against the cold.

Neither stepped near enough to touch.

“The party is ready?” Shi Feng asked.

“Almost,” Ling Qingzhu replied. “One ingredient chest had the wrong seal. They found it before loading.”

He nodded. An ordinary delay, fixed by someone doing their work carefully.

She wished she had something else equally ordinary to tell him. That the roof at the last inn had leaked. That Hongxiu had packed too many hairpins. That Ling Rong had somehow argued with the same driver twice without learning to lower his voice.

Any of those things might once have made him smile.

Now she couldn't find a reason to keep him beside the carriage while she tried.

“I brought something,” Ling Qingzhu said.

She took the violet ribbon from her sleeve.

It rested across her palm, narrow and soft from use. He recognized it immediately. The colour belonged to evenings when he had still looked too long at her hair and she had pretended his staring annoyed her more than it did.

Ling Qingzhu held it out.

“Would you keep it?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

Shi Feng looked at the ribbon.

His hand didn't rise.

Taking a token from her hand at the carriage step would be a promise to wait for the next road to join. He had no such promise to give.

“Keep it,” Shi Feng said evenly. “You kept it this long.”

Ling Qingzhu's fingers closed slowly.

“I thought you might,” Ling Qingzhu said, then stopped.

Shi Feng waited without asking her to finish.

She folded the ribbon once and put it back beneath her sleeve. The care she took with it hurt more than if she'd pulled it away in anger.

“All right,” Ling Qingzhu said.

Ling Rong approached with the final travel papers. He glanced at Shi Feng, then kept his attention on Ling Qingzhu.

“The elder is ready,” Ling Rong said. “Your family copies are packed with Hongxiu's case.”

Ling Qingzhu accepted the papers. One sheet concerned her Valley entry. Another recorded the clan's travel arrangements. None dissolved the marriage registered in Great Liang.

Their temporary private terms and later extensions had not become a public divorce merely because they slept in separate inns and chose different roads.

She and Shi Feng were still husband and wife in the register.

Neither used the fact to demand anything here.

Ling Rong withdrew after a careful bow. He didn't try to make them say a warmer farewell for the sake of the servants watching.

The departure clerk checked the Valley seal against the travel list. Two porters counted the trunks and closed the luggage rack. The reporting office kept a copy of Ling Qingzhu's withdrawal; her tournament place would be filled before the new draw. A second wagon waited for the first to clear the gate. Its driver rested the reins across his knees and watched the clerk finish.

Hongxiu climbed into the second carriage and closed the case beside her feet.

The teaching elder called for the last passengers.

“Will you write after the final?” Ling Qingzhu asked.

Shi Feng looked toward the travel list, then back at her.

“I don't know where I'll be staying afterward,” Shi Feng replied.

It was true, and not the whole answer. She heard both parts.

“The reporting hall can forward a letter to the Valley,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“I understand,” Shi Feng replied.

He didn't promise one. She didn't ask again.

For a few breaths, they stood with the small space between them unchanged. The horses shifted. A porter secured a rope over the last chest and checked the knot with both hands.

Ling Qingzhu looked at the cloak fastening once more.

It was still exactly where she'd placed it.

“Take care of yourself,” Ling Qingzhu said.

“You too, Fairy Ling,” Shi Feng replied.

He stepped aside so she could reach the carriage.

Ling Qingzhu climbed the narrow step and paused with one hand on the frame. If he called her name, she would turn. She knew it with a clarity that left no room to pretend otherwise.

He didn't call.

She entered and sat beside the window. Her fingers found the ribbon beneath her sleeve before the curtain was lowered.

Shi Feng gave the teaching elder a courteous nod and turned toward the inner street.

He didn't stand at the gate to watch the carriages.

The first wheel began moving after he had passed the grain shop. He heard the harness bells, then Hongxiu's voice answering a driver. He kept walking until the sounds joined the rest of the waking city.

The blue cloak moved against his sword hilt.

He left it fastened.

At the reporting hall, Zhou Ke was checking the eligible replacement against the final trial sheet.

Cen Ruchen's name stood at seventeenth. Sima Lan remained the original sixteenth qualifier. Ling Qingzhu's withdrawal had opened a place under the rule every candidate had heard before the trials.

No one had yet drawn the new bracket.

Shi Feng stopped at the public water trough and washed the cold from his fingers. His mid Foundation Establishment qi remained steady beneath the cloak. The sword at his waist was plain, worn and fully usable.

He had a match to prepare for.

When he lifted his head, the candidates' gate was opening.

Shi Feng walked toward it without looking back at the road beyond the southern wall.

chapters.title: The Draw of Sixteen
chapters.html:
“Trial rank seventeen, Cen Ruchen,” Lu Yong announced. “Step forward.”

A young swordsman in dark blue robes walked through the waiting candidates. His late Foundation Establishment aura was carefully restrained, but he couldn't hide his excitement.

The previous evening, seventeenth place meant going home. This morning, Ling Qingzhu's withdrawal left a place in the main bracket.

Cen Ruchen didn't need anyone to explain how valuable that was.

Lu Yong checked the swordsman's plate against the trial list. Then he turned toward the stands.

“The replacement rule was announced before the trials,” Lu Yong said. “Cen Ruchen takes the withdrawn place. He enters under the same rules as everyone else.”

A few spectators looked toward the empty section beneath Great Liang's banner. Rumours about Hundred Flower Valley's early offer were already spreading through Qingyun City.

Shi Feng stood beside the passage and watched the official hand over the new token. He didn't look for a white veil among the candidates.

She'd left.

Knowing that didn't stop him noticing the space where she usually stood.

He thought, Look at the board. The carriage isn't coming back because I stare at an empty seat.

Duan Yichen approached with his heavy sabre resting against his shoulder. His expression was unusually cheerful for someone who spent the morning waiting to learn his next opponent.

“Sixteen people left,” Duan Yichen said. “Now nobody can complain about fighting a nobody.”

“They'll find another complaint,” Shi Feng replied.

“True,” Duan Yichen said. “I heard one man blame his boots for the Pressure Stair.”

“Did they climb without him?” Shi Feng asked.

Duan Yichen laughed. He stopped beside Shi Feng without asking whether a kingdom's third qualifier deserved the company. After the trials, such questions sounded especially foolish.

Sima Lan waited a short distance away. She wore Moon Lake Sect robes, and her late Foundation Establishment qi remained steady beneath them. The princess's trial token carried the sixteenth position.

She qualified before Ling Qingzhu withdrew. Nobody had given her the new place.

She noticed several people examining her token and raised it slightly.

“Read carefully,” Sima Lan said. “Sixteen isn't seventeen.”

A nearby candidate looked embarrassed and turned toward the board.

Shi Feng almost smiled. The princess knew exactly which insult she wanted to stop before it became gossip.

The first draw slips reached the board beneath the three sect banners. An attendant called each pair while Lu Yong checked the order.

Shi Feng's name appeared beside Lu Ting of Great Wu.

The late Foundation Establishment cultivator looked across the waiting area at once. Lu Ting's face tightened, but he didn't protest. At this point, complaining about a difficult draw would only make him look afraid.

Duan Yichen leaned toward the board.

“That's yours,” Duan Yichen said.

“I can read,” Shi Feng replied.

“I'm offering encouragement,” Duan Yichen said.

“You should offer it to him,” Shi Feng replied.

The sabre user laughed again. Lu Ting heard it and looked away sharply.

The next pair placed Xiahou Lie against Han Zhuo, a prince of Great Han. The body cultivator rolled his shoulders and grinned. His opponent immediately asked an attendant whether defensive armor counted as a refined artifact.

“It does,” Zhou Ke answered. “Use whatever the rules permit. Don't ask me to wear it for you.”

Han Zhuo stopped asking.

Gongsun Ce faced Cen Ruchen, the newly admitted royal swordsman of Great Wei. The prince's gaze moved briefly over his opponent's sword before returning to the puppet case beside his feet.

Cao Zhenyu, another prince of Great Wei, drew Chu Ning of Great Chu. Both men looked pleased, which meant one would soon be disappointed.

Bai Chenxi's name appeared beside Sima Lan.

The princess's fingers paused on her token. Bai Chenxi stood beneath the far awning, calm and pale, with frost gathering briefly around her sword guard.

That wouldn't be an easy match.

Sima Lan put the token away without changing her expression.

The sixth pair placed Tan He of Qingya Sword Sect against Qi Yuan of Great Qi. Yuan Kuang of Great Qin faced Zhou Yan of Great Zhou in the seventh.

Then the final slip appeared.

Gu Zhan against Duan Yichen.

Duan Yichen stared at the board. His cheerful expression changed into a long silence.

Shi Feng looked at him.

“Encouragement?” Shi Feng asked.

Duan Yichen lowered the sabre from his shoulder.

“Give me a moment,” Duan Yichen replied.

Across the waiting area, Gu Zhan lifted his spear and waved enthusiastically. The single clear eye on his scarred face was bright with interest.

“A sabre!” Gu Zhan called. “Good! Don't spend the whole match running!”

Duan Yichen looked at Shi Feng again.

“I hadn't planned to,” Duan Yichen said.

“Now?” Shi Feng asked.

“Still no,” Duan Yichen replied, straightening. “But I might regret it.”

Lu Yong waited until the crowd finished reacting before raising his hand.

“One more rule needs repeating,” Lu Yong said. “The eight defeated candidates will enter the placement bracket. Every one of them.”

Sima Lan looked up immediately.

“Eight become four,” Lu Yong continued. “Four become two. Those two earn the remaining recruitment places. They will then fight for ninth and tenth.”

Duan Yichen's grip loosened slightly around his sabre.

Losing the main match wouldn't end every chance. It also wouldn't excuse a careless fight. The placement opponents would be the same people who survived both opening rounds and the sect trials.

“You don't receive tenth because you qualified sixteenth,” Lu Yong said. “You don't receive it because your family sent a letter either. Earn it.”

Sima Lan's expression didn't change. Several spectators who were looking at her abruptly found the main bracket more interesting.

Cen Ruchen listened with open relief. Even the replacement candidate would have the same second route as everyone else.

The rules weren't comfortable. They were clear.

Shi Feng preferred that.

The candidates separated to prepare. Duan Yichen checked the edge of his sabre, then looked toward Gu Zhan again.

The spear user was practising a short thrust beside a pillar. An attendant moved the flowerpot from its path before a second thrust could break it.

“He really only thinks about fighting,” Duan Yichen said.

“You're giving him what he wants,” Shi Feng replied.

“Then he'd better remember it,” Duan Yichen said. “I'll make him use that spear properly.”

Shi Feng nodded. He didn't offer a secret technique or promise to avenge a sporting defeat. Duan Yichen wanted to test himself, and there was nothing foolish about that.

“Come find me afterward,” Shi Feng said. “Unless you're too busy blaming your boots.”

Duan Yichen grinned.

“I'll blame the draw first,” Duan Yichen replied.

Lu Ting came toward the entrance while they were speaking. His hand rested on his sword, but he didn't draw it in the passage.

“I watched your second round,” Lu Ting said to Shi Feng.

“Then you know where the platform is,” Shi Feng replied.

“I know the Crown Prince used a forbidden pill,” Lu Ting said. “I don't carry one.”

“Good,” Shi Feng answered.

Lu Ting looked toward the protective pillars around the arena. The officials hadn't removed them after Sima Yu's violation. Nobody could pretend the rules would become weaker for a less important family.

“I'll fight properly,” Lu Ting said. “Don't expect me to surrender before drawing.”

Shi Feng nodded. That was a much better opening than another speech about kingdom rank.

“Then draw when the bell rings,” Shi Feng said.

Lu Ting moved into the passage. Duan Yichen watched him go and shrugged.

“At least he won't blame the boots,” Duan Yichen said.

The bell rang above the platforms. Zhou Ke lifted the first match token.

“Shi Feng. Lu Ting. Enter,” Zhou Ke called.

Shi Feng checked his plain sword once and stepped toward the passage. Behind him, the newly finished bracket board caught the morning light.

Sixteen names remained. He intended to leave one at the top.

chapters.title: Round of Sixteen
chapters.html:
“Begin,” Lu Yong said.

Lu Ting drew his sword with both hands. Late Foundation Establishment qi spread along the edge as Great Wu's Rapid Wind opening sent three attacks toward Shi Feng's throat, ribs, and leading knee.

Shi Feng turned the first aside with a short parry. He caught the second near the hilt and stepped past the low third cut. The three exchanges rang across the platform without either man losing the centre.

Lu Ting changed the rhythm immediately.

His fourth attack came from below. The fifth followed the retreating blade instead of its owner. Shi Feng blocked both, but the sixth carried a sudden shoulder turn that brought the edge toward his head from the opposite side.

He ducked and answered with a straight thrust.

Lu Ting's guard closed around it.

The seventh exchange became a contest at close range. Lu Ting pressed the trapped blade downward while moving his leading foot across Shi Feng's retreat. Shi Feng turned out of the lock before the eighth stroke could follow him.

The Great Wu swordsman didn't chase. He shortened his stance and used his third variation.

Shi Feng's expression sharpened. The man's qi was stronger than his own visible stage, but the changing sword rhythm was the more useful part. Each variation prepared a different return instead of simply adding force to the first opening.

On the ninth exchange, Lu Ting covered the obvious path to his wrist.

On the tenth, his blade swept back through the space Shi Feng expected it to leave.

Silver light cut across Shi Feng's left sleeve.

Cloth split from elbow to cuff, and a thin line of blood welled across his forearm where the edge grazed his skin. The hanging strip fell onto the stone between them.

The crowd cried out.

Lu Ting pressed forward before his opponent could reset the guard.

Shi Feng changed methods.

Piercing Current drove through the narrow opening beneath the advancing sword. Lu Ting twisted his guard across it, but Shi Feng's wrist was already turning into Turning Wave.

The twelfth exchange forced Great Wu's swordsman half a pace off line. He recovered with a heavy cross-cut, aiming to regain the centre before the next thrust.

Returning Tide drew Shi Feng's blade back an inch and hooked the crossguard wide.

Lu Ting's chest opened.

Shi Feng stepped inside on the fourteenth exchange and planted his palm against it. The Great Wu candidate flew backward over the boundary. His sword struck the outer flagstones beside him.

“Shi Feng wins,” Lu Yong declared.

The stands roared.

“Fourteen exchanges!”

“Lu Ting drew blood!”

“He made him change sword methods!”

“And that returning hook still broke the guard!”

Shi Feng checked the torn cloth before sheathing his weapon. The shallow cut along his forearm had already stopped bleeding against his golden bone, leaving a narrow red stain on the cuff. Lu Ting's final return had been worth taking seriously.

The defeated swordsman stood slowly and picked up his blade. He looked disappointed, but nobody could say he'd fallen without showing his skill.

Duan Yichen waited in the passage with two cups of water.

“All three variations,” Duan Yichen said. “I thought the first six strokes were his whole opening.”

“The return cut was good,” Shi Feng replied, accepting a cup.

Duan Yichen glanced at the bloodied sleeve and nodded.

Bai Chenxi and Sima Lan entered soon afterward.

The princess opened carefully. Her late Foundation Establishment qi settled around her feet before her sword moved. Moon Lake Sect's method gave her a light first step and a quick second cut.

Bai Chenxi met both without retreating.

Pale frost formed along the stone. Her sword crossed Sima Lan's guard and forced the princess to change direction before finishing the next strike.

Shi Feng watched from beneath the awning. Sima Lan understood the difference in their control. She wasn't wasting qi trying to overpower a stronger opponent in the first three exchanges.

She drew Bai Chenxi toward the edge, turned, and attacked from the narrow side.

For an instant, the opening looked good.

Then frost spread beneath her leading foot.

Sima Lan stopped herself from slipping, but the correction cost her the attack. Bai Chenxi's frost-edged sword grazed her already stiff shoulder, splitting the cloth with a shallow, freezing cut before halting against her collarbone.

“I surrender,” Sima Lan said.

Bai Chenxi withdrew at once.

The princess bowed stiffly and left the platform. She was angry at losing, but not foolish enough to mistake the result for an injustice.

Her chance at recruitment now depended on the placement bracket.

She passed Shi Feng in the corridor and noticed him watching the next match.

“You won't offer comfort?” Sima Lan asked.

“You'd charge for listening,” Shi Feng replied.

Her mouth curved briefly.

“Only if the advice was poor,” Sima Lan said.

“Then win the next ones,” Shi Feng replied.

She nodded once and continued toward the treatment rooms. The frost-stiffened cut on her shoulder wasn't the part of the defeat that troubled her.

The remaining matches moved quickly.

Xiahou Lie battered Han Zhuo's shield aside and carried the Great Han prince over the boundary with one shoulder strike. The body cultivator laughed while his opponent complained that the shield was bent.

Gongsun Ce's first puppet pinned Cen Ruchen's sword. The second stopped a wooden fist beside the swordsman's temple. The replacement candidate surrendered before discovering how hard that fist could hit.

Cao Zhenyu defeated Chu Ning after a long exchange near the boundary. Tan He caught Qi Yuan's wrist with the flat of his blade and forced a surrender. Yuan Kuang swept Zhou Yan's weapon from his hands, then stood waiting until the defeated man admitted what everyone could see.

Six places among the final eight were settled.

Shi Feng kept his attention on the last pair.

Duan Yichen rolled his wrist and walked onto the platform. Gu Zhan came from the opposite passage carrying his spear across both shoulders.

“Use the heavy cut!” Gu Zhan called. “The one you practised before the draw!”

Duan Yichen stopped.

“You watched that?” Duan Yichen asked.

“It looked good,” Gu Zhan replied. “Don't make it worse now!”

The sabre user laughed despite his tension. He drew the blade and lowered his stance.

Lu Yong announced the start.

Duan Yichen attacked immediately. His sabre descended with a heavy arc of qi meant to close the space on both sides. Gu Zhan didn't retreat. The spear slid beneath the descending blade and lifted at the exact point where the force thinned.

The sabre passed over his shoulder.

Duan Yichen turned the failed cut into a second strike. Gu Zhan grinned and stepped inside it.

A short blow from the spear shaft struck Duan Yichen's ribs. He staggered, caught himself, and raised his sabre again.

“Good!” Gu Zhan shouted.

His next thrust stopped beneath Duan Yichen's chin.

The sabre user looked down at the point and slowly lowered his weapon.

“I surrender,” Duan Yichen said.

Gu Zhan withdrew the spear with obvious disappointment.

“The second cut was better,” Gu Zhan said. “Why don't you start with that?”

“Because I wanted a second cut,” Duan Yichen replied.

Gu Zhan considered that seriously, then nodded as though receiving useful advice.

Shi Feng smiled beneath the awning. The spear user wasn't mocking his opponent. He really wanted the fight to last longer.

Duan Yichen walked back holding his side. Shi Feng offered the water this time, and the sabre user accepted without pretending the blow didn't hurt.

“That was fast,” Duan Yichen said.

“Yes,” Shi Feng replied.

“You could lie a little,” Duan Yichen said.

“You could duck a little,” Shi Feng answered.

Duan Yichen laughed, then winced and pressed a hand against his ribs.

Shi Feng took out an ordinary recovery pill from his own stock. It wasn't a failed pill or a secret medicine. He put it in the sabre user's hand.

“Take it,” Shi Feng said. “You'll need your ribs for the placement matches.”

Duan Yichen looked at the pill, then at him.

“I'll pay you back,” Duan Yichen said.

“Fight properly first,” Shi Feng replied.

The sabre user swallowed it and sat beneath the awning. His respect had become something easier than another discussion of rank or profit.

Shi Feng didn't mind that.

Above the passage, attendants changed the board. Eight names remained in the main bracket, and eight moved to the lower placement list.

Gu Zhan stood beneath both boards, practising the thrust that ended his match.

He looked delighted with the whole morning.

chapters.title: Top Eight
chapters.html:
“Eight names,” Zhou Ke said, fixing the new board in place. “Don't crowd the passage.”

The candidates crowded it anyway.

Shi Feng stood far enough away to read without being pushed. His next opponent was Xiahou Lie. Beside them, Gongsun Ce faced Cao Zhenyu. Bai Chenxi would fight Tan He, and Gu Zhan drew Yuan Kuang.

The quarter-finals were settled.

Duan Yichen stood beside him, one hand still resting on his bruised ribs. The recovery pill had helped, but he wasn't foolish enough to believe a fresh injury vanished because he disliked it.

“Xiahou Lie,” Duan Yichen said. “He'll want you to hit him.”

“That's convenient,” Shi Feng replied.

“He might ask you to do it again,” Duan Yichen added.

“Then he should stay on the platform,” Shi Feng said.

The sabre user laughed quietly and checked the lower board. His own placement opponent was Qi Yuan. Sima Lan would face Han Zhuo, while Lu Ting drew Chu Ning and Cen Ruchen drew Zhou Yan.

Nobody could enter the final ten merely by pointing at the main bracket.

They still had work to do.

By afternoon, the surviving eight couldn't cross the waiting courtyard without receiving an invitation.

Yuan Kuang accepted Martial Palace's congratulations with the ease of someone who expected them. Gongsun Ce listened to He Zhen while checking the joint of a puppet's wrist. Bai Chenxi spoke quietly with Mu Shuyun beneath the shade.

Xiahou Lie asked whether the sect kitchens served enough meat.

Shi Feng found that the most useful question of the day.

Wei Chengyuan stopped him beside the outer gate. The Martial Palace delegate's late Golden Core aura was concealed, but the surrounding attendants stepped aside without needing a gesture.

“You've done well,” Wei Chengyuan said.

Shi Feng nodded politely.

“The tournament hasn't finished,” Shi Feng replied.

“Which is why it's sensible to think ahead,” Wei Chengyuan said. “Martial Palace rewards ability. Your sword deserves proper teaching.”

Shi Feng thought of the worn journal he'd returned to He Zhen. Xu Changhe's teaching already proved useful against stronger-looking opponents. He wasn't going to dismiss it because another sect wore finer robes.

“I'll decide when the choice is offered,” Shi Feng said.

Wei Chengyuan studied him.

“Don't assume an offer waits forever,” Wei Chengyuan said.

“Then don't wait for my answer today,” Shi Feng replied.

The delegate's smile thinned. He stepped aside, allowing the young cultivator to pass.

Duan Yichen waited beyond the gate with a small paper bag of food.

“You refuse powerful people very calmly,” Duan Yichen said.

“I answered a question,” Shi Feng replied.

“He might not think so,” Duan Yichen said.

“Then he'll have something to consider,” Shi Feng answered.

The sabre user offered him a steamed bun. Shi Feng took one and asked about the ribs rather than Martial Palace.

“They'll hold,” Duan Yichen said. “The placement match isn't going to fight itself.”

“Don't ask them to hold a spear again,” Shi Feng replied.

Duan Yichen looked offended, then began laughing before the first bite.

He stopped when Shi Feng pointed at the angle of his wrist.

“Your second cut was good,” Shi Feng said. “You kept turning after it missed.”

“I wanted to recover the weight,” Duan Yichen replied.

“You offered him your side,” Shi Feng said. “Next time, stop the wrist first. Move your feet before pulling the whole blade back.”

Duan Yichen tried the motion with an empty hand. His expression became serious.

“That would've saved the ribs,” Duan Yichen said.

“Some of them,” Shi Feng replied.

The sabre user grinned and repeated the movement once more before finishing the bun. He wasn't too proud to use advice that made sense.

He Zhen found Shi Feng near the inn later that day. The Artificer Hall delegate carried no great gift box, only a folded note and a wooden brush case.

“Xu Changhe's things are safely packed,” He Zhen said.

“Good,” Shi Feng replied.

“The sect will want the location when we return,” He Zhen added.

“I marked it,” Shi Feng said. “You already have the account.”

He Zhen nodded. He didn't ask the young man to swear lifelong service because a dead elder's journal changed hands.

That improved Shi Feng's opinion of him.

“You don't have to choose us because of him,” He Zhen said.

“I know,” Shi Feng replied.

The delegate looked relieved, though a little disappointed. He'd come prepared to say something difficult and found no argument waiting.

Then he noticed the alchemist's new certification token.

“Golden Core medicine at your age,” He Zhen said. “That will make the other invitations louder.”

“It won't make the medicine refine itself,” Shi Feng replied.

He Zhen smiled and left the folded note. It listed the quarter-final time and the official rest period. Nothing about it promised a divine sword or a fortune.

Shi Feng put it away with the other tournament papers.

Gu Zhan didn't notice the invitation waiting beside his door.

He thrust the spear forward, stopped it an inch from the wall, and drew it back. The motion was so direct that a nervous inn servant moved the water jug away before being asked.

Wei Chengyuan stood in the courtyard for three whole thrusts before clearing his throat.

“Gu Zhan,” Wei Chengyuan said.

The spear user turned with obvious interest.

“Do you fight?” Gu Zhan asked.

Wei Chengyuan paused.

“I'm a Martial Palace delegate,” Wei Chengyuan replied.

“That doesn't answer it,” Gu Zhan said.

From beneath the awning, Nie Wufeng laughed into his tea. The old master wore a plain robe and sat with one leg stretched across a second stool.

“Answer him,” Nie Wufeng said. “He'll keep asking otherwise.”

Wei Chengyuan looked from the old man to the one-eyed young cultivator.

“Martial Palace has excellent teachers,” Wei Chengyuan said.

“Good!” Gu Zhan replied. “Do the disciples fight them?”

“Under proper instruction,” Wei Chengyuan said.

“How often?” Gu Zhan asked.

The delegate began explaining a training schedule. Gu Zhan's attention drifted toward his own spear before the second sentence ended.

Nie Wufeng covered another laugh with the cup.

“Tell him after tomorrow,” Nie Wufeng said. “Right now, Yuan Kuang is the only lesson he'll listen to.”

Gu Zhan nodded enthusiastically and returned to the thrust.

Wei Chengyuan stood aside before the spearhead passed his sleeve. The courtyard servant picked the invitation up and placed it safely beneath the water jug.

For once, a Great Sect's offer was mostly useful for keeping paper from blowing away.

chapters.title: The Last Two Places
chapters.html:
“Every match counts,” Lu Yong said. “The main bracket isn't the only road left.”

Eight defeated candidates stood beneath the lower board. Their cultivations hadn't become weaker because they lost. Most could still make an ordinary kingdom clan treat them as honoured guests.

Here, only two would earn recruitment places.

Shi Feng watched from the waiting section while Duan Yichen checked the edge of his sabre. Sima Lan stood farther along the passage with her injured shoulder carefully warmed beneath a cloth.

Neither looked interested in going home with a story about an unlucky draw.

The first four matches ended before noon.

Sima Lan defeated Han Zhuo after drawing his shield out of position. Lu Ting forced Chu Ning across the boundary with a strong sequence of straight cuts. Duan Yichen broke Qi Yuan's rhythm and won without taking another blow to the ribs.

Cen Ruchen defeated Zhou Yan in the longest of the four. The swordsman who entered as the replacement now stood only one victory from a top-ten place.

Lu Yong ordered a rest period before the decisive matches. Nobody objected. Even the loudest spectators could see the sweat on the candidates' faces.

Duan Yichen returned to the awning and accepted water from Shi Feng.

“The wrist first,” Duan Yichen said.

“It helped?” Shi Feng asked.

“Ask Qi Yuan,” Duan Yichen replied.

Shi Feng glanced toward the defeated man rubbing his forearm. The answer was clear enough.

Sima Lan faced Lu Ting in the first qualifying match.

Both were at late Foundation Establishment. Both already lost to someone they couldn't overcome. Now they had an opponent close enough that one careless movement could decide everything.

Lu Ting attacked the princess's injured side.

She expected it. Her first step carried her clear, and Moon Lake Sect's sword method returned a low cut toward his knee.

He blocked and pushed forward again.

The exchange lasted far longer than either wanted. Sima Lan's shoulder weakened each time she raised the blade too high. Lu Ting noticed and pressed harder, forcing her to defend where the injury hurt most.

“She can't keep doing that,” Duan Yichen said quietly.

Shi Feng watched her feet.

“She knows,” Shi Feng replied.

The princess retreated toward the boundary. Several spectators stood, certain the next blow would throw her out.

Lu Ting gathered his qi into a heavy descending cut.

Sima Lan didn't raise her sword to meet it.

She dropped her shoulder, stepped across the line of attack, and let the blade tear her outer sleeve. Her own point drove toward Lu Ting's waist from below.

He twisted away, but the correction placed one foot beyond the boundary.

Sima Lan followed with the flat of her sword.

The blow struck his chest and sent the second foot after the first.

“Out of bounds,” Lu Yong declared. “Sima Lan wins.”

The princess stood with her sword lowered. Blood stained the torn sleeve, and her breathing was rough.

For a moment, she seemed unable to believe the announcement.

Then her fingers tightened around the hilt.

She'd earned a place.

Not because Sima Yu was her brother. Not because a delegate wanted the royal family's gratitude. She fought through the lower bracket and won the decisive match by less than a full step.

Lu Ting sat outside the boundary, furious with himself.

“One step,” Lu Ting muttered.

Sima Lan looked at him, exhausted enough that her usual cold smile didn't appear.

“It was the right one,” Sima Lan replied.

Duan Yichen and Cen Ruchen entered after the next rest bell.

The Great Wei swordsman opened with quick, narrow attacks. Duan Yichen didn't chase them. He kept the sabre close until the lighter blade struck his guard, then stepped sideways before returning the cut.

Shi Feng watched his wrist stop exactly where they discussed.

Better.

Cen Ruchen gave ground and tried to draw him into a longer exchange. The sabre user let him retreat twice, then changed the timing of the third step.

The heavy blade struck the sword aside.

Cen Ruchen's hand trembled. Before his guard recovered, Duan Yichen's shoulder drove into him and pushed him beyond the boundary.

The sabre user didn't follow with another strike.

“Duan Yichen wins,” Lu Yong announced.

Duan Yichen stared at the official, then laughed in open relief.

He'd lost to Gu Zhan in a few exchanges. Now he stood among the final ten.

The defeat hadn't ended his road.

Shi Feng met him beside the passage. Duan Yichen raised a fist, and Shi Feng tapped it once with his own.

“Properly fought,” Shi Feng said.

“I'll accept that,” Duan Yichen replied. “Before you mention the ribs again.”

Ninth and tenth still needed ordering.

Lu Yong gave both surviving candidates time to recover. Sima Lan accepted treatment for the shoulder but refused to withdraw from the final placement match.

“I came this far,” Sima Lan said.

Duan Yichen waited without arguing. There was no pleasure in asking an exhausted opponent to concede before she tried.

When the bell rang, he fought seriously.

Sima Lan's footwork remained sharp. Her body couldn't follow it with the same speed. The injury and three hard matches had taken too much from her.

Duan Yichen stopped her first combination, turned the second aside, and caught her sword against the weight of his sabre.

She tried to move clear. Her shoulder failed before the blade did.

The sabre's flat touched her ribs.

“I surrender,” Sima Lan said, breathing hard.

Duan Yichen withdrew at once.

“Duan Yichen, ninth,” Lu Yong declared. “Sima Lan, tenth.”

The princess closed her eyes briefly. Tenth wasn't the splendid placing her family once expected from the royal children.

It was enough to keep choosing her own road.

She bowed to Duan Yichen and left the platform under her own strength.

Shi Feng watched the new ranks appear beneath the eight quarter-finalists. The recruitment list was complete, but the championship remained undecided.

Xiahou Lie slapped his own chest beside the next passage.

“Your turn!” Xiahou Lie called to Shi Feng. “Come hit something that won't fall over so quickly!”

Shi Feng turned toward the body cultivator.

“Stay inside the boundary first,” Shi Feng replied.

chapters.title: The Iron Buddha
chapters.html:
“Put the sword away,” Xiahou Lie said.

Shi Feng stopped at the centre of the platform and looked at the body cultivator opposite him. Xiahou Lie wore a sleeveless dark robe, and his bare arms were thick enough to make most weapon sellers nervous.

Late Foundation Establishment qi moved through them steadily.

“Why?” Shi Feng asked.

“If it breaks, you might blame me,” Xiahou Lie said.

Shi Feng looked at his plain refined artifact sword. Its quality was ordinary. There was no reason to test its edge against a man who clearly preferred being struck with heavier things.

He placed the sword beside the platform entrance.

Xiahou Lie's grin grew.

“Good!” Xiahou Lie said. “That's how a proper body cultivator fights!”

“I didn't say I was one,” Shi Feng replied.

“Your hands did,” Xiahou Lie said.

Shi Feng glanced at them. There were no visible golden traces and no reason for the man to understand what lay beneath his skin.

Xiahou Lie simply recognised strength.

That was harmless enough.

Lu Yong checked that both stood inside the marks, then raised one hand.

“Begin,” Lu Yong said.

Xiahou Lie came forward like a charging beast. His feet struck the stone heavily, and his fist carried a thick layer of qi straight toward Shi Feng's chest.

Shi Feng raised his palm.

The impact cracked across the arena.

Dust lifted around their feet. Xiahou Lie's grin vanished for one breath as he felt his whole arm stop against the smaller hand.

Then the grin returned, wider than before.

“Again!” Xiahou Lie shouted.

His second fist came from the side. Shi Feng turned his wrist, pushed the first arm aside, and caught the next strike on his forearm.

Xiahou Lie drove forward with his shoulder.

Shi Feng let himself slide half a step rather than breaking the opponent's balance immediately. He wanted to feel how the body art carried force through the man's stance.

It was direct and practical. Strong legs supported a hard torso, and the qi reinforced the joints before the impact reached them.

Against an ordinary cultivator at the same realm, Xiahou Lie's method would be troublesome.

Against Shi Feng, it was something to examine.

He wasn't approaching the limit of his body.

Duan Yichen watched from the waiting area with his arms folded.

“They're smiling,” Duan Yichen said.

Sima Lan stood beside a pillar, her injured shoulder wrapped beneath clean cloth. She looked tired enough to dislike everyone who still had energy.

“Men find strange things enjoyable,” Sima Lan replied.

“You just fought four matches,” Duan Yichen said.

“I didn't smile when someone hit me,” Sima Lan answered.

On the platform, Xiahou Lie shouted in delight as Shi Feng's fist struck his chest.

The blow pushed him back two steps. His protection held, but the force passed through it deeply enough to make him cough.

He looked down at the spot, then up at Shi Feng.

“That's better!” Xiahou Lie said.

Shi Feng lowered his hand.

“You asked,” Shi Feng replied.

The crowd couldn't decide whether it was watching a serious quarter-final or two madmen discussing bruises.

“That was a direct blow!”

“Xiahou Lie didn't block it!”

“He's testing the other man's body!”

“Then why does Shi Feng look less worried?”

Xiahou Lie heard the last question and glanced at his opponent's unmarked robe. His own sleeves were missing by choice. Shi Feng hadn't lost even a thread.

Interesting.

The body cultivator planted his feet and gathered more qi.

“Iron Buddha Art,” Xiahou Lie said. “Don't stop halfway.”

A bronze sheen spread across his arms and shoulders. It wasn't the gold inside Shi Feng's bones. It was condensed qi reinforcing a practised body technique.

Shi Feng understood the difference at once. His own golden bones remained hidden beneath unchanged skin. He could study this ordinary body art without explaining what supported his strength.

The knowledgeable people watching recognised Xiahou Lie's method too. Several body-cultivation manuals described similar reinforcement. The sect delegates judged its density and control rather than treating the bronze light as some unexplained miracle.

He struck again.

This time, Shi Feng didn't catch the fist.

He stepped inside its reach and struck Xiahou Lie's upper arm from below. The attack shifted the elbow and opened the chest. A second blow landed before the body cultivator could close his guard.

Xiahou Lie slid backward, his heels digging two pale lines into the platform.

The bronze light held.

Shi Feng stopped advancing and watched the qi settle. The technique distributed force well, but it needed the shoulders and hips aligned. Break that alignment, and the reinforced body couldn't use all its strength.

He thought, There. The body isn't one solid piece of metal. He still has joints.

Xiahou Lie rubbed his chest and laughed.

“You found it quickly,” Xiahou Lie said.

“You kept pointing at it,” Shi Feng replied.

“I don't usually need to worry about the opening,” Xiahou Lie said.

“Now you do,” Shi Feng answered.

The body cultivator's expression became serious at last. He lowered his stance and brought both arms close. The bronze light deepened around his elbows.

He wasn't afraid. He was excited by the first opponent who made him change the way he stood.

Shi Feng liked that better than another candidate inventing an unfair rule after losing.

Lu Yong watched from the edge without intervening. Both men remained clear-headed, and neither was trying to attack after a surrender.

Still, the official moved closer. A heavy exchange between body cultivators could cause injuries faster than either fighter admitted.

Xiahou Lie noticed the movement and grinned again.

“Don't stop us too early, Senior Lu,” Xiahou Lie said.

“Then surrender before you need carrying,” Lu Yong replied.

Shi Feng almost laughed.

Xiahou Lie lifted both fists.

“One proper exchange,” Xiahou Lie said. “No running around my feet.”

“Your feet are large enough already,” Shi Feng replied.

The body cultivator burst forward with a shout. Bronze light covered his fists, and the stone shook beneath his stride.

Shi Feng raised one hand and chose exactly how much strength to show.

chapters.title: Two Bodies, One Platform
chapters.html:
The fists met above the platform's centre mark.

A heavy crack echoed through the stands. Xiahou Lie's bronze protection shuddered, and his whole body stopped despite the force of his charge.

Shi Feng's arm bent slightly because he allowed it to bend.

His golden bones weren't damaged. The strength beneath them was far beyond what this ordinary body art could overcome. He'd chosen enough force to stop the charge without showing how easily he could end it.

Xiahou Lie felt the difference before the audience understood it.

His grin faded. He twisted his shoulders to bring the second fist across, but Shi Feng's free hand caught the elbow.

The body cultivator's stance opened.

Shi Feng pushed.

Xiahou Lie staggered backward three steps. The bronze light around his arm flickered where the elbow moved out of line with his shoulder.

Before he could settle again, Shi Feng struck the same point with a short palm.

The protection broke.

A sharp pain shot through Xiahou Lie's forearm. He pulled it close, shocked to find that he could no longer lift it properly.

Shi Feng stopped attacking.

“Enough?” Shi Feng asked.

Xiahou Lie looked at his injured arm. His expression was so disappointed that several spectators thought he might insist on continuing.

Then he laughed.

“That's enough,” Xiahou Lie said. “I surrender.”

Lu Yong entered between them at once and checked the injury. The bone was damaged, but it wasn't shattered beyond repair. Proper medicine and rest would handle it.

The official looked at Shi Feng's unmarked hands.

“You stopped the next strike,” Lu Yong said.

“He surrendered,” Shi Feng replied.

“He would've needed carrying otherwise,” Lu Yong said.

Xiahou Lie looked offended.

“I can walk!” Xiahou Lie protested.

“Then walk to the physician,” Lu Yong replied.

The crowd finally found its voice.

“He broke the Iron Buddha guard!”

“Mid Foundation Establishment against late Foundation Establishment!”

“His own arm isn't even swollen!”

“Xiahou Lie's still laughing!”

The body cultivator raised his good hand toward the stands, delighted to confirm that last observation.

Shi Feng retrieved his sword from the entrance. The edge remained safe in its scabbard, which was more useful than having it bent against reinforced flesh.

Xiahou Lie followed him with the injured arm supported by his opposite hand.

“Rematch,” Xiahou Lie said.

“Healing first,” Shi Feng replied.

“After healing,” Xiahou Lie said. “And more practice. I need a better way to turn when someone catches the elbow.”

“Move your feet before you throw the second punch,” Shi Feng replied.
