At dawn, he went downstairs for hot water and found Gu Zhan asleep on a bench in the front hall.

The spear lay across his knees. Kang Liu stood behind the counter with the exhausted expression of a man who'd argued against several different kinds of foolishness before sunrise.

“He came to ask whether you wanted breakfast,” Kang Liu whispered.

Shi Feng looked at the sleeping cultivator.

“With the spear?” Shi Feng asked.

“He said he carries it everywhere,” Kang Liu replied.

“That part's true,” Shi Feng said.

Gu Zhan opened his eye when they mentioned the weapon. He sat upright immediately.

“You're awake!” Gu Zhan said.

“Yes,” Shi Feng replied.

The spear user examined him for a moment. His expression changed into open interest.

“Late Foundation Establishment,” Gu Zhan said. “You advanced!”

“After the final,” Shi Feng replied.

Gu Zhan looked delighted enough to forget breakfast.

“So the next fight will be better!” Gu Zhan said.

“Not before eating,” Shi Feng answered.

Kang Liu hurried to order two bowls before either visitor could prove how large a courtyard a spear needed.

Duan Yichen arrived while they ate. He stopped beside the table, looked at Shi Feng's slightly changed aura, and shook his head.

“You won yesterday,” Duan Yichen said. “You could've waited a little before making the rest of us work harder.”

“I wasn't waiting for applause,” Shi Feng replied.

“That was obvious,” Duan Yichen said. “The rest of the city hasn't finished applauding.”

Gu Zhan was drawing a spear angle beside his bowl with one finger.

Duan Yichen moved the bowl away before the finger reached the soup.

“Eat,” Duan Yichen said.

Gu Zhan looked at him, then at the displaced food.

“You sound like my master,” Gu Zhan said.

“Then he must be tired,” Duan Yichen replied.

Shi Feng laughed softly and finished his own bowl.

He felt steadier than the previous morning. He still wanted a better sword, a proper furnace, and the chance to see Artificer Hall with his own eyes.

Zhou Ke appeared at the gate with a sealed invitation bearing all three sect marks.

“The recruitment hall,” Zhou Ke said. “They're waiting for your decision.”

Shi Feng wiped his hands, stood, and accepted the paper.

“Then I'll give it,” Shi Feng replied.

chapters.title: Three Sects at One Table
chapters.html:
“Sit,” Wei Chengyuan said.

Shi Feng took the empty chair without treating the word as a personal favour. He Zhen sat opposite him with a brush case beside one hand. Mu Shuyun occupied the third side of the table.

Three sect delegates. One champion's choice.

Outside the recruitment room, attendants waited with prepared documents. The remaining successful candidates would hear their own offers after the champion answered.

Wei Chengyuan noticed Shi Feng's changed aura immediately.

“Late Foundation Establishment,” Wei Chengyuan said.

“Yes,” Shi Feng replied.

“A successful night,” Mu Shuyun observed.

“The medicine was useful,” Shi Feng said.

He Zhen looked pleased, then remembered that looking pleased didn't improve the offer he could make.

Wei Chengyuan opened the first document.

“Martial Palace,” Wei Chengyuan said. “Direct inner entry, as the champion's right provides. Three thousand spirit stones on arrival. A personal sword instructor selected from the inner court. Proper access to our technique halls.”

He paused, allowing the numbers and promises to settle.

Shi Feng listened without interrupting. The offer was good. He didn't need to pretend otherwise because the man making it had threatened him the previous night.

Wei Chengyuan added a replacement refined artifact sword and priority in the first year's training allotments.

The delegates outside would hear how generous Martial Palace had been.

So would the other candidates.

“What do you expect in return?” Shi Feng asked.

Wei Chengyuan's smile tightened slightly.

“The duties of an inner disciple,” Wei Chengyuan replied. “Loyal service to the sect, proper conduct, and progress worth supporting.”

“Anything else?” Shi Feng asked.

“Nothing that should concern a capable young man,” Wei Chengyuan said.

Shi Feng looked at him quietly. The Yunze threat wasn't printed on the document, but leaving it unprinted didn't make it disappear.

He would remember the difference between the offer and the conversation that preceded it.

Mu Shuyun opened her own paper before the silence became a quarrel.

“Hundred Flower Valley offers the same rightful inner entry,” Mu Shuyun said. “Our resources suit careful sword cultivation. You would have access to the sword pavilion and the medicinal gardens under the ordinary inner-court rules.”

She named the stipend and the instruction available. The sum was lower than Martial Palace's first gift, but the practical benefits were clear.

Shi Feng asked two questions about the teaching. She answered both directly.

Then her gaze moved briefly to the violet cord on his everyday purse.

“Your wife is already with us,” Mu Shuyun said.

The room became quieter.

Shi Feng didn't look down at the cord.

“She chose a useful teacher,” Shi Feng replied. “I'm choosing my own.”

Mu Shuyun studied him for one breath, then nodded.

“Naturally,” Mu Shuyun said.

She didn't repeat the marriage as though naming it twice would decide him. Ling Qingzhu's place belonged to her own recruitment. It wasn't a rope tied around another candidate's neck.

Shi Feng appreciated the restraint.

He Zhen unfolded the smallest paper last.

“Artificer Hall,” He Zhen said. “Direct inner entry. The standard lodging, library access, and inner-disciple allotment.”

He stopped.

Wei Chengyuan waited. Mu Shuyun waited. Shi Feng waited too, because the delegate seemed embarrassed enough that another sentence might need time to escape.

“There isn't an arrival gift?” Shi Feng asked.

“Not one to match theirs,” He Zhen replied.

“How much?” Shi Feng asked.

He Zhen named the ordinary allotment. It wouldn't make a successful alchemist rich.

The delegate's expression became more uncomfortable.

“I won't invent a treasury to win an argument,” He Zhen said. “You'd find out after arriving.”

Shi Feng nodded. That answer was more useful than a flattering promise about resources nobody could explain.

He wasn't confusing limited funds with virtue. A poor sect could still contain greedy elders and cruel disciples. Honest figures on one piece of paper didn't make every person behind its gate trustworthy.

But at least he knew what this offer actually contained.

“Teaching?” Shi Feng asked.

“Crafting is our broadest strength,” He Zhen replied. “There are sword methods too. Xu Changhe didn't invent being an enforcer by himself.”

Shi Feng smiled slightly.

“I didn't think he had,” Shi Feng replied.

“Must every inner disciple become a crafter?” Shi Feng asked.

“No,” He Zhen said. “The Hall needs people who can protect its work too. Different instructors handle different paths.”

“And alchemy practice?” Shi Feng asked.

“You can arrange a room and buy your own materials,” He Zhen replied. “Your certification doesn't make you a refiner, and we won't pretend it does.”

Shi Feng liked the clear distinction. Mo Tianheng's expertise gave him medicine, not mastery over every puppet joint and weapon channel. Xu Changhe's useful crafting notes were a separate, much smaller beginning.

He could study more if it served his purpose. He didn't need a sect to rename the things he already knew.

The three documents lay before him.

Wei Chengyuan tapped the Martial Palace paper once.

“Compare them properly,” Wei Chengyuan said. “Your future shouldn't depend on gratitude for a dead man's notes.”

“It doesn't depend only on that,” Shi Feng replied.

“Then consider what the stronger sect can provide,” Wei Chengyuan said.

“I am considering it,” Shi Feng answered.

The delegate looked unsatisfied. He'd wanted agreement, not confirmation that the young man understood the words and still intended to think for himself.

Mu Shuyun folded her hands and waited. He Zhen checked the cap on his brush, apparently wishing he'd brought a larger treasury inside the case.

Shi Feng read the final line of each document.

His alchemy could earn resources. His sword path already had a beginning. A Great Sect would open a wider world, but it wouldn't replace his own choices with the most expensive offer on the table.

He knew where he wanted to go.

“The formal announcement is outside?” Shi Feng asked.

“Yes,” He Zhen replied.

“Then I'll answer there,” Shi Feng said.

Wei Chengyuan stood first, certain that public comparison would favour the richest promise. Mu Shuyun rose without showing what she expected.

He Zhen gathered the plainest document and followed them.

Beyond the doors, the recruitment courtyard was already full.

chapters.title: The Weakest Sect
chapters.html:
“Artificer Hall,” Shi Feng said.

For one breath, the recruitment courtyard made no sound at all.

Then He Zhen dropped his brush.

The wooden handle struck the stone beside his shoe. He looked down at it as though the brush might explain what he just heard.

Wei Chengyuan's smile froze.

Mu Shuyun raised one eyebrow and turned toward the champion more carefully.

“Artificer Hall,” Lu Yong repeated. “That is your choice?”

“Yes,” Shi Feng replied.

The stands beyond the courtyard rail erupted.

“The weakest of the three!”

“After Martial Palace offered all that?”

“His wife is in the Valley!”

“Did he hear the wrong offer?”

Shi Feng heard them clearly. None had read his mind better than the man who made the decision.

He didn't need to correct each guess.

Lu Yong waited until the crowd quieted enough for the record to be heard.

“Champion Shi Feng chooses direct inner-disciple entry to Artificer Hall,” Lu Yong declared. “Let the agreement be witnessed and entered.”

An attendant unrolled the formal paper.

He Zhen finally bent to pick up the brush.

Wei Chengyuan stepped closer before the signing began.

“You understand the difference in support?” Wei Chengyuan asked.

“Yes,” Shi Feng replied.

“Three thousand spirit stones. A sword instructor. A proper refined artifact to replace what broke,” Wei Chengyuan said.

“I heard the offer,” Shi Feng answered.

The delegate's expression darkened. His late Golden Core presence made nearby attendants draw back, but Lu Yong remained beside the document without moving.

The champion's choice wasn't a favour Martial Palace could withdraw because it disliked the answer.

“Then explain it,” Wei Chengyuan said.

“I chose Artificer Hall,” Shi Feng replied. “Not your approval.”

A sharp silence followed.

Duan Yichen, standing among the other recruits, pressed his lips together to stop a badly timed smile. Sima Lan looked from the champion to the delegate and understood how much face the latter just lost.

Every expensive promise was heard in public.

So was the refusal.

Mu Shuyun spoke before Wei Chengyuan's temper made the event uglier.

“The champion earned the right to choose,” Mu Shuyun said. “He has chosen.”

Lu Yong nodded and pointed toward the paper.

“Proceed,” Lu Yong said.

Wei Chengyuan stepped back. His expression became controlled again, which didn't make it friendly.

Shi Feng signed without shaking the brush.

He Zhen inspected the finished signature, then looked at Shi Feng.

“I wasn't expecting this,” He Zhen admitted.

“You offered,” Shi Feng replied.

“Yes,” He Zhen said. “Offering and believing are different things.”

The champion almost laughed. The delegate sounded too relieved to hide the truth elegantly.

He Zhen took out the preliminary inner-disciple token and checked its seal before handing it over. The final registration would be completed at the Hall itself, but the right was settled here.

Shi Feng accepted it.

The token was ordinary-looking. No light split the sky when he held it. It still represented a step he'd worked toward from the day he learnt Foundation Establishment was required to enter a kingdom's qualification.

He was satisfied.

Lu Yong checked the final entry and paused at the cultivation line.

“Late Foundation Establishment now?” Lu Yong asked.

“Since last night,” Shi Feng replied.

The official wrote the date beside the change. Several people nearby immediately began arguing over whether the final should be described differently.

Lu Yong looked up.

“He won at mid Foundation Establishment,” Lu Yong said. “The record is clear. Today's advance doesn't change yesterday's match.”

The argument stopped.

Shi Feng appreciated that more than another speech about his future. The public didn't need his deepest secrets, but what it did receive should at least be correct.

He Zhen copied the updated cultivation into the Hall's preliminary record. His hand shook less now that the choice was signed. The champion wasn't going to vanish because the delegate finally remembered to breathe.

Mu Shuyun watched the extra line being entered and smiled slightly. Great Liang's supposed cripple had given the tournament officials plenty of new writing.

Sima Lan watched the token from behind the waiting line. She hadn't heard the remaining recruitment offers yet. The Hall's decision about her would be its own, not a reward automatically attached to Shi Feng's choice.

Gongsun Ce looked at He Zhen's brush case and smiled faintly.

“Pick up the cap too,” Gongsun Ce said.

He Zhen looked down. The little cap had rolled beneath the chair.

The prince retrieved it before the delegate could decide whether to laugh at himself.

Outside the courtyard, the gossip changed faster than the attendants could clear a passage.

Some insisted Shi Feng must've received a secret promise. Others claimed he'd fallen out with his wife and chosen the third sect to avoid seeing her.

He heard that version and felt a brief, cold annoyance.

Ling Qingzhu didn't choose his path for him while they lived together. Their separation didn't choose it for him now.

She had her own teacher and her own reasons.

So did he.

Duan Yichen caught up near the gate.

“You really chose them,” Duan Yichen said.

“Yes,” Shi Feng replied.

“Good,” Duan Yichen said. “I would've had to hear you complain about Martial Palace's invitations every morning.”

“You might still hear it,” Shi Feng replied.

The sabre user laughed, then became serious.

“I'll come find you when the training permits,” Duan Yichen said.

“Bring a better second cut,” Shi Feng replied.

“Bring a whole sword,” Duan Yichen answered.

They exchanged a brief grin. Different sects didn't require turning a useful friendship into another feud.

He Zhen approached with the signed copy and a relieved expression that still hadn't entirely left his face.

“There's time before departure,” He Zhen said. “If you have questions, ask.”

Shi Feng looked toward the old token at his waist and the new one in his hand.

“There are a few,” Shi Feng replied.

He Zhen nodded and led him toward a quieter table. Behind them, Wei Chengyuan's attendants were already telling people that Martial Palace never forced a candidate who failed to appreciate its offer.

Nobody seemed entirely convinced.

chapters.title: Why the Weakest
chapters.html:
“Was it only Xu Changhe?” He Zhen asked.

Shi Feng sat at the quieter table behind the recruitment courtyard. The public argument had ended, but the delegate's curiosity hadn't.

“No,” Shi Feng replied.

He Zhen waited instead of supplying the answer himself.

“His sword art helped me,” Shi Feng said. “His notes gave me a useful beginning. I want to see the place where he worked and study what suits me there.”

“You don't owe the whole Hall your life because of that,” He Zhen said.

“I returned his badge and journal,” Shi Feng replied. “I didn't sell myself with them.”

The delegate nodded slowly. The answer was blunter than a speech about repaying an immortal kindness, but it was easier to trust.

Shi Feng looked toward the signed agreement.

“Martial Palace offered more,” Shi Feng said. “I heard it. I still prefer this choice.”

“A sect with nothing to lose doesn't sell its disciples,” He Zhen said.

Shi Feng looked at him steadily.

“Then keep that promise after we arrive,” Shi Feng replied.

He Zhen nodded without adding another grand claim.

“You know we're weaker overall,” He Zhen said.

“Yes,” Shi Feng replied.

“And the inner court won't have endless resources waiting because you're a champion,” He Zhen added.

“Then I'll earn what I need,” Shi Feng said. “I've done that before.”

He Zhen smiled at last. He wasn't being promised a grateful disciple who'd accept every demand without thinking. He was receiving someone who knew what he wanted.

He Zhen checked the preliminary record before closing it.

“One point,” He Zhen said. “Learning from Xu Changhe's notes isn't the same as being formally accepted as his disciple.”

“I know,” Shi Feng replied.

“Some people may ask,” He Zhen added.

“Then I'll answer honestly,” Shi Feng said. “I found his remains, learnt useful things, and returned what identified him. He wasn't alive to promise me a place.”

He Zhen nodded, clearly relieved that the distinction wouldn't become an argument at the gate.

Shi Feng didn't need a dead man's name to replace the result he'd earned. The champion's token already opened the way. What he learnt after entering would depend on his own work.

That might cause trouble later. It might also be useful.

Duan Yichen found him outside the courtyard with the old sword wrapped beneath one arm.

“Repairing it?” Duan Yichen asked.

“Having someone inspect it,” Shi Feng replied.

“I know a materials shop,” Duan Yichen said.

“Do they know weapons?” Shi Feng asked.

“They sent me away when I asked for cheap good ones,” Duan Yichen replied. “That seems promising.”

Shi Feng laughed and followed him through the market.

The shop stood beside a narrow forge yard. A plain Sky Pavilion certificate hung near the entrance, naming Qin Zheng as a 1 Mark refiner. The craftsman himself was at early Golden Core, with grey sleeves and a small burn above one eyebrow.

He checked the broken blade without asking who won the final.

Then he looked at Shi Feng.

“You put this against Golden Core force?” Qin Zheng asked.

“Yes,” Shi Feng replied.

“Repeatedly?” Qin Zheng asked.

“Once. It broke,” Shi Feng said.

Qin Zheng placed the two pieces side by side.

“It did well to hold your counterstrike before parting,” Qin Zheng said.

Duan Yichen leaned over the counter.

“So it can be repaired?” Duan Yichen asked.

“It can be reforged with better materials,” Qin Zheng replied. “That's nearly another sword. A simple join won't give the old metal a new limit.”

Shi Feng nodded. That was what he needed to know.

He understood some ordinary crafting from Xu Changhe's notes. Mo Tianheng's alchemy experience wasn't going to tell him how to remake every weapon channel through a damaged blade.

Asking a proper refiner was faster than pretending.

Qin Zheng showed them two examples of stronger work, explaining the materials and the way each blade accepted qi.

The explanation was clear. The prices were equally clear.

Shi Feng could afford more now. He didn't need to buy the first expensive weapon placed in his hands simply because the previous one broke.

He tested the weight and returned both.

“I'll examine the Hall's stores after arriving,” Shi Feng said.

“Artificer Hall?” Qin Zheng asked.

“Yes,” Shi Feng replied.

The refiner's expression changed into interest.

“Then ask to see the channel before praising the polish,” Qin Zheng said. “Their younger disciples sometimes make fine work look like an unfinished farm tool.”

Duan Yichen laughed.

“That's encouragement?” Duan Yichen asked.

“That's advice,” Qin Zheng replied. “You can recognise it because I haven't charged for it.”

Shi Feng paid for the inspection and accepted the sword pieces back in clean wrapping. The craftsman didn't insist that a champion ought to spend more before leaving.

An ordinary fair transaction could end there.

They stopped for food near the forge street. Duan Yichen unfolded his Martial Palace offer while waiting for the bowls.

The sabre user read the training allotment again and looked pleased.

“You're certain?” Duan Yichen asked Shi Feng.

“About Artificer Hall?” Shi Feng asked.

“Yes,” Duan Yichen replied.

“I am,” Shi Feng said.

Duan Yichen folded the paper.

“Then good,” Duan Yichen said. “I can stop trying to understand the part you already decided.”

Shi Feng smiled. The sabre user wanted his friend to do well. He didn't need identical sect tokens to make that possible.

They ate while the forge hammers sounded beyond the wall. Nobody at the table required a speech about the strongest sect or the noblest debt.

There was work ahead in either place.

When they separated, Shi Feng returned to the inn and packed the broken sword carefully. He didn't place it in the ordinary sheath as though the blade were whole again.

The new token rested beside the wrapping.

His choice wasn't proof that Artificer Hall was full of good people. He hadn't met its disciples or tested its rules yet. He expected greed, arrogance, useful teachers, and ordinary fools there just as elsewhere.

He'd decide how to handle each when they appeared.

For now, the important thing was simple.

The choice belonged to him.

Outside, Kang Liu began telling a guest that the champion chose his inn for its excellent roof. Shi Feng closed the window before the claim reached a divine level.

chapters.title: The Other Recruits
chapters.html:
“Do your disciples fight every day?” Gu Zhan asked.

Wei Chengyuan paused beside the recruitment table.

“Martial Palace provides regular instruction,” Wei Chengyuan replied.

“Every day?” Gu Zhan asked.

“Not every lesson is a fight,” Wei Chengyuan said.

“Then no,” Gu Zhan replied.

The courtyard went quiet enough to hear Nie Wufeng laughing beneath the awning.

Mu Shuyun covered a small smile with the edge of her sleeve. He Zhen looked as though he'd already decided not to begin an explanation about workshop schedules.

Gu Zhan turned toward them anyway.

“Yours?” Gu Zhan asked.

“Some disciples spend days on one difficult piece of work,” He Zhen replied.

“Does it fight?” Gu Zhan asked.

“Occasionally, if someone makes it badly,” He Zhen said.

Gu Zhan looked interested for one breath, then shook his head.

“No,” Gu Zhan said. “I'll stay with Master.”

Nie Wufeng stopped laughing long enough to look annoyed.

“You haven't asked me,” Nie Wufeng said.

Gu Zhan pointed toward the spear beside his chair.

“You still fight,” Gu Zhan replied.

The old master considered the explanation, then grunted and returned to his tea.

Lu Yong marked the refusal clearly. Runner-up Gu Zhan declined recruitment from all three sects. Nobody needed to pretend he vanished from the top ten because the offers didn't interest him.

Bai Chenxi accepted Hundred Flower Valley's offer after asking two practical questions about sword instruction.

Mu Shuyun answered without repeating the speeches she used for the champion. The swordswoman had already shown discipline, skill, and a willingness to learn from a defeat.

That suited the Valley's instruction.

Yuan Kuang accepted Martial Palace. His expression remained proud, though the public ceremony was quieter than the triumph he expected before meeting Gu Zhan.

Xiahou Lie chose the same sect after confirming that its body-cultivation teachers would correct his stance rather than forbid rematches.

Cao Zhenyu and Tan He followed under their own offers. Neither received the champion's right to dictate direct inner entry. They took the terms the sect chose to provide and signed them clearly.

Duan Yichen stood last among Martial Palace's new recruits.

“Ninth place,” Wei Chengyuan said, checking the record.

“Yes,” Duan Yichen replied.

“Hard earned,” Wei Chengyuan said.

“Yes,” Duan Yichen said again.

The delegate looked up at the repetition. Duan Yichen wasn't being rude. He simply didn't intend to apologise for the place that qualified him.

He signed the agreement and accepted the token.

From beside Artificer Hall's table, Shi Feng nodded once.

Duan Yichen returned the nod with a grin.

He Zhen called Gongsun Ce forward next.

“Inner court,” He Zhen said.

The prince looked at the paper and lifted one eyebrow.

“Because I finished third?” Gongsun Ce asked.

“Because you understand the work and keep correcting it,” He Zhen replied. “Third place helped us notice.”

Gongsun Ce smiled. That answer suited him better than being told the same reward belonged to every third-ranked candidate in the world.

He checked the workshop access and signed.

Sima Lan approached when her name was called.

The Moon Lake robe made several spectators whisper again. Great Liang's younger princess had left her household's expected path, reached the final ten, and declined to stand beside her injured brother's attendants.

None of those choices was free of consequence.

He Zhen put the offer in front of her.

“Outer court,” He Zhen said.

Sima Lan read it without changing her expression.

“The same rules as the other outer disciples?” Sima Lan asked.

“Yes,” He Zhen replied.

“No royal allowance?” Sima Lan asked.

“No,” He Zhen said.

She nodded and signed.

The delegate watched her finish.

“I like a patient fighter,” He Zhen said. “You kept looking for a useful step when the easy ones failed.”

“That step almost came too late,” Sima Lan replied.

“It came,” He Zhen said.

She accepted the outer-court token and closed her fingers around it. It wasn't the grandest offer in the courtyard. It was one she could use without waiting for her brother to approve.

That was enough.

Lu Yong checked the completed recruitment list before declaring the ceremony finished. The top ten received their offers. Gu Zhan refused his. Ling Qingzhu's earlier discretionary invitation remained a separate Valley decision, without a final tournament placing attached to her name.

A disappointed spectator asked whether the next candidate could inherit the runner-up's refusal. Lu Yong answered the question publicly before it became another argument.

“An invitation declined isn't a new tournament,” Lu Yong said. “The announced results stand.”

The courtyard began emptying in a rush of relatives, attendants, and excited new disciples.

Shi Feng stood beside the gate while Duan Yichen checked the Martial Palace departure time.

“Different boats,” Duan Yichen said.

“Same region,” Shi Feng replied.

“Then don't hide in a workshop for a year,” Duan Yichen said. “I'll come looking.”

“Bring medicine money,” Shi Feng replied.

Duan Yichen laughed and tucked the new token inside his robe.

Gu Zhan pushed through the crowd carrying his spear and looking pleased that no sect had managed to give him a training schedule.

“You'll have time to fight later?” Gu Zhan asked Shi Feng.

“Later,” Shi Feng replied.

“Good,” Gu Zhan said.

Nie Wufeng caught him by the back of the robe before he could turn later into another argument about the current afternoon.

The old master dragged him toward the street. Gu Zhan kept talking about spear angles until the crowd swallowed both voices.

He Zhen gathered the Hall's three signed records and finally let himself smile.

Gongsun Ce returned before the delegate packed the last paper.

“The workshop benches,” Gongsun Ce said. “Can an inner disciple use them immediately?”

“Under the posted rules,” He Zhen replied. “Expensive materials need approval. Break your own mistakes first, not the sect treasury.”

The prince looked at the puppet case and nodded seriously.

Sima Lan listened from nearby. Her outer token would give her fewer resources, but it didn't forbid study or advancement. She asked where those rules were posted and received an ordinary answer, not an assurance that a princess would be spared them.

Shi Feng liked that beginning. He'd see how fairly the rules were applied after arriving.

For He Zhen, it had been a good recruitment trip.

chapters.title: The Princess and the Champion
chapters.html:
“We'll be fellow disciples,” Sima Lan said.

Shi Feng looked up from the travel medicines spread across his inn table. The princess stood outside the open doorway, holding her new outer-court token.

“Yes,” Shi Feng replied.

“After you defeated my brother,” Sima Lan added.

“That happened too,” Shi Feng said.

She studied his face. There was no apology in it, and she hadn't expected one. Sima Yu's violation was entered publicly. His own forbidden pill and the backlash ruined his foundation. He'd tried to yield a breath too late; the rules kept him alive.

None of that made his earlier killing orders disappear.

“The court is asking who signed Guo Zhen's storehouse pass,” Sima Lan said.

Shi Feng looked at her more carefully.

“They can ask whoever kept the gate record,” Shi Feng replied.

“They are,” Sima Lan said. “Not every name on that paper belongs to someone who wants my brother speaking freely.”

She left the hint there instead of pretending she had come to offer loyalty.

“I didn't come to ask you to forgive him,” Sima Lan said.

“Good,” Shi Feng replied.

She smiled faintly and stepped inside after he moved the spare stool toward the table.

The room was plain. The champion's reward didn't turn the bed into precious jade or the window into a sect pavilion.

His broken sword rested in clean wrapping beside the new token.

Sima Lan looked at it, then at the sorted medicine.

“You pack your own things,” Sima Lan said.

“They're mine,” Shi Feng replied.

“Some people would find that beneath their new position,” Sima Lan said.

“Then they can lose their own jars,” Shi Feng answered.

She laughed softly. He didn't sound as though he was performing humility for a princess. He simply knew what each jar contained and wanted it where he could find it.

Sima Lan placed her token beside the edge of the table.

“Outer court,” Sima Lan said.

“You read it before signing,” Shi Feng replied.

“I did,” Sima Lan said. “I'm not complaining.”

“Then why tell me?” Shi Feng asked.

“Because people will assume I expect something from yours,” Sima Lan replied.

She looked at the champion's inner token without reaching for it.

“I'd rather hear the answer clearly before someone starts speaking on my behalf,” Sima Lan said.

Shi Feng closed one medicine box and turned toward her properly.

“If you want something, ask,” Shi Feng said. “I won't promise it because you came from the same kingdom. I won't refuse it just because Sima Yu is your brother.”

Her expression became serious.

“That's fair,” Sima Lan said.

“It depends what you ask,” Shi Feng replied.

She nodded. The distinction mattered. Fair treatment wasn't a promise to provide anything she named.

At the royal residence, people often agreed before the request was finished and complained behind the nearest closed door. She preferred knowing where the refusal would come from.

It left her something real to work with.

Outside the window, Kang Liu was trying to persuade a new guest that the room below the champion's was nearly as fortunate.

Sima Lan glanced toward the sound.

“He'll keep your name after you leave,” Sima Lan said.

“He can keep the room clean too,” Shi Feng replied.

She smiled and picked up her token again.

“My brother will hear where I chose,” Sima Lan said.

“Yes,” Shi Feng replied.

“He won't approve,” Sima Lan said.

“Did you sign for his approval?” Shi Feng asked.

“No,” Sima Lan replied.

“Then there's your answer,” Shi Feng said.

She looked down at the outer-court mark. The answer was simple. Living with the consequences would take longer.

Her late Foundation Establishment cultivation didn't give her authority over the whole royal household. Leaving Moon Lake Sect's familiar robes for Artificer Hall wouldn't make all its claims vanish either.

She understood that.

She still intended to go.

“You're very calm about other people's anger,” Sima Lan said.

“Not all of it deserves my time,” Shi Feng replied.

“And the anger that does?” Sima Lan asked.

He looked at her quietly.

She remembered the broken prince being carried from the platform and decided that question already had an answer.

A small glass bottle rolled when Shi Feng moved the cloth beneath it. Sima Lan caught it before it reached the floor and set it beside the correct box.

“External wash,” Sima Lan said, reading the label.

“Yes,” Shi Feng replied.

“Not a recovery pill,” Sima Lan added.

“The label helps,” Shi Feng said.

She gave him an annoyed look. He smiled and finished tying the box shut.

She didn't ask for a free bottle or assume that visiting entitled her to medicine. Her injured shoulder already had proper treatment from the tournament physicians.

That made the conversation easier.

“Your alchemy will earn more at the sect,” Sima Lan said.

“It'll also cost more to practise,” Shi Feng replied.

“Then you'll need people who can count properly,” Sima Lan said.

“I can count,” Shi Feng answered.

“I noticed,” Sima Lan replied.

Her smile turned a little sharper. She wasn't offering to become a servant or trying to turn tenth place into an obligation to obey the champion. She simply noticed how much work sat outside the refining itself.

Perhaps it would matter later.

For now, she stood and put the token away.

“I'll be at the landing on time,” Sima Lan said.

“Good,” Shi Feng replied.

“And if He Zhen's boat looks ready to fall apart?” Sima Lan asked.

“Ask whether the repairs are useful,” Shi Feng said. “Not whether they're pretty.”

She glanced at the broken sword once more and laughed.

“That's advice from experience,” Sima Lan said.

“An expensive piece of it,” Shi Feng replied.

Before leaving, she paused beside the stool.

“What do you think I should study first?” Sima Lan asked.

“What do you want to learn?” Shi Feng replied.

“Something I can't receive just by being a princess,” Sima Lan said.

“Then you'll have plenty of work,” Shi Feng answered.

She considered that and nodded. It wasn't a promise to teach her everything. It was a reminder that the choice was still hers to make.

She left through the open door without asking him to escort her or explain what fellow disciples ought to owe each other.

Shi Feng returned to the medicines.

A princess would be entering the outer court beside two inner recruits. The titles made that sound unusual. The sect's actual rules and the people applying them would decide what happened next.

He wasn't going to invent the whole future from three tokens.

He put the final box into the ring and reached for the clean wrapping around his sword.

chapters.title: Lu Qingxue's Farewell
chapters.html:
Lu Qingxue waited outside the inn while the White Crane wagons loaded at the next crossing.

Shi Feng found her when he came back from the reporting office. She stood beside the wall, out of the doorway, with a travelling cloak folded over one arm. Her white disciple's robe looked dusty at the hem.

For a moment he remembered the well in Yunze Town. She had stood in somebody's way then, holding an envelope she should have delivered much earlier.

Today her hands were empty.

“I'm leaving with the Pavilion,” Lu Qingxue said.

Shi Feng stopped beside the step.

“Safe travels,” Shi Feng said.

She nodded, but didn't leave. Behind her, a wagon driver shouted for the final luggage. Somebody on the roof of the cart lowered a trunk too quickly and received an angry answer from below.

“I won't keep you long,” Lu Qingxue said.

He waited. She had come this far to speak. He could give her a few minutes without pretending the meeting meant more than it did.

“The record sent back to my household will include the tournament result,” Lu Qingxue said. “Your recovery and your choice of sect. I checked that myself.”

“It should include what the officials verified,” Shi Feng said.

“It does,” Lu Qingxue said.

Not his meridians. Not the ring or the physique. She knew only what the arena had shown everyone, and she didn't ask him to fill the empty spaces in her account.

That made the conversation easier.

A porter squeezed past carrying a rolled mattress. Lu Qingxue moved closer to the wall before the man needed to ask. Shi Feng shifted his everyday bag to the other shoulder.

“The earlier report is still wrong,” Lu Qingxue said. “Not the physician's uncertainty. The way the Pavilion made it certain afterward.”

“I know,” Shi Feng said.

“I knew enough to question it then,” Lu Qingxue said. “I didn't.”

Her voice stayed low. There was no crowd to hear an apology and turn it into another story about a fallen engagement. Kang Liu stood inside the inn counting cups, but the road noise covered their words.

Shi Feng looked at her properly.

Lu Qingxue didn't look like a woman hoping a champion would offer to rescue her from a lesser sect. She looked tired of choosing the easier account of something she had done.

“I'm sorry,” Lu Qingxue said.

He felt none of the anger he once expected from that sentence. The lost months remained lost. Her apology didn't return them, and refusing to hear it wouldn't return them either.

“I heard you,” Shi Feng said.

She drew a careful breath. He hadn't said everything was forgiven. She didn't try to make his answer larger.

“I wanted you to know before I went,” Lu Qingxue said.

“Then now I know,” Shi Feng said.

For a little while they stood without speaking. A wheel struck a loose stone near the crossing. The driver blamed his helper, and the helper pointed at the wheel as though the wood could testify.

Lu Qingxue almost smiled at the argument. She remembered how quickly Shi Feng would once have answered such a complaint. Now he simply let other people's journey remain their business.

“Artificer Hall,” Lu Qingxue said. “You chose it quickly.”

“I had reasons before the offers,” Shi Feng said.

She nodded. He didn't explain Xu Changhe's journal, and she didn't ask whether a more prestigious offer might change his mind. The choice was his, just as leaving Qingshi Town had been his.

“You always disliked people deciding for you,” Lu Qingxue said.

“Most people dislike it,” Shi Feng said.

That was true. She had simply thought his ruined future made the decision easier to make on his behalf. Remembering that brought heat to her face.

The wagon driver called again.

Lu Qingxue put the folded cloak over her shoulders and fastened its plain tie. The knot slipped on the first attempt. She retied it without waiting for help.

“Goodbye, Shi Feng,” Lu Qingxue said.

“Goodbye, Lu Qingxue,” Shi Feng said.

She turned toward the crossing. He went into the inn.

Neither looked back to see whether the other had stopped.

Kang Liu lifted a clean cup from the counter.

“Tea before you pack?” Kang Liu asked.

“Water,” Shi Feng said.

The innkeeper poured it without asking who the woman had been. He had seen enough visitors during the tournament to understand that curiosity didn't always improve a customer's mood.

Shi Feng drank while Kang Liu separated the cups with chipped rims. The work reminded him of the tea house in the capital, the cracked handle and the first proposal that changed his life.

He let the memory come. Then he set down the cup.

Lu Qingxue's departure had settled an old conversation. It hadn't settled the one he still carried from Qingliu Lane. Those hurts belonged to different people and different choices. He wouldn't use an easy goodbye to pretend the difficult one no longer mattered.

He climbed to his room and checked the reporting receipt. Champion. Artificer Hall. Direct inner entry. The ink was ordinary; the road it recorded was new.

He put the receipt with his travel papers.

At the crossing, Han Zheng checked the luggage against a list without looking toward the inn.

Lu Qingxue took her place near the rear wagon. The chief disciple helped a younger junior tie down a loose case, then climbed aboard after making sure the driver had room for his feet.

Nobody began a speech about the honour White Crane had lost. They had supplies to secure and a border road to reach before dark. Defeat didn't remove the need to travel sensibly.

Han Zheng finally looked at Lu Qingxue.

“You spoke to him?” Han Zheng asked.

“Yes,” Lu Qingxue said.

The steward's brush stopped. Perhaps he wanted to ask what a champion had promised. Perhaps he feared what she might have repeated. She gave him no answer to either question.

“The result goes into the report,” Lu Qingxue said. “As it happened.”

Han Zheng lowered the list and told the driver to move.

The wagons rolled away from the crossing. Lu Qingxue watched the road ahead until the wheels settled into a steady rhythm. She had training to return to and mistakes of her own to stop repeating.

chapters.title: The Price of Choosing
chapters.html:
The message arrived in an ordinary envelope.

Kang Liu brought it upstairs with Shi Feng's final room account. The paper bore no official order. A narrow strip inside carried the name of Martial Palace's elder Wei Chengyuan.

“The courier wants an answer,” Kang Liu said.

“Where is he?” Shi Feng asked.

“By the front door,” Kang Liu said. “He wouldn't buy tea.”

Shi Feng checked the account first. The extra kettle had been included, and the last night's charge matched what they agreed. He paid, put away the receipt and went downstairs with the unopened envelope.

The Martial Palace courier Liu Cheng stood beside the inn's entrance. His Bone Refinement aura was ordinary, but the Martial Palace badge on his chest had been polished until the edges shone. He straightened when Shi Feng appeared.

“Elder Wei Chengyuan asked that you read this before departing,” Liu Cheng said.

Shi Feng opened it.

The words were brief. Martial Palace had offered proper resources and proper protection. Artificer Hall could not promise the same. A young man who chose to stand outside the Palace's door should remember that the Wei family's grievances would remain outside with him.

No signature confessed to an unlawful act. No date named a coming attack. The warning was meant to be understood without becoming useful evidence of anything more precise.

Shi Feng read it once.

The courier watched his face. The courier had probably expected anger, an anxious question or an attempt to soften yesterday's refusal. He found none of them.

“Tell Wei Chengyuan I chose Artificer Hall, and any lawful complaint can go to the proper office,” Shi Feng said.

He folded the message and put it inside his everyday bag.

The courier waited. Shi Feng stepped around him and walked toward the materials street. After two breaths, the courier understood that the answer was finished.

He left without buying tea.

Kang Liu looked after both men, then picked up the envelope Shi Feng had left on the counter. Ordinary paper. Nothing about it explained why a powerful sect couldn't simply accept a young man's choice.

The innkeeper dropped it among the waste wrappers and went back to his cups.

The materials street was quieter now that the tournament had ended.

Several stallholders were taking down signs that promised special prices for candidates. One turned his board over and discovered he'd painted an even better promise on the other side last year.

Shi Feng stopped at a shop selling travelling cases.

Huang Bin placed two on the counter. The first had a carved lid and bright brass corners. The second was plain wood, with a dry lining and a clasp that didn't wobble.

“For a sword?” Huang Bin asked.

“Pieces of one,” Shi Feng said.

He unwrapped the broken refined artifact carefully. Huang Bin's eyes widened when he saw the channel running along the steel. Then recognition reached him.

“The final,” Huang Bin said.

Shi Feng nodded.

The shopkeeper touched neither piece. He measured them with a strip of cord and took a shorter case from beneath the counter. Both halves fitted without the broken edges pressing against each other.

“This one,” Huang Bin said. “Keep the padding between them.”

Shi Feng checked the clasp and paid the ordinary price. No discount for fame, no charge for a famous sword's history. He appreciated the straightforward work.

Outside, he put the closed case into the ring. The weapon had failed in the final. His injured arm had healed after the fight, but the broken steel still needed replacing. He would find a better blade after seeing what Artificer Hall could actually supply. Until then, he had a sound knife and more strength than the road's ordinary dangers required.

He wasn't going to buy the next sword because somebody praised its handle.

A delivery cart passed carrying dismantled benches from the arena. Two men argued over which end went into storage first. Shi Feng stepped aside and watched a boy run after the last fallen cushion.

The gathering that had filled Qingyun City was becoming furniture again.

Tomorrow he would leave it behind.

He Zhen found him near the reporting office before noon.

The elder carried three sealed recruit packets beneath his arm. One was thicker than the others, with a list of materials folded around it.

“Your room token will be issued at the sect,” He Zhen said. “This confirms the entry offer. Keep it with your identification.”

Shi Feng checked his name and the inner-disciple terms before accepting it.

He Zhen didn't look offended that he read the document. He stood in the shade and waited until Shi Feng finished.

“Something wrong?” He Zhen asked.

“No,” Shi Feng said.

“Then the eastern landing,” He Zhen said. “After the morning bell. Bring what you need, not what a servant thinks makes you important.”

“I don't have a servant,” Shi Feng said.

“That saves time,” He Zhen said.

The answer made Shi Feng smile. He Zhen had a tired look suggesting that somebody else's luggage had already cost him an argument.

The elder noticed the narrow message strip sticking from Shi Feng's bag.

“Martial Palace?” He Zhen asked.

Shi Feng handed him the paper. He Zhen read it without making a show of anger. His fingers tightened only when he reached the last sentence.

“The recruitment decision is recorded,” He Zhen said. “A private warning doesn't change it.”

Shi Feng took the message back.

He Zhen didn't promise that every elder on his mountain would be brave or fair. He didn't claim a poor sect could make every stronger rival disappear. The useful fact was simpler: the offer remained in place, and they would travel as arranged.

That was enough for today.

“Keep the paper,” He Zhen said.

Shi Feng put it with the Wei hearing receipt. He had kept accounts when nobody believed him. A champion's plate didn't make written evidence less useful.

They parted at the office steps. He Zhen went to settle the vessel's departure permit. Shi Feng returned to the inn to finish packing.

His room looked bare once the tools and medicine bottles were stored.

The everyday bag held identification, a little money and the things he might need without opening the ring. He checked each once, then placed it beside his folded cloak.

The violet purse string remained tied where it had been. He checked the medicine cases' lids, then stored them beside the broken sword's wooden box inside the ring.

Shi Feng opened the window. Below, a cart driver asked Kang Liu whether a departing guest had forgotten a bowl. Kang Liu examined it, recognised his own kitchen mark and took it back with injured dignity.

Shi Feng laughed quietly.

Wei Chengyuan had sent a warning. The road still belonged to the person walking it. Shi Feng closed the window and lay down to rest before choosing his next steps himself.

chapters.title: News for Great Liang
chapters.html:
Wen Shou read the regional report twice before signing the capital copy.

The first reading confirmed the names. The second confirmed that nobody had written the results in the wrong order.

Shi Feng, champion. Artificer Hall, direct inner-disciple entry.

A clerk waited beside his desk with a fresh sheet and the worried expression of a man who had to carry facts into the royal household.

“Should the crown prince's result go first?” Lu Sen asked.

“The stages go in order,” Wen Shou said.

Lu Sen lowered his brush.

Sima Yu had been eliminated in Round Two after taking forbidden medicine. The officials' account recorded the forbidden-pill violation and his removal alive under medical care. There was no later placing to make the sentence more comfortable.

Below that came Ling Qingzhu's withdrawal after the trials, following Hundred Flower Valley's direct inner-disciple offer. No final rank was assigned to her.

Then the ten recruited places.

“Princess Sima Lan, tenth,” Lu Sen read. “Artificer Hall, outer court.”

“Yes,” Wen Shou said.

“The princess?” Lu Sen asked.

“The name hasn't changed since you read it,” Wen Shou said.

Lu Sen wrote carefully. Great Liang had sent three representatives and somehow received news about four of its most discussed young people. The one who had left without a royal place had entered through Moon Lake Sect and finished above most of the field.

The copy for the palace needed no jokes attached.

By afternoon, the market had supplied its own.

“Round Two! Before the sect trials!”

“The princess took tenth!”

“The first fairy went straight to the Valley!”

“And the cripple won?”

“He's not a cripple, you fool. How many reports do you need?”

Bao Shun stood outside Qingliu Lane holding a new rental notice. He had written that the kingdom's champion once lived in the courtyard before remembering that Jiang Meilan owned the lease.

Jiang Meilan took the notice from him.

“Once lived?” Jiang Meilan said. “The rent period isn't even over.”

“That's better,” Bao Shun said. “Still paying. Excellent tenants.”

“The roof leaked while he was here,” Granny Qin called from her brazier.

Jiang Meilan folded the notice over the offending line.

“The roof was repaired,” Jiang Meilan said.

“After his blanket got wet,” Granny Qin said.

Bao Shun looked at the courtyard gate, then at the three women listening nearby. A promising advertisement was becoming a record of complaints.

He took the paper back to correct it.

Granny Qin turned her cakes over. For once none had burned. She put two aside before remembering that the young man who warned her about the brazier was far beyond the capital now.

She sold them to a labourer instead, with an extra one because he looked hungry.

Ling Zhen received the clan copy while checking travel expenses.

He read Ling Qingzhu's entry first. Direct inner disciple. Her choice had carried her beyond the household's careful plans, and he felt relieved enough to put down his account brush.

Then he read Shi Feng's result.

For a moment he remembered laughing at an empty pale bag.

He didn't laugh now.

Ling Rong stood beside the table holding a list of gifts somebody wanted to send to Artificer Hall. Eleven names filled the margin. Apparently relatives who once needed free medicine now needed introductions.

“Should I prepare these?” Ling Rong asked.

“Prepare our congratulations,” Ling Zhen said. “Ask before sending anything in his name.”

Ling Rong looked at the list, crossed out the heading and took a fresh sheet. The instruction was plain enough to make the old shortcuts uncomfortable.

Ling Zhen kept the result beside his niece's letter. He would send her the official copy. Whether she answered her husband, or he answered her, wasn't a matter a clan steward could arrange.

The news reached Qingshi Town with a merchant carrying winter cloth.

By the time the written copy reached the Shi household, the street had already given Shi Feng three different titles. One version claimed he had become a sect elder. Another insisted he was travelling in a royal carriage drawn by spirit beasts.

Shi Rong put the actual report on the council table.

“Champion,” Shi Rong said. “Artificer Hall inner disciple. Read the rest before adding anything.”

Shi Hong leaned across the table. His finger stopped above Sima Yu's result, then moved lower until it found Shi Feng's name again.

“Perhaps his opponents were injured,” Shi Hong said.

“By everyone else's opponents?” Shi Rong asked.

Two elders coughed into their sleeves. Shi Hong sat back, red around the ears.

Shi Zhen kept his face stern. On the shelf behind him stood the ledger that had once made a courtyard and its medicine allowance look like gifts from his own hand.

“Clan rules still matter,” Shi Zhen said.

“They do,” Shi Rong said. “So do records.”

He tapped the date on the report before folding it closed.

“He'll be expected at the year-end test,” Shi Rong added.

Shi Hong looked up sharply. That test once sounded like an easy way to disgrace the eastern household. A champion returning from a Great Sect would make it a very different gathering.

Nobody needed to explain which old record he meant. The eastern household's settlement remained tied in red cord where the clan head had ordered it kept.

Shi Zhen reached for his tea and found the cup empty. He set it down without calling for more.

The elders began discussing a congratulatory letter. For once, Shi Hong offered no suggestion about what Shi Feng ought to contribute in return.

Shi Yulan heard the street version first and refused to believe the carriage.

“He'd ask what feeding the beasts costs,” Shi Yulan said.

Meng Shou laughed. He had come from the clinic with the merchant's written copy, folded carefully away from a packet of ordinary medicine.

Shi Yulan read it in the eastern courtyard. When she reached the champion's name, she stopped pretending to be calm.

“He got there,” Shi Yulan said.

“He did,” Meng Shou said.

She read the line again, then checked the recruitment entry. Artificer Hall. She knew little about its mountain and less about its teachers. She knew it was a place Shi Feng had chosen after the whole field heard his name.

That mattered.

“Your living root?” Shi Yulan asked.

“Still alive,” Meng Shou said. “I keep it in its mineral bed. The delivery boy was more careful with it than with his lunch.”

“He remembered to send it,” Shi Yulan said.

Meng Shou nodded. The physician hadn't forgotten the small parcel or its receipt. A young man who kept that promise deserved to have this piece of news read properly.

Shi Yulan folded the report and carried it inside. There was no official trumpet in the courtyard, only a kettle beginning to boil and a neighbour calling that the merchant still had cloth to sell.

“Let him wait,” Shi Yulan said. “Today I'm buying better tea.”

chapters.title: Su Wanning's Letter
chapters.html:
Su Wanning's letter arrived folded around the tournament results.

Ling Qingzhu knew who had sent it before she saw the name. Nobody else underlined a question three times and then drew an angry face beside it.

She sat at the little table in her assigned courtyard at Hundred Flower Valley. Flowering trees stood beyond the wall, and the morning air carried more qi than the capital's crowded streets. Her white veil stayed tied. This was a new place, not the home she once shared with Shi Feng.

The first line was written larger than the rest.

You left before the final?

Ling Qingzhu read on.

He won? Shi Feng won the entire tournament? I asked the messenger twice. He seemed offended the second time. Why didn't you tell me he could beat all those princes?

There was an ink blot where Su Wanning had stopped, then a fresh paragraph squeezed beneath it.

And don't tell me you chose him only because he was convenient. When you were sixteen, you found excuses for talking about the Qingshi boy. You found a new one after marrying him.

And he ignored you? Him? The same man who forgot his own question when you tucked your hair behind your ear? Don't tell me he was looking at someone else. I'll be angry for you after you've explained what happened.

Ling Qingzhu's fingers tightened around the page.

Su Wanning had seen too much during that outing. She had seen Shi Feng watching his supposed wife, then watched him pay the bill without complaining. At the time, Ling Qingzhu had enjoyed both things. She thought the first proved her charm and the second belonged to their agreement.

She had paid nothing.

The money was settled now. That fact still couldn't change the memory.

At the bottom, Su Wanning's writing became large again.

The princess is joining HIS sect? Sima Lan? Artificer Hall? Are they recruiting disciples or collecting Great Liang's finest scandals? Write back properly this time. Don't send me three polite lines about the weather.

Ling Qingzhu lowered the letter.

For a moment she felt a sharp, foolish jealousy. Sima Lan would travel where Shi Feng traveled. She would see him at meals, hear his blunt replies, and perhaps learn which jokes made him laugh.

Ling Qingzhu thought, That isn't something I can forbid.

She had no right to turn his new sect into another condition of their private agreement. He hadn't left to make her jealous. He had left because living beside her hurt.

Knowing the reason didn't make it easier to picture somebody else taking the place she'd treated carelessly.

A bell rang beyond the flowering trees.

Ling Qingzhu folded the letter and went to the morning practice court. Six other new disciples were already waiting. A pale stone tablet listed the day's training, and a woman in a blue sash checked their attendance.

Lin Yue was at early Foundation Establishment. She had trained at the Valley for several years and had no interest in treating a new disciple's title as a reason to arrive late.

“The sword forms first,” Lin Yue said. “No one leaves an unfinished set because the dining hall opens.”

One girl looked disappointed. Another adjusted her grip and pretended she hadn't been thinking about breakfast.

Ling Qingzhu took her place at the end of the row. Her inner-disciple token had made people curious, but she gave them no display that answered every question. Her movements were clean, measured and within what she chose to show.

The depth behind her publicly known cultivation remained her own affair.

On the seventh turn, a strand of hair slipped across her temple. She tucked it back without thinking.

Then she looked toward the empty edge of the court.

Nobody stood there staring at her.

The ache hit so suddenly that her next step was late. She corrected it before the form broke, but Lin Yue noticed.

“Your feet,” Lin Yue said. “Keep your attention with them.”

“Yes, Senior Lin Yue,” Ling Qingzhu said.

She began the sequence again. The second time, she didn't look beyond the court. She finished the set and accepted the correction without pretending her distraction was part of some secret technique.

After practice, the others talked about the tournament results. One had a brother who wagered on Yuan Kuang and now claimed he always admired Gu Zhan instead. The girls laughed. Ling Qingzhu heard Shi Feng's name twice and said nothing.

She didn't want his victory to become another excuse for people to question her marriage.

It was his victory. She could at least let it belong to him.

Back in the courtyard, she placed Su Wanning's letter beside a clean sheet.

The brush hovered over the first line.

What could she write? That he wasn't the man they'd assumed? That she had watched his meals grow smaller and called him greedy? That he told her the payment bag was empty and she chose to believe he was bargaining?

Su Wanning would read it. Then she would ask the obvious question: why didn't you listen?

Ling Qingzhu had no good answer.

She set the brush down.

A little packet lay inside her travel chest. It held things too ordinary to count among a cultivator's treasures: a household receipt, the end of a cooking cord, a folded note in Shi Feng's plain handwriting. The note named the jars on the kitchen shelf so she wouldn't mix the medicines after he left.

He had still remembered to tell her that.

Ling Qingzhu read the labels again, though she knew them already. His careful writing hurt more than an angry farewell would have. It showed how much of him had stayed considerate even after he stopped expecting her to understand.

She thought, I can't ask him to forget it because I finally feel ashamed.

Outside, someone called that the meal bell would ring soon. Ling Qingzhu put the note away and stood. She ate at the dining hall, listened to Lin Yue explain the next day's work, and returned without inventing a reason to send another urgent letter.

That evening, Su Wanning's questions still lay unanswered on the table.

Ling Qingzhu folded the sheet along its old creases. She didn't tear it up or write that everything was well. Her friend deserved a proper answer when she could give one.

For now, she put it beneath the travel chest's lid and closed it gently.

chapters.title: The Road to Artificer Hall
chapters.html:
Artificer Hall's traveling boat had three different kinds of wood along one side.

Shi Feng stood at Qingyun City's eastern landing and examined the repairs. One strip was dark with age. Another still showed fresh tool marks. The third had been painted to match both and failed.

Gongsun Ce crouched beside the mooring post.

“Was that section replaced after a fall?” Gongsun Ce asked.

“A hard landing,” He Zhen said.

“Is there a difference?” Sima Lan asked.

“There's a boat left to travel in,” He Zhen said.

The princess considered the answer, then stepped aboard. Her late Foundation Establishment cultivation let her balance easily on the narrow plank. She carried her own bag. No palace servants followed with cushions or a second carriage.

Gongsun Ce checked the wooden rail once before joining her. Shi Feng stepped on last and put his everyday bag beside a bench. The storage ring kept the prize medicines and other valuables out of sight.

He had reached late Foundation Establishment. The broken sword from the final stayed wrapped separately. He wasn't going to throw away the weapon merely because Gu Zhan's spear exposed its limit.

A shabby bundle landed beside his feet.

Li Changyuan climbed aboard holding a packet of buns.

“You're coming too?” Shi Feng asked.

“The road goes the same way,” Li Changyuan said.

He Zhen stopped checking the boat's controls for a moment. Then he returned to his work without adding an explanation.

The old man sat at the least damaged bench and began eating.

Shi Feng thought, He chose that seat quickly. He's traveled in this thing before.

He didn't ask why. A man could have friends at a sect without announcing his whole history at a landing.

The mooring rope fell away. He Zhen fed qi into the boat, and the old artifact rose slowly above the wooden platform. A porter below waved them clear of the nearest roof. The vessel tilted, straightened, and carried them east.

Sima Lan gripped the rail.

“Does it always make that sound?” Sima Lan asked.

A wooden fitting clicked near the stern.

“Only when it moves,” Li Changyuan said.

He Zhen's mouth tightened. Gongsun Ce laughed before checking the rail a second time.

By noon, Qingyun City had disappeared behind the hills.

The boat flew above the road rather than the highest peaks. Its pace was steady, not impressive. A sleek vessel bearing Martial Palace's mark passed them with a bright trail and enough noise to make the patched rail tremble.

One passenger on the faster vessel looked back. His laughter reached them before the distance swallowed it.

He Zhen kept the old boat level.

“We could travel faster,” He Zhen said. “We'd spend more stones and replace the left balancing plate afterward.”

“Then this pace works,” Shi Feng said.

He wasn't racing somebody else's transport for applause. The sect had promised him inner-disciple entry. It hadn't promised that every piece of furniture would look expensive.

Gongsun Ce watched the passing vessel until it vanished.

“They had a new three-part balancing array,” Gongsun Ce said.

“And six people doing nothing on deck,” Li Changyuan said. “Buy the fitting if you like it. Don't buy all six fools with it.”

Sima Lan laughed. He Zhen found something worth inspecting beside the stern.

Shi Feng looked at the small wooden figure in Gongsun Ce's lap. The prince had removed its damaged shoulder cover and was comparing two replacement pins. This was a better use of the journey than arguing about another sect's paintwork.

“Does it still move?” Shi Feng asked.

“The arm does,” Gongsun Ce said. “The elbow keeps catching.”

Shi Feng held the cover while Gongsun Ce tested the joint. He didn't pretend to know the whole design. He could see where the fresh scrape met the wood, and that was enough to keep the cover clear while the prince adjusted it.

The arm bent properly on the next try.

Gongsun Ce nodded his thanks and put the tools away. His choice of Artificer Hall had a clear purpose. The sect could teach work he wanted to learn, whether its boat looked grand or not.

They stopped beside a road station before dusk.

He Zhen lowered the boat onto a prepared bed of sand and went to register the vessel. Sima Lan stretched her legs. Gongsun Ce carried the repaired puppet under one arm as if worried the inn might charge it for a room.

Li Changyuan remained on the bench.

“You aren't coming down?” Shi Feng asked.

“The buns aren't finished,” Li Changyuan said.

“They've gone cold,” Shi Feng said.

“They were cold when I bought them,” Li Changyuan said. “That seller had no talent for lying.”

Shi Feng laughed and went to the station kitchen. He bought a simple meal, checked the returning merchant notices, and sat where he could see the boat. There was no reason to keep staring west while supper cooled.

For a moment he remembered how Ling Qingzhu used to sit across from him, pretending she hadn't waited for the first dish.

The memory hurt. He let it pass without blaming the people eating nearby.

Sima Lan joined the table after paying for her own bowl. She asked which hills belonged to Artificer Hall. Shi Feng didn't know, and he said so. He Zhen returned in time to point out the route on a board beside the kitchen door.

“By tomorrow morning,” He Zhen said. “We'll pass the outer workshops before reaching the main gate.”

“Before the main gate?” Gongsun Ce asked.

“People still need tools outside a sect,” He Zhen said. “Not every furnace makes a treasure.”

That pleased Shi Feng. Xu Changhe's notes had held ordinary repairs beside sword practice and patrol records. A sect could have thousands of people doing useful work without every one being a hidden immortal.

After the meal, they returned to the boat. Li Changyuan had saved one bun, though nobody wanted it. He ate it himself and used the empty paper to wrap a loose wooden wheel in his bundle.

By morning, the road station was behind them.

Ahead, smoke rose from a line of workshops beneath the mountain. Artificer Hall's territory had begun.

chapters.title: The Gate of the Weakest Sect
chapters.html:
The outer workshops appeared before Artificer Hall's main gate.

Shi Feng saw water wheels, stone yards and rows of sheds with their doors open to the morning. Men hauled ore while apprentices carried baskets of charcoal. One boy chased a rolling barrel downhill and shouted for everyone to save the barrel before saving him.

The boy reached the flat road first. The barrel struck a post and stopped. His master hit him on the back of the head, then hurried over to inspect the hoops.

Sima Lan leaned over the boat's rail.

“Is that part of the sect?” Sima Lan asked.

“Outer workshops,” He Zhen said. “Families, hired workers, disciples learning the ordinary trades.”

A bell rang from farther up the slope. Several apprentices immediately began walking faster. Their master pointed at the unfinished charcoal baskets until they returned to collect them.

Shi Feng felt more curious than disappointed. He had never expected a sect to consist only of experts seated above clouds. Someone had to carry the charcoal before somebody else refined an artifact.

The old boat passed above the last sheds and settled beside a broad stone stair.

At the top stood Artificer Hall's gate.

One roof corner had fresh tiles. The other still wore moss. A split wooden panel was held straight by two iron bands, and the great characters above it had faded unevenly in the sun.

The name was grand. The entrance badly needed work.

Gongsun Ce looked at the bands.

“They repaired the hinge properly,” Gongsun Ce said.

“You notice that before the roof?” Sima Lan asked.

“The roof isn't holding the door,” Gongsun Ce said.

Li Changyuan stepped onto the landing with his shabby bundle. He looked at the gate for a long moment, then began climbing without comment.

Cui Hong met them halfway up the stairs.

The gate supervisor was at mid Foundation Establishment. He wore a plain robe with a burn mark near the hem and carried a board covered in arrival notes. A younger disciple, Zheng Yu, followed with a brush tucked behind each ear.

“Elder He Zhen,” Cui Hong said, bowing. “The rooms are ready.”

“All of them?” He Zhen asked.

“The rooms,” Cui Hong said. “One bed still needs a leg.”

He Zhen closed his eyes briefly.

Zheng Yu hurried to explain. He was in Qi Condensation and looked more frightened of an unfinished bed than of the three tournament recruits.

“The carpenter's replacing it now,” Zheng Yu said. “Nobody will sleep on the floor.”

Shi Feng looked at the open gate. He had spent enough nights on a floor to know a bed leg could become an important sect matter very quickly.

Before He Zhen replied, the courier Liu Cheng came down from the gate carrying an empty delivery case. He wore Martial Palace's badge. His Bone Refinement cultivation was ordinary, but he polished the badge often enough that it caught every scrap of light. Shi Feng recognized the man who had delivered Wei Chengyuan's warning. The faster Martial Palace transport had brought him ahead of them.

“So these are the new recruits,” Liu Cheng said. “We heard the champion chose this mountain. Our outer court was surprised.”

His gaze moved from the patched boat to the iron bands on the gate. He smiled with obvious contempt.

“They expected him to choose somewhere with a roof,” Liu Cheng said.

Cui Hong's face darkened. Zheng Yu opened his mouth, looked at He Zhen, and held his tongue.

He Zhen took the signed delivery receipt from Cui Hong.

“Your goods arrived. Your case is empty. You can go,” He Zhen said.

The courier hesitated. He'd hoped somebody would shout so he could carry back a story about Artificer Hall losing its temper. Instead, an early Golden Core elder was calmly telling him his errand had ended.

He bowed stiffly and continued down the stairs.

Shi Feng didn't chase him. A courier's joke wasn't an attempt to kill him, and the man had already spent more attention on a gate than it deserved.

Li Changyuan watched him leave.

“He nearly tripped while looking at the roof,” Li Changyuan said. “His Palace should train the feet as well.”

Zheng Yu laughed, then straightened when Cui Hong looked at him. Sima Lan hid her smile poorly. The old man's face remained quite serious, which made it worse.

Inside the gate, the main court was swept clean.

The paving stones were old but level. Workshop signs stood along one side, a practice ground along the other. From a distant hall came the steady ring of metal meeting metal.

Two disciples stopped sparring when they saw He Zhen's guests. One recognized Shi Feng and elbowed his partner so hard the man dropped his practice sword.

“The champion!”

“He really came?”

“Which one is the prince?”

“The one carrying the wooden man!”

Gongsun Ce looked down at the puppet beneath his arm. Sima Lan finally laughed aloud.

Cui Hong sent the watching disciples back to their work. Zheng Yu brought three room tokens and checked the names carefully. Inner court for Shi Feng. Inner court for Gongsun Ce, under the sect's own offer. Outer court for Sima Lan.

Nobody changed her token because she was a princess. She examined the mark, nodded and put it away.

He Zhen pointed out the dining hall and the practice court. The work schedules were posted openly. Sect resources would follow their rules, and expensive materials needed permission. He explained the essentials without promising that joining made any of them rich overnight.

Shi Feng thought, Good. I'll see what the rules are before deciding which are useful.

His alchemy could still earn money. His cultivation still needed pills, and his swordsmanship needed better weapons and more practice. A new token hadn't completed any of those things for him.

At the far end of the court, the tall bronze-bound doors of the reception hall stood open. Six inner-court elders waited inside beside an empty high-backed chair on the central dais.

Li Changyuan slung his shabby bundle over one shoulder and walked through the doors first.

He Zhen motioned for the three recruits to follow, and Shi Feng stepped across the threshold into Artificer Hall.

chapters.title: The Seat at Artificer Hall
chapters.html:
The high-backed chair at the head of the reception dais stood empty.

Shi Feng stopped two paces inside the threshold. Six inner-court elders waited along the pillars, with Nascent Soul Elder Tian Luo standing nearest the steps, a closed register beneath one hand.

Gongsun Ce adjusted the puppet case under his arm. Sima Lan checked the outer-court token at her waist, then lowered her hand. Both had expected the journey to end with a formal greeting.

He Zhen entered behind them and closed his brush case.

Li Changyuan didn't stop with the recruits.

The old man crossed the polished floor in his patched brown robe. His shabby bundle bumped against his leg, carrying cracked furnace lids, bent pins, and the same broken puppet joints he'd bought in Qingyun City.

Shi Feng watched him pass the first pillar.

Then the second.

The elders turned toward him, but nobody challenged the old man's place in the hall. He Zhen looked down at the papers he already knew by heart.

Gongsun Ce shifted the puppet case to his other arm. The movement brought him closer to Shi Feng.

“That's the central dais,” Gongsun Ce said quietly.

“I can see it,” Shi Feng replied.

Li Changyuan climbed the three stone steps.

A bent wooden wheel slipped from a fold of his bundle. He caught it, placed it on the side table, and settled the shabby bundle beside it. Only then did he turn toward the high-backed chair.

Shi Feng remembered the market well. The old man had asked him to inspect an ordinary crack. Later, he'd complained about cold buns and chosen the least damaged bench on He Zhen's patched boat.

His cultivation had remained unreadable through every conversation.

Now he sat down squarely in the sect master's chair.

Gongsun Ce's breath caught. Sima Lan went completely still.

Along both sides of the hall, Tian Luo, He Zhen, and the other five inner-court elders placed their fists together and bowed.

“Sect Master!” Tian Luo and He Zhen greeted him together.

Li Changyuan glanced at the wooden case holding Shi Feng's broken sword.

“Don't call cheap steel humility on my mountain,” Li Changyuan said.
